6.3 CT Calibration
Calibration to Air (Baseline, then daily) - An initial baseline followed by daily
scans will be obtained. This calibration is part of the daily scanner start-up
routine. These procedures will follow the manufacturer’s recommended
procedure.
Calibration to Water (Baseline)
An initial baseline calibration will be obtained and analyzed using a
water phantom. These procedures will follow the manufacturer’s
recommended procedure and will include zeroing and calibrating
the scanner unit.
Calibration to Calcium (Baseline, then bi-weekly)
Each CT scanning site will be provided a standardized Calcium
QCT Calibration Phantom which includes a Torso QA phantom for
scanner calibration (Image Analysis Inc, Lexington, KY). The center
plug of the Torso QA phantom contains a region with a known
concentration of calcium hydroxyapatite (100mg/ml). The Calcium
QCT Calibration phantom contains four cylindrical rods with the
following concentrations of calcium: 0, 50, 100, 200 mg/ml calcium
hydroxyapatite. On the first and 15th of each month quality
assurance scans of the torso phantom will be performed at the CT
scan site. The analysis of these scans by the CT Reading Center
allows convenient and quick verification of accuracy and precision
of the CT scanners at different sites.
Positioning the Calibration and Torso Phantoms.
The table height of the CT couch will be positioned such that the
center of the Torso Calibration phantom will be located at isocenter
of the scanner field of view.
Place the torso phantom on top of the calibration phantom
(positioned in couch pad) and using your laser alignment light;
adjust the table height until the torso center insert is at the location
of isocenter on the CT scanner. This is the table height you will use
for QA scans with your Torso phantom.
Scanning the TORSO QA Phantom
After the correct position has been determined, take a vertical axial
slice through the center of the TORSO phantom. Use the same
parameters as with participant exams. Each site will perform a
scout of the phantom followed by an axial scan (identical
parameters to the heart series). Reconstruction should be done
with the same parameters as in scanning study subjects. Then
display your axial image on your CT monitor and examine it to
ensure that it is free of artifacts, such as air gaps and streaks.
Ensure that the calibration phantom is included in the field of view.

complete before the interview. Some of the interview questions are determined by
responses to self-administered questions.
8. Form 31 (Interim Healthcare Contacts) involves obtaining information about
hospitalizations and permission to request related hospital records. In order to
prevent duplicate requests for medical records, Hospitalization Reports providing
information about previously-reported hospitalizations (on the annual follow-up
contact questionnaires) will be printed along with the form set prior to the
participant’s visit. These reports will be used by the interviewer when administering
Form 31.
9. The Diet Interview will take 50-60 minutes and should be planned to follow-up other
core measures, especially for participants with limited time available for the exam.
10. The Carotid Ultrasound will take approximately 35 minutes.
11. The Anthropometry measurements take approximately 15 minutes and will require
that the participant be dressed in light-weight clothing. Participants may be required
to change into clinic-supplied clothing if theirs restricts anthropometric
measurements. Wheelchair-bound participants are excluded from all anthropometric
measurements, while pregnant women are excluded from weight and waist girth
measurements.
12. The Pulmonary Function testing must be done sometime after the anthropometry
measures are completed. The participant’s height and weight are required to be
entered into the Pulmonary Function device’s software before testing can commence.

C. GREETING AND INFORMED CONSENT
1. General Information
Pleasantly greeting the participant sets the tone for the entire exam. During the
greeting, each participant should be reminded that:
(cid:131) they are participating in an important national study;
(cid:131) they will receive valuable information about their own health;
(cid:131) they will receive a specially-designed CARDIA examination available at only four
sites in the United States; and
(cid:131) their test results can be provided to them for sharing with their health care provider,
if desired.
Stressing these important points is helpful in establishing and maintaining rapport
with the participant. The staff at each Field Center should discuss their approach to
greeting the participants and address these items in ways that are most suitable for their
own populations.
2. Guidelines for Greeting
Verify that the participant has arrived on his/her scheduled exam date. If a
participant arrives outside his/her scheduled appointment time, he/she may be told Your
appointment is not recorded on today's exam schedule; however, it may be possible to fit
you in today or Our records show that you are scheduled for an exam at (time); there's a
chance we may be able to see you sooner. The Clinic Coordinator should then be
consulted for further instructions.
If the participant appears to be ill, verify that he/she feels well enough to complete the
examination. The participant may be asked Do you have a fever? If Yes, his/her
appointment should be rescheduled according to local Field Center appointment
procedures. If the participant is unable to complete the entire exam, unfinished
components should be rescheduled as soon as possible according to local Field Center
appointment procedures. The participant's ID, unfinished components, and reason for the
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 15November06 GUI-5

incomplete exam should be recorded on the Field Center log.
Pregnancy, regardless of gestational stage, excludes a participant from CT exam as
well as measurement of weight and waist girth; however, height should still be obtained.
It is vitally important to ascertain pregnancy status during the greeting in order to plan the
exam flow appropriately.
Prior to starting the Y20 Exam, a brief description of CARDIA should be given to the
participant. The following is an example:
As you know, CARDIA is a major study of the lifestyles and health of
young adults. It is sponsored by the National Institutes of Health. Here in
Birmingham, the study is conducted by the Division of Preventive Medicine
at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.
Let me tell you again about what will be included in your exam today.
As in past CARDIA exams, we will explore several aspects of your health and
your lifestyle. You will be asked questions about:
(cid:131) current general health status;
(cid:131) past illnesses or injuries;
(cid:131) medications you take;
(cid:131) the amount of exercise you get;
(cid:131) what you’ve eaten the past month and other dietary questions;
(cid:131) the way you deal with everyday problems and how you feel about
things in your life; and
(cid:131) your background, education, marital status, career/job status,
and other similar questions.
We will:
(cid:131) take your blood pressure several times;
(cid:131) measure your height, weight, and waist circumference;
(cid:131) do an ultrasound of the carotid artery in your neck;
(cid:131) measure your breathing;
(cid:131) obtain blood and urine specimens for specific measurements,
such as cholesterol and albuminuria.
NOTE: At this point, each female participant should be asked if she is currently
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 15November06 GUI-6

menstruating. If she is, it must be recorded on the urine sample form (#51) and she will
be excluded from this measurement.
3. Guidelines for Obtaining Informed Consent
The participant should be asked to read and sign a Field Center-specific informed
consent form. He/she must also understand what is going to happen to him/her during the
exam and any risks involved. The greeter should make certain that the participant is
actually reading the form and then specifically ask if he/she has any questions about the
form. The greeter should be prepared to answer the questions himself/herself or have
someone else on-site answer them. If the participant is struggling to read the form,
assistance in reading the form may be given. When reading a form to a participant, care
should be taken to read the content exactly as written.
After the consent form has been read and signed, the greeter should ask the
participant if he/she would like the test results mailed to him/her. The participant should
be informed that a second copy can be included in the mailing for sharing with the
healthcare provider, if desired.
D. VERIFICATION OF DEMOGRAPHIC DATA
After the participant has signed the informed consent, the greeter will refer to the
Verification of Demographic Information form included in his/her form set. The
participant will be asked his/her birth date, to be compared (for verification) with the
demographic data from his/her most recent exam. Changes in sex and race should be
questioned only if there appears to have been an error. The participant is now ready to
continue with the Y20 Exam.
E. EXAMINING PARTICIPANTS AT A CLINIC DIFFERENT THAN THE YEAR 0 EXAM
If the participant is being examined at a clinic different than the Y0 Exam, the
interviewer should record and circle the clinic number (1, 2, 3, or 4) for the current exam
site in the upper right corner of the demographic form. The form set will be scanned at

the examining clinic. In addition, the examining Field Center will be responsible for
distributing the results letters to the participant. When the entire Y20 Exam is over and
all edits are completed, the original form sets should be forwarded to the "home" clinic
(where the Y0 Exam was performed) for permanent storage with a copy retained in the
examining clinic.
NOTE: A copy of the follow-up contact worksheet should be forwarded to the home
clinic as soon as the exam is complete. The Recruitment Coordinator will need the
worksheet for the next follow-up contact.
Results forms should be printed from the CARIDA Internal Web site; two copies sent
to the participant and one copy put into the participant’s record.
Each Field Center will have the ability to print any participant’s form set and labels,
regardless of where that participant was examined at the baseline exam. At the Y15
Exam, over 100 participants were examined at a Field Center different from his/her
baseline or “home” Field Center.

2. Abbreviated Examinations
The length of the Y20 Exam may preclude some participants from completing all

G. OUT-OF-CLINIC EXAMS
1. General Instructions
a. The possibility of an out-of-clinic exam should be brought up with a CARDIA
participant only after it has become clear that the participant will not come into
the clinic for any kind of exam including an abbreviated exam or an a-typically
scheduled exam (e.g., evening).
b. All exam components must be performed by certified personnel.
c. The consent forms must be completed as for an in-clinic exam.
d. All forms must be printed for each participant from the scheduling system.
e. An out-of-clinic exam will be denoted on the Verification of Demographic
Information form with an "H" in the upper right corner and circled. The form
will be scanned with the form set and the data entry person at the Coordinating
Center will record exam performed away from clinic.
f. All out-of-clinic exams must be recorded on the General Log Form. The
participant ID, exam date, and forms completed should be recorded on the Log
Form and the CARDIA Participants Examined Outside the Clinic box should be
marked (see Appendix 2). The Log Form should be forwarded to the
Coordinating Center with the participant’s form set.
2. Components
The following priority order should be applied to components for home visits:
a. Blood pressure measurement with the OmROn HEM907XL, identical to the
protocol used in the clinic exam (refer to Y20 Blood Pressure Manual of
Operations).
b. Full core blood draw, if possible (refer to Y20 Phlebotomy Manual of
Operations). Given the time constraints, it may be advisable to draw the blood at
the end of the home visit (rather than immediately after blood pressure).
Note: Participants examined out of the clinic will NOT participate in the OGTT and will
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 15November06 GUI-11

NOT be identified as QC participants.
3. Blood Draw
Blood draw procedures for an out of clinic exam are the same as those for the in
clinic exam. Procedures for collecting blood are found in the Phlebotomy section of the
Y20 MOO (pages 7 – 14) and are not repeated here. Due to the complexity of the
aliquoting scheme for the full core blood draw, priority for drawing and aliquoting blood
specimens is as follows:
a. 10 ml lavender top vacutainer
b. 12.5 ml red top vacutainer
c. 4.5 ml blue top vacutainer
d. 10 ml lavender top vacutainer
e. 4.5 ml blue top vacutainer
f. 5 ml SCAT (anti-protease) vacutainer
4. Handling the Core Samples
a. Place the two 10-ml lavender top tubes into ice water. Cool the sample on water
and ice for 30 minutes but not more than 60 minutes.
b. Place the 12.5-ml red top tube in test tube rack and allow the sample to clot by
standing for 30 minutes but not more than 60 minutes at room temperature (65-75
degrees).
c. Place the two 4.5-ml blue top tube into ice water. Cool the sample on water and
ice for 30 minutes but not more than 60 minutes.
d. Place the 5-ml SCAT 1 tube into ice water. Cool the sample on water and ice for
30 minutes but not more than 60 minutes.
e. All samples must be centrifuged, aliquoted and in the freezer (if indicated) within
90 minutes of the blood draw.
NOTE: Label blood tubes with labels as outlined in the Y20 CARDIA MOO.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 15November06 GUI-12

5. Transporting Core Specimens
Special precautions must be taken during transportation of specimens to the
laboratory. All specimens must be appropriately labeled with the participant’s ID labels
and must be placed in bio-hazard bags during transport. Specimens that are required to
go on ice should be carefully positioned in a small cooler (such as a Styrofoam box) on
wet ice (ice with water). The specimens should be maintained in an up-right position
during transport. Placing a Styrofoam cut-out in the bottom of the cooler is a good way to
secure the vacutainers in an upright position. The cooler must also be labeled with a bio-
hazard label. Specimens that are to remain at room (ambient) temperature should be
placed in a separate Styrofoam container (no ice) and remain in an up-right position. The
container must also be labeled with a bio-hazard label. Care should be taken to position
specimens so that they will not be jarred or broken during transit. Specimens should not
be left in direct sunlight and should not be left in any extreme temperature, e.g. in a car.
6. Aliquoting Scheme:
Once the specimens have reached the laboratory, aliquoting of the core specimens
should follow the same aliquoting scheme as an in clinic exam. Specific instructions for
aliquoting of core samples are included in the Phlebotomy section of the Y20 MOO
beginning on page 26.
7. Weight and Waist Circumference
Weight will be obtained using a portable scale (following the Y20 Anthropometry

H. CONSENT FORMS
Participant consent forms for the Y20 Exam are included in the participant forms
packet. A separate consent form for CT scanning is included, as it may be required by
some Field Centers.
Many new guidelines have been developed to protect the confidentiality and rights of
research participants regarding the collection and analyses of genetic material. Thus, in
addition to requesting permission to perform the core components of the Y20 Exam,
specific permission from each participant will be requested, by way of a checklist
included as part of the consent form, for each of the following:
• Participate in the Year 20 exam to measure weight, cholesterol, blood pressure
and other physical factors related to heart disease including an ultrasound image
of the arteries in my neck;
• Donate a blood and urine sample to be frozen, stored, and used for future
research;
• Have a CT exam to look for calcium in the arteries of my heart;
• Other findings that may be related to heart disease;
• Allow DNA to be extracted from blood samples to be analyzed for genetic
information related to heart disease, obesity, blood pressure, diabetes and other
conditions affecting people in midlife understanding that the information will be
kept confidential at all times;
• Allow genetic/DNA samples and data to be released, for research purposes only,
to other qualified non-CARDIA investigators who have met CARDIA’s standards
for confidentiality;
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 15November06 GUI-14

• Allow researchers from private or non-profit organizations to have access, in a
way that cannot identify me, to specimens, DNA or other CARDIA information in
order to develop diagnostic laboratory tests, medications, or other therapies that
could benefit many people;
• As a participant in the CARDIA Study, he/she also has the right to ask that we do
not inform him/her of any genetic condition that we find and may elect to be
informed of his/her results if a gene is found that is related to a medically treatable
genetic disease.
Due to these additional levels of agreement to participate in the Y20 Exam, obtaining
informed consent will require more time than in past exams. The interviewer must be
prepared to answer questions regarding the long-term storage of genetic material; in
addition, these specific permission levels provide them with the choice of full, partial, or
no participation in the analyses of their genetic material, while still participating in the
other aspects of the exam.
I. FOLLOW-UP CONTACT INTERVIEW
1. General Information
During this interview, information will be obtained to help maintain contact with the
participant during the time interval between exams. Participant contact information will
be verified, his/her name and residence plans for the next two years will be ascertained,
and information on other sources (friends, employer, school) that will help contact the
participant, if necessary, will be collected.
2. Instructions for Follow-up Contact Interview
a. The Follow-Up Contact Interview should be administered after the informed
consent has been signed.
b. Q5 asks about the Follow-Up Contact Worksheet. The participant will receive
this worksheet for recording contact information in the mail prior to his/her
scheduled appointment. He/she will be asked to bring this completed form to the
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 15November06 GUI-15

clinic on the day of the exam. The interviewer should check the form for
completeness and attempt to complete any missing information. If the participant
does not bring the form to the clinic, the interviewer should provide the form and
ask the participant to complete it at that time. The interviewer should assist the
participant in completing the form in whatever way is necessary (e.g., read it
aloud).
J. DETERMINING IF SELF-ADMINISTERED QUESTIONNAIRES NEED TO BE
INTERVIEWER ADMINISTERED
After completing the Follow-Up Contact Interview, the greeter should inform the
participant that during the exam he/she will be given some questionnaires to complete.
The greeter should ask the participant if he/she will need assistance in reading the
questionnaires. If the participant answers Yes, the Yes response box for Q6 on the
Follow-Up Contact Interview form should be marked.
K. INCIDENT REPORTS
If a participant experiences any unusual medical-related incidents during the course
of the exam, the clinic is responsible for documenting these incidents for future reference
by the CARDIA Study, whether or not a physician is notified.
Incidents are defined as events such as fainting, uncontrolled bleeding, any unusual
reports of pain, accidents, etc. Staff members should report any dangerous situations to
the Clinic Coordinator and document the incident. These reports should be documented
on the General Log Form with the Incident Report box checked and details written out,
and scanned with the participant’s form set to the Coordinating Center.

L. CT EXAM SCHEDULING AND PREGNANCY TESTING
All female participants must be screened for potential for pregnancy prior to having a
CT exam. This screening is completed using Form 73, the CT Screening Form Female
participants who are not excluded from pregnancy testing should receive a pregnancy test
prior to the CT exam. There are two possible scenarios for this:
1. CT exam scheduled within three days of core exam
If the CT exam is scheduled within three days, a pregnancy test should be completed
on the day of the core exam as described in the Phlebotomy Manual.
2. CT exam scheduled more than three days from the core exam
If the CT exam is scheduled more than three days from the core exam, the participant
should be given a home pregnancy kit with both verbal and written instructions to use it
the day of the CT exam, prior to going to the exam. An example of the written
instructions are found in Appendix 5.
M. EXIT INTERVIEW
1. Overview
The exit interview serves two very important functions as part of the Y20 Exam. It
provides an opportunity for the participant to express his/her feelings, and, if necessary,
summarize any problem(s) experienced during the exam. The exit interview also
provides a time for the Field Center staff member to complete the Exit Interview Form, to
review for missing data and to close the exam.
2. Instructions
a. If the participant has not already been recruited and scheduled for a CT scan,
he/she should be. The CT scan is performed in order to evaluate the presence of
coronary calcium. This component is part of the core Y20 Exam and should be
presented as an extension of the examination that the participant has just
completed. (See CT section of this Manual of Operations.) There will be a
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 15November06 GUI-17

separate reimbursement at some sites, as the scan will be performed at a second
visit and at a separate site.
b. If the participant has not already been recruited and scheduled for the CARDIA
Fitness Study (CFS), this should be done at this time. CFS involves a full body
DXA, a graded treadmill exercise test to assess physical fitness, and wearing an
accelerometer and keeping a Daily Activity Monitor Log for eight days. This
study is scheduled for a separate day and the in-clinic appointment should take
approximately 1 hour 15 minutes and is consented and reimbursed separately.
c. The designated Data Editor of each Field Center should retrieve the set of forms
toward the end of the exam and review them for gross omissions and/or
incomplete sections on the forms. It is vital that the data editor be extremely
familiar with the forms in order to efficiently note any missing data, whether skip
patterns are observed, etc.
The Data Editor is responsible for reviewing each self-administered form in
order to note whether or not the participant received help in completing the form.
If no help was required, the appropriate clinical code number should be written
in the space provided for the Interviewer ID number.

Pregnancy precaution procedures for CARDIA study coronary artery calcium CT scans
The CARDIA Year 20 exam includes a CT scan (also known as a CAT scan) to look for calcium
in your coronary arteries. CT scan is an x-ray procedure that should not be performed in
pregnant women. The National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (NHLBI) of the National
Institutes of Health provides the funding for the CARDIA study and is committed to ensuring
participant safety in its sponsored studies. NHLBI has requested CARDIA centers to develop
procedures to assure that the chance that a pregnant woman undergoes a CT scan is minimized.
1) Any woman who has NOT had a hysterectomy (removal of the uterus with or without
the ovaries) or a tubal ligation (“tubes tied”) is required to have a pregnancy test
within two days prior to the CT scan. If the pregnancy test is positive, the CT scans
should not be performed.
2) Regardless of the results of the pregnancy test, any woman who has not undergone a
hysterectomy or a tubal ligation should reschedule the CT scan to a later date if she
has had sexual intercourse without using an effective method of birth control at any
time within the 7 days prior to the scheduled CT scan. This is because the pregnancy
test may stay negative (indicating no pregnancy) for 7 days after a woman becomes
pregnant.
If your CT scan is scheduled within two days after your CARDIA exam, we will perform the
pregnancy test on the urine we collect as part of your exam. If your CT scan is scheduled either
before the CARDIA exam or more than two days after the CARDIA exam, we will provide you
with a simple pregnancy test that you should perform before your CT scan on the same day of
the scan.
Thank you for your cooperation with this policy. Please feel free to call [Insert name of staff],
the [Insert title], at [Insert phone number] with any questions.

A. CARDIA DIET HISTORY INSTRUMENT
1. Introduction
The prospective study, Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) was
designed to examine the influence of diet and other lifestyle factors on the evolution of risk factors
for the major cardiovascular diseases in black and white men and women aged 18 to 30 years at
baseline during 1985-86 (1). CARDIA recruited 5,115 young adults with a wide range of
educational attainment in four geographic areas: Birmingham, Alabama; Chicago, Illinois;
Minneapolis, Minnesota; and Oakland, California. At baseline and Year 7, usual eating habits of
CARDIA participants were assessed by an interviewer-administered dietary history developed for
this study to obtain detailed information about food intakes of this racially and geographically
diverse population during the preceding month. Our method was based on that of Burke (2) as
modified and used in the prospective Chicago Western Electric Study (3).
The Diet History (4). The criteria for choice of diet assessment were that it be non-
interventional, be applicable to a wide range of socioeconomic and literacy levels, encompass
appropriate regional and ethnic food choices, and not stimulate dietary change. Issues of time
and expense also had to be considered as dietary assessment was only one of several
measurements used in CARDIA and no more than 1 hour could be allocated. Interviewer skill
and level of expertise necessary for collecting and processing the dietary data were further
considerations. Furthermore, compared to the Block or Willett food frequency questionnaires,
sufficient detail about usual food eaten is obtained with the diet history, including brand names
of selected foods and fats typically used in food preparation are obtained. Therefore, the diet
history method was chosen over other methods.
Before use in the study, the CARDIA dietary history was tested in 100 young adults similar
to the CARDIA population at the four CARDIA centers to evaluate interview content,
procedures, and duration. The pretest also enabled the CARDIA nutritionists to become familiar
with the history and its implementation before use at the baseline examination. The validity
(accuracy) and reliability (repeatability) of the Questionnaire was also tested in 128 similar to
CARDIA participants (ref). The average nutrient intake from seven 24-hour recalls was
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-1

correlated to the average nutrient intake from the diet history. Nutrient values estimated from the
diet history were generally higher than from the average of the seven recalls with correlations
greater than 0.50 for most nutrients among whites. For blacks, correlations were lower. For
reliability, the first history tended to yield higher values than the second, the differences were
significant only for blacks.
1. Friedman CD, Cutter GR, Donahue RO, Hughes GH, Hulley SB, Jacobs DR, K Liu, PJ Savage.
CARIDA: study design, recruitment, and some characteristics of the examined subjects. J Clin
Epidemiol. 1988; 41: 1105-16.
2. Burke BS. The dietary history as a tool in research. J Am Diet Assoc 1947; 23: 1041-46.
3. Paul O, Lepper MH, Phelan WH, Dupertuis GW, MacMillan A, McKean H, Park, H. A longitudinal
study of coronary heart disease. Circulation. 1963; 28: 20-31.
4. McDonald A, Van Horn L, Slattery M, Hilner J, Bragg C, Caan B, Jacobs D, Kiu K, Hubert H,
Gernhofer N, Betz E, Havlik D. The CARDIA dietary history: development, implementation, and
evaluation. J Am Diet Assoc. 1991; 91:1104-12.
2. Nutrient Database
The nutrient database (Version 36) selected for analyses of dietary data for CARDIA was
developed by the Nutrition Coordinating Center (NCC) at the University of Minnesota. This
database is a food composition table containing values for 139 nutrients.
3. Format
The Diet History is comprised of three parts, including the Dietary Practices, Quantitated
Food Frequency, and a Self-Administered Questionnaire.
The first section, Dietary Practices, consists of nine questions related to the participant’s
usual meal pattern, frequency of eating at fast food establishments and restaurants, fat use, use of
nutrient modified products, and recent changes in the diet. This section was designed to obtain a
maximal amount of information about the participant’s usual dietary practices with a minimal
expenditure of time. Portions of the responses obtained will be used to complete the Quantitated
Food Frequency portion of the form after the interview, thereby minimizing the need for
repetitious questioning. The Dietary Practices can also be used as a cross-check on information
obtained from the Quantitated Food Frequency.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-2

The second section of the history, Quantitated Food Frequency, consists of a series of
questions about the usual intake of various food groups, followed by lists of food items.
Questions were designed to standardize the interview and minimize inter-interviewer differences.
The questions establish whether a participant consumes a particular food or foods within a
particular food group, usual serving size, frequency of consumption (by day, week, or month),
and preparation method, if applicable.
All foods have been divided into food groups to facilitate recall. The food groups are the
major headings with items contained within each group listed beneath. In some food groups,
sub-grouping may be necessary for greater specificity (e.g., “Grains/Cereals” is a food group
with bread, cereal, pasta, and rice as sub-groups). This arrangement will enable the interviewer
to skip entire sections if, after key questions within each food group or sub-group are asked, the

There are also numerous “additions” sections which contain food items that are not usually

CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-5

Recording the intake of such food items is important since they contain significant amounts of
calories, fat, and sodium. Additions sections are located after major food groups or sub-groups.
Some of the items in the food table have one or more food preparation codes, a three letter
code indicating the use of a fat in preparation, and designating a pre-calculated amount of fat to
be added to each serving. CARDIA uses two preparation codes for meat (PAN, BDF), one for
vegetables (SES), and one for recipe items (APF). Each code represents a preparation method
specific to the type of food and denotes differences in amount of fat absorbed by those foods.
When a preparation code is selected, it is always accompanied by a four letter fat code.
Fats are identified by both four letter codes and numerical Food IDs. The letter code for fat
is used only with the preparation code. The Food ID is used to list fats separately, such as to
indicate use as a spread. With a few exceptions, any fat code may be selected to accompany a
preparation code. However, certain recipe items may either require a specific fat code or
disallow a specific fat code. When a fat is not used in preparation, all preparation codes with the
exception of APF may be disregarded. If an item accompanied by an APF code does not include
a fat added in preparation, NAP 0000 must be substituted to override the computer rule for
addition of fat to these items.
The NCC database contains codes for margarine, and for various forms of margarine (diet,
spread, stick, tub, whipped and squeeze). Margarine codes are identified by brands and also
include default codes for each form when brand is unknown. Oil, fast foods, cereals,
convenience foods, cookies, crackers, and candy also have codes designated for various brand
names as well as codes for the unknown types when brands are not specified.
Cue cards are used throughout the Quantitated Food Frequency to indicate the type of
responses required for given questions or to facilitate the participant’s recall. Questions that
require a cue card are denoted with an asterisk (*) to the left of the question and the words (Cue
Card) at the end of the question.
The Quantitated Food Frequency was designed so that data entry may be made directly from
the form. Information provided for each food item in the Quantitated Food Frequency will be
the Food ID, a description of the item, serving size units allowed, and preparation codes allowed.
Extra lines are provided within major food groups as needed to accommodate different
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-6

preparation methods and fat codes for various items, as well as foods reported by the participant
that are not listed on the form.
At the end of the Quantitated Food Frequency, there is a question regarding intake of foods
not mentioned during the interview to permit the participant to report foods not appearing on the
form. There is also a place to document both participant and interviewer perception of recall
ability.
The Quantitated Food Frequency ends with two questions to determine if the foods reported
represent the participant’s usual diet.
The Self-Administered component of the Diet History is included in the packet of self-
administered questionnaires and completed by the participant during the exam.
B. CONDUCT OF INTERVIEW
1. Staff Preparation for Participant’s Visit
The physical setting where the interview takes place should be quiet, attractive, and private
so that the participant can feel relaxed and at ease. A small desk and two chairs should be
provided and arranged so that the interviewer and participant are facing each other and the
interviewer can comfortably sit at the desk to write responses. Standardized food models, cups,
dishes, etc. should be accessible to the interviewer and the participant. Food models need to be
individually wrapped with a light weight plastic wrap (e.g., Saran Wrap) or in zip-lock bags to
keep them clean. To help the interviewer utilize food models efficiently, they should be
arranged on a portable cart in food groupings (i.e., meats together, fruits together, vegetables
together, etc.).
Prior to the interview, make sure that the participant’s bar code identifier is on the form and
record the exam date on the form. Be certain that the food models are in order and that the room
is clear of distractions. Record the time that the interview starts in the space provided on page
one.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-7

The interviewer should have the digital recorder set for recording, with a blank CD in the
recorder. Instructions for using the digital recorder can be found in Section 9 of the Diet
History Manual.
2. Introduction to Participant
Greet the participant warmly. Do not introduce yourself as a nutritionist. Read the
question asking permission to record the interview to the participant. Record the response. If
interview is not recorded, record the reason why it is not, e.g., participant refuses, recorder
malfunctioned, etc.
Briefly state that the purpose of the interview is to get information about usual dietary intake
and that the past month will be used as a point of reference. Usual dietary intake will be
ascertained by (1) asking about dietary practices; (2) asking about foods commonly consumed;
and (3) questions about how this represents usual intake. Explain that the interview will be
conducted in three parts (1) Dietary Practices; (2) Quantitated Food Frequency; and (3) Self-
Administered Questionnaire.
It is also important to explain that the interview will take approximately 45 to 50 minutes to
complete and that the time for the interview will be minimized if responses are as succinct and
concise as possible. Assure the participant, however that she/he should feel free to ask questions
or have instructions repeated at any time and that she/he should not feel inhibited from
answering as completely as possible the questions that are being asked.
STATEMENT TO PARTICIPANT: Hello, my name is __________. The purpose of this
interview is to determine what you usually eat, using the past month as a guide. The interview
will be conducted in three parts and will take approximately 45 to 50 minutes.
The first part of the interview consists of questions about your usual dietary practices. The
second part will deal with the specific foods you eat. The last part asks a few more questions
about your usual diet practices.
3. Part I: Dietary Practices
The Dietary Practices section is an important component of the Diet History and serves three
basic purposes:

4. Part II: Quantitated Food Frequency
Prior to initiating this portion of the interview, explain to the participant that a series of food
groups will be reviewed and that specific items within these food groups will be queried. The
general approach to ascertaining dietary intake will be determining usual intake, focusing on the
past month as a point of reference. Emphasize that foods not eaten in the past month should
not be reported. Explain that usual serving size, preparation method, and frequency of
consumption must be ascertained for each reported food item. Provide the participant with the
cue card containing examples of appropriate responses. Encourage the participant to provide as
much information as possible in a single response.
There is a general tendency for participants to be distracted by the food models if they are
unaccustomed to the dietary interviewing process. Spend a few seconds explaining that the food
models are to be used as a point of reference for serving size. Guide the participant’s use of the
models by suggesting that she/he indicate that her/his portion of any given food was the same,
half as much, twice as much, or any other simple fraction to provide a general idea of intake.
Approximate serving sizes are sufficient for this history.
Explain to the participant that quantities of food may be stated in terms of days, weeks or
months. Inform the participant that cue cards will be provided throughout this section of the
history to facilitate recall.

portion of the diet history. Please tell me about the foods you usually eat. Use the past
month as a guide for your usual intake. I will ask if you eat any foods from various food
groups, such as dairy products. I will then ask you how much you usually ate, how often you
ate that food, how it was prepared, and whether anything was added to the food.
(INDICATE FOOD MODELS) These food models can be used as a reference to help
determine your usual serving size. When you look at them, please let me know if you ate the
same amount, or if you had, for example, half as much, twice as much, or another amount.
I will also ask how often you ate the foods, per day, per week, or per month.

the participant cannot be entered directly in the appropriate columns. Provide cue cards as
indicated throughout the food frequency.
“Additions” sections contain those dietary items usually consumed with other foods and are
included after most food groups and/or sub-groups. The purpose of having the additions sections
is to decrease poor reporting of dietary items added to other foods which may contribute large
amounts of fat, carbohydrate, and sodium to the diet and to decrease the number of times a
participant will be asked to report any given food. Use of this section will increase accuracy and
decrease the time needed to complete the interview.
“Additions” are different from any other sections on the form in that serving size is not

in a particular additions section, the food should be recorded under “other” and both a serving
size and frequency of consumption determined. A code must also be determined after the
interview and entered in the appropriate space on the form.
At the end of the Quantitated Food Frequency, Q101 asks the participant to evaluate
how well the history represents her/his usual intake.
INSTRUCTION TO INTERVIEWER: Ask the question as stated on the form. Hand the
participant the cue card and review the meal pattern reported by the participant in Q1 of the
Dietary Practices section. Check only one response.
Q102 helps determine if the past month has been typical with regard to the participant’s
usual dietary intake.
INSTRUCTION TO INTERVIEWER: Ask the question as stated on the form. If the
participant’s response is Yes, proceed to the possible responses in the second part of Q102.
Ask What occurred? Record only one response. If the response is No, the interview is
completed.

At the close of the interview, record the time that the interview ended. Thank the participant
for her/his time. Explain to the participant that the third part of the exam, the Self-Administered

complete during the exam.

the participant’s recall ability. It is important to complete these two questions before beginning
another interview. Record your Interviewer ID on the form.

C. INSTRUCTIONS FOR THE QUANTITATED FOOD FREQUENCY
1. Information Required by the Interviewer to Complete the Form
The Quantitated Food Frequency part of the CARDIA Diet History is designed to collect
usual dietary intake over the past month. The form was constructed so that data could be entered
directly into the computer with minimal additional coding. Therefore, the information must be
handled in a very specific manner. The form is arranged to assist the interviewer in obtaining the
information and in locating the correct place to record it. Notes are provided throughout the
form to instruct the interviewer how to handle information obtained. Conversions, calculations,
and other types of information will be dealt with after the interview so that the interview does not
take longer than necessary. At the completion of the interview, the interviewer should review
the form, making sure that all foods with a check mark in the select column have a Food ID,
serving size, and frequency included as well as method of preparation and fat code, when
applicable.
To complete the form, the interviewer should be familiar with the function of each of the
columns. Each page of the section will have nine columns with the following titles:
Serving
Food Item Prep Fat
√ Comments Size Freq Unit
ID Description Code Code
Amount
*Food ID: Each food item in the database is identified by a numerical Food ID. It is the
code that corresponds to nutrient information in the database for each food in the
Quantitated Food Frequency. The Food ID is listed in this column.
* √ (Select): This column is used to identify those food items consumed over the previous
month as reported by the participant. The interviewer checks this column opposite the
specific items reported by the participant.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-15

* Item Description: This column provides a brief description of each food in the
Quantitated Food Frequency. The interviewer should obtain enough information from the
participant to check the appropriate dietary items reported within each group.
* Comments: The Comments column provides space for the interviewer to record
comments made by the participant. Description of items that cannot be identified by a
specific code as well as information that cannot be entered directly into the appropriate
space or column during the interview should be written in the Comments column. (Lengthy
descriptions and/or extensive information should be recorded on the Floating Sheet).
* Serving Size: The amount of each item consumed, as described by the participant, is
recorded in this column. Serving size will be estimated by using the appropriate food model
as a guide. Items not represented by a specific food model can be quantitated using a food
model of similar size and/or shape. The interviewer should record the amount specified on
the underside of the food model if the participant indicates that the serving size is the same
or similar to that represented by the food model, or record that fraction or multiplier of the
food model indicated by the participant. It is also important to direct the participant to
express serving size in units appropriate to the item to avoid misrepresentation (e.g., fluid
ounces derived from a measuring cup should not be used to express quantities of dry items
since this could be confused with weight). For example, if the participant reports a 4 ounce
serving of cereal, the interviewer should clarify weather this is a weight or measuring cup
amount since 4 ounces by weight of dry cereal may be equivalent to 2 cups, not ½ cup as
indicated by 4 fluid ounces.
Acceptable serving units are listed in the Serving Size column. The serving unit and
amount described by the participant should be circled, even for items with only one legal
serving unit.
When the participant describes items in units other than those acceptable, those units are
recorded as reported under Comments, and conversions to appropriate units are made after
the interview. The interviewer will select the appropriate serving unit:
1. from information provided directly by the participant;
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-16

2. after conversion of quantity to “legal” or acceptable units if reported by participant
in unacceptable units; and
3. after conversion of quantity provided by dimensions to appropriate units.
One or more representative usual serving size will be used for most food groups. There are
some food groups where serving size for each item must be ascertained.
*Freq/Unit: The frequency with which items were consumed over the previous month
should be reported in days, weeks, or month. The participant should be free to report
frequency in the easiest manner. Multiple frequency units may be reported for a single item
and should be recorded as such. Frequencies of less than one per month should not be
recorded.
If a participant reports an amount of food as a total consumed over a period, for example, a
gallon of milk per week, probe to determine the serving size amount and the frequency that
the food was consumed. If the amounts vary, determine the overall frequency. The serving
size amount can then be determined by dividing the total amount by the frequency. For
example, the participant reports drinking milk 12 times during the week. The gallon of milk
(128 FO), would be divided by the frequency (12) resulting in a serving size amount of
10.66 FO.
Rule of Four: In some food groups, such as cereals, crackers or cookies, a participant may
eat four or more different types or brands of a particular food item. In such cases, obtaining
a frequency of consumption for each type or brand may prove time-consuming.
When a participant reports more than four different types or brands in a food group,
ascertain the four products used most frequently. Determine the overall frequency for the
total of the products consumed, then divide the overall frequency by four (4) and record the
result in the Frequency column.
For example, a participant reports eating four different cereals. The interviewer obtains
an overall frequency for consumption of cereal of 5 times per week. After the interview, the
interviewer divides the overall frequency of cereal consumption (5) by (4), and places 1.25
in the Frequency column and W in the Unit column for each cereal reported.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-17

Example 2: The participant eats 7 different cereals. She/he eats cereal 26 days per
month. Ascertain the four most commonly eaten cereals and record the names with the
Food IDs on the Quantitated Food Frequency, then divide 26 by 4 and record 6.5 in the
Frequency column and M in the Unit column for each of these four cereals.
*Food Preparation Code (Prep Code): This column is used to designate how a food was
prepared and is used only for food items that may require fat or had fat added during
preparation. Therefore, for many food items this column is not applicable. The prep code
indicates that a calculated amount of fat be added for each serving unit of that given food
item. All prep codes must be followed by a fat code (see next section on Fat Codes).
The preparation codes to be used for the CARDIA Quantitated Food Frequency are:
• Meat, fish or poultry:
pan-fried or grilled with fat other than its own fat PAN
basted or braised with fat while oven-cooked, broiled or grilled PAN
marinated in mixture used for basting during cooking PAN
breaded with flour or crumbs in moderate to deep fat BDF
• Vegetables, rice and pasta:
seasoned with any type of fat in cooling SES
stir-fried SES
• All items containing fat as an ingredient or as a variable part of the composition: APF
• Not applicable: No fat added to an item that would normally have added fat NAP
The APF code stands for “Add Principle Fat” and is already listed on the form for those
food items that usually have fat added during preparation (i.e., cakes, cookies, sauces,
pancakes/waffles). The APF code will be followed by either an “I” or a “C”, e.g., APFI or
APFC. The “I” indicates that the ingredient fat should be ascertained and reflected in the fat
code. The “C” indicates that the cooking fat should be ascertained and reflected in the fat
code. The interviewer is not permitted to write in APF as a prep code for foods printed on
the form since APF codes are already indicated for appropriate food items. However, if the
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-18

participant reports a food that does not appear on the form, an APF code may be required and
should be entered, when applicable (the CARDIA Diet Center will advise if a new food
resolution should be coded with SPF).
The PAN and BDF prep codes will be entered on the form in the meat, poultry and fish
sections only. No prep code is needed if fat is not added during preparation, and in such
cases, the Prep and Fat code columns should be left blank. Several lines have been provided
to allow room for listing the same item with different preparation methods.
For example, if the participant reports that steak is consumed twice a week, she/he may
indicate that once a week steak is prepared on a gas grill and once a week it is pan-fried in
oil. Such a response would require two entries for steak, one with no prep code (grilled) and
one with PAN (pan-fried in oil).
The SES prep code will be entered on the form in the vegetable, rice, or pasta sections
only. As previously stated, if fat is not added during preparation, no prep code is required
and the Prep and Fat code columns should be left blank.
* Fat Code: This column will be used only when a food has an APF code or a prep code
entered by the interviewer. A prep code must always be followed by a fat code. The fat code
will indicate what type of fat was used during the preparation. Fats have different codes
depending on the type. The interviewer will need to assign the appropriate four letter fat
code depending on information obtained from the participant. Fat codes and brand name
guides are located in the Coding Manual.
Question 5 in the Dietary Practices section deals with the type of fats used at home for
cooking, baking or seasoning. Information obtained from this question will be used to
complete fat codes for foods prepared at home. If the type of fat is unknown, the unknown
home fat code (HOME) should be used. This code will also be used if a food was prepared,
for example, at a friend’s home, from a recipe, but the type of fat used is unknown. For
foods prepared commercially, for example by a restaurant or deli, or prepared with a
commercial mix, the fat code BCOM should be used.
If an APF code is required on the Diet History form, but that food was prepared without
fat, do not cross off the APF. Instead, on a blank line in that section, record the Food ID and
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-19

the name of the food, but record NAP in the Prep Code column, and 0000 in the Fat Code
column. When NAP is used to override the APF prep code, 0000 needs to follow in the Fat
Code column. This indicates that no fat was added during the preparation of the food item.
2. Diet History Floating Sheet
The Diet History Floating Sheet should be available for each interview. The purpose of this
sheet is to permit the interviewer to record comments that the participant may make about food
eaten in a food group other than the one currently being asked about. The Floating Sheet can
also be used to record an extensive and/or lengthy description of a food item that will not fit in
the comments column. There are several large boxes on the Floating Sheet so that the
interviewer can label food categories that the participant reports. For example, if the participant
reports eating hot dog buns with franks about twice a month in the Rolls section, the interviewer
can label a box on the Floating Sheet as MEATS and make a note that the participant eats franks
twice during a usual month. When questioning in the Meat section, the interviewer can look at
the sheet to see if any meats have been mentioned. If the participant does not mention franks, the
interviewer can then state, “You said that you eat franks about twice a month. Have you
forgotten them here?”
3. Multiple Serving Units, Preparation Codes, and Frequencies
If any item is prepared in several different ways or consumed in several different serving
sizes, with different frequencies of consumption, the interviewer will use a separate line to record
each type of preparation method and each serving size and frequency. Blank lines exist at the
end of food groups for this purpose. When an item is entered in a blank space on the form, the
interviewer must enter the Food ID, the item description, serving size, frequency and prep/fat
codes, if applicable.
4. Procedures for Handling Missing Foods
Overview: Occasionally, a participant reports eating a food that is not on the Diet History
form or in the Food Code List Manual (FCLM). If the food item is not similar to another food
listed on the Diet History form or FCLM, the Chief Nutritionist sends a New Food Request form
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-20

to the Diet Center. A number is assigned to the new food (or form) prior to sending the request to
the Diet Center.
a. Steps for finding and entering problem (missing) foods:
Overview: There are times during the Diet History interview when a food is reported
that is not listed on the Diet History form. When this occurs, document details about the
food ingredients, flavors, fat, (e.g. low fat), preparation, etc. and the amount eaten. After
the participant departs, the Dietary Interviewer tries to locate the food code in the
FCLM. If the food item still cannot be found, the Dietary Interviewer consults with the
Chief Nutritionist and completes a New Food Request form.
When a food cannot be found in the Diet History or FCLM, try the steps below:
• If the item is a homemade casserole or other dish, select a generic food code.
For example: Several generic Casserole Recipe codes are listed that give the option of
different ingredients, such as beef, pork, and ham with pasta or rice, cream sauce with
vegetables (13278) and without vegetables (12353).
• Matches may be made from generic food items in the DHx.
For example: Byerly’s fat-free Italian dressing can be entered as generic fat-free clear
salad dressing. Gummy Super Heroes can be entered as gummi candies.
If no close matches are available, or if you are unsure if it is a close match, then the
Chief Nutritionist submits a New Food Request Form to the Diet Center. See the next
section for instructions on using the New Food Request Form.
b. Keeping Track of Decisions
The Chief Nutritionist keeps track of all missing foods and resolutions made at the site.
After a New Food Item has been resolved by the Diet Center, the resolution and food ID
for entering the food is returned to the Chief Nutritionist. The Dietary Interviewer enters
the new food onto the appropriate Diet History and continues with other quality control
procedures. The Chief Nutritionist is responsible for communicating all food
resolutions to Dietary Interviewers. New food resolutions (food IDs) will be made
available periodically in updates of the FCLM sent to all the field centers.

c. Submitting a New Food Request Form
If an item is not on the Diet History form or FCLM, use a New Food Request Form to
report nutrient (e.g. kcal, protein, fat, total carbohydrate, sodium) and ingredient

website. You may also be able to find nutrition and ingredient information for brand
name products at online shopping sites, such as Simon Delivers or Net Grocer. The
instructions for completing the New Food Request form are below. The Chief

Overview: The New Food Request Form is used by interviewers to request data entry
assistance for foods not found on the Diet History or FCLM. The form is completed by the

ii. Determine the New Food Request number by numbering sequentially by request

For example:
The first request is 0 0 0 1.

5. Actual vs. Usual Intake
Due to the nature of the history, the participant is asked to use the past month as a frame
of reference. Even if the participant reports that his intake over the past month has been
atypical due to travel, illness, dieting, etc., record the foods the participant actually ate. While
the food items selected during the past month may not be typical, they are still reflective of the
participant’s food selection behavior. The “unusual” food items have been substituted for usual
food items and should be recorded on the form.

7. Handling Nutrition-Related Questions During the Interview
It is likely that some participants will inquire about the adequacy of their diets or other nutrition-
related topics during the interview. Due to the nature of this study as well as the time constraints of
the interview, such questions should be deferred as politely as possible. If the participant inquires as
to the adequacy of his own particular diet, the interviewer can respond with the following statement:
I cannot answer your question at this time, but I will be sending you an evaluation later through the
mail. If the participant asks more general questions related to nutrition, the interviewer can respond
as follows: Time does not permit a discussion about that now. As I explained earlier, we need to
move through the interview as quickly as possible. If a participant is persistent in questions of a
nutritional nature, suggest that he speak to his physician.

a. Forms should be as neat as possible to make it easier for the data entry personnel.
i. Avoid unnecessary writing in data entry columns (i.e., Select, Serving Size
