4. Calculating Frequencies for Additions
During the interview, the interviewer should record the additions reported by the participant
as well as the foods to which these additions are added. After the interview, the frequency for
each reported addition must be calculated by multiplying the serving size amount by the
frequency of consumption for the food(s) to which the addition was added. For example, a
participant reports that she/he usually eats four pancakes, three times a month, and that regular
syrup is always used on her/his pancakes. After the interview, the interviewer would multiply 4
(serving size) by 3 (frequency) and enter 12 in the Frequency column on the line for regular
syrup in the additions section.
It is possible that the same additions will be used in the same frequencies for different food
items. If the frequencies of food items to which an addition is added are the same (day, week, or
month), the same step outlined above would be followed for each food item to which the
addition was added. The products should then be added and this sum entered in the Frequency
column in the Additions section. For example, a participant reports that she/he usually eats four
pancakes, three times a month, and three slices of French toast, twice a month, and that regular
syrup is always used on these items. After the interview, the interviewer would first multiply 4
(serving size for pancakes) by 3 (frequency for pancakes) for a product of 12, then multiply 3
(serving size for French toast) by 2 (frequency for French toast) for a product of 6. The
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-31

interviewer would then sum the 12 and 6 and enter 18 in the Frequency column on the line for
regular syrup in the Additions section.
If the frequencies of the food items to which an addition is added are different, the
frequency of the additions is reported twice in the same additions section. The interviewer
should not convert frequencies to obtain a common denominator. For example, a participant
reports that he usually eats four pancakes, three times a month, and three slices of French toast,
twice a week, and that regular syrup is always used on these items. After the interview, the
interviewer would multiply 4 (serving size for pancakes) by 3 (frequency for pancakes) and enter
12 in the Frequency column on the line for regular syrup in the Additions section. The
interviewer would then enter the Food ID for regular syrup and descriptive data, “REGULAR
SYRUP”, in block letters on a blank line in the Additions section. The serving size for French
toast (3 slices) would be multiplied by the frequency for French toast (2) and the product 6
entered in the Frequency column on the line for the second syrup entry. The serving size amount
would be entered on the second syrup entry using the “Standard Additions” list in the Coding
Manual.
E. DEALING WITH PROBLEM INTERVIEWS
1. Introduction
Most CARDIA participants will respond favorably to the Diet History interview. By
conveying a friendly, interested attitude and by proceeding through the history in a direct but
flexible manner, the CARDIA nutritionist will be successful in obtaining the necessary
information. Subtle cues such as a warm greeting, an occasional smile, frequent eye contact, and
a cordial atmosphere are extremely effective in eliciting cooperation and candor from the
participant. A pleasant tone of voice and a sincere interest in the person being interviewed will
help to ensure optimal response.
Despite mastery of these interviewing skills and a working knowledge of proper technique
for administering the history, CARDIA nutritionists are apt to encounter problems with some
interviews. It is unlikely that these situations can be predicted. Nutritionists should be ready and
willing to adapt their interviewing style to the particular needs of the participant. Simple
changes such as increasing or decreasing the speed of the questions being asked, shifting position
of the chair, or offering to repeat questions if necessary may be all that is required.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-32

Consideration of whether the participant understands the instructions and the purpose of the
interview, and also has reasonable expectations of the time needed to complete the dietary
component, are all important factors.
Although the CARDIA Diet History documentation procedures have been standardized as
much as possible throughout the study, each Diet History interview is a unique experience
depending on the personality and perspective of the individuals involved. Certain kinds of
problematic behavior are more likely to occur than others and nutritionists should be prepared to
respond accordingly. Some of these types of problem interviews, and ways of handling them,
are summarized below.
2. The Unresponsive Participant
For numerous reasons, i.e., shyness, lack of understanding, or inability to recall past eating
habits, some participants will not want to talk. This situation requires patience in both
interpreting the reason for the silence as well as in encouraging greater response. If the first five
minutes have lapsed and the participant seems overly shy or quiet, try to assess the reason. Some
of the following techniques may also be helpful:
• Ask open-ended questions and use food models to help the participant explain types of
food as well as serving size, preparation, etc.
• Ask questions more slowly, offer to repeat questions, give examples of appropriate
responses, and/or rephrase questions.
• Engage in brief conversation regarding the common difficulty of remembering food
intake and lead the participant into recalling general eating patterns.
• Ask about general food preferences or dislikes.
• Ascertain who typically does the cooking for the participant and whether he/she
discusses the process with the participant.
• Assure the participant that it is not unusual for someone who typically eats out or has
someone else preparing food to disregard the nature of the food being served and/or be
unable to accurately report on content.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-33

• Without leading the answers, suggest different food groups to determine whether the
participant eats a variety of foods or has a limited intake within one or two food groups.
• Allow the participant a chance to see the Diet History form and the manner in which the
data are recorded to facilitate his/her understanding of the interview process.
• Ask the participant to recall activities often associated with eating, e.g., watching
television, reading, listening to music, etc. to help remember particular meals and
snacks.
3. The Hostile Participant
• First, try to determine the source of the hostility, i.e., fatigue, discomfort from blood
draw immediately preceding the dietary interview, anxiety over missing work, leaving
children unattended or with babysitters, etc. Offer assistance for physical discomfort or
other aid when appropriate.
• Express appreciation to the participant for extending the time and effort to attend the
CARDIA exams.
• Before beginning, explain that the interview will take about 45 to 50 minutes. Allow
the opportunity for a stretch break, drink of water or other temporary diversion during
the interview if necessary.
• Ask the participant if there is anything that can be done to help him/her be more
comfortable.
• Try a little humor and accept the fact that diet is not necessarily a topic of interest to all
participants.
4. The Bored or Hurried Participant
• Warn the participant before the interview begins of the expected length of the interview.
Indicate that the procedure can be most efficient by providing concise but complete
information.
• Try to speed up the interview by shortening the sentences and/or anticipating questions
from the participant
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-34

• Obtain information in the most expedient manner possible, saving complete
documentation for the editing period post-interview.
• Encourage the participant to endure the process and to cooperate in order to shorten the
time needed to complete the interview.
• Use caution so as not to proceed with excessive haste thereby limiting complete
information.
• Use food models and cue cards to help focus the participant’s thoughts on the process at
hand rather than on the boredom.
5. The Uninformed Participant
Some participants will not have a practical understanding of food purchasing, brand names,
serving sizes or much of anything related to her/his eating habits. This is likely to be a person
who eats many meals out or away from home and/or may have someone else preparing meals,
doing the shopping, etc. This may also be a person who has little knowledge of qualitative
differences within food groups and differences in measurement, or someone who is unfamiliar
with cooking terminology.
• Carefully explain and reiterate the types of information being sought.
• Give frequent examples.
• Briefly define and differentiate certain terms, i.e., boiling vs. frying, cup measure vs.
spoon measure, differences between fats, margarine, oils, etc.
• Seek less specific brand name information using the least common denominator
approach.
• Suggest that the participant point to the food models and the serving size models
whenever possible.
• Forego use of cue cards if the participant is obviously illiterate and read the options
instead.
• Be patient and allow the participant the opportunity to ask or paraphrase questions
before responding.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-35

• Obtain data in whatever terms are familiar to the participant, probing for details when
necessary. Following the interview, items written in the “comments” section of the
form may be edited as needed.
F. PERSONNEL RECOMMENDED REQUIREMENTS
1. Chief Nutritionist
The Chief Nutritionist is responsible for all aspects of the dietary data collection in the
clinical centers including the planning, organization, development, and execution of nutrition
components of CARDIA. The Chief Nutritionist coordinates the nutrition activities as well as
the supervision and evaluation of the work of all other members of the nutrition staff. In
addition, she/he is responsible, in part, for the training of the local clinical personnel.
The recommended education and experience requirements for a Chief Nutritionist are: (1) a
master’s degree in foods and nutrition or in public health nutrition and two years of progressively
responsible experience in these fields; (2) or an equivalent combination of training and
experience, such as dietetic internship with a nutrition clinic or pubic health component and three
or more years of work in the field. Experience in conducting dietary interviews is highly
desirable.
2. Staff Nutritionist/Interviewer
The Staff Nutritionist/Interviewer in CARDIA will be responsible for collecting accurate
dietary information from study participants. Each Nutritionist/Interviewer will be trained and
certified to:
• obtain information on dietary practices;
• administer a 28-day quantitated Diet History; and
• edit forms for data entry.
The time required to administer and edit one Diet History is approximately 1.5 to 2 hours.
Each center should calculate nutritionist(s) time on the basis of the number of participants to be
seen daily by the individual center.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-36

The recommended qualifications for persons selected to interview CARDIA participants are:
• minimum of a two year Diet Tech degree or a BS in nutrition or food science;
• some experience in conducting dietary interviews;
• demonstration of good mathematical skills;
• fluent in English; and
• familiarity with American eating patterns and food supply specific to CARDIA
participants.
3. Nutrition Coordinator
The dietary component of CARDIA will involve the collection of a large volume of diverse
data. Standardization of mechanisms for handling this data across centers is important to assure
quality control. In addition, the NCC nutrient database used for nutrient analyses must be
continually updated to provide current estimates of nutrient intake. To maintain consistency and
quality in the collection of dietary data across centers, a Nutrition Coordinator will be selected
for CARDIA and should meet the qualifications previously described for the Chief Nutritionist.
The Nutrition Coordinator works with other team members at the CARDIA Diet Reading
Center, including the PI, programmer, and another nutritionist. The responsibilities of the
Nutrition Coordinator are:
• to answer all questions regarding the recording of dietary information obtained in the
interview on the form;
• to document answers to questions regarding dietary data to provide consistency in
responses;
• to maintain contact with the NCC to receive current information on compositional
changes in food products and new additions to the food supply for updating the
database;
• to supervise ongoing quality of interviewer skills in conducting the Diet History
interviews;
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-37

• to report monthly regarding progress and status of the flow and quality of the dietary
data collection;
• to summarize the quality of the dietary data collection for reports to the Quality Control
Committee and the Review Board.
G. CERTIFICATION
Certification for Diet History interviewers will be made upon satisfactory completion of:
• CARDIA Diet History centralized (or local) training session; and
• A total of eight interviews and the corresponding Diet History forms – two of which may
be completed during training, and eight completed back at the interviewer’s center.
The last two interviews performed for certification must be observed by the Chief
Nutritionist or a certified nutritionist. The evaluation forms for these interviews (Appendix 6—
Diet History Certification Interview Checklist) must be submitted to the Diet Center along with
the interviews. The interview forms will be evaluated for completeness by the Nutrition
Coordinator. An error rate of less than 3% must be achieved on both of the submitted forms. If
this error rate is not achieved on both forms, four additional interviews and the corresponding
forms will be completed. The last two of these additional forms must be submitted to the
Nutrition Coordinator and evaluated for completeness.
In addition, the last interview should be digitally recorded and forwarded to the Nutrition
Coordinator for evaluation. Fewer than ten errors for incorrectly recorded information and
deviations from protocol (combined) must be achieved.
Certification must be completed before the start of the pilot testing period.
H. QUALITY CONTROL
Dietary data will be monitored during the period of data collection on an ongoing basis to
insure the complete and accurate recording of dietary information. This will insure consistency
across centers in recording the information by providing input regarding interpretation and
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-38

recording of reported dietary intake among different nutritionists and with an individual
nutritionist over time. The Nutrition Coordinator will be responsible for implementing and
overseeing the procedures for quality control for the dietary data.
1. Completeness of Recorded Information
The completeness of information recorded on the Diet History form will be reviewed by the
nutritionist conducting the interview and checked again by a second nutritionist. A monthly 10%
random sample of Diet History forms will be checked for completeness at the Diet Center
(Appendix 8).
The following items will be reviewed:
• sufficient information was obtained for each item reported to satisfy the requirements
for processing the data, e.g., “Select” column checked, serving amounts provided,
serving units indicated, preparation codes indicated, and fat codes provided, where
appropriate;
• items described under “Comments” and on the Floating Sheet were recorded in the
appropriate places on the form;
• Food IDs were selected and recorded on the form for those items requiring the use of
food guides; and
• answers are clearly marked for all questions and that no questions were omitted during
the interview.
2. Accuracy of Recorded Information
The accuracy of recording reported dietary intake on the Diet History form will be
monitored as follows (Appendix 9):
• each nutritionist will make a digital recording of every interview throughout the Year
20 Exam. One recording per month per nutritionist will be selected and reviewed at the
Diet Center. The Coordinating Center will select the interview for evaluation and send
the digital file and a copy of the completed Diet History form to the Nutrition
Coordinator;
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-39

• the Nutrition Coordinator will check the form for accuracy and completeness while
listening to the recorded interview;
• the Nutrition Coordinator will report to each Chief Nutritionist any errors made by
nutritionists in their center;
• the Diet Center will monitor the progress of nutritionists and will generate a report to be
distributed to the PIs, the Coordinating Center, the Diet Committee, the Quality Control
committee and the Review Board; and
• the Diet Center will file the digital recordings, interviewer-completed history forms, and
error reports.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-40

APPENDIX 1
CONFIDENTIALITY
Maintaining confidentiality is one of the most important tasks of the survey interviewer. It is
important to assure the respondent that information given during an interview will not be directly
linked to his/her household.
The rights of human subjects are a matter of primary concern to your Institutional Review Board and
all study procedures are reviewed to ensure that individual respondents are protected at each stage of
research. While it is the University’s policy to make study findings public, the utmost care is taken
to ensure that no data are released that would permit any respondent to be identified. All information
that links a particular interview to a specific respondent is removed as soon as the interview is
completed; this information is maintained in special confidential files while the study is in progress,
and is destroyed after the study closes. Interviewers themselves are identified only by numbers.
The University’s strict precautions to protect the anonymity of respondents will be undermined if
you do not treat information concerning respondents with equal regard. You perform a professional
function when you obtain information from individuals in personal interviews, and you are expected
to maintain professional ethical standards of confidentiality regarding what you hear from a
respondent. All information about respondents obtained during the course of the research is
privileged information, whether it relates to the interview itself or includes extraneous observations
concerning the respondent’s home, family, and activities.
IMPORTANT POINTS TO REMEMBER ABOUT CONFIDENTIALITY
• All information received in connection with a survey is considered privileged. The
respondent trusts you not to betray any confidence
• No information gathered is ever directly linked to a respondent. Names are never attached
to a survey.
• Do not discuss details of a survey with others.
• Do not offer opinions about survey results either to respondents or in discussions you may
have with friends or family. In the course of a survey you may find yourself developing
opinions about the information received. Remember, however, that your conclusions are
drawn from the very small number of people you interview. Your conclusions may not
accurately reflect the population as a whole
When asked by others what your work involves, explain it in the same broad terms used to introduce
the survey to respondents. Try not to make interpretations about the survey findings. If you talk
with someone interested in the results of the study, refer them to your supervisor.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations ver 1.2 05December06 Diet-41

APPENDIX 2
DETERMINING AMOUNT OF EXTRA ALCOHOL CONSUMED
Q96-Q98 ask How often during the month do you drink more than this amount?, as an
additional question after asking the usual amount. The following procedure should be followed for
these questions:
• Ascertain and record the usual amount of alcohol consumed and the frequency.
• Ask How often during the month do you drink more than this amount? If the participant
replies that this happened at least once, ask Are those separate occasions from the times
you just described or are they included in those times?
• If the participant states that these occasions are included in those already reported :
o Ask How much more do you drink?
o Probe to determine whether the response included the usual amount reported. If the
base amount was included, code only the extra alcohol. If the base amount was not
included, code the total amount consumed.
• If the participant states that these occasions are separate from those already reported:
o Ask How much do you have on those occasions?
o Record the amount of alcohol consumed.

APPENDIX 3
CONVERTING FRACTIONS TO DECIMALS
ROUNDING RULES BY SCIENTIFIC NOTATION
When converting a fraction to a decimal: divide the numerator by the denominator.
• Example: 5/8 = 0.625 (5 ÷ 8)
To round a decimal to two decimal places, use Rules by Scientific Notation.
If a calculation results in a number from 1 to 4, round down.
If a calculation results in a number from 6 to 9, round up.
If a calculation results in a number ending in 5:
• If the number before the 5 is odd, round up.
• If the number before the 5 is even, drop the 5.
The justification is that in the coursed of a series of many calculations, any rounding errors will be
averaged out.
• Example: 0.245 rounds to 0.24
• Example: 0.235 rounds to 0.24
• Example: 0.465 rounds to 0.46
• Example: 0.435 rounds to 0.44

A. OVERVIEW
This document is the Manual of Operations for the National Heart, Lung, and Blood
Institute's Coronary Artery Risk Development in (Young) Adults (CARDIA) Study Y20
Exam (also called Exam VII). The examination process covered by this manual
represents the seventh examination of the CARDIA cohort, which was created by the
initial screening process for the Y0 Exam, conducted from March 1985 to June 1986.
The selection process utilized in this initial examination created a cohort of 5115 persons
randomly selected from the four populations identified for the study by the four CARDIA
Field Centers: Chicago, Minneapolis, Birmingham, and Oakland. The selection
procedures and methods used are described elsewhere (1, 2) and the baseline results have
been reported (3, 4).
Subsequent examinations were held at Y2 (June 1987-June 1988), Y5 (June 1990-
June 1991), Y7 (June 1992-June 1993), Y10 (June 1995 - June 1996), and Y15 (June
2000 – May 2001). The contents and methods used in these examinations are described
in the relevant Manuals of Operations and Protocols (5-15).
B. Y20 EXAMINATION
The CARDIA Y20 Exam includes a set of core examination components, including a
measurement of subclinical disease via computed tomography (CT) scanning for coronary
calcium and intima medial thickening via carotid ultrasound. (See Appendix 1 for a list of
data collection items for all seven of the CARDIA examinations, as well as sub-studies
and ancillary studies.) Sub-studies are typically undertaken by fewer than all four of the
Field Centers with funding from the CARDIA contracts. Ancillary studies are defined as
those undertaken by some, or all, Field Centers with funding from sources outside the
contracts for the central CARDIA Study.
This document provides instructions for Field Center personnel regarding their data
collection responsibilities for this examination. No sub-studies are included in the Y20

B. INTERVIEWING PRINCIPLES AND PROCEDURES
Interviewing is, in part, a science. There are definite rules that produce valid results.
Interviewing is also an art. Frequently there are only general guidelines to follow, and
much depends on the sensitivity of the interviewer. The procedures and techniques that
follow will help interviewers conduct interviews which will yield valid data.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-1

1. Developing a Good Interviewing Relationship
Interviewing is one of the major parts of the CARDIA Study, and therefore it is
crucial that interviewer present questions appropriately, record participant responses
precisely and accurately, and probe meaningfully. To promote an objective information-
gathering atmosphere, the interviewer must convey an understanding persona accepting
of information in a non-judgmental manner, as well as interest in what the participant is
saying. The participant must find satisfaction in talking to a receptive person without the
fear of judgment.
It is the interviewer's responsibility to obtain full and accurate information by
eliciting cooperation from each participant by establishing and maintaining rapport, and
encouraging the participant to answer honestly in a strictly neutral way. Interviewers
with professional skills make it possible for participants to give frank, complete, relevant
answers to questions.
In general, the majority of participants are willing to be interviewed. A confident,
enthusiastic approach that assumes people are willing to be interviewed is a most
effective technique.
a. Increasing the Participant's Cooperativeness. Previous studies have identified
several factors that increase a participant's receptiveness.
i. The interviewer must be prepared by knowing the material. Participants need to
feel that the interviewer is interested in the Study and interested in what
information they have to give. The interviewer must be an active listener and
establish comfortable eye contact with the participant.
ii. The interviewer must offer convincing statements about the purpose of the Study
and show appreciation for the participant’s cooperation.
iii. The interviewer must describe the beneficial uses of the research findings to both
the participant and to the community.
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-2

2. Two Main Kinds of Questions
a. Pre-coded Questions: An “X” is placed in the box that matches the participant’s
answer. Whenever there is any question about which response option is
appropriate, it is very important that the interviewer record the participant's
verbatim response.
b. Open-ended Questions: The question is followed by a blank box for the
interviewer to record the participant's answer verbatim. This kind of question
suggests no possible answers, so the participant's own words must be recorded in
the box provided. The interviewer should encourage him/her to express ideas as
fully and as clearly as possible.
3. Interviewer-Administered Questionnaires
There are several standard procedures for reading questions: Read in a natural
conversation rhythm and in a normal tone of voice. The interviewer should read as
speaking, but be cautious of reading questions too rapidly, as a participant may not feel
comfortable asking that a question be repeated. A question should be repeated as written,
if answered inappropriately.
a. Interview instructions are provided throughout the interview. These instructions
are not to be read to participants but are intended to guide the interviewer.
Interviewer instructions appear in all capital letters.
b. Only those code categories which appear in the question should be read, unless:
i. the interviewer has special instructions to the contrary;
ii. there is an instruction to READ CHOICES; or
iii. a question ends with a dash or colon and it is obvious that the codes must be
read for the question to make sense.
c. Questions are to be asked exactly as worded and in the same order as they appear
in the questionnaires. Minor changes in wording can completely change the
meaning of a question. This will help to insure that comparable information is
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-3

being obtained from all the participants in the Study. The interviewer should not
ask questions out of order unless given special instructions.
d. Every question should be asked, unless instructed to SKIP TO another question.
Often a previous statement by the participant will partially answer another
question, but rarely does it answer that question completely. The interviewer
must not omit questions and not assume answers to questions.
4. How to Get Satisfactory Answers
a. Learn the Purpose of Each Question. In order to do a good job of interviewing,
the interviewer needs to understand the kind of information sought by each
question. Unless the question’s purpose is understood, the interviewer will not be
able to judge when a response is adequate and when a probe for clarification is
necessary.
b. Don't Attempt to Explain the Question—Maintain Neutrality. If a participant
does not seem to understand a question, the interviewer should repeat the
question slowly, clearly, and exactly as written. The participant should be given
time to think about the question. Unless instructed otherwise, the acceptable
reply to a participant asking what a question means is whatever it means to you.
The interviewer should not attempt to explain the purpose of a question.
c. Don't Define Terms Used in Questions. Some participants may ask what is
meant by a word or phrase used in a question. The interviewer must leave the
matter of definition to the participant, suggesting whatever you think XYZ means
or however you use the term XYZ.
d. The interviewer should not leave a question until 1) an adequate answer has been
given, 2) the participant cannot give a clearer answer, or 3) No response is a
response category option.
5. Probing Techniques
a. Silence. The value of silence cannot be overestimated. Many people, including
interviewers, react to silence as a vacuum that must be filled with constant
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-4

chatter. The interviewer who can wait quietly and patiently will soon find that
fifteen seconds of silence is sufficient for a participant to expand or clarify a
previously inadequate answer.
b. Repeat the Question. When repeating a question, the interviewer should read the
question verbatim. This probing technique is particularly useful when a
participant answers a question irrelevantly. The interviewer should acknowledge
the participant’s answer and then repeat the question.
c. Do Not Accept a "Don't Know" Answer Without Probing at Least Once. If a
response is Don't know, the interviewer should probe by asking Well, what do
you think? or I'd like to know your opinion. If the question requires a factual
answer (rather than opinion), an approximation is preferred to no answer at all.
The interviewer might probe by asking What's your best guess? or
Approximately? to convey that 100% accuracy is not required.
d. Neutral Probes. Probes are needed to obtain more complete, accurate answers.
All probes must be non-directive and not suggest any particular answer. The
interviewer should use a neutral probe when a participant is hesitant to answer a
question, seems to have trouble expressing him/herself, seems too shy to speak at
length, or has not given a complete report of his/her thoughts. Additionally, the
interviewer should use reassuring probes if a participant seems to lack
confidence. Probes that are leading should be avoided, as participants tend to say
yes to any suggestion, either because it's easy or because they think it's the right
answer.
A listing of sample neutral probes and leading probes follows:
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-5

Acceptable Neutral Probes Unacceptable Leading Probes
In what way? Do you mean...?
Why do you feel that way? Then you feel...?
I would like your opinion. So, you think…?
What do you think? So, you think…?
Can you give me an example? For example, …
Can you explain that in a little more detail?
What else can you tell me about that?
6. How to Record the Interviews onto the Forms
Interviewer Recommendations:
(cid:131) Be prepared to write.
(cid:131) Periodically establish eye contact with the participant while writing.
(cid:131) Use abbreviations to help record as much as possible.
(cid:131) Always record responses in participant’s exact words. If the response is too
wordy, the participant should be asked to summarize his/her response.
(cid:131) If a response is recorded incorrectly, it should be erased and recorded correctly.
The Y20 Exam form sets will be scanned and transmitted to the Coordinating Center
for data entry. Most forms will be entered via electronic scanning device; therefore, the
following recording techniques are mandatory to ensure clarity and quality of answers:
a. Boxes that require a mark (other than a character or number) should be marked
with an X like this: X
b. When recording numbers, such as amounts or dates, one number should go in
each box provided, and every box should have a number in it. Therefore, it may
be necessary to provide leading zeros when the number requires fewer boxes than
provided. For example:
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-6

0 2 3
c. Written responses (text) should be kept within the textbox provided. Text written
outside a textbox will not be read by the scanning device.
d. The box same date as blood pressure should be marked on all forms completed
the same day as the participant’s blood pressure is taken. The date field on these
forms should be left blank. If forms are completed, the date should be recorded,
using leading zeros when necessary. No spaces should be left blank. For
example: 0 6 / 0 4 / 2 0 0 5
e. A No. 2 pencil should be used to record responses. The interviewer should write
clearly, pressing with enough pressure to leave dark writing on the forms.
f. When recording text responses, print should be legible and in all capital letters,
following the Alpha-Numeric Design Template found in Appendix 1. This will
be easiest for the data entry person to enter or the electronic scanner to read.
Illegible printing will result in queries being returned to the clinic for
clarification.
g. If no answer is given by a participant, the interviewer should mark the No answer
response, if available; if this option is not available, the interviewer should circle
all responses and write NA for no answer in the left margin.
h. Numerals should be printed clearly and legibly following the Alpha-Numeric
Design Template found in Appendix 1.
C. SOCIODEMOGRAPHIC QUESTIONNAIRE (FORM 3)
General Information
The Sociodemographic Questionnaire is an interviewer-administered form designed
to collect information about the basic socioeconomic and demographic characteristics of
the study population.
Question 1: Education of Participant
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-7

“Regular school” means school that advances a person toward an elementary school
certificate, high school diploma, or college or university degree. It includes schooling the
person may have received in night school and special classes toward a high school
diploma. (If foreign schooling, the interviewer should probe for closest equivalent to
U.S. grades.)
Technical, vocational, or business schools are not considered regular school. If a
participant answers in terms of vocational school, the interviewer should indicate that the
question refers specifically to grade school, high school, college, and graduate school.
The interviewer is to check one entry from response options 01 to 20 to indicate the
highest grade or year of schooling completed.
Question 2: Highest Degree
All participants should be asked Q2, as the number of years of regular school
completed does not necessarily indicate whether or not a degree was earned. For
example, a participant may have earned a college degree after completing less than four
years of college. Response option Other, specify should be marked if the participant
responds that his/her highest degree earned is a technical school degree or vocational
school degree. The participant’s specific response should then be recorded in the box
provided.
Question 3: Currently in School
The interviewer should mark the response that applies.
Question 4: Usual Activity
The interviewer should read Q4a-Q4f and allow the participant to answer each
question Yes or No.
The term working in these questions means working for pay at a job, running one's
own business or profession, or working without pay in a family business. The interviewer
is to always accept a participant’s definition of full-time and part-time work. As well, the
interviewer should never define these terms for a participant. If the participant responds
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-8

Yes to Q4f, then Q4f1 should be asked to determine his/her relationship to the children
being raised; check all that apply. Adopted children and stepchildren living with the
participant full-time, are considered own children.
Note: Q4e and Q4f cannot be Yes if either Q4a or Q4b is Yes. If a participant responds
Yes to either full-time or part-time work and also responds Yes to full-time housework or
raising children, the interviewer will need to clarify by saying “If you work for pay full-
or part-time, then keeping house or raising children cannot also be considered full-time.”
Question 5a: Occupation of Participant (Employer)
The emphasis of this question is on the participant's current or most recent job. If the
participant has more than one job, the interviewer should probe for the primary job, i.e.,
the job at which the person spends the most hours. If the hours are equal, the interviewer
should ask the questions in reference to the job the participant considers primary or most
important. The interviewer is not to press for the name of the company or employer if
there is any hesitancy on the participant’s part. The name is not necessary, and in most
instances will not tell what the participant actually does in his/her job. If the participant
has never worked, Never Worked should be recorded in the box provided.
Although coding of occupation will not be performed during the Y20 Exam, detailed
occupation information will still be collected for use at a later date. If having difficultly
determining the participant’s occupation, the interviewer can refer to the Census Bureau’s
instructions for determining a worker’s classification which can be found in Appendix 2.
Question 5b: Occupation of Participant (Kind of Business)
The kind of business or industry is crucial to properly classifying the participant’s
job. A description such as automobiles is not sufficient, as it describes a number of
different businesses, including auto factory, new car dealership, used car lot, car rental
agency, and car wash. The interviewer should probe fully to determine the specific
business or industry in which the participant works. If appropriate, the interviewer may
ask if the industry is manufacturing, wholesale, retail or other (construction, service,
school, bank, etc).

The interviewer must find out specifically what kind of work the participant does.

3. Medication Follow-up Forms (Form 9-MED-ADH, Form 9-MED, Form 9 MED-
ASP, Form 9 MED-BCP)
Participants will be asked to bring physician prescriptions and/or medication
containers with the prescription labels to the clinic for their CARDIA appointment. If a
participant does not have a physician prescription or medication container, he/she should
prepare a list of prescription medications (prescribed by a physician and filled by a
pharmacist) to bring to his/her exam. The prescription list should contain the complete
medication name, strength and units, and dosage.
Each participant’s form set will contain four medication-related forms: 9 MED-ADH,
9 MED, 9 MED-ASP, and 9 MED-BCP. If the participant reports using more than three
medications, then a copy of Form 9-MED made from the master set should be completed
for each additional medication reported and one of the participant’s ID label affixed to the
form.
Forms 9-MED and 9-MED-BCP require coding of the medication using the Master
Medication Database (MMD) Code Book. The MMD contain two sections. In the first
section, medications are organized alphabetically by generic name and in the second
section, medications are organized alphabetically by brand name. The interviewer will
look for the generic name or brand name and write the code associated with that
medication. If the name of a medication is not found, 9999 should be recorded. If the
name of a medication is unknown (e.g., the name is not clearly written on the label or on
the participant’s list), then 0000 should be recorded, and UNKNOWN should be recorded
for the medication name. If the name of the medication is known, but details about it are
not, and there are multiple listings in the MMD by that name, use the code for the first
listed medication of that name.
Form 9 MED-ADH
The interview related to medications will start with Form 9 MED-ADH. This form is
generic, therefore, questions refer to medications in general, not to any specific
medication. If a participant is currently taking ANY medication (other than birth control

proceed with the remaining questions. The following cue card is available to assisting the

Scoring and Reliability of Form 18—Physical Activity History
Q2 - Q14
Scores related to energy expenditure are computed from intensity levels and the
months of less frequent and more frequent performance of each activity (see Table 1).
The intensity level assigned to each activity is roughly the number of kilocalories
expended in one minute of activity. Intensities were patterned after those used by Taylor,
et al. (2) and Folsom, et al. (3) which, in turn, are based on formulation by Reiff, et al.
(4). Exceptions are bicycling, which was set at an intensity code of 6 to reflect the
wording faster than 10 miles per hour; and vigorous job activity, which was set at an
intensity code of 5, somewhat less than that for weight lifting.
Amount of activity performed is based on months of participation and an assumption
about relative duration of activity for frequent versus infrequent participators. The
duration of activity in more frequent participation months (in which the activity was
performed more than the activity-specific cutpoint of 2 to 5 hours per week) is assumed
somewhat arbitrarily to be three times as great as the duration of activity in less frequent
participation months. The sum of the products of Intensity*Amount is computed for each
activity group 2 through 14 running/jogging through home maintenance/gardening, i.e.,
bi*(mi + 3*ni), where i ranges through the activity classes, bi is the intensity, mi is the
number of months of less frequent participation, and ni is the number of months of more
frequent participation. The Heavy Intensity Score sums these computed values over the
class of eight vigorous intensity activities (2-9), the Moderate Intensity Score is restricted
to the class of the five remaining moderate intensity activities, and the Total Score is the
sum of these two subscores. Since the number of minutes of performance in any month is
unknown and likely to vary substantially across activities, no interpretation as caloric
expenditure per week is available, and the score is left unaltered in Exercise Units.

G. INTERIM HEALTH CARE CONTACTS (FORM 31)
1. Overview
The CARDIA Study tracks major health events (i.e., injuries, surgeries, illnesses)
requiring hospitalization or outpatient treatment reported by CARDIA participants.
Whether or not the participants report any Other Major Health Problem on the Medical
History Form (Form 8), the interviewer should ask about health care contacts. Participants
will be questioned about hospitalizations since their last CARDIA examination or contact.
The information will be recorded on the Interim Health Care Contact, Hospitalizations,
Serious Illnesses and Injuries Form (Form 31).
2. General Instructions for Completion of Form 31
A hospitalization is defined as an admission which involves an overnight stay in a
hospital, alcohol or drug abuse treatment center or a mental institution. Emergency room
visits with no admission, same day surgery, and outpatient clinic services will not be
considered hospitalizations, but will be queried separately.
3. Administering the Interim Health Care Contact Form (Form 31)
Completion of Form 31 requires a significant amount of text and will not be
processed using the TeleForm system. It is, however, very important that the interviewer
record clearly and legibly on the form.
At the top of the form, just below the date to the right, is box with a question that asks
if the participant traveled more than 50 miles from their home to this exam. Record the
participant’s response as Yes or No. Do not leave this blank. If participant is unsure how
far they traveled, note the name of the town they live in so that the exit interviewer can
code the response. If the participant traveled from somewhere other than their home
today, ask how far they live from the Field Center to respond to this question.
A Hospitalization Report Form will be generated for each participant when his/her
form set is printed. The Hospitalization Report Form summarizes hospitalizations
reported by the participant at the most recent follow-up contact or last CARDIA exam,

Hospitalization Report Form will provide the hospital admission date, reason for

Is the information about the hospitalization(s) on the Hospital Report Form accurate? If
not, the information should be corrected, and a copy sent to the Coordinating Center.

4. CARDIA Hospitalization Coding Schemes
A Hospitalization Coding Scheme has been developed to facilitate systematic and
consistent identification of hospitalization records of interest to the Study. The coding
scheme also provides standardized information about the reasons for hospitalization,
facilitating data entry and retrieval of information about CARDIA participants. The goal
of the coding is to classify illnesses in a broad sense, with greater specificity in coding
cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases. The standardized coding permits
identification of the hospitalizations for which the Study will request more detailed
information (medical records). Information collected by the interviewer on Form 31 is
the basis for the coding, and in some instances, may be the only information available for
use in identifying endpoints (those diagnoses of special interest to the Study).
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-51

Interviewers must be familiar with the CARDIA Hospitalization Coding Scheme to
ensure accurate collection of information during the interview (see Tables 1-3). CARDIA
coding is included in the Interviewer Training. All interviewers are required to pass a
written test using the CARDIA Hospitalization Coding Scheme to become certified to
perform CARDIA coding.
There are two types of CARDIA coding:
a. CARDIA Coding Scheme One permits commonly occurring reasons for
hospitalization (e.g., heart attack, pregnancy delivery, diabetes, asthma,
pneumonia, AIDS) to be coded using only one code (Table 1). The reasons for
hospitalizations listed in Table 1 were included for three reasons: 1) the systemic
nature of the illness (e.g., diabetes, AIDS); 2) the regular association of a specific
illness with a specific body part (e.g., heart attack, stroke, pneumonia); and 3) the
frequency of occurrence in CARDIA participants. In general, these codes are
grouped according to body systems. The following are examples of these types
of hospitalizations: pregnancy with a vaginal delivery (code P2), diabetes (code
E1), hypertension (code V2), stroke (code V1), lupus (code R2), depression (code
M1), AIDS (code G1) and pneumonia/bronchitis (code L2).
b. CARDIA Coding Scheme Two requires a minimum of two codes; the first code
identifies the general or medical problem (e.g., cancer, fracture/broken bone,
burn). The second code identifies the body part affected (e.g., breast, leg,
foot/ankle). For example, breast cancer would be coded as 51 (cancer) and 32
(breast).
When the hospitalization is the result of an injury or surgery, the cause
code should be listed first, followed by the problem and the body part. For
example, an automobile accident resulting in a broken leg would be coded W4
(auto accident); 75 (fracture); 45 (leg).
If the participant does not provide enough information for the specific
coding, the injury would be coded as injury, unspecified. This coding scheme is
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-52

flexible, permitting a degree of detail, but without requiring an extensive list of
codes.
In review, many hospitalizations require a code for illness or injury and
additional codes for affected body part. When coding these hospitalizations, the
illness or injury codes are placed first, followed by the body part codes. In
the case of surgery, the illness code is placed first, followed by the surgery code,
and the body part code.
5. Coding Hospitalizations
Form 31 provides space for coding three two-digit codes for each reported
hospitalization. The primary (main) reason for the hospitalization should be coded first,
followed by secondary reasons. If any of the reasons for hospitalization result in
code: H1–H7, V1-V6, V9, 01, or 02, the code should be listed among the codes
whether or not it was the primary reason for the hospitalization. In the event that
more than the provided spaces are required for documenting CARDIA codes, additional
codes may be documented in the margin of Form 31.
Interviewer questions regarding the coding of a hospitalization should be directed to
the Clinic Coordinator. If questions remain, the Coordinating Center should be contacted
by phone at (205) 934-0786 or fax at (205) 934-0777. When faxing Form 31, any
personally identifying information should be covered/removed. The Coordinating Center
will notify all Field Centers of identified problems or questions about the coding schemes.
6. Requesting Hospitalization Records
After the reasons for reported hospitalizations have been assigned CARDIA codes,
clinic staff will determine which medical records should be requested for further review
by CARDIA investigators. The first step in making this decision is to confirm that the
participant has provided written consent on the Medical Record Release Form. If the
participant has NOT given consent, the medical record will not be requested. If the
participant has given consent, clinic staff may pursue request of the hospitalization
record.

The request for records will be initiated by sending a photocopy of the participant’s
signed Medical Record Release Form, along with a cover letter, to the appropriate
hospital’s (healthcare agency) medical records department. The cover letter should
include request for all admitting medical history and physical exam documentation; daily
lab work; ECG tracings; radiology reports; results of all special procedures performed
(CT scans, ultrasounds, MRI, etc.); face sheet; and discharge summary (see Appendix 5).
A separate request should be made to each hospital or facility in which the participant
has had a procedure performed.
If medical records are not received within two to three weeks of the initial request,
follow-up telephone calls should be made. The original request may have been lost or
misdirected within the hospital; there may be confusion regarding the specific information
requested; and study requests often receive low priority in busy medical records

departments. A telephone call may stimulate a search for the records and will certainly be
a reminder of the request.
Many hospitals have established time-frames for considering a consent signature as
valid. It is important to request the medical records as quickly as possible after the
hospitalization has been reported and the Medical Record Release Form has been signed
by the participant. The Morbidity Electronic Tracking Program was designed to assist in
tracking requests and responses.
7. Processing Medical Records
Once the clinic has received the requested record, it should be reviewed for
completeness by comparing the record with the request letter. A copy of Form 31 should
be placed at the front of the medical record and a copy both should be made.
Coordinating Center staff may NOT have access to any personally identifying
information about a participant. The medical record should be de-identified before
reaching the Coordinating Center. The participant’s name, social security number,
address, date of birth, telephone numbers, medical record number, and any other
personally identifying information must be removed from the record prior to forwarding
to the Coordinating Center. The participant’s twelve digit CARDIA ID, however, must
be recorded on appropriate forms. It is extremely helpful if the participant ID is written
on each page of the medical record.

H. TELEPHONE INTERVIEW FOR PARTICIPANT NOT ATTENDING Y20 EXAM
Historically, the Study has attempted annual contact of CARDIA participants for the
purpose of collecting information about their health status, hospitalizations, visits to
doctors, and health practices, such as smoking. The Annual Follow-Up Questionnaire is
used to collect and report this information. Because collection of this information is
included in the CARDIA exam, the Annual Follow-Up Questionnaire has been omitted
during an exam year in the past. However, for the Y20 Exam, an attempt to contact
individuals who do not participate in the Y20 Exam will be initiated, utilizing a form
similar to the Annual Follow-up Questionnaire, labeled Form 83.
Field Center recruiting staff will make every effort to schedule as many participants
as possible for the Y20 Exam. Completion of the Annual Follow-Up Questionnaire will
be attempted only after the Clinic Coordinator has determined that it is highly unlikely the
participant will be examined. Once this decision is made, effort should be made to
contact the participant to administer the Questionnaire by telephone. If the participant is
not available for a telephone interview, the Questionnaire can be mailed to the participant
for completion.
Question 1: Hospitalizations
If the participant reports no hospitalizations since their last CARDIA contact, proceed
to Q2. If hospitalizations are reported, document these in the same manner as previously
described for Form 31, but without coding the reason for the hospitalization. The follow-
up questionnaire has space for documenting three hospitalizations. If more than three
hospitalizations are reported, use an additional page 1 of the form 83.
Question 2: Coronary Angiogram/Heart Catheterization
If the participant answers no to Q2, proceed to Q3. If procedures are reported,
document the date, name of the procedure and the hospital or clinic where the clinic was
performed. There is space to record up to three procedures, if more are needed, use an
additional page 1 of Form 83.
If the participant has reported hospitalizations or procedures, he/she should be asked
CARDIA Y20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.4 17January07 INT-62

for consent to obtain the records. If consent is given, instruct the participant that a
Medical Record Release form will be mailed to him/her for signature. The interviewer
should review the release form with the participant to confirm that the form is understood
by the participant. Instruct the participant that the form should be read, signed and
returned to the clinic.
Question 3: Doctor Visit
If the participant reports that he/she has been to a doctor, ask Q3a, number of visits.
If the participant cannot recall the exact number of visits, encourage the participant to
provide the number that they believe is accurate.
Question 4: Medical Problems
This question asks about diagnoses that have been assigned during the past year.
Read each item and record the participant’s response in the correct box. Note that Yes
responses for items F – I lead to additional queries to better define this diagnoses.
Question 5: Smoking
This question asks specifically about cigarettes (not cigars or other forms of tobacco).
The average number of cigarettes smoked per day is to be recorded; it the participant
denies smoking, record “00.”
Questions 6 through 9: Medications
These questions ask the participant about medications that he/she may be taking for
specific medical problems. Document the participant’s response to each question.
You will see a box at the bottom of page 3 that indicates for staff use only. There are
two items of information that should be included in this box; 1) whether additional forms
for reporting hospitalizations were used and 2) the interviewer’s ID number.
If the participant is not available for a telephone interview, the follow-up contact
questionnaire may be mailed to the participant for completion. Once the form is returned

A. MORTALITY REPORTING
The CARDIA Study attempts to acquire as much data as possible regarding the death
and cause(s) of death for any CARDIA participant. Death certificates are requested for
all deaths, and depending upon the cause of death, hospital records, autopsy records,
coroner's report, and/or emergency room records are sought.
The CARDIA Steering Committee approved the implementation of a Decision Matrix
for Forms to Be Obtained When a Participant Dies, along with the associated forms
(Forms 33 A - D) for use in obtaining data on deceased CARDIA participants. The
decision matrix indicates which forms should be completed, depending upon the cause of
death. For all deaths, Forms 33A (Initial Notification of Death) and 33B (Final Report of
Death) are required. For cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, renovascular, pulmonary, and
"ambiguous" reasons for death, Form 33C (Interviews with Witness or Next of Kin) and
Form 33D (Physician Interview) should be completed when there is indication to pursue
additional information about the death of a participant If you are unsure about
completion of Forms 33C and/or 33D, consult with your PI.
Full hospital records (see Decision Matrix for contents request) for all participant
deaths occurring in a hospital should be requested EXCEPT for those participants who
died of AIDS, unintentional injury and homicide. Autopsy reports and/or coroner's
reports (as indicated on the death certificates) should be requested for all deceased
participants. Emergency room records are requested when the participant dies in an
emergency room.
It is necessary to obtain written permission from a relative to access the hospital (or
emergency room) records and autopsy/coroner's reports. Always use a permission form
which requests hospital records as well as autopsy records. Obtaining consent may take
considerable time and effort, as some of these deaths may have occurred years earlier than
reported, and it may be difficult to locate the next of kin. However, because this data is
very important to the study, every effort should be made to obtain the information.
Progress in obtaining records/information may be tracked using the electronic tracking
package. Additionally, the CC will forward Mortality Tracking Logs as indicated.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.0 01June05 MORT-1

Death certificates should be requested from the family (when appropriate) or from the
state health department. These documents, along with Form 33B and the necessary
accompanying documents should be forwarded to the CC as soon as possible. Death
certificates will be forwarded to a nosologist, who will assign standardized ICD-9 code
numbers to causes of death (on the death certificates). The CC will batch the death
certificates and forward them to the nosologist for coding.
In summary, when a participant's death is discovered, Form 33A should be

A. CARDIA 20-YEAR FOLLOW-UP SPIROMETRY MANUAL OF PROCEDURES
Prepared by Paul Enright and John Hankinson
1. BACKGROUND
Follow-up surveys of community populations in the United States and Europe have
shown that impaired lung function is an independent predictor of mortality (even after
adjustment for gender, age, race, and smoking). Surprisingly, the mortality excess among
those with impaired ventilation is due to a variety of causes (especially cardiovascular
and cancer) and not to respiratory cause alone. The risk of mortality increases with the
degree of spirometry impairment. Spirometry is the simplest, most effective, and least
expensive test for assessment of pulmonary function. Spirometry is being included in the
CARDIA Y20 exam to determine its value in evaluating the progression of
cardiovascular disease in this group of younger individuals. Spirometry was included in
the CARDIA Y0, Y2, Y5 and Y10 exams, as well as in many other cardiovascular heath
studies funded by the NIH-NHLBI specifically for that reason.
The important spirometry measurements are the forced vital capacity (FVC), which is
greatest volume of air exhaled from a maximal inspiration to a complete exhalation; the
forced expiration volume in one second (FEV ), which is the volume of air exhaled in the
1
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 05July06 PUL-1

first second of the FVC maneuver; and the ratio between these two values: FEV /FVC.
1
Two professional societies publish widely recognized spirometry guidelines: the
American Thoracic Society (ATS) and the European Thoracic Society (ERS), and both
have recently met to produce a combined ATS + ERS spirometry guideline. The
instruments and methods in this manual conform to these guidelines and exceed their
accuracy and repeatability recommendations. The spirometers, software, and quality
assurance program are the same as those, which will be used by the 4th National Health
and Nutrition Examination (NHANES 4).
2. THE TESTING ENVIRONMENT
The testing room must be quiet and private, without distractions. No other tests will
be conducted in the room during spirometry testing.
The ambient temperature in the testing room must be maintained between 17 and
40ºC (63-104ºF). The humidity is maintained at a level consistent with patient comfort.

4. FEATURES OF THE SPIROMETRY SYSTEM
a. Accuracy: The volume accuracy of this system is within 1.5 percent (better than
the ATS-ERS accuracy recommendation of 3%).
b. Return Spring: The spirometry system is designed to use the spring (negator)
which is standard on most dry rolling seal spirometers. The advantages of using
the return spring are:
i. The spirometer piston is returned to the zero position at the end of each
maneuver, reducing the time required to test a participant.
ii. Any leak in the spirometer or between the participant and his/her mouthpiece
is easily detected because of the obvious loss in volume as a result of the
positive pressure (0.4 cmH O) generated by the return spring.
2
iii. There is a clear indication when the participant comes off the mouthpiece,
avoiding the slight increase in volume which can occur in some dry rolling
seal spirometers when not used with return spring (due to seal “memory”).
iv. The spirometer is always stored with minimal volume in the spirometer,
which eliminates the development of a seal memory within the measuring
volume.

6. LEAK AND CALIBRATION CHECKS
Volume calibration checks are performed using a standard three-liter calibrating
syringe. Leak and calibration checks are performed before each testing session, at least
every 4 hours, and whenever the snout plate is reattached.
a. Double click OMI-HMF windows icon.
b. Enter user’s initials
c. Select “Calibration” main heading.
d. Select Leak Test from pull-down
“Calibration” menu.
e. A leak test is performed by checking that
the negator (return spring) is engaged and then adding 3 liters of air into the
spirometer with a calibrating syringe.
f. Click on “Start Timing”. The computer will then monitor the spirometer volume
for 60 seconds and determine if the volume is maintained. A progress bar shows
the time left until completion of the leak test.
g. The result of the leak test are written to a calibration/leak test log file, including
the date and time of the test, by clicking on the “Save” button. A warning is
displayed if a leak larger than the 20ml is observed. If the leak is larger than 20
ml, check the spirometer for the following and then re-run the leak test:
1) the face plate is secure (all hand tightened nuts are tight) and that the O-ring
is properly in place.
2) check the hose for small holes or tears; these occur most commonly where
the ridges meet the smooth ends.
If the spirometer still fails the leak test, call Dr. Jensen (LDS) and contact OMI
for other on site trouble shooting.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 05July06 PUL-6

h. Select “Perform Cal/Leak Check” button on the main screen or in the
“Calibration” menu.
i. Check that the “Current Volume” is zero.
j. Fill the calibrating syringe and connect it securely to the spirometer hose.
k. Click on “OK” or type any key, inject the full 3-liters from the syringe into the
spirometer, and then pull back on the syringe. (NOTE: When injecting air from
the syringe, do not “Slam” the syringe at the end of the injection by pushing the
air out too vigorously as this may cause erroneous calibrations.)
l. The computer determines the volume injected. The user then verifies the
calibrating syringe’s volume and the computer compares this volume with the
volume measured by the spirometer. The computer displays the difference
between the syringe and spirometer-determined volume in both absolute volume
and as a % Error. As with the leak test results, the calibration test results are
written to the calibration database file as “Save” is clicked.
m. Detach the calibration syringe and store it near the spirometer.
n. Print Calibration: This option, under “Calibration” menu, will print the
calibration results to the printer using all dates or a selected date range. This
report includes leak and volume calibration check.
o. View Calibrations: The “View Calibrations” menu item allows the user to view
all previous calibration results.
NOTE: The calibration and leak tests are the same if the syringe remains connected and
stays connected to the spirometer for 1 minute.

8. TEST PROTOCOL
The accuracy of the spirometry examination depends on the effort exerted by the
participant and the conscientiousness of the user. Consequently, it is crucial that the
examination protocol be observed consistently. The participant must be carefully
prepared and “coached”. Insufficient effort on the part of the participant will cause the
results to be inadequate for analysis.

(Form 80) upon beginning the spirometry procedure.

stroke in last month), DO NOT PROCEED with spirometry. Instead,
complete Question 6 (reason spirometry was not completed) of the
Spirometry Completion Form. Check “No” and proceed to the box
listing reasons that PFT not completed.

b. Examination
i. Press “Proceed with testing”

will prompt “Start Test?” When ready, the user clicks “OK.”

take a deep breath, place the mouthpiece in his/her mouth, and BLAST the
air out!
iv. Continue to coach the participant to exhale until the “Plateau Achieved”
message is displayed and 6 seconds of exhalation has occurred. The
participant is then instructed to come off the mouthpiece.

viii. A result screen is then displayed on a table that lists: Trial Number, FVC,
FEV1, and PEF. After the second and successive trials differences from the
largest observed values (expressed in milliliters and as a percentage), and a
6-item acceptability code are displayed. All of the flow-volume and
volume-time curves are also displayed (superimposed on top of each other.
The last maneuver is highlighted in dark blue and the best curve is lime
green. All of the remaining curves are black. Any deleted or unusable
curves (cough or large extrapolated volume) are red. The quality assessment
information should be used to judge whether a curve should be accepted or
rejected. Curves previously obtained during the current session may also be
reassessed based on better curves being achieved after them. Clicking on
the quality code box, a pop-up window is displayed allowing the user to
over-ride any acceptability code or delete the curve (Delete, nonspecific
error, omit from future processing, extra breath at end of maneuver, cough).
This same pop-up window also provides a legend of acceptability codes.
The reproducibility criteria are applied and a messages as to whether the test
is reproducible is displayed.
Criteria for an acceptable spirogram; No hesitation or false starts; the
volume of back extrapolation (Vext) less than 5% of the FVC or 0.15 L,
whichever is the greater. No coughing during the first second; no glottic
closure, no mouthpiece obstruction by the tongue or dentures, no leaks
should be present. There should be a plateau in the volume-time spirogram;
and the breath should last at least 6 seconds.
Criteria for a reproducible spirogram; after three acceptable maneuvers,
the two highest values for FVC and FEV1 taken from acceptable forced
expiratory maneuvers must show minimal variability. The two largest FVC
values should agree within 150 ml, and the two largest FEV1 values should
also agree within 150 ml. Testing should continue until three acceptable
tests (all green in the code box) and reproducibility criteria are met

9. QUALITY CONTROL
Machine quality assurance is maintained by cleaning, calibration, leak correction
(summarize from previous section.) Technician (user) quality assurance is maintained by
training and certification, plus periodic feedback on quality of tests performed.
Upon completion and review of each batch of incoming data, users will be notified
quickly of any errors with calibration and procedures. Each month, statistics will be
compiled for each user summarizing the quality of the tests done. Five percent (5%) of
spirograms will be re-read at the PF Reading Center to assess the within and between
readers variability.
In addition to the quality control summary report, a calibration summary report is
also generated for each study. The quality controls reports will be provided to each Field
Center for review by the PI, the Clinic Coordinator, and shared with each technician for
review. Depending on the results, the users will receive additional training as necessary.
Several improvements in the software, in particular, error warnings with override
requirements, have been made to the original versions of the spirometry system software.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 05July06 PUL-18

Therefore, fewer errors should be observed in future studies due to software
improvements and increased user experience.
10. TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION
a. Training: Technicians from each Field Center will be trained centrally for
pulmonary function (PF) testing. Each technician will complete a course in
spirometric testing.
b. Certification: The examination includes 50 multiple choice questions (50 points),
calculation of spirometry results from a spirogram (25 points), and a practical
demonstration of skills including leak and calibration checks, cleaning, and
testing of a naive subject (25 points). A passing score of at least 75 points is
necessary for certification. Only certified technicians will perform pulmonary
function testing in this study.
PF technicians should test at least one person (participant, another technician or
staff member) per week between the training session and the start of the
examination of CARDIA participants. To retain certification, technicians must
test at least four participants each month during the recruitment period.
Certification of new technicians after the initial central training sessions may be
performed by a centrally trained, certified PF technician. The written exam will
be administered locally, and the first 10 PF test performed will be observed by a
certified PF technician and then examined by the PF Center and found to be
satisfactory before the new technician is certified.
c. Site Visits: The results of the first 50 spirometry test sessions performed by each
technician will be closely examined by the QC Supervisor. Copies of
suboptimal quality test sessions with comments for improvements will be mailed
to the Clinic Coordinator and the technician the same day as they are evaluated.
A site visit to each of the four clinical centers may be made during the first three
months of recruitment. Complete calibration, leak, and complete PF testing of at
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 05July06 PUL-19

least three participants by each PF certified technician will be observed. Copies
of suboptimal quality test sessions will be reviewed. More efficient methods as
well as protocol violations will be discussed during the site visits and later in a
written report.
d. The Need for Spirometry QC: Examination of spirograms from the Framingham
study revealed that more than 18% were of clearly unacceptable quality. Two
more recent studies, with over 12,000 adults each, found that 40-50% of the
spirometry maneuvers were of unacceptable quality. Manual measurements
from spirograms are tedious and prone to error and deviations in test
performances and lack of regular leak checking and calibration can result in loss
of study data (16-18).
The Epidemiology Standardization Project, the American Thoracic Society
spirometry standards, and recent evaluations of commercially available
spirometers emphasize the importance of spirometry quality control
procedures. Factors which affect spirometry quality include:
i. Participant
ii. Maneuvers
iii. Technician
iv. Equipment
v. Analysis
e. Implementation of QC Procedures: There are five separate levels of quality
control implemented for spirometry testing which address the five factors known
to influence the results:
i. Daily spirometer leak and calibration checks using a 3.00 liter syringe as the
“gold standard” check maneuver immediately after it is performed.
ii. Eight computerized checks of FVC maneuver acceptability and
reproducibility check every maneuver immediately after it is performed.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 05July06 PUL-20

iii. The PF technician is trained to recognize the patterns of acceptable
maneuvers, watching the participant during the performance, and reviewing
the colorfully displayed flow-volume curves on the computer monitor.
iv. The results of the leak and calibration checks and the best 3 FVC maneuvers
are stored and sent to the PF Reading Center for review by the PF QC
Supervisor. Monthly reports are compiled for each technician’s performance.
v. Results from all of the above are taken into account during the analysis of the
data by the PF reading Center. The calibration factors, PF tech’s impression
of the participant and the maneuver quality, and the QC supervisor’s
impression of test session quality are all integrated to obtain the final FEV1
and FVC results reported to the Data Coordinating Center.
11. SAFETY PROCEDURES
a. All equipment will be plugged into a grounded electrical outlet.
b. To minimize cross-contamination:
i. Each participant will have a disposable, filtered mouthpiece.
ii. The participant’s mouth will always be higher than the spirometer snout.
iii. Participants will be instructed to remove their mouth from the hose when
inhaling to avoid inhalation of potentially infectious agent.
iv. The spirometer and accessories will be cleaned and disinfected at regular
intervals, but no less than weekly.
a. Tubing will be cleaned and disinfected daily
b. Seal will be inspected and cleaned at the same time.
In rare cases, a participant may hyperventilate and feel dizzy during the examination.
Ammonia capsules are available in the event of a participant becoming faint. A
participant who feels faint should be assisted to a chair and positioned with head down
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 05July06 PUL-21

towards knees and encouraged to breathe slowly and deeply until recovered. A physician
should be summoned whenever a participant fails to recover normal breathing, faints or
reports feeling ill.
