15. DEFINITIONS AND SYMBOLS
ATPS is the condition of air inside the spirometer - Ambient Temperature and
Pressure, and Saturated with water vapor. The ambient temperature of the spirometer is
usually lower than body temperature; this has the effect of cooling and contracting the
volume of air exhaled into the spirometer.
ATS is short for American Thoracic Society, the scientific branch of the American
Lung Association - the Easter Seal folks. The ATS promotes accurate spirometers by
recommending spirometry standards.
BACK EXTRAPOLATION is the standard method used to determine "time zero"
when measuring the FEV1. The amount of slowly exhaled volume at the start of the
maneuver excluded from the FEV1 by this technique is called the back extrapolated
volume (BEV or EV). The BEV should be less than 5% of the vital capacity, otherwise
the maneuver is considered to have started too slowly.
BTPS stands for Body Temperature (usually 37 degC) and Pressure, and Saturated
with water vapor (100% humidity), which is the condition of air inside the lungs before it
is exhaled into a spirometer. ATS standards require that volumes and flows be reported
as if they were under these conditions.
CALIBRATION SYRINGE is a large metal cylinder with a rubber sealed piston used
to check the volume accuracy of spirometers. The ATS recommends that it be 3.00 liters
in size.
COPD stands for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, a general term for lung
disease caused by cigarette smoking - a mixture of emphysema, bronchitis, and hyper-
reactive airways.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 05July06 PUL-30

DIAPHRAGM is the large, dome-shaped muscle between the lungs and the
abdomen. Its strength is measured by the MIP test.
EV (see Back Extrapolation)
FET is short for Forced Exhalation Time. The FET should be at least six seconds,
while attempting to obtain a ten exhalation, for the FVC maneuver to be considered
acceptable, otherwise the FVC may be underestimated. Unfortunately, the FET cannot be
seen on a flow-volume curve, and must be displayed separately.
FEV1 is the most important spirometry variable, short for Forced Expiratory Volume
in one second. It is convenient to think of it as the average flow rate during the first
second of the FVC maneuver. It is reduced with airflow obstruction.
FEV1/FVC RATIO is the most sensitive and specific index of airways obstruction
measured by a spirometer. It is normally above 70%.
FLOW-VOLUME CURVE is the graph obtained from a forced exhalation maneuver
plotted with flow on the vertical axis and volume on the horizontal axis. When compared
with the traditional spirogram, it has the advantage of allowing easy recognition of
unacceptable or poorly reproducible maneuvers and disease patterns.
FVC is the Forced Vital Capacity, the volume of air exhaled during the maneuver
named after it. The subject takes as deep a breath as possible and then quickly exhales as
much air as possible. The FVC is reduced with restrictive disorders.
MEP stands for Maximal Expiratory Pressure, a measure of the strength of the
expiratory muscles.
MIP is Maximal Inspiratory Pressure, a measure of the strength of the diaphragm, the
primary muscle of breathing.
MRP is Maximal Respiratory Pressures, including both inspiratory and expiratory
pressures.
NHLBI is the government agency paying your salary this year.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.3 05July06 PUL-31

OBSTRUCTION is a decrease in maximal airflow rates caused by airway narrowing.
The FEV1/FVC ratio and the FEV1 are both decreased.
PEFR stands for Peak Expiratory Flow Rate, the highest flow measured during the
FVC maneuver. It is a good index of effort used at the onset of the maneuver. It can be
seen on a flow-volume curve but not on a spirogram.
PF is short for Pulmonary Function (lung tests).
PRED is short for the predicted value of a PF parameter. It is determined from the
regression equation from a large population study of supposedly normal people.
RESTRICTION is a decrease in lung volumes. Scarring of lung tissue (fibrosis),
heart failure, pneumonia, and simple obesity are some of many causes. The FVC is
reduced while the FEV1/FVC ratio is normal or increased.
VOLUME-TIME TRACING is the graph produced by a water-sealed spirometer. It
is traced by a pen connected to the spirometer bell with volume on the vertical axis.

A. REFERRAL CRITERIA
Below are listed the criteria for referral by exam component and the recommended
action. These criteria are summarized in Table 1.
1. Blood Pressure
Blood pressure referral levels will correspond to the recommendations given in the
Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee on Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment
of High Blood Pressure. The average of the second and third resting blood pressure
readings will be used. Recommended follow-up is according to Joint National Committee
6 guidelines. Referral will be made for hypertension (systolic ≥140 or diastolic≥ 90)
based on the highest recorded blood pressure, regardless of whether participant is already
being treated.

Note: If recommendations for follow-up of DBP and SBP are different, the shorter
recommended time period supersedes, and a referral supersedes a recheck
recommendation.
All CARDIA Field Centers should offer blood pressure rechecks. Each Principal
Investigator can decide whether to provide follow-up of diastolic blood pressures of 85 to
89 and systolic blood pressures of 130 to 140 at the CARDIA Field Center.
2. Body Size Measurements
No standardized referrals.
3. Lipids
Participants will be referred for the triglycerides values >500 mg/dl. Based on the
summary of the Third Report of the National Cholesterol Education Program (NCEP), an
HDL-cholesterol level <40 mg/dl will be noted as a risk factor, but not as a referral. A
participant with an LDL level > 160 mg/dl will be referred.
High triglycerides or LDL conditions should result in the Field Center generating a
standard referral letter using preprogrammed options in the data entry system. The
referral letter will give the value of the test result and recommend the appropriate action
to be taken by the participant. Ideally, the letter should contain values from previous
exams.
4. Blood Chemistries
Glucose: Participants with a fasting glucose level >126 mg/dl or <60 mg/dl
will be referred to a physician for re-measurement. Participants
with a 2-hour glucose level ≥200 will be referred.
Insulin: No standardized referrals.
Any referral levels noted above should result in the Field Center generating a
standard referral letter with the value of the test result and recommended action.
5. Inflammatory Markers
No standardized referrals.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 13December06 REF-2

6. Urine Assays
Albuminuria: Participants will be referred for albumin excretion of >300 mg/g
[estimated from (albumin mg/dl)/(creatinine mg/dl.) This measure can vary from day-to-
day, so participants will be urged to have a repeat evaluation.
GFR: <60
7. Computed Topography (CT) Scans
No standardized referrals. Participants who had an abnormal finding at Y15 not
related to coronary calcium (“noncoronary pathology”) are the only participants for
whom CT scans will be reviewed for noncoronary pathology. Because of the range of
findings, possible referral will need to be individualized for these participants.
8. Carotid Ultrasound
Participants with a Doppler flow velocity value greater than or equal to 250 cm/sec
will receive immediate alert referrals. This indicates at 75% or greater stenosis of the
carotid artery. Participants with a Doppler flow velocity value greater than or equal to
150 cm/sec but less than 250 cm/sec will receive routine referrals.
9. Pulmonary Function
Participants with pulmonary function scores <70% of expected values based on their
ethnicity, height, age and gender will be referred for follow-up and notified that their
function is less than normal.
10. Diet
No standardized referrals.
11. Best Clinical Judgment
Any condition or finding which, in the judgment of the clinic physician, needs
referral will be referred.

B. DISTRIBUTION OF RESULTS
Letter of Participant’s Results
Because of new federal privacy laws, Field Centers will not routinely mail results to
participants’ physicians. Participants may request extra copies of their results for
distribution to physicians as they wish. In special circumstances, a participant may
specifically request that the Field Center mail results to a physician(s). In that case, the
participant should sign a release of medical information form that is complaint with the
Field Center’s institutional guidelines and the federal HIPAA regulations.
Participants will be provided with the clinical results of their CARDIA examination
on component specific forms, as follows:
a. The In-Clinic Results forms, provided on the day of the CARDIA exam, include:
i. current blood pressure – any referral information will be included
ii. anthropometric measurements; Body Mass Index (BMI) should be looked up
on the table in Appendix 4 of the Anthropometry section of the Manual of
Operation.
b. Other results letters: mailed to the participant when results are available (there
may be separate mailings due to the time lapse of the exam and receipt of various
results); results forms include the participant’s values with reference to
categorical interpretations. Tests which generate results letters include:
i. lipids (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides)
ii. serum chemistries: fasting glucose, 2-hour glucose and Glomular Filtration
Rate (GFR)
iii. albumin/creatinine ratio
v. CT scan for coronary findings (other incidental findings only for those with
positive findings at Y15 and Birmingham participants)
vi. Carotid Ultrasound - Left and Right Doppler values
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 13December06 REF-4

vii. Pulmonary function (% of expected based on gender, age and ethnicity)
viii. Diet results – percent of calories from fat, saturated fat, carbohydrate,
protein, cholesterol/1000 calories; fiber/1000 calories and calcium
An example of the participant’s results forms can be found in Appendices 1-10 of this
section.
Each clinic should edit and revise its own cover letters. All cover letters should
include information about referrals for blood pressure, lipids, glucose, albuminuria, GFR,
pulmonary function, and carotid ultrasound, even if the status is normal. To evaluate the
urgency of any referrals, the participant's past values will also be reviewed. A condition
identified for the first time during the Y20 exam will be emphasized more strongly than
one which has been observed during previous CARDIA exams. Past exam results, related
current medical history, and all Y20 results for all participants are provided on the
CARDIA internal webpage. This information is available to all Field Center Principal
Investigators.

APPENDIX 4. AMENDMENT TO SPECIMEN PROCESSING PROTOCOL FOR PLASMA CITRATED
SAMPLES IN FUTURE CARDIA EXAMS........................................................71

A. OVERVIEW
The blood drawing station is designed to provide a safe and comfortable environment
for obtaining blood samples to test for important risk factors of cardiovascular disease
and other parameters of interest to the CARDIA Study. Because obtaining blood samples
may cause increased anxiety in some individuals, and because breaking the skin is known
to increase the risk of infection, the blood drawing station should be considered an area of
potential risk. However, if collection procedures are carefully planned and implemented,
the risk of anxiety and injury to the participant can be minimized. Obtaining the required
blood sample will take approximately 10 –15 minutes. This chapter of the Manual of
Operations documents the Study’s approach and serves as a training manual for the
phlebotomists at the Field Centers.
1. Tests
a. The following laboratory tests are planned for all participants during the
CARDIA Year 20 Exam:
i. Serum glucose, insulin and serum creatinine (fasting);
ii. Plasma lipid profile (total and HDL Cholesterol, triglycerides);
iii. Plasma CRP, IL-6, fibrinogen;
iv. Urinary albumin and creatinine.
v. Consenting participants will have a two hour oral glucose tolerance test
(OGTT) performed.
b. The following laboratory tests are planned for the YALTA Study:
i. Serum PLA2;
ii Serum SOD;
iii. Serum GGT;
iv. Serum s-ICAM;
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-1

e. No particular restriction need be made for smoking since the blood drawing
station will be approximately one half hour after clinic arrival.
f. Blood drawing should occur early in the CARDIA visit, but must follow the
blood pressure measurement and precede the snack.
3. General preparation for Core Exam and YALTA Study
The blood drawing should take place in an isolated room or one enclosed by dividers.
The temperature in the room should be 65 o-75o F and there should be no direct sunlight.
If a reclining chair is used, the chair should be placed in a space sufficient to allow the
chair to fully recline. The chair may be elevated on a wooden box to facilitate comfort of
the phlebotomist when drawing the blood.
The room should be equipped with all the necessary supplies. A table or counter
should be prepared with the materials and vials needed for blood handling and aliquoting.
The centrifuge, refrigerator and freezer should be nearby and ready for use.
The Daily Temperature Record must be completed each day the clinic is in operation.
Freezer, refrigerator and room temperatures are to be recorded. The acceptable
temperatures are: freezer: -75o to -65oC; refrigerator: 35o to 40oF; room: 65o to 75oF.
The phlebotomy station will be staffed by a technician with documented class time
and experience in phlebotomy. Certification will occur at the centralized training session.
Recertification will occur once as requested by the Coordinating Center, and will be
authorized by the clinic supervisor or medical director. The technician should be properly
attired in a laboratory coat. Long hair should be tied back. Gloves must be used at all
times while handling blood specimens.
4. Blood volume to be obtained
a. CARDIA Exam
i. All participants will have 52 mls of blood drawn for the core exam, using the
following vacutainers:
(cid:131) Two 10-ml lavender top (EDTA) vacutainers;
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-3

(cid:131) One 12.5-ml red top (SST) vacutainer;
(cid:131) One 5-ml red top serum vacutainer;
(cid:131) Two 4.5-ml blue top (citrated) vacutainers;
(cid:131) One 5-ml anti-protease (SCAT 1) tube.
ii. The quality control (QC) participant selected will have an additional 14.5 mls
of blood drawn, as indicated below, using the following vacutainers:
(cid:131) One 5-ml lavender top (EDTA) vacutainer tube (lipids);
(cid:131) One 5-ml red top (SST) vacutainer tube (insulin, glucose, and
creatinine);
(cid:131) One 4.5-ml blue top (citrated) vacutainer tube (C-reactive protein,
IL-6, and fibrinogen).
b. YALTA Study
i. All participants consenting to participate in the YALTA Study will have 18
mls of blood drawn in addition to the 52 mls for the core exam, using the
following vacutainers:
• One 10-ml lavender top (EDTA) vacutainer;
• One 5-ml red top vacutainer;
• Two 3 ml syringes (1.75 and 1.25 ml) of whole blood
ii. The QC participant selected will have an additional 18 mls of blood drawn,
as indicated above.
Due to the volume of blood to be drawn for the core exam and the YALTA Study,
QC participants selected for core QC will be excluded from selection as the YALTA QC
participant and vice-versa.

C. BLOOD DRAWING PROCEDURES
1. The following steps outline the procedures for blood drawing:
a. Wash hands at the beginning of the work day, between participants, and as
needed during and after processing specimens.
b. Prepare vacutainers (collection tubes) by affixing the Participant ID (PID) label
to each tube. Remove the appropriate label from the prepared sheet of labels and
affix vertically to the tube. Labels must be placed vertically to facilitate bar-
coder accuracy. Place a bar-coded label on the DNA blood spot card.
c. Greet the participant. Confirm that you have the correct PID labels. Locate Form
5—Phlebotomy in the participant's form set, and check that it has a bar-coded
PID printed on the form and that the boxes indicating the blood collection
procedures for which the participant has consented is/are checked. Write the
participant’s name in the lower left corner of the DNA blood spot card AND affix
a PID label.
d. Explain the procedure to the participant. An example might be: "I am going to
collect blood from a vein in your arm. The purpose of this is to check the blood
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-7

levels of specific substances such as cholesterol or glucose. I will collect the
specimen in six small tubes for the CARDIA Study and four small tubes for the
YALTA Study. Do you have any questions?"
NOTE: The number of tubes and the total amount of blood drawn will vary
depending on whether the participant is selected for QC. This script should be
adjusted accordingly.
e. If the participant asks when he/she will receive the results of this test, direct the
participant to ask the Clinic Coordinator during the exit interview.
f. Request that the participant remove his/her jacket or sweater and instruct the
participant to sit upright in the chair with the sleeves
rolled up to expose the antecubital fossa (inner side of
the elbow). The chair should be completely upright.
Only when the participant has indicated that he/she has
a history of fainting, should the technician have the participant sit in the reclining
chair. In this event, the chair should be placed in the reclining position for the
procedure. The technician may recline the chair by: (1) pulling the lever
forward; (2) pulling up and forward on the arm rest; or (3) gently pushing the
chair back. This reclining position is an exception to the protocol and should
only be used in the specific circumstances described. Its use is left to the
discretion of the phlebotomist. It may be helpful to reassure an apprehensive
participant that he/she may recline following the blood drawing. The chair
position should not be changed from sitting to reclining during the blood
drawing. Attempt to collect as much blood as possible with the participant in the
upright position.
g. Use of evacuated tubes (vacutainers):
i. Before applying the tourniquet, screw the Luer adapter into the plastic
vacutainer tube guide. Insert the butterfly tubing onto the adapter.
ii. Insert the first blood collection tube (10-ml lavender top) into the holder. Do
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-8

not push the tube beyond the guideline, as premature loss of vacuum may
result. The tube will retract slightly. Leave it in this position.
iii. If a tube has been previously or unsuccessfully used, it should be
immediately discarded into an appropriate biohazard sharps container.
iv. Inspect the bevel (tip) of the needle visually to ensure that it is free of hooks
or barbs at the end of the point, and that the
opening is clear of any small particles that
might obstruct the flow of blood. The needle
must be sterile. Do not use a needle from a
package which is open or appears
contaminated. A 21-gauge collection set should be used, unless the
individual has small vessels that can be accessed using a smaller gauge.
h. Wearing gloves palpate and trace the path of veins several times with the index
finger. Unlike veins, arteries pulse, are more elastic,
and have a thick wall. Thrombosed veins lack
resilience, feel cord-like, and roll easily. If
superficial veins are not readily apparent, instruct
the participant to close the fist or lower the
extremity over the arm of the chair to allow the veins to fill.
i. Identify the best available vein.
j. A tourniquet is used to increase venous filling and causes the veins to be more
prominent and easier to enter. PRECAUTIONS WHEN USING A
TOURNIQUET: The tourniquet should be on the arm for the shortest time
possible. Never leave the tourniquet on for longer than two (2) minutes. To do
so may result in hemoconcentration and a variation in blood test values. If a
tourniquet must be applied for the preliminary vein selection, it should be
released and reapplied after a wait of two minutes. If the patient has a skin
problem, place the tourniquet over the participant's shirt or use a piece of gauze
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-9

or paper tissue to avoid direct contact with the skin.
i. Wrap the tourniquet around the arm 3 to 4 in. (7.5 to 10.0 cm) above the
venipuncture site.
ii. Tuck the end under the last round.
iii. If a Velcro tourniquet is used, adhere the tabs to each other.
k. Cleanse the venipuncture site:
i. Remove the alcohol prep from its sterile package.
ii. Cleanse the vein site with a circular motion from the
Field Center to the periphery.
iii. Allow the area to dry to prevent possible hemolysis of the specimen and a
burning sensation to the patient when the venipuncture is performed.
iv. If the phlebotomist needs to palpate the vein again, the site should be
cleansed again with an alcohol prep sponge.
l. Perform the venipuncture:
i. Grasp the participant's arm firmly, using your thumb
to draw the skin taut. This anchors the vein. The
thumb should be 1 or 2 in. (2.5 or 5.0 cm) below the
venipuncture site.
ii. With the needle bevel upward, enter the vein in a
smooth continuous motion.
iii. Make sure the participant's arm is in a flat or downward position while
maintaining the tube below the site when the needle enters the vein. It may
be helpful to place a rolled towel under the elbow for support or have the
participant make a fist with the opposite hand and place it under the elbow.
iv. Grasp the flange of the needle holder and push the tube forward until the butt
end of the needle punctures the stopper, exposing the full lumen of the
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-10

needle.
v. Remove the tourniquet within the two minute limit. Once the collection has
started, do not change the position of the tube until
it is withdrawn from the needle. During the
procedure, avoid allowing the contents of the tube
to come into contact with the vacutainer top
(stopper).
vi. Maintain constant, slight forward pressure (in the direction of the needle) on
the end of the tube. This prevents release of the shut-off valve which may
stop the flow of blood. Do not vary pressure nor reintroduce pressure after
completion of the draw.
vii. Fill the vacutainer tube as completely as possible, i.e., until the vacuum is
exhausted and blood flow ceases. A partially filled lavender top tube should
be avoided if possible, because the higher resulting final concentration of
anticoagulant will affect lipid values.
viii. When the blood flow ceases, remove the tube from the holder. The shut-off
valve recovers the point, stopping blood flow until the next tube is inserted
(if necessary). Gently invert each tube as it is removed from the collection
tube holder.
ix. Once the blood collection is complete, immediately
and thoroughly mix the contents of all tubes by gently
inverting eight (8) times. To prevent hemolysis, do
not shake tubes. Place the tube in a collection rack.
x. To obtain additional core specimens, insert next tube (12.5ml red top
vacutainer, the first 4.5 ml blue top vacutainer, the
second 10-ml purple top vacutainer, the second 4.5 ml
blue top vacutainer, and the 5-ml anti-protease
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-11

[SCAT 1] tube) using the procedure described in Section C v-viii.
NOTE: For the SCAT 1 tube, attention should be paid to minimizing turbulence
whenever possible. Small steps, such as slanting the needle in the tube to
have the blood run down the side of the tube instead of shooting all the way
to the bottom, may result in significant improvement.
m. YALTA specimens should be collected immediately following completion of the
core blood draw. Begin by inserting the 10-ml lavender
vacutainer followed by the 5-ml red-top vacutainer into
holder and repeat procedure from Section C v-viii.
Remove the red-top vacutainer and attach a 3 ml syringe.
Collect 1.75 ml of blood; slide the lock on the collection set close the tubing;
remove the syringe and attach the 3 ml heparinized syringe. Slide the lock on the
collection set to open the line and collect an additional
1.25 ml of blood into the heparinized syringe.
NOTE: see specific instructions below for processing
whole blood collected in syringes.
n. If difficulty is encountered during sample collection, you may:
i. Change the position of the needle. If it has penetrated too far into the vein,
pull it back a bit. If it has not penetrated far enough, advance it farther into
the vein. Rotate the needle half a turn.
ii. Change to a different tube; the tube in use may not have had sufficient
vacuum.
iii. Loosen the tourniquet; it may have been applied too tightly, and obstructed
the blood flow. Reapply the tourniquet loosely. If the tourniquet is a Velcro
type, quickly release and press back together. Be sure however, that the
tourniquet remains on for no longer than two minutes at a time.
iv. If the specimen cannot be collected, selection of another site for the
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-12

venipuncture is required. Probing is not recommended as this may be painful
to the participant.
v. A syringe and needle may be used instead of a vacutainer, particularly in
women whose veins are often smaller. Use a syringe and needle only as
specifically indicated for collecting a specimen or as a last resort for
collection.
vi. Do not attempt a venipuncture more than twice. Ask the participant if he/she
would be willing to have your supervisor attempt to draw the specimen.
vii. If no staff member is able to obtain a blood sample or if a participant refuses
to have blood drawn, indicate this on the form (Q4).
o. Ask participant to open his/her hand after the blood has been collected.
p. To remove the needle, lightly place clean gauze over
the venipuncture site. Remove the needle quickly and
immediately. Apply pressure to the site with a pad.
Appropriately discard the needle into the used-needle
box. Instruct the participant to hold the pad firmly over the site for one to two
minutes to prevent development of a hematoma.
q. Bandage the arm.
i. Under normal conditions: Slip the gauze pad down over the site, continuing
mild pressure. Apply an adhesive or gauze bandage over the venipuncture
site after assuring that blood flow has stopped.
ii. If the patient continues to bleed: Apply pressure to the site with a gauze pad.
Keep the arm elevated until the bleeding stops. Wrap a gauze bandage tightly
around the arm, over the pad. An ice pack may be placed over the pad for a
short time to stop the bleeding.
iii. If bleeding persists longer than five minutes, the supervisor should be alerted.
Continue pressure on the site as long as necessary to stop the bleeding.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-13

iv. Instruct the patient to leave the bandage on for at least 15 minutes.
v. If the participant is participating in the OGTT, follow the instructions for
OGTT (Item 5, below). If the participant has declined to participate in the
OGTT, indicate this on Form 5, Q13.
2. Managing a participant who becomes faint following the blood collection:
a. Have the person remain in the recliner, recline the chair if necessary or have the
participant sit with their head between their knees.
b. Crush an ampule of spirits of ammonia (or ammonia swab), and wave it beneath
the participant's nose for a few seconds, taking care not to allow the ammonia to
come into contact with the skin.
c. Provide a leak-proof biohazard bag if he/she feels nauseous.
d. Instruct the participant to remain reclined until color returns and the participant
reports feeling better.
e. Place a cold wet cloth on the back of the neck.
f. If the participant continues to feel faint or sick, take a blood pressure and pulse
reading. Contact a medical staff member who will advise you on further action.
3. Managing participants who are extremely apprehensive about having blood
drawn:
Do not, under any circumstance, coerce or force the participant to have blood drawn.
It is sometimes best to let the participant continue with another part of the visit, and ask
them to return when the phlebotomist is available to spend more time with the person.
(NOTE: the participant should not be given a snack until a final decision regarding the
blood draw has been reached.) It may also help to allow the participant to recline in the
blood drawing chair while the phlebotomist assesses the veins in the participant's arms,
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-14

without actually attempting to collect blood. If the participant refuses to have any blood
drawn, Form 5 should be completed as follows:
a. Record the exam date on page 1 and the phlebotomist ID on page 5;
b. Leave the first three questions blank; and
c. Record No for Q4—Was any blood drawn? and record Refused for the reason.
4. Caution in handling blood samples:
Improper handling of blood collection tubes and needles is extremely dangerous. All
blood samples should be handled using universal precautions, treating the specimens as if
the participant has a blood-borne transmissible disease. The following procedures should
be implemented:
a. ALL needles must be disposed of in proper biohazard
disposal containers.
b. Avoid contact with plasma, gloves should always be
worn.
c. If the phlebotomist accidentally sustains a contaminated needle stick, the wound
should be immediately and thoroughly cleansed with
soap and water. The medical director should be notified
immediately.
d. All used vacutainer tubes are to be placed in a biohazard
box. Blood products are to be placed in biohazard containers or bags for
disposal.
5. Instructions for Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)
a. Instructions to Clinic Coordinators
Participants from all Field Centers will be recruited for the OGTT. The OGTT
will provide information about whether the participant is diabetic or has impaired
glucose tolerance. Each participant will be informed about the OGTT prior to
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-15

signing the informed consent form. Only those participants who have consented
to the test and whose appointment is earlier than 10:00 AM will be offered the
opportunity to participate in this test. Participants wishing to participate in
OGTT whose appointment is after 10:00 AM may elect to return to clinic at a
later date to have a delayed OGTT.
i. If the participant has been recruited to participate in the OGTT, explain that
the test requires a fasting blood collection and one additional blood collection
that will take place two hours after the participant has consumed a glucose
solution.
ii. If the participate has agreed to participate in the OGTT, indicate this on the
scheduling sheet.
iii. If the participant checks into the clinic after 10:00 AM, instruct the
participant that, because of the varying levels of glucose throughout the day,
he/she will have only the fasting glucose measured, but will have the
opportunity to return on a future date to participate in the OGTT.
iv. The pulmonary function test (PFT) is to be conducted after the second blood
collection (OGTT blood draw). Participants ineligible for OGTT should
perform PFT after the initial blood collection (fasting blood draw).
v. Confirm that the participant knows to return to the phlebotomy station ten
minutes prior the assigned time for the second blood collection.
b. Instructions to the Phlebotomist for the OGTT
i. Indicate whether the participant agreed to participate in the OGTT (Q11).
ii. Determine whether the first blood draw occurred before 10:30 AM by
referring to Q6, page 1 of Form 5. If the blood was drawn after 10:30 AM,
mark Yes for Q12 on page 3; the participant is not eligible to participate in the
OGTT at that visit.
iii. Determine whether the participant fasted for at least eight hours by referring
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-16

back to Q2 on page 1 (Q13). If the participant fasted less than eight hours,
he/she will not be eligible for the OGTT.
iv. Ask the participant:
Has he/she ever been told by a physician that he/she is diabetic? (Q14). If
the answer is Yes, ask whether he/she is taking insulin and/or oral
medications for diabetes treatment. If the participant is taking insulin and/or
oral medications, the participant is not eligible for the OGTT.
Is he/she using steroids (e.g., prednisone) for any reason? (Q15). If the
answer is Yes, the participant is not eligible for the OGTT. The only
exception to this exclusion is the use of oral steroid inhalers (e.g., Albuterol);
they do not exclude the participant from the OGTT and the response should
be marked as no.
Is she pregnant? (Q16). If the participant is male, do not ask this question,
but do mark the Not applicable response on the form. If the participant is
pregnant or not sure whether she is pregnant, she is not eligible for the
OGTT.
In summary, the following participants are not eligible for the OGTT:
o those arriving at the clinic after 10:00 AM (although may
participate on a future date);
o those who did not fast for at least eight hours (although may
participate on a future date);
o those who are diabetic and take insulin and/or oral diabetes
medications;
o those using steroids (not including oral inhalers); and
o those who are, or may be, pregnant.
v. If the time for the first blood collection is prior
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-17

to 10:30 AM, provide 75gm glucose solution (Glucola) within a period
not to exceed five minutes. Encourage the participant to drink the solution
as quickly as possible, and confirm that the entire volume of the glucose
solution has been consumed.
NOTE: A participant may become nauseous and/or vomit following
ingestion of the glucose drink. Providing a leak-proof biohazard bag can
prevent exposure to bodily fluids and may also improve the comfort of the
participant.
vi. Record the time that the participant started the glucose
drink (Q17).
vii. Record the time that the participant completed the
glucose drink (Q18).
NOTE: Do not exclude the participant from the OGTT if the time for
consuming the glucose solution exceeds five minutes.
viii. Record the expected time (two hours from time glucose drink is consumed)
of the second blood collection on the form (Q19).
Record the time that you want the participant to return
to the phlebotomy station (ten minutes prior to the
expected blood collection time) on an adhesive label
and ask the participant to stick the label on the left side of his/her chest or
shoulder.
ix. Inform the Clinic Coordinator of the time for the second blood collection to
ensure that the PFT will be completed at least thirty minutes before the
assigned time for the second blood collection.
x. Instruct the participant to refrain from smoking and heavy physical activity
and to return to the phlebotomy station at the assigned time for the second
blood collection.

xi. When the participant returns to the phlebotomy station, check the expected

xii. Record the time of the completion of the PFT (Q20).
xiii. If at any time after consuming the glucose solution, but prior to the second

xiv. If the phlebotomist is unable to obtain blood for the OGTT sample, indicate

xv. Within + five minutes of the expected time for

i. Complete Form 5A—Phlebotomy-Delayed OGTT.
ii. Perform fasting blood draw before 10:30 AM.
iii. Instruct the participant to consume the 75gm glucose solution (Glucola)
within a period not to exceed five minutes. Encourage the participant to drink
the solution as quickly as possible, and confirm that the entire volume of the
glucose solution has been consumed.
NOTE: A participant may become nauseous and/or vomit following
ingestion of the glucose drink. Providing a leak-proof biohazard bag can
prevent exposure to bodily fluids and may also improve the comfort of the
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-19

participant.
NOTE: Do not exclude the participant from the OGTT if the time for

iv. Record the time that the participant should return to the phlebotomy station

D. BLOOD HANDLING
1. Description
The proper handling of the collected samples is critical. Deviation from the protocol
can significantly affect the analyte being measured in the blood. It is particularly
important to comply with time deadlines while handling specimens so that samples will
not be left open to the atmosphere longer than necessary. A total of ninety (90) minutes
is permitted between blood drawing and final placement of samples in the freezer;
schedule your time accordingly.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-20

2. Procedure for Core and YALTA Blood Components
a. Confirm that the correct PID label is on each of the six
core vacutainers, two YALTA vacutainers, two 3-ml
syringes, and the DNA blood spot card. This is
absolutely necessary in order to identify which tubes belong to which participant
and to avoid any mix-up and/or mislabeling of samples. Verify that the
participant’s name, written in the lower left corner of the DNA blood spot card,
matches the PID label.
b. Immediately following the blood collection, place the three lavender top tubes
(two for core and one for YALTA), the two blue-top
vacutainers (core), and the SCAT 1 tube into a container
of water and ice. Cool the samples on water and ice for
at least 30 – 45 minutes. The samples should never be
kept on water and ice for more than 60 minutes.
c. Place the two red-top tubes (one for core and one for YALTA) in the test tube
rack. Allow the samples to clot by standing for at least 30 – 45 minutes, but not
more than 60 minutes at room temperature (65-75oF).
3. Procedure for drawing blood into two 3-ml syringes
a. Gather supplies:
i. 2 A-tubes stored at -70° C
ii. 2 B-tubes stored at -70° C
iii. 2 empty 2 ml cryovials (referred to as C-tubes)
iv. hemoglobin A kit (1 capillary tube, 1 Sample Preparation Vial, 1 capillary
1c
tube holder)
v. 1 DNA blood spot card
vi. 1 - 3 ml syringe
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-21

vii. 1 - 3 ml syringe with heparin
viii. 1 empty plastic box to transport B-tubes
ix. Sample storage boxes (both plastic and fiber)
b. Preparatory Work:
i. Remove the necessary number of tubes from the -70° C freezer (both A- and
B-tubes; each participant requires two of each tube) for the collection
procedure.
ii. Place the B-tubes into a plastic box and then onto a glass tray. Bring both
sets of tubes to room temperature before use.
NOTE: The B-tubes have been prepared and provided by the University of
Minnesota, and contain a preservative that requires special shipping
precautions; see shipping instructions.
iii. Place the necessary number of A-tubes (two per participant), C-tubes (two
per participant) and hemoglobin Sample Preparation Vials (one per
participant) into the aliquoting board. Label all tubes (including the B-tubes
in the glass tray) and a DNA blood spot card the long way and covering the
large white block. Also, take out a capillary tube (one per participant), and
attach it to the capillary tube holder. Take the tubes (excluding the B-tubes),
the card, and a hemoglobin kit with you to the blood draw.
4. Blood is drawn into the syringes following all vacutainers tubes drawn for the
study.
5. Sample collection with first syringe:
a. Using the same butterfly needle used for the vacutainers,
slide the lock to obstruct the tube so that no blood flows
out, remove the holder and attach the 3 ml syringe
without heparin onto the butterfly port.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-22

b. Draw approximately 1.75 ml of blood into the syringe.
c. Remove the syringe from the butterfly needle and connect the second 3 ml
heparinized syringe onto the butterfly port. Care should be taken to ensure
that the syringe is securely locked to the hub of the port.
d. Immediately aliquot the specimen that was collected into the first syringe in the
following order:
i. Aliquot 0.5 ml into each of two A-tubes, cap securely, and mix by slowly
inverting the tube twice, being careful not to hemolyze the sample.
Accuracy is very important for this aliquot, so be as precise as possible.
NOTE: If you have trouble reading the graduations, pre-mark the
graduations on the syringe using a correction fluid pen or a small piece of
tape.
ii. Drop enough blood from the syringe to fill the circles on the DNA blood spot
card. When the blood has dried, place the card and a desiccant packet in the
envelope provided, but do not seal the envelope. The card does not require
refrigeration, and may be stored in a file cabinet. At the end of that day, or
within two days, the PID label and the participant’s name
on the card should be compared against the list of
participants examined from the Scheduling System. Use
this comparison to verify that the participant’s name and PID label match. If
they do match, the name should be cut off the card, taking care to not
compromise the blood sample. If the participant’s name and PID label do
NOT match, all other specimens from that collection date should be checked
for possible mislabeling (between the card and the other specimens) and for
confirmation that the participant’s name is correctly documented on the card.
In the event that a card’s owner absolutely cannot be verified, the card
should be destroyed by removing the PID label and placing the card in a
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-23

biohazard container. Otherwise, the envelope should be sealed after
verification is complete, and stored at room temperature in secure storage.
e. These steps must be done within two minutes of the blood draw into the syringe.
f. Discard the syringe in the appropriate biohazard container.
6. Sample collection with second syringe:
a. Using the second syringe already attached to the
butterfly port, draw 1.25 ml of blood.
b. Remove the syringe, mix to prevent clotting, set aside,
and complete the blood draw procedure within two
minutes.
c. Immediately aliquot the specimen that was collected into the second syringe by
dripping and using the graduations on the side of the syringe in the following
order:
i. Aliquot 0.5 ml into two C-tubes.
ii. For hemoglobin determination, insert the
capillary tube into the tip of the syringe using
the capillary holder. Allow the capillary tube to
fill, and process the sample immediately after (see Item 7).
d. Discard the syringe in the appropriate biohazard container.
7. Sample processing:
Process the samples in the following order:
a. Hemoglobin vial:
i. Transfer the filled capillary tube into the sample preparation vial.
ii. Cap the vial and invert it to rinse the blood completely from the capillary
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-24

tube. It is important to make sure that no blood remains in the capillary
tube.
iii. Place the tube into a sample box and store at
-70° C.
b. A-tube:
i. Depress the timing button on the micro-centrifuge and spin the A-tube for 30
seconds at 12,000 rpm to remove blood cells. If there is any evidence of
hemolysis, the sample should be discarded.
ii. Place the A-tubes onto the glass tray with the B-tubes.
iii. Being careful not to spill the B-tubes, remove the caps from the B-tubes.
iv. Aliquot 0.2 ml of supernatant from the A-tube into the B-tube and cap
immediately after supernatant is transferred.
v. Slowly invert to mix and store sample at -70° C in a plastic storage box.
c. C-tube processing:
i. Centrifuge the tube for 30 seconds at 12,000 rpm in a micro-centrifuge.
ii. Remove and discard the plasma and white blood cells as completely as
possible including the top ⅛ inch of the red blood cells.
iii. Add 0.1 ml of saline to the tube, mix, place the sample into a sample box,
and store at -70° C.
8. Do not allow any of the samples to stand in direct sunlight or become exposed to
extreme temperatures.

E. OPERATING THE CENTRIFUGE
1. Set the POWER switch to ON.
2. Following the manufacturer’s specific instructions, ensure the centrifuge is pre-
cooled at the Study-directed temperature of 4°C.
NOTE: The shields should be refrigerated if they are removed from the centrifuge,
so that they will be chilled prior to spinning blood. These instructions may vary by
type of centrifuge; check manufacturer’s directions.
3. Maintain the temperature of 4°C by keeping the centrifuge door closed and
locked until ready for loading.
4. Set the TIMER control to 20 minutes and the speed to 3000 RPM (1000-1500
RCF{g} depending upon equipment).
5. Balance the load.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-26

a. Place opposite shields containing filled vacutainers on the balance.
b. To the lighter centrifuge shield, add tubes filled with water (or 50/50
water/alcohol) to equal the volume of processing specimens. A balanced load is
essential for the safe operation of all centrifuges. An unbalanced load produces
vibration and can damage the unit, therefore, always make sure that the rotor is
loaded symmetrically with a full complement of accessories, and with a full (or
paired) set of tubes. Tube adapters should also be installed symmetrically
correspondence in size, shape, and relative position of parts or opposite sides.
To obtain good dynamic balance, the opposite loads must not only be equal in
mass, but must also have the same center of gravity. Opposing containers must
be alike in shape, thickness, and distribution of glass or plastic.
6. Load the rotor, being careful to place balanced shields directly opposite each
other.
7. Recheck the centrifuge preset parameters for temperature, speed, time and
brake position.
8. Close cover and lock.
9. Push the RUN button to begin the run cycle. Record the time the samples were
placed in the centrifuge in Q7 of Form 5.
10. The centrifuge will stop automatically at the pre-selected time and the stop
indicator will light. Remove samples one at a time and carefully place them in
the appropriate aliquoting board space.
11. Consult the Centrifuge Service Manual for other guidelines and for
troubleshooting.

4. Frozen Sample Packaging and Shipment
Packaging and shipping of frozen samples is the responsibility of each Field Center.
Different carriers, e.g. FedEx or UPS, have specific packing instructions which may vary
slightly. It is the responsibility of the Field Center to be aware of and comply with the
specific requirements of the carrier. Additionally, the Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention (CDC), Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), and
International Air Transportation Association (IATA) have specific guidelines and
recommendations that must be followed. The following information is generally
applicable for all carriers, the CDC, OSHA, and the IATA.
Individuals who are responsible for collecting, storing, packing, and shipping medical
specimens must have appropriate education and training in handling of specimens to
protect themselves and others from possible exposure. Records of the training must be
maintained. The CDC has published specific regulations addressing the transportation of
biological agents. The regulations are designed to ensure the public and workers are
protected from exposure to any substance that is being shipped. Protection includes
requirements for packaging; labeling of shipping containers; documentation regarding the
hazardous contents of a package; and training of individuals who will be in contact with
the package during shipment. Safe shipping of medical samples includes “triple packing”
procedures.
a. Safe shipping of liquid specimens includes the following basic requirements:
i. leak-proof primary receptacles;
ii. leak-proof secondary receptacles;
iii. absorbent materials;
iv. sturdy outer packaging;
v. an itemized list of the contents of the package.
b. The storage vials are shipped in the storage boxes in which they have already
been stored at the Field Center.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-48

c. Samples must be frozen for at least twenty-four hours before they are packaged
to be shipped.
d. When ready to ship the samples to the laboratory, check the condition of the
fiberboard box. Boxes that are of poor integrity should not be used for shipping.
e. If QC samples are to be included with the shipment, place the QC samples in the
box.
f. Assess the specimens for obvious leakage, loose or improperly placed caps, etc.
g. Before securing the cover on the box, place an absorbent material over the
samples inside the box. The absorbent material must be of sufficient size to
absorb the entire contents of the box in the event of breakage/spillage/thawing.
h. Place a rubber band around the box.
i. Place the box containing the specimens inside a waterproof biohazard bag and
seal the bag.
j. Place the biohazard bag, with the frozen samples upright, into the insulated
shipping container and, wearing the appropriate protective gloves, surround with
dry ice pellets. At least 10 pounds of dry ice is necessary to keep the samples
frozen for up to 48 hours; 15-20 pounds is recommended.
k. The two shipping forms (Shipment Contents Facesheet and Shipment Contents
Form) must be enclosed with each shipment. Instructions for completion of
these forms are found in Appendix 1. A separate Facesheet should be used for
each type of specimen enclosed.
l. Samples must be shipped so that they arrive at the laboratory by 10:30 A.M. the
following morning. The Field Centers must request that laboratories return the
containers as soon as possible at the Field Center's expense. Return need not
be overnight and the Field Centers should provide an account number to the
laboratories for the return shipping costs.
m. On the day of shipment, the technician responsible for shipping samples must
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-49

notify each laboratory that the samples have been shipped (to arrive by 10:30
AM the following day). (Due to differences in time zones, the technician may
need to call the laboratory the morning that the shipment will be arriving). If the
shipment is not received by noon, the laboratory personnel should contact the
Coordinating Center and the Clinic Coordinator of the pertinent Field Center
immediately. This will permit the clinic to initiate a trace on the missing samples
and increase the likelihood of recovering the samples prior to thawing.
n. Shipments MUST be made according to the shipping schedule.
o. Label each shipment with "CONTENTS TO REMAIN FROZEN."
p. Effective January 1, 2005, IATA regulations require an additional label or
marking on the outside of shipping boxes containing diagnostic specimens.
These shipping boxes must be marked with the following:

J. LABORATORY QUALITY CONTROL
In order to assess the reproducibility of the measurements made at the centralized
laboratories, a split sample external surveillance program has been developed. The
purpose of the program is to produce data which may be used: (1) to identify problems as
they occur and to communicate this information to the clinic and laboratory for corrective
action; and (2) to document the performance of the entire process, i.e. sample collection,
preparation, handling, shipping and analytical performance.
The QC procedures will consist of providing the laboratories with duplicate
specimens, one sample labeled with the PID and the other with a QC ID. Duplicate
samples will also aid in measuring "across assay" reproducibility. In order to accomplish
this, the duplicate blood specimens must be split across shipments to the laboratories.
Otherwise, the sample is analyzed in the same manner as all other specimens in that
particular month.
Each of the Field Centers will draw a QC sample on an approximate seven percent
sample of the participants for the each type of analysis sample.
The QC participant will be identified by the QC portion of the local data system at the
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.5 06December06 PHL-58

start of each week. The Clinic Coordinator at each Field Center will provide this
information to the phlebotomist at the beginning of each clinic week. In the event that the
additional sample could not be drawn on the identified participant, the phlebotomist
should draw the QC sample from the NEXT PARTICIPANT.
1. Duplicate Core Exam Specimens
The volume of additional blood that will be drawn for the core QC is: one 5ml
lavender top (EDTA) vacutainer tube for duplicate plasma lipids measurements; one 5-ml
red-top (SST) vacutainer for duplicate serum insulin, glucose, and creatinine
measurements; and one 4.5-ml blue top vacutainer for CRP, IL-6 and fibrinogen
measurements.
The plasma from the 5-ml lavender top vacutainer is aliquoted into a red labeled 2-ml
cryovial (lipids); the plasma from the 4.5-ml blue-top vacutainer is aliquoted into a blue
labeled 2-ml cryovial (inflammatory markers). The serum from the 5-ml red-top
vacutainer is aliquoted into a purple labeled 2-ml cryovial (chemistries).
2. Duplicate YALTA Specimens
The volume of additional blood that will be drawn for the YALTA QC is: one 10-ml
lavender top vacutainer; one 5-ml red top (SST) vacutainer and 3 ml whole blood drawn
into two 3-ml syringes (1.75 and 1.25 ml each) for duplicate YALTA QC measures.
The plasma from the 10-ml lavender top vacutainer is aliquoted into one red stripe-
labeled 2-ml cryovial; three pink stripe-labeled 2-ml cryovial; one blue stripe-labeled 2-
ml cryovial; and three orange stripe labeled 2-ml cryovials. The serum from the 5-ml red
top vacutainer is aliquoted into five green stripe labeled 2-ml cryovials. The blood from
syringe # 1 will be used for the two yellow stripe 2-ml cryovials, and the blood from
syringe #2 will be used for HbA1c (black striped label) and for two light blue stripe 2-ml
cryovials.
3. Shipping Duplicate Specimens
When an additional amount of blood is drawn and aliquoted for the QC duplicate

should not be shipped with the original specimen; shipments of original and

APPENDIX 4
AMENDMENT TO SPECIMEN PROCESSING PROTOCOL FOR PLASMA CITRATED
SAMPLES IN FUTURE CARDIA EXAMS
Due to the observation of clots in blue-top citrate tubes by laboratory technicians at
the University of Vermont’s Laboratory of Clinical Biochemistry Research during the
Year 20 Exam, and following the results* of a subsequent Fibrinogen Comparability
Study**, the Laboratory Subcommittee recommended revision of the sample processing
protocol to include the icing of plasma citrated samples immediately following
centrifuging in future CARDIA exams.
* Fibrinogen Comparability Study results are posted on the CARDIA Internal Website in
the Laboratory Subcommittee “Meeting 2006-09-12” folder.
** Fibrinogen Comparability Study: 50 randomly-selected Y20 EDTA samples from
participants who had observable clots in their citrate samples and another 50 sex-race
matched Y20 EDTA samples from participants who did not have observable clots in their
citrate samples were selected—the fibrinogen values from the Y20 EDTA assays were
compared with the fibrinogen values from the Y20 citrate assays. In addition, the
differences of the fibrinogen (EDTA-citrate) were also compared between the 50 samples
with observable clots and the 50 samples without observable clots.

Excerpt from CARDIA Laboratory Subcommittee Meeting Minutes
CARDIA Laboratory Subcommittee
Minutes of Meeting
September 12, 2006
5:00 p.m. — 7:00 p.m. Eastern Time
Present: Pam Schreiner; Myron Gross; Mike Steffes; David Jacobs; Kiang Liu; Nancy
Jenny, Alex Arynchyn; Jennifer Wammack
5. Topic: Review Fibrinogen Comparability Study Results
Discussion: Nancy Jenny from the University of Vermont (UVM) joined the QC and
Laboratory Subcommittee meetings to discuss the early fibrinogen data. Lab technicians
at UVM noted the presence of clots in the citrate tubes and stopped analysis after 1,914
samples out of the Year 20 cohort were processed. Values were substantially lower than
expected, and this was attributed to the citrate samples being processed last in the
phlebotomy scheme and the omission of a final ice step in the protocol after processing.
A sub-sample of the clotted tubes were rerun with their EDTA stored sample and the
values were consistently higher with EDTA, potentially due to the calcium chelating
properties of EDTA that may have inhibited excess clotting. Because there is no way of
determining if the samples without clots have micro-clots or are adequate, the Laboratory
Subcommittee believes that the citrate samples are not useful. Discussions with the
Laboratory of Clinical Biochemistry Research at UVM suggest that the processing time
of the citrate samples did not affect the CRP or IL-6 data.
Recommendation: Amend Year 20 protocol (manual of operations) for specimen
processing to add an ice step after processing all plasma citrated samples for historical
and future records.
Recommendation: Rerun all Year 20 samples using stored EDTA.
Recommendation: Calibrate the new fibrinogen data to the Year 7 (nephelometry)
fibrinogen data.

B. GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS
1. Recording Responses
Form responses are read automatically by a scanning device. Therefore, it is
very important that the responses be recorded by the participant within the space
allotted. The instructions in Appendix 1 should be given to the participant to read
prior to completion of self-administered forms.
The following guidelines should be emphasized:
a. When choosing a response option, the participant should place an X inside the
X
box beside his/her answer, like this:
b. When recording a text response, the participant should write only within the box
provided, as markings outside the box will not be read by the scanning device.
c. When recording numerical responses, such as amounts or dates, one number
should be entered in each box and every box should have a number in it.
Therefore, it may be necessary to record leading zeros when the number requires
fewer boxes than provided.
d. The date on the top of the form is not to be completed by the participant. The
form reviewer should enter the date if the form is completed on a different day
than the participant’s blood pressure was taken, otherwise the same date blood
pressure taken box should be marked.
e. Forms should be completed using a No. 2 pencil; errors should be erased as
completely as possible and corrections written clearly.
2. Questionnaire Instructions
Brief written instructions are provided on individual questionnaires. If a
participant appears to have difficulty understanding a form’s instructions, the
interviewer should clearly read the instructions aloud, periodically making eye
contact with the participant.

3. Clarifying Questions for a Participant
Question wording is very precise and may not be altered. If a participant does
not understand the meaning of a question, the interviewer should clearly read the
question aloud, periodically making eye contact with the participant. If he/she still
does not understand the question, a neutral probe should be used, such as Answer
what's right for you. If the participant still does not understand the question, the
interviewer should state You may leave that question blank. The interviewer should
then circle all the answers and write NA (not answered) in the left margin. If a
participant asks a CARDIA interviewer for ANY help in reading or completing a
self-administered questionnaire, the interviewer should record his/her Interviewer ID
in the space located on the last page of the form.
4. Reading Questions Aloud
Before giving participants any self-administered questionnaires, clinic personnel
should be certain that the Prefers to have forms read box on the Clinic Flow Sheet
has not been checked. If this box has been checked, an interviewer must read all self-
administered questionnaires to the participant according to the instructions in Section
C, below.
5. Requesting a Participant to Complete Missing Data
If the Exit Interviewer in each Field Center has to ask that a participant complete
a portion of a form, or fill in missing data, the Exit Interviewer should not record
his/her Interviewer ID on that form. This does not constitute helping the participant
read a form.
Once the exam is completed, the Data Editor should review the form set prior to
scanning. If the Interviewer ID space located on the first page of a self-administered
form is left blank, it is the Data Editor's responsibility to fill in the Interviewer ID:
199 (Birmingham), 299 (Chicago), 399 (Minneapolis), or 499 (Oakland). This
procedure serves to eliminate missing fields and is a quality control measure, as well.

C. INSTRUCTIONS FOR INTERVIEWER ADMINISTRATION OF SELF-ADMINISTERED
QUESTIONNAIRES
1. Each question should be read aloud, exactly as it appears.
2. GO TO or SKIP TO instructions should not be read aloud.
3. All* response options should be read for questions requiring one response only. The
participant should not be given time to answer until all options have been read.
4. All* response options should be read for questions allowing multiple responses. The
participant should be given time to answer after each option has been read.
5. Repetitive response options, such as True/False or Yes/No do not have to be repeated
for each question if the participant appears to understand the questions and provides
plausible answers.
6. After a self-administered questionnaire is interviewer-administered, the interviewer
should record his/her Interviewer ID.

information about participants’ disease status and medication usage. This form is
somewhat difficult to navigate, so participants should be encouraged to request assistance
when needed. Additionally, the participant should be given some specific information
prior to completing the form.

E. TOBACCO USE (FORM 10)
The Tobacco Use Questionnaire is designed to collect information about the
participant's history of tobacco use and exposure to environmental tobacco smoke. The
path through Form 10 is indicated by arrows and GO TO statements. Instructions to the
participant appear capitalized and in parentheses. The questionnaire contains thirteen
primary questions and two additional response-dependent follow-up questions. Q1 asks
if the participant has ever used any form of tobacco. Q2-Q7 pertain to use of specific
forms of tobacco, and are to be completed only by participants who indicate ever using
tobacco. Q8-Q12 pertain to exposure to environmental tobacco smoke, and are to be
completed by all participants. Q13 pertains to workplace smoking policy, and is also to
be completed by all participants.
F. HISTORY OF LUNG PROBLEMS (FORM 12)
The History of Lung Problems form is a two-category questionnaire designed to
collect information about the participant's pulmonary problems, including cough, phlegm,
wheezing, breathlessness, and chest colds. The participant is asked to mark a Yes/No
response box indicating whether he/she has experienced problems in the defined area.
Q1 is split into two questions based on whether or not the symptom is present in a
defined situation. When a Yes response is given to an initial question the participant

should complete the appropriate follow-up questions; a No response means the follow-up
questions are to be skipped.
G. FRAMINGHAM TYPE A (FORM 16)
The Framingham Type A form is designed to collect information about participant
personality traits, especially related to time-pressure and type of work. There are
nineteen items with two skip patterns. Those participants whose primary role is other
than Homemaker (any response to Q7 except 4), answer all questions except Q12-Q15.
Those participants whose primary role is Homemaker (response to Q7 is 4), answer all
questions except Q7-Q11.
H. NON-MEDICAL DRUG USE QUESTIONNAIRE (FORM 17)
The Non-Medical Drug Use form is designed to collect information about
participants’ use of illegal (recreational) drugs. The path through this questionnaire is
indicated by GO TO statements and arrows. All participants should answer Q1, Q3, Q5,
Q7, and Q9. Q2 applies only to participants who have ever used marijuana. Q4 applies
only to participants who have ever used crack cocaine. Q6 applies only to participants
who have ever used other forms of cocaine. Q8 applies only to participants who have
ever used amphetamines. Q10 applies only to participants who have ever used opiates.
One of the most common concerns of participants completing this questionnaire is
confidentiality. Should a participant ask about this, the interviewer should reassure
him/her that information collected is strictly confidential. His/her answers will be
combined with other participants’ answers to help provide a better understanding of
general or average use. If a participant does not wish to complete the questionnaire,
he/she should not be pressed to do so. In this case, the interviewer should write
intentionally blank on the form and record his/her (interviewer’s) initials in the
Interviewer ID space at the bottom of the second page.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.1 06June06
SA-6

I. LONELINESS (FORM 14B)
The Loneliness questionnaire is comprised of four questions that address loneliness.
Participants are to respond to each question by choosing the response that best describes
how they feel. Each statement is followed by four response options, including
Frequently, Occasionally, Rarely, and Never. No time-frame is given for these feelings.
J. CES-D DEPRESSION SCALE (FORM 36)
The CES-D (Center for Epidemiological Studies) Depression Scale is a twenty-item
questionnaire designed to collect information about the participant's mood during the
previous week. Participants respond to a series of statements by indicating: Rarely or
none of the time, Some of the time, Much of the time, or Most or all of the time.
Definitions of these options follow, and may be conveyed to participants:
Rarely or none of the time = less than one full day
Some of the time = 1-2 days
Much of the time = 3-4 days
Most or all of the time = 5-7 days
Since the CES-D measures recent mood, the interviewer should remind the participant
that the questions apply only to the previous week, with the day of the interview acting as
the last day of the week.
The CES-D is scored by the addition of points for each item, with points for each
item ranging from 0 to 3. Note that the points scale is reversed in Q4, Q8, Q12, and Q16,
in that Rarely or none of the time receives a score of 3, not 0, while Most or all of the
time receives a score of 0, rather than 3, as in all other questions.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.1 06June06
SA-7

K. ANGER IN EXPRESSION (FORM 38)
The Anger in Expression Questionnaire consists of three statements describing the
ways in which a person might deal with anger. The response options for each statement
are Very likely, Somewhat likely, and Not too likely. The participant should select the one
response for each statement that best describes him/her. The Anger in Expression
Questionnaire is scored by the addition of points for each item.
L. NEIGHBORHOOD COHESION (FORM 56)
The Neighborhood Cohesion form is designed to collect information about the
participant's perception of his/her social environment. This questionnaire queries a
participant’s beliefs about the people in his/her neighborhood. Each statement is to be
ranked on a five-point scale: Strongly Agree, Agree, Neutral, Disagree, Strongly
Disagree.
M. SOCIAL SUPPORT AND CONFLICT (FORM 62)
The Social Support and Conflict Questionnaire assesses the social support and
conflict a participant perceives from his/her family and/or friends. The questionnaire
contains eight items, each requiring a response from a four-point response scale: Not at
all, A little, Some, A lot.
N. SOCIAL NETWORK (FORM 63)
The Social Network form is designed to collect information about the participant's
social ties with individual people and groups around him/her. Three questions, regarding
the number of friends and/or relatives the participant is connected with on a regular basis,
require a response on a five-point response scale: None, 1 or 2, 3 to 5, 6 to 9, 10 or more.
Six items, regarding group affiliation, require a Yes/No response.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.1 06June06
SA-8

O. CHRONIC BURDEN (FORM 64)
The Chronic Burden form is designed to collect information about the participant's
chronic problems (those lasting longer than six months). Eight items require a response
on a four-point response scale: No, Yes-but not very stressful, Yes- moderately stressful,
and Yes-very stressful.
P. QUALITY OF LIFE SF-12 (FORM 65)
The Quality of Life form has twelve questions and is designed to collect information
about the participant's perceived physical and emotional health, as they relate to quality
of daily living.
Q1 asks the participant to rank his/her general health on a five-point response scale:
Excellent, Very Good, Good, Fair, Poor. Q2 and Q3 address the extent to which a
participant’s health limits his/her activities regarding moderate activities and climbing
stairs, using a three-point response scale: No-not limited, Yes- limited a little, Yes- limited
a lot. Q4-Q7 ask the participant to assess whether physical and emotional problems have
impacted his/her ability to perform work tasks or regular daily activities during the
previous four weeks. A Yes or No response is required. Q8 asks the participant how
much pain interfered with his/her normal work during the previous four weeks, using a
five-point response scale: Not at all, A little bit, Moderately, Quite a bit, Extremely. Q9-
Q12 ask the participant how he/she has felt during the previous four weeks, using a six-
point response scale: All of the time, Most of the time, A good bit of the time, Some of the
time, A little of the time, None of the time.
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.1 06June06

Q. SUBJECTIVE STANDING (FORM 66)
The Subjective Standing form has two items and is designed to collect information
about the participant's perceived social standing. Participants rank themselves (1) in
terms of standing within their community and (2) in terms of their standing in the nation.
For each of these two items, a drawing of a ladder with nine rungs is presented. Q1
has the participant place a large X in the box on the rung where he/she thinks he/she
currently stands in his/her own community. Q2 has the participant place a large X in the
box on the rung where he/she thinks he/she stands relative to other people in the United
States.
Note: The Data Editor should make sure the X is marked in a box on a rung, not between
rungs.
R. SLEEP HABITS (FORM 67)
The Sleep Habits Questionnaire is designed to collect information about the
participant's sleep quality and quantity. The questionnaire contains seven primary
questions and two additional response-dependent follow-up questions. Specific areas
addressed include: sleepiness, snoring, falling asleep, staying asleep, waking up, quality
of sleep, and number of hours of sleep per night in the past month.
Q1-Q5 provide Yes, No, Don’t know response categories. Q6 has the participant rate
his/her sleep quality on a five-point response scale: Very good, Fairly good, Good, Fairly
bad, Very bad. And Q7 pertains to hours of sleep per night.
S. WOMEN’S REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH (FORM 68)
The Women’s Reproductive Health form is designed to collect information about the
female participant's menstrual function. If the participant asks why additional menstrual
information is being collected, the interviewer can use this explanation:
CARDIA Year 20 Manual of Operations Ver. 1.1 06June06

Menstrual function is a marker of both a woman’s reproductive health and her
health in general. These questions will help us to understand the changes that
a woman goes through as she moves through her 30s, 40s, and 50s (prior to
menopause, in many cases), and how these changes relate to risk factors for
heart disease.
Note: When the participant is given the Women’s Reproductive Health form, she should
be told to pay particular attention to the time-period of interest for each question.
Q1-Q3 deal with menopause at any age. If a participant asks about this, it is
appropriate to clarify the time-frame. If a participant answers No or Not sure to Q1, she
should skip to Q4. If a participant answers Yes to Q1, she should answer Q2 and Q3,
then skip to Q12.
Q4-Q11 all deal with reproductive health during the previous twelve months.
Participants may have difficulty following the skip pattern for Q4. If a participant
answered No or Not sure for Q4, she should have answered Q4a and Q4b only. If a
participant answered Yes to Q4, she should have answered Q4c only.
If the participant asks about a Became more regular option for Q5, the interviewer
can prompt Did this mean your periods became closer together or farther apart? The
participant’s answer to this prompt should help her choose an appropriate option.
Q12-Q18 address different time intervals (e.g., three months, one year).
If a participant asks how Q17 relates to women’s reproductive health, the interviewer
can tell her that this question relates to her health in general. The question itself is meant
to capture symptoms that often accompany perimenopause or menopause.
T. GOAL-STRIVING STRESS (FORM 74)
The Goal-Striving Stress form is a four-question questionnaire designed to collect
information about the participant's perceived progress toward achieving goals and
reaction to potential lack of goal-achievement. A drawing of a ten-rung ladder is

presented for use in Q1-Q3. Q3a has the participant rank disappointment related to lack
of goal-achievement on a four-point response scale: Very disappointed, Fairly
disappointed, Slightly disappointed, Not at all disappointed.
U. CAREGIVING STRESS (FORM 75)
The Caregiving Stress form is designed to collect information about whether the
participant has a caregiving role due to the needs of a family member, and the level of
stress associated with performing that role. The questionnaire contains two primary
questions, each of which has two response-dependent follow-up questions. Q1 addresses
providing for personal care needs and Q2 addresses assistance given with everyday
chores.
V. CSQ MEDICAL HISTORY (FORM 78)
The CSQ Medical History questionnaire focuses on joint and skin complaints,
specific blood test outcomes, and specific physical symptoms. The form has thirty
primary questions, three of which have response-dependent follow-up questions. This
history is not time-limited, and queries whether a participant has ever had each specific
complaint or diagnosis.
W. DIETARY HABITS (FORM 79)
The Dietary Habits form is a seven-question self-administered questionnaire
designed to collect information about the participant's salt and water intake. Questions
included in this form were originally part of the interviewer-administered Diet History
form. The Diet Subcommittee and Diet Center developed the Dietary Habits form for
questions that could be self-administered without losing data quality. Q1-Q4 and Q7
require the participant to choose one response. Q5 requires rating his/her response on a

to rank order a list of responses, one of which is Other (if chosen, this needs a written
