Appendix 9
Heart Failure Case Law
(Updated 9/10/2009)
1. If there is no evidence of exacerbation or decompensation until a fatal cardiac arrest and there is no
other evidence of heart failure, then there is not sufficient evidence for a diagnosis of definite
decompensated HF (option 2) or possible decompensated HF (option 2).
2. If there is no history of symptoms or evidence from echocardiography or other imaging to suggest
LV systolic or diastolic dysfunction, then there is not sufficient evidence for a classification of chronic
stable Heart Failure (option 4).
3. Assign a classification of unclassifiable (option 8) if you can’t decide between chronic Heart Failure
(option 4) and HF unlikely (option 1). Do not use “unclassifiable” if you are uncertain between
“definite decompensated HF” and “possible decompensated HF”; in such a case, record “possible
decompensated HF” (option 3).
4. In the context of an acute exacerbation of COPD with symptoms of heart failure but with no direct
or clear evidence of right or left ventricular dysfunction from imaging, then classify as unclassifiable
(option 8).
5. When deciding between Heart Failure unlikely (option 1) and unclassifiable (option 8) consider the
completeness or sufficiency of the evidence. If there is sufficient or substantial amount of
information provided in the reports to suggest that the patient did not have heart failure, choose HF
unlikely (option 1). Use unclassifiable (option 8) in the cases where the level or amount of
documentation is simply insufficient to make a clear diagnosis (whether heart failure is present
versus absent).
6. Evidence of dilated ventricle alone is not sufficient to record abnormal LV/RV dysfunction.
7. Use all of the data available which is provided by the field center for your diagnosis in question 7,
even it is seems old, because it is relevant to the case/admission under review. However, for
recording LVEF or LV/RV/Diastolic dysfunction, use only the documentation related to the current
hospitalization rather than records that pre-date the hospitalization.
8. Do not put too much weight on one piece of evidence. For example, when the discharge summary
appears inconsistent with a HF diagnosis (i.e., does not list HF as a problem/diagnosis when there
was an obvious problem of heart failure based on other documents like chest x-rays or description
of treatment), make sure to weigh the totality of the evidence in the chart in order to classify the
case.
9. If left ventricular compliance is normal, record no for 7.2.3.
10. If the event summary form indicates an ejection fraction was recorded, but there is no supporting
information provided in the materials included in the case, record Unknown for 7.3.
11. If there are multiple echocardiography reports containing ejection fraction from old admissions and
current admissions, make sure to use the lowest ejection fraction from the CURRENT admission.
CARDIA Endpoint Events Manual of Operations v0312/2018/20154
67

12. For patients with specific types of cardiomyopathies that are not described as heart failure, (e.g.,
hypertrophic cardimyopathy/IHSS), use supporting evidence to determine that the condition exists
(either as a chronic stable type of heart failure or a decompensated state). If the available evidence
(e.g., treatment, past history) does not confirm that this condition exists as a “heart failure”
condition, and you are trying to choose among “chronic stable HF,” “HF unlikely,” and
“unclassifiable,” then choose “unclassifiable”.
13. When deciding between “chronic stable HF,” “HF unlikely,” and “unclassifiable”: if the record only
mentions history of HF, and there is no other information to substantiate the diagnosis, choose
“unclassifiable” (not “chronic stable HF”). However, in order to choose “chronic stable HF”, there
must be no contradictory evidence AND some kind of supporting information; for example, a
statement about previous hospitalization for HF, low ejection fraction, medications specifically for
heart failure, or X-ray finding like cardiomegaly. The ESF can be used to provide this supporting
evidence, but a previous diagnosis alone may not be sufficient. Evidence of HF treatment should
come from the medical record (sole mention of treatment in the ESF is not sufficient). (This case law
is a similar but an expanded version of Case Law #2.)
14. When patients with severe or late stage kidney disease that are not currently on dialysis and no
history of clinical HF have symptoms/signs of pulmonary edema which respond to specific heart
failure treatment then choose “3” (Possible decompensated heart failure) rather than “2” (Definite
decompensated heart failure) because of the confounding comorbidity of renal failure. However,
“1” (HF unlikely) should generally be chosen if the patient is on chronic dialysis and symptoms are
due to inadequate dialysis with no evidence of cardiac systolic or diastolic dysfunction or history of
clinical heart failure. Patients with ESRD on dialysis may be classified as “3” (or possibly “2”) when
there is appropriate supporting evidence for heart failure and the primary cause of the exacerbation
is unlikely due to inadequate or missed dialysis. Patients with ESRD and low LVEF who had
inadequate dialysis as the cause of volume overload should be classified as “1”. The following
hierarchy of supporting evidence can be used to determine the “diagnosis”:
 Heart Function including past or present systolic and diastolic measurements;
 Therapy for chronic or acute heart failure;
 Chest x-ray that shows pulmonary edema or cardiomegaly (pulmonary vascular congestion
is not sufficient);
 Totality of evidence.
15. RV strain noted in the case materials is insufficient to consider it RV dysfunction unless there are
further details suggesting RV dysfunction. If only RV strain is present, abnormal RV systolic function
is unknown.
16. If a patient has an acute pulmonary embolus resulting in right ventricular dysfunction, but is
without signs or symptoms, the patient does not have heart failure; the reviewer should choose “1”
(heart failure unlikely).
17. Patients with obvious HF signs and symptoms secondary to arrhythmia (e.g. atrial fibrillation) severe
valvular disease, or cor pulmonale, and with no documented evidence of diastolic or systolic
dysfunction, may still be classified as “2” (definite decompensated HF) is there is clear evidence for
right- or left-sided heart failure.

A4REF - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Demographic Data)

This file contains the demographic variables which should be
used in any analyses of the CARDIA cohort requiring stratification
by the demographic variables. The variables EXAMAGE, SEX and RACE
are based on the original demographic variables collected in Exam
1 and verified at Exam 2 for those participants attending Exam 2.
AO3ED is the number of years of education as reported at Exam 1.
A number of edits have been applied to this variable (see A4F03
documentation for more information).

In addition to the standard demographic variables, this data
set contains the date of Exam 1 (AO2DATE) and the participant's
birthdate (BIRTHDT) which was verified at Exam 2.

The following SAS code can be used to stratify the four
demographic variables on two levels (i.e., create the 16-cells).
The new variables are renamed RCCD, SEXCD, AGECD, EDCD.

RCCD = "WHITE";

IF RACE = 4 THEN RCCD = "BLACK";
SEXCD = "MALE";

IF SEX = 2 THEN SEXCD = "FEMALE";
EDCD = "< = HS ";

IF AQ3ED >12 THEN EDCD = "> HS ";
AGECD = "18-24";

IF EXAMAGE >24 THEN AGECD = "25-30";

Computed Variables
EXAMAGE - the age of the participant at Exam 1 calculated using
BIRTHDT and AO2DATE.

NOTE: There are 12 participants less than 18 years old and 46
participants greater than 30 years old. When age is used
as a categorical variable, these individuals should be
grouped with the 18-24 and 25-30 year olds, respectively.
When age is used as a continuous variable (as in linear
regression), the individual’s actual age should be used.

A4F02_- NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Blood Pressure)

The corrected systolic and diastolic blood pressure measures
have been deleted from this file due to a large number of
subtraction errors made in the calculation of these corrected
readings by the technicians. Please use the calculated variables
AQ2SBP and AO2DBP as described below. These measures are the
average of the 2nd and 3rd corrected readings.

Four corrected diastolic blood pressures were verified as 0
mmHg. These include ID=205417230658 (3rd DBP=0), ID=206137119651
(3rd DBP=0) and ID=400291323301 (2nd and 3rd DBP=0). The zero was
treated as were all other non-zero values; that is, the final DBP
measure (AO2DBP) is the mean of the 2nd and 3rd DBPs.

Four SBP measures and four DBP measures were calculated as
the average of one missing and one non-missing value. In these
situations, the MEAN function in SAS outputs the non-missing value
as the mean value.

Computed Variables

AO2SBP - mean of second and third SBPs (the SBPs for this
algorithm were calculated by subtracting the random zero
reading from the SBP reading).

AO2DBP - mean of second and third DBPs (the DBPs for this
algorithm were calculated by subtracting the random zero
reading from the DBP reading).

A4F03_- NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Sociodemographic Questionnaire)

For the variable AQ3SDGRE (highest degree spouse earned -
Question a-2, page 6), a code of 0 was used in some clinics to
designate "less than high school", while other clinics used 0 as
a missing response. This occurred because the code of 8, the usual
designation for <HS, was inadvertently left off the data collection
form. Thus, one should use caution in the interpretation of this
variable.

A number of discrepancies between reported education at Exam
1 and Exam 2 have been identified. The following discussion
documents these discrepancies.

1. The first comparison was made between the number of years of
regular school completed between the exams. Ten percent of
participants examined at both exams reported a lower number
of years of education at the second exam (69% of these
decreases were of one year).

Increases in education of three or more years were reported
by 2.6% of the cohort (71% of these increases were three
years).

Only two data entry errors were found in 362 of these edits
sent to the clinics for verification.

Participant records reflecting increases >3 years and
decreases >2 were compared to verify that the same participant
was examined at each examination.

2. Similarly, a comparison of the highest degree earned was made.
136 unusual discrepancies were sent to the clinics to check
for data entry errors. Examples of unusual discrepancies
include a high school degree reported in Exam 1 and a master’s

or doctoral degree reported at Exam 2 or a master’s degree in
Exam 1 and a bachelor’s degree in Exam 2. Seven total data
entry errors were found in three of the clinics. In addition,
one clinic recoded 29 of their 32 problem records based on
information written in the margins of the form.

3. Problems were noted even within an exam. At Exam 1, education
was collected at the recruitment phone call by asking, "What
is the highest grade (or year) of regular school you have
completed?". However, no standardized protocol was utilized
to probe for and verify that the reported education was
correct.

Education was also collected on the interviewer- administered
sociodemographic questionnaire using the same question. Only
73% of participant records agree exactly on these two
education questions (92% agree to within one year). of
course, it is to be expected that a few participants would
have completed a grade between the phone call and the exam.

4. Also within an exam, a comparison between the reported years
and degree can be made. These are the first two questions on
the interviewer administered sociodemographic form, implying
that some internal validity checking might have been done by
the interviewer. A range of 7 to 12 years of education was
found for each of the Exam 1 degrees except for the doctoral
degrees (the 13 with Ph.D.’s reported either 19 or 20 years
of education). It is important to note however, that the two
measures are not exactly comparable, e.g., a Bachelor’s degree
can be completed in less than the usual 16 years.

The lack of a standardized probing protocol may be the
explanation for these inconsistencies. One clinic has reported
examples of problems which were observed in reviewing some of the
records sent as edits.

1. Vo-tech/business education - sometimes counted and
sometimes not counted.

2. GED - sometimes checked as 12 years of education and
sometimes not.

3. College - specific degree given various years of "credit"
- e.g., AA degree marked as 13 years when finished in
less than the usual 14 years.

4. College - 2 Bachelor degrees, 20 years of education
checked. There appears to be a tendency to give people
credit for extra degrees that are at the same level.

These comments indicate that the problem is not restricted to the
interviewers only, but also to the participants themselves.

A4F07_~- NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Alcohol Use Questionnaire)

Skip patterns were not incorporated into the Form 07 data
entry system. For this reason, one should be cautious in analyzing
this data, qualifying responses based on question 1 when
appropriate.

Computed Variables

Total amount of absolute alcohol consumed in milliliters per
day has been calculated using the following algorithm for those
answering "yes" to AO7DRINK:

AO7MLALC = ((AOQ7BEER*16.7) + (AO7WINE*17.02) + (AO7LIQR*19.09))/7

Participants responding "no" to AQ7DRINK had AO7MLALC set to 0.
Participants responding "don’t know" or "no answer" had AOQ7MLALC
set to missing.

NOTE: In contrast to the above algorithm, the algorithm for
AO7MLALC used in Versions 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 slightly overestimated
the milliliters of alcohol per day. The algorithm used in Version
1.4 is thought to provide a more accurate quantification of alcohol
consumption (Dyer et al, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 1990,
in press).

A4FO9MED —- NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Medication Follow-up)

Multiple observations (up to 9) may occur for a given
participant ID in the A4FO9MED file, since a participant may
be taking several prescription medications. Typically, a
participant will have from 0 to 3 observations in this file.

In the A4FO9MED file, there are two text fields which may

contain missing values specified by either " " (blank) or "M":
AOSMDNM (medication name)
AO9MDRSN (reason for taking medication)

To test for both types of text missing values, SAS statements
modeled on the following should be used:

IF text_variable name EQ ’ ’ OR
text_variable name EQ ‘M’ THEN...

This version of the SAS file is sorted by participant ID,
medication type (medication follow-up page name) and
medication type sequence number (SAS variable names: ID,
AOQMDTYP, and AO9MDNBR).

Medication follow-up records with a medication sequence number
(AOSMDNBR) greater than or equal to "2" and having missing
values ("." or ".M") for all participant response fields have
been deleted from the SAS file.

The interviewer ID for the Medication Follow-up (SAS variable
name: AO9IVIDM), although defined in the Data Dictionary, is
not included in this version of the SAS file.

In Exam 1, the value of this field was assumed always to be
the same as that entered for the General Medical Follow-up
A4FO9GEN, and was left blank.

There apparently was some inconsistency among clinics with
respect to medication coding practices: some participants
had all medications coded, whether they were prescription or
not, whereas the same medications were not coded at other
clinics. Medications were coded according to chapter names
of the book AMA Drug Evaluations, 1983, included here for
reference.

Some of the medication codes were entered as 0 (zero), to
indicate a missing value. These have been left as zero to
facilitate verification and editing.

Some participants showed years and months of use of a
medication as 0 (zero). While this may represent a total time
of use of less than one month, it may also represent an effort
to indicate a missing value. This seems particularly likely
where the numeric classification codes are also missing or

zero.

Recently in papers submitted for verification and in
presentations using Exam 1 data, we have experienced a number
of problems with SAS algorithms used to determine whether
individuals were taking specific current medications (e.g.,
hypertension medication, asthma medication, etc.). We have
included an example of the SAS algorithm used by the
Coordinating Center to determine these individuals. This
example is used to determine which individuals were current
users of hypertension medication at the time of Exam 1.
(Note: these are SAS program statements. )

DATA A; SET HISTORY.A3FO9MED;

BY ID AO9SMDTYP;

IF AOSMDTYP=’HBP’ AND AO9IMDNOW=2;
DATA B; SET A;

BY ID;

IF FIRST.ID;

In this example, the SAS dataset A will contain X observations
(i.e., all individuals who reported current use of
hypertension medication BUT these are not X unique individuals
since a few individuals reported more than one hypertension
medication). The SAS dataset B will contain Y observations
(i.e., all unique individuals who were on hypertension
medication at the time of Exam 1).

This code can be used for all the other medications in
A4FO9MED by changing HBP in line three of the code to the
specific medication of interest (e.g., AOQ9MDTYP=’ASTH’ for
asthma medications).

Note, this may not be the only SAS code which will accomplish
this task, but it is the easiest we have found. This code can
also be modified to determine past users of the medication.
We would appreciate utilization of this code (when
appropriate) in all further analyses since it would expedite
the verification process at the Coordinating Center.

medication since first began use; in months.

A4F08 —- NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Medical and Weight History)

Sex-specific questions should have been skipped by persons of
the opposite sex. We have set these to missing in the SAS code.

The following discrepancies in the FORM08 weight data have
been discovered. These include:

The weight that some subjects listed as the most they have
ever weighed was found to be less than what they weighed at the
anthropometry station (n=782). The age at which subjects weighed
this maximum amount was also examined; a number of subjects were
found for whom this age was older than their age at the time of
the exam (n=28). The third problem involved subjects who answered
"No" to ever being on a diet, but "Yes" to currently dieting
(n=12).

The following suggestions regarding editing the data for
analysis have been made: (Note: These suggestions have not been
implemented in the SAS code.)

1) If the subject’s current weight is greater than his
stated maximum weight, and:

a. The difference is 15 lbs or less, then the maximum
weight will be replaced by the current weight.

b. The difference is greater than 15 lbs, then the
maximum weight will be made "missing."

NOTE: This will also eliminate unreasonably low
weights.

2) Regarding the subject’s age at maximum weight:

a. If it is greater than the subject’s age at the time
of the exam, and if the difference is 1 year, then
"exam" age shall replace the "maximum weight" age.
If the difference is greater than 1 year, then the
"maximum weight" age shall be made "missing."

b. If the "maximum weight" age is less than 10 years
old, then that age shall be made "missing".

3) If the subject answered "No" to ever being on a diet but
answered "Yes" to being on a diet now (unacceptable by

the structure of the questions), then both answers shall
be made "missing."

missings will be found for this question when the status variable

A4F13 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Cook Medley)

Computed Variables

A13SCORE The sum of the 'hostile' responses, derived from the
MMPI.

Note that for the first 50 variables, a 'true' response
is the hostile response except for variables A13SYMPA,
A13FRNDL and A13ANGER, for which a 'false' response is
the hostile response.

A13SCORE is missing when one or more of the variables
used to compute it are missing.

In the SAS data set, the responses to the questions
appear as they were entered by the centers and thus
recoding must be performed if the Cook Medley score is
recomputed.

Scores may range from 0 to 50, with higher scores
indicative of greater levels of hostility.

A13CIGMI The sum of the responses to the ten questions numbered
51-60 is a predictor of cigarette smoking behavior and
of the strength of the relationship between cigarette
smoking and myocardial infarction. (Friedman, GD et al,
Prev Med 12:533-40, 1983).

A13CIGMI is missing when one or more of the variables
used.

IF text_variable name EQ * ’ or

A4F14 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Social Support Questionnaire)

Computed Variables
Scoring
1. Instrumental and Emotional Support (Questions 1-5) - A value
of 1 is assigned for a "yes" response to "your friends", "your
spouse or mate", or "another family member". All other
responses receive a value of 0.
| Response Category | Value |
|---|---|
| |Yes | No |
| no one, you rely on yourself | 0 | 0 |
| your friends | 1 | 0 |
| your spouse or mate | 1 | 0 |
| another family member | 1 | 0 |
| you pay for help | 0 | 0 |
2. Network Adequacy (Questions 6-9) - Values of 1 through 4 are
assigned as indicated for questions 6, 7, and 9.
| Response | Value |
|---|---|
| frequently | 1 |
| occasionally | 2 |
| rarely | 3 |
| never | 4 |

In question 8, scoring is reversed.
| Response | Value |
|---|---|
| frequently | 4 |
| occasionally | 3 |
| rarely | 2 |
| never | 1 |

3. Social Network Index (Questions 10 and 11) - Questions 10 and
11 will be analyzed independently and as part of a combined
measure. The social network score will be derived as follows:

Analysis
1. Instrumental Support (Questions 1-4) - The sum of the values

for these four questions provides one overall score of
instrumental support. This score may range from 0-12. The
higher the score, the greater the level of instrumental

support. This cumulative score may be analyzed as a
continuous variable. Each question may also be examined
independently.

Missing data: At least two responses are necessary to compute
the cumulative score. When data are missing, but at least two
responses are given, two scores will be computed: (1) a "true
score" consisting of the actual point total of the complete
responses, and (2) a weighted point total. The weighted value
for any question is the mean value of the non-missing

responses. For example, a subject answering to questions,

with a "true score" of 4 for these two questions, would have
a cumulative weighted score of 8 for Instrumental Support.
If more than two questions are not answered, the instrumental
support score is not computed and is defined as missing.

2. Emotional Support (Question 5) - Scores for emotional support
May range between 0-3, with 3 indicating the highest level.

3. Network Adequacy (Question 6-9) - Scores in this section may
range between 4-16, with higher scores indicating a more
adequate social network.

Missing data should be dealt with as for the instrumental
support questions above.

4. Social Network Index (Questions 10, 11) - We would like to
examine the relationship between affiliation with both formal
(question 10 ) and more informal (question 11) organizations
with outcome.

(The above information was extracted from a memorandum from Leonard
Syme, Ph.D. to the Coordinating Center.)

to compute each of the above scores appear as they were input by
the centers. Thus, recoding must be performed if calculation of
instrumental support, weighted instrumental support, emotional
support, weighted network adequacy, or social network index are
recomputed in a program.

A4F15 -— NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(John Henryism)

Computed Variables

A15SCORE

John Henryism is measured by a twelve item Likert-type
scale, which contains five response options per item.
On the CARDIA form, the response DON’T KNOW was not
included (n.i.) and thus individuals had four responses
to choose from for each question. The score (A15SCORE)
is based on the sum of values assigned to the responses
for all twelve questions and can range from a low of 12
to a high of 60. If a response to a question is missing,
the score was not calculated but set to missing. Prior
to summing the values for the responses, recoding was
performed so the appropriate values were given to each
response. These were:

CARDIA JOHN HENRY
RESPONSE VALUE VALUE
completely true 1 5
somewhat true 2 4
somewhat false 3 2
completely false 4 1
don’t know n.i. 3

In the SAS data set, the responses to the twelve
questions appear as they were input by the centers and
thus recoding must be performed if the John Henry score
is recomputed.

Due to the change in format (omitting the "don’t know"
response), the CARDIA John Henryism score is not directly
comparable to the John Henryism scores reported in the
literature.

The following information concerning analysis and
interpretation was supplied by S. Leonard Syme, Ph.D.:

High scores connote physical vigor, tenacity, and a
strong sense of personal efficacy when confronting
behavioral stressors.

The actual score can be used as a continuous variable in
analyses. An alternative use of the score is to use the
median value to define dichotomous categories for
analysis purposes. Median values may be determined for
race-sex specific subgroups and for the entire group of
participants as desired.

A4F16 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Framingham Type A/B)

On FORM16, questions 8-11 (SAS variables A16TIME, A16LIMIT,
A16WELL) should have been answered by all individuals who were not
full-time homemakers. Questions 12-15 (SAS variables A16HWPRS,
A16DISAT, A16HSTAY, A16STRAN) should have been answered by full-
time homemakers only. Thus, an individual should have answered
questions 8-11 or questions 12-15, but not both. In some clinics,
many individuals answered both sections. To determine who were
full-time homemakers, the Coordinating Center program checked to
see if an individual responded that they were a homemaker (i.e.,
A16HOME=2) but responded negatively (i.e., 1) to all of the other
classifications to question 7; otherwise, it was assumed that an
individual was not a full-time homemaker. This information was
used in determining which variables to use in calculating A16SCORE
(Framingham type A/B).

Computed Variables

Al6SCORE The Framingham Type A/B scale is derived by calculating
the mean of the recoded responses for questions 1-6 and
either 8-11 (for non-full-time homemakers) or 12-15 (for
full-time homemakers). To determine whether a person was
a full-time homemaker, the program checked whether a
person responded yes (i.e. 2) to HOMEMAKER and not yes
(i.e. not a 2) to the other resonses to question 7. If
any responses in the appropriate set of questions for an
individual were missing (i.e. 1-6 and 8-11 for non-full-
time homemakers, 1-6 and 12-15 for full-time homemakers )
the score is set to missing. In the calculations, the
following recoding was performed for questions 1-5:

CARDIA FRAMINGHAM

RESPONSE VALUE VALUE
very well 1 1
fairly well 2 0.67
somewhat 3 0.33
not at all 4 0

In the calculations, the following recoding was performed
for questions 6, 8-15:

CARDIA FRAMINGHAM
RESPONSE VALUE VALUE
no 1
yes 2 1

In the SAS data set, the responses to the questions appear as
they were input by the centers and thus recoding must be performed
if calculation of the Framingham score is recomputed in a program.

The following information concerning analysis and
interpretation was supplied by S. Leonard Syme, Ph.D.:

Categorization by behavior type: Subjects are
categorized into Type A and Type B behavior groups using
sex-race specific median cut points. Subjects with

scores equal to or below the median are categorized as
Type B; those with scores above the median are
categorized as Type A.

Life Satisfaction: (Questions 16-18): Analyses of these
items are exploratory. Although each item will be
considered as a separate variable, they will be evaluated
as a group. Construction of scales will be explored.

A4F12_ - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(History of Lung Problems and Pulmonary Function Testing Results)

Both reconstructed and hand-measured lung function test data
are included in the Form 12 data file. This data is flagged as
such by the variable A12FLAG. Data was reconstructed for 291
Minneapolis participant lung function tests for which the original
test results were stolen (A12FLAG=R). Al2FVC1, A12FEV11, and
A1l2RATA1l were reconstructed from the ‘’percent of predicted’
reported to the participant in a results letter. These values were
taken from the Eagle II "summary" print-out thus reflecting maximum
values as chosen by the Eagle II. These are the only three
variables in the data file for these 292 individuals.

Lung function spirograms which were done without the aid of
the Eagle II microprocessor (usually due to malfunction), or tests
for which the microprocessor print-out was difficult to read, were
hand-measured (A12FLAG=H). For these 352 participants, only the
Al2FVCn, A12FEVn, A12FEV3n and Al12TIMEn (and A1l2MMEF from the
maximum trial) are present (although it appears that 25% also have
flow rates, perhaps entered from the pale strips prior to the hand-
measurement).

A third category of flagged data is designated by Al2FLAG=E.
A hand-measurement was made of the spirogram but when an operator
attempted to enter the hand-measured data, data already existed,
perhaps entered from a pale strip. For these 22 records, no
changes were made and the data is assumed to have come from the
original microprocessor strip. The note in the above paragraph
indicates that the program which set this flag variable was not
operable at all times.

Participant records not containing at least two trials of 3
or more seconds duration (n=296) were reviewed by Dr. Jonathan
Samet for judgement of acceptability. Most records were judged as

unacceptable (n=226) and have been deleted from the data file using
the Al2TnACC code (see SAS code).

Of the 5115 CARDIA participants, 29 participants did not
perform the lung function test and 226 records were judged as
totally unacceptable as described above. Thus, 4861 (95%)
participants have data for the three major variables of interest,
Al2FVC, A12FE1 AND A12RATIO.

For each participant, a series of summary measures have been
selected and are included in the data file. These variables
include the maximum FVC, FEV1 and FEV3 (Al2FVC, Al2FE1, Al2FE3) in
addition to the exhalation time (Al2FVCTM, Al2FE1TM, Al2FE3TM) and
trial number (A12FVCTR, Al2FE1TR, Al2FE3TR) of the trial from which
each were chosen. The reproducibility of these maximum values were
also calculated and stored as the volume difference between the
maximum and submaximum (Al2RPFVC, Al2RPFE1, Al2RPFE3). Summary
flow rates (A12PEFR, Al2MMEF, Al12FF25, Al2FF50, Al2FF75) were
selected from that curve identified as the maximum curve (curve
with the maximum FVC+FEV1). The exhalation time (Al2FRTM) and
trial number (Al12FRTR) of the maximum curve is also included.

In analyses you may wish to exclude certain categories of
flagged data. Flagged data should not be considered erroneous
although the summary statistics are generally incomplete, e.g.,
flow rates are not present for all H and R flagged data. For each
of the flag categories, summary statistics of the data for the
first trial are included in the summary statistics manual to assist
you in decision making.

When examining some of the small discrepancies in volumes,
e.g., FVC versus FEV3, and flow rates, e.g. PEFR versus FEF25, the
limits of accuracy of the Eagle II should be borne in mind. These
are + 3% or + 0.05 L, whichever is greater, for volumes, and + 5%
or +t 0.1 L/s, whichever is greater, for flow rates.

Also, when using the exhalation time in analyses, it is
important to understand how that time is measured. It is the time
elapsing between the start of expiration and the end of the FVC
plateau, i.e. it does not include time after the highest point in
the tracing (FVC) when the subject continues the maneuver but air
is leaking out around the mouthpiece. Since many of these young
subjects reach their FVC quickly (perhaps in 3 seconds), their
exhalation time will not include the portion of the maneuver when
they are straining to exhale the last bit of air and in SO
straining, leak air out around the mouthpiece.

A number of corrections/exclusions were executed in the
creation of the SAS file. It is important that you review the SAS
code for these comments.

A4F19 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Physical Activity Recall)

Several discrepancies have been found in the FORM19 data. In
such areas as “hours employed per day", "total hours of activity
per week", and "total hours of work activity per day", the number
of hours listed are sometimes greater than the maximum number of
hours possible (n=61). In other instances, the total hours of work
activities exceed the listed number of hours of employment (n=71).

One suggestion is to handle the data in analyses as follows:

1. In a case of total hours of weekday activities >=100,
total hours of weekend activities >40, hours of
employment >24 per day, or total hours of work activity
>24 per day, the entire record will be deleted from
analysis.

2. If the total hours of work activity is greater than the
number of hours of employment, and the difference is >1
hour, then all work-related variables will be set to
"missing".

3. If the hours of sleep plus activities (moderate, hard,
very hard) are greater than the maximum hours possible
for weekdays or weekends, then the entire record will be
deleted from analysis.

Computed Variables
Moderate activity per week is the sum of the moderate activity for

5 week days and the moderate activity for 2 weekend days, similarly
for hard activity and very hard activity. Total activity per week
is the sum of the moderate, hard and very hard activity.

Moderate activity/week = A19MODWK

Al9WDMOD + A19WEMOD

Hard activity/week = A19HRDWK = A19WDHRD + A1lQWEHRD
Very hard activity/week = Al19VRYWK = A19WDVRY + A19WEVRY
Total activity/week = A19YTOTWK = A19MODWK + A19HRDWK + Al19VRYWK

(Physical Activity Questionnaire)

Edit checks of the FORM18 data have turned up some
inconsistencies. For subjects who answered "No" to whether they
participate in a specific activity, several have values greater
than zero for one or both of the two follow-up questions. These
have been verified by the clinics. In addition, there are those
who answered "Yes" to specific activities, and give a number of
months in which they participated; however, when asked "How may of
these months...", the number given is greater than the number of
stated months of participation. These have also been verified.

A suggestion was made to handle the data in analyses in the
following manner:

1. For those who answer "No" to a specific activity, but list a
number of months of participation greater than 0, their
response for that activity shall be changed to "Missing".

2. If the response is "No" and the following number of months is
"0", "M", or "88", the response shall remain "No", and both
follow-up questions shall be treated as "0", (regardless of
the answer to the second follow-up question, which in some
instances is greater than 0).

3. If the answer is "M", the final response will depend upon the
answer to the follow-up questions: if greater than 0, then
the response shall be "Yes"; if 0, then the response shall be
"No".

4. When the second follow-up response is greater than the first
follow-up response, the second answer will be made to equal
the answer of the first.

In calculating the summary statistics for the data tape, the
Coordinating Center chose to compute individual activity scores
when the response to the first question was "Yes" or "M" and there
were non-zero responses to the two follow-up questions.

Computed Variables

Scoring is accomplished by adding a weighted sum of the number
of months for each activity below and again above the hours per
week cutpoint. Algebraically, where ‘m’ is the number of months
below the cutpoint and ‘n’ is the number of months above the
cutpoint, and the coefficients ‘b’ and ‘c’ are described below.
The coefficient ‘c’ has been selected to be 3*b for each activity.

Heavy intensity score = b;*m;+c,;*n,; for activities A-H

Moderate intensity score is similar in form, but summed over
activities I through M; the total score is the sum of the two
subscores.

The coefficient ‘b’ is the intensity level assigned to each
activity which is roughly the number of kilocalories thought to be
expended in one minute of activity by a 70 kg man. Intensities
were patterned after those used by Taylor et al and Folsom et al.
Exceptions are bicycling, which was set at an intensity code of 6
to reflect the wording "faster than 10 miles per hour"; and
vigorous work activity (which was not included in Taylor’s or
Folsom’s work), which was set at an intensity code of 5, somewhat
less than that for weight lifting.

D1REFA - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Demographic Data)

This file contains the demographic variables (age [Exam 1 and
Exam 4], sex, race, education [Exam 1 and Exam 4]) and should be
used in any analysis of the CARDIA cohort requiring stratification
by the demographic variables. EXAMAGE is the age of the
participant at Exam 1. EX4_AGE is the age of the participant at
Exam 4. The variables EXAMAGE, SEX and RACE are based on the
original demographic variables collected in Exam 1 and verified in
Exams 2, 3 and/or 4. Only participants who were examined at Exam
2, Exam 3 or Exam 4 have their demographic data updated. The
demographic variables for those participants who did not return for
the second, third and fourth exams are as they were recorded in the
first exam. AO3ED is the number of years of education as reported
at Exam 1. DO3ED is the number of years of education as reported
at Exam 4. Fourteen Hispanic race codes have been changed to
white.

This reference file is the only file in this version of the
CARDIA data that contains information on all 5115 original
participants; all other files contain only participants examined at
Exam 4 (n=4086).

In addition to the standard demographic variables, this data
set contains the date of Exam 1 (AO2DATE), the date of Exam 2
(BO2DATE), the date of Exam 3 (CO2DATE), the date of Exam 4
(DO2DATE), the participant's birthdate (BIRTHDT), which was
verified at Exam 2, Exam 3 and/or Exam 4, and the participant's
pregnancy status at Exam 4 (DO8PREG) .

This data set also contains scheduling information on each of
the original 5115 participants seen in Exam 1 (X4DATE, X4STATUS,
X4WINDOW, and X4EXPDT). X4DATE will be the same as DO2DATE for all
examined participants. If the participant was not re-examined,

X4DATE reflects scheduling dates or pending dates, not an exam

date. X4STATUS reflects whether a participant was seen in Exam 4.
An explanation of each code is provided.
CODE | EXPLANATION
E | examined
H | home visit
1 | For participants examined in a
2 | clinic other than their home clinic,
3 | this number reflects the site of the
4 | exam (1=BHAM, 2=CHIC, 3=MINN, 4=OAKL).
D | died prior to Exam 4
Z | death known prior to exam recruitment
U | uncontacted
P | pending
N | no-show
R | refused
L | lost

Thus, examined participants are coded as E, H, 1, 2, 3 or 4 and
those not examined are coded as U, P, N, R, and L.

X4WINDOW reflects the participant's window status as of the
end of the exam. (See the Exam 4 Manual of Operations for more
detail on window codes.) All clinics did not use this aspect of
the scheduling system for the entire exam, thus these codes are not
all accurate. If you are planning to use these, please contact
each clinic for more specific information on how this variable was
handled.

X4EXPDT is the target week for the participant's fourth
examination. This is a character variable and uses codes from 'A'
through 'Z ' and 'a' through ' z.' The coding scheme for each week
of Exam 4 follows.

A4HCY - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(Homocysteine)

This file contains the homocysteine measurement made from
frozen Year 0 samples of 805 CARDIA participants. To be included
in the sample, an individual must have been examined and had
dietary history data at both the baseline examination (Year 0)
and the third exam (Year 7). Participants with self-reported
renal disease were excluded prior to the sample selection. From
the eligible participants, approximately 200 individuals were

randomly selected from each race-gender group.

Samples were analyzed by the Nutrition Research Support
Laboratory. The assay used was a high performance liquid
chromatograpic mechod as published by Cornwell et al. This isa
nonstandard assay for homocysteine. If two readings were done of
the same sample, the value included in this file is the average
of those readings. For further details on the assay, please

contact the CARDIA Coordinating Center.

(Treadmill Exercise Test)

New Release of Version 1.4

During Exam 4, it was discovered that technicians from
Birmingham and Oakland used heart rates from the right side of the
ECG strip while Chicago and Minneapolis used heart rates from the
left side of the strip. The Steering Committee decided that the
heart rates from the left side of the strip were the appropriate
ones to record. Staff at the Minnesota ECG Coding Center re-read
the strips from the Birmingham and Oakland clinics to obtain
consistent heart rate information. These corrected values are
included in this version of the data set (A4F22A).

Missing Values

Although supine HR appears on Form 22, the data was not
collected and hence is not included in the SAS data set.

Values of 0O for heart rate (pre-exercise, exercise, or
recovery), SBP, or rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were set to
missing. DBP was set to missing if the DBP was recorded as 0 and

SBP was also recorded as 0 (or missing).

Variable Names

For each stage (#), the variables collected are recorded as
A22_S#. For example, for stage 2, the variables collected are
A22HRS2, A22SBPS2, A22DBPS2, and A22RPES2. These correspond to
heart rate, SBP, DBP, and RPE (a scale from 6-20) for stage 2,
respectively.

3/94

Change in ECG Criteria for Stopping Treadmill Test

During Exam 4, it was observed that many more participants
were being stopped during the treadmill test due to ECG criteria
than had been stopped during Exam 1. A panel of physicians
determined that the ECG criteria could be relaxed with no increased
risk to participants.

In order to make the data comparable, the Minnesota ECG Coding
Center reviewed the ECG strips of all participants who had been
stopped due to ECG criteria during Exam 1 (N=54) to determine which
participants would have been allowed to continue the test with the
relaxed criteria. The variable A22CRIT reflects this review with
the following coding.

Would have been stopped with relaxed criteria

Would have been allowed to continue with relaxed criteria

A22HRMAX: Maximum heart rate recorded for stage 1 through stage 9
A22HRMAX = MAX (A22HRS1, A22HRS2, ..., A22HRS9)

A22STGFN: Number of stages (2 minute periods) completed

A22STGFN = FLOOR (A22DURTN/60/2)

where A22DURTN = exercise test duration in seconds

A4FO6A/A4FO6VA - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Nutrient Data - Dietary History)

New Release of Version 1.4

During preparation for Exam 4, it was discovered that NCC had
modified the formulae for adding fat to foods based on the
preparation codes. The changes are based on laboratory analysis of
fat absorption in foods and, thus, are more accurate. The data
were re-analyzed with these new formulae and are contained in this
release. Thus, there are two nutrient data sets: (1) nutrients
with the vitamin supplement data excluded (A4F06A, variable prefix:
A06); and (2) nutrients with the vitamin supplement data included
(A4FO6VA, variable prefix: AV6). The SAS code and PROC CONTENTS
for these files are located in this section. These replace the two
nutrient data sets distributed in December 1989 (A4F06 and A4FO6V).

General Considerations and Comments

Dietary data were collected using a dietary history method.
Nutrients were calculated with Version 10 of the Food Table from
the Nutrition Coordinating Center (NCC) at the University of
Minnesota. Appropriate use of these data should consider the
following factors.

1. Absolute mean intakes may be overestimates of actual
intakes obtained as other dietary methods, e.g., 24-hour
recall or food records. This should not interfere with
analyses comparing means for various subgroups within the
CARDIA population. However, mean nutrient intakes of the
CARDIA population may be higher than that of other
populations if methodology other than the history was

used.

2. Nutrient densities (intakes expressed relative to caloric
intake) may be used to adjust for the tendency towards

overestimation of actual intakes in the dietary history
methodology.

3. Although group mean intakes may be overestimated, ranking
of individual intakes should be preserved. This permits
analyses of relationships between nutrient intakes and
other variables for the individuals.

The dietary history referenced intake for the previous month.
When average daily intake was calculated, it was assumed that one
month had 30.42 days and 4.35 weeks.

General information about the dietary interview, such as
length of interview and nutritionist's rating of the participant's
ability to recall information can be found in A4FO6A/A4FO6VA. Data
concerning dietary practices can be found in A4F06Q18.

Outliers and Missing Values

In accordance with the decisions made by the Nutrition Working
Group during Exam 1, we have made the following decisions regarding
outliers and missing values.

1. Include all out-of-range amounts in the participant
records. These values have been checked for data entry

errors and have been verified.

2. Do not exclude any participant from the data set.
Outliers will be handled in the analysis of the data.

So Do not impute values for missing serving amount or
frequency data.

Edits of Participant Food Records

Prior to nutrient processing, the participants' food records

3/94

were extensively edited. The following describes the edits done
for each of the data fields from the Quantitated Food Frequency
portion of Form 6.

1.

NCC Code: Check that the code is in the NCC Version 10
database.

Serving Size Amount: Check that the amount is non-
missing and greater than 0.

Serving Size Unit: Check that the unit is valid for the
specific food in the NCC Version 10 database.

Frequency Unit: Check that the unit is D, W, or M.

Prep Code: Check that the code is a valid code (APF,
BDF, BVF, NAP, PAN, SES) and that it is allowable for
that food in the NCC Version 10 database.

Fat Code: Check that the code is a valid code in the ncc
Version 10 database.

Average Daily Intake (calculated from serving amount and
frequency amount): Check that the average daily intake
is less than or equal to the maximum intake amount
specified in the NCC Version 10 database.

Processing of Food Items with Errors

Included in the data set is information regarding the total

number of food items reported, the number processed with errors,

and the number of food items processed for each specific error
(AxX6ERR1 - Ax6ERR16). The following are the error codes used:

3/94

Missing/Invalid Food Code
Serving Size missing

3 = Frequency Size missing
4 = Frequency Unit missing
5 = Serving Unit missing; Multiple Serving Units available in
database
6 = Serving Unit missing; only one Serving Unit available in
database
7 = Amount eaten > maximum allowed in database
8 = Prep Code of BDF for a vegetable
9 = Prep Code reported for food that does not allow added fat
10 = Prep Code missing or invalid
11 = Prep Code present, Fat Code missing
12 = Fat Code invalid
13 = Prep Code is SES or BVF but CP not valid Serving Unit
14 = Prep Code is PAN but OZ not valid Serving Unit
15 = Fat Food Code not found
16 = Fat Food Code does not have needed Serving Unit

Foods with Errors 1-5 are not processed when calculating
nutrients. Foods with Error 6 are processed with the default
Serving Unit. Foods with Error 7 are processed with no changes.
Foods with Errors 9-16 are processed without the added fat.

Computed Variables

A06PRCOR: percent of the total number of food items reported by the
participant that were processed without error(s)

A06TIME: length of the diet history interview in minutes

GUIDELINES FOR EXAMINATION #1

PURPOSE

The first set of examinations is scheduled over a fourteen-month period. Since this
will be the first initial contact of the participant with the clinical center staff, it is
especially important that this experience be viewed favorably by the participant.

The total time for the first examination should not exceed 4 hours. The results of

the examination will be sent to the participant's family physician if he/she so indicates.

PREPARATION OF PARTICIPANT FOR THE FIRST VISIT

All participants are required to fast from all food, except water, 12 hours prior to.
the exam; they should not have participated in any vigorous exercise on the day of the
appointment; and should not have used tobacco 30 minutes prior to the exam. The
participant should bring to the appointment a list of any prescription medications they
are currently using. Additional pre-exam instructions will be related by phone to the

participant prior to the day of the appointment.

STAFF PREPARATION FOR THE PARTICIPANT'S VISIT

In preparation for the participant's arrival to the clinic, a designated staff member
should retrieve the expected participant's file which should contain the completed
telephone interview. The staff member will then proceed to collate the CARDIA
questionnaires into a form set which will accompany and be administered to the
participant throughout the course of the examination.

Upon receipt of the forms from the NHLBI, each clinical center should separate or

package the forms according to the following guidelines:

FORMS

The staff member will collate the CARDIA form sets according to the center's
anticipated clinic flow for ease of administration. The CARDIA forms were formatted
and coded by the Coordinating Center and then forwarded to the NHLBI for printing and
binding. The CARDIA forms will be saddle bound (bound at the side) and printed on front
and back, with the exception of the Nutrition form. The Nutrition form will be bound at
the top and printed only on the front. Each form will be printed on different color
paper. Those forms that are bound together will have a colored top sheet but inside
pages will be all one color. Bound will be: Framingham A/B, John Henryism, Cook-
Medley, Social Support, and Drug Abuse Questionnaires. Also to be bound are: Weight
History, Medical History, Tobacco, Lung Function, Family History, and Aleohol Use.

The identification codes and labels to be placed on each CARDIA form will be
designed, prepared, and distributed by the Coordinating Center to each clinical center.
Only after the participant actually enters the clinic situation should the staff member
affix the ID labels to each form of that particular participant's form set in the upper left
hand corner of the first page of each form. (Form sets can be assembled at any time).
Once the form set is complete, the entire package should be placed into a notebook
provided for each participant. Each participant's form set should remain assembled in
the 3-ring notebook until the Data Editor has entered all of that participant's data.
Following data entry, the form set should be filed and stored.

The identification labels will be precoded by the Coordinating Center and will
consist of a one-digit center code, a four-digit participant number, a digit check number,
a quality control number, and a five-digit cross reference.

Extra labels remaining may be used if one of the coded labels is torn or if an error is
made. If an extra label is used in place of one of the coded labels, the code should be
written on the substitute label and placed in the upper left hand corner. Only one label

should be affixed to a bound set of forms.

GENERAL INFORMATION
The greeting is very important because it sets the tone for the entire exam. Each
participant has been told during the recruitment interview that:
* they are participating in an important new national study
* they will receive valuable information about their own health
* they will receive a specially designed CARDIA examination available at only
four centers in the United States
* if they wish, their physicians can be sent their test results
* they will receive a CARDIA t-shirt and lunch and may be reimbursed for exam
expenses.
In the greeting we want these general points to be stressed again, but each center

should do this in ways that are most suitable for their own populations.

Guidelines for the greeting and informed consent are listed below:
GUIDELINES FOR GREETING

Verify that the participant has arrived on the right day at the right time. If the
participant has not arrived on the correct day or at the correct time, say something like,
"Your appointment is not recorded on today's exam schedule. There's a chance we may
be able to fit you in today," or "our records show that you are scheduled for an exam
at o'clock. There's a chance we may be able to see you sooner." Then, consult
with your on-site clinic coordinator for further instructions.

If the participant appears to be ill, verify that he/she feels well enough to complete
the examination. One way to do this is to ask, "do you have a fever?" If the participant

answers "ves," reschedule the appointment according to local center appointment

GUIDELINES FOR OBTAINING INFORMED CONSENT

At this time the participant should be asked to read and sign the consent form. Each
center has a different form. It is not enough to have a participant to read and sign the
form; the participant must understand what is going to happen to him/her during the
exam and the risks involved. The greeter should make certain that the participant is
actually reading the form and then specifically ask if he/she has any questions about it.

aloud. If so, the greeter should read it aloud.

participant if he/she would like the test results mailed to him/her and/or to his/her
physician. The responses to these questions should be marked in the appropriate spaces
on the medical release form. If the participant would like the results mailed to a
physician, the name and address of the physician, as well as the participant's signature on

the medical release form should be obtained at this time. Results may not be released to

a physician without the participant's signature on the medical release form.

BLOOD PRESSURE MANUAL OF PROCEDURES

HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE (HYPERTENSION)

As blood pressure rises, so does risk of ischemic heart disease and its
complications. The range of normal blood pressures is wide. Even within the "normal"
group, risk increases as the upper limits are approached. Usually, blood pressures are
expressed as systolic pressure/diastolie pressure; values exceeding 140/90 mmHg are
considered to be hypertensive for adults. Middle-aged persons with a diastolic blood
pressure of 90-104 mmHg or greater (so-called "mild" hypertension) have a risk of heart
attack that is about 70 percent higher than that of persons with a diastolic pressure
under 80 mmHg (normal value). Persons with a diastolic blood pressure exceeding 104
mmHg (moderately severe to severe hypertension) have a risk more than twice that of
those with a normal value. Hypertension is an especially strong risk factor for stroke
and, to a lesser extent, for peripheral vascular disease.

Blood pressure is measured in a resting state, using 3 measurements with a random
zero sphygmomanometer. The random zero machine has two advantages over the fixed
zero manometer. Digit preference does not appear in the data, though it may still exist
in the reading itself, and be randomized out of the data by the use of the randomly
chosen zero point. More importantly, it deprives the blood pressure technician of
knowledge of the actual value, and therefore of the ability to make judgements about
blood pressure levels for readings close to critical values such as 90 diastolic. It should
be noted, however, that the random zero machines tend to yield blood pressures which
are about 1.5 mmHg less than those obtained when using a fixed zero machine. Within
person variation in blood pressure is substantial; 3 replicate readings tends to reduce this

variation.

BLOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT INSTRUCTIONS

The purpose of blood pressure measurements in CARDIA is: to compare levels of
this risk factor between blacks and whites; to observe the interaction with other CHD
risk factors over time; and to observe variables that will predict changing levels of blood
pressure.

Blood pressure measurements (systolic and fifth phase diastolic) will be recorded
with a random-zero (RZ) sphygmomanometer, by trained and certified technicians at
baseline and subsequent intervals. The methods of measurement will be standardized - as
set out in the Manual of Operations. The pulse rate for 30 seconds will be recorded with
each blood pressure measurement.

As many confounders of blood pressure measurement as possible will be controlled
by standard settings and technique of blood pressure measurement or by recording
uncontrollable confounding factors. So that the following will be recorded:

1). Time of day (AM/PM)

2). Room temperature

3). Arm circumference at the midpoint of the upper arm

4). Technician 1.D. number

The blood pressure will be measured three times on each occasion. Caffeine (from
tea, coffee, pop), eating, heavy physical activity, smoking (30 minute proscription) and
alcohol intake will be proscribed for two hours prior to recording blood pressure level.
The requirement for a fasting state in the basic exam will assure much of the dietary
compliance. Recording of current drug intake, including medications affecting blood
pressure, non-prescription drugs and "recreational" drugs will be made on medical history
forms on the day of the examination.

Detailed history of alcohol intake patterns will be recorded along with the nutrition

history because of the known, but ill-understood, relationship of alcohol intake to blood

TECHNICIAN TRAINING AND QUALITY CONTROL

Technicians will be trained centrally prior to participant intake in five half-day
sessions. New technicians after the start of the study will be trained locally by a
designated "BP Supervisor". Recertification will occur every six months with
instructions being found in the Manual of Operations. Prior to certification, each
technician will be tested for vision (reading) and with an auditory test (by Korotkoff
sound tape).

The Coordinating Center will direct a BP certicification committee to review six-
monthly data. This same committee will review three-monthly tabulations of blood
pressure levels (systolic and diastolic separately) comparing group means of each
technician with the values for all technicians by center and controlled for weight, age
and sex - by use of Z-seores. Arbitrary levels of Z-seores, (depending on experience) but
initially 3 will be used to flag possible systematic deviations in blood pressure
measurement by individual technicians. Digit preference will also be monitored.

CLINIC PROCEDURE

It will take approximately 10-15 minutes to make three blood pressure
measurements including the initial five minute rest and recording of pulse rate. The
blood pressure measurements will be made very early in the clinic visit sequence
immediately following the greeting and informed consent. Measurements will be made
before the physical exam, blood drawing, treadmill test, or any potentially stressful
interview. The blood pressure measurements on each participant will be make in a
separate room or, at minimum, in an area properly screened from all other activity and

other participants.

BLOOD PRESSURE TRAINING/CERTIFICATION

At the beginning of the first session, a description and demonstration of the correct
BP procedure is given. Trainees are to listen to the 1st (training) tape, taking the test
sequences until they are comfortable with what they are listening to. Then, they take
the 2nd tape until they have passed the test. After passing the second tape, they are
given the 3rd tape test. Alternated with the tapes are actual live practices under the
instruction and observation of the training supervisor. Some live practices may be done
with a standard stethoscope, but most should employ the Y-tube stethoscope. The
optimum size of a group is 8. This allows 4 people to do live practices while 4 are on the
tape training device. The group can interchange and practice on each other.

After the first day of training, each trainee should be given a cuff and manometer
(no stethoscope) to take home and practice just the control of the valve. This can be
done by wrapping the cuff on a jar or bottle and alternately pumping up and dropping the
mercury at a steady rate of 2 mm per second. After two or three sessions, they could
also be given a stethocope to practice on family and/or friends. This out of class
practice is very important to build confidence. This time allowed for class is not enough
without outside practice time.

Once each trainee has passed tape #3, he or she should do at least 2 live readings
with the training supervisor on the Y-tube stethoscope. The readings should agree within
4 mm and the average should agree within 3 mm. If they do not, the trainee needs
additional practice with tapes and live subjects. The training supervisor should also
assure that the trainee understands and follows proper procedures.

If the trainees are also to use the Random Zero device, additional time should be

4 and one or two readings with the training supervisor on a Y-tube stethoscope.

BLOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT PROCEDURES

TRAINING
Standardized training sessions are required for blood pressure measurement. Some
initial training sessions will be conducted centrally with subsequent training taking place
in individual clinics. Other training will take place in the Clinical Centers only. Central
training will take place prior to recruitment (Appendix 3).
A. Blood Pressure Measurements
Blood pressure observer/trainers will be trained initially in a central location over 5
x 1/2 days. Training methods consist of a pre- and post-test, audio cassette tape
instruction and split-stethoscope testing. Blood pressure observers will be trained
to observe and record the onset of 1st and 5th phase Korotkoff sounds. Each
clinical center will have one blood pressure trainer who will have the responsibility
for training any new blood pressure observers and for conducting recertification
procedures.
CERTIFICATION AND RECERTIFICATION
The Coordinating Center will notify each clinical center when certifications and
recertifications are required. It will be the responsibility of each clinical center to
conduct these procedures at the specified times and to notify the Coordinating Center
when the procedures are complete.
A. Blood Pressure
Blood pressure observers are required to be initially certified after training by a
designated trainer. Recertification is required every six months using audio
cassette tapes and double-stethoscope testing by a certified trainer.
EQUIPMENT MAINTENANCE
Each clinical center is responsible for the proper operation and maintenance of its

equipment. Maintenance responsibility should be assumed by the quality control officer

and all staff should be instructed to report any real or suspected equipment problems to
that person promptly.

All checks, inspections, cleanings and problems indicated will be documented and
recorded by date in a permanent log and/or electronically. Problems and solutions should
also be recorded. The local quality control officer will send copy of this log monthly to
the Coordinating Center.

An inspection and maintenance schedule is summarized below. Specific
instructions for the cleaning and maintenance of R-Z and standard sphygmomanometers
is found in Appendix 1.

A. Random Zero and Standard Sphygmomanometers

These devices will be checked thoroughly and cleaned if necessary every three

months, The R-Z manometer should be inspected once a week and the Standard

device once a month. In general, these inspections should include a check of zero
levels, mercury leakage, operation of valves, manometer columns for dirt or
mercury oxide deposit, and condition of all tubing and fittings. More specific
instructions are included later in this chapter.

STANDARDIZED CLINIC PROCEDURES

Correct measurement of indirect blood pressure is of the utmost importance and
concern to the success of this study. It is essential that the standardized format
described below for measuring blood pressure on the Random Zero be followed exactly.

Major differences in blood pressure measurement methodology among health
professionals from several countries have been observed despite the fact that written
international recommendations of blood pressure measurement were established in 1939
by a joint committee of the American Heart Association and the Cardiac Society of
Great Britain and Ireland. It is also well known that precision is essential for valid
comparisons of blood pressure between groups of people and in individuals on different

occasions. A number of elements can be identified in measuring blood pressure and each

6/85 BP-8

is explained briefly in subsequent subsections of this chapter ending with a subsection on
technique that is presented in detail. Study organizers consider all of these elements
equally important and ask that the strictest attention be paid to each in order to insure
that the blood pressure measurments have a standard and high level of accuracy and
precision.
A. SOUND
For purposes of this study, SBP level is recorded at the level when phase 1
Korotkoff sounds are first heard and DBP is recorded at the beginning of phase 5
with disappearance of sounds. The onset of phase 1 and 5 sounds are the points of
clinical importance.
B. EQUIPMENT
The following blood pressure measurement equipment will be used and standardized
for the study: stethoscope, random-zero and standard sphygmomanometers, cuff
and bulb.
1, STETHOSCOPE
A standard Littman stethoscope having a bell will be use. Korotkoff sounds are
best heard with the bell because of their low pitch. Stethoscope tubing should be
about 10-12 inches from the bell piece to "Y" branching. This length provides
optimal acoustical properties and allows the observer to read the
sphygmomanometer at eye level and in a comfortable position. Earpieces should fit
comfortably and snugly in the ears. Four points should be observed in using the
stethoscope.
a. The ear pieces should be directed downwards and forwards into the
external ear canal.
b. The ear pieces should be tight enough to exclude outside sound but

not so tight that they cause discomfort.

3. CUFFS AND BULBS
Clinies will have four standardized cuffs available - adult, pediatric, large adult,
and thigh cuff (by the Baum Company). Proper size of the cuff is essential for
accurate blood pressure measurement. To select proper cuff size, hold the end of
the cuff containing the rubber bladder over the upper arm and pull the other end
toward the subject under the arm. The top edge should lie within the range
markings for cuff size. If it does not, select the next smaller or larger cuff. The
range markings which are on the commercial cuffs actually overlap from size to
size and are not considered to be optimum correcot measurements. The pediatric
cuff should be used for an arm circumference (AC) of us to 24.5 em. The standard
adult cuff should be used for AC of 24.5 - 33 em, large adult cuff for AC of 33 - 41

em, and thigh cuff for AC above 41 em.

STAFF PREPARATION FOR PARTICIPANT'S VISIT

A minimum of three clinic staff persons will be responsible for measuring blood
pressure, They need not be health professionals, but they must be trained and certified
in blood pressure measurement and technique. Observers should have some experience in
relating to and dealing with people. While it is difficult to standardize demeanor, the
observer should strive to present a non-discriminatory, reassuring and professional
approach. The observers will be required to have a simple vision test in addition to the
training process. .

It should be remembered that participation in the study is a voluntary procedure.
Participants will be given full explanation and instructions about the preparation for the
blood pressure examination as well as an opportunity for discussion. The setting for
making repeated blood pressure measurments must be standardized for clinic visits. The
examination should take place in a quiet room where no other activity is taking place and
where temperature fluctuations are minimal. Clinic scheduling procedures will establish
consistent appointment times to minimize problems that stem from systematic variation
of blood pressure during the day.

Once the participant has been given instructions and explanations, the equipment
has been checked, and he has been sitting in a quiet and relaxing room with no change of
position or posture, blood pressure measurement can begin. The following steps should be
followed as precisely as possible.

1. Seat the participant with right arm on table. The inner aspect of
the bend at the elbow (cubital fossa) should be at heart level. (If the
right arm is missing or injured, reverse chairs and use left arm - noting
this change on the form.) Legs should remain uncrossed.

2. Palpate for the brachial artery (just medial to and above the cubital
fossa). Choose the correct cuff size and wrap the cuff on the arm with

the center of the bladder over the brachial artery. If the participant

PROCEDURE FOR RECORDING

If for any reason the observer is unable to determine (or forgets) any phase, write a
dash in the space on the form. This is the correct way to indicate missed information. If
an entire reading is missed, completely deflate the cuff and start over with a
replacement reading. However, under no other circumstances may a replacement
reading be obtained. Always wait at least 30 seconds between readings.

After averaging the 2nd and 3rd corrected R-Z readings, record the average on the
form. Provide the participant with a copy of the blood pressure measurement.
PROCEDURE FOR CHANGING THE PEAK INFLATION LEVEL

Occasionally the Korotkoff sounds may be heard as soon as one places the
stethoscope over the brachial pulse and begins to listen. If this happens, the observer
should immediately deflate the cuff by releasing the thumbscrew and disconnecting the
euff tube. Then have the participant hold the cuff-wrapped arm vertically for five

seconds.

USING THE CRONUS STOP WATCH WITH THE PRINEAS BLOOD PRESSURE TAPES

1. Turn on the stop watch and press reset button.

2. Start the tape, wearing headphones. At the beginning of each tape is a timing
sequence, with no Korotkoff sounds. When you hear the beep, start the watch by
pressing the button at the top. Stop the watch with the button at the top when you
hear the second beep. Record the time elapsed to the nearest 10th of a second on
the top of the student form.

3. Press reset button.

When the tape announces sequence 1, start the watch at the beep.

4. | When you hear the first Korotkoff sounds, stop the watch with the button at the
top. Record the time elapsed to the nearest 10th of a second. The watch continues
to run internally.

5. | When you hear the Phase 4 (muffling), stop the watch. There will not be enough
time between Phases 4 and 5 to record - so just remember that number until Phase
5 (disappearance). Then stop the watch again and record the remembered number

for Phase 4 and the final one for Phase 5 on the stop watch. Press reset.

Repeat steps 3 thru 5 for each sequence.
Remember that the tapes were designed for a special timing devie~ The answers
given will be double the stop watch values.
At the end be sure to turn off the stop watch in order to save batteries.
The cronus stopwatch, model 3-S, is an interval timer. Of the various types we
have tried, it seems to be the simplest and easiest to read. They may be available at a
loeal sporting goods store. The address of the manufacturer is:

If only Phase 1 and Phase 5 are to be learned, two ordinary stop watches may be

TAPES

There are a series of four tapes of Korotkoff sounds. Tape 1 is a training tape.
Tape 2 is a practice tape. Tapes 3 and 4 are test tapes. A new trainee should listen to
tape 1, go to tape 2 and repeat if necessary until passed. Tape 3 is taken as a test. It
too, may be repeated if necessary. Tape 4 is held in reserve for the six month
recertification. Tapes 3 and 4 are to be alternated thereafter for recertification.

Y¥ TUBE STETHOSCOPE OBSERVATIONS

Y Tube stethoscope observations should be made in conjunction with blood pressure
tapes during initial training and for recertification. The trainer should have the
observer-trainee go through the entire BP measurement procedure using the quality
control checklist (Table 1). The observer and trainer listen with the Y Tube and record
the values on separate sheets (Table 2, parts 1 and 2). Two measurements on one subject
should be observed. Measurements should agree within 4 mmHg on any one reading
(systolic or diastolic) and averages should agree within 3 mmHg. Additional observations

may be made if needed.

RANDOM ZERO SPHYGMOMANOMETER

Check cap of manometer column to be sure it fits properly and is tight. The 0 ring
or seal must be seated correctly. Clean cap of any mercury beads or dust. The cap
should be firmly finger tight. Any time the mercury seems to ‘bounce! in the
column of either a standard manometer or random zero (RZ) manometer, it may be
due to a loose cap. Check the opening. If it becomes blocked, the mercury column
falls too slowly due to a vacuum effect. This may result in false high readings and
an erratically oscillating column. This procedure should be carried out for both
standard manometers and RZ's.

Remove back of case (two screws at top of face and two at bottom rear of ease),
Swing back from the left around the thumb serew on the right side. Check for
spring placement — it should be in line. Tighten all screws except the one holding
the bellows plate in place.

Wrap an arm cuff around a bottle or can.

With reservoir, valve (newer models do not have a reservoir valve) open and bellows
valve closed, pump mercury to top of column (270-290 mmHg). If the mercury will
hold at a steady level for 10-15 seconds or drops 2-4 mm, that system is airtight.
With the high pressure still in the system, close the reservoir valve and disconnect
cuff to see if that valve will hold steady pressure. If a leak is discovered in the
reservoir valve, remove hose and valve (with Allen wrench). Valve handle unscrews
or lifts off. There are two 0 rings on the valve stem. Clean stem and replace 0
rings. Use stopcock grease on 0 rings and valve.

If the closed reservoir valve is tight, but there was a leak with it open, check the

inflation assembly. There may be a leak in the bulb, valve, or cuff.

To test the inflation assembly, immerse each section, especially valves and tubing
connections in water while the pressure is high and watch for air bubbles. To test
the tubing of the Hg reservoir, put soapy water on it. Most leaks occur at or near
tubing connections or from valves. If a valve leaks, sometimes a shot of silicone
lubricant on the thumb screw and worked in will solve the problem. Otherwise it
may need to be replaced Tubing leaks near a connector can be repaired by
removing the connector, cutting off 1/2 to 3/4 inches and replacing the connector.
Lubricate a sharp knife with soapy water to make the cut, and similarly lubricate
the cut tube to make it easier to reattach.

Turn RZ with back toward you. With bellows valve open, retract mercury to just
below the plexiglass valve chamber. Close the bellows valve, pump mercury to top
and visually check that leakage does not occur at that valve point. If Hg does rise
into the chamber, the valve needs repair. Replacing 0 rings on that valve can be
done locally if someone is qualified to do it. It is a more difficult job than on the
reservoir valve. Otherwise it should be sent to Baum. A serious leak in this valve
ean affect BP readings.

Whenever the manometer tube seems dirty in the area of your 'zeros' or if the Hg
seems to hang up there, the tube should be cleaned. A dirty tube can affect 'zero'
readings. To clean tube, set cam at lowest zero. Pump up, close bellows valve,
release pressure. This leaves little mercury in the column. Tilt manometer,
getting rest of mercury out of glass and into reservoir. Close reservoir valve.
Lean manometer at angle so that no mercury is in glass. Remove tube and clean
tube and seats. Check to be sure the rubber gaskets are seated properly. Replace
tube.

This procedure should only be done by a qualified person in a controlled setting.
The manometer should be set in a catch basin so that no mercury can escape and

there should be a trap-type vacuum pump available to pick up any small spills.

9. Check "maximum" and "minimum" zeroes and of bellows and cam function. (This
needs to be done only if there are doubts about the values of those zeros or
functions; or if Hg has been added or lost).

a. Release all pressure and open the bellows valve. The large thumb wheel with
the black rubber "tire” and the cam against which it is pressed should turn

freely without binding. If they do bind, bring in the RZ.

b. Inflate the system while watching the large (about 2-1/4" diameter) dise above
and to the left of the bellows valve chamber. (bellows valve is still open).

As pressure rises you will see the dise, a piston, pushed toward the back

plate until a ring around the center of the dise touches the forward rim of

the cam. That rim is tapered, and thus determines how far the piston can

move, depending on the position of the taper in relation to the ring at the

center of the piston — a matter of chance in normal operation of the RZ. The distance

that the piston can move before being stopped by the cam

determines the volume of Hg in the bellows chamber, hence the volume of Hg

left in the rest of the manometer.
ec. To read "maximum" zero, release pressure with bellows valve still open.

Turn the cam so that the point of its taper nearest the piston will be hit

by the ring of the piston. (It may take an inflation and deflation or two

before you find the correct cam position, which allows the minimum volume of Hg in the

bellows chamber, hence maximum Hg in the rest of the system.)

Inflate to about 200 mmHg, close the bellows valve, release pressure and

read the zero as usual; this is the "maximum". Repeat the procedure once

or twice, checking the cam position to make sure you get the same reading. Note that

this is not a fixed value for if you were to inflate to 300 before closing the bellows valve,

the reading would be lower; and inflation to 120-130 would give a higher value. For this

reason, always record what you read when taking blood pressures.
