BIRMINGHAM SAMPLING PROCEDURE

Our sample will be drawn from the City of Birmingham utilizing random digit
dialing. This method of random sampling is expected to produce a study sample within
the limits (45-55% race and sex split with appropriate age divisions) approved by the
Steering Committee on 3/10/84. There are relatively few Hispanics, Orientals, or other
minorities within the Birmingham area. We will accept a probability approach to achieve
a balance on such factors as SES. A relatively small percentage of CARDIA age eligibles
reside in group quarters (2%) which facilitates enumeration and identification. Our
sampling plan is expected to produce a representative sample of the City of Birmingham
with the only known exception being the exclusion of those whithout telephones. To
include these individuals (less than 10% overall) would require procedures expensive and
laborious, such as door to-door-screening, in comparison to the expected return.
Specifically, our sampling procedure is as follows:

1. There are 20 telephone exchanges (NXX) that include all the area within the city
limits of Birmingham. These exchanges are known to us. Several exhcanges
overlap the city boundary and will require screening by area in order to restrict our
sampling to the city.

2. We will identify from the Birmingham city directory (which includes areas not in
Birmingham) the range of working numbers within an exchange. This procedure will
reduce the number of non-working numbers given the phone company which will
reduce costs.

3. From a program available, we will generate 15,000-20,000 telephone numbers to be
given to the phone company. The phone company will identify working numbers and
names and addresses of residents. Unlisted numbers (approximately 10%) will be
labeled as "no information available" (NIA). The phone company updates their
information on a daily basis. Our requests will be made in four batches (organized
by exchange) to insure that the names and addresses are as up-to-date as possible.
It is estimated that 30 - 40 percent of the numbers selected will be businesses
which will result in approximately 9,000 households, of which half should have a
CARDIA age eligible. This volume is intended to ensure a sufficient number of
house holds to meet any anticipated shortfall within strata without the need for
resampling.

4. Blocks of 10 numbers from each exchange will be contacted until all exchanges are
included and then the cycle will be repeated. This procedure insures that no one
block fills the quota and that the different attributes of the several exchanges will
be represented and known. A sample of those telephone numbers listed as NIA will
receive a telephone screen to determine eligibility for and willingness to
participate in CARDIA.

5. Mail recruitment letters to 600 participants per month.
6. As part of initial call we will ask if respondent is located within the city limits of

Birmingham and if not, the person is excluded. This filtering process is cheaper
than checking address prior to calling.

CHICAGO SAMPLING PROCEDURE

The Department of Planning of the City of Chicago has divided the city into 77
community areas and maintains census data for these 77 areas. The Chicago Center of
CARDIA proposes to recruit its sample of 1,100 participants from Community Area 8.
Community Area 8 includes the Northwestern University Medical school and is bounded
on the East by Lake Michigan, on the South and West by the Chicago River, and on the
North by North Avenue. Based on the 1980 census, the population in Community Area 8
in Area 8 in 1980 was 67,167. Of this total, 62.7 per cent were white, 32.5 per cent were
black, 2.9 per cent were Hispanic, and 1.5 per cent were of Asian ancestry. It is
estimated that in 1980 there were 18,728 men and women age 18-30 in Community Area
8. By sex and race, it is estimated that in 1980 there were 5,453 white males age 18-30
living in Community Area 8, 7,2225 white females, 2,536 black males, and 3,270 black
females.

The Chicago Center proposes to recruit 275 white males, 275 white females, 275
black males, and 275 black females. If these four cells cannot be filled from the
population in Community Area 8, then Community Area 7 is directly North of
Communtiy Area 8 and Community Area 41 is the area around the University of Chicago
on the South side of the city. Community Area 41 will also be utilized in the event that
Community Area 8 does not provide an adequate number of moderate and high income
blacks for the sample.

The sample will be recruited using random digit dialing. Ten thousand phone
numbers will be randomly selected from Community Area 8. These 10,000 numbers will
then be divided into 10 equal pools of 1,000 members each. Sampling will be
accomplished by moving successively through these pools. Only one age eligible per
household will be allowed to participate. If there is more than one person eligible in a
household, a Kish table will be used to randomly select one person to be invited
participate.

In working through the first pool of phone numbers, for each household for which
there is at least one person age 18-30, one person will be randomly selected to be invited
to particpate in CARDIA. If the person randomly selected is present in the household at
the time of the enumeration phone call and is available to speak to the recruiter, that
person will be invited to participate, irrespective of race or ethnicity. As indicated
above, the population in Community Area 8 in 1980 was 95.2 per cent black and white.
We will, however, limit the number of non-white and non-black respondents examined in
the first pool to 5 If the person randomly selected is black or white and is not present in
the household at the time of the enumeration phone call, we will attempt to obtain the
address of the household so that we can mail a letter to that person about CARDIA.
That person will then be recalled and invited to participate. Non-whites and non-blacks
who are not present at the time of the enumeration phone call will not be recalled.

When the first pool of phone numbers is completed, the distribution of respondents
will be reviewed by age, sex, and race. If the first pool of phone numbers does not
provide approximately equal numbers of respondents in the four sex-race cells
adjustments in the probability of selection will be made. For example, if in the first pool
of respondents there are twice as many whites as blacks, then we will set up & scheme
through which we invite only one-half of the whites contacted. An attempt will be made
to accomplish this first, if possible, by recalling only a portion of the whites who were
not avaiable at the time of the enumeration phone call. For example, if 60 per cent of
the white respondents were not available at the time of the enumeration phone call, we

REC-4
6/85

would invite all whites who were present at the time of the enumeration in the next pool,
and, in addition we would randomly select one-sixth of the randomly selected persons
from these households for recall. All blacks would continue to be recalled. In this
approach, if the response rates are different depending on whether or not recruitment is
attempted at the time of the enumeration phone call or a subsequent call, because of
having received a letter about CARDIA, then we would assign probabilities of being
invited to individual phone numbers. For example, if we only wish to recruit half of the
eligible whites in the second pool, we might only invite those whites whose telephone
numbers end with an odd digit.

The number of non-whites and non-blacks contacted in the first pool will also be
carefully reviewed. If only 1-2 such persons are actually examined, then we will make no
changes in how we handles such persons. However, if 3-5 such persons are actually
examined, then we will reduce their probability of selection by assigning probabilities of
being invited based on the digits in the phone number. These probabilities will be
adjusted so that we take no more than 20-25 non-white and non-black participants. Since
this group makes up less than 5% of the population in Community Area 8, it is likely that
the procedure of only taking non-white and non-black participants, if they are available
at the time of the enumeration phone call, will not need to be altered during the course
of recruitment.

The distribution of respondents by age, sex, and race will also be examined as each
pool of numbers is completed. Probabilities of selection will be altered as needed to
maintian balance in the four cells. Socioeconomic status of the participants will also be
monitored as we work through the pools. If it is determined that the numbers of
moderate and high income blacks is inadequate, we will do supplemental sampling in
Community Area 41.

When a household is contacted, and the eligible selected is a member of the armed
forces or is away at college, the recruiter willask if that person may be contacted at
his/her base or school. An attempt will then be made to determine if that person will be
in the Chicago area in the next three months or before the end of the exam peiod.
Persons meeting these criteria will be recalled and invited to participate when they are
in Chicago.

The Chicago Center will also attempt up to 180 face-to-face interviews. Persons
scheduled for a face-to-face interview will be persons who completed the enumeration
and the short interview, but who declined the invitation to participate. These interviews
will be targeted at those persons who are most difficult to recruit, in terms of filling the
four cells.

Women who are pregnant at the time of the enumeration phone call, or who have
been pregnant within the last three months, will be placed in a hold file for recontact.
Women not currently pregnant will be recontacted in three months, and women who are
currently pregnant will be recontacted three months after the due date.

Each participant will be allowed a minimum of one 'no show'. If a person no shows
twice, he/she will not be rescheduled a second time unless there are special
circumstances surrounding the no show. Persons who reschedule their exams must
complete the exam within 3 months of the initial examination appointment. Persons who
come to the examination center but are too ill to complete the exam on that day will be
rescheduled.

MINNEAPOLIS SAMPLING PROCEDURE

Population description

CARDIA recruitment will occur in Minneapolis Census Tracts 94, 95, 100 and
109 (south) and 27, 28 and 32 (north). The combined population of these areas is
estimated to be 52% black, 46 white, and 2% other (Asian and American Indian).
About 1% of the population is considered to be of Hispanic origin.

In the seven selected Census area there are estimated to be 2,293 age-
eligible white persons and 1,775 age-elibible black persons. From the pilot
telephone survey, we estimate that 36% of these individuals will be made ineligible
by virtue of living in households with other age-eligible persons. About 5% will be
ineligible for all other reasons. This gives us a total of 1,353 age-eligible whites
and 1,047 age-eligible blacks. With a recruitment success rate of 60%, we will be
able to recruit 812 whites and 628 blacks to CARDIA.

Construct recruitment frame

A complete listing of households in the selected Census Tract areas will be
generated using maps, direct observation, and the telephone company address-based
directory. The address-based directory will be used to provide telephone numbers
for as many housing units as possible.

Sampling

All househods in the targeting Census tracts are included in the sample. No
sampling will be done within Census tracts.

Recruitment (Details in attached flow diagram)

A. The initial contact letter will be mailed to all 7,233 housing units in the
selected area, in batches of about 500 each month.

B. Census tracts will be ordered for recruitment, with recruiting completed and
eleaned up within each area pior to moving on.

Cc. Telephone and door-to-door (DDR) recruitment will proceed
simultaneously. Housing units with no telephones will be immediately
assigned to DDR recruitment. When no contact is made by telephone after
12 attempts (six weekday evenings, two weekday mornings and afternoons,
and one weekend morning and afternoon), the household will be assigned to
DDR Four attempts will be made on contact housholds assigned to DDR;
two on weekday evenings, on on a weekday, one on a weekend. If no contact
is made, a note will be left asking someone in the household to call the
recruiting office.

D. When contact is made with a household, enumerate gender and age of all

age-eligible (18-30 year old) residents. Select one respondent by Trodahl-
Carter technique. Interview respondent and recruit to CARDIA.

REC-10

5. Monitor recruitment

Monitor age, sex and race of selected respondents (refuse clinic, no-show to
clic, attend clinic). This can be compared 1) to the household rosters of all age
eligibles; and 2) to Census data in order to evaluate possible bias in sampling.

OAKLAND SAMPLING PROCEDURE

The sampling frame will consist of health plan members whose names are not

identified as Asian or Hispanic, aged 17-30 as of July 1984 in the Oakland residence area.

There were 35,733 health plan members aged 17-30 as of July 1984 in the Oakland

residence area. Information on address, zip code, sex, and age is available for these
members. Identification of names as Asian or Hispanic will be done by visual check. It is
estimated that 20-25% of the names will be identified as Asian or Hispanic which gives a
sampling frame of approximately 26,000 - 28,000 names.

1.

6/85

Selection of one individual per address:

Only one individual per address will be used for further sampling. To
determine which individual is to be included when more than 1 health plan member
has the same address, individuals who share an address will be randomly ordered;
the first individual at each address will be selected. We estimate that this will
leave approxiamtely 20,000 individuals.

Stratification by racial composition of zipcode

To insure a smaple with the desired racial composition, the individuals
selected in step 1 of the sampling procedure will be divided into 3 strata according
to the racial composition of the zipcode: predominantly black ( = 60% black),
mixed (30-60% black), and predominantly non-black ( =30% black). Estimates of
racial composition for a given zipcode will be obtained from 2 sources: (1) 1980
census data, all ages and (2) 1983 multiphasie health checkup data, health plan
members aged 17-30. Non-geographic zipcodes will be assigned to the mixed
strata.

Selection of names for recruitment

Individuals in each of the strata will be randomly ordered. A block of
individuals will be selected from each stratum and pooled. This pooled sample will
be randomly ordered to produce a recruitment list.

Recruitment of study subjects

Individuals will be recruited in the order in which they appear on the
recruitment list. If an individual has an address that differs from that on the listing
(e.g., away at college) but still considers his/her permanent address to be in the
Oakland residence area, attempts will be made to recruit that individual at the new
address.

The first recruitment list will include equal numbers of individuals from each
stratum. We will periodically monitor the race and sex composition of the recruits,
and if necessary, adjust the size of the blocks to be drawn from each stratum for
subsequent recruitment lists. For example, if we find too few black males among
our recruits, we will include more males from the predominantly black stratum in
subsequent recruitment lists.

RECRUITMENT INSTRUCTION MANUAL

The CARDIA Recruitment Form is used to provide the Coordinating Center with
basic information necessary to monitor the age, race, sex, education balance of
participants in the CARDIA clinics; to provide a check on certain aspects of the
selection and recruitment process; to provide the initial data elements in each CARDIA
participant record; to evaluate any medical exclusions from CARDIA; and to invite
potential participants to CARDIA.

The form has two parts, the first called Selection and Monitoring, and the second
ealled Recruitment Interview.

PART I: SELECTION AND MONITORING

PURPOSE: The purpose of this form is to monitor CARDIA participants. It contains
basic information about participants, including how they were selected to participate and
their final status. This information provides a basis for monitoring recruitment efforts
by centers. It contains information that will enable investigators to determine the
proportion of their study population that is of various age, race, sex, and education
levels.

USE: This form is used to summarize information obtained both during the
enumeration/selection interview and during the Recruitment Interview (Part II of the
Recruitment Form). It is not filled out in a participant interview. It may be partially
completed during the recruitment process, but must be completed for each potential
eligible within one month of the date of selection. Information from this form is
forwarded to the Coordinating Center upon completion.

SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS: There are 16 questions on this form. The information is
obtained from a variety of places, some of which are center specific. This information

should be available in part at the date of selection, except in Oakland where the

digit Kaiser ID, in Minneapolis it is a 10 digit number comprised of census tract,
area, sequential household, persons number, and in Chicago and Birmingham it is the
9 digit telephone number/person number. This number is assigned at an early stage in
the local recruitment process, as potential participants are identified, i.e. by
telephone numbers.

CARDIA RECRUITMENT INTERVIEW CORE QUESTIONS

PURPOSE: The purpose of the core interview questions is to obtain basic demographic
information on people whose eligibility for CARDIA cannot be determined through the
selection process. Some of these people will be actual CARDIA participants,others may
be determined medically ineligible or refuse to participate in CARDIA. The information
obtained from this questionnaire can therefore be used to characterize non-participants
so that they can be compared to participants. This information can be used to determine
differences between the two groups and to help investigators determine the extent that
selection bias may be present in the CARDIA population.

USE: This form should be completed once an age, race and address eligible person is
identified. The interview may be completed over the telephone or in person, i.e. at the
person's house. The core questions comprise a major part of the Recruitment Interview.

other eligibility criteria may be done.

1. PURPOSE
The blood drawing station is designed to obtain a blood sample to test for important
risk factors for cardiovascular disease and for other blood parameters of interest to
CARDIA. It is potentially a difficult station because of the anxiety caused in most
people by blood drawing and the potential for injury. However, if carefully and
professionally done, it provides a positive safe experience for the participant and for
CARDIA. Blood drawing will take about 5 minutes of the participant's time.
This protocol was designed as a training manual for the phlebotomist at the clinical
centers.
II. DESCRIPTION
A. TESTS
The following tests are planned in CARDIA:

CLINICAL CHEMISTRIES: glucose, uric acid, SGOT, alkaline phosphatase,
GGT, total bilirubin, protein, albumin, calcium, phosphorous, creatinine.
CBC: hematocrit, white blood cell count with differential.
LIPIDS: total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol and subfractions
(HDL2, HDL3), estimated LDL cholesterol, estimated VLDL cholesterol,
apolipoproteins A-I, B.
4.
OTHER: Insulin, cotinine.
The methods of measurement for each of these tests is found in the CARDIA
Laboratory Operations Manual and the Rationale for Assessment is found in the CARDIA
Protocol.
B. RESTRICTIONS
The Lipid Research Clinic's Manual of Operations identifies several factors which
may influence lipid and lipoprotein values, which should be standardized.
1.
A standardized seated posture will be followed. The adverse reactions which
occurred in the pre-test have warranted the use of a recliner, although the

known fainting).

2. Prolonged venous occlusion: Elevations of 2-5% can be seen after two minutes
of continuous tourniquet use. Therefore, trained, efficient staff and a total
tourniquet time of less than two minutes are required.

3. State of fasting: Clearly influences parameters such as triglycerides, giucose,
insulin. CARDIA subjects should have fasted for 12 hours (except water) prior
to blood drawing. Blood will be drawn on all participants, regardless of fasting
status.

4, Vigorous exercise should be avoided for six hours prior to the visit.

5. Subjects must have signed the consent form. No particular restriction need be
made for smoking, since the blood drawing station will be approximately one
half hour after clinic arrival.

6. Blood drawing should occur early in the CARDIA visit but following the blood
pressure measurement. It must precede the exercise test and the snack.

C. GENERAL PREPARATION

Site: The blood drawing should take place in an isolated room or one enclosed by
dividers. Temperature should be 65-75°F, There should be no direct sunlight. The
recliner should be placed in a space sufficient to allow the chair to fully recline. The
chair may be elevated on a wooden box to facilitate comfort of the phlebotomist when
drawing the blood.

The room should be equipped with all the necessary supplies. A work-table or
counter should be prepared with the materials and vials needed for blood handling and
aliquotting. The centrifuge, refrigerator and freezer should be nearby.

Staff: This station is staffed with a technician with documented class time and
experience in phlebotomy. The clinic supervisor or medical director will conduct training

for this technician. Recertification will take place on a quarterly basis and will be

2) Wrap a gauze bandage tightly around the arm over the pad.

3) Tell the patient to leave the bandage on for at least 15 minutes.

The venipuncturist should be alert to excessive bleeding. If bleeding persists
longer than 5 minutes, the supervisor should be alerted. Continue pressure on the
site as long as necessary to stop the bleeding.

PRECAUTIONS - IF A PARTICIPANT FEELS FAINT OR LOOKS FAINT

FOLLOWING THE BLOOD DRAWING:

A. Have the person remain in the recliner, recline the chair if necessary or have
him sit with head between knees.

B. Take an ampule of smelling salts and crush it and wave it under the person's

nose for a few seconds.

C. Provide the person with a basin if he/she feels nauseous.

D. Have the person stay reclined until the color returns and he/she feels better.

E. Place a cold wet rag on the back of the person's neck.

F. If the person faints, use smelling salts to revive.

G. If the person continues to feel sick, take a blood pressure and pulse reading.
Contact a medical staff member, who will advise you on further action.

17. HANDLING PARTICIPANTS WHO ARE EXTREMELY APPREHENSIVE ABOUT

HAVING BLOOD DRAWN:

Do not under any circumstances force the participant to have blood drawn. It
is sometimes best to let the participant go on with another part of the visit, and
have them return when the phlebotomist has more time to talk with the person. It
also helps to have the participant recline in the blood drawing chair just so the
Phlebotomist can check the veins in the participant's arms, without actually drawing
blood. If the participant has "good veins" the phlebotomist can reassuringly say,
"Oh, you have good veins; there should be no problem."

WITH THE AIDS VIRUS (HTLV-II)
DECEMBER 1985

The phlebotomy form is the only specific means by which the CARDIA study has to obtain
information concerning possible infection by the AIDS virus.

The form itself queries the participant whether he/she has had AIDS. The Steering
Committee has requested that this question be read as "Do you have any reason to
believe you have been exposed to... AIDS ?"

A positive response to this question of exposure should prompt the phlebotomist to probe
discretely for more specifie information, particularly because many people erroneously
believe that the AIDS virus can be transmitted through casual contact. We recommended
that the technician record any comments which the participant volunteers on the
phlebotomy form.

Besides the technician taking the necessary precautions, the phlebotomist should also:

1) Flag the blood sample in the same manner as other contaminated
specimens,

2) and most importantly, on the shipping form sent to each of the
laboratories with this contaminated specimen, include a detailed statement
describing the circumstances of exposure as related to the phlebotomist by the
participant.

This protocol is designed to give the laboratory enough information to allow for an
objective decision concerning their safety.

We are operating on the assumption that an individual afflicted with AIDS will self-

exclude him/herself. Parenthetically, current figures show that only 5-15% of persons
carrying the AIDS virus (HTLV-II) will eventually develop the disease.

IX. LABORATORY QUALITY CONTROL

In order to assess the reproducibility and validity of the measurements supplied by
the centralized laboratories, a split sample external surveillance program has been
developed. Its purpose is to produce data which may be used (1) to identify problems as
they occur and to communicate this information to the appropriate laboratory for
corrective action and (2) to obtain historical data about the performance of the entire
process, i.e. sample collection, preparation, handling, shipping and analytical
performance,

The quality control procedures will consist of split patient samples providing
duplicate specimens for assessment of performance. Duplicate samples will aid in
measuring 'within assay' or 'within day' reproducibility.

In order to accomplish these quality control measures, the duplicate blood
specimens will be interspersed among the blood samples and shipped to the respective
central laboratory for analysis. The sample is handled in the same manner as all other
specimens.

REFERRALS FOR SPECIFIC BLOOD TESTS
Chemistries:
In the case of the blood chemistries, repeat analysis on all tests with results in the
alert value range (as noted on the following page) should be performed by Bio-Science on
the same serum sample, if possible, or on frozen serum stored at the center. Calcium
and total protein should be adjusted for abnormal albumin levels to determine if they
need to be repeated. If repeat analysis is abnormal, a participant may be invited to come
into the center for another determination or referred to appropriate medical care. At
the Oakland center, a participant may be sent to the Oakland Kaiser-Permante
Foundation Hospital laboratory for the second determination.
CBC:
In the case of the CBC, subjects with abnormal hematocrits and white blood counts
would be invited to come into the center for another determination or referred to
appropriate medical care. Individuals with white blood counts between 11,000 and 15,000
would not need repeat tests if the increase reflected an illness which was evident at the
clinic visit (though, these individuals should have probably been screened out for that
visit).
Lipids:
As per the medical history protocol, subjects with a total plasma cholesterol of 250
mg/dl or greater and LDL level of 180 mg/dl or greater will be invited to return to the
study clinic to have these tests repeated. If repeat results are above these thresholds,
subjects will be referred to an appropriate medical provider.

the following individuals: R. Crow, G. Friedman, F. Gosch, R. Havlik, A. Oberman, S.

NUTRITION INSTRUMENT

NUTRIENT DATABASE

The nutrient database selected for analyses of nutrition data for CARDIA has been
developed by the Nutrition Coding Center (NCC). This data base is a food composition
table containing values for 60 nutrients in over 1300 items. Each item is identified by a
five digit numerical code. A maximum of four serving size units are assigned to each
item indicating the specific factor used to convert the nutrient values found in the food
compostion table in per 100gm amounts to those found in the specified serving sizes. No
conversions are necessary when serving size is expressed as "serving" since the food table
nutrient values are expressed per serving for these items.

Some of the items in the food table have one or more preparation codes, a three
letter code indicating the use of a fat in preparation and designating a pre-calculated
amount of fat to be added for each serving. There are four preparation codes for meat
(PAN, MAR, BDF, BST), two for vegetables (SES, BVF), one for eggs (EGF) and one for
recipe items (APF). Each code represents a preparation method specific to the type of
food and denotes differences in amount of fat absorbed by those foods. When a
preparation code is selected, it is always accompanied by a four letter fat code. Fats are
identified by these four letter codes in addition to the usual five digit numerical codes.
The letter code for fat is used only with the preparation code. The numerical code is
used to list fats separately such as to indicate use as a spread. With a few exceptions,
any fat code may be selected to accompany a preparation code. However, certain recipe
items may either require a specific fat code or disallow a specific fat code. When a fat
is not used in preparation, all preparation codes with the exception of APF may be
disregarded. If an item accompanied by an APF code does not include a fat added in
preparation, NAP 0000 must be substituted to override the computer rule for addition of

specified amounts of fat to these items.

6/85
NUT-1

An important feature of the NCC coding system is its specificity in codes for
individual items while also providing general codes for these items when detail is not
available. For example, there are four codes for chicken salad: made with mayonnaise,
made with mayonnaise-type dressing, made with unknown type of dressing and a code
without dressing so that a specific type might be added in an amount specified by a
coding rule. In addition there are over 40 codes for margarine covering seven ranges of
P/S ratio, and specific for five forms (diet, spread, stick or tub and whipped). Margarine
codes are identified for over 300 brands and include codes for each form when brand is
unknown. Oil, cereals, cookies, crackers and candy also have codes designated for
various brand names as well as codes for the unknown types when brands are not

specified.

FORMAT
The nutrition history is comprised of two parts. The first section, "Dietary
Practices", consists of eighteen questions related to fat use, consumption of "fast" foods
and salt use in cooking and at the table. This section was designed to obtain a maximal
amount of information about the participant's usual dietary practices with a minimal
expenditure of time. The responses obtained will be used to complete the second portion
of the form after the interview, thereby eliminating the need for repetitious
questioning. This first portion can also be used as a cross check on information obtained
from the second section of the history.

The second section of the history, "Quantitated Food History", consists of series of
questions about the usual intake of various dietary items, followed by lists of food items.
Questions were designed to standardize the interview and minimize inter-interviewer
differences. The questions establish whether a participant consumes a particular food or
foods within a particular food group, usual serving size, frequency of consumption by day,
week or month, and preparation method, if applicable.

All foods have been divided into food groups to facilitate recall. The food groups
are the major headings with items contained within each group listed beneath. In some
food groups, subgroupings may be necessary for greater specificity (e.g.,
"Grains/Cereals" is a food group with bread, cereal, pasta and rice as subgroups). This

The physical setting where the interview takes place should be quiet, attractive and
private, so that the respondent can feel relaxed and at ease. A small desk and two chairs

DEALING WITH PROBLEM INTERVIEWS

Most CARDIA participants will respond favorably to the nutrition interview. By
conveying a friendly, interested attitude and by proceeding through the history in a
direct but flexible manner, the CARDIA nutritionist will be successful in obtaining the
necessary information. Subtle cues such as a warm greeting, an occasional smile,
frequent eye contact and a cordial atmosphere are extremely effective in eliciting
cooperation and candor from the participant. A pleasant tone of voice and a sincere
interest in the person being interviewed will help to ensure optimal response.

Despite mastery of these interviewing skills and a working knowledge of proper
technique for administering the history, CARDIA nutritionists are apt to encounter
problems with some interviews. It is unlikely that these situations can be predicted.
Nutritionists should be ready and willing to adapt their interviewing style to the
particular needs of the participant. Simple changes such as increasing or decreasing the
speed of the questions being asked, shifting position of the chair or offering to repeat
questions if necessary may be all that is required. Consideration of whether the
participant understands the instructions and the purpose of the interview and also has
reasonable expectations of the time needed to complete the nutrition component are all
important factors.

Although the CARDIA Nutrition History documentation procedures have been
standardized as much as possible throughout the study, each nutrition interview is a
unique experience depending on the personality and perspective of the individuals
involved. Certain kinds of problematic behavior are more likely to occur than others and
nutritionists should be prepared to respond accordingly. Some of these types of problem

interviews and ways of handling them are summarized below.

INTERVIEWING PRINCIPLES AND PROCEDURES

Interviewing, in part, is a science: There are definite rules that produce valid
results. Interviewing is also an art: Frequently there are only general guidelines to
follow and much depends on the sensitivity of the interviewer. The procedures and
techniques that follow will help you to conduct interviews which will yield valid data.

L DEVELOPING A GOOD INTERVIEWING RELATIONSHIP

Interviewing is one of the major parts of the CARDIA study and therefore it is
crucial that interviewers present questions appropriately, record the participants' replies
precisely and accurately and probe meaningfully. In order to maintain an objective
information gathering atmosphere, the interviewer must convey that he/she is an
understanding person capable of accepting information in a non-judgmental manner as
well as convey an interest in what the subject is saying. The subject must find
satisfaction in talking to a receptive person without the fear of appearing inadequate.

It will be the interviewer's responsibility to obtain full and accurate information by
eliciting cooperation from participants, establishing and maintaining rapport,
encouraging active participation of participants' answers in a strictly neutral way.
Interviewers are skilled professionals. Their skills make it possible for subjects to give
frank, complete, relevant answers to questions.

In general, you will find that the majority of subjects are willing to be
interviewed. They will have received the CARDIA initial contact letter and are aware
that they will be called. We would like to emphasize that a confident, enthusiastic
approach which assumes people are willing to be interviewed is a most effective

technique.

Il. THE TWO MAIN KINDS OF QUESTIONS

A. Precoded Questions. With precoded questions, you circle the appropriate
code number (or check the right answer box). In addition to checking a box or
circling the right answer, it is very important that you record the participant's
verbatim response whenever there is any question about which code is appropriate.

B. Open-ended Questions. With open-ended questions, the question is followed
by a blank space for you to record the participant's answer word for word. This
kind of question suggests no possible answers, so it is your job to fill in that blank
space with the participant's own words and to encourage him/her to express ideas

as fully and as clearly as possible.

Il. INTERVIEWER ADMINISTERED QUESTIONNAIRES

There are several standard procedures for reading questions: Read in a natural
conversational rhythm and in a normal tone of voice. Read as if you are speaking. Be
cautious about reading questions too rapidly; the subject may not feel comfortable asking
you to repeat questions and consequently the answer will not reflect his/her true
thoughts on that issue. Be aware of the participant's facial expressions, e.g., puzzled,
confused. Repeat the question if it is answered inappropriately, but repeat it exactly as
written. Show no impatience when being asked to repeat a question.

Each question must be asked of each participant in the same way, and in the same
order to insure that comparable information is being obtained from all the respondents in
the study.

V. PROBING TECHNIQUES
The two most effective neutral probes are silence and repeating the original
question.
A. Silence. The value of silence cannot be overestimated. Many people, including
interviewers, react to silence as a vacuum that must be filled with constant
chatter. The interviewer who can wait quietly and patiently will soon find that 15
seconds of silence is more than most participants can take, and the participant will
often expand or clarify a previously inadequate answer.
B. Repeating the Question or Answer Categories. Be sure to repeat the question
as stated in the questionnaire. Tis is particularly useful when the participant
answers a question irrelevantly. In some cases it will be necessary to remind the

subject of your frame of reference, i.e., to acknowledge what the participant has

C. Do not Accept _a "Don't Know" Answer Without Probing at Least Once. If a
response is a "don't know", probe by asking: "well, what do you think?" or "I'd like
to know your opinion" (if the question asks for an opinion rather than facts). If the
question deals with facts, we prefer an approximation to no answer at all, and you
might probe "what's you best guess?" or "approximately?" to convey the idea that
100% accuracy is not required.
D. Use Neutral Probes That Do Not Suggest Answers. Probes are needed to obtain
more complete, accurate answers. All probes must be non-directive, i.e., the probe
must not suggest any particular answer to the participant. Probes should be used
whenever the participant is hesitant in answering questions; when he/she seems to
have trouble expressing him/herself; when he/she seems too shy to speak at length;
whenever there is any reason for the interviewer to believe that the subject has not
given a complete report of his/her thoughts; and finally, reassuring probes are
needed when a participant seems to lack confidence.

margin. Be sure to label these continuations clearly when you edit each

2. Don't ask "do you mean...". People tend to say "yes" to any suggestion
either because it's easy or because they think it's the right answer.

wrong part of the answer.
H. Make Probes Consistent with the Purpose of the Question. We cannot stress
enough the importance of choosing a probe that is appropriate for the particular
kind of inadequate answer given. Think through each response, evaluate it for
relevance and clarity and choose the right kind of probe. Any probe which does not
suggest answers and which is non-threatening is acceptable provided it is
appropriate to the particular interviewing problem.
I. Watch for Irrelevant Answers. Irrelevant answers can be interesting, but with
interviewers must bear in mind what we want to know. Acknowledge the response
and make it clear that you have been listening; also make clear your frame of
reference before repeating the question. Repeat the question word-for-word, but
preface it in such a way that you now need additional information.
J. Watch for Vague, Incomplete Answers. A probe such as "tell me more
about..."is effective.
K. Avoid "Depends" or "Qualified" Answers. When the participant gives a response
of this nature, we advise using probes such as repeating the question; preface the

question with a phrase such as "well, in general...".

L. Record and Document Fully and Clearly.

that you do not repeat them on subsequent interviews. Study the instructions thoroughly

INSTRUCTIONS FOR CODING OCCUPATION

During the initial period, until a determination is made on the final coding
procedure, the occupations of the Respondent, Spouse and Parents will be coded at the
Centers.

It is recommended that the person who is conducting the interviews on the
Sociodemographie Questionnaire be the person to assign the occupational code. The
interviewer will become aware of deficiencies in responses to the occupation questions
and will be sensitized to the need for careful probing for full and accurate responses.
Also the interviewer may recall statements that were not recorded but may provide clues
to the appropriate code in uncertain cases.

The basic resource for coding occupation is the Alphabetical Index of Industries and
Occupations, 1980 Census of Population, Final Edition, November, 1982. The document
is available from the Superintendent of Documents, U.S. Government Printing Office,
Washington, D.C. 20402, or from any U.S. Department of Commerce District Office.
(Prepayment is required if ordering by mail. Check price before ordering. For
information call GPO, Washington D.C. 202-783-3238.

A eompa ion volume, the Classified Index of Industries and Occupations, is
available from the same source.

Both indexes list some 20,000 industry and 29,000 occupation titles. The
Alphabetical Index lists titles in alphabetical order, the Classified Index lists them in
numerical order. The Alphabetical Index is the basic resource to use in identifying the
appropriate occupational code. The Classified Index helps the user understand how the
titles fit into the classification structure. This volume is also useful when dividing
between two or more categories. It gives a broad picture of all the titles included within
a category. This volume is also useful when deciding between two of more categories. It

gives a broad picture of all the titles included within a category.

6/85 INT-20

Both indexes are divided into two sections: the "white pages" list the industry
codes; the "yellow pages" list the occupation categories. Each industry and occupation
title has a 3-digit number or a letter which can be translated into a 3-digit number. Our
task is to identify the 3-digit occupational code which best fits the respondent's answers
to the occupation questions. Basically, the procedure is a similar to looking words up ina
dictionary. Once you get the hang of using the index, the 3-digit code is relatively
simple to assign for most cases. We do expect problems with a proportion of eases and
will set up a mechanism for resolving problem cases. Please note, the Industry "white
pages" has a section on SELF-EMPLOYED with an extensive listing.

The Coder uses the description given by the. Respondent to identifv the
occupational code in the "yellow pages". In those cases where specific industries are
associated with an occupational title, the Coder uses the industry information to select
the appropriate code. Industry information, even though we are not coding it directly
may help to identify the appropriate occupation code. Industry information is available
only for the Respondent. For the Spouse and Parents, the best we can do is to look for
industry clues in the description of occupation. If no clues are found, we will take the
most general or "not elsewhere specified" category.

The use of the 3-digit Census occupational codes provides maximum analytic
flexibility. The codes can be aggregated into a common system across centers or into a
system tailored to particular research objectives.

LIFE EVENTS QUESTIONNAIRE INSTRUCTIONS

In this interviewer-administered questionnaire, we will ask respondents about their
experiences during the past year.

SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
1. Interviewer instructions are CAPITALIZED.

2. Whenever "(MONTH/YEAR)" appears, give the current month, last year.
3. Ask all respondents the events listed on the first two pages.

4. Ask all respondents the first event listed on the third page of the questionnaire. If
yes, skip to section B and ask all remaining questions. If no, ask A: For any part of the
past year, since (MONTH/YEAR), were you married or living with someone in a
marriage-like relationship? If yes to A, ask all remaining questions in sections B through
E. If no to A, skip to section E.

5. Try to help the respondents move quickly through this interview. If he or she takes
a long time to respond, you may choose to say something like, "Try not to dwell on any
one question."

BE SENSITIVE; Remember that many of these events are quite painful. Try to respect
the respondent's feelings.

6. Do not define the events. If a respondent asks you for a definition or an opinion,
answer, "Do you consider it to be (EVENT)?"

GLOSSARY OF CARDIA MEDICAL TERMS

angina -- chest pain due to inadequate blood supply to part of
the heart.

aortic stenosis -- narrowing of the valve between the main pumping chamber
of the heart, the left ventricle, and the major blood vesse}
supplying blood to most of the body, the aorta.

cardiomyopathy -- a disorder in which the heart muscle becomes weak. This
may be the result of any of a number of medical conditions.

chorea -- (please see rheumatic fever)

cirrhosis -- hardening of the liver with the loss of normal liver function,
often as the result of excessive alcohol intake over a prolonged
period of time; may be due to other causes, too, such as viral
infection.

congestive heart failure -- accumulation of fluid in the lungs and in other
parts of the body as a result of a poorly functioning heart.

coronary occlusion -- blockage of a blood vesse! to the heart leading to death
of part of the heart muscle (heart attack, myocardial infarction).

coronary thrombosis -- same as coronary occlusion.

duodenum -- the first part of the small intestine. It is the part of the
intestinal system that occurs right after the stomach.

glomerulonephritis -- a kidney disorder characterized by inflammation of parts
of the kidney called the glomeruli. In its acute form, it is
characterized by the presence of large amounts of protein in
the urine, fluid retention (swelling of the ankles and other
parts of the body with fluid), and high blood pressure.

hepatitis -- inflammation of the liver, generally as a result of viral
infection or excessive alcohol intake.

hysterectomy -- surgical removal of the uterus (womb ).

kidney stones -- stones formed in the kidney, resulting form abnormal concen-

tration of minerals and other substances; stones can cause severe
pain if released from the kidney into an area in which they
block urine flow.

mitral valve prelapse -- an abnormality, usually harmless, of the mitral valve,
which is in between the two chambers of the left side of the
heart. This abnormality is found relatively frequently in
young women and usually requires no treatment.

myocardial infarction -- death of part of the heart due to loss of blood supply
to that part of the heart (heart attack).

TNHTA-41

GLOSSARY (2)

myocarditis -- a rare condition in which inflammation of the heart muscle
occurs, generally as the result of a viral infection.

nephritis -- inflammation of the kidney, occurring as the result of
infection or of a number of other medical conditions.

pyelonephritis -- bacterial infection of the kidney.

rheumatic fever or chorea -- an illness which may result from untreated
streptococcal (a bacteria) infections which is characterized
by fever, joint pain, and may affect the heart and cause damage
to the heart valves. If the brain is involved, chorea or
abnormal movements may occur.

rheumatic heart disease -- abnormalities of the heart valves (valves which keep
blood moving in the right direction through the heart) resulting
from rheumatic fever. These abnormalities usually do not
manifest themselves until several years after the episode of
rheumatic fever.

sickle cell trait -- a blood condition in which red blood cells have a slight
tendency to form sickle shapes. This conditions causes no
symptoms or physical damage, as opposed to sickle cell disease,
in which so many red blood cells can form sickle shapes that
anemia and a number of other medical problems can occur. The
presence of sickle cell trait can be determined by a blood test.

thyroid -- a gland located in the neck which helps to regulate the metabolic
rate, that is, the rate at which the body burns up energy.

valvular heart disease -- disease of the heart valves (valves which keep blood
moving in the right direction through the heart) which cause
the valves to malfunction. Valvular heart disease may result
from congenital disorders, infection, degenerative changes,
or rheumatic fever.

vasectomy -- a surgical procedure to make men sterile in which the vas deferens,
the sperm-carrying tubes, are cut.

THE CARDIA PROTOCOL FOR A/B BEHAVIORAL ASSESSMENT

The purpose of this protocol is to provide a standardized procedure for conducting
behavior type interviews and making behavior type judgments. Much of the protocol
includes procedures that have been used in previous research. However, because
CARDIA involves a special population of young adults, minor modifications in the
question content were made. A second purpose of the protocol is to document the
assessment methods for future use in the analysis, interpretation, and publication of
results.

The protocol is organized into three sections. The first section is concerned with
the selection and training of interviewers, and with the materials and procedures they
are to use. The second section is concerned with procedures for providing quality control
of the interviewing techniques. This section is divided into two parts: the first part
deals with a qualitative review of interviews by Michael Hecker, Ph.D. at SRI, and the
second part deals with a quantitative analysis conducted by Larry Scherwitz, Ph.D. The
third section, to be developed later, is concerned with the procedures for making
behavior type ratings from the audiotapes.

Each section is ordered according to the chronology of behavior type assessment,
beginning with investigator roles and ending with the final assessments of behavior
type. All instruction for intervieweing techniques and procedures for behavior type

rating are in the text.

b) ‘Training selected behavior type interviewers.

ce) Maintaining quality control of the interviewing techniques used.

2. INTERVIEWER CRITERIA AND SELECTION
Behavior type assessment requires that the interviewer have the ability to deftly
elicit discriminative expressions of Type A and Type B behaviors. An effective
interviewer must be able to bring out the Type A behavior in an individual whose
characteristics are less overt. Therefore, CARDIA and SRI have been careful in
selecting qualified interviewers. The first step was to identify desirable interviewer
characteristics. Accordingly, SRI provided the following characteristics to each
CARDIA clinic as criteria for inteviewer initial selection:
a) The ability to develop an engaging, assertive and professional style with
participants.
b) The ability to adhere to the structure of the interview, while at the same time
engaging the participant enough to make the interview relevant to the
participant's lifestyle.
c) Someone who is mature, 25-50 years old, male or female, somewhat hystrionic
and extraverted, able to maintian eye contact, somewhat Type A, smart, alert,
and not hostile; someone who can think on their feet, has a vigorous voice, and
has some prior experience with interviewing.

Each candidate was asked to do the following things during the 45 minute job
screening:
a) In order to see if they were extraverted and comfortable in talking with
people, the interviewer asked each candidate to describe their feelings about
working with people, their previous interviewing experience, and their general
work interest. To see if they had the personal characteristics noted above, the
candidates were asked to conduct a mock, spontaneous interview of the
interviewer regarding health, educational background, and present job. The

6/85
A/B-2

candidates were given 5 minutes to complete this mock interview.
Afterwards, without their awareness that this would be done, candidates were
asked to close their eyes and describe the interviewers gestures and body
language during the mock interviews.

Then, three questions from the structured interview were asked. The
candidates were then asked to read the same questions back to the
interviewer. Candidates were asked to query the interviewer again using the
three questions from the structured interview. The candidates were told that
the interviewer was going to: 1) try to take control of the interview, 2)
ramble incessantly, 3) give verbal answers that were inconsistent with body
language. The candidates were instructed to: 1) try to keep control of the
interview without resorting to hostility, 2) keep the participant focused when
rambling occurred, 3) use probes that were not in the script to elicit more
information to see if verbal answers would be given that would be more
consistent with the body language.

b) Next, to see if the candidates rated themselves as having Type A
characteristics, the interviewer read a list of Type A and B characteristics and
asked the candidates to rate themselves. The interviewer was looking to see if
the candidates that were thought to be somewhat Type A also thought of
themselves as Type A.

Candidates were rejected if: 1) they were not able to talk about
themselves comfortable, 2) they were not observant, 3) they were unable to
establish rapport, 4) they became hostile or were intimated, 5) were unable to
maintain sufficient eye contact, 6) were unable to probe spontaneously.

BEHAVIOR TYPE DESCRIPTIONS

Although the interviewers will not assess the behavior type, they need to know

what characteristics comprise each behavior type so that they will be able to

interpret observed behavior during the interview. Type A behavior was

summarized with the following characteristics:

1) Behavioral dispositions: ambitious, aggressive, competitive, impatient

2) Specific behaviors: tense muscles; alert; rapid emphatic speech; rapid
pace of most activities

3) Emotional responses: irritation, potential for hostility, and anger either
held in or expressed

4) Absence of excessive: anxiety, depression, worry, fear, nurotic

symptoms

It was indicated that the Type B is more than the absence of Type A in at least two

important ways. First, Type B's do not find themselves as frequently in situations

that normally elicit Type A behavior. Second, Type B's have different perceptions

and coping responses than Type A's.

GAINING RAPPORT, ELICITING RESPONSES, AND STIMULATING THE
PARTICIPANT
The following instructions to interviewers were derived from the three-day
training sessions, and from new information from the MRFIT study about
appropriate interviewing styles.

It is important to get the participants involved in the content of the

questions so that they will review their memories, and have the content of

A/B-5

these memories connect with their feelings. It is also important that the
participants feel positively toward the interviewer so that they will share their
feelings. While the interviewer has to be the judge of what will work in a
particular situation, there are some techniques that effectively engage the
subjects:
1) The interviewer should focus on being a good listener and a good
observer. Although the interviewer may refer to the interview script
while conducting the interview, all of the interviewer's attention should
concentrate on what the participant is saying. Nonverbal expressions
may be used to empathize with the participant's feelings: maintaining
eye contact, nodding, acknowledging what the subject says (e.g., "That's
interesting.").
2) Whenever possible, the questions should be made contingent upon what
the participant has just said or how he/she reacted to a particular
question. The interviewer should follow up with open-ended questions
when the participant is not generating enough speech material (a full
sentence or more).
3) The participant's first name should be used two or three times during the
interview. This serves to personalize the interview, and to show that the
interviewer regards the participant as an individual (not just an ID
number).
4) The participant's interest and involvement may be increased by referring
to his or her own answer content or expressions of feelings.
5) Because the interviewer's feelings about a participant could be a bias,
feelings must be carefully monitored so that they do not affect the
interviewer's verbal or nonverbal behaviors. And especially, the
interviewer must not act differently for Type A's than for Type B's.

6/85

Questions must not be asked faster just because the participant is
answering them faster. Questions must not be asked more emphatically
of Type B's than of Type A's to provoke them into becoming Type A's.
The interviewer must not distract the participant's attention with
repetitive movements or other distracting behaviors while the subject is
answering.
6) If the participant volunteers material that a subsequent question asks, it
is better to either acknowledge the previous answer or probe deeper than
to ask the question again, which could communicate to the participant
that the interviewer either wasn't listening or is mechanically going
through the interview. If the participant thoroughly answered the

7) If the participant asks a question of the interviewer, the interviewer
should respond in a way that will neither encourage further questions nor

clarification. If a participant asks, "Why are you taping this interview?",

participant's lifestyle, or smile and avoid an answer.
8) When the interviewer is talking more than the participant, the

9) If a participant seriously objects to a particular question, let that

PREFACE TO INTERVIEW SCRIPT
The interview questions are a guide to aid interviewers in covering all

the SI topic areas; interviewers should take care not to follow the script too

rigidly, but to adapt the questions to fit the participants’ lifestyles, and to use
the participants’ actual answer content to develop spontaneous probes for
further information.

One of the most important questions in the interviewer is, "What kind of
work do you do?" and the probes following this question. It is important
because:

1) ‘It is the beginning of the interview, a time where the interviewer must
be careful not to slip into a pattern of mechanical questions asking or
hurrying though the interview.

2)‘ The interviewer needs to know what activities the participant is doing so
that they will know how to phrase subsequent questions.

3) It is a good time to gain rapport because most participants are interested
in their major daily activity.

4) The interviewer needs to consider the participant's answers to think
about how to phrase subsequent questions and to find clues about what
activities grab the participant's interest.

A creative task for the interviewer is to find the participant's major daily

activity when they are not working nor going to school full time. The general

strategy is to find out the activity participants normally engage in and base
the work-oriented questions upon this activitv. Listed below are some general
guidelines:

1) A job will qualify as a major activity if they did it for 2 months or more.

2) If the job is important and you can see that they were invested in the

CHANGES IN STRUCTURED INTERVIEW PROTOCOL

After the first batch of interviews was conducted and sent to SRI and UCSF
for auditing, the decision was made to change the interview script and some
aspects of the procedure so as to better approximate the interviewer style and
participant response in the WCGS. In this section the rationale for that change
is given.

The objective of administering the Type A Structured Interview (SI) is to
assess Type A behavior as it was measured in the Western Collaborative Group
Study (WCGS). In the course of training the CARDIA interviewers and auditing
their practice interviews, it became apparent that certain changes in the SI
protocol would facilitate administering the SI in the style of the WCGS
interviews while staying within the limitations of the CARDIA examination.

Specifically, in the WCGS interviews the interviewer adapted the
wording of the written questions to the participant's personal situation in order
to make the questions more appropriate and meaningful for the participant.
The purpose of this adaptation, which did not change the intent of the

questions, was to increase the ability of interviewers to build and maintain

A/B-11

6/85

good rapport with the participants. The WCGS subjects were middle-aged
employed men, and the questions were designed to be appropriate for that
population. Because the CARDIA participants are younger and have less work
experience, some changes in the written questions were made to assist the
interviewers in adapting the questions to the CARDIA participants. Although
the CARDIA interviewers were trained to adapt the wording of the questions,
as was done in the WCGS, their practice interviews administered after training
showed that the extent of the required adaptation was considerable and that
additional changes in the written questions were necessary.

As in the WCGS, the changes in the SI protocol for CARDIA are directed
at making the interview relevant to the participants while maintaining the
intent of the questions. These changes included modifying certain questions to
make them reflect informal spoken language, as used in conversation, rather
than formal written language. While the questions used in the WCGS primarily
addressed middle-aged workers, the modified questions are designed to be
more appropriate for the CARDIA population. In addition, the structure of
some questions was made more open-ended so that participants would be more
responsive, as was the case in the WCGS interviews.

Other changes in the SI protocol are directed toward keeping to the time
limitations of the CARDIA examination. Unlike the WCGS interviews, which
had a less stringent time limit, the CARDIA interviews must not exceed an
average duration of 12 minutes. The previously described changes will provide
a more valid assessment of Type A behavior than that afforded by simply
reading the questions as they are written. However, the changes are likely to
increase the length of the interview. In order to compensate for this
anticipated increase, certain questions that were found to be inappropriate for

the CARDIA population during pilot testing were deleted from the protocol.

A/B-12

These questions not only failed to elicit meaningful responses from most
participants, but their presence interfered with the establishment of rapport.
Despite the removal of these questions, it is likely that the interviews will be
slightly longer than desired while the CARDIA interviewers become familiar
with the new protocol. Once this familiarity is achieved, however, the
interviewers should be able to administer the SI within the allotted 12 minutes
while following the style of the WCGS interviews.

QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS OF INTERVIEWER STYLE BY DR. LARRY SCHERWITZ

As part of an intensive analysis of MRFIT and WCGS structured interviews to
assess Type A behavior, Dr. Scherwitz and his colleagues have uncovered clues which
suggest that some interviewers’ assessments of Type Al's (when compared with A2's,
X's and B's) are more predictive of CHD than others. Within MRFIT, he has found
the "more predictive" interviewers to speak more slowly when asking questions, and
to be less empathetic. In addition, a pilot study indicated that the more predictive
interviewers asked more non-structured questions and interrupted less often than the
"less predictive" interviewers. Clinically, auditors described the more predictive
interviewers as more friendly, and the less predictive interviewers as more irritating
though easy to score (because they mechanically followed the protocol and elicited
so little speech from the participants).

More importantly, the differences within the MRFIT interviewers are
consistent with the even larger differences in interviewer style between MRFIT and
WCGS. Asa result of these clues, Dr. Scherwitz trained his interviewers at Pacific
Medical Center to be more engaging in their style by asking more nonstandard
questions and disrupting the subjects less often than they were originally trained.
Recently their assessments of Type A behavior from 156 male and female patients
were found to be positively correlated with angiographically determined coronary
artery disease severity.

Based upon the above clues, Dr. Scherwitz has developed a quantitative

A/B-15

measure of interviewer behaviors that may reflect the predictiveness of their
assessments. These measures, referred to collectively as "interviewer engagement",
are being used to score 627 MRFIT interviews. They are also the measures that will
be used to score the CARDIA interviews:
a) Speed of asking questions
b) Speed of speaking when asking questions
c) Number of times the interviewer interrupts the subject.
d) Number of standard probes (indicated on script) and nonstandard probes
(tailored to the subjects' answers) used.
e) Number of times the interviewer acknowledges the subject's answers.

Interviews will be scored on a regular basis (at least one interview per
interviewer for each batch) throughout the data collection period, with closer
monitoring in the early stages.
The quantitative scores will be compared with similar scores from MRFIT.
The goal is to have the CARDIA interviewers more engaging than the MRFIT
interviewers.

OVERVIEW

While increases in coronary heart disease risk factors occur in young adulthood in
eonjunetion with significant changes in physiological measures and in lifestyle, the
interrelationships among these risk factors and changes have not been rigorously
investigated. Both epidemiologic and clinical research in coronary heart disease have
increased our awareness that some risk factors for disease such as obesity, hypertension,
and hypercholesterolemia may be partially determined by genetic factors or behaviors
which are formed in infancy, childhood, and adolescence. Studies to date also suggest
that some of the coronary heart disease risk factors do not change dramatically before
the late teenage years and that differences in characteristics by sex or race emerge and
are most pronounced after this time. However, relatively little work has been done to
identify the characteristics of young adult life which may be precursors to, or coincident
with, the increase in risk factors prior to middle age.

Cross-sectional data, for example, suggest that weight gain is pronounced during
the late teens through age 30, particularly in males, and that positive relationships exist
between weight and lipoprotein fractions during these ages. The reasons for, and
consequences of, this increase in adiposity need further investigation. The interaction of
life events, behavior, changes in physical activity, and dietary intake that may influence
weight gain and lipoprotein levels should be assessed as well as the relative importance
of weight gain in relationship to risk factor changes during this age span.

Investigators have examined the consistency of blood pressure levels in children to
determine whether "tracking" oecurs into the teenage years. The results of these studies
have raised other interesting and important questions. Is there evidence for "tracking" of
other coronary risk factors? Does "tracking" persist into young adult life, a time during
which dramatie changes in lifestyle are often taking place? Are the changes a function
of these changes?

An important component of this study is the study of young blacks. Since the
Black Health Task Force on High Blood Pressure Control pointed out the lack of
knowledge about coronary heart disease in blacks as applied to this country, a greater
focus on the nature of disease in blacks has been a topic of increasing consideration.

"Coronary Artery Risk Factor Development in Young Adults" (CARDIA) is the
study of the evolution of coronary heart disease risk in a cohort of black and white men
and women initially 18-30 years old. Such studies will not only contribute to our
understanding of the development of atherosclerotic disease, but more importantly, help
to suggest strategies for prevention before individual lifestyle patterns become well
established.

OBJECTIVES

Overall Goals

1.

To document at baseline and after one or more biannual intervals, risk factors and
changes for coronary heart disease (CHD) in young (black and white) adults, 18-30

To identify lifestyles during this age span, which influence these changes in risk
factors. The interrelationships among risk factors and lifestyles, and changes in
these characteristics will be considered.

The Secondary Objectives of this Study are:

1.

To observe age-related trends in risk factors during young adulthood and to
compare cross-sectional with longitudinal findings

To perform subpopulation analyses on, sex, race, or sociodemographic groupings,
and to compare trends and processes involved in risk factor development between
these subgroups

To develop and apply effective methods of follow-up during these young adult
years to achieve maximum participation of the study populations.

Objectives of each Clinical Center

race and sex

To recruit and enroll at least 1100 of those identified, willing to participate and

To maintain, via mail and phone calls at semiannual intervals during the two year

ADMINISTRATIVE STRUCTURE

The Steering Committee is the representative body of the CARDIA study and is
supported by ten working groups: Blood Chemistry, Blood Pressure, Data Management,
Nutrition, Exercise, Lipids, Medical History, Objective Smoking, Psychosocial, and
Sampling/Recruitment/Consent. The working group members were assigned from a pool
of experts consisting of Principal Investigators, Clinical Center personnel, Coordinating
Center personnel, and consultants as needed. There is an NHLBI representative on each
working group. All working groups have specific responsibilities for the conduct of all
phases of the study and will assume such other responsibilities as requested by the
Steering Committee.

Role and Composition of Steering Committee

The Steering Committee is the representative body of all investigators (Table 1).
It is composed of six voting members: the Principal Investigator from each of the four
clinical centers, the Director of the Coordinating Center and the NHLBI project
officer. The Steering Committee provides overall scientific direction for the study
through consideration of recommendations flowing to it from the working groups and
others as appropriate. The Chairperson of the Steering Committee is the NHLBI Project
Officer.

The Steering Committee will meet regularly to review study progress. Each
center is required to be represented by an investigator, or by proxy, at each meeting of
this committee. If a vote is needed, it will require a two-thirds majority of all six
voting members, Minutes will be taken by a member of the Coordinating Center.

The Steering Committee will perform the following functions:

1. Guide and oversee the development of the Study Protocol and the Manual
of Operations

2. Review and approve major changes in the Manual of Operations

3. Review and approve ancillary studies

4. Provide advice and assistance to the Coordinating Center, clinical centers

or NHLBI on operational matters.

5. Resolve problems brought to the Steering Committee by investigators, the
Coordinating Center, and any other of the Central units (Central labs,
NHLBI, etc.)

6. Monitor the performance of all participating clinical centers through site

visits according to information provided by the Coordinating Center in
order to insure that an adequate number of participants are recruited; that
the clinical centers adhere to the protocol; and that quality data is
collected.

POLICIES

Informed Consent

In order to be eligible for the study, each participant must be willing to sign a
statement of informed consent prior to examination/evaluation. This will document
the agreement of the subject to participate in the study activities. No subject will
be recruited who is less than 18 years of age; therefore, no parent or guardian
consent will be necessary. Changes will be adopted only if they are required to
insure participant safety or will significantly enhance the study.

General Principles of the Informed Consent
1, Explanation of the purpose of the study.

2. A description of the primary outcome of interest, examination schedule and
follow-up methods.

3. Permission for, and information about withdrawal from participation
information

4, Participant confidentiality

5. Participant safety measures

6. An offer by clinic staff to answer any inquiries concerning the study
procedures.

The Steering Committee recognizes that individual collaborating centers may
require, or be required by their local Institutional Review Boards (IRB), that the
recommended Informed Consent Form be amended to include additional statements
or be reworded to clarify existing statements. All such modifications to the
Informed Consent Form will be reviewed by the Steering Committee, and those
which do not detract from the content of the suggested CARDIA form will be
approved.

Informed Consent Procedure

No signed informed consent will be obtained for the telephone recruitment. This
follows well established principles of survey research; however the participants will be
informed of the intent to keep the information confidential. The sequence of procedures
for obtaining the patient's consent is as follows: it is desirable that the Principal
Investigator and/or Clinic Coordinator be involved in the early stages of the sequence.
The consent form obtains the participant's permission for the examination to be
performed.

Training/Certification

Each working group is charged with the development of training procedures,
certification/recertification requirements, and selection and assignment of
obser ver/trainers appropriate to the tasks proposed.

The requirement of standardized training procedures implies most initial training
sessions should be conducted centrally with subsequent training occuring in individual
clinics. The following rationales support centralized training: the overlap within study
centers of personne] performing specialized testing; the need to gain understanding of
the problems in implementation of the various facets as they piece together logistically;
and the psychological benefit to the study allowing interaction to take place among study
personnel. The Steering Committee will request recommendations for trainers from the
members and the Coordinating Center will subsequently contact all trainers and set time
schedules.

The CARDIA Coordinating Center will assume the organizing role for the major
training that will occur. As a facilitator, the Coordinating Center will work with the

Sessions and assist in the monitoring of certification and recertification.

The Coordinating Center will make all reservations for the Steering Committee,
Coordinating Center, trainers, and trainees. Equipment and space needs for centralized
training will be handled through a representative of the host city where training will
occur.

Privacy of Records

The CARDIA study will maintain confidentiality of stored records according to the
following guidelines: all records will be kept by assigned study numbers. Conclusions and
final results will be presented for appropriate scientific review in conferences and in
journals in the form of statistical analyses, with no disclosures of specific cases.
Collected information will not be released without the explicit consent of the
participant, according to the Privacy Act. The clinical centers will maintain locked files
and permit access only by authorized individuals. No personal identifying information
will be released from any clinical center to any other clinical center, the Coordinating
Center or NHLBI.

REFERRAL POLICY

Blood Pressure

Blood Pressure referral levels will follow the Joint National Statement. The CARDIA
Policy statement reflects the fcllowing:

1. The average of the second and third resting blood pressure readings, will be
used instead of an average of all blood pressure readings,

2. A systolic reading of less than 140 will be rechecked within 2 years.

3. A systolic reading of 140-199 will be confirmed at a 2 month interval.

4. A systolic reading above 200 will be evaluated im mediately, or referred to a
source of care within 2 weeks.

5. A diastolic reading of 85-89 will be rechecked at a 1 year interval.

6. A diastolic reading of 90-104 will be confirmed within 2 months.

7. A diastolic reading of 105-114 will be evaluated or referred to a source of
care within 2 months.

8. A diastolic reading of 115 and above will be referred immediately to a
source of care.

Lipids

Participants with a total plasma cholesterol of 250 mg/dl or greater and LDL level
of 180 mq/dl or greater will be referred to an appropriate medical care provider. Re-
evaluation can occur for public relations purposes. These referral levels are based on the
high likelihood of the local physician initiating therapy. They may change with future
implementation of the NIH census recom mendations.
