PROTOCOL
CARDIA QUALITY CONTROL

PURPOSE

The CARDIA Coordinating Center will carry out quality control measures during the
eourse of the study. There are two primary purposes for quality control. One is for
assessing errors and historically documenting the level of quality. Second, and more
importantly, is the impact of these quality measures on maintaining or improving the
quality of the subsequent collection of study data.

Quality control involves the collection of certain types of data and the subsequent
analysis of that data. It is primarily a measure of the quality of data that is 1) being
collected by the clinical centers, and 2) measured by central laboratories and centers
associated with the CARDIA study.

Quality control is accomplished in many different ways depending upon the type of data
being collected, the type of procedure being analyzed, and the associated outcome
variable in question. The types of quality control measures that will be used in the
CARDIA Study inelude:

1) Monitoring reports - primarily a tool used to monitor errors in forms; also used to
document recruitment procedures.

2) Calibration of instruments - used in any section which employs a measurement
instrument, e.g. calipers, seales, sphygmomanometer.

3) Log sheets - sometimes supplied to the Coordinating Center noting periodic
calibration procedures such as room, refrigerator, and freezer temperatures,
inventories, ete.

4) External surveillance - used when data is reported from outside the CARDIA
community, i.e. central laboratories, CARDIA storage centers (ECG).

A Manual will be developed which outlines those particular steps that will be taken for

each of the sections of the CARDIA visit in order to assure that quality data is being
collected and reported.

POL-9

The RESPONSIBILITIES of the Coordinating Center in developing and carrying out
quality control measures are listed below:
1) Identifying and notifying clinical centers of the quality of performance of
interviewers, technicians, and other responsible personnel in upholding proper
certification standards.
2) As a back-up in identifying calibration problems and/or performing the corrective
action by notifying the clinical center and/or correcting or flagging the data.
3) Identifying problems as they occur within the external reporting centers and
communicating this information to them for corrective action.
4) Obtaining historical data on all accounts which describes the quality and
performance of the entire CARDIA study.
5) Reporting selected information to the appropriate groups and the CARDIA Steering
Committee.
6) Design protocol and procedures for periodic site visits which check for quality of
performance and adherence to CARDIA standardized procedures within the clinical
center.
7) Develop protocol within the Coordinating Center for handling, filing, and promptly
analyzing incoming data and forms which have been created for use in quality
control, e.g. log sheets, blood chemistry results.
8) Develop protocol for alerting clinical centers when periodic quality and performance
reports are past due.
9) Keep an up-to-date file of all completed personnel certification forms.

CARDIA POLICY REGARDING ANCILLARY STUDIES

The CARDIA Steering committee has adopted the following policy regarding

ancillary studies.

5.

CARDIA investigators are encouraged to consider ancillary studies.

Any CARDIA center can conduct, or agree to participate in an ancillary study,
subject to the final approval by the Steering Committee.

The Steering Committee's major criterion for judging a proposed ancillary study is
its effect on the conduct and goals of the CARDIA study itself. An ancillary
study will ordinarily be approved unless it is judged to interfere significantly with
the objectives of CARDIA. Interference may take a variety of forms; for
example, too much additional blood to be drawn, premature thawing of frozen
specimens, excessive exam time required, or decrease in acceptability of exam to
participants.

If the ancillary study meets the test of non-interference with CARDIA it may still
compete with other proposed ancillary studies for limited additional time, blood,
subject matter, ete. Ordinarily such competition can be resolved according to
the preferences of each center. However, if this question arises for studies
requiring more than one center, we will request that the competing applicants try
to combine their efforts. If this is not possible, the Steering Committee members
will individually assign priority scores to the competing proposals. The proposal(s)
with the highest average priority score will be selected until the available
resources (time, blood, ete.) are exhausted. Acceptable proposals not of sufficient
priority to be included in one examination cycle can be resubmitted to compete
again for a subsequent cycle. Although the Steering Committe is reluctant to pass
judgement on the scientific merit of proposals for ancillary studies, scientific
merit and relevance to the goals of CARDIA will inevitably be involved in the
setting of priorities.

The investigator applying for an ancillary study must supply all additional funds
needed for it. The Steering Committee will be concerned with both the obvious
and the hidden costs to CARDIA entailed by an ancillary study.

Confidentiality of individually identifiable data about CARDIA subjects must be
assured,

A CARDIA investigator must be a principal investigator or co-investigator on an
ancillary study; be responsible for presenting the study to the Steering
Committee; and for the study's continuing compatibility with CARDIA.

All the publications, presentations and abstracts from an ancillary study must be
reviewed and approved by the Steering Committee prior to submission or
presentation.

No personal identification will be provided to ancillary studies staff. There are no

assurances that ancillary studies will be able to identify and contact subjects in
the future, particularly after the CARDIA study ends.

RECRUITMENT

The CARDIA study recruitment plans were designed to address the following
population requirements identified in the RFP:

"Study populations should be composed of biracial (black and white non-hispanic)
men and women, initially aged 18-30 years. Existing data on risk factor distributions and
change suggest that comparisons within and between these age-sex-race groups will be of
most interest. The best study design for pooling purposes should include a broad range of
ages, both sexes and both races. A choice of three to six contractors will be made to
insure a total combined sample of 3,000-4,000 individuals and about equal representation
across all age ~ sex -race groups on a pooled basis. Each offerer should propose to study
at least 500 young adults.

The study population should be limited to healthy, free-living individuals residing
in the continental United States. Chronically ill, disabled or institutionalized groups (e.g.
persons in prisons or mental hospitals) will be excluded from consideration. "Due to
alterations in lipoprotein and blood pressure measurements during pregnancy, expectant
women should not be examined until at least three months after delivery..."

The study centers chosen provide opportunities to achieve the goals stated in the
RFP and enable important comparisons among centers. Each center has demonstrated
the availability of a representative biracial population. All centers will examine free-
living populations. A major strength among the centers is the ability to compare a
previously enrolled population (Kaiser) versus various recruited populations at baseline,
and more importantly, on follow-up.

A second concern was the level of uniformity necessary in sampling the individual
center populations. Although the need for common sampling is recognized, experience
with recruitment from free-living populations suggests that issues of differential
nonresponse and missing data often overshadow the sampling issues. For example, in the
National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 95% of households selected were
interviewed, 75% were examined with over 15% missing several key measures. From an
analytical perspective, there is a paucity of statistical methods available to study
relationships from complex sampling designs. CARDIA will achieve poolability by
identifying a general approach to sampling, which is common to all centers, but not
necessarily identical. The minor modifications have been made to provide for the most
effective approach to maximizing recruitment within the various centers.

Each of the four clinical centers (Birmingham, Chicago, Minneapolis, Oakland) will
attempt to recruit a sample which is heterogeneous in age and social class, and is
aproximately one-quarter black male, black female, white male, white female. The
general process is shown in Figure 1.

All four centers will randomly select only one age-eligible person per household

Since Oakland is using its membership information to target age-eligible

Once a potential study candidate is contacted, his/her eligibility for CARDIA will

1. Age: Participants must be aged 18-30 years at the time of the initial

2. Residence: Participants must have a permanent address in the target area.

SAMPLE SIZE

Data from which to adequately estimate sample size needs for CARDIA is scant,
particularly for black men and women. There are a large number of hypotheses to be
assessed. This provides added difficulty due to the adjustments to the significance levels
necessary to protect against Type I errors. For detecting correlations from the cross-
sectional data, there is ample power even within small subgroups. In order to detect
significant changes in the characteristics of interest over a short time period, data from
the Lipid Research Clinics (LRC) Prevalence Study were used to estimate mean changes
within age, race and sex subgroups. Assuming only minimal correlation between the
characteristic at two points in time (r=0.50), a Type I error of 0.05 and a power of 0.90,
age-race-sex specific sample size should be approximately 400-500 per subgroup. A total
population of 4000 persons evenly distributed would be adequate to detect significant
changes in weight (2-3 Kg), cholesterol (5-6 Mg), systolic blood pressure (2-3 Kg), blood
pressure (1.5-2 mm Hg) and LDL cholesterol (4.5-6 Mg) based upon the cross-sectional
data provided by the LRC.

The necessary sample size estimated at 4000 participants assume measurements
at two points in time. The goal for the study is to re-examine at least 85% of the
participants at the second exam. If we are to have an adequate sample size within
subgroups, oversampling must be done at the initial exam to achieve these goals. Thus,
the CARDIA study has as its recruitment goal a total sample size of 5100.

I. INTRODUCTION
Accurate spirometrie pulmonary function testing has three essential
components: a) a frequently calibrated spirometer that accurately records exhaled
volume in relation to time during the forced expiration; b) a subject who inspires
maximally and exhales as forcefully, smoothly, and completely as he* can; and ¢)
technician who can calibrate the spirometer, coach the subject to perform maximal
efforts, and detect poor subject effort and/or expirations that are not continuous,
maximal, and completely recorded (1,2). The goal of the present manual is to assist the
technician in producing accurate spirometrie pulmonary function measurements using the
Survey Spirometer and the Eagle Il Microprocessor (Warren E. Collins, Inc., Braintree,
MA).
Section II of this manual deseribes the equipment to be used in the CARDIA
Study, and discusses a list of supplies necessary for pulmonary function testing. Section
Ill presents cleaning of the spirometer and breathing tubes. Section IV presents
calibration of the spirometer, including checks of the chart speed and volume deflection
and tests for leakage. Section V presents general principles of spirometrie testing, such
as: a) how to perform forced expiratory maneuvers; b) problems that are often
encountered in conducting the forced expiratory maneuver; c) the number of trials to be
performed and reproducibility criteria; d) measurements of the Foreed Expiratory
Volume in One Second (FEV1), the Forced Vital Capacity (FVC), the FEV1/FVC ratio, the
Forced Expiratory Flow Rates (FEF) at 25%, 50%, and 75% of the FVC exhaled, and the
Maximal Mid-Expiratory Flow Rate (MMEF); e) correction of these measurements to
Body Temperature and Pressure, Saturated (BTPS); and f) the racial correction factor.
Section VI presents the procedures to be followed in testing study objects using the Eagle
II Microprocessor and the Survey Spirometer.

Il. EQUIPMENT

All pulmonary function tests will be conducted using the Collins Survey 8-liter
water sealed spirometer, shown in Figure 1. As shown in Figure 2, the expired volume is
measured as it displaces a lightweight plastic bell riding in a narrow water well. A pen
moves directly with the bell, recording a tracing of volume versus time on a kymograph
drum, rotating at a speed of 32mm/sec. In addition to the information presented in this
manual, further details of the operation and maintenance of the spirometer are given in
the Instruction Manual for the Collins Survey Spirometer-

The Eagle II Microprocessor will be used in conjunction with the Survey
Spirometer during spirometer volume calibration, Eagle If time standard checks, and
patient testing. The Eagle II attaches to the survey spirometer via a Computer
Input/Output Connector Cable, as shown in Figure 3. The Eagle II primarily assists the
technician in two otherwise time-consuming tasks: calculation of expired volumes and
flow rates and calculation of predicted pulmonary function values.

A linear motion potentiometer attached to the spirometer bell converts
spirometer bell volume changes into electrical signals. As the spirometer bell is
displaced during a forced expiration, signals are sent to the Eagle II through the
computer connector cable. In this way, the Eagle I measures how fast the expiration is
proceeding, and calculates instantaneous flow rates at several points during the forced
expiration.

In addition, using the subject's age, height, and sex, which are entered into the

6/85 PUL -4

Eagle II prior to subject testing, the Eagle II computes the predicted pulmonary function
values using Knudson's prediction equations (3). After each expiration is recorded, the
Eagle II will print the test results and compare the subject's observed measurements with
those predicted for his age, height, race, and sex. Further details on the Eagle II are
available in the Instruction Manual for the Collins Eagle If Pulmonary Function Testing
System.

It is recommended that the Survey spirometer be placed on a high surface, at
least as high as a laboratory table (37" off the floor), and preferably a surface that is 46-
48" high. However, the Eagle II microprocessor can be positioned at any level, and the
length of the computer connector cord will permit a considerable discrepancy in height
between the two units. There are two advantages in placing the spirometer at a level
well above a normal desk level: (1) the spirometrie testing can be performed in the
standing position even for tall subjects without constricting the patient breathing tube or
forcing tall subjects to bend over; and (2) it is easier for the technician to watch the

Vv. The Forced Expiratory Maneuver

Measurements of pulmonary function made during a forced expiratory maneuver are
among the sinmplest and most repeatable tests of the pulmonary mechnics of breathing.
However, the accuracy of these measurements depends, in large part, on the technician
conducting the testing. The technician must guide the subject through the procedure,
and he must be able to judge the adequacy of the subject's effort. To make the
spirometric testing results as accurate and consistent as possible, the testing should be

done in a standardized fashion by all technicians, for all subjects.

A. Preparing for the Maneuver

Performance of the pulmonary function test should be postponed on the grounds of
(1) use of a bronchodilator within the past hour, or (2) acute illness. The questions listed
in Figure 29 should be asked, and the answers noted, before conducting spirometric
testing.

Whenever possible, testing should be conducted in the standing position, particularly
for obese subjects, since slightlv larger volumes are observed in the standing than in the
sitting posture (4). A sturdy chair, without wheels, should be positioned behind the
subject, to be used in the rare event of fainting or dizziness. Smelling salts should
always be kept on hand for this possibility.

The subject's neck should be slightly extended, the spirometer hose should be
adjustable to the subject's height, so that he stands erect, and is not hunched over, and

his chin should be slightly elevated. The position in which the testing is done, whether it

be standing or sitting, should be noted on the graph paper and the computer printout.

6/85 PUL-18

Tight clothing, such as a tie or belt, which might restrict the subject's maximal
breathing and efforts, should be loosened.

Dentures if they are loose, should be removed, since they will prevent a tight seal from
being formed around the mouthpiece. If they are not loose, they should be left in place.

A noseclip will be used during the maneuver to prevent nasal leakage during expiration.
The best time for the subject to put on the noseclip is just before he takes in his maximal
inspiration. This way he will avoid swallowing while wearing the noseclip, which blocks the
ears and is uncomfortable. Though the noseclips are "disposable", they should be cleaned and

re-used for as long as possible.

B. Explaining and Demonstrating the Maneuver

First, explain to the subject that he is about to do a test to determine how much air he
can exhale, and how hard and fast he can exhale it. Then, explain to the subject that he will (1)
attach the noseclip, (2) take in as deep a breath as possible, and when full, will (3) place the
mouthpiece in his mouth, (4) close his lips tightly around the mouthpiece, and (5) exhale through
the mouthpiece into the spirometer, pushing his air out as hard, fast, and completely as
possible. He is not to take any additional breaths until he has finished the forced expiration,
and he should continue to actively push out his air until the technician instructs him to stop
exhaling. He should be able to exhale until the tracing flattens out and draws an FVC plateau
of at least one second in length. The technician should continually urge the subject to "PUSH"
his air out, until the FVC plateau is recorded. In middle-aged subjects, six seconds of
expiration is usually possible, and should be aimed for in a group of young adults. However,
some young adults with very high flow rates reach the FVC plateau within four seconds, and
this should be accepted if it occurs. After a subject's testing session is completed, the
Exhalation Time of each of his tracings will be measured and recorded, as described below in
Section V.F.

The technician must check to be sure that the subject's lips form a tight seal around the
mouthpiece, especially if the subject wears dentures. The subject's lips should not be pursed
behind the mouthpiece, like a trumpet player's and his tongue should not block the mouthpiece
during the expiration.

A demonstration by the technician of the completeness of the inspiration, and the
forcefulness, completeness, and smoothness of the expiration is sometimes helpful. Such a
demonstration may prevent time and effort from being wasted on unacceptable forced
expiratory efforts (Section V.D below), which are caused by the subject's failure to understand
a verbal explanation of the procedure.

Be sure to tell the subject that you (the technician) will be forcefully coaching him

through the maneuver, so that he is not taken by surprise.

Conducting the Maneuver and Recording the Forced Expirations

Prior to the testing, using the rubber stamp provided, record the subject's ID number,
the date of testing, the room temperature, and the technician's ID code in the upper left corner
of the kymograph chart paper. If this is done, the chart paper can still be interpreted even if it
gets seperated from the subject's computer printout. Specific comments on subject testing
using the Eagle II microprocessor are presented below in Section VI.

Insert the mouthpiece into the spirometer hose, trying not to handle the end that the
subject will put into his mouth. During the testing, number the tracings as they are recorded.
When the Eagle If is used, the FEV1, FVC and the flow-volume curves that are printed on the
computer strip will aid the technician in monitoring subject effort and in checking the

reproducibility of the curves (see Section V.E below).

6/85 PUL~20

After the subject has been instructed to inhale maximally, turn on the kymograph drum
so that the drum will be turning at 32 mm/sec for the expiration, and so that the timing of the
expiration will be accurately recorded and a short baseline will be drawn.

During the inspiration, encourage the subject to inhale as much as possible, exhorting
him to go “IN, IN, IN". During the expiration, encourage him to "PUSH" as soon as he has his
mouth on mouthpiece, and to "KEEP PUSHING, KEEP PUSHING" as long as his exhalation line
is still climbing on the chart paper.

After the first trial, indicate the areas where you think that he could improve.
Emphasize that he should inhale just a little more air next time, even if he felt he was full
and/or exhale it for just a little bit longer, even though he thought it was empty. If the subject
did not reach an FVC plateau, point out that even though he may feel empty, he was still
exhaling and should only stop pushing when you tell him to do so. Although the final results are
checked for reproducibility, the emphasis should always be placed on maximal efforts, and not
on simply reproducing what has already been recorded. If the subject continually makes his
best effort, the results should be reasonably consistent. By emphasizing maximal efforts, the
technician can feel confident that he has elicited the subject's best efforts in that testing
session.

Always let the subject rest as long as needed between trials. If the participant has
problems with the maneuver, try to determine exactly what his problem might be and direct
your remarks to that problem. Do not simply repeat the entire set of instructions. The
participant is often unable to distinguish where his problems lie, and it will generally help
increase his interest and cooperation and make him feel that an excellent effort is expected if
you are able to direct his attention to particular trouble spots. For example, did his tongue get
in the way of the mouthpiece, resulting in a low amount of air exhaled, or did he leak around
the mouthpiece? Sometimes this latter problem can be heard as it occurs. Did the participant
inhale or exhale less air than he could have? Did he push out as hard and as long as he could

have? If his onset of exhalation was only a gradual push, urge a sharper push on the next trial.

If a choppy line was drawn, his throat may be dry (offer a drink of water), or he may not have
tried to push out continuously.

nose to absorb the oil.

A second demonstration by the technician (cheerleader style) of a smooth and complete
exhalation versus a choppy and hesitating exhalation can help a subject who has difficulty
maintaining a smooth exhalation. Breathing along with the subject may be helpful (and
automatic). It seems to increase the technician's attention to the routine and to improve the

timing of the maneuver.

D. Quality of the Forced Expiratory Tracings

A "good quality" spirometric test requires a maximal inspiration, to completely fill the
lungs, and a subsequent forceful, complete, and continuous expiration. The accuracy of the
measurements made from the spirograms, the Forced Expiratory Volume in One Second (FEV1),
the Forced Vital Capacity (FVC), and the Forced Expiratory Flow Rates (FEF) depends on the
quality of the spirograms.

The FEV1 is the maximum volume of air that a subject can exhale within the first
second of expiration following a maximal inspiration. The accuracy of the FEV1 depends on
whether the subject inhales maximally and whether he expels his air as fast and as hard as he
ean, and not with a sub-maximal effort.

The FVC is the maximum amount of air that can be expelled in one forced expiration
after a maximal inspiration. The accuracy of the FVC depends on how maximal the subject's

inspiration is and how complete his expiration is.

6/85 PUL-22

Both of these measurements, and the flow rates, will be discussed in more detail below.
Measurement of the FEV1 and FVC are shown in Figure 12.
There are several different types of errors that can occur during the forced expiratory
maneuver: (1) mechanical problems with the spirometer; (2) submaximal inspirations; (3)
submaximal effort on expiration; (4) hesitations, glottis closure, cough or tongue blocking
mouthpiece during expiration; (5) incomplete expirations; (6) taking in another breath during
expiration; and (7) procedural errors such as turning the chart drive on after expiration has
begun, or leakage through the subject's nose or around the mouthpiece. These errors, described
in detail below and pictured in Figures 13-26, may invalidate the FEV1, FVC, and the flow
rates.
1) Mechanical Problems with the Spirometer
If the pen does not make contact with the chart paper during the entire forced
expiration, the trial should be repeated. If the water level is low (Figure 7) or if any other
mechanical problems occur, especially if a leak develops (Figure 13), the test should be
repeated. However, daily water level checks and leak tests should prevent these problems from
occuring during a testing session.
2) Submaximal Inspiration
If this problem consistently occurs, it may not be visible on the tracings, since tracings
recorded after a submaximal inspiration look normal, but small. Comparison of the spirogram
in Figure 14 with the normal tracing in Figure 12 reveals the effect of a submaximal inspiration
on both the FEV1 and the FVC. The FEV1 recorded after a maximal inspiration (2850 ml) is
reduced to 2160 ml after a submaximal inspiration. The FVC recorded after a maximal
inspiration (3575 ml) is reduced to 2760 ml after a submaximal inspiration. Submaximal

inspirations invalidate all the pulmonary function measurements.

Submaximal Efforts on Expiration

If the subject pushes his air out slowly during the entire expiration (Figure 15) or
gradually increases his push (Figure 16) or purses his lips behind the mouthpiece and blows into
it like a trumpet (Figure 17), the FEV1 from that tracing will be invalid, though the FVC may
be valid if the expiration is complete (See (5) below). The flow rates will be invalid. The

subject must be encouraged to blast his air out as he begins his exhalation.

4) Hesitations, Glottis Closure, Cough, or Tongue Blocking the Mouthpiece

If the subject hesitates in his push during the first second of expiration (Figure 18), the
FEV1, the FVC, and the flow rates generally will be invalid. A cough anywhere during the
expiration prior to the FVC plateau will usually invalidate the FVC (Figure 19), but if the cough
occurs after the first seconds, the FEV1 may still be valid. A drink of water may relieve a
problem with coughing on subsequent trials. However, if the subject stops pushing but keeps his
mouth on the mouthpiece, or has glottis closure or his tongue blocks the airflow near the end of
the expiration (Figure 20), the FVC will be invalid, though the FEV1 would still be acceptable.
Figure 20 shows that these problems appear in the tracing as an abrupt flattening of the
expiratory tracing, forming a "knee", which does not occur during the usual gradual lessening of

flow rates as the FVC plateau is reached.

6/85
PUL=24

5) Incomplete Expirations

The expirations must be recorded to the FVC plateau, which occurs after six seconds of
expiration in adult males, but may occur after a shorter exhalation time in young adults, due to
their very high flow rates during expiration. Obstructed subjects may well need 10 or more
seconds of exhalation to reach their FVC plateau has been reached when a horizonal line is
inscribed on the chart paper. Incomplete expirations can have a profound impact on the
measurement of the FVC, the FEV1/FVC, and the Forced Expiratory Flow Rates. The FVC
plateau should be maintained for at least one second before terminating the forced expiratory

maneuver. Figure 21 shows two examples of incomplete expirations.

6) Taking in a Second Breath During the Expiration

As with the other hesitations in expiratory flow discussed in (4) above, if a second breath
is taken in during the first second of expiration (Figure 22), the complete test is invalid.
However, if the second breath is taken in after the first second of expiration, the FEV1 may be
invalid, but the FVC and the flow rates will not be valid, unless the breath is taken in after the
FVC plateau has been drawn for at least one second. Taking a second breath will either cause a
vertical excursion of the pen (Figure 22) if the mouthpiece is not blocked by the tongue, or it
may result in a second small plateau after the FVC plateau has already been reached (Figure
23). This will only happen if the tongue blocks the mouthpiece and no noseclip is used, thus
permitting extra air to be taken through the nose without being recorded as a vertical

deflection. This problem will not occur when a noseclip is used.

PUL-25
6/85

7) Procedural Errors: Turning the Chart Drive on After the Expiration Has Begun, and Leakage
Through the Nose or Around the Mouthpiece

If the chart drive is turned on after the start of the exhalation, the timing of the
expiration is not recorded accurately, since the onset of expiration cannot be determined. The
vertical motion of the pen resulting from this problem is shown in Figure 24. The FEV1 is
invalidated by this problem, unless the vertical excursion is less than 200 ml or 20% of the
FVC, whichever is smaller. However, if the expiration is complete, the FVC may be valid. The
flow rates will not be valid unless the FEV1 is valid.

Leakage of air can occur during the forced expiration through the nose, around the
mouthpiece, or from the spirometer. Use of a noseclip will prevent nasal leakage from
occurring; sealing the lips tightly around the mouthpiece will prevent air from leaking around
the mouthpiece; and daily leak testing should prevent spirometer leaks from going undetected.
However, if leakage from one of these three sources does occur, it will appear as in Figure 13,

and should be recognized.

E. Number, Reproducibility, and Quality of Tracings Required

Every subject should perform a minimum of three trials. If, at the end of three trials,
there are at least three tracings free of the above mentioned procedural errors, and with the
maximum FVC and FEV1 reproduced to within 5% or 100 ml, whichever is greater, no more
trials are needed. As mentioned earlier, the primary goal of each trial is to obtain maximal
efforts, and a series of such efforts will usually be reproducible at this desired level.

If the first three attempts do not yield three good quality tracings, up to two more
attempts should be made to get three such tracings. After five attempts, regardless of their
quality, testing should be stopped. If the subject refuses to continue with the required number
of trials, it should be noted on the kymograph chart paper.

6/85 PUL-26

F. Measuring the Tracings; FEV1, FVC, MMEF, and Exhalation Time

The FEV1 and FVC should be measured in all tracings that are free of the procedural
errors discussed above. Even if the tracings are smaller or don't "look good" in comparison with
the other tracings, they should be read if they are not technically inaccurate. Therefore, the
first step should be to look through the tracings and decide which ones will yield invalid
measurements of the FEV1 and the FVC, based on the above mentioned categories of errors in
(Section V.D)

If the spirometer is empty, the felt pen should rest at and draw a baseline along the "0"
line of the chart paper. The measurements are easiest to read if the baseline is set at "0"
before the testing. The daily baseline check should insure that the baseline remains on "0"
line. However, if the baseline was not exactly on the "0" line during the testing, draw in the
correct baseline and make all the measurements from the corrected baseline.

The FEV1 is greatly affected by the point selected for the start of the expiration.
Therefore, a uniform method has been established to correct for the varying degrees of
eurvature that appear at the beginning of the expiration, due to submaximal efforts in the
split-second when exhalation is starting (Figure 25). The method, called "back-extrapolation",
requires a tangent to be drawn from the steepest portion of the curve back to the baseline.
The starting point of the expiration, the origin, is then taken from the point where the back-
extrapolation line intersects the baseline. The curved tail to the right of the back-
extrapolation line is ignored. If the "extrapolated volume", measured as the height of the
tracing vertically above the new origin, exceeds 10% of the total FVC, the tracing is too

curved to be back-extrapolated, and should not be used for measurement of the FEV1.

PUL-27
6/85

Having determined the onset of the expiration for measurement purposes, the FEV1 is
found by placing a "one-second wide" (32 mm) ruler at the new origin, and reading the FEV1
where the tracing emerges on the left side of the ruler. Position the ruler with the right edge
touching the back-extrapolated origin for accurate FEV1 measurement. Also, be sure that the
ruler is vertical. The FEV1 should be read to the nearest 10 ml.

Measurement of the FVC is less difficult, being simply the volume between the baseline
and the tracing at the FVC plateau. If a plateau is not drawn, the "FVC" will be submaximal.
As with the FEV1, measure the FVC to the nearest 10 ml.

Agreement between the tracings may not be checked. The maximum FVC and FEV1
should be reproduced to within 5%.* Only the best FEV1 and the best FVC will be used to
characterize the subject's pulmonary function.

One additional, and somewhat more difficult measurement is shown in Figure 26, that is,
the FEF 25-75% (MMEF). Only one measurement of the MMEF is made from all the subject's
tracings. The "best" tracing, with the greatest sum of FEV1 plus FVC is chosen for MMEF
measurement. Compute 1/4 and 3/4 of the FVC from this tracing (do not compute 1/4 and 3/4
of the sum of FEVI plus FVC). Carefully place a small dot on the tracing at each of these
volumes. Using a ruler, draw a line that passes exactly through the centers of the dots. (If the
line passes even slightly to one side of the dots, and accurate MMEF will be ealculated).
Extend this line so that it crosses a one-second interval on the graph paper. (If the line is so
steep that it does not cross one-second within the scaled portion of the graph paper, one of the
vertical lines on the graph paper must be extended up or down so that a one-second wide
interval is crossed by the line connecting the dots.) The volume at which the line intersects the
beginning and end of one second are measured, and the difference between the two volumes is

ealculated. This difference is the MMEF, in milliliters expired per second.

PUL-28
6/85

All three of these measurements - the FEV1, FVC, and MMEF - must be corrected from
room temperature to body temperature and pressure, saturated (BTPS). Each of the
measurements is multiplied by the BTPS correction factor appropriate for the spirometer
temperature, inflating the measurements by 8-10%. The BTPS-corrected measurements can
then be compared with predicted values to evaluate the state of this subject's pulmonary
function. Though the Eagle II removes the burden of regularly performing these calculations,
the technician should still know how to measure the spirograms in case of Eagle II failure.

The Exhalation Time is the final measurement to be made on each tracing. It is the
number of seconds that elapsed between the back-extrapolated origin of the tracing and the
FVC. For each trial, the number of one-second intervals crossed by the tracing are counted, to
the nearest 0.25 seconds, and recorded on the computer printout, as described in Section VI.C
below. Exhalation Times are recorded in Figures 12, 25A, and 26. Since the Eagle II does not

compute the Exhalation Time, this measurement must always be performed by the technician.

VI.

Subject Testing Using the Survey Spirometer and the Eagle Il
Microprocessor

As described above in Section V, at least three forced expiratory maneuvers should be
attempted, recorded, and labelled on the kymograph chart paper. In addition, when the Eagle II
miscroprocessor is attached to the spirometer, a small printout of the values for the FEV1,
FVC, and flow rates should be generated after each trial, as outlined below in Section VLC. a
small flow-volume curve will also be printed after each expiration, to aid in coaching the
subject. At the end of the testing session, a summary printout will be obtained. As described
below, the computer printout should be labelled with the subject ID, technician ID, and testing
posture. The Exhalation Time should be measured for each tracing, and recorded on the

computer printout.

A. Preparing the chart paper and the kymograph drum

1. Label the chart paper using the rubber stamp which has been provided. Before attaching
the paper to the drum, the chart paper should be labelled in the upper left hand corner with
the subject's ID number, the temperature (C), the data of testing, the technician's code
number, and the posture in which the testing is conducted.

2, Attach the chart paper to the kymograph drum, as described in Section IV.D save the
adhesive strip backing.

3. Place the kymograph drum on the drum base, and draw a short baseline. If the baseline
is not on "0", the baseline should be adjusted as discussed in Section IV.G.

4. Place the kymograph switch in the neutral position.

B. Preparing the Eagle II

1. Turn the switch "on" and be sure that the computer connector cable is correctly

attached, as shown in Figure 3. Note: Keep all of the results from a subject's testing

session on one printout after a subject's testing session is completed.

2. Enter the Code Number: 200. This code number prints a flow-volume curves, but

suppresses "interpretation" of the spirometry results. The Knudson predicted values for

pulmonary function are used.

3. Enter the Preliminary Data:

a) Date: 6 digits (month/day/year); leading zeros must be entered e.g., "06".

b) Barometric Pressure "(BP)": 3 digits (enter the barometric pressure, in mm, or enter
"760" if no barometer is available).

ce) Temperature "(Temp)": 2 digits (C).

4, The Eagle II prints out the BTPS correction factor it will use for the temperature

and barometric pressure entered ("BTPS=").

5. Enter Subject Data:

a) Patient No.: 10 digits (enter subject ID, number only, no letters. If fewer than 10

digits, push "M" button after ID has been entered).

b) Height: 2 digits (inches, rounded to the nearest inch).

c) Age: 2 digits (years, as of most recent birthday).

d) Sex: Enter "M" (male) or "F" (female).

e) Israce correction factor desired ("Race correction?"): Enter "Y" (yes) if subject is

black, enter "N" (no) if subject is not black.

6. The Eagle II prompts with "Function Select:". Push the "Paper Feed" button to

advance about 1 1/2 inches of paper for labelling the printout after the testing session is

completed.

You are now ready for subject testing.

C. Subject Testing with the Eagle I
1. Explain the test to the subject as described in Section V.B and have the subject attach
noseclips.
2. As the subject is inhaling, depress the "FVC" key and keep it depressed until the
expiration is completed. If the "FVC" key is not held down, the Eagle H will stop
accumulating volume before the expiration is completed. Figure 27 was recorded with the
"FYC" key released after the start of the maneuver. The effect of releasing the "FVC" key
during testing is seen when the FVC in Figure 27 is compared with the FVC of the same
subject in Figure 12. The effect will be more pronounced for a less healthy subject.
Depression of the FVC key will cause the kymograph drum to rotate.
3. Watching the chart paper for the FVC plateau, and watching the subject for signs of
lightheadedness, urge the subject to exhale continuously until an FVC plateau is drawn. The
"FVC" button must remain depressed throughout the expiration, until the FVC plateau is
drawn,
4. When the FVC plateau has been reached, release the "FVC" key and let the subject
relax. When the key is released, you will hear a beep.
5. Label the tracing that was just recorded with its trial number (usually, 1-3). Label it
beneath the start of the tracing, and above its FVC plateau. Label in pencil if possible.
6. The Eagle II will prompt with "SAVE?". Unless it was an invalid tracing, reply yes ("Y"),
and then push "N" to generate a printout of that trial's results.
7. After the printout is completed, do not detach the printout, but save it as part of the
continuous strip.
8. Push "Paper Feed" twice.
9. The Eagle II prompts with "Function Select:"; push "M" (Manual Mode), and then "6".
This will cause a small flow-volume curve to be printed out from the trial just completed.
As shown in Figures 12-26, the flow-volume curves are helpful in monitoring some of the

aspects of patient effort during the successive trials.

10. When the flow-volume curve is drawn, the Eagle II will prompt with "Manual Mode"; push
"M" again, and "Function Select:" will reappear.

11. You are now ready for the next trial: repeat steps (1-9) for all three trials.

12. After at least three trials have been attempted, and at least three tracings are
acceptable as described in Section V, this subject's testing is complete.

13. Before detaching the computer printout for this subject, depress the "Print" key to
generate a summary of the best results and the best flow-volume curve from the entire

14. Detach the printout, record the trial numbers on the printout, label the summary portion

code, and the testing posture at the top of the computer printout.

15. Stamp "Time: __ seconds" between the pulmonary function results and the flow-volume
curve for each trial recorded. Measure the Exhalation Time for each tracing, as described in

16. If another subject is to be tested immediately and the temperature has not changed
since the previous test, depress the "Data" key. The Eagle II will respond with "Patient No.".
17. If another subject will not be tested immediately, depress the "Clear" button, but leave
the power on if more subjects are to be tested that day.

18. Begin testing the next study subject by entering "Preliminary Data" (Section VI.B above).

Eagle Il Diagnostic Comments
The Eagle If prints the following comments after a trial is completed, in the form of
symbols near the FVC and FEV1.
1 Reproducibility not within 10% of the maximum FVC or FEV1. If the FVC or the FEV1
of the present trial was not within 10% of the maximum value obtained so far in the testing
session, a caret symbol () appears below the measurement that is too low. Absence of a caret
does not indicate that the values are reproduced within the desired limits of 5% or 100 ml,
whichever is greater, but the presence of a caret certainly indicates that the values are not
within the acceptable reproducibility limits.
2. Extrapolated Volume unacceptably large for FEV1 measurement. If the extrapolated
volume exceeds 10% of the FVC for a particular trial, an asterisk (*) is printed to the right of
the FEV1. If such a symbol appears, back-extrapolation will not be performed by the Eagle I

before determining the FEV1.

Vi. Technician Certification and Quality Control

Following attendance at a "CARDIA Standardized Pulmonary Function Testing
Workshop", a technician should conduct: (1) four calibration sessions, recording the obtained
values on a calibration log sheet; and (2) four pulmonary function testing sessions for non-
CARDIA Subjects, preferably using subjects inexperienced in spirometric testing. The
calibration logs, chart papers, and computer strips should be forwarded to the CARDIA
Coordinating Center for review. Similarly, the pulmonary function tracings and computer
strips from the Subject testing should be properly labelled and forwarded to the Coordinating
Center. After the technician's calibration and testing techniques are judged to be

satisfactory, the technician will be certified to conduct pulmonary function testing.

PHLEBOTOMY
Description:
The blood drawing station is designed to obtain an adequate blood sample to test for
several important risk factors for cardiovascular disease and for other blood parameters
of interest to the overall CARDIA assessment. It is a potentially difficult station for
several reasons:
1. The anxiety caused in most people by blood drawing
2. The potential for injury
3. The complicated logistics in the handling and shipping of the specimens.
However, if carefully and professionally done, it will provide a positive safe
experience for the participant and valuable information for the participant and for
CARDIA.
Forty-seven ml of blood will be drawn, using 4 vacutainers. This sample will be
aliquotted and shipped for storage and to four centralized laboratories for clinical
chemistries, CBC, lipids, insulin and cotinine analyses.
The blood drawing, handling, aliquotting, and transporting procedures have been
standardized and can be found in the Manual of Operations.
Quality Control measures including both split samples and pooled samples will be
employed to assure the reliability of measurements within assays and over time.
Additional blood (not to exceed 15 ml) will be drawn on up to 5% of the CARDIA
population for these Quality Control studies.
Training/Certification
The station will be staffed with a technician with documented class time and
experience in phlebotomy. The Center supervisor or medical director will conduct
training and quarterly recertification for this technician. Training in the logistics of
handling and shipping specimens will take place at the CARDIA training sessions in
Oakland.
PHL-1

RATIONALE FOR MEASUREMENT OF BLOOD LIPIDS, LIPOPROTEINS AND
APOLIPOPROTEINS IN CARDIA

CARDIA is a study in young adults of the evolution of risk factors for coronary
heart disease. Each of the major established risk factors, including elevated blood
cholesterol, are of paramount interest in CARDIA. Evolution of risk is studied by
following the course of blood cholesterol levels and the levels of related lipoproteins and
apoproteins through young adulthood, and by examining the relationships of these blood
levels to other biologie and behavioral aspects of life. Each of the blood lipid levels and
the levels of related lipoproteins and apolipoproteins are therefore primary outcome
variables in CARDIA.

Many volumes of reports have been published dealing with blood cholesterol and
its influence in the atherosclerotic process. An exhaustive interpretative review of this
body of literature was published in 1981 by the Working Group on Arteriosclerosis of the
National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (1,2). The importance in the atherosclerotic
process of blood lipids, lipoproteins and apoliproteins is established in the following
quotation from Volume 1, pp.16 and 17:

Hypercholesterolemia (High Blood Cholesterol)

"The average concentration of cholesterol in the blood plasma of middle-aged
American men is presently on the order of 210-220 mg of cholesterol per 100 ml. The
risk of premature coronary heart disease and its consequences, expecially acute heart
attacks, increases rapidly as the level of cholesterol in blood exceeds 220 mg/dl. Men
between 40 and 49 years of age with a cholesterol level 240 mg/dl or above are more
than twice as likely to develop premature coronary heart disease as are men of the same
age whose blood cholesterol levels are less than 220 mg/dl. Men in the same age group
with levels of 270 mg/dl and higher have almost three times the risk of a premature
heart attack than those with levels less than 220. The relationship is similar for women.

Cholesterol and other fats are transported in the bloodstream in a soluble form as
components of lipoproteins. Hypercholesterolemia may reflect a disorder in the proteins
transporting the fat (apolipoproteins) and/or in the metabolism of fat per se. The
coneentration of other blood fats may also be inordinately high from a disorder of
lipoprotein metabolism. For clinical purposes, severe hyperlipoproteinemias have been
categorized using biochemical and genetic techniques. Distinctions have been made
between the common hyperlipoproteinemias in the population and the rare genetic
types. Hyperlipoproteinemias may also result from endocrine disturbances and most
commonly from dietary excesses. These types of hyperlipoproteinemia are all strongly
related to the risk of premature atherosclerosis.

One of the several lipoproteins that transport cholesterol - high density
lipoproteins - may confer some protection against atherosclerosis; an inverse relationship
has been identified between the concentration of HDL cholesterol in the blood and
coronary heart disease. Thus, individuals with high levels of HDL tend to have a lower
risk of coronary heart disease compared to those with low HDL levels. In contrast, the
higher the LDL level, the higher the incidence of coronary heart disease. These
observations have led to a reexamination of the interactions of the two lipoproteins with
cells of the arterial wall. Although the reasons for the different effects of the different
cholesterol-carrying lipoproteins are not yet clear, the information provides new ways of
identifying persons at high risk and new prospects for preventing, and even reversing,
atherosclerosis.

PHL-2

CARDIA will measure plasma levels of total cholesterol, high, low and very low
density cholesterols (HDL, LDL, and VLDL), HDL-2 and HDL-3 cholesterols, and levels of
apolipoproteins A-1 and B.

The methodology for lipid and lipoprotein measurement which has been selected
was developed and used by the Lipid Research Clinics (3), except that the more modern
enzymic methods will be used instead of the Autoananlyzer methods. Use of this
methodology has the advantage of maximizing comparability with the findings of this
very large study (4-8). The methodology gives a direct measurement of total and HDL
plasma cholesterol (the latter by analysis after precipitation with dextran
sulfate/magnesium chloride ($)) and plasma triglycerides. It estimates VLDL cholesterol
as 1/5 of the triglycerides value, and LDL cholesterol as total cholesterol less HDL
cholesterol less VLDL cholesterol.

Blood lipoprotein cholesterol is far more complicated than the classification as
HDL, VLDL and LDL allows. Standard methodology does not exist for measurement of
the many subclasses which may be defined within each of the lipoprotein classes. There
exists some evidence that the protection against atherosclerosis afforded by higher HDL
cholesterol levels is actually carried in a subclass called HDL-2 while the remainder of
HDL, called HDL-3 is less closely associated with risk. A standard methodology for the
determination of HDL-2 and HDL-3 (a second precipitation with dextran
sulfate/magnesium chloride (10)) will be used in CARDIA.

Cholesterol is carried in the blood in combination with proteins; these proteins are
called apolipoproteins. Evidence for the relationship of apoproteins to the prevalence of
atherosclerotic disease is strongest for Apo A-l and for Apo B, among many
apoproteins. Apo A-1 is closely (see above) associated with HDL-2 and Apo B is elosely
associated with LDL cholesterol. Although these associations are strong, as quoted
above it is not known whether hypercholesterolemia is primarily a disorder of the
proteins which transport the fat, the fat itself, or both. It is possible that changes in the
lipid moiety will not be reflected in corresponding changes in the protein moiety. For
these reasons it is felt to be important to monitor these two apoproteins for which the
evidence is strongest for a relationship to the atherosclerotic process (11-13). These
apoproteins will be measured by the enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay (ELISA).

Ideally, this same battery of lipids, lipoproteins and apoproteins will be measured
at each CARDIA examination.

RATIONALE FOR STORED BLOOD IN CARDIA

No study can predict discoveries which will be made some years hence. The great
majority of blood constituents remain stable when blood is stored deep-frozen, i.e., -70
C. It may be desirable to measure blood constituents on frozen samples to investigate
discoveries yet to be made. In the first examination, CARDIA will store four vials of
frozen serum for such future needs. Subsequent examinations should contribute lesser
amounts of stored frozen samples.

PHL-7

RATIONALE FOR CARDIA OBJECTIVE MEASURE OF SMOKING - COTININE

The recent U.S. Surgeon General's Reports on Smoking and Health (1,2) have clearly
delineated the multiple health hazards of cigarette smoking. Smoking is a major
contributor to cardiovascular (CVD) morbidity and mortality in industrial societies and
warrants measurement in any study of CVD risk. Smoking habits are established early in
life, and may undergo changes during the young adult years, making it an important
factor for measurement in CARDIA.

Traditional survey measures of smoking behavior have focused on self-reports of
number and type of cigarette smoked and of inhalation style. This straightforward
method has become increasingly less desirable recently when the type of cigarettes
smoked and the social attitude towards smoking began to change radically. Thus, the
validity of self-reported smoking levels has recently been questioned (3). For example,
the Multiple Risk Factor Intervention Trial found that smokers appeared to invalidly
report abstinence and generally under-reported their level of smoking (4). Such under-
reporting might clearly be a problem in a longitudinal study of young adults, in that there
may be a tendency to misrepresent smoking habits. Furthermore, self-reports of
cigarette number show obvious digit preference and therefore pose analytic difficulties.

While self-reported level of smoking remains a primary measure of exposure in
CARDIA, the need for some form of biochemical validation is generally accepted. There
are a variety of biochemical measures which can be performed on blood to assess
smoking exposure (5). Cotinine has been chosen for the following reasons:

1. It is a fairly stable compound with a half life of 19 to 40 hours (6,7).

2. Since the nicotine alkaloid is a portion of the particulate phase of cigarette
smoke, it is very likely that cotinine level can provide a reasonable estimate
of exposure to the total particulate phase in addition to nicotine itself (8).

3. Compared with other biochemical measures of smoking, continine has the
highest specificity to confirm smoking status, and offers the potential to
detect small changes in number of cigarettes or other reductions in tobacco
"dose."

One potential difficulty with cotinine is that use of nicotine gum will interfere. In
the few cases that use nicotine gum, self reports of smoking habits will be accepted.

Cotinine analyses for CARDIA will be performed by the American Health

Foundation. These investigators have extensive experience in cotinine measurement in
epidemiologic studies (5,9).

RATIONALE FOR SERUM CHEMISTRY ANALYSES FOR CARDIA

Specimens will be obtained from CARDIA participants for measuring blood
chemistries and hemotologic values. The tests to be included in the CARDIA exam are:

1. CLINICAL CHEMISTRIES: glucose, uric acid, SGOT, alkaline phosphatase,
GGT, total bilirubin, total protein, albumin, calcium, phosphorous, creatinine
2. CBC: Hematocrit, white blood cell count with differential

These blood parameters warrant measurement for one or more of the following
reasons:

They are known or suspected to be related to CHD incidence,

They are known or suspected to be related to other risk factor levels.

They reflect behaviors of interest to CARDIA; for example, alcohol intake.
They are part of a routine screening battery and are felt important for
inclusion in a health study.

em ON
oes

Fasting blood glucose is being measured in CARDIA because in some studies it has
been positively associated with CHD incidence (1,2). It also provides a relatively good
screening test for diabetes mellitus. Because glucose intolerance increases with age,
CARDIA will also be interested in the development of hyperglycemia or diabetes mellitus
over time. In addition, in the Framingham Offspring Study, glucose levels were
positively associated with blood pressure (3).

Serum urie acid has been positively and independently related to CHD incidence in
a few studies (4,5), although other studies suggest this is not an independent association.
Uric acid was negatively associated with HDL cholesterol and positively with VLDL
cholesterol in one study (12). Uric acid is also included as a screening test, although
hyperuricemia would likely be rare in the CARDIA populations.

The serum enzymes, SGOT, alkaline phosphatase, GGT, as well as total bilirubin,
are included as reflectors of hepatic function. It is deemed important to identify heavy
alcohol consumption, which may be highly prevalent in CARDIA populations.
Furthermore, there is evidence to indicate that metabolism of serum lipids and
lipoproteins (particularly HDL) is related to hepatie function (6,12). Individual serum
enzyme levels have generally not been independently related to CHD incidence.

Serum total protein, albumin, phosphorous, and hematocrit have all been
independently related to blood pressure in the Framingham Offspring Study (3). Some of
these associations may be due to changes in blood volume with hypertension (3). These
blood tests also screen for potential, albeit rare disease. .

There is recent evidence to suggest that calcium May contribute to the
pathogenesis of hypertension (7). Serum total calcium has been positively and
independently related to blood pressure level (8). The relationship to blood pressure is
likely complex with interactions among calcium, phosphorous, magnesium, and renin (9).
The association between changes in blood pressure and ehanges in calcium are of interest
of CARDIA. Finally, serum calcium has been associated positively with HDL cholesterol
and LDL cholesterol levels (12).

Creatinine is included in the CARDIA exam as a screen for renal disease and
secondary hypertension.

PHL-11

The Multiple Risk Factor Intervention Trial and others have shown that white
blood cell count is positively related with CHD incidence, independent of smoking
(10,11). This relationship may be a direct one in that white blood cells may contribute to
the atherosclerosis process, or an indirect one. As well as associations with smoking,
leukocyte count has been negatively associated with HDL cholesterol and positively
associated with LDL cholesterol and VLDL cholesterol (12). MRFIT and most previous
studies have not examined individual white blood cell types, which CARDIA proposes to
do.

The laboratory performing the chemistry analyses is American Bio-Science Labs.

RATIONALE FOR FASTING INSULIN CONCENTRATION

Although the sex difference in mortality from coronary heart disease (CHD) is well
known, the reasons for it are poorly understood. Studies indicate that even after
adjusting for behavioral, physiological and socioeconomic differences, a significant sex
differential remains (1-3). However, among diabetic populations, the sex difference in
CHD mortality appears to be largely eliminated (4-6). The Framingham Study (4) showed
diabetes was not an independent predictor of cardiovascular disease in men, while among
women, diabetes was a significant factor even after adjusting for HDL-C, LDL-C,
systolic blood pressure and left ventricular hypertrophy. In the Evans County Study (5),
diabetes was a weak risk factor among men, while diabetic women were at nearly 3 times
the risk of death from CHD than nondiabetic women. A more recent study of white men
and women in Rancho Bernando, California (7) confirmed the excess risk of CHD death
among diabetic women but additionally found that diabetes was a significant predictor of
fatal ischemic heart disease in men. Thus, while these studies are not totally consistent
in regard to their findings in males, the consistent female associations suggest that the
sex differences in CHD mortality seen in normal populations and the lack of difference in
diabetics may be linked. None of the currently recognized risk factors appear to exert a
strong enough sex-specific effect upon CHD mortality to explain the potent effect of
diabetes in women.

Studies of asymptomatic hyperglycemia have failed to show a clear and consistant
relationship to CHD. Recent findings from the Whitehall Study (8) indicate that the
relationship between plasma glucose and CHD is not linear. The threshold may be
limited to those individuals above the 95th percentile of post-load glucose concentration,
suggesting perhaps that hyperglycemia is not itself causing the disease.

It has been postulated that the relative: advantage women enjoy over men may
relate to their greater insulin sensitivity (i.e. greater insulin concentration per unit
glucose). Studies have shown that women produce more insulin in response to an oral
glucose tolerance test (OGTT) than similarly aged men, this difference being most
significant in adolescent and young adult women (9). The difference in insulin response
was independent of obesity and blood glucose concentration. This implies that young
women, for reasons other than blood glucose concentration and obesity, secrete more
insulin in response to an OGTT. It is hypothesized that women not only have a better
capacity to produce insulin but also that peripheral insulin resistance may be less,
enabling them to have lower glucose concentrations. It is also hypothesized that in
nondiabetic populations insulin is linked to the female "protection" and resistance to its
actions (in non insulin dependent diabetes) or absence (in insulin dependent diabetes)
leads to increased CVD mortality.

Raised plasma insulin concentrations have been shown to be predictive of future
cardiovascular disease in men (10-11) although apparently not in women (12). A five year
study among policemen in Helsinki (10) found that elevated insulin concentrations one
and two hours after an OGTT was an independent predictor of CHD risk, while blood
glucose was not. Similar findings for men were found in the Busselton Study (12) (though
not for women). The Paris Prospective Study (11) found that among men, fasting insulin
and fasting insulin glucose ratio were independent predictors of CHD risk over 5 1/2
years followup.

There is much evidence in the literature which suggests that raised insulin may
promote atherosclerosis (14). One proposed mechanism is via its association with lipid
and lipoprotein metabolism. Briefly, insulin stimulates lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity,
an enzyme system which promotes the peripheral catabolism of VLDL-C resulting ina

PHL-15

fall in triglyceride concentration and a possible rise in HDL-C, one source of which is
thought to be VLDL-C catabolism (15). Further, Nikkila (16) has found that adipose
tissue concentrations of LPL are higher in females than males and further that LPL
activity was positively correlated with HDL-C concentration. The Bogalusa Heart Study
(17) has reported that fasting glucose and/or fasting insulin concentrations were
Positively related to obesity, systolic blood pressure and triglycerides and inversely
related to HDL-C in 15-17 year olds.

Recently, the insulin-lipids relation was examined in over 300 individuals (18) who
underwent an OGTT. In multivariate analyses, insulin sensitivity largely accounted for
the associations of sex and obesity with the atherogenic lipids i.e. total cholesterol, LDL
and triglycerides. Thus, the more efficient a person's insulin in controlling blood sugar,
the greater may be the stimulation of LPL with consequent removal of VLDL.
Conversely, since obesity and insulin resistance are positively related, the greater may
be the triglyceride concentration among obese insulin resistant individuals based upon the
same mechanism. The well known inverse relationship between triglycerides and HDL-C
would predict HDL concentration to be positively related to insulin sensitivity.

It is proposed that fasting insulin and glucose concentrations be determined in all
participants except insulin dependent diabetics. As noted previously, both fasting insulin
and fasting I:G ratios (10) have been prospectively related to risk of CHD, as well as
cross-sectionally associated with risk factors in both sexes and both races (16). Because
an OGTT will not be performed, the 1:G ratio cannot be used to adequately measure
insulin sensitivity.

The major hypothesis under study is that insulin mediated glucose homeostasis is
better in women than in men and relates to the sex difference in lipid and lipoprotein
levels in adults. Thus, adjusting for differences in insulin will reduce or eliminate some
of these differences. From this, a number of other hypotheses are suggested: 1) Fasting
insulin concentration is positively related to total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides in
both sexes and inversely to HDL-C. 2) These relationships will be stronger in black males
than black females and in white males than white females and these sex differences may
decrease somewhat with age. 3) No significant race-sex interaction with insulin
concentration will be found. 4) The relationship between HDL-C and insulin will be due
largely to the inverse relationship between insulin and the HDL-2 subfraction. 5) The sex
difference in total cholesterol and LDL will largely be explained by controlling for the
sex differences in insulin concentration and obesity while a significant sex difference in
HDL-C will remain even after adjusting for other covariates. However, the sex
difference in the HDL-2 subfraction will be considerably reduced. 6) Insulin
concentration will be positively related to cigarette smoking and obesity and inversely
related to physical activity, fitness and education level. 7) The physical activity and
fitness relationship with HDL and triglycerides is at least partially mediated by insulin
sensitivity. 8) Longitudinally, change in insulin will be most stongly related to change in
weight. 9) Change in HDL-C and HDL-2 will be inversely related to change in insulin
concentration and change in weight. _ 10) Sex differences in change in lipids and
lipoproteins will be largely explained by sex differences in change in insulin sensitivity
and change in weight. Glucose measures may often enter the multivariate analysis in
place of the insulin measures since 1) both measures reflect similar aspects of a
nondiabetic's physiology and 2) glucose concentration may be measured more precisely
than insulin concentration. Other relationships of interest include associations between
insulin concentration and apoproteins A-1 and B, as well as systolic blood pressure. Also
of importance is the question of how much of the racial difference in CHD risk profile is
due to differences in insulin concentration.

RATIONALE FOR MEASUREMENT OF BLOOD PRESSURE IN CARDIA

CARDIA is a study in young adults of the evolution of risk factors for coronary
heart disease. Each of the major established risk factors, including elevated blood
pressure, are of paramount interest in CARDIA. Evolution of risk is studied by following
the course of blood pressure and the appearance of new hypertension through young
adulthood, and by examining the relationships of these blood pressure levels to other
biologic and behavioral aspects of life. Blood pressure and hypertension are therefore
primary outcome variables in CARDIA,

Many volumes of reports have been published dealing with blood pressure and its
influence in the atherosclerotic process. An exhaustive interpretative review of this
body of literature was published in 1981 by the Working Group on Arterioselerosis of the
National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (Arteriosclerosis 1981, Volume 1, Summary,
Conclusions and Recommendations, NIH Publication Number 81-2034, June 1981; and
Volume 2, Detailed Report, NIH Publication Number 82-2035, Sept 1981), The
importance in the atherosclerotic process of blood pressure is established in the following
quotation from Volume 1, p 17:

High Blood Pressure (Hypertension)

As blood pressure rises, so does risk of ischemic heart disease and its
complications. The range of normal blood pressures is wide. Even within the "normal"
group, risk increases as the upper limits are approached. Usually, blood pressures are
expressed as systolic pressure/diastolic pressure; values exceeding 140/90 mmHg are
considered to be hypertensive for adults. Middle-aged persons with a diastolic blood
pressure of 90-104 mmHg or greater (so-called "mild" hypertension) have a risk of heart
attack that is about 70 percent higher than that of persons with a diastolic pressure
under 80mmHg (normal value). Persons with a diastolic blood pressure exceeding
104mmHG (moderately severe to severe hypertension) have a risk more than twice that
of those with a normal value. Hypertension is an especially strong risk factor for stroke
and, to a lesser extent, for peripheral vascular disease.

Blood pressure is measured in a resting state, using 3 measurements with a random
zero sphygmomanometer. The random zero machine has two advantages over the fixed
zero manometer. Digit preference does not appear in the data, though it may still exist
in the reading itself, and be randomized out of the data by the use of the randomly
chosen zero point. More importantly, it deprives the blood pressure technician of
knowledge of the actual value, and therefore of the ability to make judgements about
blood pressure levels for readings close to critical values such as 90 diastolic. It should
be noted, however, that the random zero machines tend to yield blood pressures which
are about 1.5mmHg less than those obtained when using a fixed zero machine. Within
Person variation in blood pressure is substantial; 3 replicate readings tends to reduce this
variation.

BP-1

Blood Pressure Measurements

The purpose of blood pressure measurements in CARDIA is: to compare levels of
this risk factor between young blacks and whites; to observe the interaction with other
CHD risk factors over time; and to observe variables that will predict changing levels of
blood pressure.

Blood pressure measurements (systolic and fifth phase diastolic) will be recorded
with a random-zero (RZ) sphygmomanometer, by trained and certified technicians at
baseline and subsequent intervals. The methods of measurement will be standardized - as
set out in the Manual of Operations. The pulse rate for 30 seconds will be recorded with
each blood pressure measurement.

As many confounders of blood pressure measurement as possible will be controlled
by standard settings and technique of blood pressure measurement or by recording
uncontrollable confounding factors. So that the following will be recorded:

1) Time of day (AM/PM)

2) Room temperature
3) Arm circumference at the midpoint of the upper arm
4) Technician ID. number

The blood pressure will be measured three times on each oecasion. Caffeine (from
tea, coffee, pop), eating, heavy physical activity, smoking, and alcohol intake will be
proscribed for two hours prior to recording blood pressure level. The requirement for a
fasting state in the basic exam will assure much of the dietary compliance. Recording of
current drug intake, including medications affecting blood pressure, non-prescription
drugs and "recreational" drugs will be made on medical history forms on the day of the
examination.

Detailed history of alcohol intake patterns will be recorded along with the
nutrition history because of the known, but ill-understood, relationship of alcohol intake
to blood pressure level. For similar reasons physical activity at work and leisure will be
ineluded in a separate history.

TECHNICIAN TRAINING AND QUALITY CONTROL

Technicians will be trained centrally prior to participant intake in five half-day
sessions, New technicians after the start of the study will be trained locally by a
designated "BP supervisor". Recertification will occur every six months (details in
MOO). Prior to certification each technician will be tested for vision (reading) and with
an auditory test (by Korotkoff sound tape).

The Coordinating Center will direct a BP certification committee to review six
monthly data. This same committee will review three-monthly tabulations of blood
pressure levels (systolic and diastolic separately) comparing group means of each
technician with the values for all technicians by center and controlled for weight, age
and sex ~ by use of Z-scores, Arbitrary levels of Z~scores, (depending on experience) but
initially 3 will be used to flag possible systematic deviations in blood pressure
Measurement by individual technicians. Digit preference will also be monitored,

Order of Measurement

It will take approximately 10-15 minutes to make three blood pressure
Measurements including the initial five minute rest and recording of pulse rate. The
blood pressure measurements will be made very early in the clinic visit sequence
im mediately following the greeting and informed consent. Measurements will be made
before the physical exam, blood drawing, treadmill test, or any potentially stressful
interview. The blood pressure measurements on each participant will be made in a
separate room or, at minimum, in an area properly screened from all other activity and

other participants.
Referral of Hypertensives

Blood Pressure referral levels will follow the Joint National Statement. The
CARDIA policy statement reflects the following:

a. The average of the second and third resting blood pressure readings, will be
used instead of an average of all blood pressure readings.

b. A systolic reading of less than 140 will be rechecked within 2 years.

[om A systolic reading of 140-199 will be confirmed at a 2 month interval.

d. A systolic reading above 200 will be evaluated immediately, or referred to
a source of care within 2 weeks.

e A diastolic reading of 85-89 will be rechecked at a1 year interval.

f. A diastolic reading of 90-104 will be confirmed within 2 months.

g. A diastolic reading of 105-114 will be evaluated or referred to a source of
care within 2 months,

h. A diastolic reading of 115 and above will be referred im mediately to a source
of care.

Tf these levels are maintained, the participant will be referred to his physician. If
the participant does not have a physician, study personnel will obtain a list of locally
available physicians, Follow-up to check if the participant has contacted a physician will
be carried out within six months, For DBP 115 mmHG, same day referral to a physician
will be made, and a phone call follow-up, to confirm participant contacted physician, will
occur within one week.

BP-3

Blood Pressure Training/Certification

At the beginning of the first session, a description and demonstration of the
correct BP procedure is given. Trainees are to listen to the Ist (training) tape, taking
the test sequences until they are comfortable with what they are listening to. Then, they
take the 2nd tape until they have passed that test. After passing the second tape, they
are given the 3rd tape test. Alternated with the tapes are actual live practices under the
instruction and observation of the training supervisor. Some live practices may be done
with @ standard stethoscope, but most should employ the Y-tube stethoscope. The
optimum size of a group is 8. This allows 4 people to do live practices while 4 are on the
tape training device. The group can interchange and practice on each other.

After the first day of training, each trainee should be given a euff and manometer
(no stethoscope) to take home and practice just the control of the valve. This can be
done by wrapping the cuff on a jar or bottle and alternately pumping up and dropping the
mercury at @ steady rate of 2mm per second. After two or three sessions, they could
also be given a stethoscope to practice on family and/or friends. This out of class
practice is very important to build confidence. This time allowed for class is not enough
without outside practice time.

Once each trainee has passed tape#3, he or she should do at least 2 live readings
with the training supervisor on the Y-tube stethoscope. The readings should agree within
2mm. If they do not, the trainee needs additional practice with tapes and live subjects.
The training supervisor should also assure that the trainee understands and follows proper
procedures.

If the trainees are also to use the Random Zero device, additional time should be
allowed for instruction and mastering that procedure. Observers are certified after
passing the tape tests 2 and 3 (tape 4 is held in reserve for recertification) and at least 2
live readings. Observers are recertified every six months by taking and passing tape 3 or
4 and one or two readings with the training supervisor on a Y-tube stethoscope.
