MEDICAL HISTORY

It is important to ascertain illnesses and medications as these May affect risk
factor levels and life-style. For example, thyroid disease, oral contraceptives, and
thiazide diuretics are known to affect lipid levels and should be considered when
determinants of Hpid levels are assessed. Although, in the targeted age group, most
medical conditions will be infrequent and not of great importance to the study, the study
results will lose considerable credibility among the medical com munity if some effort to
ascertain basic health status and illnesses is not undertaken.

Genetic factors are important determinants of coronary risk factor levels as
evidenced by familial aggregation of these factors. Therefore, some basic information
about the longevity and premature development of cardiovascular and related illness in
close relatives is essential. Because of time and resource limitations in the first
CARDIA examination, we will not attempt to obtain detailed family histories or genetic
Measures such as HLA and/or blood groups even though these would be valuable to have
eventually.

Smoking, particularly of cigarettes, constitutes a major established coronary risk
factor. This will be a key dependent variable in CARDIA and changes in smoking habits
will be observed in many participants as the study progresses. Therefore, it is important
to measure tobacco consumption with care and in some detail as well as to employ
objective measures of smoking.

Alcohol consumption is another important life-style component that may vary
considerably among participants and from exam to exam. It is known to positively affect
blood pressure and HDL cholesterol, and has been negatively associated with the
development of coronary heart disease in some studies, Although time allotted for
alcohal questions is limited, we are attempting to get information about intake of
different beverages since they may have different effects. These questions also cover
"binge" drinking and past alcohol drinking which are not covered in the nutrition
interview.

Nonmedical drugs are used by many young people. We believe that we will be
ignoring an important aspect of life-style of the young unless we ask some questions
about this area. Because drug use is a sensitive subject, the questions have been kept
few and limited to marijuana use. Assurance of confidentiality will be important.

Several miscellaneous items are of interest or are necessary for interpretation of
other tests (e.g., time since last food in relation to blood glucose and triglycerides) and
the questions will attempt to cover these items,

In general, the method of administration will first be self-administered

questionnaires to screen most aspects with positive answers followed up by interviewer
administered questions to obtain some specific details,

BODY SIZE MEASUREMENTS

There are three primary reasons for including body size measurements in
CARDIA. First, they provide a standardized basis for examining the association between
physical size, stature, or ponderosity, and risk for developing coronary heart disease,
hypertension and other diseases of interest (e.g., chronic obstructive lung disease,
diabetes). Second, repeated measurements of body mass over time permit investigation
of whether changes in body size directly contribute favorably or unfavorably to an
individual's risk profile. Further, because the data will be collected using standardized
methods employed in previous investigations, the representative nature of the CARDIA
data set can be determined using existing data from similar age, sex and ethnic groups.

All of the body size measurements to be used have been reported, either
independently or collectively, to be correlated with a specific risk factor or clinical
manifestations of disease. These measures also represent important indicators of growth
and nutritional status. Although numerous additional anthropometric and/or body size
measurements have been identified, the intent of this study is to focus on indices
particularly relevant to the risk of developing coronary heart disease or systemic arterial
hypertension. Measurements must be limited to those that are the most relevant and
that can be performed using standardized methodology within and between survey
centers because of time limitations and other practical constraints of the study.

Specifically, the anthropometric and body measurements included in studies such
as the Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (HANES), Framingham, and the Lipids
Research Clinies Prevalence Survey have served as a model for the measurements
proposed (1,2,3). In addition, the age group involved in CARDIA suggests the need for
monitoring growth and development inherent in the aging process which may be unrelated
to environmental influences such as dietary or exercise patterns.

Rationale for Specific Meausurements

Body Height and Weight. Among all the possible measurements, height and weight
are universally accepted as primary indices of body size. Weight for height standards are
available for both men and women from studies such as the Build and Blood Pressure
Study and the recently updated Metropolitan Life Insurance tables. Based on standards
such as these, relative weight can be determined. In addition, several ratios of
weight/height have been correlated with selected risk factors. Indices such as body mass
index or Quetelet's Index or Ponderal Index also have been associated with hypertension,
hyperlipidemia and diabetes.

Not only the existence of obesity, but the age of onset of obesity are reportedly
related to susceptibility to hypertension (5). Weight gained early in adult life may be a
sensitive indicator of increased risk for cardiovascular disease. Hyperplastie obesity
experienced during adulthood may impose different risks than hyperplastic obesity
developed during youth and these risks may vary among different age,sex, and ethnic
groups (7). For these reasons it is important that CARDIA include measures of height
and weight during each successive examination.

However, it is well known that there are numerous limitations to indices of
relative weight (6). Although individuals may be classified as being overweight or
underweight compared to age and sex specific means, the terms obesity and overweight
are not necessarily synonymous. Furthermore, height and weight tables do not reflect
the variations across different ethnic, socioeconomic and/or occupational groups. Thus,
in order to determine not only body weight but also a better index of body composition,
additional measurements are proposed to CARDIA.

Skinfold Meausures. No single measure of obesity or body mass is optimal or uniformly
representative for all ages, races, and sexes, making the use of several indices desirable,
if not necessary (3,8). It is recommended that the body size index should not be
Gependent on height and should have a strong association with independent indices of
fatness, e.g., skinfold thickness, body density, etc.

Blair, et al (7) recently reported evidence from HANES (1971-1974) that risk for
hypertension increases with centrally located body fat as measured by triceps and
subscapular skinfolds. They reported that subscapular skinfold was a better predictor of
both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in each race-sex group... " sharing all the
association of triceps with blood pressure and having significant predictive power
unshared by triceps " (7). These data support the need to differentiate between central
versus peripheral deposition of body fat.

Despite its reported superiority in predicting hypertension, subscapular skinfold
measures may not be as sensitive in predicting other risk factors relative to coronary
heart disease. Population data for triceps skinfold measure are available for both sexes
and race groups ages 18 to 30 years thus providing a means of comparing the data
coliected in CARDIA. The third most commonly measured skinfold site is the suprailiac
crest. Given its location at the hip, it offers a means of comparing upper versus lower
body fatness and may, either separately or in conjunction with the other two skinfold
measures, provide unique information regarding the evolution of CHD or hypertension.

Elbow Breadth. Subcutaneous fat constitutes approximately fifty percent of total body
fat in young adults (1). Therefore, the skinfold measures of height and weight provide
indicators of body size and relative body weight. However, weight varies not only with
height but is also influenced by factors such as body width, bone size and density,
muscularity and length of trunk relative to total height (4). It is thus recommended that
an index of frame size be included in the CARDIA survey. Numerous, often complex and
cumbersome measures of frame size have been used, each having some relationship to
other anthropometric indices. Recent evidence reported from HANES indicated that
elbow breadth provides a useful, reliable estimate of frame size. Mean values of elbow
breadth demonstrated significant age, sex, and ethnic differences in frame size within
the HANES population.

Waist and Hip Girth. Measures of girth or body thickness contribute additional
information for accurately characterizing body size and composition. Here again,
numerous sites have been used in the past but two circumferences, one representing
waist girth and the other hip girth, will be used in CARDIA. These measures are
sensitive to recent loss or gain in weight and appear to be differentially associated with
future risk of disease (9). Of particular interest is the waist to hip girth ratio in relation
to the development of high blood pressure and diabetes (10).

Upper Arm Girth. Upper arm girth is related to blood pressure level independent of body
weight or BMI. The size of the upper arm may be an index of adiposity, influence the
pressure needed to occlude the artery, or influence the amplitude of the Korotkoff
sounds.

SEVEN DAY PHYSICAL ACTIVITY RECALL

Rationale

Physical inactivity has been established as a coronary heart disease (CHD) risk
factor for both men and women. Decreased CHD risk is associated with recent job
related as well as leisure-time activity, and some dose-relationship appears to exist.
Also, there is preliminary evidence that inactivity is associated with increased risk for
hypertension, Type II diabetes and osteoporosis. Data relating physical activity to CHD
prevalence or incidence has been collected primarily on men over age 30 with very little
data available on men and women ages 18-30 years, a time when major changes occur in
exercise habits as well as other major CHD factors.

While it appears that recent activity and not past activity has an association with
CHD risk, physical activity experiences during school years may be an important
determinant of activity habits as an adult. One objective of CARDIA should be to try
and determine what influence various experiences during youth have on CHD risk factors
in the young adult. We are thereby proposing to collect information on the past exercise

experiences of CARDIA participants.

Attitudes about potential health performance and appearance effects of exercise
differ for adults who exercise regularly versus those who are sedentary. Also, some
evidence exists that people who exercise more have different attitudes about time
constraints, lack of exercise facilities and exercise opportunities than their non-
exercising counterparts. Such relationships have not been reported for black
populations. These attitudes appear to be related to SES and they differ with age.
Questions regarding attitudes about exercise are proposed in an attempt to determine if
these relationships exist in the CARDIA population and if there are significant ethnic and
sex differences. Also, we would like to know if previous exercise experiences influence
these attitudes and how these attitudes relate to current activity habits.

General Information

Scientists have found it difficult to accurately measure the amount of physical
activity performed by people in a free-living population. Some of the methods have
included using occupational titles, activity diaries, self-administered questionnaires, and
interviewer-administered questionnaires. Some questionnaires have focused on leisure-
time activities, some on occupational activities, and some on both types. Some
questionnaires cover a short time period (one day or one week-end) while others have
been based on a strict recall approach (for example, remember all your activities for the
past two days). Another approach has been to average the amounts of various activities
over a specified time period.

For CARDIA, we have selected an interviewer-administered recall method that
attempts to obtain the major activities a person has performed during the past seven
days. It covers all physical activity (occupational, leisure, and home). As with any

approach to measuring total physical activity in a population, it has its weaknesses:

EX-6

(1) Some people may have trouble remembering what they did.

(2) Some respondents (as with any questionnaire) may, consciously or
unconsciously, " gild the lily " and tell us what they think we want to hear.

(3) This approach inevitably calls for subjective judgement by the interviewers
and there may be some difficulty establishing consistency within and among
the various CARDIA centers. Ideally, an interviewer should get the same
data today as he/she, or another interviewer, would get next month if
interviewing the same participant whose activity was constant.

Our method of measuring physical activity also has its advantages. Since we ask
about the number of hours spent in sleep, moderate, hard, and very hard activities, we
can obtain the time spent in light activities by summing those categories and subtracting
from 24 hours. This then allows us to calculate the total daily caloric expenditure as the
physical activity index. We think that our questionnaire approach is efficient since
respondents will sleep 6-8 hours per day, and for the majority, most of their waking
activity will be in the light category. Therefore, our interview efforts need only
specifically account for relatively small amounts of time, usually less than 3-4 hours per
day.

The purpose of the seven-day physical activity recall (PAR) is to determine an
estimate of the energy output by a person during a day. The energy output is measured
in calories, just as an individual's energy from food is measured in calories. We are
always expending energy whatever we do. The amount of energy we expend is related to
how strenuous our activities are. One activity is more strenuous than another one, in this
sense, if it causes our bodies to operate at a higher metabolic rate than the other
activity. The unit which has been devised to measure the strenuousness of an activity is
the MET. One MET is the lowest level of activity and corresponds to our metabolic rate
while we sleep. A very hard activity, such as running, may correspond to a level of 10
mets. In our survey, light activities correspond to levels of up to 3 METS, moderate
activities to levels between 3 and 5 METS, hard activities to levels between 5 and 7
METS, and very hard activities to levels greater than 7 METS. An individual's caloric
expenditure during any activity is directly related to the MET level of that activity. For
example, one burns up twice as many calories during a 6 MET activity than during a 3
MET activity. If we know both the MET level of ‘an activity and the amount of time
spent performing that activity, then we can estimate the total calorie expenditure
associated with that activity. With the PAR, we determine the amount of time spent in
activities of different MET levels during the week, and can estimate an individual's daily
energy output, as measured in calories, from this as demonstrated in Table 1.

CARDIA PHYSICAL ACTIVITY QUESTIONNAIRE
RATIONALE

The presumption is strong based on epidemiologic evidence that physical inactivity
is a risk factor for coronary heart disease. It is certain that it is relevant to weight
control, and in turn is therefore related to the genesis of obesity, hypertension and
hyperlipidemia. Through its relationship to HDL cholesterol, physical activity level may
be related in general to the lipid profile.

Physical activity is a behavior, consisting of many different components. It is
important for CARDIA to measure which activities are prevalent, and how this activity
spectrum changes as the CARDIA population ages. Further it is important to reliably
rank people for overall level of all and of intense physical activity.

The existing questionnaires which might be best suited for use in CARDIA were the
Minnesota Leisure Time Physical Activity Questionnaire and the Seven Day Physical
Activity Reeall. The former, which spans 12 months, has been validated against
physiologic endpoints, but has not been shown to be adequately reliable on reapplication,
and takes too long to administer. The latter spans only seven days, has considerable
accuracy, has passed some validity studies and is suitably brief. It is included in the
CARDIA protocol. However, it too suffers from low repeatability since one week's
physical activity is often not representative of general patterns.

In devising a briefer new questionnaire, it was theorized that people could
accurately recall or summarize for themselves what and how much activity they do
within broad categories. Therefore details were avoided as being both poorly repeatable
and irrelevant.

Using an extensive database from the Minnesota Heart Health Program, tabulations
were made of activity participation for men and women aged 25-29. Based on these
tabulations questions were worded for sets of activities which might be logically classed
together. For each, the number of months of minimal performance, at least one hour
total in the month, was queried. Finally the number of months in which the activity was
performed frequently, i.e. at least an activity-specifie number of hours/week, was
queried.

RATIONALE FOR EXERCISE TESTING IN CARDIA

A general impression exists that increased physical fitness or physical working
capacity is inversely associated with coronary heart disease CHD risk (1). However,
limited data are available that directly address this association: few studies have been
published that have acquired accurate measures of fitness on a population free of
clinically evident CHD and followed them for an adequate period of time. Data from
MRFIT and the LRC Prevalence Survey may provide data on this issue but such data have
not been published yet. In patients with established CHD, functional capacity, as
measured by symptom-limited exercise testing, is a powerful predictor of recurrent
cardiac events but this association is due more to the effects of poor left ventricular
function in some of these patients than fitness as modified by exercise habits (2). Some
resting indicies of physical fitness, most notably resting heart rate, have been inversely
associated with CHD risk in several major studies (3,4).

Vigorous physical activity, as assessed by recall questionnaire, is associated with
exercise test performance and adults at all ages that regularly perform vigorous leisure-
time or job-related exercise have significantly higher exercise capacities than their
sedentary counterparts (5). The characteristics of exercise (type, intensity, duration and
frequency) required to enhance physical working capacity have been reasonably well
defined (6).

A high physical working capacity has been associated with an improved CHD risk
profile (7). Various studies have demonstrated that the more fit tend to have less
adiposity, higher HDL-Cholesterol, lower plasma triglycerides and somewhat lower
systolic blood pressures. Some of these apparent benefits probably are due to selection
factors (heredity), as it has been much more difficult to demonstrate changes of similar
magnitude when sedentary adults have undergone exercise training (8).

Electrocardiographic abnormalities at rest and during exercise are powerful
independent predictors of clinical CHD events in individuals initially free of CHD
manifestations as well as cardiac patients (9,10). Conduction disturbances at rest and
changes in the ECG during exercise, especially shifts of the ST-segment of more than 0.1
millivolts, have been strong predictors of CHD. Also in CARDIA, ECG indications of left
ventricular hypertrophy will be of interest, especially ethnic differences in young adults
occuring overtime.

There is some preliminary evidence that in adults with normal resting blood
pressure, a rapid rise in systolic blood pressure at low intensities of exercise is predictive
of future elevations in resting pressure (11). The CARDIA population provides an
excellent opportunity to investigate this possible predictor of blood pressure rise in a
young population.

A maximal treadmill exercise test with measurement of the ECG, blood pressure
and rating of perceived exertion was selected for CARDIA for the following reasons:

EX-9

A valid, highly precise, and reproducible measure of physical working capacity is
considered an important measure for CARDIA and the maximal treadmill exercise
test is considered the " gold standard " of such measurements. The treadmill
provides a better measure of capacity than a test on a cycle ergometer; accuracy
and reproducibility are somewhat less using a submaximal test procedure and the
Balke-type protocol provides reasonably equal physiologic increments in work and
allows nearly all subjects to complete the test while walking (aids in ability to
eoliect high quality ECG and blood pressure information).

Given the biracial nature of the CARDIA population, exercise blood pressure
responses and those factors associated with different magnitudes of response are
of great interest: how does resting and exercise blood pressure relate in young
adults, does " exercise hypertension " precede rest hypertension in some people?
The recording of blood pressure during treadmill exercise testing requires special
training but can be accurately performed by well trained technicians.

The measurement of greatest cost and logistic challange is the recording of the
ECG at rest and during exercise. Very little is known about the evolution of ECG
exercise abnormalities in this population or the precursors of these abnormalities. A
follow-up of 10 years or more probably would be needed to determine the
relationship of the evolution of these exercise ECG changes to the development of
the clinical manifestations of CHD.

A secondary reason for including the ECG recording during exercise is that without
it, a submaximal exercise test would have to be performed, thus reducing the value
of the test as a measure of physical working capacity. Most experts advise that if
maximal exercise testing is to be performed by adults, it should only be performed
if the ECG is continuously monitored.

EX-10

GENERAL TESTING PROCEDURE

The test procedure selected for CARDIA is a graded, maximal symptom-limited
treadmill exercise test to be performed by all CARDIA participants except those
excluded for medical reasons or who refuse to volunteer. The testing procedure
includes the following components:

1. Screening for medical eligibility

2. Participant preparation for ECG

3. Resting (supine) 12-lead ECG

4. Pre-exercise (standing) 3-lead ECG and blood pressure
5. Exercise on the treadmill

6. Recovery following exercise

7. Participant discharge

SCREENING FOR MEDICAL ELIGIBILITY

Once the participant has finished the body size measurements the technician will
check the medical questionnaire and resting blood pressure values and ask the participant
the additional medical screening questions for the purpose of determining the
participant's eligibility for exercise testing (Graded Exercise Treadmill Test
Rescheduling and Exclusion Criteria Form). The blood pressure to be considered for
determining eligibility is the average of the last two resting measurements recorded
using the random zero machine.

A limited examination of the heart and lungs should be performed on all
participants before preparation for the electrocardiogram commences. The examination
may be performed by the exercise test supervisor or the clinic physician. Training of the
exercise test supervisor in the examination will be the responsibility of the local
CARDIA physician (s). The examination should be performed with the participant in the
standing position. The examination should include at a minimum, oscultation of the lung
bases and oscultation of the apical and aortic areas of the precardium. A more extensive
routine examination may be performed if desired by local centers. Any abnormal
findings on examination should be verified by the clinic physician. Any participant witha
history of asthma, @ chronic respiratory disorder other than asthma or a cardiac disorder,
should be examined by the clinie physician. In addition to these guidelines, the clinic
physician may be requested to perform this examination in other situations at the
descretion of the exercise test supervisor.

CARDIA QUALITY CONTROL PROCEDURES

INTRODUCTION

The CARDIA Coordinating Center will carry out quality control measures during the

course of the study. There are two primary purposes for quality control. One is for

assessing errors and historically documenting the level of quality. Second, and more
importantly, is the impact of these quality measures on maintaining or improving the
quality of the subsequent collection of study data.

Quality control involves the collection of certain types of data and the subsequent

analysis of that data. It is primarily a measure of the quality of data that is 1) being

collected by the clincal center, and 2) measured by central laboratories and centers
associated with the CARDIA study.

Quality control is accomplished in many different ways depending upon the type of data

being collected, the type of procedure being analyzed, and the associated outcome

variable in question. The types of quality control measures that will be used in the

CARDIA Study include:

1) Monitoring reports ~ primarily a tool used to monitor errors in forms; also used to
document recruitment procedures.

2) Calibration of instruments - used in any seetion which employs a measurement
instrument, e.g. calipers, scales, sphygmomanometer.

3) Log sheets - sometimes supplied to the Coordinating Center noting periodic
calibration procedures such as room, refrigerator, and freezer temperatures,
inventories, ete.

4) External surveillance - used when data is reported from outside the CARDIA
community, i.e. central laboratories, CARDIA storage centers (ECG).

A Manual has been developed which outlines the particular steps that will be taken for

each of the sections of the CARDIA visit in order to assure that quality data is being

collected and reported.

OBJECTIVE: To assess the quality of the CARDIA occupational coding.

Assessment of the reproducibility of an assigned occupation code in the CARDIA study will be
conducted internally by the individual clinical centers. A round robin approach as described
below would control for some review bias within a center. The administration and control of
the procedure would be handled by the Coordinating Center. The Occupational Code
Committee (Johnson, Orden, Collette) will act as the adjudicator for mismatches. The Census
Bureau may also be utilized to handle codes which cannot be resolved by the adjudicator.

METHODS:

Clinical Center Responsibilities:

As a center to be assessed:

1. Xerox pages 4, 8, and 11 of Form 3 (responses to the occupation questions for respondent,
spouse, and parents). Always send a complete set of these 3 response pages even when no
response is given for spouse or parent.

- On the sets to be sent to the review center, black out all assigned occupation codes.

2. Compile a list of these participant ID's on an Occupation Code (OCC) Report Form. Xerox
3 copies of this form to prevent transcription errors,

- On the form to be sent to the reviewing center, only the respondent ID numbers are
to be filled in.

- On the form to be sent to the Coordinating Center, also fill in the initial codes for
respondent, spouse and parents.

- Retain a copy for your files.

3. Mail (via USPS) the response pages and OCC form to the review center and to the
Coordinating Center.

As a reviewing center:

1. One individual preferably, or more than one if appropriate, should be selected to recode the
occupation responses.

2. Upon receipt of Form 3 pages and Occupation Code Report Form, the designated coder is
to assign occupation codes for each participant form set received, entering responses on the
eode report form in the review center column (R).

3. The completed report form is then forwarded to the Coordinating Center.

8/85 QC-40

Coordinating Center Responsibilities:

1. Compare initial codes with reviewer assigned codes to identify mismatches.

Code all comparisons on the OCC Report Form in the error code column using the following
scheme (see attachment for description of groups):

(1) agreement between initial and reviewer assigned code

(2) mismatch - difference falls within same census category of 15

(3) mismatch - difference falls within the same census major group of 6, but not in
the same category of 15

(4) mismatch - difference falls outside census major group of 6

2. Report mismatches to the adjudicator with copies of the textual Form 3 data and the OCC
form for placement of the final codes.

3. Compare adjudicator codes given to mismatches. Identify those participant responses
which cannot be consistently coded.

4. Compute the initial vs. adjudicator error rates by coder, center, and overall study.
Compute specific error type rates using the error codes assigned in #1.

5. Report rates and problem responses to the Committee.

Adjudicator Responsibilities:

1. The adjudicator will be supplied by the Coordinating Center with Form 3 pages and
previously assigned codes in which a mismatch between initial and reviewer code appeared. The
adjudicator will decide which code most closely describes the occupation, or whether yet
another code is more appropriate.

2. The adjudicator will enter code and any explanation of the difference and return the form
to the Coordinating Center.

Committee Responsibilities:

1. The Committee will monitor quality control results and will supply detailed feedback to the
Steering Committee and the clinie coordinators.

2. Special instructions will be communicated to coders.

requires correction in the database.

PULMONARY FUNCTION TESTING AND HISTORY

Measures of pulmonary function and history are included in the CARDIA protocol
primarily to gain a better understanding of the factors that contribute to pulmonary
growth and decay prior to middle age and only secondarily to investigate the possible
interplay between pulmonary factors and the development of coronary heart disease and
other cardiovascular outcomes.

Numerous studies have identified cigarette smoking as an important contributor to
the decline in pulmonary function over time and to the development of chronic
obstructive airway disease (1-7) However, there is little concensus regarding other
environmental or social influences on pulmonary function or disease that might account
for differences observed between and within populations. Since the lungs continue to
develop through childhood and into young adulthood, it has been suggested that certain
factors during the formative years such as recurrent respiratory illness may predispose
individuals to later pulmonary symptomatology or disease (8,9). Existing data also
indicate that there may be racial differences in pulmonary function which are
unexplained by differences in smoking habits or simple measures of body size such as
height and weight (10-15). In addition, more research is needed on asthmatic conditions
which are poorly understood but not uncommon in younger populations. The CARDIA
pulmonary protocol has been designed to add to the existing knowledge in these areas.
Specifically, CARDIA will attempt to:

a) describe the evolution of pulmonary function and symptomatology
through young adulthood in relationship to influences such as early
cigarette exposure and childhood respiratory history. Passive as well
as direct exposure to cigarettes will be measured by blood cotinine
levels.

b) provide data on black-white differences in pulmonary function and
change which may be related, at least in part, to differences in body
build (measured by height, frame size, girths), childhood disease
experience, and cigarette exposure.

ce) gain further insight into those factors (e.g., allergies, sensitivity to
exposures) that predispose to the development of asthmatic
symptomatolgy and concomitant pulmonary function changes.

A secondary objective of characterizing the pulmonary profile of this young adult
population at baseline is to investigate the relationship between pulmonary function and
coronary risk. Some studies suggest that pulmonary function is predictive of subsequent
cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, irrespective of smoking habits (16-18). However,
it has been hypothesized that decreased pulmonary capacity is more likely an early
marker of ill-health and probably does not contribute to disease outcome either directly
or indirectly through the cardiovascular risk factors. In any event, it can not be
anticipated that CARDIA participants will be followed for disease end points at the
present time.

PUL-1

Data Collection

The following pulmonary measures are pert of the CARDIA examination protocol:

lung volumes and flow rates obtained from several forced expiratory
maneuvers on the Collins Survey Spirometer (forced vital capacity, forced
expiratory volume in 1 and 3 seconds, peak expiratory flow rate, mid-
maximal expiratory flow rate, flow rates at 25, 50 and 75 percent of total
expired volume). These measures will be taken at the first, but not second,
CARDIA examination.

information on current respiratory infections, medication use, chest injuries
and operations for interpretation of the pulmonary tracings.

respiratory symptomatology including cough, phlegm and wheeze for
ascertainment of the development of chronic obstructive airway disease and
asthma.

history of pulmonary diagnoses in childhood and adulthood.

history of allergies as well as sensitivity to dust, pollen, smoke and animals
as they relate to the development of asthma and decline in pulmonary
function.

Methods of Measurement

Accurate spirometric pulmonary function testing has three essential components:
a) a frequently calibrated spirometer that accurately records exhaled volume in relation
to time during the forced expiration; b) a subject who inspires maximally and exhales as
forcefully, smoothly, and completely as he can; and c) a technician who can calibrate the
spirometer, coach the subject to perform maximal efforts, and detect poor subject effort
and/or expirations that are not continuous, maximal, and completely recorded. CARDIA
has as its goal to produce accurate spirometric pulmonary function measurements using
the Survey Spirometer and the Eagle Il microprocessor (Warren E. Collins, Inc.,
Braintree, MA).

The equipment to be used in the CARDIA Study, and the supplies necessary for
pulmonary function testing will be standardized, with routine cleaning of the spirometer
and breathing tubes, plus frequent calibration of the spirometer, including checks of the
chart speed and volume deflection and tests for leakage. General principles of
spirometrie testing, are: a) how to perform forced expiratory maneuvers; b) problems
that are often encountered in conducting the forced expiratory maneuver; c) the number
of trials to be performed and reproducibility criteria; d) measurements of the Forced
Expiratory Volume in One Second (FEV1), the Forced Vital Capacity (FVC), The FEV1
FVC ratio, the Forced Expiratory Flow Rates (FEF) at 25%, 50%, and 75% of the FVC
exhaled, and the Maximal Mid-Expiratory Flow Rate (MMEF); e) correction of these
measurements to Body Temperature and Pressure, Saturated (BTPS); and f) calculation
of the predicted lung volumes and flow rates, the racial correction factor, and
comparison of the observed with these predicted values will also be detailed along with
procedures to be followed in testing study subjects using the Eagle fl microprocessor and
the Survey Spirometer.

PUL-2

It will be seen that use of the Eagle II, in conjunction with the Survey spirometer,
relieves the technician of hand measurement of the spirograms, BTPS correction, and
ealeulation of and comparison with predicted pulmonary function values. However, it is
still essential that the technician calibrate the spirometer and that he insure, by active
eoaching and by vigilant attention to the spirograms, that maximum and good quality
forced expirations are performed and recorded.

Equipment

All pulmonary function tests will be conducted using the Collins survey 8-liter
water sealed spirometer. The expired volume is measured as it displaces a lightweight
plastie bell riding in a narrow water well. A pen moves directly with the bell, recording
a tracing of volume versus time on a kymograph drum, rotating at a speed of 32mm/sec.
In addition, to the information presented in this manual, further details of the operation
and maintenance of the spirometer sre given in the Instruction Manual for the Collins
Survey Spirometer.

The Eagle 0, microprocessor will be used in conjunction with the Survey
spirometer during the spirometer volume calibration and patient testing. The Eagle I
attaches to the Survey spirometer via a Computer Input/Output Connector Cable. The
Eagle I primarily assists the technician in two otherwise time-consuming tasks:
ealculation of expired volumes and flow rates and calculation of predicted pulmonary
function values.

A linear motion potentiometer attached to the spirometer bell converts
spirometer bell volume changes into electrical signals. As the spirometer bell is
displaced during a forced expiration, signals are sent to the Eagle I through the
computer connector cable. In this way, the Eagie Ii measures how fast the expiration is
proceeding, and calculates instantaneous flow rates at several points during the forced
expiration.

In addition, using the participant's age, height and sex, which are entered into the
Eagle Il prior to participant testing, the Eagle Il computes the predicted pulmonary
function values using Knudsons's prediction equations (16). After each expiration is
recorded, the Eagle II will print the test results and compare the participant's observed
measurements with those predicted for his age, height, race, and sex. Further details on
the Eagle I are available in the Instruction Manual for the Collins Eagle Il Pulmonary
Function Testing System.

Details of the approach to pulmonary function testing are outlined in the
"CARDIA" Standardized Pulmonary Function Testing Manual" which is part of the
CARDIA Manual of Operations. Pulmonary history and symptomatology questions are
part of the medical history and medical data collection for the study.

Technician Certification and Quality Control

Following attendance at a "CARDIA Standardized Pulmonary Function Testing
Workshop", technician should conduct: (1) four calibration sessions, recording the
obtained values on a calibration log sheet; and (2) four pulmonary function testing
sessions for non-CARDIA participants, preferably using participants inexperienced in
spirometric testing. The calibration logs, chart papers, and computer strips should be
forwarded to the Coordinating Center for review. Similarly, the pulmonary function
tracings and computer strips from the Participant testing should be properly labelled and
forwarded to the Coordinating Center. After the technician's calibration and testing

PUL-3

techniques are judged to be satisfactory, the technician will be certified to conduct
pulmonary function testing.

Following certification, the Coordinating Center will draw a random sample of
several pulmonary function tests per technician at the end of each month, and request

NUTRITION

A role for diet in the development of cornary heart disease (CHD) is supported by
findings that dietary factors may influence risk factors for this disease. The CHD risk
factors shown to be most affected by patterns of nutrient intake are serum cholesterol
and blood pressure.

Serum Cholesterol

Hypercholesterolemia is one of the three major established risk factors for CHD.
Many studies have indicated a strong relationship between dietary factors, especially
dietary lipid intake, and serum cholesterol and heart disease. These studies can be
classified in to four different eategories: inter-population comparison studies, metabolic
ward studies, studies on free-living individuals, and dietary trials.

Inter-population Comparisons

Many investigators have examined the relationships among dietary factors and
CHD mortality utilizing data published by the United Nations Food and Agriculture
Organization (FAO), and the World Health Organization (WHO), (1-8). All of the studies
have consistently shown statistically significant univariate associations between dietary
constituents and mortality from CHD. These encompassed significant positive
associations between dietary saturated fat, cholesterol, animal fat, total fat, total
protein, animal protein, animal foodstuffs, refined and processed sugars, total calories
and CHD mortality rates in middle age. Significant negative correlations were observed
for vegetable protein, vegetable foodstuffs, vegetable fat and CHD mortality rates.
Intakes of these dietary factors are also related to one another, i.e., high intake of
animal fat is correlated with low intake of vegetable fat, as a reflection of the
economies of these countries. Therefore some of the relationships may be spurious. A
recent study analyzed these data using bivariate techniques (9). The results indicated
that the significant relationship between dietary lipid and CHD persisted with control for
vegetable products or refined sugars. The latter two, on the other hand, did not relate
significantly to CHD mortality when dietary lipid was controlled.

Similar comparison among living population cohorts demonstrated similar positive
associations among dietary lipid, serum cholesterol and CHD rates (10-15). For example,
the Seven Countries Study examined the 5- and 10-year incidence rates of CHD for 16
population in seven countries -- Finland, Greece, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, the
United States, and Yugoslavia (10-12). Baseline saturated fat intakes and CHD rates for
these populations samples were highly and significantly correlated, as were saturated fat
intake and serum cholesterol, and serum cholesterol and CHD rates. The Ni-Hon San
Study compared men in Japan, Japanese~American men in Hawaii, and Japenese men in
San Francisco (13-15). Nutrient analyses indicated that the group mean intakes of total
fat, saturated fat, and animal protein were much lower in the Japanese than in the
Japanese-American men. The mean serum cholesterol level of Japanese men was 37
mg/dl lower than that of the Hawaiian men and 47 mg/dl lower than that of the
California men.

NUT-1

The data from the international autopsy studies, epitomized by the International
Atherosclerosis Project, also showed a relationship across populations between dietary
fat and severe coronary atherosclerosis, and, in addition, between dietary fat and serum
cholesterol and between serum cholesterol and severe coronary atherosclerosis (16),

Within the U.S. population, comparisons of various ethnic or religious groups
yielded similar findings. For example, the comparison of vegetarians and non-
vegetarians in a Seventh-Day Adventist group, and the comparison of Boston vegetarian
commune residents with Framingham men showed that dietary fat composition and serum
cholesterol were strongly associated (17-18).

In summary, analyses of FAO-WHO data and comparisons of international living
populations, in international autopsy studies, migrants, ethnic and religious groups
within-countries have all yielded similar findings, i.e., dietary lipid composition and
cholesterol intakes are strongly associated with serum cholesterol and CHD incidence
and mortality rates.

Metabolic Ward Studies

In a series of metabolic studies, Keys et al. showed that the mean change in serum
cholesterol in men can be expressed as a linear function of mean changes in saturated
fat, polyunsaturated fat and dietary cholesterol intakes (19). Similar findings were also
obtained by Hegsted et al. (20). Connor et al. studied the effects of dietary cholesterol
on serum lipids and showed that mean serum cholesterol levels of a group of men changed
as dietary cholesterol intake changed (21-23). Their findings were confirmed by Mattson
et al. (24). Moreover, Erickson and Mattson showed that serum cholesterol level changed
as the ratio of polyunsaturated to saturated fatty acids changed (25). In summary,
results from metabolic ward studies have indicated that dietary cholesterol, saturated
fat and polyunsaturated fat intakes have a strong impact upon serum cholesterol level.

Cross-Sectional Studies

Results of the cross-sectional studies on the relationship between dietary lipid
intake of individuals within a population and serum cholesterol are inconsistent (26-31).
Several studies, e.g., the Framingham and Tecumseh Community Studies, and the Israeli
Civil Servant Study reported no association, or a low-order non-significant association,
between the dietary lipid intake in individuals and their serum cholesterol level (26-28).
On the other hand, the Tarahumara Indian Study found a highly significant relationship,
with a very high correlation coefficient (r=.9), between dietary cholesterol and the
plasma cholesterol (29). The Western Electric Study reported a highly significant
association between dietary lipid intake and serum cholesterol at baseline (30). In the
Western Electric Study, dietary lipid intake was measured by the lipid scores derived by
Keys and Hegsted in their metabolic ward studies (19-20). These scores measure the
combined impact of the saturated fat, polyunsaturated fat and dietary cholesterol intake
on serum cholesterol. For both univariate and multivariate analyses, the lipid scores
were highly correlated with serum cholesterol level. In addition, the changes in these
lipid scores between baseline and the first year were highly significantly related to the
corresponding changes in serum cholesterol level. Similar findings were also obtained
between saturated fat, dietary cholesterol and serum cholesterol.

NUT-2

Several reasons may explain the inconsistent results of these studies. First, within
a homogeneous population, the intra-individual variation of dietary factor is as large as,
or larger than, the inter-individual variation (32). Therefore, a single measurement—
e.g., the 24 hour recall used in the Tecumseh Study—is inadequate for validly
characterizing individuals within a population. On the other hand, the Tarahumara
Indians eat almost identically day after day. There is little intra-individual variation in
dietary cholesterol intake and thus a strong association between dietary and serum
cholesterol can be observed. Second, a large proportion of people with high serum
cholesterol levels will change their diet after being informed of their cholesterol level.
Consequently, if the dietary data are collected after the serum cholesterol data, the
relationship could be attenuated (31). Third, the intrinsic factors (under gentic influence)
of serum cholesterol may dilute a true relationship between a dietary factor and serum
cholesterol in a cross-sectional study (33). The analysis of change over time eliminates,
or at least markedly reduces, the interfering effect of genetically controlled inter-
individual differences in endogenous biochemical regulation.

The Western Electric Study did not limit itself to either a short dietary history of
what the men usually ate or to a 24-hour recall. Rather, for both the baseline and the
first year, the recent habitual diet of the participants was characterized in depth by the
modified Burke method, requiring about an hour per person. The positive findings
between dietary lipid intake and serum cholseterol and between the changes in both
variables merit emphasis.

With respect to the relationship between dietary lipid and the CHD mortality or
incidence, the results are fairly consistent. The Western Electric Study found that the
baseline lipid scores (both Keys and Hegsted) and dietary cholesterol intake (analyzed
separately) were significantly associated with the 20 year mortality from CHD (30).
These associations were independent of the three major risk factors, i.e., high blood
pressure, high serum cholesterol and cigarette smoking at baseline. Gordon et al.
analyzed the 6 year follow-up data from the Framingham Study, the Honolulu Heart
Study and Puerto Rico Heart Health Program (34). Men who developed myocardial
infarction (MI) or died of CHD, consumed a significantly higher percentage of calories
from total fat (in some cases, saturated fat) and less starch than the men without CHD.
In this study, the CHD group also consumed less calories and alcohol than average. More
recently, McGee et al. found that the baseline percentage of calories from protein, fat,
saturated fat and dietary cholesterol (per 100 calories) were significantly related to the
10 year incidence of MI or CHD death in the multivariate analysis of the Honolulu Heart
Study (35). Several other variables—calories, carbohydrates and aleohol—were inversely
related to MI or the CHD death. Similar findings were also reported by Kromhout and
Coulander on the 10 year mortality follow-up the of the Zutphen Study (36). Moreover,
Cahn et al. reported in the 21 year follow-up of adult Seventh-Day Adventists that intake
of eggs and meat were significantly positively related to, and intake of green salad was
negatively related to, the subsequent mortality from all causes (37).

In summary, the findings on the relationship between dietary lipid intake and
serum cholesterol for free-living individuals within a population are inconsistent.
However, the inconsistency can be explained at least in part by the methodological
problem in dietary assessment and the genetic factors related to serum cholesterol. The
experiences of the Western Electric Study deserve some attention, and the positive
findings need to be confirmed.

NUT-3

The results on the relationship between the baseline dietary intake of fat,
saturated fat and cholesterol, and the subsequent incidence or mortality from CHD
obtained in these prospective studies, further support the importance of diet in relation
to CHD.

Dietary Trials

Most of the dietary trials were not designed to test only the effect of dietary
change on serum cholesterol level. Usually dietary modification is a part of a
multifactor intervention program to reduce CHD. However, the National Diet Heart
Study, the Oslo Diet Heart Study, the Coronary Prevention Evaluation Program, the New
York Anti-Coronary Club Study, the Los Angeles Veterans Administration Domiciliary
iliary Facility Study, and the Lipid Research Clinic Coronary Primary Prevention Trial
have all shown that group mean serum cholesterol of free living people can be reduced
significantly by changing from a diet high in saturated fat and cholesterol to a diet low in
saturated fat and cholesterol, with or without high polyunsaturates (38-43). Results from
these studies suggest that it is feasible to change diet for a large group of people and
that the average serum cholesterol can be lowered by reducing the total fat intake and
by changing the fat composition in the diet.

Summary

The studies reviewed in this section are a few representative examples of a large
amount of literature on the relationship between diet and serum cholesterol level and/or
CHD. It does not include studies on the relationship between dietary intake and
lipoproteins, e.g., alcohol intake increases high density lipoprotein (44). However, based
on these study results, it can logically be concluded that diet plays a very important role
in the determination of serum cholesterol and in the development of atherosclerosis and
CHD. The CARDIA Study intends to identify the lifestyle or the change in lifestyle that
eauses the change in the major risk factors in young adults, serum cholesterol and blood
pressure. It is therefore imperative to measure the dietary intake of these young adults
over time. In order to characterize accurately the dietary intake for individuals, it is
necessary to select an appropriate dietary assessment method.

In most of the cross-sectional or prospective studies, either a single 24-hour recall
or a short quantitative food frequency method was used. Due to the problems described
before, either no or low-order associations were observed in these studies. The Western
Electric study, on the other hand, used a thorough dietary history method which took
about one hour per person. Consequently, the baseline dietary lipid scores (Keys and
Hegsted), saturated fat (percent from calories) and dietary cholesterol (per 1,000
ealories) were all significantly related to serum cholesterol. The changes in these
dietary variables from baseline to one year were also significantly related to the
corresponding changes in serum cholesterol. Moreover, these dietary variables were
significantly associated with the 20 year mortality from CHD. The significant finding is
not only limited to cardiovascular epidemiologic research. The Western Electric Study
also reported a highly significant inverse association between the baseline Vitamin A
intake from vegetable sources and the 20-year incidence and mortality from lung and
eolon cancers (45), All these results suggest that CARDIA should adopt a dietary method
that is similar to that used by the Western Electric Study. In this way, CARDIA is likely
to use the best method currently available and, the CARDIA study can have the
opportunity to confirm the Western Electric Study findings.

BLOOD PRESSURE

The influence of diet on blood pressure is a complex one involving both adverse and
favorable responses to intakes of individual nutrients as well as to the interactions of one
or more of these nutrients. Nutrients shown to adversely affect blood pressure are
sodium, total calories, sucrose, aleohol, and type and amount of protein: Those favorably
influencing blood pressure are potassium, calcium, magnesium, polyunsaturated fat and
fiber.

Sodium

A substantial amount of data supports an effect of dietary sodium on blood
pressure. Epidemiologic studies have shown that among populations consuming habitual
diets high in sodium, the prevalence of hypertension is high, in contrast to populations
consuming habitual diets low in sodium, where hypertension is rare and the tendency of
blood pressure to increase with age is not observed (1-6). Clinical investigations have
also shown that blood pressure may be successfully reduced in hypertensive individuals by
lowering dietary sodium intake (7-11). Studies in animals have revealed that the age at
which exposure to high sodium intake begins and the duration of this exposure may be
important factors in determining the level of blood pressure and the severity of
hypertension which develops (12-13). Intrapopulation studies of the relationship of
dietary sodium to blood pressure have yielded conflicting results (14-15). Methodological
Problems with assessment of sodium intake as well as individual differences in sensitivity
to sodium and other environmental influences may have contributed to the inconsistency
in the findings from these studies (16-17).

Calories

Total caloric intake may influence blood pressure through weight (18-22), the
amount of sodium consumed (23) and effects on sympathetic nervous system activity
(24). These factors may be interrelated in their effects on blood pressure as weight and
sodium also influence sympathetic activity (25-27). However, findings in animals suggest
a et effect of caloric intake on sympathetic activity independent of weight or sodium
intake (28).

Sucrose

The relationship between sucrose intake and blood pressure is not well defined.
Acute pressor effects of high sucrose intakes have been demonstrated in normotensive
humans without any changes in body weight (29-30). There are no data examining long-
term effects of sucrose on blood pressure in humans, but studies in normotensive animal
models have shown increased blood pressures with sucrose supplementation over a period
of 2-3 months at constant carbohydrate intake (31-32) independent of weight (32). High
sucrose intakes also augmented the hypertensinogenic effect of high sodium intake in
monkeys (33).

NUT-9

Protein

Although the total amount of protein in the diet may influence blood pressure
through effects on renal function (34), the type of protein may be a more important
determinant of blood pressure response. Much of the eveidence for this has been derived
from studies showing lower blood pressures among vegetarians compared with
omnivorous A significant decrease in diastolic pressure was noted when ominivores
consumed a vegetarian diet for six weeks, with blood pressures returning to baseline
levels when normal dietary intake was resumed (37), Although blood pressure has been
significantly associated with reported consumption of foods of animal origin (35), lacto-
ovo vegetarians who consume dairy protein also have lower pressures than omnivores
(38). In addition, fish protein fed at high levels resulted in decreased blood pressures and
complete inhibition of the development of stroke in stroke-prone spontaneously
hypertensive rats (39). However, vegetarian diets also differ from omnivorous diets in
many other factors such as P/S ratio and intakes of potassium and fiber, which have also
been shown to influence blood pressure (36, 40).

Alcohol

An association between prevalence of hypertension and regular consumption of
large amounts of alcoho] has been demonstrated in several cross-sectional population
studies, independent of body weight (41-45), age (41-43), serum cholesterol, pulse (42),
sex, race, coffee use, former heavy drinking, and educational attainment (43). The
available data suggest that the relationship between alcohol and blood pressure is not a
continuous one, but that a threshold level may exist with elevated pressures at and above
these levels, and with similar pressures below these levels for drinkers compared to those
who abstain (43).

Potassium

Dietary potassium has been associated with lower blood pressure in both
normotensives (46-47) and hypertensives (48-49). Acute experiments in humans indicate
that this potassium effect on blood pressure may be related to the enhanced urinary
excretion of sodium with potassium supplementation (49-51). These findings support
early work by Dahl et al (52) showing that less hypertension developed in animals fed high
sodium diets when the Na/K molar ratio was low, than in animals fed the same level of
sodium with a high Na/k ratio.

Calcium

High intakes of calcium have also been shown to have a favorable effect on blood
pressure. Data from 24-hour recalls revealed that a group of hypertensives consumed
less calcium than a group of normotensives matched for age, sex and race (53). Calcium
intake was also significantly and inversely associated with blood pressure among a group
of normotensive men age 30-79 (54). Furthermore, calcium supplementation of young
normotensive adults resulted in a decline in mean diastolic pressure of 6% in women and
9% in men (55). This protective effect of calcium on blood pressure is also supported by
studies with animals (56-60).

NUT-10

Magnesium

Limited data suggest that magnesium intake may also favorably influence blood
pressure. An analysis of the epidemiologic data showing an inverse association between
blood pressure and hardness of the water supply suggested that the magnesium
concentration in the water was the important factor related to blood pressure (61). A
significant decrease in blood pressure was noted with magnesium supplementation in a
group of hypertensive patients in the absence of changes in urinary sodium and potassium
concentrations or body weight (62).

Polyunsaturated

A significant negative association has been demonstrated between adipose tissue
linoleate and blood pressure in both men and women controlling for age and relative
weight (63-64). Blood pressure has also been significantly reduced in healthy adults by an
increase in the P/S ratio while decreasing intake of total fat (65-66). Similar findings
have also been reported for hypertensives with either a decrease in total fat, and
inerease in P/S ratio or both (66-67). Although the amount of fat intake may also be
important, data from a study with animals indicate that the blood pressure effect is due
to the increase in polyunsaturated fat rather than to the decrease or absence of
saturated fat (68).

Fiber

Studies examining the effect of dietary fiber on blood pressure have also involved
changes in other dietary factors as well. However, it appears that dietary fiber may
influence blood pressure through its effect on dietary fat absorption as has been
suggested by studies with animals (69-70). Increased P/S ratio was associated with a
significant reduction in blood pressure among individuals consuming low fiber diets, but
was without a further effect on blood pressure in fiber-supplemented individuals who had

reviously shown a significant decrease in blood pressure when fiber intake was increased
(71). Usual intakes of fiber were found to be signifeantly lower among a group of
hypertensives compared with normotensives (71). However, fiber supplementation of
hypertensives resulted in a significant decrease in blood pressure with a reduction in
total fat intake only if the P/S ratio was low (71). If the P/S ratio remained high, no
change in blood pressure was observed when fiber intake was increased (71), unless levels
of fiber were very high, e.g., 30-35g (72).

Summary

The evidence reported here supporting an association of dietary factors with blood
pressure represents only a sample of the most representative epidemiologic,
interventional and clinical research with humans. A significant amount of corroborating
findings in animals has been omitted except where these findings were provocative in
their extrapolation to humans or where research with humans was limited. With the
exception of sodium, the relationships between dietary factors and the interactions of
these factors with blood pressure have not been studied extensively and is a rapidly
growing field of investigation. CARDIA presents a unique opportunity to examine these
relationships in a young population where data concerning dietary behavior, exercise and
psychosocial factors will also be available to contribute to the interpretation of the
findings.

METHOD OF MEASUREMENT

To assess patterns of nutrient intake of importance to the development of CHD, a
28-day dietary history based on the Western Electric dietary history format will be
used. This method was selected because it can characterize individual intakes without
the bias created by methods which increase awareness of diet or require a minimal level
of education to complete. Several validated dietary histories are available but they are
not comprehensive regarding a broad range of nutrients, and none are satisfactory in
providing the specificity for those nutrients of importance to CHD.

The Western Electric 28-day dietary history was chosen on the basis for developing
a new history to achieve this aim. Previous use of this particular history provided
information on intakes of saturated fat and cholesterol which were significantly
associated with subsequent levels of serum cholesterol and development of CHD. Based
on 24 hour recall results of NHANES II regarding the foods most frequently consumed by
Amerieans during the 1970's, the Western Electric history has been modified to reflect
the current food supply and the intakes of a younger and more ethnically diverse
population. In addition, the format has been adapted to incorporate information required
for nutrient analysis using the database developed for NHLBI by the Nutrition Coding
Center (NCC).

The 28-day period will serve as the basis for estimating usual nutrient intake for
the following reasons:

° to provide a time-frame for reasonable recall as proven feasible in the
Western Electric Study

° to correlate with measures of serum variables which are influenced by diet
within this period of time

° to minimize the length of the interview.

The 28-day period will not reflect seasonal intakes of certain foods. Since histories
will be obtained throughout the year, seasonal intakes for the group will be determined.
To eliminate the influence of seasonal variations in nutrient intakes on serum variables in
individuals, follow-up examinations for each individual will take place in the same
season.

Use of a dietary history to measure nutrient intake can only provide estimates of
actual intake since it is limited by recall ability. The validity of this method is based on
its ability to preserve individual rank within the distibutions of intakes for each
nutrient. This ability may be enhanced by the following:

° providing a standardized list of items to elicit recall rather than relying on
recall alone

° assuring more accurate estimation of quantity through the use of food
models

° assuring more complete estimation of quantity by listing food items

individually rather than by grouping them.

Description

The nutrition history consists of three components: 1) questions regarding usual
dietary practices, 2) an assessment of sodium intake, and 3) a specific quantified food
frequency questionnaire.

1) Dietary practices will be evaluated by

° the use of food group indices developed to categorize foods in the nutrition
history according to behavior reflected in the choice of those foods

o additional questions to assess the use of fat in the preparation of various
foods.

2) Patterns of sodium intake will be categorized using answers obtained from a
short series of questions pertaining to

° addition of salt at the table

° addition of salt or sodium-containing spices in preparation of foods

° selection of foods having a lower sodium content rather than the usual
products

° use of specially prepared low-sodium products

° frequency of eating meals in commercial establishments.

3) The food frequency questionnaire will obtain

° the frequency of intake over the past month of various foods contained
within the NCC nutrition database file to provide qualitative and
quantitative data regarding key nutrients of interest

° information regarding usual serving size
° information on preparation technique and use of added fat,
Comparative Study

The nutrition instrument will be tested for both accuracy and feasibility. Although
the development of this instrument was based on the Western Electric dietary history, it
is a modified version of the original history and it is essentially a tool. Thus, it is
important that the relative validity of the CARDIA nutrition history in estimating usual
nutrient intake be assessed.

Accuracy. Nutrient intakes estimated from the nutrition history will be compared
with those obtained from seven 24-hour recalls randomly distributed over a one month
period. The agreement between the two methods in estimating intake of calories, total
fat, saturated fat, polyunsaturated fat, cholesterol, total carbohydrate, fiber, potassium,
eaicium, vitamin A and vitamin C will be used as the basis for validation.

Quality Control

A system for quality control of the nutrition data will be implemented to assure
completeness and accuracy of recorded dietary information and to monitor inter and
intra-interviewer differences in interpretation of reported dietary information for
recording it on the nutrition history form.

Completeness of Recorded Information

Each nutritionist will review the form upon completion and submit it to a second
nutritionist for review to check if all data required to process the form has been
recorded in the appropriate places. All columns will be checked to be sure that all
information for entry has been included. Items recorded under comments and on the
floating sheet will be checked to determine if they have been adequately documented on
the form. Items noted by asterisks as requiring codes will be checked to see that codes
have been entered.

Accuracy of Recorded Information

Each nutritionist will make a tape recording of one interview each month for the
first three months of the study. After the first three months, each nutritionist will make
a tape recording on one interview every six weeks. The tape and a eopy of the
corresponding nutrition history form will be sent to the Nutrition Coordinator who will
review the completed forms for accuracy in recording the dietary information.

NUT-21

Inter-interviewer Differences
The Nutrition Coordinator will prepare four video tape recordings emphasizing
various sections of the nutrition history. Each nutritionist will complete a nutrition
history form while viewing the taped interview. The nutritionist will review the form for
completeness and submit it to another nutritionist for a second check as described
previously in the "Completeness of Recorded Information". The completed form will be
returned to the Nutrition Coordinator who will compare nutrient data obtained from the
forms completed by each nutritionist to assess differences between interviewers in
interpreting reported dietary information for recording it on the history form.

Intra-interviewer Differences
The Nutrition Coordinator will send one of the four prepared videotapes to each
nutritionist twice. The nutritionist will complete a nutrition history form viewing the
taped interview, review the form for completeness and submit it to a second check by
another nutritionist as described previously in the section "Completeness of Recorded
Information". The completed form will be returned to the Nutrition Coordinator who will
compare nutrient data obtained from this form to that obtained from the original form
completed by the same nutritionist to assess intra-interviewer consistency in interpreting
reported dietary information for recording it on the history form.

SYSTEM DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION PLAN:
SYSTEM START-UP

The data management implementation plan is basically a three step plan focused on
getting the system functional with data entered and edited via microcomputers,
transferred to the central study database.

Step 1: Centralized Data Entry/Edit at the Coordinating Center.

Data processing is to begin with distributed data entry and editing at the Clinical
Centers via micro-processor-based equipment. Paper forms used for initial data capture
to record participant responses will be utilized as the primary source document for data
entry and editing. Data will be entered at stand-alone workstations with preliminary edit
ehecking done at data entry utilizing screen oriented input to minimize typing errors and
obvious inconsistencies such as numeric data, alphabetic data, range checks, ete.

Initial entry will be stored on hard disks, then transferred and transmitted to the
central study computer (VAX 11/750) for consolidation and updating of the central study
database. Backup for data entered will be provided. A standard, commercially available
teleeommunications software package, will be used for telecommunications to the VAX
11/750 at the Coordinating Center.

Step 2: Analysis

As development of the central study database proceeds, analysis will be effected
initially in 2 ways:

1. Machine readable tape in SAS formats will be provided to NHLBI. Data in
machine readable form would also be available in whole or part to the
Clinical Centers for analysis, as authorized by NHLBI and the Steering
Committee.

2. Dial-up access is also planned for those investigators who, with authorization
from NHLBI, desire access to the main study database.

Step 3: Distributed Data Analysis

Further capabilities for distributed analysis will be provided utilizing previously
provided dial-up access to the main study database with investigators extracting data
subsets or partitions of interest, and storing them on micro-proccessor-based equipment
for further analysis locally.

Such distributed analysis would require micro-processor based equipment with
sufficient memory to accommodate data sets of interest, and analytical and computing
hardware and software power for accomplishing analysis.

Use of similar software packages utilizing the same basic computational methods
and algorithms, and equipment produced by the same manufacturer may help in
minimizing the inherent discrepencies often found in results originating across different
machines utilizing various software packages.

DATA FLOW

The dynamics of the data flow process ean be divided into three distinct phases -
data entry, file transfer, and storage on the host machine.

Data Entry

The data entry process can be viewed from two levels. The first level is the more
abstract since it views data entry as a multi-modal operation incorporating the addition
of new records and the deletion, modification, and viewing of current records. It views
these processes as individual modules, each implementing the necessary error checking,
correction, verification, and journaling required to insure data integrity. The first view
is reflected by data flow diagram 1.

The second level is the more concrete since it actually describes a method of data
entry (i.e. electronic forms), implementation of specifie error checking mechanisms, and
master file preparations. The second view is shown in data flow diagram 2.

File Transfer

Data is to be transferred from the clinic data entry stations to the host system,
utilizing an asynchronous file transfer protocol enabling the up-loading and down-loading
of data files. The advantages of this method would be that data could be incorporated
into the central data base almost immediately and it would simplify distributed analysis
of data. A general scheme of file transfer is shown in data flow diagram 3.

Storage on the Host Machine

Once data is transferred to the host, it is integrated into the main data base.
Facilities must be available for on-line updates as well as the batch processing of data
received from laboratories in machine readable form (tape diskette or file transfer from
machine to machine). Other facilities must include data display and retrieval
mechanisms, statistical software, report generators, and capabilities to create tape files
for purposes of analysis or archiving. Refer to flow diagram 4.

DATA MANAGEMENT
Software

The initial priority of the CARDIA study from a data mangement perspective is the
development of a distributed data entry sytem that provides rapid and easy data entry,
while simultaneously insuring optimum data integrity. The ability to create special data
checking and editing features not provided by the software itself will be used.

An additional requirement to that of flexibility is one of high programmer
productivity. Due to stringent time requirements for system development, there is a
need to optimize development time.

The two above requirements are best met by forms management software
complete with a high-level programming language interface. In some ways the use of
this type of package is a compromise from the productivity standpoint since it requires
more programming than other packaged software (i.e. data base management systems).
However, forms managment software provides the ability to build the needed edit and
control features which are specifically required for this project.

Computer and Equipment

In considering a specific machine for data entry, a great deal of weight is placed on
the availability of required software for that machine. In this respect, the IBM PC/XT
seems a good choice. There appears to be no shortage of good quality application and
utility software available for the PC. The numerous forms managment packages and
communieations protocols written for the IBM give it the ability to perform adequately
both in the area of data entry and in micro-to-mainframe file transfer.

Data Analyses

Subsequent to data entry, file transfer, and data storage on the host machine, will
come data analysis, the primary objective of the study. An important facet of the
preparation of data for analysis is the management of data on the host. The essential
considerations are data integrity, data security, data independence, and the ability to
view and retrieve data in any and all combinations necessary for subsequent analysis.
