PSYCHOSOCIAL COMPONENT

The CARDIA study presents an excellent opportunity to study the effects of life
change on a cohort of young adults prior to the existence of major disease and in
conjunction with an extensive set of biomedical data. The basic goals of the psychosocial
portion of the exam will be:

1. To develop basic demographic information suitable in deseribing the study
population adequately in this age group.

2. To describe the development of psychosocial risk factors over a minimum of
two years.

3. To identify psychosocial factors predictive of CHD risk factor development.

The basie strategy that was followed in the selection of variables were their
demonstrated association with CHD, hypertension or other CHD risk factors in at least
two epidemiological studies. Additionally, variables were chosen that were useful or
necessary for the description of the study population (socioeconomic status, race, etc).
Questionnaire selection was based on the criteria of being appropriate for the study
population in terms of age, race, gender, socioeconomic status and literacy demands.
Attention to the length of the forms were considered as well as having documented
reliability and/or validity in prior research. While the list of variables was quite long,
the basie classes include sociodemographic indicators, life changes, and ways of eoping
with life situations and life changes. Several measures have been suggested for initial
exams only, while others will be obtained at the second exam. Rationales and
descriptions of the individual components follow.

PSY-1

SOCIODEMOGRAPHIC QUESTIONNAIRE
1

Description .

The basie sociodemographic descriptors included in this questionnaire are: age, sex,
race, marital status, socioeconomic status, parental socioeconomic status, spouse's
socioeconomic status, living situation, and residential mobility. Socioeconomic status is
measured by education, occupation and income, the traditional indicators of social
class, These measures may be analyzed separately or combined into an index of
socioeconomic status (SES). Questions on occupation have been formulated to correspond
to those used by the Bureau of the Census. :

Evidence

The evidence presented here is limited to risk for CHD, in accordance with the
criteria for selection of variables set by the Psychosocial Committee. Evidence of the
association of sociodemographic characteristics with specifie risk factors will be
considered by others,

Social Class

A change in the social class distribution of risk for CHD, at mid-century was noted
(Antonovsky, 1968; Jenkins, 1971; Marmot et al., 1978). Prior to the 1950's coronary
heart disease was widely held to be a disease of affluence with upper socioeconomic
classes at elevated risk (Osler, 1910; Price, 1941; Spain, 1966). Antonovsky reported that
this perception was clearly not supported by the data. In an extensive literature review,
he found some studies reported inverse class gradients, others reported direct gradients
and still others reported no gradient at all in the association between social class and risk
for CHD. Although there was no consistency, he noted that a majority of the studies did
show class differences which were substantial. He observed that several studies done in
1930-50 reported a direct gradient for the older age group and an inverse gradient in the
younger age group. Since the 1950's there has been a marked change in the view that
CHD is a disease of the rich . CHD has been reported as progressively more common
among lower socioeconomic classes (Marmot et al., 1978;Cooper et al., 1978).
Consequently lower classes are now generally at greater risk for CHD than middle
classes. An inverse relationship between social class and CHD risk has been reported in a
number of studies (see Education and Occupation for details). Kraus and his colleagues
noted that the inverse relationship between SES and risk for CHD held for whites, Asians,
and Spanish Americans, but not for blacks (Kraus et al. 1950).

Education

An inverse relationship between education and CHD risk has been reported with
reasonable consistency in several prospective epidemiological studies since the 1950's
(Liu et al., 1981; Hinkle et al., 1968, Rosenman et al. 1975; Dawber et al., 1959). Liu and
his colleagues found an inverse association between education and risk factors at entry in
the Chicago Heart Association cohort. They also found that the inverse relationship
between education and CHD risk was independent of risk factors at entry. The
Framingham study found an inverse relationship in its six year follow-up but it was not
significant (Dawber et al., 1959).

PSY-2

Occupation

Differences in CHD risk have been identified both within a particular occupation,
as well as across occupations. In the Whitehall study, men in lower employment grades in
the London civil service were at higher CHD risk than men in higher employment grades
(Rose and Marmot, 1981). In comparisons across occupations, people in those which
require a higher standard of education are at lower CHD risk compared to those with
lower educational requirements (Holme, et al., 1976; Sauli, 1979; Marmot et al., 1978;
Logan, 1954). On the other hand, the National Health Survey found no strong evidence of
any class gradient measured by either occupation or income with prevalence of CHD
(NCHS, Series 11, No.10, 1965).

Age-sex-race

Older people are at higher risk for CHD than younger ones, men are at higher risk
than women, black women are at higher risk than white women, and black men are
similar in risk to white men ( Cooper et al, 1978; Moriyama et al., 1971; Kitagawa and
Hauser, 1973; Gillum, 1982; Gillum and Grant, 1982). Death rates for black women have
been consistently higher than for white women since the late 1940's. The picture is
different for black men. Death rates were lower than for white men in the 1940's, then
rose rapidly and exceeded the rates for white men in 1968 and 1969, and in the years
following remained lower or close to the rates for white men (Cooper et al., 1978).
Contrary to a belief held by some that blacks are immune to CHD, CHD is the leading
cause of death in blacks, as it is in whites (Gillum, 1982).

Marital status

Death rates from CHD of the single, widowed and divorced are substantially
higher than rates for married persons (Moriyama et al., 1971). Men and women in
marriages in which the wife works out of economie necessity report more tension and
negative affect than people in marriages in which the wife works by choice (Orden and
Bradburn, 1968, 1969).

Status incongruities

Several studies indicate that men whose wives have a higher level of education than
they themselves have attained are at higher risk of CHD than men whose wives have less
education (Suarez, 1984; Haynes et al., 1983; Jenkins, 1976; Shekelle, 1969),

Occupational and residential mobility

Many studies have shown increased rates of disease among occupationally and
residentially mobile people (Syme et al., 1969; Syme et al., 1966; Cassel and Tyroler
1961; Kaplan 1971; Shekelle, 1979; Jahne, 1980). However several studies failed to find
increased rates of disease among mobile persons (Hinkle et al., 1968; Rosen and Rosen,
1978).

PSY-3

Living Situation

An association between social isolation and mortality has been shown. People living
alone are at greater risk than those living with others (Gove et al., 1980; Carnahan et al.,
1974).

Hypotheses

Social class and other sociodemographic variables will be used to describe sub-
groups of the sample population and to explain variations in levels of risk factors for
coronary heart disease, as well as changes in the development of risk factors over time.
The risk factors include biological and behavioral risk factors such as high blood pressure,
cigarette smoking, diet, alcohol consumption, etc.; psychological variables such as
hostility, anger, ways of coping and bringing a sense of coherence to life events; access
to and utilization of health care services; exposure to social factors such as social
supports and social disruption; and other factors yet to be identified. The pattern and
direction of the associations between sociodemographic characteristics and risk factors
for coronary heart disease will be as follow:

PSY-8

LIFE EVENTS

Description

Many studies on human behavior and social change have viewed change, especially
rapid social change as a time of stress for the individual. The most compelling evidence
for the negative impact of change on the individual comes from the literature in
psychosomatic medicine. From this developed the concept of stressful life events,
events in a person's life that, for better or worse, interrupted or changed the pattern of
usual activities. The incidence of change/interruption in usual activities leads to the
development of stress and the consequent onset of illness in the affected individual.
Recently a number of psychometric scales have been developed to measure the
magnitude of stress from a list of typical life events.

Justification and Hypotheses

There exists a vast literature citing a positive relationship between the incidence
of stressful life events and the onset of illness - both organic and psychiatric. Several
studies (Theorell and Rahe, 1970; Rahe and Paasikivi, 1971; Theorell and Rahe 1971;
Rahe, et al., 1974; and Theorell, 1974) have found a positive relationship between
stressful life events and myocardial infarction. The major hypothesis examined in these
studies (and many other similar investigations) is that significant stressful life events will
increase the probability of the onset of illness, including CHD. In addition, the incidence
of illness onset is a consequence of the rapid accumulation of stressful life events over
time. Finally, those stressful life events most closely related to lifestyle and lifestyle
changes will be most closely associated with illness onset, including CHD. In addition,
the incidence of illness onset is a consequence of the rapid accumulation of stressful life
events over time. The measurement of stressful life events is most important for
CARDIA as 18-30 years olds do experience rapid social change in lifestyle. Thus, for this
group the stressful effects of this change may be a definite risk factor for CHD. The
literature on stressful life events is not without its ecrities (Rabkin and Struening, 1974;
Wershow and Reinhart, 1974). Most of these criticisms, however, deal more with
methodological than substantive issues. Recently questions have been raised as to the
linearity of the relationship between stressful life events and illness (Wildman and
Johnson, 1977) and the additivity of the relationship (Lin, et al., 1979). These lead to
additional hypotheses concerning the meditating effects of social support mechanisms as
a buffer between stressful life events and illness onset and to the relationship between
the absence of life events and illness onset in a sub-population for which rapid social
change may be the norm.

Methods of Measuring and Scoring Stressful Life Events

Following the work by Holmes and Rahe (1967), a number of modifications of and
variations on their Social Readjustment Rating Scale have been developed in order to
measure stressful life events. To date, the revision by Dohrenwend et al. (1978) appears
to be the most successful from two perspectives: applicability to the target population
of CARDIA and methodological rigor. Each of the 102 events on the Psychiatric
Epidemiology Rating Interview (PERI) Life Events Scale: was assigned a weight,
indicating its stress magnitude. These weights were empirically derived from a sample
of persons similar in their characteristics to the proposed CARDIA population. From the
PERI seale, a sub-scale of 64 items was selected by the Psychosocial Working Group.

PSY-9

These events, linked to educational attainment, family formation ,and career
development, etc. may be scored by one or all of three methods. First, the number of
events experienced during a fixed time period (usually one year) may be utilized; second,
the sum of weighted life events may be used as a ratio measure; and third, the sum of: the

ranks of the weighted life events may be used as an interval measure of the level of
stressful life events.

PSY-11

SOCIAL SUPPORT AND SENSE OF COHERENCE

Rationale

The 18-30 age period is a time when young adults first assume the responsibilities
of adult life. It is a time of substantial life changes and challenge. Several sections of
the psychosocial battery identify and assess these environmental demands. The 18-30
age period also is a time when young people first need to develop adult ways of coping
with challenges and demands, We hypothesize that (a) those who cope ineffectively and
inappropriately with environmental demands will exhibit greater increases in CHD risk
and (b) those young adults who cope well, even in the face of massive demands and
burdens, will experience lower CHD risk. Several questionnaires dealing with coping
have been described elsewhere (e.g., type A behavior, hostility and anger). Here we
discuss social support and sense of coherence.

Description

Social Support.

A substantial literature exists showing that strong social support networks
can act as a mediator between environmental demands and disease (Nuckolls,
Cassel, Kaplan, 1972; Boyce, Jensen, Cassel et al, 1977; Lin, Ensel, Simeone et al,
1979). Data are now available from large prospective studies that inadequate social
support networks predict the subsequent occurrence of CHD, angina, and mortality
from all with relative risks ranging from 2 to 3 after account has been taken of
other major CHD risk factors (Berkman and Syme, 1979; House, Robbins and
Metzner, 1982; Blazer, 1982). On the other hand, research on Japanese-American
men living in Honolulu found no relationship between social support and CHD
incidence (Reed, 1983). However, a 10-year follow-up study of social support and
CHD among 10,000 men and women in Finland is now nearing completion and data
from this study (after adjusting for major CHD risk factors) shows a two-fold
relative risk in disease among those with poor social support networks (Kaplan and
Syme, 1984, unpublished). Since young adults 18-30 tend more often than other to
leave home, leave school, get married, find jobs and move geographically, the issue
of social support is of special importance in this group.

Sense of Coherence

Three investigators recently have suggested the importance of a particular
"world view" for successful coping with environmental demands and burdens.
Kobasa (1979) has referred to one such style of coping as "hardiness" — having an
overall direction and purpose in life, a feeling of control and an acceptance of
change. Kobasa has shown (1982) that hardy individuals have significantly fewer
symptoms of illness than non-hardy people even in the face of considerable life
change and burden. Boyce (1983) has shown the importance of "sense of
permanence" in predicting upper respiratory infections in children and

PSY-22

ANGER/HOSTILITY/AGGRESSION - (AHA)

Anger, hostility and aggression are not conceptually distinet and in practice have
been used inconsistently and even interchangeably. Current definitions describe hostility
as an overall generic trait characterized by cynicism, malevalence, anger, and
aggression; anger as an emotional state including irritation, rage, ete.; and aggression as
the behavioral response. Data indicate significant overlap among the measures of each
construct, yet each appears to contribute to the prediction of CHD and its risk factors.

Hostility

Anger/Hostility/Aggression (AHA) has a long history of being related to coronary
heart disease (Alexander 1939, Miller 1965). Barefoot et al (1982) administered full scale
MMPI's to freshman medical students and recorded CHD and all cause mortality over a
25 year follow-up period. He found that hostility was the single best predictor in a
multivariate analysis using classical risk factors of smoking, age, family history of
hypertension, and current hypertensive status. Williams et al (1984) showed that women
who were type A and hostile have a relative risk of 3.6 for significant occlusions.
Matthews et al. (1977) reanalyzed the Western Collaborative Group Study data and found
potential for hostility strongly differentiated men who developed CHD. Dembrowski et
al (In press) found potential for hostility to be a predictor of total number of coronary
arteries occluded. His data show that increases in potential for hostility were associated
only for patients who held their anger in, Shekelle et al (1983) found that higher hostility
seores predicted increases in both CHD and total mortality among men in the Western
Electric Study over a 20 year follow-up period. He also showed that hostility is
independent of classical risk factors.

Anger

CHD factors are related to anger including style of coping with anger as to whether
it is expressed (anger-out) or contained (anger-in) and the dimension of anger as a
personality trait (trait-anger) and the experience of anger (state anger). Dembrowski et
al (In press) shows anger-in influenced the effect of hostility on coronary occlusions.
Harburg et al (1979, 1973, 1980) show that individuals in high stress areas and classified
as anger-in had a significant higher incidence of hypertension. Johnson (1984) found a
significant positive correlation between anger-in and blood pressure, after controlling for
age, race, weight, and sex. Framingham data show that holding anger in was predictive
of cerebral vascular accidents in women. Crane (1981) showed hypertensives to score
higher on both state and trait anger dimensions.

Measurement
Hostility may be measured by a number of different instruments with the Cook-
Mediey subseale (50 items) of the MMPI and component anaylsis of the structured

interview (See Structured Interview Presentation) commonly used in CHD research. It is
not known if the interview and questionnaire are measuring the same variable.

PSY-12

Hypotheses
Numerous hypotheses are available e.g. high hostility scores will function as a
prime risk factor for CHD, anger-in will modify the effect of hostility, anger-in will be
related to hypertension.

PSY-14

STRUCTURED INTERVIEW TO ASSESS TYPE A BEHAVIOR

Description of Instrument and Variables.

The Structured Interview (SI) is a standardized interview of 24 questions
concerning ambitiousness, competitiveness, time urgency and impatience. The SI was
originally designed to assess Type A behavior, and it was validated as a predictor of CHD
in a prospective epidemiological study (WCGS) (1).

Purpose of the SI.

All questionnaire measures of psychosocial risk rely upon the respondents' ability
and willingness to evaluate themselves—something which may be more difficult for those
most "risk prone". Since we conceive of risk factors, e.g., hostility and lack of social
support, as social processes, it is best to study these processes during actual social
interactions. The SI is a social interaction between the interviewer and respondent; it
provides behavioral components that have been linked with CHD. Assessments of these
components are based upon observing the social interaction rather than relying upon the
respondents subjective evaluations.

Research Support for Psychosocial Measures in the SI
Type A Behavior

Two prospective studies have linked Type A behavior to the incidence of CHD. The
first study, the WCGS found that male Type A's assessed by the SI were twice as likely to
incur CHD in an 8.5 year followup as Type B's (1). This study indicated that the SI
assessments of Type A behavior were more predictive of future CHD than a
questionnaire (2). In a second study, using data from Framingham, female Type A's were
significantly more likely to ineur CHD than Type B's (3). In a third prospective study
(MRFIT), Type A behavior was not found to predict CHD (4). An intensive analysis of
the MRFITS SI's indicated that some interviewers assessments of Type A were
significantly related to CHD, whereas others were not (5). The predictive interviewers
were more like the WCGS interviewers in that they asked questions more slowly and
interrupted the respondents less than the nonpredictive interviewers. As discussed
below, CARDIA interviewers will be trained using the WCGS as the ‘gold standard’. In
addition to Type A behavior, other behaviors to be scored from the SI will include self-
involvement—have recently emerged as successful predictors of CAD severity and CHD
incidence and they are proposed for study in CARDIA.

Hostility

Repeated studies have shown that hostility is correlated with severity of coronary
artery disease (6), and prospectively related to CHD and all cause mortality (7), Yet, we
do not fully understand hostility, particularly how its aspects are manifested and
integrated. The SI provides a behavioral measure of hostility providing a basis for
studying how different expressions of hostility or anger are related to one another, to the
other psychosocial variables, e.g., social support, and to blood pressure reactivity.

PSY-18

JOHN HENRYISM

Conceptual Definition

John Henryism refers to a strong personality predisposition to cope actively with
behavioral stressors in one's environment. The concept is rooted in the legend of John
Henry, in which the protagonist - a physically powerful, uneducated, black steel-driver -
purportedly won a drilling contest against a mechanical steam drill but dropped dead
immediately thereafter from exhaustion.

Assessment

John Henryism is measured by a 12 item Likert-type scale, which contains five
response options per item. Hence, scores on the scale can range from a low of 12 toa
high of 60. High scores connote physical vigor, tenacity, and a strong sense of personal
efficacy when confronting behavioral stressors. The assessment tool is called the John
Henryism Scale for Active Coping, or the JHAC12. Alpha coefficients have typically
ranged between .70 and .75.

The John Henryism Hypothesis

When actual coping resources (e.g. education, income, social supports, ete.) are
high, John Henryism is expected to be inversely associated with risk for cardiovascular
diseases, However, when such resources are low, John Henryism is expected to be
positively associated with risk for cardiovascular diseases.

Evidence in Support of the John Henryism Hypothesis

In a community study of 132 working class, black men, James et al! found that
men scoring above the median on John Henryism but below the median on education (i.e.
were not high school graduates) had the very highest mean blood pressures. Men who
scored above the median on John Henryism and who were high school graduates had the
very lowest mean blood pressures, ghe remaining two groups of men had intermediate
blood pressure values. James et al“ have also determined that there is a relationship
between high John Henryism mediates and between some psychosocial job stressors and
mean blood pressures in these working class black men.

In a recently completed study, James, Paul Obrist, and colleagues at UNC-Chapel
Hill found that the SES background of male undergraduates, in combination with high
John Henryism scores, predicted level of cardiovascular reactivity to controlled
laboratory stressors which required active coping. The least reactive subjects scored
above the median on John Henryism and came from homes where the head of the
household was a college graduate. In contrast, there was a tendency for subjects who
scored above the mean on John Henryism and who came from non-college backgrounds to
be the most highly reactive. In this sample of 180 college males (90% white), John
Henryism scores were inversely correlated with anger and hostility, as measured by the
Buss-Durkee Inventory. Also in this sample, JHAC12 and JAS Type A scores correlated
37; but, interestingly, JAS scores and Buss-Durkee anger/hostility scores were
eompletely uncorrelated.

PSY-19

Puture Research Challenges

JHAC12 data have recently been collected from a new, community probability
sample of eastern North Carolina residents. This sample includes 322 black men, 361
white men, 452 black women and 413 white women. Resting blood pressure data are also
available on these individuals. During 1984-85, the John Henryism Hypothesis will be
tested in this new study population to determine its applicability to whites and women.

The CARDIA project provides the first opportunity to test the John Henryism
Hypothesis in urban populations. The opportunity to collect 2 year (and possibly beyond)
follow-up data on CARDIA participants - in order to determine if high John Henryism (in
combination with selected social and economic resources) predicts undesirable changes in
CHD risk factors - represents an important step toward establishing the validity of the
John Henryism Hypothesis.

LIFE SATISFACTION

Rationale

Life satisfaction questions have been used widely in studies of quality of life and
health. Data exists on age, sex, and race specific responses.

Life satisfaction has been shown to be intermediate between the apparent
expectations and objective circumstances (achievements). The smaller the gap between
expegtations and achievements, the greater the level of subjectively reported quality of
life.

Studies which have addressed the subjective quality of life experience have
produced more consistent findings than those using objective social indicators.

A number of studies have demonstrated that the objective conditions of life (e.g.
income, education, and many other sociodemographic characteristics) are only marginally
related to the subjective experience of a better quality of lite.4~

APPENDIX

HYPOTHESES

This appendix provides a compendium of the hypotheses developed in the
generation of the protocol for CARDIA, While it is not meant to be mutually exclusive
and/or exhaustive, it represents the basic working hypotheses generated by the centers
and the working groups. The cover page attempts to index the hypotheses by relevant
component of the exam. Several of the hypotheses overlap and apply to more than one
component of the protocol. Generally, these are only shown once when the overlap is
obvious (e.g. objective smoking and tobacco questionnaire),

CENTER
MINN 1. HYPOTHESIS
CHD risk wil be greater in lower than higher socioeconomic status
groups. This will be partly a reflection of more smoking in the lower
socioeconomic status groups, along with a diet higher in fat and
sodium.
MINN 2.
Significant cross-sectional differences will be seen between white and
black subjects, congruent with the data showing higher blood pressure,
HDL-C and smoking rates in blacks than whites, but changes in these
factors in response to changes in other factors such as physical
activity, weight and diet will be comparable between blacks and
whites, and between men and women.
MINN 3.
Persons with more social networks will report more positive health
behaviors.
MINN 4.
Person who report negative life events and who have more social
networks will report fewer lapses in positive health behavior than
those who have fewer social networks.
MINN 5.
A tendency to form extensive social networks will be consistent over
time.
MINN 6.
Persons who report more recent negative life events will report more
lapses in positive health behavior (i.e. weight gain, started or returned
to smoking, stopped exercising) at a later time.
MINN 7.
Persons who report negative life events and who are rated internal on
the Multidimensional Health Locus of Control will report fewer lapses
in positive health behavior than those who are rated as external.
MINN 8.
Entering the workforce and increasing marital and family
responsibilities will reduce the opportunities for physical activity, and
therefore cause weight gain.
MINN 9.
Weight gain will be greater in those who have experienced major life
changes such as marriage, divorce, first job, or birth of their first
child. This weight gain will be caused by decreases in physical
activity and changes in eating patterns.
MINN 10.
Behavior change attempts in this population will generalize; that is,
those reporting behavior change attempts in one area will be more
likely than others to report behavior change attempts in other areas
of health at a later time.
MINN 11. More women will attempt weight loss than will men.
MINN 12.
There will be a curvilinear relationship between self-reported life
satisfaction and weight loss. Persons who are very content with their
lives will be unlikely to attempt weight loss regardless of initial

weight. Those who report low levels of satisfaction may attempt it
but are unlikely to be successful. Those with moderate reported
levels of life satisfaction are more likely to both attempt and achieve
weight loss.
MINN
13.
Persons with positive family history of heart disease will make more
attempts to improve health and reduce risk than will those with
negative family histories.
MINN
14.
Type A'S will make more health behavior change attempts than will
Type B's, including attempts to lose weight, increase physical activity
and quit smoking.
MINN
15.
Type A behavior pattern will be less stable in those who are 18-24
than in those who are 25-30 years old.
MINN
16.
Type A behavior will increase in those who enter the work force; it
will decrease in young women who leave the work force (i.e. for
marriage and/or childrearing.)
MINN
17.
There will be little change in smoking habits in early adult years.
MINN
18.
There will be little relation of smoking to vital capacity measures due
to the limited exposure time of the smokers. Smoking will
nevertheless be associated with more chronic cough and respiratory
problems.
MINN
19.
The observed relationship in which smokers weigh less than
nonsmokers will not be observed due to the limited exposure time of
these smokers to smoking. Weight gain in smokers who quit will not
be as great in these young people as has been observed in middle aged
people.
OAKL
20.
"...vitamin use may provide insights about life-style and health
conciousness of the subjects."
OAKL
21.
"The scientific questions about smoking that will be of primary
concern for this study will be directed chiefly at the identification of
factors associated with various aspects of the smoking habit and with
changes in the smoking habit. What leads to starting or to stopping
smoking? How persistent is the smoking havit in this age group once
it has begun? What determines the choice between low and high tar
and nicotine yield cigarettes and how often and why do persons
change to cigarettes with differenlt yields?
OAKL
22.
We also want to examine the relationship between changes in physical
activity and psychosocial parameters, such as Type A/B. One
particularly interesting question to examine would be the role of
physical activity in coping with the stress of major life events.
MINN
23.
Black men will be thinner than white men, but black women will be

The interactions of physical activity and nutrition in weight control

The interaction between physical activity and lipoproteins profiles
also deserve investigation. Some studies have demonstrated an
increase in HDL cholesterol with exercise (Wood et al., 1983). It
would be interesting to examine this issue in young adults, since
differences at relatively young age might have a cumulative effect
over the years and be related to the development of CHD. It would
also be of general interest to determine the interactions with other
lipoproteins and apoproteins as little work in this area has been done
with this age group, especially with women in general, and
particularly with blacks. We hypothesize that changes in lipids and
lipoproteins in the direction of lower CHD risk will be observed in
association with increased physical activity.

It should be clear that the Physical Activity Recall (PAR) provides a
vehicle for performing the types of analyses noted above not only by
total energy expenditure and by fitness level, but also by the energy
expenditure at various levels of exercise intensity. For example, it
has been suggested that a certain weekly threshold of very hard
activity (i.e., jogging) is associated with significant increases in HDL
cholesterol (Wood et al, 1983). The PAR can be used to validate this
and to determine whether a high level of moderate activity might
have the same effect.

A careful assessment is needed of the correlation between fitness
level as measured by the low level fitness test... and the total energy
expenditure as estimated by the PAR. If the correlation is
sufficiently high, it may be possible to use either of these methods
interchangeably as a valid measure of physical activity and fitness in
future epidemiological studies. If they do not correlate well, then it
would be necessary to use both types of methods as measurement
tools in future studies.

We would like to study the relation of job activity to fitness level as
measured by the exercise test and to CHD risk factors. Job activity
will be measured by the PAR, by a self-administered question about
work connected physical activity ... and by published information
about the energy expenditure involved in a wide variety of jobs
(Durin, 1967).

BODY SIZE MEASUREMENTS

All measurements are to be made with the participants wearing a short sleeve shirt
or blouse (or surgical gown) , shorts and socks and without shoes. A supply of shirts and
shorts should be maintained at the survey center for participants who forget to wear or
bring the appropriate clothes for exercise testing and body size measurements. Men
should be sure pockets are empty.

All measurements should be taken by a team of two persons, if possible - one acting
as observer and the other as recorder. The observer takes the measurements, calling out
the results to the recorder, who repeats them and then calls out the name of the next
measurement. The observer keeps the measuring instrument in place until the recorder
repeats the number. The recorder generally checks the examinee's position during the
procedure. Any values should be rounded to the nearest unit indicated for each
measure. If the value is exactly between two units, round up if the lower unit is even and
round down if the lower unit is odd (e.g, if value is 10.5 round up to 11.0; if value is 11.5
round down to 11.0).

Any modification in measurement techniques—such as left-side rather than right-
side measurements required because of amputations or casts, abnormal conditions such as
height decreased from a hunched condition, or girth increased from pregnancy—should be
noted on the recording form, where they could be taken into consideration in data

analysis.

BODY WEIGHT. Be sure the seale is balanced so that the indicator is at zero when
no weight is on the scale. The scale should be level and on a firm surface (not a
carpet). The participant should be instructed to stand in the middle of the platform of
the balance scale (Detecto, model #439) with head erect and eyes looking straight
ahead. Adjust the weight on the indicator until it is balanced. Record the results to the

nearest 0.2 pounds.

BODY HEIGHT. The participant stands erect on the floor or the horizontal platform
with his/her back against the vertical mounted metal centimeter ruler, looking straight
ahead with his/her head in the Frankfort horizontal plane (the horizontal plane which
includes the lower margin of the bony orbit-the bony socket containing the eye-and the
most forward point in the supratragal notch-the notch just above the anterior
cartilaginous projections of the external ear) (Figure 1). The carpenter square is brought
down snugly but not tightly on the top of the head. The participant's height is recorded
to the nearest 0.50 centimeters. The participant should be instructed to stand as straight
as possible but with feet flat on the floor. A check should be made to be sure the floor is
level, the wall is at a 90 degree angle to the floor, the wall is straight and the metal
ruler. is mounted perpendicular to the floor. A chart converting centimeters to inches
should be on the wall or available for use in informing the participant of his/her height in

inches (Figure 2).

SKINFOLDS. There are no special directions for the participant to follow prior to
this test since these are relatively stable measurements. Skinfolds should be taken prior
to active tests since sweating and increased blood flow to the skin makes measurement
more difficult. Men can wear gym shorts for the test; women should wear shorts and a
loose-fitting, sleeveless blouse or surgical gown which is also loose at the waist. The
Harpinden skinfold caliper will be used for taking all skinfold measurements.

Taking skinfolds requires practice to assure reliability and validity as previously
stated. The following suggestions for taking skinfold measurements should be observed:

All measurements are taken on the right side of the person being measured. The
fold of skin should be firmly grasped between the left thumb and forefinger (for right
handed persons) and then lifted up. Pinch and lift the fold several times to make certain
that no musculature is grasped. Continue to hold the skinfold firmly with the thumb and
finger and place the contact surface of the calipers below the thumb and finger. Do not
let go of the fold. When the movement of the needle on the caliper dial stops, take the
reading to the nearest millimeter. Release the grip on the caliper completely, allowing
the spring to compress the fold. Remove the caliper, then release the fold. (NOTE: the
Harpinden caliper needle makes more than one revolution; the small pointer on the the
number of revolutions.) Each revolution of the large needle is 20mm. The maximum
skinfold thickness than can be measured is 50mm. Keeping the left hand above the
skinfold (see pictures) allows the dial to be read easily.

The "skin" should be lifted by grasping firmly the fold between the thumb and
forefinger. A firm grip, not exceeding the pain threshold, eliminates or at least
substantially reduces the variations in the apparent thickness of skinfold that would

result from wide differences in the pulling force of the fingers.

6/85 EX-3

The width of the skin that is enclosed between the fingers is an important factor. It
cannot be standardized, in its absolute size, for all the sites of the body. With a thick
subcutaneous layer a wider segment of the skin must be "pinched" in order to form a fold
than when the adipose tissue is poorly developed, as it is on the dorsum of the hand. For
a given site the width of the skin should be minimal, still yielding a well defined fold.

The depth of the skinfold at which the calipers are placed on the fold also requires
comment. The two sides of the fold are not likely to be parallel, when the skin is lifted
by one hand, being narrower near the crest and larger toward the base. When the

calipers are placed at the base, the resulting measurement is too large. Here, again,, the

eorrect distance from the crest_at_which a true fold, with surfaces approximately

parallel to each other and to the contact surfaces of the calipers, is obtained upon the

application of the calipers to the skin.

It is extremely important to measure skinfolds accurately. Even after extensive
practice it is possible to make errors due to slight misplacement of the caliper or
misreading the dial. To avoid such errors the following procedure is recommended.

a. If possible, the person measuring the skinfolds should not be the one to record
them. An assistant should record the values as the measurer reads them from
the caliper. It is helpful if the assistant repeats the values aloud as they are
recorded.

b.  Skinfolds should be lifted two or three times to determine the fold to be
measured before placing the calipers. Too many individuals are overly anxious
to put the calipers in place before determining what is really to be measured.
Do not lift the skinfold away from the body or the actual location of the

calipers will then be too far forward.

6/85 EX-4

e Place the calipers below the thumb and forefinger and read the dial. The jaws
of the calipers must be on the exact site. Adjust the finger grip as
necessary.The skinfold must be released between measurements.

d. At least two measurements at each site are to be performed on each
participant. If these two values are within 2 mm. go to the next site. If the
difference between these first two measurements is greater than 2 millimeters
(or greater than 10% of the value if greater than 25mm), two additional
measurements are to be made and recorded as #3 and #4 on the recording

forms. A maximum of four measurements are to be made.

TRICEPS SKINFOLD. The participant stands with his/her arms hanging loosely at
the side. Using the tape measure, the observer measures from the tip of the acromion
Process on the shoulder to the tip of the olecranon process on the back of the right
elbow. Make a mark (+) at the midpoint between the shoulder and elbow in the midline of
the back of the upper arm. Using his thumb and forefinger, the observer grasps a
skinfold parellel to the long axis of the right arm over the triceps area (back of arm, not
side) and 1 centimeter above the mark made at the midpoint of the upper arm. The
caliper is applied at the mark (+), The observer counts silently, 1-2-3, and calls out the
reading (to the nearest millimeter) to the recorder who repeats it and then records it.
The measurement is repeated a second time, releasing the skinfold between
measurements. Both measurements are recorded to the nearest millimeter. If the
difference between the first two measurements is greater than two millimeters (or
greater than 10% of the value if it is greater than 25mm), two additional measurements

are recorded as #3 and #4 on the recording form.

6/85 EX-5

SUBSCAPULAR SKINFOLD. This measurement is made 1 centimeter below the tip
of the right scapula. Palpatate the bottom of the right scapula and mark a point (+) that
is one centimeter below the tip. To aid in locating the tip of the scapula have the
participant reach his right hand to the rear and place the back of his hand on the middle
of his back. This move will cause the tip of the scapula to point rearward and make it
easier to locate. The observer then grasps a skinfold below the lower border of the
scapula with his fingers on top, thumb below, and forefinger at the lower tip of the
seapula. The skinfold should be angled about 45 degrees from the horizontal, going
medially upward and laterally downward. The calipers should be placed 1 centimeter
below the forefinger (on the mark). Measurement and recording are performed and
recorded as for the triceps skinfold. If the difference between the first two
measurements is greater than two millimeters (or greater than 10% of the value if it is
greater than 25mm), two additional measurements are recorded as #3 and #4 on the

recording form.

SUPRAILIAC (HIP) SKINFOLD). This measurement is made on a diagonal fold just
above the crest of the ilium, i.e., highest peak on the side of the pelvic girdle on the mid-
axillary line (be sure not to make the measurement forward of this line). Identify this
point and mark it (+). Measure this skinfold twice, releasing the skinfold between
measurements. Both measurements are recorded. If the difference between the two
measurements is greater than two millimeters, (or greater than 10% of the value if it is

greater than 25mm), two additional measurements are recorded as #3 and #4 on the

recording form.

6/85 EX-6

UPPER ARM CIRCUMFERENCE. Arm circumference at the midpoint of the right
upper arm is to be measured using the anthropometric tape. Using the mark made at the
midpoint of the line from the acromion process to the olecranon process on the posterior
midline of the upper arm (made for the measurement of the triceps skinfold), measure
the circumference of the arm. The arm should be hanging loosely at the person's side.
Make the measurement in duplicate and record each measurement to the nearest

centimeter on the blood pressure recording form.

ELBOW BREADTH. The participant's right arm is extended forward perpendicular
to the body. With the arm bent so the angle at the elbow forms 90 degrees with the
fingers pointing up and the dorsal part of the wrist toward the examiner, the greatest
breadth across the elbow joint is measured with the sliding caliper along the axis of the
upper arm. The measurement is made in duplicate and recorded to the nearest

millimeter.

WAIST (ABDOMINAL) GIRTH. A cloth anthropometric centimeter tape is applied
horizontally at a level laterally that is midway between the iliac crest and the lowest
lateral portion of the rib cage and anteriorly midway between the xyphoid process of the
sternum and the umbilicus. This level usually is the natural waist and is identified as the
level of minimal abdominal width when the site profiles are slightly concave (in some
people it will not be concave), Have the participant bend sideways, to identify the
natural indentation at the waist (have examiner place finger on this spot before
participant stands upright again). The objective is to measure the smallest
circumference around the waist. Be sure that the tape is kept horizontal when making
the measurement. A second observer/recorder can help observe the position of the

tape. Make one measurement, remove the tape from the participant and then make a

second measurement. Record both measurements to the nearest 0.5¢em.

6/85 EX-7

HIP GIRTH. Hip girth is measured at the level of the symphysis pubis anteriorly and
posteriorly at the level of the maximal protrusion of the gluteal muscles. This level
usually is the greatest circumference of the hips (but not always). Keep the
anthropometric tape horizontal at this level and record the measurement to the nearest
0.5em. Remove the tape and repeat the measurement. Only two measurements will be
made. The greatest source of error for this measurement is due to not having the tape

horizontal.

CALIBRATION CHECK OF HARPINDEN SKINFOLD CALIPERS

AND MICROMETER USED TO MEASURE ELBOW BREADTH.

The Calibration block is designed so that each step is 10mm (1em) wide. To check the
calibration of the skinfold caliper, place the jaws on the base and first step. The calipers
should read 10.22mm ( not 10.0 because the angle of the jaws increases this reading by
.22mm). When the jaws are placed on the second step, the reading should be 20.50mm; at
step 3 it should be 20.70; step 4 should be 40.95mm, and at step 5 it should read

51.20mm. Readings should be + .20mm.

The long base of the measuring block is 120 mm (12cm) and the short base is 80mm
(8em). These two sides can be used to cheek the accuracy of the micrometer used for

measuring elbow breadth.

Technicians should record calibration of calipers once per week and forward a copy of

this log at the end of each month to the Coordinating Center for quality control

purposes.

GENERAL TESTING PROCEDURE

The test procedure selected for CARDIA is a graded, maximal or symptom-limited
treadmill exercise test to be performed by all CARDIA participants except those
excluded for medical reasons or who refuse to perform the test. The testing procedure
includes the following components.

1. Sereening for medical eligibility

2. Participant preparation for ECG

3. Resting (supine) 12-lead ECG

4, Pre-exercise (standing) 3-lead ECG and blood pressure

5. Exercise on the treadmill

6. Recovery following exercise

7. Participant discharge

SCREENING FOR MEDICAL ELIGIBILITY

Once the participant has finished the body size measurements the technicians will
eheck the resting blood pressure values and pulmonary test results, and ask the
participant the additional medical screening questions for the purpose of determining the
participant's eligibility for exercise testing (See Graded Exercise Treadmill Test
Rescheduling and Exclusion Criteria Form: Figure 1). The blood pressure to be
considered for determining eligibility is the average of the last two resting

measurements recorded using the random zero machine.

Any questions regarding medical eligibility should be referred to the survey

If the participant is ineligible for exercise testing he still is to be hooked-up for a

PARTICIPANT HOOK-UP FOR THE ECG

All participants will have a resting 12-lead ECG whether or not they are going to

have an exercise test. The location of the electrodes for the resting and exercise ECG
are described below and illustrated in Figure 2. For the resting ECG, electrodes will be
placed on the wrists and ankles in their standard Position. All the leads will use fluid
column, silver-silver chloride, disposable electrodes that are also used for the exercise
ECG.

While the participant is standing, connect all the chest electrodes required for
exercise testing using the technique described below. Once they are connected, have the
participant lie supine on the examination table and connect the three limb leads (LR, LL,

RL) for the resting ECG.

ELECTRODE PLACEMENT

The participant is instructed to stand with shoulders straight and arms relaxed at
sides, He/she is asked to avoid movements which may cause errors in marking the
electrode locations, but encouraged to converse with the technician. Men should be

gown that opens in the front.

He/she is questioned as to their experience with electrocardiograms and in
particular stress tests, and is informed of the test procedure. Any questions the
participant poses are answered. The exercise staff, using a kind and friendly approach,
should strive to keep the participant comfortable and relaxed,

SKIN PREPARATION AND ELECTRODE ATTACHMENT
Proper electrode placement and attachment is absolutely essential for obtaining
useful ECG data. The electrode sites need to be accurately selected, the skin needs to
be prepared properly so that the skin electrical impedance is reduced and the electrodes
stay attached during exercise and the ECG wires need to be adjusted and fixed so that
tension does not develop on the electrodes during exercise.
Carefully follow the procedures as outlined.

6/85

Locate and mark the proper electrode sites. Use a surgical felt pen designed

for marking on the skin.

If the skin where an electrode is to be placed has hair on it, ask the participant
if it is OK to shave the hair. If he gives this permission, carefully shave the
hair with a clean razor. If he refuses permission, try to place the electrode so

that it makes the best contact possible. Shave as small an area as possible.

At each electrode location, in turn, the outer horney layer of the epidermis is

light pressure is required. If skin preparation with the sandpaper has removed
the felt pen markings at any electrode site, these should be accurately re-
established by carefully repeating the electrode position measurements. It is
important that the electrode sites be marked accurately using the procedure

described previously.

PERCEIVED EXERTION INSTRUCTIONS
The Perceived Exertion Rating Scale contains numbers from 6 to 20, (Figure 6). We
use this scale so that you may translate into numbers your feelings of exertion while
exercising. The range of numbers should represent a range of feelings from "No exertion
at all" (number 6) to "Maximal exertion" (number 20). In order to help you select a
number which corresponds to your subjective feelings, every other number has an
attached verbal expression (for example, 7 is associated with feelings of Very, Very Light
Exertion, while 19 is associated with feelings of Very, Very Hard Exertion). Your goal is
to rate your feelings which are caused by the work and not the work itself. These
feelings should be general, that is, about the body as a whole. We will not ask you to
specify the feeling but to select a number which most accurately corresponds to your
perception of your total body feeling.
Keep in mid that there are no right or wrong numbers. Use any number you think is

appropriate.
In summary:

1. Try to estimate the degree of exertion as accurately and naively as possible,

2. Do not underestimate or overestimate the exertion; simply rate your feelings

caused by the work at the moment.
3. The rating should be based on a subjective evaluation of your total body
feelings.
4. Use the attached expressions to help you rate your feelings.

5. Enter the seale at any point — there are no right or wrong numbers.

EXERCISE ON THE TREADMILL

Once the standing pre-exercise ECG and blood pressure have been recorded and the
exercise test procedure has been explained and demonstrated to the participant, then
begin the test as soon as possible adhering closely to the following steps (See Figure 7).
1. Check to see that the CARDIA protocol has been selected. If it is not listed on the
sereen of the monitor push "select proto" key until the name appears.
2. Push "start belt" key: The treadmill will start and the speed indicator will go to 2.0
MPH and the grade indicator to 0%.
3. Have the participant step on to the belt holding on to the front handrail with either
one or both hands. Instruct him to walk normally looking ahead and not at the belt and
holding lightly on to the handrail with both hands at first. After 10 seconds or so have
him let loose with one hand and then the other. If balance is a problem or the participant
becomes anxious, have him hold on lightly with the left hand (so that blood pressure can
be taken in the right arm). As the test progresses attempt to get all participants to walk
without holding on to the handrail (holding on to the handrail reduces the energy cost of
treadmill exercise and can produce a large error in estimating maximal oxygen uptake).
After 10 or 15 seconds and the participant is walking comfortably, you are ready to start
the test.
4. Push the "start exer" key and the monitor will start the exercise timing, begin to
analyze the ECG, register the heart rate and regulate the treadmill speed and grade.
The treadmill speed will increase to 3.0 MPH and the grade will go to 2.0%. If the test
response is normal and the equipment is working properly you should not have to touch
the key board again until you are ready to stop the test. At the end of each stage of
exercise (last 10 seconds of each stage) an "exercise lead" tracing and an "averaged"

tracing will be recorded automatically by the strip chart recorder and at the end of the

Outline of Recording Procedures
1. Record 12-lead ECG at supine rest.

2. Record exercise leads (II, V1, V5), averaged ECG and blood pressure after standing for 30

seconds of the exercise. If ECG not recorded during last 30 seconds, record it immediately at the
beginning of the recovery.

5. During recovery, record the exercise ECG leads and averaged ECG at minutes 1 and 2 anda
12-lead (supine) ECG at the end of 3 minutes of recovery. Record blood pressure when standing
after end of 3-minute recovery period.

6. If ECG abnormalities appear during exercise or recovery (arrhythmias, conduction defects or
ischemic type ST changes) record ECG as necessary to document changes.

SYMPTOM MONITORING

(a) Perceived Level of Exertion:
Throughout the exercise test, the participant will be asked to evaluate his
"perceived exertion level". This will be done at the end of each stage by
having him indieate exertion from a rating scale posted on the wall (see Table
2). This seale is useful in evaluating how much longer a participant will be
able to continue exercise before fatigue becomes a limiting factor. (Adding a
zero to the perceived rating will give a rough estimation of heart rate.)

(b) Chest Discomfort:
During the course of exercise, the participant is frequently questioned
regarding the appearance of any even slightly unpleasant feeling about the
upper chest — beneath the sternum, between the seapulae, in either shoulder

or arm, in the neck, angle of the jaw or in the teeth. It must be realized that

participants experiencing angina pectoris frequently will deny that this is an
actual PAIN and insist that it is only a feeling of fullness, pressure,
constriction or other sensation which is simply moderately disagreeable,
During treadmill testing it is very unusual to encounter angina pectoris located
below the epigastric region or lateral to the left midclavical line. It is almost
never described as sharp, knife-like, stabbing, lightning quick or very sharply
localized. It is much more likely to be dull and aching.

Other Pain or Discomfort:

In the course of exercise, participants have been known to experience
headaches which may be dull or throbbing; this may cause discomfort in the
arms and shoulders due to muscular aching. Probabley the most common
discomfort is aching in the calves while walking at grade elevation of 15% or
more. In the case of any pain or discomfort, whether it is thought to be angina
or not, the time course of behavior after its first appearance is important.
Participants should be requested to announce whether and when the discomfort
becomes better or worse and, in the absence of spontaneous reporting from
them, they should be questioned about every thirty seconds regarding the
status of any previously reported discomfort.

Painful fatigue of the calves will get progressively worse with exercise. With
this particular exercise schedule, angina pectoris pain will also get
Progressively worse, since the "walkthrough phenomenon" is effectively
prevented by the progressive load of the test. Other kinds of pain, particularly
chest wall pain, are likely to stay the same or get better as the kinetie sensory
input from the body increases during progressive exercise.

Shortness of Breath:

Any participant normally becomes short of breath in the course of performing

the graded exercise test. In the normal participant, there will be no

6/85

significant shortness of breath in Stage 1 to Stage 3, although the breathing
will become deeper and more rapid in Stage 3. During Stage 4, mild shortness
of breath may be expected and, in Stage 5 or 6, it is typically pronounced,
although in an ostensibly normal participant it is not cause for termination of
exercise. Some individuals develop an anxiety reaction on beginning the
treadmill exercise and will hyperventilate during Stage 1, rarely to the point of
respiratory alkalosis. As soon as hyperventilation is recognized, the staff
should attempt to talk the participant out of his anxiety attack without
interrupting exercise. If it is necessary to terminate an exercise test for
hyperventilation, have the participant sit up on the edge of the examining
table and direct the participant in a kind but imperative way to stop breathing
for a few seconds. As soon as he is forced to begin breathing again, he is
directed to take very shallow breaths and only as often as these are absolutely
necessary. With this method, attacks are regularly terminated in thirty
seconds. In the abnormal participant, shortness of breath may be a limiting
factor during exercise, particularly when pulmonary emphysema, bronchial
asthma, or other form of chronic pulmonary disease is present.

Skin Temperature:

In the course of performing vigorous work, the cardiac output is redistributed
in favor of the heart, brain and working muscles. During moderate exercise at
eomfortable, ambient temperature, cutaneous circulation is also increased
since the skin serves as the principal means of body temperature regulation for
the marked increased heat production from physical work. As one exceeds
moderate work levels, perhaps 50% of maximum work capacity, the cardiac
output is further conserved at the expense of skin circulation. During maximal
or near maximal intensity of work, which ean be sustained only for brief sprint

interval, there is absolutely minimal skin circulation and the skin will become

EX-27

cold, moist, and ashen ("clammy"), although body core temperature is rising
rapidly. If, in the course of exercise, the skin loses its normal heat radiating
warmth and becomes cool with or without cold sweat, this must be presumed a
sign of maximal or near maximal cardiac output adaptation and should be
appropriately noted and exercise promptly discontinued.
(f)
Dizziness:
Although there are numerous possible causes of dizziness during exercise
testing, the two most common causes are anxiety with or without
hyperventilation, and cerebral circulatory insufficiency. Functional dizziness
when associated with hyperventilation is usually accompanied by an air of
detachment or extremely flat effect. A blankness of facial expression, a lack
of interest in the procedure, and sometimes closure of the eyes goes along with
this reaction. If the participant cannot be coaxed into normal responsiveness
to the situation, the test procedure should be terminated. In the case of
cerebral circulatory insufficiency, dizziness may be due either to a deficiency
of cardiac output for the degree of external work being performed, or to
stenotic lesions in vessels supplying the brain. This is frequently associated
with a staggering gait developing during fairly strenuous exercise following a
normal gait and responsiveness to prior testing.

(h)
Disturbance of vison, skin sensation or of other sensory modalities is a rare
occurence during exercise testing. If it occurs and persists or progresses, this
should be an indication for discontinuing exercise and for evaluating the
participant to determine the etiology of the disturbance.

RECOVERY FOLLOWING EXERCISE

Once the "stop exer" key is pushed, the treadmill speed goes to 2.0 MPH and the
grade to 0%. Have the participant continue to walk on the treadmill for the first two
minutes of recovery at 2.0 MPH and 0% grade. An "exercise lead" ECG will be recorded
automatically at minutes 1 and 2 of recovery. After 2 minutes of recovery stop the
treadmill by pushing the "stop belt" key and have the participant lie supine on the
examination table. At 3 minutes of recovery a 12-lead ECG will be recorded. Have the
participant lie quietly during this time.

The general criteria for discontinuing electrocardiographie monitoring, at the end of
the post exercise recovery period, is that the ECG has returned to baseline status for the
participant exept for heart rate or is reverting toward normal. Specifie criteria include
the following:

1) T wave inversion if occuring during exercise in asymptomatic participant be clearly
improving.

2) $S-T depression occuring during exercise should be resolving and should be less than
0.5mm before monitoring is discontinued.

3) Fewer than 25% of heart beats should be ventricular ectopic beats. There should be
no pairs, runs or multifocal ventricular ectopic beats. Bundle branch block, if occuring
during exercise, should be resolved.

6) The clinic physician should be consulted about any questions regarding post exercise
status.

If the participant appears reasonably well recovered with no specific problems
brought on by exercise, have him stand quietly for 10 seconds or so and then record a

Check once again to see how the participant is feeling. If OK, give him some

Q-QS Waves (1-Codes)
Injured regions of the heart may become electrically inactive. Heart attacks are the most frequent cause of this.
The normal excitation wave may be altered by this nonfunctioning part of the heart, thus changing the ap-
pearance of the QRS complex. In this situation the early part of the QRS complex appears as a deep, wide
negative Q- or QS-wave in certain leads. Smaller areas of injury cause lesser Q-waves.
Ideally, one would measure the amplitude and duration of all Q-waves and refer to standard values for
classification. Practically, this is too tedious for visual-manual coding. Instead, the code provides classes which
generally reflect degrees of Q-QS abnormality according to lead.

APPENDIX C
Self-Evaluation of ECG Quality and Identification of Problems
I. Self-Evaluation of Technical Performance

Rough estimates of the noise level and amount of baseline drift of the ECG can be
obtained by examining a paper tracing, and an indication of technical performance level
thereby obtained. The method for self-evaluation is given below and summarized in
Table C-1 at the end of this section. This self-evaluation should be performed by each
exercise test technician once per month.

The test paper tracing should first be examined for obvious errors such as waveform
clipping, missing tracings, or excessive noise and drift. Once satisfied that the
waveforms are basically correct and no obvious errors are present, the baselines (PR, ST,
and TP segments) should be checked for the level of noise. No 60 Hz noise should be
present, and the baseline should be steady and free of transients. Converting the rms
noise levels given in Table C-2 to peak-to-peak values, and noting that recording
sensitivity is 1mV/em, the allowable noise levels in terms of the number of small paper
divisions (one small paper division equals 1 mm) are obtained as indicated for each grade
level in the self-evaluation table (Table 6-1). These "eyeball" measurements only serve
as rough indications of the noise level performance grade. However, baseline
fluctuations approaching 5 small paper divisions (500 mV peak-to-peak) are certainly
indicative of unacceptable noise levels.

The overall drift criteria may be checked and an indication of the overall drift grade
level obtained by searching the record for the maximum and minimum baseline levels (as
determined by the PR and TP segments) and measuring the vertical distance between
them (amplitude difference). This distance must be less than 10 small (2 large) paper
divisions (1 mV) to satisfy Grade 4 requirements for overall drift.

Paper tracings will always display the leads in a given group in

Remedial Actions:
Muscle tremor is the involuntary muscle activity of a parti-

This is why a clear explanation of the electrocardiogram
test and reassurance is necessary for the participant. The
participant is asked if the temperature of the room is too
low for him and is covered with a blanket if so. During
exercise testing this problem is difficult to avoid, but
minimizing arm movement and anxiety will help.

Faulty skin-electrode interface is the usual cause of base-

limb leads (i.e., in two of leads I, II, and III) brings sus-

picion to the extremity which is common to them.

Lead I is the potential difference between LA and RA.
Lead II is the potential difference between LL and RA.
Lead III is the potential difference between LL and LA.

Therefore, if only leads II and III show AC interference,
the left leg, being the common member, must be at fault.

It must, therefore, be checked with regard to:

i. quality of skin preparation and electrode contact;
ii. secure attachment of the LL cable tip to the electrode;

iii. possible contact to left leg with any metal part of
bed or other equipment (or proximity to a wall with
hidden wiring);

iv. a partially broken cable.

Safety Measures

(a) All participating technicians conducting tests must be able
to recognize common important cardiac dysrhythmias. A chart
illustrating the ECG waveforms for these dysrhythmias should
be displayed in the exercise room.
(b) Participant's attention must be drawn to correct method of
stepping onto the treadmill to avoid tripping and potential
accidents because of curling of the edge of the treadmill
belt.
(c) Avoid undesirable levels of anxiety with the attendant
tachycardia or bradycardia by firm kindly reassurance of
all participants by all members of the staff conducting 3rd
screening procedures prior to exercise.
(d) Stop the treadmill on recognition of collapse or dysrhythmic
event.
(e) Move patient quickly to flat surface-floor or bed and place
in recumbency.
(f) Activate alarm system to alert resuscitation team.
(g) Institute ABC's of resuscitation as clinically indicated with
use of oxygen adjunct. (Posters displaying the ABC's - avail-
able from AHA - should be on display.)
(h) Identify rhythm status on oscilloscope and record on Q 3000
strip chart recorder.
(i) Record Blood Pressure.
(j) If cardiopulmonary arrest state -
i. Activate alarm system to obtain Ambulance and inform
Hospital of admission probability.
ii. Institute appropriate resuscitative management:
Ventilation with oxygen: applied external cardiac com-
pression. Defibrillate if ventricular fibrillation or
Cardiovert is indicated. Institute pharmacotherapy via
intravenous or intracardiac routes, with special emphasis
to oxygenation and correction of acidosis.
Chest "thump" conversion may be used at individual
discretion.
(k) Those centers electively using a separate cardioverter with
synchronous mode may disconnect patient from Marquette unit
and connect to a separate EKG recorder/cardioverter/scope,
and monitor appropriately.

ST Elevation:

This is an uncommon manifestation and may be due to either
transient myocardial hypoxia (the angina phenomenon) or it

may be due to actual myocardial infarction such as hypotension,
pale and clammy skin, faintness, progressive chest pain,
nausea, vomiting, general feeling of illness and weakness

and persistence or further increase in the ST segment ele-
vation following exercise. The tentative diagnosis of in-
farction should be made and emergency procedures instituted
immediately.

Admission to Coronary Care Unit:

Operational details for transferring a participant with acute
infarction will have been worked out in advance so that at
the time of emergency the precise steps and the order in
which they are taken are already known and familiar to the
personnel involved. This will include notification of the
cooperating Coronary Care Unit and setting in motion the
details involved in the transportation of the participant

to the Unit.

Immediate care of the participant should not be in the least
delayed by the procedures in (a). If the blood pressure is
normal, the participant is given sublingual nitroglycerin
immediately. The largest accessible brachial vein is selected
and an intravenous drip of 5% glucose is started. Atropine
and lidocaine are drawn up into syringes ready for immediate
use. The defibrillator is checked to make certain it is
charged at 200 watt seconds, the paddles disposed conveni-
ently and electrode paste is opened for instant use. If the
participant is in severe pain, 25 mg of merperidine (demerol)

6/85

is given by gradual intravenous injection. This may be
repeated at three-minute intervals as necessary. The
physician and staff prepare themselves to remove the examining
table mattress pad in order to administer external cardiac
massage effectively in case there is circulatory arrest.

If the participant has low blood pressure, weakness, and
pale cold skin, shock should be considered and the partici-
Pant examined for evidence of ventricular failure such as
distention of the neck veins, third heart sound gallop on
auscultation or a development of rales in the lungs. If
heart failure is not present, normal saline solution shoulda
be substituted for the glucose solution, and it should be
infused rapidly while continuing to observe the participant
for signs of cardiac failure. In the meantime, an eight
microgram vial of norepinephrine (levophed) or aramine
50-100 mgs is mixed into 500 ml of 53% glucose for cautious
intravenous use if saline infusion is insufficient alone in
improving the blood pressure. If there are any signs of
heart failure, norepinephrine or aramine in 5% D/W is used
first instead of saline infusion alone.

If the heart rate is below 70/minute or if there is any
degree of atrioventricular block, 1 mg of atropine may be
given intravenously.

If the participant is short of breath or cyanotic, oxygen

is given by face mask. If there is insufficient spontaneous
respiration, an airway is inserted and artificial respiration
is administered.

In transporting the participant to a Coronary Care Unit, the
intravenous needle is stabilized and the infusion set and
flask are brought with the patient, along with the sphygmoman-
ometer. If the participant obviously needs oxygen, this is
brought with him, but otherwise it is left behind. The

ST Elevation as an Atypical Manifestation

of Transient Myocardial Hypoxia:

In this case, the ST segment elevation will gradually diminish
in the minutes following exercise. If there was hypotension,
this will quickly disappear. If there is chest pain, it should
begin to improve within sixty seconds following exercise.

If it does not, sublingual nitroglycerin should be given.

By the end of five minutes post exercise, the participant
should be at least 90% improved from his attack of angina.

If the electrocardiogram has become normal or nearly so, the
recording procedure may be terminated ten minutes after exer-
cise and the participant asked to rest another ten minutes

in the office, making sure that he feels entirely all right
before dismissing him. If this represents a previously
undiagnosed case of angina pectoris, the findings should be
explained to the participant and his physician notified.

ST Seament Depression Brought on by Exercise is most likely
a manifestation of transient myocardial hypoxia as listed

above (2) and should be treated in the same way. If chest
pain develops and did not improve promptly after exercise
or after nitroglycerin, and especially if this prolonged
chest pain is accompanied by further ST segment depression,
the possibility of subendocardial infarction should be
entertained and preparations should be made for dealing
with a case of acute myocardial infarction as described
above. Continued observation of the participant over the
next few minutes should help answer the question of whether
he is experiencing transient hypoxia or acute infarction,
and he is treated accordingly as soon as this decision is

reached.

6/85

Heart Block:

If atrioventricular or intraventricular block occurs in the
course of exercise testing, it is likely to be transient and
to disappear in the early post-exercise period. If it should
be present, it is a suggestion of myocardial injury, and the

articipant should be observed in a hospital emergency room,
intensive care unit, or coronary care unit for evaluation to
see whether evidence of myocardial injury becomes apparent.
This observation does not represent quite the degree of
urgency as is present with frankly apparent acute myocardial
infarction, however.

Cardiac Arrhythmias:

Those arrhythmias likely to be encountered in the course of
exercise testing include isolated ventricular and atrial pre-
mature beats, coupled ventricular beats and runs of ventricu-
lar tachycardia, runs of paroxysmal atrial tachycardia or of
atrial fibrillation. These are usually self-terminating in
the post-exercise period. If PAT occurs and is not self-
terminating, an effort should be made to terminate it with
carotid sinus pressure applied to one side at the time and

assisted if necessary with the valsalva maneuver.

If ventricular tachycardia develops and persists, the first
step is to determine whether the participant has adequate
systemic circulation. If his circulation is satisfactory,
additional ECG strips should be examined to help determine
whether this is really ventricular tachycardia or is supra-
ventricular tachycardia with bundle branch block. Trial of
carotid sinus pressure may abort the arrhythmia and unmask
its mechanism. If unsuccessful with carotid sinus pressure,
then an intravenous infusion should be started immediately
and the defibrillator made ready, a lidocaine syringe pre-
pared and norepinephrine 8 ug diluted to 500 cc. If it is
thought likely that supraventricular tachycardia is present

rather than ventricular tachycardia, norepinephrine infusion
should be begun carefully in an effort to raise the blood
pressure to the range of 160 to 180 mm/Hg systolic. This

is likely to terminate atrial tachycardia but not ventricular
tachycardia,

If the participant has what appears to be ventricular tachy-
cardia and also has low blood pressure or other evidence of
circulatory instability, the decision must be made whether

to give countershock within the next few seconds or whether
additional time can be taken to establish an intravenous
infusion. If no delay is acceptable, countershock should

be given with the participant lying on his side (or in the
Supine position if the defibrillator used has a flat paddle)
so that one paddle is centered over the midprecordium and

the other paddle is on the participant's back immediately
Opposite the anterior paddle. A great excess of electrode
Paste is used on each paddle. A 400 watt seconds discharge

is administered and the ECG examined, which is likely to

show normal sinus rhythm, continuation of ventricular tachy-
Cardia, or ventricular fibrillation. In the later two cases,
the defibrillator should be recharged to 400 watt seconds and
countershock repeated immediately. At this point, if the par-
ticipant is in normal sinus rhythm, he should be hospitalized
for observation. If he still appears to have ventricular
tachycardia, he should be transferred to a hospital for further
treatment with intravenous infusion started and a physician

in attendance. If ventricular fibrillation persists, standard
cardiopulmonary resuscitation procedure should be followed
from this point on.

If immediate countershock was not elected, an intravenous
infusion should be started and a bolus of 50-100 mgs lidocaine
injected. If this does not terminate the arrhythmia, it may
be repeated once or twice more at three-minute intervals.

This will probably terminate ventricular tachycardia. If

it does not, countershock may be elected at this time, and

it should be decided whether to premedicate with diazepam
(Valium) if the Participant is alert. If Valium is elected

All patients who develop ECG abnormalities in the course of

Emergency procedures are designed to meet two levels of emergencies.
Those that are life threatening and most likely would oceur in association
with exercise stress testing and less acute situations as might occur
following blood drawing or pulmonary function (Hypotension). For the
less acute emergency situations, "Code Green" will be broadcast over

the intercom network with the room in which the situation has occurred.
This will signal the physician or physicians to come to the specific
area and render help as needed. For more serious emergency situations ~
