SEVEN DAY PHYSICAL ACTIVITY RECALL QUESTIONNAIRE INSTRUCTIONS

GENERAL INFORMATION

Scientists have found it difficult to accurately measure the amount of physical
activity performed by people in a free-living population. Some of the methods have
included using occupation titles, activity diaries, self-administered questionnaires, and
interviewer-administered questionnaires. Some questionnaires have focused on leisure-
time activities, some on occupational activities, and some on both types. Some
questionnaires have been for a short time period (one day or one week-end) while others
have been based on a strict recall approach (for example, remember all your activities
for the past two days). Another approach has been to ask for the average amounts of
various activities over a specified time period.

For CARDIA, an interviewer-administered recall method has been selected that
attempts to obtain the major activities a person has performed during the past seven
days. It covers all physical activity (occupational, leisure, and home). As with any
approach to measuring total physical activity in a population, it has its weaknesses:

(1) Some people may have trouble remembering what they did.

(2) Some respondents (as with any questionnaire) may, consciously or

unconsciously, "gild the lily" and tell us what they think we want
to hear.
(3) This approach inevitably calis for subjective judgment by the interviewers

and there may be some difficulty establishing consistency within
and among the various CARDIA centers. Ideally, an interviewer should
get the same data today as he/she, or another interviewer would get
next month if interviewing the same subject whose activity was constant.

Our method of measuring physical activity also has its advantages. Since we ask about

the number of hours spent in sleep, moderate, hard, and very hard activities, we can

EX-35

6/85

obtain the time spent in light activities by summing those categories and subtracting
from 24 hours. This then allows us to calculate the total daily caloric expenditure as the
physical activity index. We think that our questionnaire approach is efficient since
respondents will sleep 6-8 hours per day, and for the majority, most of their waking
activity will be in the light category. Therefore, our interview efforts need only
specifically account for relatively small amounts of time, usually less than 3-4 hours per
day.

The purpose of the seven-day physical activity recall (PAR) is to determine an
estimate of the energy output by a person during a day. The energy output is measured
in calories, just as an individual's energy from food is measured in calories. We are
always expending energy whatever we do. The amount of energy we expend is related to
how strenuous our activities are. One activity is more strenuous than another one, in
this sense, if it causes our bodies to operate at a higher metabolic rate than the other
activity. The unit which has been devised to measured the strenuousness of an activity
is the MET. One MET is the lowest level of activity and corresponds to our metabolic
rate while we sleep. A very hard activity, such as running, may correspond to a level of
10 mets. In our survey, light activities correspond to levels of up to 3 METS, moderate
activities to levels between 3 and 5 METS, hard activities to levels between 5 and 7
METS, and very hard activities to levels greater than 7 METS. An individual's caloric
expenditure during any activity is directly related to the MET level of that activity. For
example, one burns up twice as many calories during a 6 MET activity than during a 3
MET activity. If we know both the MET level of an activity and the amount of time
spent performing that activity, then we can estimate the total caloric expenditure
associated with that activity. With the PAR, we determine the amount of time spent in
activities of different MET levels during the week, and can estimate an individual's daily

energy output, as measured in calories, from this.

EX-36

6/85

Interviewing Technique

Your technique should limit bias in the data and prevent the interview from
becoming tedious. It may be difficult for respondents to remember their past week's
activity. Some may not try very hard and others may get bogged down in details. You
should strive to achieve a happy medium. You should control the pace of the interview
and extraneous talk should be avoided. If a respondent is going into excessive detail, you
should remind him/her that they need not account for every minute, but that an average
or estimate is expected. Don't let a respondent sidetrack you.

It is impossible for us to develop a list of activities that covers every conceivable
possibility. When you encounter a new activity that is not on the list, you will have to
make judgment, and assign it to one of the broad categories using the criteria descibed in
the General Instructions, below.

It is important to remember that most of the respondents you interview will spend
the vast majority of their waking hours in light activity. Even many tiring, unpleasant
household and/or occupational tasks do not have a very high energy cost. A clerk in a
store, for example,may be on his or her feet all day, and may feel fatigued,but the
energy cost is in the light category. An exception to this example would be time spent in
stocking shelves,which would probably be moderate activity. Also, for most occupational
tasks that require at least moderate expenditure, it is important to accurately determine
the time actively spent in the activity. In the stock clerking example, even though a
person might do that activity for an entire shift, it probably would not equal 8 hours.

We believe that the physical activity index will be a meaningful way to separate

respondents into active and inactive groups.

For most activities, the rate at which they are performed can make a huge
difference in energy cost. It is possible to play singles tennis, for example, so as
not to move around very much and not spend much energy. The rate of digging, for
another example, could make the MET cost range from 3 to 12. Some activities
may be quite strenuous, but if they are performed intermittently, the overall
energy cost may place them in the moderate category. A good example of this is

When classifying activities into moderate, hard, and very hard activity levels, first
refer to the list used in the interview. Some activities, such as softball, basketball
and soccer are shown in only one category. An activity which as been assigned to
one specific level (moderate, hard, or very hard) should always be recorded in that
level. A respondent may disagree with this categorization. For example, a
respondent who plays softball may not feel that it is a light activity. In this case,

on the continuation page provided at the end of the questionnaire and flag the

LIST DURING THE INTERVIEW.

Other activities, such as swimming appear in three categories, depending upon the

rate at which they are performed, or are not listed at all. In this case, you will

have to determine the activity level based on the strenuousness of the activity. We
have found that walking and running provide good frames of reference for
classifying other activities. Everyone should be familiar with the relative intensity
of brisk walking, which is at about the midpoint of the moderate activity
eategory. Therefore, if some other activity subjectively seems to be about as
strenuous to the individual as walking briskly, then the activity should be coded as

seems about as strenuous to the individual as running, classify the activity as very

PHYSICAL ACTIVITY QUESTIONNAIRE INSTRUCTIONS

INTRODUCTION
The physical activity questionnaire was developed for CARDIA to help determine a
participant's usual activity patterns. There are two parts to the questionnaire. The first
part ascertains life long activity relative to peers, while the second part focuses on
activities done during the past year. Both parts of the questionnaire are summarized
below.
PART 1 Part one of the questionnaire ascertains past activity patterns relative to one's
peers. The respondent is provided with a cue card for reference. The interviewer reads
the 3 questions in Part 1. The cue card is given to the respondent while the first question
is being read. It is important that the respondent give a definite number for an answer.
The following dialogue may be typical:
I: "Compared to other people your age and sex, how would you rate your physical
activity prior to high school, or less than 14 years of age. (HAND RESPONDENT CUE
CARD 1) What number would you choose from this card, where 1 is physically inactive
and 5 is very active?
R: "Physically inactive."
I: "Could you please give me a number?", or "Would you say 1 or 2?"
R: "2."
I: "Compared to other people your age and sex, what number would you choose for
rating your physical activity during your high school years, that is between ages 14 to 18
years?"
R: "2."
I: "Compared to other people your age and sex, what number would you choose for
rating your physical activity during the past year?"
R: "3."
6/85
EX-49

PART 2. This part of the questionnaire is formatted as a list of various activities that
require various levels of physical exertion to perform. The activities listed include those
done both at work and at home or leisure. Participants are requested to select those
activities which they have performed in the past year for at least one hour in any
month. The one hour is total time, and may represent several activity sessions.
Additional information is ascertained for those activities which were performed.
Primarily, we want to determine the number of months in which they participated in
each activity, as well as the number of those months in which their usual duration of
activity was more than a specific number of hours per week. A "yes" should be given in
Al, Bl... whenever there is at least one hour of activity in only 1 month, or in any
number of months up to 12. Thirteen categories of activity, A through M are queried;
the structure of the questions is the same for each of the 13 activities. Again, a cue
eard is provided to help focus on the activities listed on the questionnaire.
Conduct of the second part of the physical activity questionnaire should begin with the
following statement:

I: "Please look at this card. (HAND RESPONDENT CUE CARD 2) I'll be asking you
whether you do the activities listed. Only include the time actually spent doing the
activity. For example, sitting by the poo] does not count as time swimming; sitting in a
chair lift does not count as time skiing.

First I'll ask you about vigorous activities. Vigorous activities increase your heart rate,
or make you sweat when doing them or make you breathe hard, or raise your body
temperature. If you do an activity, but not vigorously, please include it later when I ask
you about other nonstrenuous sports."

For the first vigorous activity performed, confirm vigorousness by asking 'So you do
breathe hard or sweat when you do this?’ If the person confirms that by this definition or

otherwise the activity is vigorous, it should be so classified.

EX-50
6/85

Otherwise, it may be included under ‘nonstrenuous sports’. Please note that only one of
the four conditions listed above is needed for the activity to be vigorous. However,
sweating, increased body temperature, ete. should be due to the activity, and not because
it is a hot day.

The first two activities questioned include the words ‘in the past 12 months for at
least one hour total time per month?! This defines the minimum criterion for including
an activity. After the first two activities these words are optional, and may be included
if clarification is needed. Reconfirm that this condition is being met at least in the next
activity which the participant reports doing. In the second question for each activity,
‘How many months did you do this activity?', several words are optional.

Proceed with the questionnaire by going through the list of items. It is important that
activities included are of the intensity required for inclusion, i.e., bieycling at least 10
mph, and that the time recorded is for the time actually spent in the activity. There are
two options for each activity listed, 1) the person did not perform the activity, 2) the
person did perform the activity. For those who report doing the activity, follow-up with
the question about number of months of total Performance, and then the number of
months of more frequent performance.

For each activity group, it is important to determine the number of months engaged in
the activity as well as the number of months during which the persons participated more
than the cutpoint for the activity. Therefore, there are a series of questions to be
asked. The first question asks if the participant engaged in the activity, the second
question asks how many months the participant participated in the activity, and the third
question asks how manv of the total months the participant spent more hours per week

than the cutpoint. An example is given below.

EX-51
6/85

I: "Did you jog or run in the past 12 months for at least one hour total time per month?
For instance, you might have done three 20 minute sessions."
R: "Yes, jog."
I: "Did you sweat or get short of breath while jogging?"
R: "Yes."
I: "How many months did you jog or run?"
R: "10."
I: "How many of these months were for at least 2 hours per week?"
R: "6."
I: "Did you do vigorous racket sports in the past 12 months for at least one hour total
time?"
R: "Yes."
I: "How many months did you play vigorous racket sports?"
R: "6."
I: "How many of these months did you play for at least 3 hours per week?"-
R: "0."
The following points may be made for clarification if needed:
A. Jog or run: Include time actually spent in the activity. The cutpoint is 2 hour/
week.
B. Vigorous racket sports: This should include only racket sports done vigorously,
which generally is the case only for singles matches. Cutpoint is 3 hours/week.
C. Bicycle faster than 10 mph or exercise hard on an exercise bicycle: 10 mph is
a constant, moderate to fast pace. When bicycling at that rate, your heart rate
should increase and you will probably start to sweat. Cutpoint is 2 hours/week.
6/85
EX-52

6/85

D. Swimming: The cutpoint time includes only that time spent swimming, not
time sitting by the pool, in the sauna, ete. The cutpoint time is 2 hours/week.

E. Vigorous exercise class or vigorous dance: It is important to only include those
exercise classes or dancing that is done vigorously. Cutpoint is 3 hours/week.

F. Vigorous job activity such as lifting, carrying or digging: It is important that
the activity be vigorous. The cutpoint is 5 hours/week.

G. Home or leisure activity such as snow shoveling, moving heavy objects or
weight lifting: Include time actually spent in the activity. Cutpoint is 3
hours/week,

H. Other strenuous sports such as basketball, football, skating or skiing: This
should only include strenuous sports or those sports that require intense exertion.
Time should only be that time spent in the activity. The cutpoint is 3 hours/week.

I, Other non-strenuous sports such as softball, shooting baskets, volleyball, ping
pong, or leisurely jogging, swimming or biking: It is important to count the time
actually spent doing the sport. The cutpoint is 3 hours/week.

J. Taking walks or hikes or walking to work: This should be vigorous walking,
rather than leisurely strolling. If hunting is included, exclude time not moving such
as time in a duck blind. The cutpoint time is 4 hours/week.

K. Bowling or golf: It is important to count the time that is actually spent in the
sport, excluding time sitting by the bowling lane or riding in a golf cart. Note that
golfing using a motorized cart will generally be classified as less frequent activity,
below the cutpoint time of 3 hours/week.

L. Home exercises or calisthenics: It is important to count the time actually spent
in the exercise. The cutpoint is 2 hours/week.

M. Home maintenance and gardening, including carpentry, painting, raking or

mowing: Include time actually spent in the activity. The cutpoint is 5 hours/week.

SCORING AND RELIABILITY

Scoring is accomplished by adding a weighted sum of the number of months for each
activity below and again above the hours per week cutpoint. Algebraically, where m is the
number of months below the cutpoint andn_ is the number of months above the cutpoint, and
the coefficients b and ¢ are described below. The coefficient ¢ has been selected to be 3*b for
each activity.

Heavy intensity score = >. bi *m,+e; *n;
ie activities A-H

Moderate intensity score is similar in form, but summed over activities I through M, and
the total score the sum of the two subscores.

Coefficients b ande for (A) jogging, (B) racket sports, (C) biking, (D) swimming,
and (H) other strenuous sports are 12 for less than the cutpoint and 36 for greater than the
cutpoint; for (E) exercise classes and dancing and (G) shoveling and weight lifting are 8 and 24
respectively; for (F) vigorous job activity are 18 and 54. For activities (I) nonstrenuous sports
and (J) walking coefficients are 6 and 18, for (K) bowling and golf and (L) home exercise and
calisthenics are 4.5 and 13.5, and for (M) home maintenance and gardening are 8 and 24.
Subscores are computed for vigorous aetivity (A. through H.) and for moderate activity (I.
through M.), and these are summed for a total score.

The coefficients have been selected to mimic intensity or caloric expenditure per minute
for each activity, and also to reflect likely duration of activity for those above and below the
cutpoint for each class of activity. However, because of the lack of detail, a score to be
explicitly interpreted in relation to caloric expenditure is deliberately avoided.

Other evaluation of the the questionnaire results may be done. These include the
description of frequency of participation of the various activity classes; as well as these
frequencies for persons who do the activities for longer durations in most months of the year.

Reliability and timing studies were done at the University of Minnesota of the

questionnaire. The questionnaire can be administered in 5 to 6 minutes. Coefficients of

B2F16 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(Framingham Questionnaire)

The Framingham Type A/B scale score is derived by
calculating the mean of the recoded responses’ for
questions 1-6 and either 8-11 (for non-full-time
homemakers) or 12-15 (for full-time homemakers) . To
determine whether a person was a full-time homemaker, the
program checked whether a person responded with a code
of 4 to Question #7 (B160CCUP). If any responses in the
appropriate set of questions for an individual were
missing (i.e., 1-6 and 8-11 for non-full-time homemakers,
1-6 and 12-15 for full-time homemakers) the score is
defined to be missing. In the calculations, the
following recoding was performed for questions 1-5:

CARDIA FRAMINGHAM

RESPONSE VALUE VALUE
very well 1 1
fairly well 2 0.67
somewhat 3 0.33
not at all 4 0

In the calculations, the following recoding was performed
for questions 6, 8-15:

CARDIA FRAMINGHAM

RESPONSE VALUE VALUE
no 1 ie)
yes 2 1

In the SAS data set, the responses to the questions are
as they were input by the centers and thus recoding must
be performed if calculation of the Framingham score is
recomputed in a program.

The following information concerning analysis and

interpretation was supplied by S. Leonard Syme, Ph.D.:

Framingham Type A/B:

Categorization by behavior type: Subjects are
categorized into Type A and Type B behavior groups using
sex-race specific median cut points. Subjects with

scores equal to or below the median are categorized as
Type B; those with scores above the median are
categorized as Type A.

Concordance with structured interview categorization:

To examine concordance, we will divide the respondents
into quintiles using the Framingham Type A/B scores. We
will then look for concordance with the five categories

derived from the structured interview.

Life Satisfaction: (Questions 16-18) Analyses of these

items are exploratory. Although each item will be
considered as a separate variable, they will be evaluated

as a group. Construction of scales will be explored.

B2F18 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Physical Activity Questionnaire)

Scoring is accomplished by adding a weighted sum of the number
of months for each activity below and again above the hours per
week cutpoint. Algebraically, where m is the number of months
below the cutpoint and n is the number of months above the
cutpoint, and the coefficients b and c are described below. The

coefficient c has been selected to be 3*b for each activity.

Heavy intensity score = = b,; * m, +c, * n;

for activities A-H

Moderate intensity score is similar in form, but summed over
activities I through M, and the total score is the sum of the two

subscores.

The coefficient b is the intensity level assigned to each
activity which is roughly the number of kilocalories thought to be
expended in one minute of activity by a 70 kg man. Intensities
were patterned after those used by Taylor et al and Folsom et al.
Exceptions are bicycling, which was set at an intensity code of 6
to reflect the wording "faster than 10 miles per hour"! and
vigorous work activity (which was not included in Taylor's or
Folsom's work), which was set at an intensity code of 5, somewhat
less than that for weight lifting.

B2REF - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Demographic data)

This file contains the demographic variables (age, sex, race,
education) and should be used in any analysis of the CARDIA cohort
requiring stratification by the demographic variables. EXAMAGE is
the age of the participant at Exam 1. The variables EXAMAGE, SEX
and RACE are based on the original demographic variables collected
in Exam 1 and verified in Exam 2. Only participants who were
examined at Exam 2 have their demographic data updated. For those
participants who did not return for the second exam, their demo-
graphic variables are as they were recorded in the first exam.
AO3ED is the number of years of education as reported at Exam 1.

Fifteen Hispanic race codes have been changed to white.

This reference file is the only file in this version of the
CARDIA data that contains information on all 5115 original
participants, all other files contain only participants examined
at Exam 2 (n=4624).

In addition to the standard demographic variables, this data
set contains the date of Exam 1 (AO2DATE), date of Exam 2 (X2DATE),
and the participant's birthdate (which was verified at Exam 2).
If the participant was not re-examined then X2DATE reflects

scheduling dates or pending dates, not the actual exam date.

This data set also contains scheduling information on each of
the original 5115 participants seen in Exam 1 (X2STATUS, X2WINDOW,
and X2EXPDT). X2STATUS reflects whether a participant was seen in
Exam 2. An explanation of each code follows.

Code | Explanation
E | examined
A | abbreviated exam
1 | For participants examined in a
2 | clinic other than their home clinic,
3 | this number reflects the site of the
4 | exam (1=BHAM, 2=CHIC, 3=MINN, 4=OAKL).
D | died prior to Exam 2
N | no-show
P | pending
R | refused
L | lost

Thus, examined participants are coded E, A, 1, 2, 3 or 4 and
those not examined are coded N, P, R, L. X2WINDOW reflects the
participant's window status as of the end of the exam. (See the
Exam 2 Manual of Operations for more detail on window codes.) All
clinics did not use this aspect of the scheduling system for the
entire exam, thus these codes are not all accurate. If you are
planning to use these, please contact each clinic for more specific
information on how this variable was handled. X2EXPDT is the
target week for the participant's second examination. This is a
character variable and uses values from A - Z and a - z. The
coding scheme for each week of Exam 2 follows.

Naming Conventions
The form set data files are named B1Fnn. 'B' signifies Exam
2, '2' signifies the second version of the data file and 'Fnn'
corresponds to the form number. Variables in each of these
files all begin with the letter 'B' followed by the two digit
form number, nn, then followed by up to five characters
describing the variable, e.g. BnnXXXXX. Variables which were
collected in both Exams 1 and 2 are named identically except
for the first character.

Unlike the first examination data tape, the data collected on
the Medical History Follow-up Forms is distributed among
numerous SAS files, each corresponding to its data collection
form. The file names are listed below under the specific
heading for which documentation can be found in this notebook.
MEDICAL HISTORY FOLLOW-UP:

B2F09HBP, B2F09CHL, B2F09HRT, B2F09DIB, B2F09KID,

Age/Race/Sex/Education Data

A reference file (B2REF) containing the four important
demographic characteristics of each participant and their
examination status has been created. Although participant age,
sex and education can be found in files other than B2REF, the data
in B2REF has been more carefully edited than any of ‘the other
variables. Thus, for any analysis which requires one or more of
these variables, THIS REFERENCE FILE MUST BE USED. Please refer
to the documentation of B2REF for more detail.

NOTE: The original 14 Hispanic participants are now coded as
white.

Number of Observations

Each file except for the Form 9 follow-ups contain 4624
observations (the total number of participants coded as Examined
or Abbreviated for Exam 2). If all data for a particular
participant is missing in a file, that particular record will
contain SAS missing values although an ID and CENTER variable will
be present. Recall that abbreviated exams were allowed in the
second exam, with some parts of the exam being eliminated more
often than others. Thus, some files will have a greater number of
missing data than others.

The Form 9 follow-up files contain only those participants
who completed the form. Most of the files are relatively small.
Some files contain multiple records per person (e.g. medication).
Please refer to the specific documentation for more information on
these files.

ID Variable

Although all the files contain an ID variable, not all contain
the 12-digit CARDIA ID (ID). A 5-digit ID (SHORT ID) is the ID
variable in all of the Form 9 follow-up files. In order to merge
one of these files with a file containing only the 12-digit ID
variable (ID), you can use the following statement to create a new
SHORT_ID in your file:

SHORT_ID=INT(ID/10**7).

Formats

The only formats used in the SAS data sets are the
conventional SAS date and time formats identified as DATE7 and
TIME5. To determine which variables have used these formats and
which format was used, please look at the PROC CONTENTS for each
data set. When using variables that were stored with DATE7 and

TIME5 formats, we recommend using these formats since without them
the variables cannot be easily interpreted.

Sorted Files

Each of the SAS data files have been sorted by the ID variable
(either ID or SHORT_ID) to facilitate the merging of files for
analysis.

Missing Values

CARDIA data entry personnel were instructed to use the letter
'M' for missing values. ee ene other conventions were
followed such as the use of zero's (0) and blanks (). In addition,
skip patterns built into the data entry system appropriately filled
the skipped fields with blanks ( ). SAS sets these blank values
to the SAS missing value of a period (.).

Please refer to the 'CARDIA DATA ENTRY PROGRAM DOCUMENTATION'!
on file at each clinic and the Coordinating Center for specific
form instructions regarding missing values and skip patterns.
Files for which specific problems with missing or skipped data have
been found and are noted in the documentation that follows.

Edits

In addition to the range checks automatically applied to the
data at entry, real-time edits were generated by the Coordinating
Center during the course of the exam on the transmission files.
A detailed listing of the "real-time" edits performed on the data
can be found in the respective documentation for that file. These
edits were corrected or verified by the field centers on a monthly
basis. Although all these edits were completed by the centers,
occasional out-of-range results (outliers) are still contained in
the data files because some values were verified as being correct
as entered. The data was entered correctly from the form, although
the form was obviously in error. The clinics were instructed not
to create data. Thus, only data entry errors were corrected and
not interviewer or transcription errors.

A listing of additional edits applied to the files after data
collection is found following this section.

These outliers should be handled appropriately in analyses.
For that reason, when you are making a decision regarding outliers,
please refer to these edits to see what has been done by the
Coordinating Center. THIS IMPORTANT STEP WILL MINIMIZE YOUR TIME,
THE COORDINATING CENTER'S TIME AND THE FIELD CENTER'S TIME.

Forms Used for the Documentation of Tape Usage

As agreed at the September 1986 Steering Committee meeting,
documentation on the use of this data tape must be completed and
forwarded to the Coordinating Center by all users. There are also
forms for use in communicating technical problems about the tape
and edit requests to the Coordinating Center. All these forms are
located in the final section of this notebook (DOCUMENT USE) with
a brief explanation of their use. In addition, a letter outlining
the analysis and publication policies of the study are also
contained there. This can be used to inform potential users of the
process before they begin any analyses on the database.

The Principal Investigator (/Project Officer) is responsible
for seeing that these forms are used and submitted at the
appropriate time.

It is important that any and all errors found in the dataset
be brought to the attention of the Coordinating Center. DO NOT
ATTEMPT TO CORRECT THESE ON YOUR OWN. THIS WILL LEAD TO
DUPLICATION OF EFFORTS BY THE COORDINATING CENTER AND THE CLINICAL
CENTERS. IT MAY ALSO RESULT IN DELAY OF PUBLICATIONS, BECAUSE ALL
OF THE CHANGES YOU APPLY TO THE DATASET MAY NOT BE APPLIED BY THE
COORDINATING CENTER (whose responsibility for signing off on
verification is required).

Computed Variables

Variables which have been calculated by the computer and
included in the SAS data files are listed in each section of the
documentation. Review these pages carefully. Several commonly
computed variables (e.g. BMI, smoking status) have been included
in order to save you time in analyses and assure consistency in
definition among the CARDIA publications.

Data Dictionaries

Data dictionaries are included for each file except for the
lipid data files. Data dictionaries describe the ASCII data files
and information pertinent to their collection in the data entry
program. The first 43 bytes of information collected on each form
is referred to as "header information" specifically characterizing
the data entry process for that particular form. This data is not
included in the SAS data sets. Thus, form specific variables begin
at column 44. For each variable the following information is
included:

1. variable name (same as SAS variable name) ;

2. ASCII character definition for storing data (e.g. 'c');

3. number of bytes allowed for the variable; and

4. comments (begin with '/*' and end with '*/'),
Comments include:
a) the beginning byte count
of the variable;
b) question number from the
form;
c) a description of the variable; and

a) edit checks performed by the Forms
Management System. These generally include
range checks and/or allowable character
checks.

Summary Counts

Print-outs of the appropriate frequency tables (for
categorical data) or univariate statistics (continuous data) for
all variables in the SAS data sets are included with this
documentation. For the univariate procedure, the five highest and
lowest values are printed along with the corresponding participant
ID (first 5-digits only).

Specifications

Version 2.2 of the CARDIA data set, distributed on June 30,
1989 is contained within 49 SAS data sets, containing 1115
variables, for a total of 17.96 megabytes.

A number of discrepancies between reported education at Exam

1 and Exam 2 have been identified indicating that one should use

caution in using this reported education variable in analyses. The

following discussion documents these discrepancies.

1.

Ten percent of participants examined at both exams reported
a lower number of years of education at the second exam (69%
of these decreases were of one year).

Increases in education of three or more years were reported
by 2.6% of the cohort (71% of these increases were three

years).

Only two data entry errors were found in 362 of these edits

sent to the clinics for verification.

Participant records reflecting increases >3 years and
decreases >2 were compared to verify that the same participant

was examined at each examination.

Unusual discrepancies between exams for the highest degree
earned were sent to the clinics to check for data entry errors
(n=136). Examples of unusual discrepancies include a high
school degree reported in Exam 1 and a master's or doctoral
degree reported at Exam 2 or a master's degree in Exam 1 and
a bachelor's degree in Exam 2. Seven total data entry errors
were found in three of the clinics. One clinic recoded 29 of
their 32 problem records based on information written in the
margins of the form.

The lack of a standardized probing protocol may be the

explanation for these inconsistencies. One clinic has reported

examples of problems which were observed in reviewing some of the

records sent as edits.

1. Vo-tech/business education - sometimes counted and
sometimes not counted.

2. GED - sometimes checked as 12 years of education and
sometimes not.

So College - specific degree given various years of "credit"
- e.g., AA degree marked as 13 years when finished in
less than the usual 14 years.

4. College - 2 Bachelor degrees, 20 years of education
checked. There appears to be a tendency to give people
credit for extra degrees that are at the same level.

These comments indicate that the problem is not restricted to the

interviewers only, but also to the participants themselves.

B2F34 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Diet Questionnaire)

The dietary data were collected using the Health Habits and
History Questionnaire: Diet History and Other Risk Factors
developed by the National Cancer Institute (Gladys Block
Questionnaire). The questionnaire was originally designed. to be
administered by an interviewer; it was modified for the CARDIA Year
2 Exam to make it self-administered. This file contains nutrient
data for each participant. The food item data were analyzed using
the DIETANAL portion of the NCI personal computer system packet
released in January, 1988.

There are five nutrients (vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin B,
iron and calcium) for which data are provided both with and without
vitamin/mineral supplements. Variables which include
vitamin/mineral supplements begin with BNV_ and those without
supplements begin with BNN_. The vitamin B variable is the sum of
thiamine, riboflavin and niacin. In addition, vitamins D and E
from supplements are provided; the analysis program does not
provide the dietary intake for these two vitamins.

Computed Variables

Five nutrients are supplied both with and without added
vitamin supplements. Those without the vitamin supplements added
begin with the characters "BNN_", those with added vitamin

supplements begin "BNV_" and are calculated as follows:

BNV_CA = BNN_CA + BN_SUPCA
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY CALCIUM INTAKE (MG)
plus EST DAILY CALCIUM FROM SUPP'T (MG)

BNV_FE = BNN_FE + BN_SUPFE
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY IRON INTAKE (MG)
plus EST DAILY IRON FROM SUPP'T (MG)

BNV_VITA = BNN_VITA + BN_SUPVA
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY VIT. A INTAKE (IU)
plus EST DAILY VIT. A FROM SUPP'T (IU)

BNV_VITB = BNN_THIAM + BNN_RIBOF + BNN_NICIN + BN_SUPVB
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY THIAMINE INTAKE (MG)
plus DIET: EST DAILY RIBOFLAVIN INTAKE (MG)
plus DIET: EST DAILY NIACIN INTAKE (MG)

BNV_VITC = BNN_VITC + BN_SUPVC
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY VIT. C INTAKE (MG)
plus EST DAILY VIT. C FROM SUPP'T (MG)

B2F16 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(Framingham Questionnaire)

The Framingham Type A/B scale score is derived by
calculating the mean of the recoded responses’ for
questions 1-6 and either 8-11 (for non-full-time
homemakers) or 12-15 (for full-time homemakers) . To
determine whether a person was a full-time homemaker, the
program checked whether a person responded with a code
of 4 to Question #7 (B160CCUP). If any responses in the
appropriate set of questions for an individual were
missing (i.e., 1-6 and 8-11 for non-full-time homemakers,
1-6 and 12-15 for full-time homemakers) the score is
defined to be missing. In the calculations, the
following recoding was performed for questions 1-5:

CARDIA FRAMINGHAM

RESPONSE VALUE VALUE
very well 1 1
fairly well 2 0.67
somewhat 3 0.33
not at all 4 0

In the calculations, the following recoding was performed
for questions 6, 8-15:

CARDIA FRAMINGHAM

RESPONSE VALUE VALUE
no 1 ie)
yes 2 1

In the SAS data set, the responses to the questions are
as they were input by the centers and thus recoding must
be performed if calculation of the Framingham score is
recomputed in a program.

The following information concerning analysis and

interpretation was supplied by S. Leonard Syme, Ph.D.:

Framingham Type A/B:

Categorization by behavior type: Subjects are
categorized into Type A and Type B behavior groups using
sex-race specific median cut points. Subjects with

scores equal to or below the median are categorized as
Type B; those with scores above the median are
categorized as Type A.

Concordance with structured interview categorization:

To examine concordance, we will divide the respondents
into quintiles using the Framingham Type A/B scores. We
will then look for concordance with the five categories

derived from the structured interview.

Analysis

1.

Instrumental support (questions 1-4) - the sum of the values
for these four questions provides onE overall score of
instrumental support. This score may range from 0-12. The

higher the score, the greater the level of instrumental

support. This cumulative score may be analyzed as a
continuous variable. Each question may also be examined
independently.

Missing data: At least two responses are necessary to compute
the cumulative score. When data are missing, but at least two
responses are given, two scores will be computed: (1) a "true
score" consisting of the actual point total of the complete
responses, and (2) a weighted point total. The weighted value
for any question is the mean value of the non-missing
responses. For example, a subject answering to questions with
a "true score" of 4 for these two questions, would have a
cumulative weighted score of 8 for Instrumental Support. If
more than two questions are not answered, the instrumental

support scores is not computed and is defined as missing.

Emotional Support (Question 5) - Scores for emotional support
may range between 0-3, with 3 indicating the highest level.

Network Adequacy (Question 6-9) - Scores in this section may
range between 4-16, with higher scores indicating a more
adequate social network. Question 6 has shown interesting
sex-specific results in previous studies. The age range of
our populatign is most likely too narrow to reveal any
significant age-specific differences.

Missing data should be dealt with as for the instrumental

support questions above.

examine the relationship between affiliation with both formal

Special Notes Regarding Pregnancy File

In order to ease handling and interpretation, the pregnancy
follow-up variables have been split into three files. These files
are named: B2F9PRG1.SSD, B2F9PRG2.SSD, and B2F9PRG3.SSD. See the
PROC CONTENTS output for detailed lists of variables contained in
these files.

B2F9PRG1.SSD contains one observation for each participant who
completed a Pregnancy Follow-up form, and the variables from page
1 of the form; an observation in this file is uniquely identified
by the 5-digit CARDIA ID (SAS variable SHORT_ID).

B2F9PRG2.SSD contains one observation for each pregnancy

reported as occurring between CARDIA Exam 1 and CARDIA Exam 2, and
the variables from pages 2 and 4 of the form; an observation from
this file is uniquely identified by the combination of SHORT_ID and
the pregnancy number (SAS variable BO9PRGNO). Note that pregnan-
cies contemporaneous with the interview are identified as pregnancy
"0" (zero); other pregnancies should be numbered, beginning with
"1" (one) from earliest to latest.

B2F9PRG3.SSD contains one observation for each infant
resulting from each pregnancy, and the variables from page 3 of the
form; observations are uniquely identified by the combination of
SHORT_ID, BO9PRGNO, and the infant number (SAS variable BO9WHICH).

Scoring
1. Instrumental and Emotional Support (Questions 1-5) A value
of 1 is assigned for a "yes" response to "your friends," "your

2. Network Adequacy (Questions 6-9) Values of 1 through 4 are
assigned as indicated for questions 6, 7, and 9.

| Response | Value |
|---|---|

| rarely | 3 |
| never | 4 |

3. Social Network Index (Questions 10 and 11) Questions 10 and

Analysis

1.

Instrumental support (questions 1-4) - the sum of the values
for these four questions provides onE overall score of
instrumental support. This score may range from 0-12. The
higher the score, the greater the level of instrumental
support. This cumulative score may be analyzed as a
continuous variable. Each question may also be examined
independently.

Missing data: At least two responses are necessary to compute
the cumulative score. When data are missing, but at least two
responses are given, two scores will be computed: (1) a "true
score" consisting of the actual point total of the complete
responses, and (2) a weighted point total. The weighted value
for any question is the mean value of the non-missing
responses. For example, a subject answering to questions with
a “true score" of 4 for these two questions, would have a
cumulative weighted score of 8 for Instrumental Support. If
more than two questions are not answered, the instrumental

support scores is not computed and is defined as missing.

Emotional Support (Question 5) - Scores for emotional support
may range between 0-3, with 3 indicating the highest level.

Network Adequacy (Question 6-9) - Scores in this section may
range between 4-16, with higher scores indicating a more
adequate social network. Question 6 has shown interesting
sex-specific results in previous studies. The age range of
our populatign is most likely too narrow to reveal any
significant age-specific differences.

Missing data should be dealt with as for the instrumental
support questions above.

Social Network Index (Questions 10, 13) - We would like to
examine the relationship between affiliation with both formal
(question 10) and more informal (question 13) organizations
with outcome.

B2HEMO - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(Hemostatic Factors)

Frozen samples from participants who attended the Year 2
examination in Chicago or Minneapolis were analyzed in the
laboratory of David Green, M.D. at Northwestern University
through ancillary funding. The ancillary study also analyzed
samples collected during the Years 5 and 7 examinations. The
Year 2 values were measured on frozen plasma collected ina
purple top EDTA vacutainer. Values for these measurements differ
when a citrated tube is used, as was done at Years 5 and 7.
Comparability analyses, performed to ascertain differences in the
measurement based on collection tube, can be obtained from the

CARDIA Coordinating Center.

B2LEPTIN - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Leptin)

This file contains leptin measurements for 502 CARDIA
participants measured from frozen Year 2 samples; a similar file
can be found within the Year 10 datasets (E1LEPTIN). The
measurements were done at the Mayo Foundation using an assay
developed by LINCO Research, Inc. The sample of participants was
selected by Aaron Folsom at the Uninversity of Minnesota, using

the following criteria in each of the four race-sex groups:

(1) 15 from those with highest weight gain from Year 2 to
Year 10;

(2) 15 from those with highest weight loss from Year 2 to
Year 10;

(3) 32 each from the tertiles of weight change between Year
2 and 10 (excluding the extremes described above); and

(4) Exclusion of participants currently or recently
pregnant or with known medical conditions (diabetes,
cancer, mental illness, chronic gastrointestinal

disease, or known HIV seropositivity) .

Five of the participants were inadvertenly sampled twice;

one value has been deleted for each of them.

CARDIA DATA DOCUMENTATION VERSION 2.2 11/98

April 5, 1991

TO: Users of CARDIA Data
FROM: Joan Hilner, M.P.H., R.D.
RE: Use of Exam 1 and 2 Dietary Data -

Calories from Alcohol

Exam 2

Alcoholic beverages were inadvertently omitted from the food
frequency questionnaire used in the second exam. When the omission
was discovered, a decision was made not to add the items to the
form since alcohol consumption was already being ascertained with
Form 7. This means that the total caloric intake obtained from the

Exam 2 dietary instrument does not include calories from alcohol.
The total caloric intake is underestimated and the percent of

calories from carbohydrate, protein and fat are thus inflated.

Prior to analyzing the Exam 2 dietary data, you may want to
"correct" the data by adding the alcohol intake data from Form 7
(Alcohol Questionnaire) to Form 34. This can be done by converting
the ml of alcohol consumed (BO7MLALC) to grams of alcohol and then
multiplying the grams of alcohol by 7 (7 kcal/gm alcohol). This
will provide an estimate of the calories from alcohol that can be
added to the total calories (BN_TOTKC) from Form 34. You will need
to re-calculate the percentage of calories from carbohydrate,
protein and fat (BN_PKCAR, BN _PKPRO and BN_PKFAT) based on the new
caloric intake. The SAS code for performing this correction is
attached.

Exam 1

Alcohol consumption was ascertained with two different instruments
in Exam 1: the CARDIA Diet History and Form 7. The two instruments
yield a somewhat different estimate of alcohol consumption. Dr.
Alan Dyer has used the data from Form 7 for his paper, "Alcohol
Intake and Blood Pressure in Young Adults: The CARDIA Study". The
total caloric intake obtained from the CARDIA Diet History includes
calories from alcohol.

Due to the omission of alcohol from the Exam 2 food frequency
questionnaire, comparison of the dietary data from the instruments
used in Exam 1 and Exam 2 becomes even more problematic than
previously anticipated: in Exam 1, alcohol was estimated in the

history itself; in Exam 2, alcohol would be estimated from Form 7.
To make the instruments more comparable in this area, the data from
the first exam would need to be altered in the following way:
alcohol consumption from the diet history would be excluded from
each participant's record and the calories from alcohol estimated
from the ml of alcohol (from Form 7) would be added to each
participant's record. Prior to analysis that compares the dietary
data from Exam 1 and Exam 2, you will need to contact the
Coordinating Center to obtain this SAS data set.

In Summary:

If you use BN_TOTKC, BN_PKCAR, BN_PKPRO or BN_PKFAT from the SAS
data set B2F34.SSD in any of your analyses, correct these variables
for alcohol intake using the attached algorithm.

To compare Exam 1 and Exam 2 dietary data, correct Exam 2 data as
described above and contact the Coordinating Center for the SAS
data set, A4F0607.SSD (alcohol intake from the diet history
excluded and alcohol intake from Form 7 included).

B2F34 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(Diet Questionnaire)

The dietary data were collected using the Health Habits and
History Questionnaire: Diet History and Other Risk Factors
developed by the National Cancer Institute (Gladys Block
Questionnaire). The questionnaire was originally designed to be
administered by an interviewer; it was modified for the CARDIA Year
2 Exam to make it self-administered. This file contains nutrient
data for each participant. The food item data were analyzed using
the DIETANAL portion of the NCI personal computer system packet
released in January, 1988.

There are five nutrients (vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin B,
iron and calcium) for which data are provided both with and without
vitamin/mineral supplements. Variables which include
vitamin/mineral supplements begin with BNV_ and those without
supplements begin with BNN_. The vitamin B variable is the sum of
thiamine, riboflavin and niacin. ~In addition, vitamins D and E
from supplements are provided; the analysis program does not

provide the dietary intake for these two vitamins.

Computed Variables

Five nutrients are supplied both with and without added
vitamin supplements. Those without the vitamin supplements added
begin with the characters "BNN_", those with added vitamin
supplements begin "BNV_" and are calculated as follows:

BNV_CA = BNN_CA + BN_SUPCA
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY CALCIUM INTAKE (MG)
plus EST DAILY CALCIUM FROM SUPP'T (MG)

BNV_FE = BNN_FE + BN_SUPFE
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY IRON INTAKE (MG)
plus EST DAILY IRON FROM SUPP'T (MG)

BNV_VITA = BNN_VITA + BN_SUPVA
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY VIT. A INTAKE (IU)
plus EST DAILY VIT. A FROM SUPP'T (IU)

BNV_VITB = BNN_THIAM + BNN_RIBOF + BNN_NICIN + BN_SUPVB
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY THIAMINE INTAKE (MG)
plus DIET: EST DAILY RIBOFLAVIN INTAKE (MG)
plus DIET: EST DAILY NIACIN INTAKE (MG)

BNV_VITC = BNN_VITC + BN_SUPVC
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY VIT. C INTAKE (MG)
plus EST DAILY VIT. C FROM SUPP'T (MG)

OVERVIEW

While increases in coronary heart disease risk factors oceur in young adulthood in
conjunction with significant changes in physiological measures and in lifestyle, the
interrelationships among these risk factors and changes have not been rigorously
investigated. Both epidemiologic and clinical research in coronary heart disease have
increased our awareness that some risk factors for disease such as obesity, hypertension,
and hypercholesterolemia may be partially determined by genetic factors or behaviors
which are formed in infancy, childhood, and adolescence. Studies to date also suggest
that some of the coronary heart disease risk factors do not change dramatically before
the late teenage years and that differences in characteristics by sex or race emerge and
are most pronounced after this time. However, relatively little work has been done to
identify the characteristics of young adult life which may be precursors to, or coincident
with, the increase in risk factors prior to middle age.

Cross-sectional data, for example, suggest that weight gain is pronounced during
the late teens through age 30, particularly in males, and that positive relationships exist
between weight and lipoprotein fractions during these ages. The reasons for, and
consequences of, this increase in adiposity need further investigation. The interaction of
life events, behavior, changes in physical activity, and dietary intake that may influence
weight gain and lipoprotein levels should be assessed as well as the relative importance
of weight gain in relationship to risk factor changes during this age span.

Investigators have examined the consistency of blood pressure levels in children to
determine whether "tracking" occurs into the teenage years. The results of these studies
have raised other interesting and important questions. Is there evidence for "tracking" of
other coronary risk factors? Does "tracking" persist into young adult life, a time during
which dramatie changes in lifestyle are often taking place? Are the changes a function
of these changes?

An important component of this study is the study of young blacks. Since the Blaek
Health Task Force on High Blood Pressure Control pointed out the lack of knowledge
about coronary heart disease in blacks as applied to this country, a greater focus on the
nature of disease in blacks has been a topic of increasing consideration.

"Coronary Artery Risk Factor Development in Young Adults" (CARDIA) is the
study of the evolution of coronary heart disease risk in a cohort of black and white men
and women initially 18-30 years old. Such studies will not only contribute to our
understanding of the development of atherosclerotic disease, but more importantly, help
to suggest strategies for prevention before individual lifestyle patterns become well
established.

OBJECTIVES

Overall Goals

1.

To document at baseline and after one or more biannual intervals, risk factors and
changes for coronary heart disease (CHD) in young (black and white) adults, 18-30

To identify lifestyles during this age span, which influence these changes in risk
factors. The interrelationships among risk factors and lifestyles, and changes in
these characteristics will be considered.

The Secondary Objectives of this Study are:

1.

To observe age-related trends in risk factors during young adulthood and to
eompare cross-sectional with longitudinal findings

To perform subpopulation analyses on, sex, race, or sociodemographic groupings,
and to compare trends and processes involved in risk factor development between
these subgroups

To develop and apply effective methods of follow-up during these young adult years
to achieve maximum participation of the study populations.

Objectives of each Clinical Center

1.

To identify 1100-1500 healthy 18-30 year olds per clinical center, balanced by race
and sex

To reeruit and enroll at least 1100 of those identified, willing to participate and be
revaluated at the 2 year follow-up exam

To assess risk factors for CHD in these participants
To maintain, via mail and phone calls at semiannual intervals during the two year

follow up period, contact with each participant in order to ensure maximum
participation at the second assessment.

(Diet Questionnaire)

The dietary data were collected using the Health Habits and
History Questionnaire: Diet History and Other Risk Factors
developed by the National Cancer Institute (Gladys Block
Questionnaire). The questionnaire was originally designed. to be
administered by an interviewer; it was modified for the CARDIA Year
2 Exam to make it self-administered. This file contains nutrient
data for each participant. The food item data were analyzed using
the DIETANAL portion of the NCI personal computer system packet
released in January, 1988.

There are five nutrients (vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin B,
iron and calcium) for which data are provided both with and without
vitamin/mineral supplements. Variables which include
vitamin/mineral supplements begin with BNV_ and those without
supplements begin with BNN_. The vitamin B variable is the sum of
thiamine, riboflavin and niacin. In addition, vitamins D and E
from supplements are provided; the analysis program does not
provide the dietary intake for these two vitamins.

Computed Variables

Five nutrients are supplied both with and without added
vitamin supplements. Those without the vitamin supplements added
begin with the characters "BNN_", those with added vitamin

supplements begin "BNV_" and are calculated as follows:

BNV_CA = BNN_CA + BN_SUPCA
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY CALCIUM INTAKE (MG)
plus EST DAILY CALCIUM FROM SUPP'T (MG)

BNV_FE = BNN_FE + BN_SUPFE
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY IRON INTAKE (MG)
plus EST DAILY IRON FROM SUPP'T (MG)

BNV_VITA = BNN_VITA + BN_SUPVA
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY VIT. A INTAKE (IU)
plus EST DAILY VIT. A FROM SUPP'T (IU)

BNV_VITB = BNN_THIAM + BNN_RIBOF + BNN_NICIN + BN_SUPVB
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY THIAMINE INTAKE (MG)
plus DIET: EST DAILY RIBOFLAVIN INTAKE (MG)
plus DIET: EST DAILY NIACIN INTAKE (MG)

BNV_VITC = BNN_VITC + BN_SUPVC
i.e., DIET: EST DAILY VIT. C INTAKE (MG)
plus EST DAILY VIT. C FROM SUPP'T (MG)

RETENTION OF PARTICIPANTS FOR EXAM I

OVERVIEW OF SCHEDULING PROCEDURES

The following recruitment/retention plan is designed to maximize the number of

Exam I participants re-examined two years later at Exam II. The plan also includes steps

for monitoring this process.

1.

Each center generates a PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST by running the
program provided by the Coordinating Center. This list orders participants by
their expected Exam II date which is in the order of their participation during
Exam I.

The Coordinating Center provides each center with a =50 MILE LIST which
ineludes participants who have moved=50 miles from their "home" center (the
site of Exam I), Participants on this list will henceforth be referred to as 250
mile participants.

INITIAL CONTACT LETTERS and EXAM Il CARDIA BROCHURES are mailed
to participants selected from the PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST and = 50
MILE LIST at least one week before scheduling attempts begin. (Centers may
also choose to send additional materials such as RETURN POSTCARDS
indicating ideal times to reach participants, ete.).

Recruiters make Initial Telephone Contacts with participants selected from
the participant lists and invite them to take Exam II. The Initial Telephone
Contact includes:

o Introduction

o Description of Exam II

o Pregnancy questions

o = Invitation/Scheduling

o Arrangements for expense reimbursement
o Arrangements for reminder phone call
o Review of pre-exam instructions

o Special arrangements for participants =50 miles away

Recruiters record the results of all initial telephone contacts on the PARTICIPANT

SCHEDULING LIST, the TRACKING AND REIMBURSEMENT FORM, and any center

specific forms which document the recruitment process. Data from the PARTICIPANTS

SCHEDULING LIST is entered into the computer at the end of each day and a list of

PARTICIPANTS TO BE EXAMINED for the next day(s) can be generated.

5.

CONFIRMATION LETTERS, including Pre-Exam Instructions and a FOLLOW-
UP CONTACT WORKSHEET are sent to all participants one to two weeks
before their exam is scheduled.

Reminder Phone Calls are made to subjects one day prior to their scheduled
exam. If a participant has moved and is travelling a few days prior to the
clinie visit, this phone call should be made the day before the participant is
scheduled to travel.

At the exam, demographic information is verified, INFORMED CONSENT
FORMS are signed and the completed FOLLOW-UP CONTACT WORKSHEET is
reviewed. Arrangements are made for further completion of the FOLLOW-UP
CONTACT WORKSHEET if necessary.

At the end of the exam, there is an Exit Interview during which the subject is
asked to: a) complete items left blank on forms, ete., and b) indicate any
problems they had with parts of the exam. The participant is given a CARDIA
gym bag, NEWSLETTER and is reimbursed for exam-related expenses.
Participants will be encouraged to keep CARDIA informed of their

whereabouts so that they may be invited back for a third exam.

10.

After the exam, the PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST, and the TRACKING
AND REIMBURSEMENT FORMS are completed by the participant's home
center. PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST data is entered on a daily basis.
Xeroxed copies of the TRACKING AND REIMBURSEMENT FORMS are sent to
the Coordinating Center on a weekly basis.

The forms of participants examined at a site other than their home center are
xeroxed and stored and the originals are sent to the home center for data
entry. The examining center is to pay the participant's expenses and will be

reimbursed by NHLBI, if these become a problem.

RECRUITMENT FLOW SHEET

1. The participant scheduling list is generated by each center using the Coordinating
Center program.

2. A sublist of participants who moved =50 miles from their home center is generated.

3. Initial contact letters and brochures are mailed* to participants (in exam date

order), at least one week before scheduling attempts begin.

4. Initial Telephone Contact are made one week later. The results are recorded on
the PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST and the TRACKING AND
REIMBURSEMENT FORM.

5. CONFIRMATION LETTERS, Pre-Exam Instructions, and FOLLOW-UP CONTACT
WORKSHEET are sent to participants one to two weeks prior to their scheduled
exams.

6. Reminder Phone Calls are made to each participant one day prior to their
scheduled exam.

7. On examination day Tracking Forms are updated, demographic information is
verified, INFORMED CONSENT FORMS are signed, and the FOLLOW-UP
CONTACT WORKSHEET is reviewed.

8. At the Exit Interview, participants are given a CARDIA gym bag and a
NEWSLETTER. They are also reimbursed for exam-related expenses.

9. The TRACKING AND REIMBURSEMENT FORMS are sent to the Coordinating
Center on a weekly basis.

* NOTE: The 50 mile participants may be scheduled at any time, but detailed fiscal
records need to be kept to document the expense of bringing in these participants.

DETAILED INSTRUCTIONS TO RECRUITERS

PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST

The PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST can be generated using selection F1 of
the CARDIA EXAM II scheduling utilities in the CARDIA data entry system. This
list ean be generated for any week of the CARDIA Exam II and includes all
participants whose target date is included in the week(s) requested excluding any
participant whose status is classifed as an S (scheduled), D (died), E (examined) or R
(refused). This list ineludes the following information: CARDIA ID, target week,
birthdate, sex, race and level of education for the participant. Space is provided on
the form for recruiters to record the participant's name, scheduled exam date, phone

number and any comments.

Onee the data from the PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST is entered (i.e.,
status code changes and scheduled examination dates), a list of "Participants to be
Examined" for a given week or number of weeks can be generated locally by each
eenter. Recruiters can generate an OVERDUE PARTICIPANT LIST using the
Coordinating Center program which includes those participants not examined and

those who are four weeks past their expected exam date.

2 50 MILE LIST
Most of the CARDIA participants will still live near their home center during

the Exam II eycle and will not need to travel extensively to participate. Others,
particularly those who have moved 2.50 miles away, are pregnant, or are students
away at school may require special recruitment procedures and separate tracking.
The primary purpose of the 250 MILE LIST is to enable recruiters to efficiently
begin contacting and scheduling these participants in the most cost effective
manner. The goal is to bring these participants back for Exam II without having to
pay high travel expenses. To do this requries flexibility on the acceptable interval
between Exams I and II. As soon as it is feasible, starting with the participants on
the 2 50 MILE LIST who were contacted at 18 months, reeruiters should initiate

eontact with these participants by sending out initial contact letters and making

initial telephone calls to invite them to the second exam. By using the participants
contacted at 18 months first, we will have the best chance of examining the 50
mile participants within the one month target window for Exam II sinee these
participants will be due for their exams first.

The = 50 MILE LIST includes the following information: CARDIA ID, target
week, race, birthdate, sex, level of education and space for comments. The
Coordinating Center will provide each center with a list which will be updated
monthly. Note, this list will only include participants who had moved = 50 miles
from their home center as of their last follow-up contact with CARDIA (which is
probably the 18-month contact). Thus, this list will not be all inclusive since some

participants will have moved 50 miles since our last contact with them.

INITIAL CONTACT LETTER, RETURN POSTCARD AND EXAM IT CARDIA

BROCHURE are designed to prepare participants for the Initial Telephone Contact.

Initial Telephone Contact
The purpose fo the Initial Telephone Contact is to schedule
participants for Exam Il. The only data to be processed centrally from these
eontacts are recruitment monitoring items which are recorded on the PARTICIPANT
SCHEDULING LIST and the TRACKING AND REIMBURSEMENT FORM. To
complete these forms use the codes which appear at the end of this section.
Recruiters should attempt to schedule participants for exams in the order that
they appear on the PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST. A participant's target date
for Exam II has been calculated based on the participant's Exam I date, adjusting for
the uneven clinic flow which occurred during Exam I. For example, a participant
examined on 7/1/85 will have an approximate target date of 7/1/87 depending on the
clinie adjustment which was necessary in the calculations. Thus, following this list

will maximize our chances of examining participants within the one month target

window and will also help to insure an even flow of participants through our clinics
during Exam Il. It is important to note that if a participant cannot come for an
exam during their one month target window, he/she will be scheduled at their

convenience. No participant willing to take Exam II will be turned away.

An example of an initial phone contact is included in Appendix 1. Appendix 2
contains a description of Exam II which can be used to deseribe the exam during the
Initial Telephone Contact.

All participants of Exam I are eligible for Exam II. If participants are not
seriously injured or ill but willing to come for the exam, they should be scheduled.
Participants can take Exam II with a broken leg, but need one unbroken arm for the
blood pressure component, and two unbroken arms for the cold pressor and video
game. Some situations may require a best judgement call.

The one condition that is necessary to probe about during the initial telephone
contact is pregancy. Remember (unlike Exam I) we are not excluding pregnant
women from Exam II — only postponing their exams. Introduce the pregnancy
questions by telling participants that while everyone is eligible for Exam II, we
prefer, if possible, to examine the women when they are not pregnant. Explain that
this is because there are radical changes in women's blood chemistries during

pregnancy.

a. Invitation/Scheduling
Invite the participant to schedule an appointment for Exam II during his/her
target week as indicated by the PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST. If a
participant is unable to take Exam II during that time, schedule an
appointment for another time -- keeping it as close to the target week as
possible. Allow the participant to schedule a tentative date with the

understanding that you will telephone them about two weeks before to

confirm. If the participant is willing to come for Exam II, but unwilling to
schedule a specific appointment, ask him/her to indicate a specifie week or
month when they think they might be able to take Exam Il. Arrange to
recontact them about two weeks before that week (or month) to schedule a
definite appointment. If the participant expects to move and/or not be in the
area of their home center during the exam year for another reason special
procedures may be needed to bring them back (see "Special Arrangements for

Participants.250 Miles Away" below).

b. Arrangements for Expense Reimbursement
Explain that as in the first CARDIA Exam, there are limited funds available
for reimbursing participants for exam-related expenses not to exceed $20 or

the center specific amount. Establish approximate amount to be reimbursed.

e. Review of Pre-Exam Instructions

SPECIAL ARRANGEMENTS FOR PARTICIPANTS = 50 MILES AWAY

A great majority of the participants will be brought to their home centers for
Exam IE within their window and without a reimbursement of exam related expenses
more than $20 or the center specific amount. The others may require special

procedures and tracking as they may require a broad window, be examined at an

alternate center and/or need to be reimbursed more than $20 for actual travel
expenses incurred. We expect that the majority of difficult to schedule
participants will be so because they have moved far from their home center.

Data from the Exam I Follow-up Contacts indicate that approximately 10% of
our sample will live at least 50 miles from there home center by the time they are
due for Exam Il. The = 50 MILE LIST includes these participants. The following are
general guidelines for making special arrangements that maximize the number of =
50 mile participants we bring back for Exam II while minimizing the costs. PLEASE
NOTE THAT IT IS PREFERABLE TO EXAMINE PARTICIPANTS OUTSIDE THEIR
WINDOWS THAN TO PAY THEIR TRAVEL EXPENSES.

Recruiters should schedule each=50 mile participant according to the
following priorities:

a. Schedule the participant's appointment at the home center for Exam II within
one month of the target date with no reimbursement for actual travel expenses
above $20.

b. Schedule the participant's appointment at the home center anytime during
Exam II with no reimbursement for actual travel expenses above $20.

ce. Arrange for the participant to go to an alternate center anytime with no
reimbursement for actual travel expenses above $20.

d. Arrange for the participant to return to the home center with reimbursement
for actual travel expenses of up to $250 for train, plane or bus fare or $.20 per
mile (this varies by center) for driving be included, but this should not always
be necessary. If necessary, $65 is the maximum allowed for one night's lodging
and $15 is the maximum per meal. The maximum any one participant can be
reimbursed would be $350.

e. Arrange for the participant to go to an alternate center with reimbursement

for actual travel expenses up to $350.

f. Arrange for the participant to take a portable exam, partial exam, ete., with
no reimbursement for travel expenses above $20.

(Note, these costs may need to be revised based on increases in airfares.)

Recruiters should begin contacting the participants on the=50 MILE LIST as
soon as possible. This will allow us to bring in those who plan to be in the area of
their home center for a vacation, family visit, ete., sometime over the next year but
would not otherwise be returning. Start by scheduling the = 50 mile participants
reached during the 18 month contact first because their expected exam date on the
PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST will be coming up soon anyway. Give the
participant an appointment as close as possible to their due date, but schedule them
whenever possible. Maximum flexibility in scheduling is necessary to insure the
return of these participants. After finishing the = 50 mile participants contacted at
18 months, go to those reached at 12 months, then 6 months, ete.

If you are unable to schedule a participant to be examined at his/her home
center, inform him/her that they may take the exam at one of the other sites if that
is more convenient. Tell them that you will make arrangements for them to be
contacted by someone from that other center. Obtain all contact information that
will be needed by the other center (other phone numbers, ete.). The home center is
responsible for giving the alternate centers all relevant information on participants
to be scheduled and examined by them. Monitoring the process is to be done by the
home center using the TRACKING AND REIMBURSEMENT FORM and center
specifie forms.

If you are unable to schedule a participant who is away and if the participant is
unable to go to an alternate center at their own expense, inform him/her that there
are some LIMITED FUNDS for assistance with actual travel costs for cases such as

theirs and ask them if they would return to their home center or travel to an

alternate center if CARDIA could defray some of their actual travel expenses.
Negotiate with participants at this point. Start by offering to help pay part of their
plane fare, ete. After determining the amount that they will be reimbursed, tell
them to be sure to bring their receipts to the exam. Make certain they understand
that they need receipts in order to be reimbursed. If appropriate, tell them that
they will be given or mailed a check after they complete the exam. (NO
ADDITIONAL TRAVEL MONEY SHOULD BE SPENT ON PARTICIPANTS
EXCLUDED FROM THE EXAMI DATA ANALYSIS.)

If none of the above are possible, tell the participant that we may arrange for
them to take a portable exam but need to call them back again to make
arrangements. Get at least one additional phone number before terminating the
contact.

The results of all telephone contacts with =50 mile participants should be

recorded on the TRACKING AND REIMBURSEMENT FORM.

RECORDING OUTCOME OF INITIAL TELEPHONE CONTACT

The outcome of the initial telephone contact is recorded on the PARTICIPANT
SCHEDULING LIST and TRACKING AND REIMBURSEMENT FORM. Note that this
initial eontact will determine the WINDOW STATUS of the participant. WINDOW
STATUS refers to target window for the participant's examination date. Most
participants will fall into a normal window, i.e. they should be seen within one month
of their target date. For participants that have moved, are pregnant, are in jail,
ete., the system allows you to change their WINDOW STATUS to reflect a possible
problem in seeing the participant in his/her target window. Note: all attempts
should be made to see these participants during their target window following the
guidelines in this document.

The initial contact should also update the participant's STATUS (that is the

examination status) into one of the following initial or temporary codes.

Initial or Temporary Status Codes:

U= Uneontacted: The participant is not currently and never has been
contacted or scheduled for an exam. Each participant has been initially
coded to U by the system and remains a U until another status code has
been recorded.

P = Pending: The participant has been contacted. A tentative exam date
should be established if possible. However, a missing date is allowed.

S= Scheduled: The participant is scheduled for an exam. S is automatically
eoded when the "DATE SCHEDULED" is entered into the scheduling
system.

N= No show: The participant has not shown for his/her scheduled
appointment and/or the participant has been examined but the information
which would update their code to E has not been entered into the

computer yet.

If a participant's initial code changes, for example a participant who was
onee pending is now scheduled, this change should be entered into the
computer. In this example, the code would be updated once the scheduled date
is entered into the computer. NOTE: For participants who are not initially
eoded in the "S" eategory, the code "P" should be entered since this indicates
that the participant has been contacted. Failure to enter a "P" will cause the
computer to interpret the participant as "uncontacted" even though the target
exam date has passed.

The following section what are considered to be final STATUS codes, that
is once a participant is given one of these codes it should be a permanent
eode. Three of these codes (E, D, R) are now available while the others (A, L)

will be available in the July 1987 update of the scheduling system.

b. Final Status Codes:

D= Died: The participant has died. Date of death must be entered into the
computer by data entry; missing date is allowed.

E= Examined: The participant has been seen by the clinic and has at least
partially completed Exam HU. E is automatically coded when the
participant's demographie data and date of examiniation is entered into

A*= Abbreviated exam completed: The participant has completed a portable
exam. This code is assigned to participants who wish to participate and

APPENDIX 2

DESCRIPTION OF EXAM I

The following information about CARDIA and Exam II may help you to answer any

questions the participants have about CARDIA in general, and Exam If. Included at the

end of the materials section is a one-page summary about CARDIA.

oO

Every Exam I participant will be re-examined — that's over 5100 young adults
nationwide from Birmingham, Chicago, Minneapolis and Oakland.
Returning participants will be given a specially designed exam that will be shorter
than Exam I — approximately 24% to 3 hours. HERE IS A BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF
EXAM If WHICH CAN BE READ VERBATIM IF YOU WISH:

The second CARDIA exam is a series of tests designed to gather
additional data as our study continues. It will include a blood pressure check,
interviews about your medical history, smoking and diet. A small sample of your
blood will be drawn so that we ean determine your cholesterol levels. We will test
your lung capacity and take your body measurements, We will ask you to clip some
of your toenails during the exam. These nail samples may provide important
information about the relationship between your health, your nutrition and disease.
Also, a special monitor will measure your blood pressure periodically as you play a
video game and trace the mirrored reflection of a star.
As in last year’s exam, we will ask you to fast for 12 hours before coming in for your
appointment.
Each returning participant will receive a copy of their test results by mail. If you
wish, we will send an additional copy to the physician of your choice. Further, at
the end of the exam itself, you will receive a copy of the CARDIA NEWSLETTER
which summarizes the results of Exam I for the overall study and also presents some

interesting highlights about the "average" CARDIA participant.

Each Exam II participant will be given a snack shortly after their arrival, since they
will have fasted for 12 hours prior to coming. Participants will have the opportunity
to select an original CARDIA gym bag designed to go with the T-shirts given out at

the last exam.
