GUIDELINES FOR EXAMINATION II

PURPOSE
CARDIA Il examinations are scheduled over a twelve-month period (June 1987 - May
1988). This will be the second contact of the participant with the clinieal center staffs.
It continues to be important that this experience be viewed favorably by the participant.
The total time for the examination should not exceed 3 hours. The results of the

examination will be sent to the participant's family physician if he/she so indicates.

PREPARATION OF PARTICIPANT FOR THE SECOND VISIT

All participants are required to fast from all food, exeept water, 12 hours prior to
the exam; they should not have participated in any vigorous exercise on the day of the
appointment; and should not have used tobacco 30 minutes prior to the exam. The
participant should bring to the appointment a list of any prescription medications they
are currently using. Additional pre-exam instructions will be related by phone to the

participant prior to the day of the appointment.

STAFF PREPARATION FOR THE PARTICIPANT'S VISIT

In preparation for the participant's arrival to the clinic, a designated staff member
should construct the expected participant's file. (Separate files should be maintained by
the clinics distinguishing Exam I information from Exam II.) The staff member will
proceed to collate the CARDIA questionnaires into a form set which will accompany and
be administered to the participant throughout the course of the examination.

Upon receipt of the forms from the Coordinating Center each clinical center should

separate or package the forms according to the following guidelines:

GUI-1

FORMS

The staff member will collate the CARDIA form sets according to the center's
anticipated clinie flow for ease of administration. The CARDIA forms are formatted,
coded, and printed by the Coordinating Center. The CARDIA forms will be printed on
front and back.

The identification codes and labels to be placed on each CARDIA form will be
designed, prepared, and distributed by the Coordinating Center to each clinical center.
The 1.D. label should be affixed in the upper left hand corner of the first page of each
form. (Form sets can be assembled at any time). Once the form set is complete, the
entire package should be placed into a notebook provided for each participant. Each
participant's form set should remain assembled in the 3-ring notebook until the Data
Editor has entered all of that participant's data. Following data entry, the form set
should be filed and stored.

The identification labels will be precoded by the Coordinating Center and will
consist of a one-digit center code, a four-digit participant number, a digit check number,
a quality control number, and a five-digit cross reference. In addition, "X2" will appear
on each label to designate that forms were completed at the second exam.

Extra labels remaining may be used if one of the coded labels is torn or if an error is
made. If an extra label is used in place of one of the coded labels, the code should be
written on the substitute label and placed in the upper left hand corner. Only one label

should be affixed to a bound set of forms, i.e. diet questionnaire.

GUIDELINES FOR GREETING AND INFORMED CONSENT

GENERAL INFORMATION
The greeting is very important because it sets the tone for the entire exam. Each

participant was told during Exam I that:

* they are participating in an important new national study
* they will receive valuable information about their own health
* they will receive a specially designed CARDIA examination available at only

four centers in the United States
* if they wish, their physicians can be sent their test results
In the greeting for Exam II we would like these general points to be stressed again,
but each center should do this in ways that are most suitable for their own populations.

Guidelines for the greeting and informed consent are listed below:

GUIDELINES FOR GREETING

Verify that the participant has arrived on the right day at the right time. If the
participant has not arrived on the correct day or at the correct time, say something like,
"Your appointment is not recorded on today's exam schedule. There's a chance we may
be able to fit you in today," or “our records show that you are scheduled for an exam
at o'clock. There's a chance we may be able to see you sooner." Then, consult
with your on-site clinic coordinator for further instructions.

If the participant appears to be ill, verify that he/she feels well enough to complete
the examination. One way to do this is to ask, "do you have a fever?” If the participant
answers "yes," reschedule the appointment according to local center appointment
procedures. If the participant fails to complete the entire exam, reschedule the
unfinished components as soon as possible according to local center appointment
procedures, and record the participant's ID#, unfinished component, and reason for the

incomplete exam on the clinical center log.

A brief description of CARDIA should be given to the participant prior to Exam II.
The following is an example: “As you know, CARDIA is a major new study of the
lifestyles and health of young adults. It is sponsored by the National Institutes of
Health. Here in Chicago, the study is being conducted by the Department of Community
Health and Preventive Medicine of Northwestern University Medical School.

First, let me tell you again a little about what will be included in your exam today.
As you know, we will explore many aspects of your health and your lifestyle...

You will be asked questions about

* your current health, in general

* any past illness or injuries

* any medications you take

* what you eat and drink

* the amount of exercise you get

* the way you deal with every day problems, and

* your background — your education, whether you are married, what you do, and

things like that.
We will take your blood pressure several times.
There will be a blood test to see how much fat there is in your blood.
We will measure your height and weight.
We will test the capacity of your lungs.

You will play a video game and have your blood pressure monitored."

LOG OF INCOMPLETE EXAMS - (see sample)

If a participant fails to complete the entire exam on their scheduled day, reschedule
the unfinished components as soon as possible. Reasons such as illness, equipment
malfunctions or breakage should be recorded on the log (see sample).

These logs should be kept by the month and forwarded to the Coordinating Center at

the end of each month,

INCIDENT REPORTS - (see sample)

If a participant experiences any unusual medical-related incidents during the course
of the exam and a physician or medical-related person is summoned (i.e., physician's
assistant or nurse) the clinic is responsible for documenting these incidents for future
reference by the CARDIA study.

"Incidents" are episodes such as fainting, uncontrollable bleeding, any unusual
reports of pain, ete. Staff members should report any dangerous situations to the clinic
eoordinator and document the incident. These reports should be forwarded to the

Coordinating Center at the end of each month.

GUIDELINES FOR OBTAINING INFORMED CONSENT

At this time the participant should be asked to read and sign the consent form. Each
center has a different form. It is not enough to have a participant to read and sign the
form; the participant must understand what is going to happen to him/her during the
exam and the risks involved. The greeter should make certain that the participant is
actually reading the form and then specifically ask if he/she has any questions about it.
The greeter should be prepared to answer those questions himself/herself or have
someone else on site answer them. If it seems appropriate (i.e., the participant is
struggling to read form), ask if the participant would prefer that the form be read
aloud. If so, the greeter should read it aloud.

After the consent form has been read and signed, the greeter should ask the
participant if he/she would like the test results mailed to him/her and/or to his/her
physician. The responses to these questions should be marked in the appropriate spaces
on the medical release form. If the participant would like the results mailed to a
physician, the name and address of the physician, as well as the participant's signature on

the medical release form should be obtained at this time. Results may not be released to

a physician without the participant's signature on the medical release form.

VERIFICATION OF EXAM I DEMOGRAPHIC DATA

After the participant has signed the informed consent, the greeter will refer to the
"Verification of Baseline Demographic Data" form, as already prepared for each
individual participant by the Coordinating Center. The participant will be asked their
birthdate, sex, and race to be compared for verification with the Exam I demographic
data. This form will not require an ID label, as the ID number will already be generated
on the form. (Specific probing instructions and a sample of the form ean be found in the
Retention (RET) section of MOO II). The participant is now ready to continue with Exam

The instrument used to collect dietary information for the second CARDIA exam
differs considerably from that used in the first exam. This diet questionnaire will be
self-administered rather than interviewer administered. The period of time covered by
this questionnaire is the past year rather than the past month. There will be no food
models used, although liquid and dry measuring cups as well as measuring spoons will be
used.

The CARDIA Exam II Diet Questionnaire is comprised of two parts. The first
section consists of sixteen questions related to fat use, consumption of "fast" foods,
vitamin use and salt use in cooking and at the table. This section was designed to obtain
a maximal amount of information about the participant's usual dietary practices with a
minimal expenditure of time. This first portion should take approximately 3 to 5 minutes
to complete.

frequency with lists of food items which have been divided into food groups to facilitate
recall. The food groups are the major headings with specific items contained within each
group listed beneath the major heading. The food groups are listed below.
(1) Fruit
(2) Vegetables
(3) Meat, Fish and Poultry
(4) Mixed Dishes/Lunch Items
(5) Breads/Salty Snacks/Spreads
(6) Breakfast Foods
(7) Sweets
(8) Dairy Products
(9) Beverages
(10) Other Food Items
Participants are asked to provide information regarding frequency of consumption and
approximate serving size for each food or group of foods listed.

BLOOD PRESSURE MANUAL OF PROCEDURES
HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE (HYPERTENSION)

As blood pressure rises, so does risk of ischemic heart disease and
its complications. The range of normal blood pressures is wide. Even
within the "normal" group, risk increases as the upper limits are
approached. Usually, blood pressures are expressed as systolic
pressure/diastolic pressure; values exceeding 140/90 mmHg are
considered to be hypertensive for adults. Middle-aged persons with a
diastolic blood pressure of 90-104 mmHg or greater (so-called "mild"
hypertension) have a risk of heart attack that is about 70 percent
higher than that of persons with a diastolic pressure under 80 mmHg
(normal value). Persons with a diastolic blood pressure exceeding 104
mmHg (moderately severe to severe hypertension) have a risk more than
twice that of those with a normal value. Hypertension is an especially
strong risk factor for stroke and, to a lesser extent, for peripheral

vascular disease.

Blood pressure is measured in a resting state, using 3 measurements
with a random zero sphygmomanometer. The random zero machine has two
advantages over the fixed zero manometer. Digit preference does not
appear in the data, though it may still exist in the reading itself, and
be randomized out of the data by the use of the randomly chosen zero
point. More importantly, it deprives the blood pressure technician of
knowledge of the actual value, and therefore of the ability to make
judgements about blood pressure levels for readings close to critical
values such as 90 diastolic. It should be noted, however, that the
random zero machines tend to yield blood pressures which are about 1.5
mmHg less than those obtained when using a fixed zero machine. Within
person variation in blood pressure is substantial; 3 replicate readings
tends to reduce this variation.

S3LOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT INSTRUCTIONS

The purpose of blood pressure measurements in CARDIA is: to
compare levels of this risk factor between blacks and whites; to observe
the interaction with other CHD risk factors over time; and to observe
variables that will predict changing levels of blood pressure.

Blood pressure measurements (systolic and fifth phase diastolic)
will be recorded with a random-zero (RZ) sphygmomanometer by trained and
certified technicians at baseline and subsequent intervals. The methods
of measurement will be standardized - as set out in the Manual of
Operations. The pulse rate for 30 seconds will be recorded with each
blood pressure measurement.

Standing blood pressure measurements will be taked at Exam II. The
cuff should be disconnected from the random zero and attached to the
standard sphygmomanometer. Upon standing, the cuff is to be inflated to
30 mmHg above the highest seated systolic reading. As many confounders
of blood pressure measurement as possible will be controlled by standard
settings and technique of blood pressure measurement or by recording
uncontrollable confounding factors. Thus, the following will be
recorded:

1). Time of day (AM/PM)

2). Room temperature

3). Arm circumference at the midpoint of the upper arm

4). Technician I.D. number

The blood pressure will be measured three times on each occasion.
Caffeine. (from tea, coffee, cola beverages), eating, heavy physical
activity, smoking (30 minute proscription) and alcohol intake will be
proscribed for two hours prior to recording blood pressure level. The
requirement for a fasting state in the basic exam will assure much of
the dietary compliance. Recording of current drug intake, including
medications affecting blood pressure, non-prescription drugs and
"recreational" drugs will be made on medical history forms on the day of

the examination.

1/88 BP-2

Detailed history of alcohol intake patterns will be recorded along
with the nutrition history because of the known, but ill-understood,
relationship of alcohol intake to blood pressure level. For similar
reasons, physical activity at work and leisure will be included in a
separate history.

TECHNICIAN TRAINING AND QUALITY CONTROL

Technicians will be trained centrally prior to participant intake
in two full-day sessions for Exam II. New technicians after the start
of the study will be trained locally by a designated "BP Supervisor".
Recertification will occur every six months with instructions being
found in the Manual of Operations. Prior to certification, each
technician will be tested for vision (reading) and with an auditory test
(by Korotkoff sound tape).

The Coordinating Center will direct a BP certification committee
to review six-monthly data. This same committee will review
three-monthly tabulations of blood pressure levels (systolic and
diastolic separately) comparing group means of each technician with the
values for all technicians by center and controlled for weight, age
and sex - by use of Z-scores. Arbitrary levels of Z-scores, (depending
on experience) but initially 3 will be used to flag possible systematic
deviations in blood pressure measurement by individual technicians.
Digit preference will also be monitored.

CLINIC PROCEDURE

It will take approximately 10-15 Minutes to make three blood
pressure measurements including the initial five minute rest and
recording of pulse rate. The blood pressure measurements will be made

physical exam, blood drawing, or any potentially stressful interview.
The blood pressure measurements on each participant will be made in a
separate room or, at minimum, in an area properly screened from all
other activity and other participants.

BLOOD PRESSURE TRAINING/CERTIFICATION

At the beginning of the first session, a description and
demonstration of the correct BP procedure is given. Trainees are to
listen to the first (training) tape, taking the test sequences until
they are comfortable with what they are listening to. Then, they take
the second tape until they have passed the test. After passing the
second tape, they are given the third tape test. Alternated with the
tapes are actual live practices under the instruction and observation of
the training supervisor. Some live practices may be done with a
standard stethoscope, but most should employ the Y-tube stethoscope.
The optimum size of a group is eight. This allows four people to do
live practices while four are on the tape training device. The group
can interchange and practice on each other.

After the first day of training, each trainee should be given a
cuff and manometer (no stethoscope) to take home and practice just the
control of the valve. This can be done by wrapping the cuff on a jar or
bottle and alternately pumping up and dropping the mercury at a steady
rate of 2 mm per second. After two or three sessions, they could
also be given a stethoscope to practice on family and/or friends. This
out-of-class practice is very important to build confidence. This time
allowed for class is enough without outside practice time.

Once each trainee has passed the third tape, he or she should do at
least two live readings with the training supervisor on the Y-tube
stethoscope. The readings should agree within 4 mm and the average
should agree within 3 mm. If they do not, the trainee needs additional
practice with tapes and live subjects. The training supervisor should
also assure that the trainee understands and follows proper procedures.

If the trainees are also to use the Random Zero device, additional
time should be allowed for instruction and mastering that procedure.
Observers are certified after passing the second and third tape tests
(tape 4 is held in reserve for recertification) and at least two live
readings. Observers are recertified every six months by taking and
passing tape 3 or 4 and one or two readings with the training supervisor
on a Y-tube stethoscope.

BLOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT PROCEDURES

TRAINING

Standardized training sessions are required for blood pressure
measurement. Some initial training sessions will be conducted centrally
with subsequent training taking place in individual clinics. Other
training will take place in the clinical centers only. Central
training will take place prior to recruitment (Appendix 3).

A. Blood Pressure Measurements

Blood pressure observer/trainers will be trained initially in a

central location over two full days. Training methods consist of a

pre- and post-test, audio cassette tape instruction and

split-stethoscope testing. Blood pressure observers will be
trained to observe and record the onset of first and fifth phase

Korotkoff sounds. Each clinical center will have one blood

pressure trainer who will have the responsibility for training any

new blood pressure observers and for conducting recertification
procedures.

CERTIFICATION AND RECERTIFICATION

The Coordinating Center will notify each clinical center when
certifications and recertifications are required. It will be the
responsibility of each clinical center to conduct these procedures at
the specified times and to notify the Coordinating Center when the
procedures are complete.

A. Blood Pressure

Blood pressure observers are required to be initially certified

after training by a designated trainer. Recertification is

required every six months using audio cassette tapes and
double-stethoscope testing by a certified trainer.

EQUIPMENT MAINTENANCE

Each clinical center is responsible for the proper operation and
maintenance of its equipment. Maintenance responsibility should be

assumed by the quality control officer and all staff should be
instructed to report any real or suspected equipment problems to

All checks, inspections, cleanings and problems indicated will be
documented and recorded by date in a permanent log. Problems and

will send copy of this log monthly to the Coordinating Center.

An inspection and maintenance schedule is summarized below.
Specific instructions for the cleaning and maintenance of R-2Z and

A. Random Zero and Standard Sphygmomanometers

These devices will be checked thoroughly and cleaned if necessary

Manometers, mercury leakage, operation of valves, manometer columns

STANDARDIZED CLINIC PROCEDURES

Correct measurement of indirect blood pressure is of the utmost
importance and concern to the success of this study. It is essential
that the standardized format described below for measuring blood
pressure on the Random Zero be followed exactly.

Major differences in blood pressure measurement methodology among
health professionals from several countries have been observed despite
the fact that written international recommendations of blood pressure
measurement were established in 1939 by a joint committee of the
American Heart Association and the Cardiac Society of Great Britain and
Ireland. It is also well known that precision is essential for valid
comparisons of blood pressure between groups of people and in

1/88 BP-7

individuals on different occasions. A number of elements can be

identified in measuring blood pressure and each is explained briefly in

subsequent subsections of this chapter ending with a subsection on

technique that is presented in detail. Study organizers consider all of

these elements equally important and ask that the strictest attention be

paid to each in order to insure that the blood pressure measurments have

a standard and high level of accuracy and precision.

1/88

A. SOUND

For purposes of this study, SBP level is recorded at the level when
phase 1 Korotkoff sounds are first heard and DBP is recorded at the
beginning of phase 5 with disappearance of sounds. The onset of
phase 1 and 5 sounds are the points of clinical importance.

B. EQUIPMENT

The following blood pressure measurement equipment will be used and
standardized for the study: stethoscope, random-zero and standard
sphygmomanometers, cuffs and bulb.

1. STETHOSCOPE

A standard Littman stethoscope having a bell will be used.
Korotkoff sounds are best heard with the bell because of their low
pitch. Stethoscope tubing should be about 10-12 inches from the
bell piece to "Y" branching. This length provides optimal
acoustical properties and allows the observer to read the
sphygmomanometer at eye level and in a comfortable position.
Earpieces should fit comfortably and snugly in the ears. Four
points should be observed in using the stethoscope.

a. The ear pieces should be directed downwards and forwards
into the external ear canal.

b. The ear pieces should be tight enough to exclude outside
sound but not so tight that they cause discomfort.

1/88

c. The bell of the stethoscope should be placed lightly on
the skin overlying the brachial artery - immediately below the
cuff and medial to the cubital fossa above the medial
epicondyle of the radius posterior to the biceps muscle. Light
pressure accentuates low-pitched sound and avoids compression
murmurs. Pressing too heavily with the stethoscope over the
brachial artery can also produce sounds that can be heard by
the observer by reducing the internal diameter of the
brachial artery in the same manner as the cuff. This causes
turbulent flow in the artery and a murmur can be heard and may
prolong the apparent duration of phase 4.

dad. The valve between the bell and diaphragm should be turned
in the correct direction.

2.  SPHYGMOMANOMETERS

Standardized Hawksley random-zero instruments will be used for all
clinic visits. Standard Baum manometers will be used for
determining peak inflation level.

3. CUFFS AND BULBS

Clinics will have four standardized cuffs available - adult,
pediatric, large adult, and thigh cuff (by the Baum Company).
Proper size of the cuff is essential for accurate blood pressure
measurement. To select proper cuff size, hold the end of the cuff
containing the rubber bladder over the upper arm and pull the other

end toward the subject under the arm. The top edge should lie
within the range markings for cuff size. If it does not, select
the next smaller or larger cuff. The range markings which are on

the commercial cuffs actually overlap from size to size and are not
considered to be optimum correct measurements. The pediatric
cuff should be used for an arm circumference (AC) of up to 24.5 cm.
The standard adult cuff should be used for AC of 24.5 - 33 cm,
large adult cuff for AC of 33 - 41 cm, and thigh cuff for AC above
41 cm.

STAPF PREPARATION FOR PARTICIPANT’S VISIT

A minimum of three clinic staff persons will be responsible for
measuring blood pressure. They need not be health professionals, but
they must be trained and certified in blood pressure measurement and
technique. Observers should have some experience in relating to and
dealing with people. While it is difficult to standardize demeanor, the
observer should strive to present a non-discriminatory, reassuring and
professional approach. The observers will be required to have a simple
vision test in addition to the training process.

It should be remembered that participation in the study is a
voluntary procedure. Participants will be given full explanation and
instructions about the preparation for the blood pressure examination as
well as an opportunity for discussion. The setting for making repeated
blood pressure measurements must be standardized for clinic visits. The
examination should take place in a quiet room where no other activity is
taking place and where temperature fluctuations are minimal. Clinic
scheduling procedures will establish consistent appointment times to
minimize problems that stem from systematic variation of blood pressure
during the day.

Once the participant has been given instructions and explanations,
the equipment has been checked, and he has been sitting in a quiet and
relaxing room with no change of position or posture, blood pressure
measurement can begin. The following steps should be followed as
precisely as possible.

1. Seat the participant with right arm on table. The inner
aspect of the bend at the elbow (cubital fossa) should be at
heart level. {If the right arm is missing or injured, reverse
chairs and use left arm - noting this change on the form.)
Legs should remain uncrossed, feet on floor.

2. Palpate for the brachial artery (just medial to and above
the cubital fossa). Choose the correct cuff size and wrap the
cuff on the arm with the center of the bladder over the

1/88 BP-10

1/88

brachial artery. If the participant seems particularly
apprehensive or nervous, wait until after the five minute wait
to wrap cuff.

3. Record the time. There must be a five minute wait before
taking the pulse and blood pressure. Conversation should be
limited.

However, a brief explanation of the procedure can be repeated
at this time if necessary.

4. Take the pulse at radial artery for 30 seconds, and record
it.

5. Connect the cuff to a standard manometer and establish the
pulse obliteration level by slowly inflating while palpating
radial artery until pulse is no longer felt. Then deflate and
disconnect the cuff. Record the pulse disappearance level and
add 30. The total is the peak inflation level for the
standard manometer. For R-Z peak inflation level, add R-2
maximum zero number (found next to mercury column) to peak
inflation level for standard manometer({i.e., pulse
disappearance level + 30 + R-Z maximum zero number).

6. Measurement 1: Connect the cuff to the random-zero
manometer. Open the Bellows control valve and wait until
mercury settles. Turn the thumbwheel two or three times.

Inflate rapidly to the R-2Z peak inflation level. Holding the
pressure constant with the bulb, wait 5 seconds. Close the
Bellows control valve. Place the bell of the stethoscope on
the brachial artery and slowly deflate the cuff (2 mm per
second) while listening. Record the first and fifth phases,
reading the pressure in mmHg to the nearest even number and
record. The first sound heard in a series of at least two
sounds is recorded for SBP (phase 1). The first silence in a
series of at least two silences is recorded for DBP (phase 5),
not the last sound heard. Disconnect cuff. Subtract zero
value from readings to get blood pressure measurement. IT IS
STRONGLY SUGGESTED THAT ALL ARITHMETIC BE DONE WITH A
CALCULATOR, GIVEN THE IMPORTANCE OF THE BLOOD PRESSURE
AVERAGES, FOR THE PURPOSE OF REFERRAL. ALL ANALYSES WILL BE
COMPUTED ON THE DATABASE FROM THE RAW VALUES.

7. Measurements 2 and 3: Have the participant raise
measurement arm for five seconds. Wait at least 30 seconds
between readings. Repeat measurement as in 1 and disconnect
cuff.

8. Standing Blood Pressure - For logistic reasons, the
standard sphygmomanometer will be used to measure standing
blood pressure and not the RZ sphygmomanometer. After the

should be disconnected and the standard sphygmomanometer
should be connected to the cuff. The participant’s arm is to

stand may be used for this purpose; the stand may also support
the sphygmomanometer. The first standing SBP should be
recorded as soon after standing as possible (no more than one
minute). A second measurement should be made 30 seconds after

PROCEDURE FOR RECORDING

If for any reason the observer is unable to determine (or forgets)
any phase, write a dash in the space on the form. This is the correct
way to indicate missed information. If an entire reading is missed,
completely deflate the cuff and start over with a replacement reading.
However, under no other circumstances may a replacement reading be
obtained. Always wait at least 30 seconds between readings.

After averaging the second and third corrected R-Z readings, record

the average on the form. Provide the participant with a copy of the
blood pressure measurement.

Wrap an arm cuff around a bottle or can.

With reservoir valve (newer models do not have a reservoir valve)
open and bellows valve closed, pump mercury to top of colum
(270-290 mmHg). If the mercury will hold at a steady level for
10-15 seconds or drops 2-4 mm, that system is airtight.

With the high pressure still in the system, close the reservoir
valve and disconnect cuff to see if that valve will hold steady

pressure. If a leak is discovered in the reservoir valve, remove
hose and valve (with Allen wrench). Valve handle unscrews or
lifts off. There are two 0 rings on the valve stem. Clean stem

and replace 0 rings. Use stopcock grease on 0 rings and valve.

If the closed reservoir valve is tight, but there was a leak with
it open, check the inflation assembly. There may be a leak in the
bulb, valve, or cuff. To test the inflation assembly, immerse each
section, especially valves and tubing connections in water while
the pressure is high and watch for air bubbles. To test the tubing
of the mercury reservoir, put soapy water on it. Most leaks occur
at or near tubing connections or from valves. If a valve leaks,
sometimes a shot of silicone lubricant on the thumb screw and
worked in will solve the problem. Otherwise it may need to be
replaced. Tubing leaks near a connector can be repaired by
removing the connector, cutting 1/2 to 3/4 inches and replacing the
connector. Lubricate a sharp knife with soapy water to make the
cut, and similarly lubricate the cut tube to make it easier to re-
attach.

Turn RZ with back toward you. With bellows valve open, retract
mercury to just below the plexiglass valve chamber. Close the
bellows valve, pump mercury to top and visually check that leakage
does not occur at that valve point. If mercury does rise into the
chamber, the valve needs repair. Replacing 0 rings on that valve
can be done locally if someone is qualified to do it. It is a more
difficult job than on the reservoir valve. Otherwise it should be
sent to Baum. A serious leak in this valve can affect BP readings.
Whenever the manometer tube seems dirty in the area of your
‘zeroes’ ox if the mercury seems to hang up there, the tube should
be cleaned. A dirty tube can affect ‘zero’ readings. To clean
tube, set cam at lowest zero. Pump up, close bellows valve,
release pressure. This leaves little mercury in the column. Tilt

manometer, getting rest of mercury out of glass and into reservoir.
Close reservoir valve. Lean manometer at angle so that no mercury
is in glass. Remove tube and clean tube and seats. Check to be
sure the rubber gaskets are seated properly. Replace tube.

This procedure should only be done by a qualified person in a
controlled setting. The manometer should be set _ in a catch basin
so that no mercury can escape and there should be a trap-type

vacuum pump available to pick up any small spills.
Check "maximum" and "minimum" zeroes and of bellows and cam

function. (This needs to be done only if there are doubts about

the values of those zeroes or functions; or if mercury has been

added or lost).
a. Release all pressure and open the bellows valve. The
large thumb wheel with the black rubber "tire" and the cam
against which it is pressed should turn freely without
binding. If they do bind, bring in the RZ.
b. Inflate the system while watching the large (about 2 -1/4"
diameter) disc above and to the left of the bellows valve
chamber. (Bellows valve is still open.) As pressure rises
you will see the disc, a piston, pushed toward the back plate
until a ring around the center of the disc touches the forward
rim of the cam. That rim is tapered, and thus determines how
far the piston can move, depending on the position of the
taper in relation to the ring at the center of the piston - a
matter of chance in normal operation of the RZ. The distance
that the piston can move before being stopped by the cam
determines the volume of mercury in the bellows chamber, hence
the volume of Hg left in the rest of the manometer.
c. To read "maximum" zero, release pressure with bellows
valve still open. Turn the cam so that the point of its taper
nearest the piston will be hit by the ring of the piston. (It
may take an inflation and deflation or two before you find the
correct cam position, which allows the minimum volume of
mercury in the bellows chamber, hence maximum mercury in the
rest of the system.) Inflate to about 200 mmHg, close the
bellows valve, release pressure and read the zero as usual;
this is the "maximum". Repeat the procedure once or twice,

checking the cam position to make sure you get the same
reading. Note that this is not a fixed value for if you were
to inflate to 300 before closing the bellows valve, the
reading would be lower; and inflation to 120-130 would give a
higher value. For this reason, always record what you read
when taking blood pressures.

d. "Minimum" zero is measured as in c above, except that the
cam is turned so that the piston can travel its maximum. It
is usually close to 20 mm lower than the “maximum” and should
not be closer than about 4 mm to the 0 on the manometer tube
scale.

e. Replace the rear case, putting it over the thumb wheel
first. Start all four screws before tightening any. Take
care not to cross thread.

f. After a series of BP readings or before transport open the
bellows valve to drain Hg from that chamber, then close it and
the reservoir valve. Between readings, the bellows valve
should be left on "open" so that pressure on the bellows is
not left in the device.

INSTRUCTIONS FOR SELF-ADMINISTERED PSYCHOSOCIAL QUESTIONNAIRES

General Information

Four self-administered questionnaires will be completed during this

section of the CARDIA exam in the order shown below:

Form

General Instructions

(1) Most problems encountered will probably be covered in the written
instruetions provided for each questionnaire. Since there are so many
questionnaires with similiar instructions, we have made these instructions
quite brief. When a respondent has trouble understanding the instructions,
read them aloud, clearly, periodically making eye contact with him/her. In
addition, you may then read the alternative sets of instructions given below

for the Framingham Type A questionnaires:

Framingham Type A Questionnaire (Question 1-5): Below is a list of

several traits or qualities that deseribe people. For each one, please
cheek the number that applies to you. Since there are no right or wrong

answers, we are mainly interested in the answers that describe you the

best.

Framingham Fype A Questionnaire (Questions 7-10): Now we would like to

know how you have generally felt during an average day in your regular
line of work. If unemployed, please refer to your last job (Questions 8-

11). If a housewife, please refer to your housework (Questions 12-15).

(2) The wording of the questions is very precise and may not be altered.

When a respondent does not understand the meaning of a question, read it aloud
clearly. If he/she still does not understand the question, try a neutral
probe, like: Answer what's right for you. If the respondent then does not
understand the question, say: Why don't you just leave that question blank.

Write "question not understood" or "question unclear" in the margin.

(3) If the respondent would rather have someone read the questionnaires aloud
to him/her, read the questions exactly as they appear in the questionnaire.
When only one response is appropriate (i.e., questions 6-11 on the Social
Support Questionnaire and the Framingham Type A Questionnaire), read the
appropriate response categories inmediately after the question, without giving
the respondent time to answer until they all have been read. (Do not read "no
answer," "don't know," responses.) When more than one response may be
appropriate (i.e. social support questionnaire, questions 1-5), allow the
respondent enough time to indieate an answer after each response category.
When the respondent categories are repetitive (such as "true or false,” "yes
or no," or questions 1-5 on the Social Support Questionnaire), and the
respondent appears to understand the questions and provides plausible answers,

you may choose not to read the response categories to each question.

(4) If a participant asks a CARDIA interviewer for ANY help in reading a
self-administered form, that interviewer should record his/her Interviewer ID#
in the space located on the last page of that form.

If the Exit Interviewer in your center has to ask a participant to
complete a portion of a form, or to fill in some missing data, this does NOT
mean that the Exit Interviewer should reeord his/her Interviewer ID# on that
form, and especially not on any self-administered form. This does not
constitute "helping the participant to read a form".

Once the exam is completed and the form set is in the hands of the Data
Editor, the Data Editor should peruse the form set, order them, and make ready
for the data entry person. When the Data Editor looks over the self-
administered forms, if the Interviewer ID space located on the last page is
left ampty, it is the Data Editor's responsibility to fill in that blank with
his/her Interviewer ID#, be it 199, 299, 399, or 499. This procedure serves
to eliminate missing fields for the data entry person and also serves as a

quality control measure.

TOENAIL SAMPLE COLLECTION

The role of trace elements in human nutrition, health, and disease has been the
subject of increased research and speculation. Accurate assessment of selenium status is
crucial in studying the relationship between selenium status and disease. Because
toenails are relatively sheltered from environmental contaminants, there is an advantage

of the use of the toenail for multiple element analyses.

PROCEDURES

Participants should be informed at the time of scheduling appointments not to trim
their toenails until they come into the clinic. Nails are collected by clipping with a
stainless steel clipper from each of the two great toes and at least two small toes.
(Small toenail clippings may be obtained from any of the small toes.) Instructions should
be given to the participants to obtain as much toenail as possible. The toenail clippings
from the great toes and the rest of the toes are stored separately in two 1.5" x 3" bags,
since the time frame represented by the great toe is different from the rest of the
toenails storage. These nail samples should be placed in a properly labeled envelope and
stored in the driest condition possible in a pre-designated area in the local clinics until
the samples can be analyzed in the future. No attempt should be made to remove nail
polish at the clinic.

If the participant has recently cut his or her toenails, give the bags to the
participant with a self addressed and stamped envelope. Ask the participant to cut the
toenails at home two weeks after the clinic visit and mail clippings from the toenails to
the clinic. Write the proposed date for cutting the toenails on the bags to help the
participant remember to cut the toenails. If the toenails are not received one week after
the proposed date, then contact the participant at least three times.

Any participant who clips his/her nails outside the clinic should be recorded on the
Toenail Log. A copy of this log should be forwarded to the Coordinating Center upon

request.

(1) Removes shoes and socks.
(2) Samples should be obtained from both feet. Clip off portion of nails from two
large toes and place into the bag labeled "LARGE", and clip off portion of the
nails of at least two small toes and place into the bag labeled "SMALL".
(3) Be sure not to include any problem nails or nails with discolorization and

PREPARATION FOR TOENAIL SAMPLE COLLECTION

INFORMATION FOR THE PARTICIPANTS: Inform the participants at the time of
scheduling appointment not to trim their toenails before they come in.

EQUIPMENT: Several high quality stainless steel clippers, 1.5" x 3" brown bags,
envelopes, labels, distilled water, liquid sterilizer (i.e., Metricide, Cidex)

DAILY PREPARATION:
(1) Store the clippers in liquid sterilizer when not in use. Rinse with tap water and
then distilled water before use. A clipper should be replaced if there is physical
damage on the cutting edge.
(2) Samples will be collected from both feet. Label two brown bags (one for the large
toes, the other for the small toes) with ID and toe specification, and label an
envelope with the ID for each participant. Place the two brown bags inside the
envelope after the collection is made.
(3) Envelopes with samples collected from toenails should be kept in proper cabinets
or boxes and placed in a dry environment with good ventilation.

BLOOD PRESSURE REACTIVITY PROCEDURES
Method
PHYSIOLOGICAL RECORDING APPARATUS

Subjects will have a total of four different physiological measures monitored during
the course of the first two tasks of the reactivity protocol, including: heart rate,
systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and mean arterial pressure. These measures will be
monitored with the use of a Vita-Stat automated measure blood pressure monitor. The
Vita-Stat will be set to manual mode so that it will inflate the cuff and determine mean
heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and mean arterial pressure when
activated by the research assistant (see Section A for description of Vita-Stat
procedures). During the remaining task of the reactivity protocol (the cold pressor), a
standard mercury sphygmomanometer and stethoscope will be used to record systolic and
diastolic blood pressure (see Section B for description of standard mercury
sphygmomanometer procedures).

Regarding clinic flow, the blood pressure reactivity procedures should be
administered last, except on the few occasions when bottlenecks occur at other
stations. The reactivity procedures may not be given prior to the administration of the
psychosocial assessments.

TASKS

A total of three tasks will be presented to subjects, including: the video-game
breakout, star-tracing, and cold pressor. The first two tasks will be presented in a
randomized order, with the cold pressor task always presented last. The two orders will
be contained on two separate tape recordings; these tape recordings will be randomly
presented to subjects with the order of the tasks noted on the data sheet. All of the
tasks will be accompanied by standardized instructions (see Section C for transcript of
tape-recording).

Breakout. The Atari Breakout video-game will be presented to subjects over a

color monitor which is situated directly in front of them. The paddle controller for the

1/87 BPR-1

game will be affixed to a wood board (approximately 12" by 12") by plastie tie-down
straps. The serving button on the paddle controller will be held down with a strap so that
balls will continuously be served during games; the research assistant will need, however,
to control the beginning of games by pushing the reset button. The research assistant

will monitor subjects’ progress by also viewing the color monitor. Scores on Super

Breakout games will be recorded on a data sheet.

Star-tracing. The star-tracing task involves subjects tracing the outline of a star
from an image displayed in a mirror while staying within narrow limits. A right-handed
apparatus (i.e., the apparatus as is arrives from Lafayette Instruments) should be used
with right-handed subjects, and a left-handed apparatus (i.e., one that is modified so that
the supports for the sereen and mirror are reversed) should be used with left-handed
subjects. Subjects will be instructed to keep the stylus on the apparatus at all times. If
subjects move out of the limits of the star, an error is scored automatically on the
counter of the star-tracing apparatus. Subjects' total number of errors for the three
minutes of play will be entered on the data sheet. The research assistant will also be
required to count the number of times that subjects make it around the star and to enter
this number on the data sheet.

Cold pressor. The cold pressor task is one in which subjects are asked to immerse
their dominant hand in a circulating ice-bath. A submersible pump will be used to
circulate the water in an ice-chest from one side of a mesh partition filled with ice to
the other side of the partition which is filled only with water. A submersible
thermometer will be used to ensure that the water is maintained at less than 1.5 degrees
Centigrade. Subjects will be required to immerse their arm approximately 9 inches in

the cold pressor so that their open palms rest against the bottom of the ice chest.

EXCLUSIONS. If a participant is taking anti-hypertensive medication, he/she should be

excluded from all blood pressure reactivity tasks.

7/87 BPR ~ 2

If a participant reports that he/she has Raynaud’s disease or
Raynaud’s phenomena, that participant should be excluded from the cold
pressor task only.

If a participant is pregnant, she should be excluded from the cold
pressor task.

If a participant reports that he/she has sickle cell anemia, then
that participant should be excluded from the cold pressor task.

Any reason for exclusion from all or any portion of the blood
pressure reactivity protocol should be recorded on the comment section
of the form.

PROCEDURE

Prior to subjects’ arrival, the Vita-Stat Monitor should be
prepared according to the instructions in Section A. In addition, the
ice should be added to the cold pressor tank at least 15 minutes prior
to the arrival of the first subject, and the submersible pump for the
cold pressor should be turned on to allow the water to circulate.
Enough ice should be added to the cold pressor tank so that the ice half
of the tank is full of ice; the level of ice should not be allowed to
get below about one-half of this amount (i.e., the level should not go
below about half full on the ice side of the partition).

When subjects arrive for the assessment session, they will be given
an explanation of the procedures and asked which is their dominant arm.
They will then be asked to sit in a comfortable chair (with the seating
arrangement reversed for right-handed subjects) while the blood pressure
cuff is affixed around subjects’ non-dominant arm (the left arm will be
used for cuff placement with subjects who claim ambidexterity -see
Section A for description of Vita-Stat procedures). The cuff will be
affixed just above the elbow with the microphone situated over the
brachial artery.

Once the microphone and cuff have been attached to subjects, and
the recording equipment is functioning properly, tape-recorded

3/88 BPR-3

instructions will presented to subjects. These instructions (see
Section C) will explain each of the tasks and will walk subject through
a practice session of the tasks, except for the cold pressor.

During the remaining portion of the procedure, the research
assistant will monitor the tape recording, subjects’ performance on the
tasks, and the physiological measures. The research assistant will also
control the function of the Vita-Stat and will arrange the task
apparatus as needed. After the practice periods, a four-minute
habituation period will follow; after the four minute habituation
period, the procedure will follow that specified in Section C. The
Vita-Stat will be activated exactly 10 seconds into each minute during
the baseline, the performance of each task, and the recovery period from
each task. Performance will be assessed by the research assistant
during the breakout task by recording game scores. A performance
measure will also be determined for the star-tracing task by recording
the total error score from the counter and by recording the number of
times subjects complete going around the star. Each entire revolution
around the star is counted as one revolution and each completion or
partial completion of a point of the star is counted as 1/6. The
technician should record the actual number of revolution on the form as
a fraction (i.e., 2/6) to the right of the phrase "number of Completed
Stars". However, the actual number should be rounded to a whole number
and recorded in the blank for data entry. Partial revolutions which are
less than half the distance around the star are rounded down to the
nearest whole number; partial revolutions which are qual to or greater
than half the distance are rounded up. For example, 3 1/6 or 3 2/3
would be rounded down to 3 whereas any value between 3 3/4 and 3 5/6
would be rounded up to 4. During the cold pressor task, the research
assistant will position the standard mercury sphygmomanometer cuff and
stethoscope and will begin inflation of the cuff 30 seconds after
immersion of the arm into the cold pressor; the deflation of the cuff
will end 10 seconds later.

Immediately following the cold pressor task, the technician will
ask the participant to rate the discomfort experienced during the cold

pressor task.

Section A

Vita-Stat Instructions and General Procedures

I. Preparation of Vita-Stat Prior to Subject Arrival

The Vita-Stat should be situated in front of the research assistant so that front
panel switches may be comfortably reached and so that the read-outs may be easily
seen. The printer should be situated next to the Vita-Stat so that it is visible to the
research assistant but is not visible to the subject (i.e., the printer should be placed on
the opposite side of the Vita-Stat from the subject). The research assistant should record
the Vita-Stat values either directly from the display or from the printer if displayed
values are missed.

Weekly calibration check. The Vita-Stat monitor should be calibrated at the
beginning of every week of use by comparing the readings on the front of the monitor
with the meniscus level of a mercury sphygmomanometer connected with the supplied T-
tube to the appropriate connector on the front of the monitor. Wrap the cuff around a
solid cylindrical object such as a thick-walled jar or can. The supplied T-tube should be
connected to one of the connectors on the front of the monitor to which one of the hoses
from the cuff normally connect. The loose connector on the hose going to the cuff then
conneets to the appropriate connector on the supplied T-tube. The remaining hose for
the supplied T-tube then connects to another T-connector with the ends of this T-
connector attached to an inflation bulb and a standard mercury manometer. The monitor
should then be set to calibrate mode after it has warmed up for 20 minutes by depressing
the DISPLAY button and pushing the CYCLE switch up. The value which appears in the
SYSTOLIC window should be recorded on the Vita-Stat Calibration form; this value
should be 010 + 005. If the SYSTOLIC display shows a value greater than 15 or less than
5, the unit should not be used, and the unit should be referred to the quality control
officer for recalibration. If the value in the SYSTOLIC window is between 5 and 15, then

the pressure should be increased with the bulb to 290 mmHg as registered by the mercury

5/87 BPR -5

manometer. This pressure should be allowed to remain in the system for at least 15
seconds. Using the valve on the manometer bulb, the system should then be bled down to
280 mmHg; the value in the SYSTOLIC window should be recorded on the Vita-Stat
calibration form. This procedure should be repeated at pressures of 150 mmHg and 50
mmHg as set with the manometer bulb and registered with the mereury manometer. The
values seen in the Systolic window of the Vita-Stat at the three pressure levels minus the
original value seen in the SYSTOLIC window with no pressure in the system should differ
from those set by bulb in the mercury manometer by no more than the following
percentages at the following pressure levels: +10% at 280 mmHg; +5% at 150 mmHg; and
+2% at 50 mmHg. If greater discrepancies than these readings are seen at any of these
three pressure levels, then the unit should not be used in reactivity testing, the quality
control officer should be contacted, and the unit should be recalibrated.

Daily preparation of monitor. The following general preparation procedures should
be followed every time that the Vita-Stat is used:

1. Warm up the monitor for 20 minutes before beginning with the first subject.
Turn on the power switch on the rear of the monitor. The self-diagnostie test will
automatically check electronie functions. Digital displays will count down from 4 to 1 in
the 4 display windows indicating proper operation. The "88.8" will appear in all displays
of the 2600 monitor when the monitor checks out as operational. Hyphens (i.e., "---")
will appear in all displays of the 2600B Monitors after "88.8" briefly appears. If the
"88.8" does not appear in the windows of the 2600 Monitor or the "-—" in the windows of
the 2600B Monitors, consult the Vita-Stat operational manual. If the "88.8" or the "---""
does appear, the unit is ready for operation.

2. Inerease the SET TIME INTERVAL switch from the default of 5 to 60 by
raising the switch. Note the change of the time interval in the MEAN ARTERIAL or
HEART RATE display windows. Once the time has been set to 60, set the SELECT
CYCLE switch to STANDBY. Each time the tone on the tape indicates that a reading is

to be taken with the monitor, the SELECT CYCLE switch must be manually moved up to

5/87 BPR - 6

SINGLE. The switch may then be released, resulting in its return to the AUTOMATIC
position. With the next tone, the SELECT CYCLE switch will need to be moved again up
to the SINGLE position. After completing the last reading with subjects, return the
SELECT CYCLE switch to the STANDBY position.

3. Make sure that AUDIO switch is "off" (ALARM indicator light should be "off"
when the AUDIO switch is set to "off").

4. Make sure that the MIC ERROR yellow light is "off"; if this light is "on" at any
point in time, either the microphone is not plugged in or the microphone circuit is
faulty. If the light is "on," first check to ensure that the microphone is plugged in
properly. If the microphone is properly connected and the light remains "on" consult the
quality control officer and the Vita-Stat manual; do not use this unit until the problem
has been corrected.

5. Make sure that an adequate amount of paper is located in the printer.

Il. After Subjects Have Arrived
1. When the participant arrives at the station, prior to applying the blood
pressure cuff the technician should review the blood pressure form (FORM 2) to assure
that his/her blood pressure levels are within the acceptable range (equal to or greater
than 160 systolic and/or equal to or greater than 100 diastolic are exclusion levels). The
technician should ask the participant if he/she is using anti-hypertensive medication as
this also excludes participation from all the blood pressure reactivity tasks.
The technician should also ask the participant if he/she has extreme sensitivity
to eold in his/her fingers. If yes, then ask if they have Raynaud's disease or phenomena.

The following description should be used in explaining Raynaud's symptoms:
"Raynaud's produces intermittent attacks of discoloration of body extremities,

especially of the fingers or toes and sometimes of the ear and nose. First a

whiteness occurs and then a blackish/blue coloration ensues. The reaction is

5/87 BPR-7

brought on by cold or emotion and sometimes results in extreme numbness and
pain in the affected areas. This phenomena does not include the typical
blueness of the hands that one experiences in winter. For example, these

symptoms can occur in response to holding a cold drink bottle.

The technician should tell the participant that on the cold pressor task, they
will be required to immerse their arm in cold water for a short period of time. The
technician should explain that some people may feel that this is uncomfortable or even

mildly painful, but their arm will be the water less than one minute.

2. Explain that blood pressure and heart rate will be automatically measured by
the Vita-Stat monitor. Indicate that the machine is safe, that after the first reading it
will inflate 25 mmHg higher than the subject's previous blood pressure reading, and that

during the rest and task periods it will inflate every 60 seconds.

3. Palpate the subject's brachial artery on the inside of the right arm
approximately 5 centimeters above the crease in the elbow. Wrap the cuff snugly around
the upper arm, placing the red arrow (and microphone) over the brachial artery (i.e., the
palpated area). Placing the cuff properly is very important to getting accurate
readings. Keep in mind the following:

a. Use the correct cuff size; the correct size should be indicated on the cuff.
Alternatively, if the Velero of the cuff does not overlap completely, the next
size larger cuff should be used. Squeeze alli the air out of the cuff before
placing it on the arm.

b. Do not place any part of the cuff over clothing as this will dampen the
Korotkoff sound. It is also important not to place the top of the cuff on the

folded up sleeve as this will cause the pressure within the cuff to be uneven.

7/87

If subjects wear clothes that do not allow the sleeve to be rolled up far enough
to keep the cuff off of the sleeve, the subject should be asked to change into a
looser top that will not compromise placement of the cuff.

Make sure the cuff is snug, not too tight and not too loose, and check to see
that the red arrow on the outside of the cuff is placed just below the area
where you palpated the brachial artery.

Make sure the cuff is level with the heart; too high above the heart will
provide a biased low reading and too low below the heart will provide a biased
low reading. If the subject is so tall that the arm rests on the table below
heart level, a support should be placed on the table to rest the arm on and

Section B

Standard Sphygmomanometer Procedures

Blood pressure measurements (systolic and fifth phase diastolic) will be recorded
with a standard mercury sphygmomanometer and a standard Littman stethoscope, having
a bell, for the one reading during the cold pressor task and for the four recovery readings
following the cold pressor. The methods of measurement will be standardized as set out
in the Manual of Operations. The research assistant who takes the blood pressure
readings will be certified in blood pressure measurement according to the CARDIA blood

pressure certification procedures.

I. Preparation of Mercury Sphygmomanometer Prior to Subject Arrival

1. Maintenance of the mercury sphygmomanometer and stethoscope should be
assumed in each clinical center by the quality control officer. All real or suspected
equipment problems should be reported promptly to the quality control officer. All other
inspection and maintenance procedures should follow those outlined in the CARDIA
Manual of Operations for sphygmomanometers.

2. The apparatus should be situated so that subjects may immerse their dominant
hand in the cold pressor, allowing the manual blood pressure readings to be taken from

the non-dominant arm.

Il. After Subjects Have Arrived

1. The correct standardized cuff size should be chosen according to the

procedures specified in the CARDIA Manual of Operations.

2. At the conclusion of the four recovery readings for the second reactivity task,

the tape recording should be put on "pause." The arrangement of the apparatus should

The certification procedures for the reactivity testing involve
several stages. These procedures are to be met by one reactivity
trainee per center; once certified, this reactivity evaluator
may certify other reactivity trainees in each center by having
each individual meet the following stages:

1. The reactivity trainee must first meet the certification
criteria for regular blood pressure assessment procedures.

2. The trainee must pass, by correctly answering all
questions, a written examination covering the use of the Vita-
Stat and the procedures to be employed during the reactivity
testing (see Attachment A).

3. The trainee must demonstrate familiarity with the Vita-
Stat by successfully completing with no prompting the following
procedures with the machine:

a. The trainee should complete the procedures for the
weekly calibration check without any errors or
prompting.

b. The trainee should complete the procedures for the
daily preparation of the monitor, describing each step
as it is completed, without any errors or prompting.

c. The trainee should correctly demonstrate the use of
the Vita-Stat with a subject.

4. The trainee must successfully demonstrate familiarity
and proficiency with the reactivity protocol by conducting the
entire reactivity protocol without any errors. The tape
recording must be started and stopped at appropriate times (e.g.,

initiated with every sound of the tone on the tape. The
evaluation sheet contained in Attachment B should be used to
evaluate trainee's performance during the practice session.

I. PURPOSE
The blood drawing station is designed to obtain a blood sample to test for important risk
factors for cardiovascular disease and for other blood parameters of interest to CARDIA. It is
potentially a difficult station because of the anxiety caused in most people by blood drawing and
the potential for injury. However, if carefully and professionally done, it provides a positive
safe experience for the participant and for CARDIA. Blood drawing will take about 5 minutes
of the participant's time.
This protocol was designed as a training manual for the phlebotomist at the clinical
centers.

II. DESCRIPTION
A. TESTS
The following tests are planned in CARDIA EXAM II:
LIPIDS: total cholesterol, triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol and subfractions (HDL2,
HDL3), estimated LDL cholesterol, estimated VLDL cholesterol and apolipoproteins A-
I and B.
The methods of measurement for each of these tests is found in the CARDIA Laboratory
Operations Manual and the Rationale for Assessment is found in the CARDIA Protocol.
B. RESTRICTIONS
The Lipid Research Clinic's Manual of Operations identifies several factors which may
influence lipid and lipoprotein values, which should be standardized.
1. A standardized seated posture will be followed. The adverse reactions which occurred
in the pre-test have warranted the use of a recliner, although the reclining position
should be allowed only under extreme circumstances (e.g. known fainting).
2. Prolonged venous occlusion: Elevations of 2-5% can be seen after two minutes of
continuous tourniquet use. Therefore, trained, efficient staff and a total tourniquet
time of less than two minutes are required.

4. Vigorous exercise should be avoided for six hours prior to the visit.

6. Blood drawing should occur early in the CARDIA visit but following the blood pressure

C. GENERAL PREPARATION

Site: The blood drawing should take place in an isolated room or one enclosed by dividers.
Temperature should be 65-75 F. There should be no direct sunlight. The recliner should be
placed in a space sufficient to allow the chair to fully recline. The chair may be elevated on a
wooden box to facilitate comfort of the phlebotomist when drawing the blood.

The room should be equipped with all the necessary supplies. A work-table or counter
should be prepared with the materials and vials needed for blood handling and aliquotting. The
centrifuge, refrigerator and freezer should be nearby.

Staff: This station is staffed with a technician with documented class time and
experience in phlebotomy. The clinic supervisor or medical director will conduct training for
this technician. Recertification will take place twice and will be authorized by the clinic
supervisor or medical director. The technician should be properly attired in a white laboratory
coat. Long hair should be tied back.

Wash hands at the beginning of the work day and as needed after processing specimens. No
personnel should smoke in this area.
Greet participant, confirm that you have the correct envelope and that it contains ID
labels. Locate the Phlebotomy forms in the participant's form set and check that they have
been properly labeled. Fill in phlebotomist code. Ask the participant questions 2-5, the
time and date he/she last ate, whether he/she has had hepatitis and whether the subject has
any bleeding disorder, and whether he/she has been exposed to AIDS. In the ease of

Explain procedure. An example might be:
"Iam going to be drawing some blood from the vein in your arm. The purpose of this is to
check levels of blood fats such as cholesterol. You will receive results of this test in about
8 weeks. I will be taking two tubes — about 1 1/2 tablespoons. Are there any questions?"
With jackets removed, have the participant sit upright in the recliner with the sleeves
rolled up to expose the antecubital fossa (elbow). The recliner should be in a complete
upright position.

Only when the participant has indicated that he/she has a history of fainting, should the
technician recline the participant for the whole procedure. The technician may recline the
participant by: (1) pulling the lever forward (2) pulling up and forward on the arm rest
and (3) pushing back smoothly on the chair back. In the event that a participant reclines,
be sure to note the 'supine' position on question #8 on the Phlebotomy form.

This reclining position is an exception to the protocol and should only be allowed in
extreme circumstances. Its use is left to the discretion of the technician. It may be
helpful to reassure an apprehensive participant that he may recline following the blood
drawing.

The chair position should also not be changed from sitting to reclining during the blood
drawing. Try to draw as much blood as possible when the participant is in the upright

position.

A tourniquet is used to inerease venous filling, it makes the veins more prominent and

PRECAUTIONS WHEN USING A TOURNIQUET: The tourniquet should be on the arm for
the shortest time possible. Never leave the tourniquet on for longer than two (2) minutes.
To do so may result in hemoconcentration or a variation in blood test values. If a
tourniquet must be applied for the preliminary vein selection, it should be released and
reapplied after a wait of two minutes. If the patient has a skin problem, put the tourniquet
over the participant's shirt or use a piece of gauze or paper tissue so as not to pinch the
skin.
A. Wrap the tourniquet around the arm 3 to 4 in. (7.5 to 10.0 em) above the venipuncture

site.
B. Tuck the end under the last round.
C. If a velero tourniquet is used, adhere the tabs to each other.
Cleanse the venipuncture site.
A. Remove alcohol prep from its sterile package.
B. Cleanse the vein site with a circular motion from the center to the periphery.
C. Allow the area to dry to prevent possible hemolysis of the specimen and a burning
sensation to the patient when the venipuncture is performed.

D. If venipuncture becomes difficult, the vein may need to be touched again with your

hand. If this happens, the site should be cleansed again with alcohol.

Use of evacuated tubes (vacutainers):

A.

Thread the appropriate 21-gauge 1-1/2" multidraw needle into the needle holder until
it is secure.

Insert the first blood collection tube into the holder and onto the needle up to the
recessed guideline on the needle holder. Do not push the tube beyond the guideline, as
premature loss of vacuum may result. The tube will retract slightly. Leave it in this
position,

If a tube has been previously or unsuccessfully used, it should be discarded in a proper
container, not re-used.

Inspect the tip of the needle visually to determine that it is free of hooks at the end of
the point, and that its opening is clear of any small particles that would obstruct the
flow of blood.

The needie must be sterile. Do not use a needle from a package which is broken or

contaminated in any way.

Perform venipuncture:

A.

Grasp the participant's arm firmly, using your thumb to draw the skin taut. This
anchors the vein. The thumb should be 1 or 2 in. (2.5 or 5.0 em). below the
venipuncture site.

With the needle bevel upward, enter the vein in a smooth continuous motion.

Make sure the participant's arm is in a flat or downward position while maintaining the
tube below the site when the needle is in the vein. It may be helpful to have the
participant make a fist with the opposite hand and place it under the elbow for
support.

Grasp the flange of the needle holder and push the tube forward until the butt end of
the needle punctures the stopper, exposing the full lumen of the needle.

Remove the tourniquet after blood is flowing. Once the draw has started, do not
change the position of the tube until it is withdrawn from the needle. During the

procedure, do not allow the contents of the tube to contact the stopper.

Keep constant, slight forward pressure (in the direction of the needle) on the end of
the tube. This prevents release of the shut-off valve and stopping of blood. Do not
vary pressure nor reintroduce pressure after completion of the draw.

Fill the vacutainer tube as completely as possible, i.e., until the vacuum is exhausted
and blood flow ceases. A partially filled purple top tube should be avoided if possible,
because the higher resulting final concentration of anticoagulant will affect lipid
values.

When the blood flow ceases, remove the tube from the holder. The shutoff valve re-
covers the point, stopping blood flow until the next tube is inserted (if necessary).
Immediately and thoroughly mix the contents of the tubes by gently inverting eight (8)
times. To prevent hemolysis, avoid jarring or shaking the tube. Put the tube into a
rack or jacket pocket; do not lay on table.

To obtain additional specimens, insert next tube into holder and repeat procedure from

#10D.

If a blood sample is unobtainable:

A.

Change the position of the needle. If it has penetrated into the vein too far, pull it
back a bit. If it has not penetrated far enough, advance it farther into the vein.
Rotate needle half a turn.

Try another tube. The tube in use may not have had sufficient vacuum.

Loosen the tourniquet. It may have been applied to tightly, thereby stopping the blood
flow. Reapply the tourniquet loosely. If the tourniquet is a velcro type, quickly
release and press back together. Be sure however, that the tourniquet remains on for
no longer than two minutes at a time.

Probing is not recommended. This is painful to the patient. In most cases, another
puncture in a site below the first site is advised.

A syringe and needle may be used instead of a vacutainer, if necessary.

Do not attempt a venipuncture more than twice. Ask the participant if they would be

willing to have your supervisor attempt to draw the specimen.

PRECAUTIONS - IF A PARTICIPANT FEELS FAINT OR LOOKS FAINT FOLLOWING THE
BLOOD DRAWING:
A. Have the person remain in the recliner, recline the chair if necessary or have him sit

B. Take an ampule of smelling salts and crush it and wave it under the person's nose for a
few seconds.
C. Provide the person with a basin if he/she feels nauseous.

D. Have the person stay reclined until the color returns and he/she feels better.

19. Caution in Handling Blood Samples:

Improper handling of blood samples can lead to infection of blood drawing personnel.

Therefore, the following procedures should be observed.

A. Needles must be disposed of in proper disposal containers. Needles should also be
safely stored in a locked cabinet when clinie is closed.

B. Avoid contact with plasma. Cover any scratches or cuts on hands before handling, or
use gloves.

C. If the phlebotomist accidently sustains a contaminated needle stick, the wound should
be thoroughly cleansed with soap and water. The medical director should be notified
so that the serum may be analyzed for possible hepatitis.

D. All used vacutainer tubes and blood products are to be placed in biohazard bags for

disposal.

Iv. BLOOD HANDLING

A. DESCRIPTION

The methods of drawing the blood have been described above. The handling
of those samples is equally critical because change from protocol can
significantly affect the chemicals being measured in the blood. It is
particularly important that time deadlines in handling be observed and
that samples not be left open to the atmosphere longer than necessary. A
total of ninety (90) minutes is allowable between blood drawing and final
placement of samples in the freezer, so schedule your time accordingly.

B. PROCEDURE

1. Immediately after drawing the sample, affix one of the large
plain white labels with the participant’s ID to each blood
tube. This is necessary to identify which tube belongs to
which participant.

2. Immediately place the purple top tube into a container of
water-ice. Cool sample on water and ice for 30 minutes but not
more than 60 minutes.

3. Place the red top tube in the test tube rack. Allow the sample
to clot by standing for at least 30 minutes but not more than 60
minutes at room temperature (65-750 F).

4. Do not let the samples stand in direct sunlight or at extreme

temperatures.

C. OPERATING THE CENTRIFUGE
After the samples have set for the 30-60 minute time period,
prepare to centrifuge.
1. If the chamber is already cool, continue operation at #2.
To precool the centrifuge, close and lock the cover, set the
TEMPERATURE control at 4 C, set the SPEED control to 1000 RPM,
set the TIMER control to 20 minutes, and push the RUN button.
- Set the POWER switch to ON.
3. Balance the load.
A. Place opposite shields containing filled vacutainers on the
balance.
B. To the lighter centrifuge shield, add water (or 50/50
water/alcohol) around the vacutainers, but no closer to the

top of the container than one-quarter inch.

B. ALIQUOTTING

1. 15 ml PURPLE TOP TUBE: After centrifuging, the plasma should be promptly
separated from the cells. Use micropipetter #1 to aliquot 1/2ml plasma into the 1
ml Wheaton vials for apolipoprotein analysis. Next, use a Pasteur pipette to transfer
3-5 ml of plasma to the plastic screw top vial. Finally, use the micropipetter to
aliquot the remaining plasma into the 2-1 ml Wheaton vials for plasma storage.

2. 10 ml RED TOP TUBE: After centrifuging, the gel in the tube should lie between
the serum and clot; if not recentrifuge for 10 more minutes. Extract the stopper
and promptly remove the serum. Use micropipetter #2 to aliquot 1/2 ml volumes of
serum into the four yellow-labled 1 ml Wheaton vials. The remaining serum is
decanted into the 3.5 ml Wheaton vial.

C. GENERAL COMMENTS FOR ALIQUOTTING SAMPLES

1. The micropipetter automatically aliquots 1/2 ml samples at a time. Two tips will be
used for each participant, one for plasma tubes and one for serum tubes. Do not mix
tips.

2. Be careful not to disturb cells when drawing plasma into a pipette. If cells mix with
the plasma, recentrifuge the sample to insure obtaining the maximum amount
possible. When using Pasteur pipets, be careful not to draw red cells into the bulb.

3. DO NOT OVERFILL VIALS. Room is needed for expansion during freezing.

4. a. The 'Aliquotting Scheme' and the Phlebotomy Form both give the minimum
amount of specimen necessary to perform the corresponding clinical test.

b. When completing the Phlebotomy Form, it is necessary to indicate whether the
minimum amount of aliquotted specimen was collected. The instructions on the
form request that a code of 'F' be placed in the box when the vial is filled at
least to the minimum volume. (For example, for the plastic screw top vial, this
would mean filling to a volume between 3 and 5 ml.) A code of 'N' indicates
that a minimum volume was not obtained. (For this vial, that would mean

VI. STORAGE AT CLINICAL CENTER
All vials, even those containing less than a minimum, are to be frozen. Freeze
samples immediately; do not allow vials to sit out. Freezer temperature should be
-10 C.
Record time of freezing on the Phlebotomy form. Samples must be placed in the
freezer within 90 minutes of blood drawing.
Any specimens known or suspected to be contaminated with AIDS or hepatitis virus
should be stored in a plastic bag and labeled with a BIOHAZARD sticker.
Store samples in the freezer in separate trays by vial size. This will aid in specimen
retrieval at shipment time. Develop a system that orders the samples in a tray by
the date drawn, for example, start at the upper left corner and move right and down

as you would read a book.
