IX. LABORATORY QUALITY CONTROL

In order to assess the reproducibility and validity of the measurements supplied by the
centralized laboratories, a split sample external surveillance program has been developed.
Its purpose is to produce data which may be used (1) to identify problems as they oceur and
to communicate this information to the appropriate laboratory for corrective action and
(2) to obtain historical data about the performance of the entire process, i.e. sample
collection, preparation, handling, shipping and analytical performance.

The quality control procedures will consist of split patient samples providing duplicate
specimens for assessment of performance. Duplicate samples will aid in measuring 'within
assay' or ‘within day' reproducibility. In order to accomplish this, the duplicate blood
specimens will be delayed in shipment to the laboratory for analysis. Otherwise, the sample
is handled in the same manner as all other specimens,

A. DUPLICATE SPECIMENS

The amount of ADDITIONAL blood that will be drawn for the lipid and apolipoprotein
analysis is a 15 ml purple top tube. This tube is handled in the same way as the 15 ml
participant tube. It is aliquotted into the plastic screw top vial and the 1 ml Wheaton vial.
The appropriate color stripe quality control labels are affixed to these vials.

Each of the clinical centers will be requested to draw the quality control tube on
approximately five percent of the participants, generally one participant per week. This
participant will be identified at the time of the clinical center's weekly phone call to the
Coordinating Center. For information regarding this procedure, see the quality control
section of this Manual. The technician will acknowledge that the additional blood was
drawn on the Quality Control subject by placing one of the quality control identification
labels in the space provided on the Phlebotomy form. In the event that the additional
sample could not be drawn, he/she will be requested to document the reason and asked to

draw the quality control sample on the VERY NEXT SUBJECT.

PHL-— 20

7/67?

The participant need not be told that he/she is having extra blood drawn for quality
cheeks, The consent form covers the maximum amount of blood that could be drawn on any
participant,

B. SHIPPING DUPLICATE SPECIMENS

When an additional amount of blood is drawn for a quality control duplicate specimen,
it is to be submitted with the following month's shipment. That is, duplicate specimens
should not be shipped together, but separated by one month. Review the quality control
shipping schedule in the preceding Transporting Samples section (VII).

C. INTERNAL QUALITY CONTROL

The laboratory will supply the Coordinating Center with periodic reports of their

internal quality control. These reports will be reviewed by the Quality Control Committee

to insure that contract requirements are met and that action is taken when problems arise.

X. RESULTS REPORTING
A. LABORATORY REPORTS SUBMITTED TO THE CLINICAL CENTERS
Each clinical center should receive from the Northwest Lipid Research laboratory,
individual hard-copy results reports (printed forms). These should arrive within 4-6 weeks
following shipment of the CARDIA specimens for analysis.
B. REVIEWING RESULTS REPORTS

When the reports arrive at the clinical center several things need to be done:

1. Indicate on your inventory forms that the results have been received.
2. Sean all reports for obvious laboratory errors.
3. Report any errors to the contact person at the laboratory and to the quality

control person at the Coordinating Center.

4. File the report in the participant's form set.

5. None of the data from these laboratory reports will be entered in the clinical
center computer. Instead, computer tapes of all the data will be sent to the

Coordinating Center to merge with the participant record.

PHL- 21

7/87

A sample of the results will be reviewed on a monthly basis at the Coordinating
Center by the Quality Control Committee in order to check for errors, to note the
frequency of alert or out-of-range values, and to analyze the results for periodic
‘monitoring reports’.

C. REPORTING OF RESULTS TO PARTICIPANTS AND REFERRALS

The clinical center is responsible for reporting specific laboratory test results to their
participants. In addition, subjects with a total plasma cholesterol of 250 mg/dl or greater
and LDL level 180 mg/dl or greater will be invited to return to the study clinic to have
these tests repeated. If repeat results are above these thresholds subjects will be referred
to an appropriate medical provider. (These medical referral criteria were developed by a
physician advisory group composed of the following individuals: R. Crow, G. Friedman, F.
Gosch, R. Havlik, A. Oberman, S. Sidney.)

D. ALERT VALUES

The CARDIA Laboratory Operations Manual (a part of the Manual of Operations) lists
the alert values for lipids. These values represent the value at which a laboratory will alert
the clinical center concerning an abnormal test. Alert values will simply be noted as such
on the results report.

Each center is requested to develop a policy regarding the reporting of alert values.
The center is discouraged, however, from having additional bloods drawn and from pulling

additional specimens from the stored samples, for the purpose of a repeat test.

SIX-MONTH FOLLOW-UP

The following are instructions regarding the mailing and logging of the six month
contact attempts:
1. The six month contact letter with accompanying postcard or letter and return
envelope should be mailed out between six and nine months after the month when the
participant was examined at Exam I, but not before the participant has been sent their
summary of test results. (Centers may choose to contact all participants by phone if
manpower is available.)
2. If within two months of the mailing of the six month contact letter no response is
received, participants and then persons named on the follow-up contact sheet should be
telephoned. If participants cannot be reached through this method, each center should
implement other tracing procedures, such as those outlined in their original proposals.
Each center should verify directly with participants any new addresses or telephone
numbers that are received from contact persons, e.g. family members, friends, etc.
3. Any changes in addresses, phone numbers, etc. should be filed with participants’
original contact form. New information should be entered into existing center-specific
computer files of participants’ addresses and phone numbers. Each center should develop
their own system for this.
4. The use of a log sheet will allow each center to keep track of changes in the
participants' addresses and phone numbers. All data collected on the log sheets (as
designed by the Coordinating Center - see sample enclosed) will be data entered locally
and transmitted to the Coordinating Center at the end of each month. Copies of these

transmissions will be sent on a regular basis to the Steering Committee for review.

Using the 30 Month Follow-up Log
In the top right corner of the log is the date and time the log
was generated. If you have more than one copy of a log you can
check the date and time to see which is the latest version.

The second line of the title gives the month (mm) and year (yy)
the participants listed are eligible for follow-up in mm/yy
format. For example, "FOLLOWUPS FOR 01/88", tells you that the
participants listed were eligible for follow-up beginning in
January 1988.

The next three lines list the allowable codes and their meanings
for some parts of the log concerning the follow-up information
collected.

The "CARDIA ID" column lists the participants eligible for
follow-up for the month stated in order by their CARDIA ID.

The "EXAM II STATUS" column shows each participant's current Exam
II scheduling system status code. These codes are:
E Examined
S Scheduled
N No-show
P Pending
R Refused
D Died
A Abbreviated exam
ப Unscheduled.

There are four other codes pertaining to examined participants on
the log, "E +", "E-", "E ++" and "E --". "E +" indicates that
the participant's exam occurred 4 weeks or more before the
expected exam date. Likewise, the "E -" means the exam occurred
4 weeks or more after the expected exam date. The "E ++" and "E
--" codes indicate exams that occurred 12 weeks or more before
or after their participants' expected exam date. The purpose of
these codes is to flag participants that recruiters may want to
contact earlier or later than their expected 30 month follow-up
date because of their exam date.

The "EXAM II STATUS DATE" column gives the effective date of the
participant's status. For "E", "A", "E+" and "E-", it is the
exam date; for "S" and "N", it is the date scheduled, etc...

"DATE OF FOLLOWUP" is the date 30 Month Follow-up is initiated
for a participant such as the date the first phone call is made
or the first letter is mailed.

"DATE OF RESPONSE" is the date the participant responds to the
follow-up and the follow-up is completed.

BODY SIZE MEASUREMENTS

All measurements are to be made with the participants wearing a short sleeve shirt
or blouse (or surgical gown) , shorts and socks and without shoes. A supply of shirts and
Shorts should be maintained at the survey center for participants who forget to wear or
bring the appropriate clothes for exercise testing and body size measurements. Men
should be sure pockets are empty.

All measurements should be taken by a team of two persons, if possible - one acting

as observer and the other as recorder. The observer takes the measurements, calling out

the results to the recorder, who repeats them and then calls out the name of the next
measurement. The observer keeps the measuring instrument in place until the recorder
repeats the number. The recorder generally cheeks the examinee's position during the

SKINFOLDS. There are no special directions for the participant to
follow prior to this test since these are relatively stable
measurements. Skinfolds should be taken prior to active tests since
sweating and increased blood flow to the skin makes measurement more
difficult. Men can wear gym shorts for the test; women should wear
shorts and a loose-fitting, sleeveless blouse or surgical gown which
is also loose at the waist. The Harpinden skinfold caliper will be
used for taking all skinfold measurements.

Taking skinfolds requires practice to assure reliability and
validity as previously stated. The following suggestions for taking
skinfold measurements should be observed:

All measurements are taken on the right side of the person being
measured. The fold of skin should be firmly grasped between the left
thumb and forefinger (for right handed persons) and then lifted up.
(Technician’s elbow should point toward the ceiling.) Firmly grasp
and lift, sweeping up the fold several times to make certain that no
musculature is grasped. When ready to take the measurement, grasp the
skinfold firmly with the thumb and finger. Do not let go of the fold
and apply the caliper. Release the grip on the caliper completely,
allowing the spring to compress the fold. Take the reading to the
nearest millimeter. Open and remove the caliper, then release the
fold. (NOTE: the Harpinden caliper needle makes more than one
revolution; the small pointer on the number of revolutions.) Each
revolution of the large needle is 20 mm. The maximum skinfold
thickness that the caliper should be opened is 50 mm. If this will
not accommodate the skinfold, mark a modification on the form. The
code ‘88’ should be used to indicate a skinfold too large to measure.
In addition, the protocol modification question should be check *‘2'
for too obese. Keeping the left hand above the skinfold (see
pictures) allows the dial to be read easily.

The "skin" should be lifted by grasping firmly the fold between the thumb and
forefinger. A firm grip, not exeeeding the pain threshold, eliminates or at least
substantially reduces the variations in the apparent thickness of skinfold that would
result from wide differences in the pulling force of the fingers.

The width of the skin that is enclosed between the fingers is an important factor. It
cannot be standardized, in its absolute size, for all the sites of the body. With a thick
subcutaneous layer a wider segment of the skin must be "pinched" in order to form a fold
than when the adipose tissue is poorly developed, as it is on the dorsum of the hand. For
a given site the width of the skin should be minimal, still yielding a well defined fold.

The depth of the skinfold at which the calipers are placed on the fold also requires
comment. The two sides of the fold are not likely to be parallel, when the skin is lifted
by one hand, being narrower near the crest and larger toward the base. When the

ealipers are placed at the base, the resulting measurement is too large. Here, again, the

correct distance from the ecrest_at which a true fold, with surfaces approximately
parallel to each other and to the contact surfaces of the calipers, is obtained upon the

application of the calipers to the skin.

It is extremely important to measure skinfolds accurately. Even after extensive
practice it is possible to make errors due to slight misplacement of the caliper or
misreading the dial. To avoid such errors the following procedure is reeommended.

a. If possible, the person measuring the skinfolds should not be the one to record
them. An assistant should record the values as the measurer reads them from
the ealiper. It is helpful if the assistant repeats the values aloud as they are
recorded.

b. Skinfolds should be lifted two or three times to determine the fold to be put
the calipers in place before determining what is really to be measured. Do not
lift the skinfold away from the body or the actual location of the calipers will

then be too far forward.

Training and Quality Control

This training and quality control program for taking body size measurements

consists of the following components:

1.

Central training and certification of at least one technician from each survey center
before each of the two examination cycles; This individual from each center should
be designated as that center's body size measurement primary technician.

If additional personnel are needed by a center to perform body size measurements
during the examination eyeles, training will be provided by the center's clinic
supervisor and the certified body size technician using the training video tape.
Training includes the performance of the body size measurements on at least ten
people by the two technicians. Discrepancies in measurements are to be discussed
and any steps necessary to improve the techniques should be taken. The new
technician and certified technician must complete body size measurements on five
new participants and submit the recording forms to the Coordinating Center in order
for the new technician to become certified,

Direct observation by the supervisor of the examination procedures on a monthly
basis, with correction of errors when necessary.

Midway through each examination cycle an intensive one day evaluation of
measurement is to be conducted by the supervisor and an outside consultant. All
body size measurements are to be performed by each technician, supervisor, and
consultant on at least two moderately fat and two lean individuals. Discrepancies in
measurements will be discussed and any steps necessary to improve the techniques
will be taken.

A daily instrument check is to be performed on the Harpinden skinfold calipers using
a standard lucite step wedge with widths in increments of 10 mm. A weekly check is
to be performed of the body weight scale using standard weights ranging from 50 to

200 pounds.

During each exam cycle, each anthropometry technician will be required to obtain
all body size measurements from ten individuals (i.e. clinie staff ete.) twice with a
one week time interval between the two measurements. Analysis of the intra-
observer reproducibility of measurement will be performed by the Coordinating
Center using these data.

Four times a month (approximately once per week) each technician will perform all
anthropometric measurements on an individual concurrently with a second
technician performing these measurements on the same individual. Copies of both
forms will be submitted to the Coordinating Center for analysis.

The Coordinating Center will direct a body size measurement certification
committee to review body size data. This committee will review three-monthly
tabulations of body size measurements comparing group means of each technician
with the values for all technicians by center and controlled for weight, race, age,
and sex by use of Z-scores. Outlying values will be based on Z-scores initially set at
3 to flag possible systematic deviations in body size meausurement by individual
technicians. The committee also will analyze each technician's data for digit

preference.

PHYSICAL ACTIVITY QUESTIONNAIRE INSTRUCTIONS
INTRODUCTION
The physical activity questionnaire was developed for CARDIA to help determine a
participant's usual activity patterns. These questions focus on activities done during the
past year.
QUESTION 1
The respondent is provided with a cue card for reference. The interviewer reads
the question. The cue card is given to the respondent while the question is being read. It
is important that the respondent give a definite number for an answer.
QUESTION 2: SECTIONS A-M
This part of the questionnaire is formatted as a list of various activities that
require various levels of physical exertion to perform. The activities listed include those
done both at work and at home or leisure. Participants are requested to select those
activities which they have performed in the past year for at least one hour in any
month. The one hour is total time, and may represent several activity sessions.
Additional information is ascertained for those activities which were performed.
Primarily, we want to determine the number of months in which they participated
in each activity, as well as the number of those months in which their usual duration of
activity was more than a specific number of hours per week. A "yes" should be given in
A1, B1... whenever there is at least one hour of activity in only 1 month, or in any
number of months up to 12. Thirteen categories of activity, A through M are queried;
the structure of the questions is the same for each of the 13 activities. Again, a cue
card is provided to help focus on the activities listed on the questionnaire.
Conduct of the second part of the physical activity questionnaire should begin with the
following statement:

Otherwise, it may be included under 'nonstrenuous sports'. Please note that only

However, sweating, increased body temperature, ete. should be due to the activity, and

The first two activities questioned include the words 'in the past 12 months for at

Proceed with the questionnaire by going through the list of items. It is important
that activities included are of the intensity required for inclusion, i.e., bicycling at least
10 mph, and that the time recorded is for the time actually spent in the activity. There
are two options for each activity listed, 1) the person did not perform the activity, 2)
the person did perform the activity. For those who report doing the activity, follow-up
with the question about number of months of total performance, and then the number of

months of more frequent performance.

B. Vigorous racket sports: This should include only racket sports done vigorously,
which generally is the ease only for singles matches. Cutpoint is 3 hours/week.

C. Bieyele faster than 10 mph or exercise hard on an exercise bicycle: 10 mph is a
constant, moderate to fast pace. When bicycling at that rate, your heart rate should
increase and you will probably start to sweat. Cutpoint is 2 hours/week.

D. Swimming: The ecutpoint time includes only that time spent swimming, not
time sitting by the pool, in the sauna, ete. The cutpoint time is 2 hours/week.

E. Vigorous exercise class or vigorous dance: It is important to only include those
exercise classes or dancing that is done vigorously. Cutpoint is 3 hours/week.

F. Vigorous job activity such as lifting, carrying or digging: It is important that
the activity be vigorous. The cutpoint is 5 hours/week.

G. Home or leisure activity such as snow shoveling, moving heavy objects or
weight lifting: Include time actually spent in the activity. Cutpoint is 3 hours/week.

H. Other strenuous sports such as basketball, football, skating or skiing: This should
only include strenuous sports or those sports that require intense exertion. Time
should only be that time spent in the activity. The cutpoint is 3 hours/week.

I, Other non-strenuous sports such as softball, shooting baskets, volleyball, ping
pong, or leisurely jogging, swimming or biking: It is important to count the time
actually spent doing the sport. The cutpoint is 3 hours/week.

J. Taking walks or hikes or walking to work: This should be vigorous walking, rather
than leisurely strolling. If hunting is included, exclude time not moving such as time in
a duck blind. The cutpoint time is 4 hours/week.

K. Bowling or golf: It is important to count the time that is actually spent in the
sport, excluding time sitting by the bowling lane or riding in a golf cart. Note that
golfing using a motorized cart will generally be classified as less frequent activity,
below the cutpoint time of 3 hours/week.

L. Home exercises or calisthenics: It is important to count the time actually spent

in the exercise. The cutpoint is 2 hours/week.

For each activity group, it is important to determine the number of months
engaged in the activity as well as the number of months during which the persons
participated more than the cutpoint for the activity. Therefore, there are a series of

the second question asks how many months the participant participated in the activity,

Coefficients b ande for (A) jogging, (B) racket sports, (C) biking, (D) swimming,
and (H) other strenuous sports are 12 for less than the cutpoint and 36 for greater than the

Subscores are computed for vigorous activity (A. through H.) and for moderate activity (1.

The coefficients have been selected to mimic intensity or calorie expenditure per minute

cutpoint for each class of activity. However, because of the lack of detail, a seore to be
explicitly interpreted in relation to calorie expenditure is deliberately avoided.

OVERVIEW

While increases in coronary heart disease risk factors occur in young adulthood in
conjunction with signifieant changes in physiological measures and in lifestyle, the
interrelationships among these risk factors and changes have not been rigorously
investigated. Both epidemiologic and clinical research in coronary heart disease have
increased our awareness that some risk factors for disease such as obesity, hypertension,
and hypercholesterolemia may be partially determined by genetie factors or behaviors
which are formed in infancy, childhood, and adolescence. Studies to date also suggest
that some of the coronary heart disease risk factors do not change dramatically before
the late teenage years and that differences in characteristics by sex or race emerge and
are most pronounced after this time. However, relatively little work has been done to
identify the characteristics of young adult life which may be precursors to, or coincident
with, the increase in risk factors prior to middle age.

Cross-sectional data, for example, suggest that weight gain is pronounced during
the late teens through age 30, particularly in males, and that positive relationships exist
between weight and lipoprotein fractions during these ages. The reasons for, and
consequences of, this increase in adiposity need further investigation. The interaction of
life events, behavior, changes in physical activity, and dietary intake that may influence
weight gain and lipoprotein levels should be assessed as well as the relative importance
of weight gain in relationship to risk factor changes during this age span.

Investigators have examined the consistency of blood pressure levels in children to
determine whether "tracking" occurs into the teenage years. The results of these studies
have raised other interesting and important questions. Is there evidence for "tracking" of
other coronary risk factors? Does "tracking" persist into young adult life, a time during
which dramatic changes in lifestyle are often taking place? Are the changes a function
of these changes?

An important component of this study is the study of young blacks. Since the Black
Health Task Force on High Blood Pressure Control pointed out the lack of knowledge
about coronary heart disease in blacks as applied to this country, a greater focus on the
nature of disease in blacks has been a topic of increasing consideration.

"Coronary Artery Risk Factor Development in Young Adults" (CARDIA) is the
study of the evolution of coronary heart disease risk in a cohort of black and white men
and women initially 18-30 years old. Such studies will not only contribute to our
understanding of the development of atherosclerotic disease, but more importantly, help
to suggest strategies for prevention before individual lifestyle patterns become well
established.

OBJECTIVES

The overall goals of this study are:

1.

To document at baseline and after one or more biannual intervals, risk factors and
changes for coronary heart disease (CHD) in young (black and white) adults, 18-30
years old.

To identify lifestyles during this age span, which influence these changes in risk
factors. The interrelationships among risk factors and lifestyles, and changes in
these characteristics will be considered.

The secondary objectives of this study are:

1.

To observe age-related trends in risk factors during young adulthood and to
compare cross-sectional with longitudinal findings.

To perform subpopulation analyses on, sex, race, or sociodemographic groupings,
and to compare trends and processes involved in risk factor development between
these subgroups.

To develop and apply effective methods of follow-up during these young adult
years to achieve maximum participation of the study populations...

The objectives of each clinical center are:

2.

To re-examine at least 85% of the 5116 participants enrolled in the study.

To maintain, via mail and phone calls at semi-annual intervals during the two year
follow-up period, contact with each participant in order to maximize the return
rate for future examinations.

To assess risk factors for CHD in these participants.

ADMINISTRATIVE STRUCTURE

Role and Composition of Steering Committee

The Steering Committee is the representative body of the CARDIA study. It is
composed of seven voting members: a Principal Investigator from each of the four
elinieal centers, the Director of the Coordinating Center, the NHLBI Project Officer,
and the Chairperson of the Steering Committee (an individual who is not a representative
of any clinical center or the Coordinating Center). The Steering Committee provides
overall scientific direction for the study and serves as the foeal point of the
organizational structure. During the planning and the execution of the Exam Il phase,
each Principal Investigator will be directly responsible for coordinating all aspects of one
or more of the following designated areas: Sampling and Recruitment, Publications and
Presentation, Content of Exam II, Retaining Participants at Exam Il, Nutrition, Clinic
Coordinator's Issues, Lipids and Chemistries, Psychosocial, Medical Issues, Pulmonary
Function, Blood Pressure and Exercise.

The Steering Committee will meet regularly to review study progress. Each center
is required to be represented by an investigator or proxy at each meeting of this
committee. If a vote is needed, it will require a two-thirds majority of all seven voting
members. Minutes will be taken by a member of the Coordinating Center.

The Steering Committee will perform the following functions:

1. Guide and oversee the development of the study Protocol and the Manual of
Operations

2. Review and approve major changes in the Manual of Operations

3. Review and approve ancillary studies

4. Provide advice and assistance to the Coordinating Center, clinical centers or

NHLBI on operational matters.

5. Resolve problems brought to the Steering Committee by investigators, the
Coordinating Center, and any other of the Central units (Central labs, NHLBI,
etc.)

6. Monitor the performance of all participating clinical centers through site

visits according to information provided by the Coordinating Center in order
to insure that an adequate number of participants are recruited; that the
clinical centers adhere to the protocol; and that quality data is collected.

continuation of CARDIA, the Exam II period will be compressed into 12 months compared
to the the 15-16 month enrollment period during Exam I. Thus, scheduling participants
will be sequential from the first person seen until the last Exam I participant over a
twelve month period. Therefore some participants will be seen as much as 4 months
beyond their second year anniversary, but only in an exceptional case will a participant
be seen at an interval much less than 2 years.

Returning participants will be given a specially designed exam which will be
somewhat shorter than Exam I. All participants of Exam I are eligible for Exam Il. If
participants are injured or ill, but willing to come for Exam II, they will be invited.
Participants must have one unbroken arm for blood pressure testing and be non-pregnant
or non-lactating. Pregnancy or lactation will not eliminate a participant, but rather
extend their window of eligibility. Similarly, participants who have moved more than 50
miles from the clinic will be permitted a larger window of eligibility in order to
maximize retention of the cohort and minimize the costs of retention. Payments will be
allowed within limits to bring participants who have moved back for examination.

The retention plan is designed to bring at least 85% of the CARDIA cohort back to
be re-examined in this second examination period. The plan also provides for extensive
monitoring of the process. Each center will be provided scheduling lists designed to
achieve the completion of the re-examination within 12 months. Participants who have
moved prior to the 18 month follow-up will be identified so that special recruitment and
eost planning can be made in advance. Initial contact letters and Exam II CARDIA
brochures will be mailed to each participant along with a series of reeruitment telephone
contacts. These telephone contacts will include an introduction, description of the
examination, questions concerning pregnancy, and an invitation and scheduling of the
exam. Arrangements for expense reimbursement and a reminder telephone call, a review
or the pre-exam instructions (i.e. fasting, ete.) and any special arrangements for
exceptional participants (i.e. those moving over 50 miles, those incarcerated, ete.) will
also be discussed. Confirmation letters, pre-exam instructions and follow-up contact
worksheets are sent to all participants one to two weeks prior to the scheduled Exam II
date.

Every effort will be made to maximize the return rate of the CARDIA cohort. The
efforts will include performing a mini-exam on participants who refuse to participate in
the clinical setting, but are willing to provide information at home or some other
eonvenient location. Implementation of this latter option will not be started until
sufficient documentation of the inability to complete the regularly schedule examination
has been documented. These specific options may include examinations administered by
mobile teams of examiners, the use of other clinics involved in NIH funded multicenter
studies, ete.

While the 85% goal return rate is set as a target, every attempt will be made to
maximize the return at Exam Hl. The CARDIA Study is well aware of the need to
demonstrate as high a return rate as possible in order to assess the long term potential of
the study to chart the natural history and/or evolution of cardiovascular disease risk
factors. Such efforts demand the retention of the cohort in sufficient number of
complete examinations to be certain that inferences regarding risk factor changes can be
made.

Quality control involves the collection of certain types of data and the subsequent

Quality control is accomplished in many different ways depending upon the type of

inventories, etc.

community, i.e. central laboratories.

each of the sections of the CARDIA visit in order to assure that quality data is being

POL- 10

INTERVIEWING PRINCIPLES AND PROCEDURES

Interviewing, in part, is a science: There are definite rules that produce valid
results. Interviewing is also an art: Frequently there are only general guidelines to
follow and much depends on the sensitivity of the interviewer. The procedures and
techniques that follow will help you to conduct interviews which will yield valid data.

I. DEVELOPING A GOOD INTERVIEWING RELATIONSHIP

Interviewing is one of the major parts of the CARDIA study and therefore it is
crucial that interviewers present questions appropriately, record the participants’ replies
precisely and accurately and probe meaningfully. In order to maintain an objective
information gathering atmosphere, the interviewer must convey that he/she is an
understanding person capable of accepting information in a non-judgmental manner as
well as convey an interest in what the subject is saying. The subject must find
satisfaction in talking to a receptive person without the fear of appearing inadequate.

It will be the interviewer's responsibility to obtain full and accurate information by
eliciting cooperation from participants, establishing and maintaining rapport,
encouraging active participation of participants' answers in a strictly neutral way.
Interviewers are skilled professionals. Their skills make it possible for subjects to give
frank, complete, relevant answers to questions.

In general, you will find that the majority of subjects are willing to be
interviewed. They will have received the CARDIA initial contact letter and are aware
that they will be called. We would like to emphasize that a confident, enthusiastic
approach which assumes people are willing to be interviewed is a most effective

technique.

A. Increasing the Subject's Cooperativeness. Previous studies have identified

several factors that will increase the respondent's receptiveness.
1. Be prepared and know your material. Participants need to feel that you
are interested in the study and interested in their opinions. Be an active
listener and establish comfortable eye contact with the subject.
2. Offer convincing statements about the purpose of the study.
3. Discuss how the respondent was selected.
4. Deseribe the beneficial uses of the research findings to both the

respondent and to the community.

B. Questions Likely to Be Asked by Participants During the Interview. Listed

are examples of questions that the interviewer should be prepared to answer:
1. How did you get my name?
2. Why don't you take my (husband, wife, etc.) instead of me?
3. What will you do with the information?
4. What if you find something wrong?
5. What kinds of questions will you ask?
6. Are you going to test me for (AIDS, syphilis, gonorrhea, ete.)? Why not?
7. Why don't you want people over 30? Under 18?
8. Can I bring (my mother/my friend/my kids) along?
9. Will anything hurt?
10. How is an EKG done?
11. What will the blood sample be used for?
12. What is the purpose of the study?

13. Why do you want to know about my diet?

Il. THE TWO MAIN KINDS OF QUESTIONS

A. Precoded Questions. With precoded questions, you circle the appropriate
code number (or check the right answer box). In addition to eheeking a box or
cireling the right answer, it is very important that you record the participant's
verbatim response whenever there is any question about which code is appropriate.

B. Open-ended Questions. With open-ended questions, the question is followed
by a blank space for you to record the participant's answer word for word. This
kind of question suggests no possible answers, so it is your job to fill in that blank
space with the participant's own words and to encourage him/her to express ideas

as fully and as clearly as possible.

Il. INTERVIEWER ADMINISTERED QUESTIONNAIRES

There are several standard procedures for reading questions: Read in a natural
conversational rhythm and in a normal tone of voice. Read as if you are speaking. Be
cautious about reading questions too rapidly; the subject may not feel comfortable asking
you to repeat questions and consequently the answer will not reflect his/her true
thoughts on that issue. Be aware of the participant's facial expressions, e.g., puzzled,
confused. Repeat the question if it is answered inappropriately, but repeat it exactly as
written. Show no impatience when being asked to repeat a question.

Each question must be asked of each participant in the same way, and in the same
order to insure that comparable information is being obtained from all the respondents in
the study.

A. Interview instructions are provided throughout the interview. These

instructions are not to be read to participants but are intended to let you know

what to do at each point.

B. Read only those code categories which appear in the question and you are
instructed to read UNLESS:

1. You have special instructions to the contrary.

2. There is an instruction to "READ CHOICES", or

3. A question ends with a dash or colon and it is obvious that the codes must

be read.

Do NOT read any codes which do not appear in the question.
Cc. Ask the questions exactly as worded and in the same order as they appear in
the questionnaires.

Minor changes in wording can completely change the meaning of a
question. Unless each interviewer asks the questions exactly as shown, the answers
are meaningless. Similarly, you must follow the sequence of questions. Do not ask
questions out of order unless you are given special instructions to do so.

D. Ask every question. It is the interviewer's responsibility to ask every
question. Often a previous statement by the subject will partially answer another

question, but rarely does it answer that question completely. Do not omit questions

and do not assume that you know the answer to the question.

Iv. HOW TO GET SATISFACTORY ANSWERS
A. Learn the Purpose of Each Question. In order to do a good job of
interviewing, you need to understand the kind of information we are trying to get
through each particular question. Unless you understand its purpose, you will not
be able to judge when a response is adequate and when you must probe for

clarification or for additional information.

B. Don't Attempt to Interpret/Explain the Question - Maintain Neutrality. Ifa

participant does not seem to understand a question, repeat the question slowly and
clearly. Give the participant time to think about the question (while simultaniously
being aware of time allowed for administering the questionnaire). Unless you have
other instructions about handling specific questions, the acceptable reply for a
participant who wants to know what a question means is "whatever it means to
you". Do not attempt to explain the purpose of a question unless the interviewer
instructions specifically authorize you to do so.

Cc. Don't Define Terms Used in Questions. Some subjects may ask what is
meant by a word used in a question. Leave the matter of definition to the
participant, suggesting "whatever you think __ means" or "however you use the

term ",

dD. Don't Leave a Question Until You Have An Adequate Answer or Have
Determined That a Participant Can't Give a Clearer Answer.

V. PROBING TECHNIQUES
The two most effective neutral probes are silence and repeating the original
question.
A. Silence. The value of silence cannot be overestimated. Many people, including
interviewers, react to silence as a vacuum that must be filled with constant
chatter, The interviewer who can wait quietly and patiently will soon find that 15
seconds of silence is more than most participants can take, and the participant will
often expand or clarify a previously inadequate answer.
B. Repeating the Question or Answer Categories. Be sure to repeat the question
as stated in the questionnaire. This is particularly useful when the participant
answers a question irrelevantly. In some cases it will be necessary to remind the

subject of your frame of reference, i.e., to acknowledge what the participant has

INT

said and then bring the participant back to the topic by repeating the question.

C. Do not Accept a "Don't Know" Answer Without Probing at Least Once. If a

response is a "don't know", probe by asking: "well, what do you think?" or "I'd like

to know your opinion" (if the question asks for an opinion rather than facts). If the
question deals with facts, we prefer an approximation to no answer at all, and you
might probe "what's you best guess?" or "approximately?" to convey the idea that
100% accuracy is not required.

D. Use Neutral Probes That Do Not Suggest Answers. Probes are needed to obtain

more complete, accurate answers. All probes must be non-directive, i.e., the probe
must not suggest any particular answer to the participant. Probes should be used
whenever the participant is hesitant in answering questions; when he/she seems to
have trouble expressing him/herself; when he/she seems too shy to speak at length;
whenever there is any reason for the interviewer to believe that the subject has not
given a complete report of his/her thoughts; and finally, reassuring probes are
needed when a participant seems to lack confidence.
E. Examples of Other Neutral Probes.

1. In what way?

2. What is that? Why do you feel that way?

3. How do you mean?

4. I would like your impression.

5. I would like your opinion.

6. What do you think?

7. Can you give me an example? or For example?

8. Can you explain that in a little more detail?

9. How are you using the term...?

10. How is that? or How does that work?

11, Anything at all—even little things?

12. If you had to choose, which would you say?
13. What else can you tell me about that?

14. In general, overall...

1. Generally Speaking, Some Probes Are Avoided in Favor of Others.

a. Instead of "anything else?" you'll find that "what else can you tell
me about that?" is more likely to elicit answers.

b. Instead of "why?" you'll find "why do you feel that way?" or "I'd be
interested in your reasons" accomplishes the same purpose and is less

likely to be threatening.

2. Questions Used in Ordinary Conversation Should Be Avoided Because
They Suggest Answers.

a. Refrain from asking "do you mean A or B". This suggests two
possible answers and there may be others which may occur to the

participant.

F. Do Not Leave a Probe Dangling. Always record the response to a probe even if

it's only "no" or "That's all I ean think of".
G. Always Cross Reference. When you probe to clarify a response, always indicate
which response you are clarifying. There will be times when a participant will say
something ambiguous and continue talking. When you probe to clarify the
ambiguous response, indicate by an asterik both the statement being clarified and
the clarifying response.
1. If there's not enough space to record the respondent's answer, use the
margin. Be sure to label these continuations clearly when you edit each

completed interview.

ENT

2. Don't ask "do you mean...". People tend to say "yes" to any suggestion

either because it's easy or because they think it's the right answer.

3. Don't ask "then you feel...?" You may be placing the emphasis on the

wrong part of the answer.
H. Make Probes Consistent with the Purpose of the Question. We cannot stress
enough the importance of choosing a probe that is appropriate for the particular
kind of inadequate answer given. Think through each response, evaluate it for
relevance and clarity and choose the right kind of probe. Any probe which does not
suggest answers and which is non-threatening is acceptable provided it is
appropriate to the particular interviewing problem.
I. Watch for Irrelevant Answers. Irrelevant answers can be interesting, but with
interviewers must bear in mind what we want to know. Acknowledge the response
and make it clear that you have been listening; also make clear your frame of
reference before repeating the question. Repeat the question word-for-word, but
preface it in such a way that you now need additional information.

J. Watch for Vague, Incomplete Answers. A probe such as “tell me more

about..."is effective.
K. Avoid "Depends" or "Qualified" Answers. When the participant gives a response
of this nature, we advise using probes such as repeating the question; preface the

question with a phrase such as "well, in general...".

L. Record and Document Fully and Clearly.

VI. HOW TO RECORD THE INTERVIEWS.
A. We recommend the following suggestions:
1. Be prepared to write.
2. Periodically establish eye contact with the participant while you are

writing.

1.

Use abbreviations to help you get down as much as possible.
Always report a response using the participant's exact words.
Always indicate when you had to probe.

Always record verbatim the response to a probe.

If you question whether you circled the correct code, be sure to record

the participant's verbatim response.

8.

If you make a recording mistake, cross out the wrong part instead of

erasing: it is faster and easier to read. Then circle and initial the correct

answer. If an answer is skipped, cirele both spaces and write "NA".

VII. FOLLOWING YOUR FIRST BASIC TRAINING SESSION.

Become familiar with the questionnaires. Read instructions carefully. Administer

questionnaires to yourself just as you would a participant and probe yourself if an answer

to a question is uncodable or otherwise inadequate. We recommend completing the

interview with a friend. Re-read the instructions watching for any errors you made so

that you do not repeat them on subsequent interviews. Study the instructions thoroughly

so that you understand the purpose of questions.

You may wish to re-read this manual following the conduct of interviews: it may

provide a different perspective and reinforce what you have experienced.

Ask all respondents regardless of number of years of school completed.

Question 7: OCCUPATION OF RESPONDENT

These questions 7 (a - e) are the ones used to collect information on
industry, occupation and class of worker in the 1980 Census of Population. Parts a and b
refer to industry, ¢ and d to occupation and e to class of worker. Together the questions
are used to determine the proper code for industry and/or occupation. Our focus is on
deseribing the respondent's occupation. Classification of occupation is difficult and we
need as much information as we can get. Probe for full deseription of occupation and
industry.

The emphasis in these questions is on the respondent's current or most_
recent job. If Respondent has more than one job, probe for the main job, i.e. the job at
which the person spends the most hours. If the hours are equal, ask the questions in
reference to the job R considers the most important.

If Respondent has never worked record "NEVER WORKED" in Q 7a and Code:
Census 3 Digit Code 998 in the space provided at the bottom of the page.
Industry (7a_and 7b)

Do not press for the name of the company or employer if there is any
hesitancy on R's part. The name is not necessary and in most instances wil! not tell us
what R actually does in his job. But, the kind of business or industry is crucial to our
properly classfying the job. It is important to have detailed information. A description
such as "automobiles" is far from sufficient — this could mean an auto factory, a new car

dealership, a used car lot, a car rental agency, a car wash, a car repair shop, an

automobile importer or something else. Probe fully to find exactly what kind of business
or industry it is. If appropriate, ask if industry is manufacturing, wholesale, retail or
other (construction, services, schools, banks ete). See CENSUS BUREAU
INSTRUCTIONS page INT 16 for description.

Occupation (7e and 7d)

In describing the kind of work R does, do not stop with a general
answer. For example, “office work" can mean many different things —- supervising
typists, being a typist, being a file clerk, supervising the entire office, or something
else. Find out what the person does in the office. If R says "laborer," find out what
he/she does as a laborer, etc.

General answers must be probed:

"manager" -- What does R manage?

"work for Jones Company" — What does R do there?

"in the computer area" — May be data entry, programmer, systems
analyst -- Find out what R does in the computer area.

"machine operator" — what kind of machine does R operate.

In describing R's most important activities or duties, don't be content
with a job title. A sophisticated title may tell very little about what a person actually
does. Probe with a bit of personal interest: "That's interesting, what do you do?"

If R is a "homemaker", ask if she works in her own home or outside the home for
pay. We need to distinguish between a homemaker in her own home who is assigned code
997, and a homemaker or housekeeper for pay in someone else's home which is coded 407.
NOTE: "Probing should be as neutral as possible, so that the respondent's answers are

not distorted. When a neutral question is asked of all respondents, there is
comparability between all the interviewers. If each interviewer asks a leading
probe, the replies would no longer be responses to the original question but

would vary from interviewer to interviewer, depending on the probe. This

thoroughly defeats the objective of standardization, and dilutes the respondent's
answer with interviewer ideas". (Current Population Survey, CPS-250, revised
January 1980, D8-5)
Probing procedures should be introduced casually as a neutral expression of
interest, such as:
1) "Yes, 1 see" - shows that you are listening and R may add something else.
2) An expectant pause - conveys impression that the question has not been fully
answered and may bring forth a further response.
3) Repeat question - useful if R doesn't quite understand the question.
4) Repeat the respondent's reply and ask him to tell you a little more about
what he does.
"You say you are a mechanic ~ could you please describe what you do?"
or
"I'm not quite sure what you do. Could you tell me a little more?"

INSTRUCTIONS FOR CODING OCCUPATION
During the initial period, until a determination is made on the final coding
procedure, the occupations of the Respondent, Spouse and Parents will be coded at the
centers.

It is recommended that the person who is conducting the interviews on the
Sociodemographic Questionnaire be the person to assign the occupational code. The
interviewer will become aware of deficiencies in responses to the occupation questions
and will be sensitized to the need for careful probing for full and accurate responses.
Also the interviewer may recall statements that were not recorded but may provide clues
to the appropriate code in uncertain cases.

The basic resource for coding occupation is the Alphabetical Index of Industries and
Occupations, 1980 Census of Population, Final Edition, November, 1982. The document
is available from the Superintendent of Documents, U.S. Government Printing Office,
Washington, D.C. 20402, or from any U.S. Department of Commerce District Office.
(Prepayment is required if ordering by mail. Check price before ordering. For
information call GPO, Washington D.C. 202-783-3238.

A companion volume, the Classified Index of Industries and Occupations, is
available from the same souree.

Both indexes list some 20,000 industry and 29,000 occupation titles. The
Alphabetical Index lists titles in alphabetical order, the Classified Index lists them in
numerical order. The Alphabetical Index is the basic resource to use in identifying the
appropriate occupational code. The Classified Index helps the user understand how the
titles fit into the classification structure. This volume is also useful when dividing
between two or more categories. It gives a broad picture of all the titles included within
a category. This volume is also useful when deciding between two of more categories. It

gives a broad picture of all the titles included within a category.

INT 49

Both indexes are divided into two sections: the "white pages" list the industry
codes; the "yellow pages" list the occupation categories. Each industry and occupation
title has a 3-digit number or a letter which ean be translated into a 3-digit number. Our
task is to identify the 3-digit occupational code which best fits the respondent's answers
to the occupation questions. Basically, the procedure is a similar to looking words up in a
dictionary. Once you get the hang of using the index, the 3-digit code is relatively
simple to assign for most cases. We do expect problems with a proportion of eases and
will set up a mechanism for resolving problem cases. Please note, the Industry "white
pages" has a section on SELF-EMPLOYED with an extensive listing.

The Coder uses the description given by the Respondent to identify the
occupational code in the "yellow pages". In those cases where specific industries are
associated with an occupational title, the Coder uses the industry information to select
the appropriate code. Industry information, even though we are not coding it directly
may help to identify the appropriate occupation code. Industry information is available
only for the Respondent. For the Spouse and Parents, the best we can do is to look for
industry clues in the description of occupation. If no clues are found, we will take the
most general or "not elsewhere specified" category.

The use of the 3-digit Census occupational codes provides maximum analytic
flexibility. The codes can be aggregated into a common system across centers or into a
system tailored to particular research objectives.

LIFE EVENTS QUESTIONNAIRE INSTRUCTIONS

In this interviewer-administered questionnaire, we will ask respondents about their

experiences since their last CARDIA exam.

SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS

1.

Interviewer instructions are CAPITALIZED.

If the respondent answers yes to "was that in the last 12 months?", then record
response in the last column. If no, then record response in the second column. It is

possible that both responses could be marked, but for data entry purposes, only the
most current response will be entered.

Whenever "(MONTH/YEAR)" appears, give the current month, last year.
Ask all respondents the events listed on the first two pages.

Ask all respondents the first question of Section B on page three. If "No" skip to
Section E. If "Yes", continue with the second question in Section B. Then proceed

with Sections C, D, and E.

Try to help the respondents move quickly through this interview. If he or she takes
a long time to respond, you may choose to say something like, "Try not to dwell on

any one question.”

BE SENSITIVE; Remember that many of these events are quite painful. Try to respect

the respondent's feelings.

Weight Questionnaire Instructions

This questionnaire contains six questions regarding the respondent's current and
past weight. It is self-administered and is to be completed by all subjects.

Instructions:

way through the questionnaire.

respondent still does not understand, leave the answer blank and write "did not
understand question," or "question not clear" in the margin.

Alcohol Use Questionnaire Instructions

In this questionnaire, we will ask respondents about aleohol use. It is interviewer-

administered.

General Instructions

(1) The path through this questionnaire is indicated by GO TO and SKIP TO
statements. These and other instructions to the interviewer are capitalized and
parenthesized. Do not read these instructions aloud.

(2) Question 1 determines whether the respondent drank any alcoholic beverages during
the past year. Questions 2-7 and 12-15 apply to those who did. For those who did not,
question 8 determines whether the respondent drank more than once or twiee in the
past. Questions 9-11 apply to those who did. Respondents who drank alcoholic beverages
once or twice a year or more will only answer two questions, 1 and 8.

(3) Use 2 digit code. If person drinks less than once a week, the answers to questions
2, 3, and 4 should be 00.

(4) If person answers "2 drinks per day," interviewers should write down subject's
answer verbatim and then convert to appropriate time slot — i.e. with 14 drinks/week,
ask the subject, "Is that 14 drinks per week?" Ask in a non-judgmental manner.

(5) If person answers 10 drinks/month, say "How many would that usually be per
week?"

(6) If a person says "I drink about 50 drinks a weekend whenever there's a party,"
repeat the question, placing emphasis on "per week". Possible probe:

"How many would that be per week?"

(7) The number given in answer to question 6 and only that number should be used in
asking question 7. No calculation should be made regarding the "about" unless the

subject asks what we mean by "about" or asks a related question.

GLOSSARY OF CARDIA MEDICAL TERMS

angina -- chest pain due to inadequate blood supply to part of
the heart.

aortic stenosis -- narrowing of the valve between the main pumping chamber
of the heart, the left ventricle, and the major blood vessel
supplying blood to most of the body, the aorta.

cardiomyopathy -- a disorder in which the heart muscle becomes weak. This
may be the result of any of a number of medical conditions.

chorea -- (please see rheumatic fever)

cirrhosis -- hardening of the liver with the loss of normal liver function,
often as the result of excessive alcohol intake over a prolonged
period of time; may be due to other causes, too, such as viral
infection.

congestive heart failure -- accumulation of fluid in the lungs and in other
parts of the body as a result of a poorly functioning heart.

coronary occlusion -- blockage of a blood vessel to the heart leading to death
of part of the heart muscle (heart attack, myocardial infarction).

coronary thrombosis -~- same as coronary occlusion.

duodenum -- the first part of the small intestine. It is the part of the
intestinal system that occurs right after the stomach.

glomerulonephritis -- a kidney disorder characterized by inflammation of parts
of the kidney called the glomeruli. In its acute form, it is
characterized by the presence of large amounts of protein in
the urine, fluid retention (swelling of the ankles and other
parts of the body with fluid), and high blood pressure.

hepatitis -- inflammation of the liver, generally as a result of viral
infection or excessive alcohol intake.

hysterectomy -- surgical removal of the uterus (womb).

kidney stones -- stones formed in the kidney, resulting form abnormal concen-

tration of minerals and other substances; stones can cause severe
pain if released from the kidney into an area in which they
block urine flow.

mitral valve prelapse -- an abnormality, usually harmless, of the mitral valve,
which is in between the two chambers of the left side of the
heart. This abnormality is found relatively frequently in
young women and usually requires no treatment.

myocardial infarction -- death of part of the heart due to loss of blood supply
to that part of the heart (heart attack).

BLOOD PRESSURE
Rationale

CARDIA is a study in young adults of the evolution of risk factors for coronary
heart disease. Each of the major established risk factors, including elevated blood
pressure, are of paramount interest in CARDIA. Evolution of risk is studied by following
the course of blood pressure and the appearance of new hypertension through young
adulthood, and by examining the relationships of these blood pressure levels to other
biologie and behavioral aspects of life. Blood pressure and hypertension are therefore
primary outcome variables in CARDIA.

Many volumes or reports have been published dealing with blood pressure and its
influence in the atheroselerotic process. An exhaustive interpretative review of this
body of literature was published in 1981 by the Working Group on Arteriosclerosis of the
National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute (Arteriosclerosis 1981, Volume 1, Summary,
Conclusions and Recommendations, NIH Publication Number 81-2034, June 1981; and
Volume 2, Detailed Report, NIH Publication Number 82-2035, Sept 1981). The
importance in the atherosclerotic process of blood pressure is established in the following
quotation from Volume 1, p17:

"As blood pressure rises, do does risk of ischemic heart disease and its
complications. The range of normal blood pressures is wide. Even within the "normal"
group, risk increases as the upper limits are approached. Usually, blood pressures are
expressed as systolic pressure/diastolic pressure; values exceed 140/90 mmHg are
considered to be hypertensive for adults. Middle-aged person with a diastolic blood
pressure of 90-104 mmHg or greater (so-called "mild" hypertension) have a risk of heart
attack that is about 70 percent higher than that of persons with a diastolic pressure
under 80mmHg. Persons with a diastolic blood pressure exceeding 104mmHg (moderately
severe to sever hypertension) have a risk more than twice that of those with a normal
value. Hypertension is an especially strong risk factor for stroke and, to a lesser extent,
for peripheral vascular disease."

Blood pressure is measured in a resting state, using 3 measurements with a random
zero sphygmomanometer. The random zero machine has two advantages over the fixed
zero manometer. Digit preference does not appear in the data, though it may still exist
in the reading itself, and be randomized out of the data by the use of the randomly
chosen zero point. More importantly, it deprives the blood pressure technician of
knowledge of the actual value, and therefore of the ability to make judgements about
blood pressure levels for reading close to critical values such as 90 diastolic. It should be
noted, however, that the random zero machines tend to yield blood pressures which are
about 1.5mmHg less than those obtained when using a fixed zero machine. Within person
variation in blood pressure is substantial; 3 replicate readings tend to reduce this
variation.

In the Hypertension Detection and Follow-up Study of Hypertensive (>90mmHg
diastolic) men and women, a drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 20mmHg from
seated to standing positions was a significant predictor of five year mortality,
independently of age and seated blood pressure level (1). A drop in diastolic blood
pressure was also a significant predictor of five year mortality. Further, excluding the
group with drops of more than 20mmHg, change in systolic blood pressure from sitting to
standing was an independent predictor of future mortality. This result was in keeping
with results from the Normative Aging Study which showed, among normotensive men,
that an inerease in diastolic blood pressure from the supine position to sitting was an

BP - 1

7/387

independent predictor of future hypertension (2).

Postural change in blood pressure is an easily obtainable measurement that may
have clinical and predictive significance in both normotensive and hypertensive people.
This measurement will be studied in CARDIA as another potential risk factor.

Methods of Measurement

The purpose of blood pressure measurements in CARDIA is: to compare levels of
this risk factor between young blacks and whites; to observe the interaction with other
CHD risk factors over time; and to observe variables that will predict changing levels of
blood pressure.

Resting blood pressure measurements (systolic and fifth phase diastolic) will be
recorded with a random-zero (RZ) sphygmomanometer, by trained and certified
technicians at baseline and subsequent intervals. For standing blood pressure
measurements, the standard sphygmomanometer will be used. The methods of
measurement will be standardized - as set out in the Manual of Operations. The pulse
rate for 30 seconds will be recorded with each blood pressure measurement.

As many confounders of blood pressure measurement as possible will be controlled
by standard settings and technique of blood pressure measurement or by recording
uncontrollable confounding factors. So that the following will be recorded:

1) Time of day (AM/PM)

2) Room temperature

3) Arm circumference at the midpoint of the upper arm
4) Technician 1.D. number

The resting blood pressure will be measured three times on each occasion. Standing
blood pressure will be measured twice. Caffeine (from tea, coffee, pop) eating, heavy
physical activity, smoking, and alcohol intake will be proscribed for two hours prior to
recording blood pressure level. The requirement for a fasting state in the basic exam
will assure much of the dietary compliance. Recording of the current drug intake,
including medications affecting blood pressure, non-prescription drugs and "recreational"
drugs will be made on medical history forms on the day of the examination.

Detailed history of alcohol intake patterns will be recorded along with the nutrition
history because of the known, but ill-understood, relationship of alcohol intake to blood
pressure level. For similar reasons physical activity at work and leisure will be included
in a separate history.

Order of Measurement

It will take approximately 10-15 minutes to make three resting blood pressure
measurements including the initial five minute rest and recording of pulse rate.
Approximately five additional minutes will be used for measuring standing blood
pressure. The blood pressure measurements will be made very early in the clinic visit
sequence immediately following the greeting and informed consent. Measurements will

be made before the physical exam, blood drawing or any potentially stressful interview.
The blood pressure measurements on each participant wilt be made in a separate room or,
at minimum, in an area properly screened from all other activity and other participants.

Referral of Hypertensives

Blood Pressure referral levels will follow the Joint National Statement. The
CARDIA policy statement reflects the following:

a. The average of the second and third resting blood pressure readings, will be
used instead of an average of all blood pressure readings.
b. A systolic reading of less than 140 will be rechecked with 2 years.

e. Asystolic reading or 140-199 will be confirmed at a 2 month interval.

d. A systolic reading above 200 will be evaluated immediately, or referred to a
source of care within 2 weeks.

e. A diastolic reading of 85-89 will be rechecked at a 1 year interval.

f. A diastolic reading of 90-104 will be confirmed within 2 months.

g. A diastolic reading of 105-114 will be evaluated or referred to a source of care
within 2 months.

h. A diastolic reading of 115 and above will be referred immediately to a source

of care.

If these levels are maintained, the participant will be referred to his physician. If
the participant does not have a physician, study personnel will obtain a list of locally
available physicians, Follow-up to check if the participant has contacted a physician will
be carried out within six months. For DBP 115mmHg, same day referral to a physician
will be made, and a phone call follow-up, to confirm participant contacted physician, will
occur within one week.

Training/Certification

Technicians will be trained centrally prior to participant intake in two full day
sessions. New technicians after the start of the study will be trained locally by a
designated "BP supervisor". Recertification will occur every six months (details in
MOO). Prior to certification each technician will be tested for vision (reading) and with
an auditory test (by Korotkoff sound tape).

At the beginning of the first session, a description and demonstration of the correct
BP procedure is given. Trainees are to listen to the 1st (training) tape, taking the test
sequences until they are comfortable with what they are listening to. Then, they take
the 2nd tape until they have passes that test. After passing the second tape, they are
given the 3rd tape test. Alternated with the tapes are actual live practices under the
instruction and observation of the training supervisor. Some live practices may be done
with a standard stethoscope, but most should employ the Y-tube stethoscope. The
optimum size of a group is 8. This allows 4 people to do live practices while 4 are on the
tape training device. The group can interchange and practice on each other.

After the first day of training, each trainee should be given a cuff and manometer
(not stethoscope) to take home and practice just the control of the valve. This can be
done by wrapping the cuff on a jar or bottle and alternately pumping up and dropping the
mercury at a steady rate of 2mm per second. After two or three sessions, they could
also be given a stethoscope to practice on family and/or friends. This out of class

of Z-seores, (depending on experience) but initially 3 will be used to flag possible
systematic deviations in blood pressure measurement by individual technicians. Digit
preference will also be monitored.

BODY SIZE MEASUREMENTS

There are three primary reasons for including body size measurements in
CARDIA. First, they provide a standardized basis for examining the association between
physical size, stature, or ponderosity, and risk for developing coronary heart disease,
hypertension and other diseases of interest (e.g., chronic obstructive lung disease,
diabetes). Second, repeated measurements of body mass over time permit investigation
of whether changes in body size directly contribute favorably or unfavorably to an
individual's risk profile. Further, because the data will be collected using standardized
methods employed in previous investigations, the representative nature of the CARDIA
data set can be determined using existing data from similar age, sex and ethnic groups.

All of the body size measurements to be used have been reported, either
independently or eoliectively, to be correlated with a specifie risk factor or clinical
manifestations of disease. These measures also represent important indicators of growth
and nutritional status. Although numerous additional anthropometric and/or body size
measurements have been identified, the intent of this study is to focus on indices
particularly relevant to the risk of developing coronary heart disease or systemic arterial
hypertension. Measurements must be limited to those that are the most relevant and
that can be performed using standardized methodology within and between survey
centers because of time limitations and other practical constraints of the study.

Specifically, the anthropometric and body measurements included in studies such as
the Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (HANES), Framingham, and the Lipids
Research Clinies Prevalence Survey have served as a model for the measurements
proposed (1,2,3). In addition, the age group involved in CARDIA suggests the need for
monitoring growth and development inherent in the aging process which may be unrelated
to environmental influences such as dietary or exercise patterns.

Rationale for Specific Meausurements
Body Height and Weight

Among all the possible measurements, height and weight are universally accepted
as primary indices of body size. Weight for height standards are available for both men
and women from studies such as the Build and Blood Pressure Study and the recently
updated Metropolitan Life Insurance tables. Based on standards such as these, relative
weight ean be determined. In addition, several ratios of weight/height have been
correlated with selected risk factors. Indices such as body mass index or Quetelet's Index
or Ponderal Index also have been associated with hypertension, hyperlipidemia and
diabetes.

Not only the existence of obesity, but the age of onset of obesity are reportedly
related to susceptibility to hypertension (5). Weight gained early in adult life may be a
sensitive indicator of increased risk for cardiovascular disease. Hyperplastie obesity
experieneed during adulthood may impose different risks than hyperplastic obesity
developed during youth and these risks may vary among different age,sex, and ethnic
groups (7). For these reasons it is important that CARDIA include measures of height
and weight during each successive examination.

However, it is well known that there are numerous limitations to indices of relative
weight (6), Although individuals may be classified as being overweight or underweight
compared to age and sex specific means, the terms obesity and overweight are not
necessarily synonymous. Furthermore, height and weight tables do not refleet the

EX - i

7/87

variations across different ethnic, socioeconomic and/or occupational groups. Thus, in

order to determine not only body weight but also a better index of body composition,
additional measurements are proposed to CARDIA.

Skinfold Meausures

No single measure of obesity or body mass is optimal or uniformly representative
for all ages, races, and sexes, making the use of several indices desirable, if not
necessary (3,8). It is reeommended that the body size index should not be dependent on
height and should have a strong association with independent indices of fatness, e.g.,
skinfold thickness, body density, ete.

Blair, et al (7) recently reported evidence from HANES (1971-1974) that risk for
hypertension increases with centrally located body fat as measured by triceps and
subscapular skinfolds. They reported that subscapular skinfold was a better predictor of
both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in each race-sex group... " sharing all the
association of triceps with blood pressure and having significant predictive power
unshared by triceps " (7). These data support the need to differentiate between central
versus peripheral deposition of body fat.

Despite its reported superiority in predicting hypertension, subscapular skinfold
measures may not be as sensitive in predicting other risk factors relative to coronary
heart disease. Population data for triceps skinfold measure are available for both sexes
and race groups ages 18 to 30 years thus providing a means of comparing the data
collected in CARDIA. The third most commonly measured skinfold site is the suprailiac
erest. Given its location at the hip, it offers a means of comparing upper versus lower
body fatness and may, either separately or in conjunction with the other two skinfold
measures, provide unique information regarding the evolution of CHD or hypertension.

Elbow Breadth

Subcutaneous fat constitutes approximately fifty percent of total body fat in young
adults (1). Therefore, the skinfold measures of height and weight provide indicators of
body size and relative body weight. However, weight varies not only with height but is
also influenced by factors such as body width, bone size and density, muscularity and
length of trunk relative to total height (4). It is thus recommended that an index of
frame size be ineluded in the CARDIA survey. Numerous, often complex and
cumbersome measures of frame size have been used, each having some relationship to
other anthropometric indices. Recent evidence reported from HANES indicated that
elbow breadth provides a useful, reliable estimate of frame size. Mean values of elbow
breadth demonstrated significant age, sex, and ethnic differences in frame size within
the HANES population.

Waist and Hip Girth

Measures of girth or body thickness contribute additional information for
accurately characterizing body size and composition. Here again, numerous sites have
been used in the past but two circumferences, one representing waist girth and the other
hip girth, will be used in CARDIA. These measures are sensitive to recent loss or gain in
weight and appear to be differentially associated with future risk of disease (9). Of
particular interest is the waist to hip girth ratio in relation to the development of high
blood pressure and diabetes (10).

EX - 2

Upper Arm Girth

Upper arm girth is related to blood pressure level independent of body weight or
BMI. The size of the upper arm may be an index of adiposity, influence the pressure
needed to occlude the artery, or influence the amplitude of the Korotkoff sounds.

Sitting Height

Ferris (11) has suggested that sitting height may be helpful in explaining the lower
volumes attained by blacks compared to whites on pulmonary function testing because
the proportion of sitting height to overall height is lower in blacks than in whites. In one
study which demonstrated a 13% difference in FVC and FEV1 between blacks and whites,
the difference in the sitting height/overall height ratio between blacks and whites was
4%, suggesting that the racial difference in lung volumes was partially explained by the
anthropometric difference (12).

Biacromial Diameter and Chest Circumference

The chest circumference/biacromial diameter ratio has been shown to be a
predictor of coronary heart disease in a cohort of U.S. railroad workers (13).

Training/Certification

The training/certification for taking body size measurements consists of the
following components:

1. Central training and certification of at least one technician from each center
before each examination cycle; This individual from each center should be
designated as that center's body size measurement primary technician.

2. If additional personnel are needed by a center to perform body size
measurements during the examination cycle, training can be provided by the
center's clinie supervisor and the certified body size technician. Training
includes the performance of the body size measurements on at least ten people
by the two technicians. Discrepancies in measurements are to be discussed
and any steps necessary to improve the techniques should be taken. The new
technician and certified technician must complete body size measurements on
five new participants and submit the recording forms to the Coordinating
Center in order for the new technician to become certified.

3. Direct observation by the supervisor of the examination procedures on a
monthly basis, with correction of errors when necessary.
Quality Control

The quality control procedures for anthropometry consist of the following
components:

1. A daily instrument check is to be performed on the Harpinden skinfold calipers
using a standard lucite step wedge with widths in increments of 10 mm. A

weekly cheek is to be performed of the body weight seale using standard

During each exam cycle, each anthropometry technician will be required to

Four times a month (approximately once per week) each technician will
