CARDIA PHYSICAL ACTIVITY QUESTIONNAIRE

Rationale

The presumption is strong based on epidemiologic evidence that physical inactivity
is a risk factor for coronary heart disease. It is certain that it is relevant to weight
eontrol, and in turn is therefore related to the genesis of obesity, hypertension and
hyperlipidemia. Through its relationship to HDL cholesterol, physical activity level may
be related in general to the lipid profile.

Physical activity is a behavior, consisting of many different components. It is
important for CARDIA to measure which activities are prevalent, and how this activity
spectrum changes as the CARDIA population ages. Further it is important to reliably
rank people for overall level of all and of intense physical activity.

The existing questionnaire which might be best suited for use in CARDIA were the
Minnesota Leisure Time Physical Activity Questionnaire and the Seven Day Physical
Activity Recall. The former, which spans 12 months, has been valided against
physiologic endpoints, but has not been shown to be adequately reliable on reapplication,
and takes too long to administer. The latter spans only seven days, has considerable
accuracy, has passed some validity studies and is suitably brief. It is included in the
CARDIA protocol. However, it too suffers from low repeatability since one week's
physical activity is often not representative of general patterns.

In devising a briefer new questionnaire, it was theorized that people could
accurately recall or summarize for themselves what and how much activity they do
within broad categories. Therefore details were avoided as being both poorly repeatable
and irrelevant.

Using an extensive database from the Minnesota Heart Health Program, tabulations
were made of activity participation for men and women aged 25-29. Based on these
tabulations questions were worded for sets of activities which might be logically classed
together. For each, the number of months of minimal performance, at least one hour
total in the month, was queried. Finally the number of months in which the activity was
performed frequently, i.e. at least an activity-specifie number of hours/week, was
queried.

PHLEBOTOMY

Rationale for Measurement of Lipids, Lipoproteins and Apolipoproteins

CARDIA is a study in young adults of the evolution of risk factors for coronary
heart disease. Each of the major established risk factors, including elevated blood
cholesterol, are of paramount interest in CARDIA. Evolution of risk is studied by
following the course of blood cholesterol levels and the levels of related lipoproteins and
apoproteins through young adulthood, and by examining the relationships of these blood
levels to other biologic and behavioral aspects of life. Each of the blood lipid levels and
the levels of related lipoproteins and apolipoproteins are therefore primary outcome
variables in CARDIA.

Many volumes of reports have been published dealing with blood cholesterol and its
influence in the artherosclerotiec process. An exhaustive intrepretative review of this
body of literature was published in 1981 by the Working Group on Arterioselerosis of the
National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (1,2), The importance in the atherosclerotic
process of blood lipids, lipoproteins and apoliproteins is established in the following
quotation from Volume 1, pp. 16 and 17.

"The average concentration of cholesterol in the blood plasma of middie-aged
American men is presently on the order of 210-220 mg of cholesterol per 100 ml. The
risk of premature coronary heart disease and its consequences, especially acute heart
attacks, increases rapidly as the level of cholesterol in blood exceeds 220 mg/dl in men
between 40 and 49 years of age with a cholesterol level of 240 mg/dl or above are more
than twice as likely to develop premature coronary heart disease as are men of the same
age whose blood cholesterol levels are less 220 mg/dl. Men in the same age group with
levels of 270 mg/di and higher have almost three times the risk of a premature heart
attack than those with levels less than 220. The relationship is similar for women.

Cholesterol and other fats are transported in the bloodstream in a soluble form as
components of lipoproteins. Hypercholesterolemia may reflect a disorder in the proteins
transporting the fat (apolipoproteins) and/or in the metabolism of fat per se. The
coneentration of other blood fats may also be inordinately high from a disorder of
lipoprotein metabolism. For clinical purposes, severe hyperlipoproteinemias have been
categorized using biochemical and genetie techniques. Distinctions have been made
between the common hyperlipoproteinemias in the population and the rare genetic
types. Hyperlipoproteinemias may also result from endocrine disturbances and most
commonly from dietary excesses. These types of hyperlipoproteinemia are all strongly
related to the risk of premature atherosclerosis.

One of the several lipoproteins that transport cholesterol - high density
lipoproteins - may confer some protection against athersclerosis; an inverse relationship
has been identified between the concentration of HDL cholesterol in the blood and
coronary heart disease. Thus, individuals with high levels of HDL tend to have a lower
risk of coronary heart disease compared to those with low HDL levels. In contrast, the
higher the LDL level, the higher the incidence of coronary heart disease. These
observations have led to a re-examination of the interactions of the two lipoproteins with
eells of the arterial wall. Although the reasons for the different effects of the different
cholesterol-carrying lipoproteins are not yet clear, the information provides new ways of
identifying persons at high risk and new prospects for preventing, and even reversing,
atherosclerosis."

FB?

CARDIA will measure plasma levels of total cholesterol, high, low and very low
density cholesterols (HDL, LDL, and VLDL), HDL-2 and HDL-3 cholesterols, and levels of
apolipoproteins A-1 and B.

The methodology for lipid and lipoprotein measurement which has been selected
was developed and used by the Lipid Research Clinics (3), except that the more modern
enzymic methods will be used instead of the Autoanalyzer methods. Use of this
methodology has the advantage of maximizing comparibility with the findings of this
very large study (4-8). The methodology gives a direct measurement of total and HDL
plasma cholesterol (the latter by anaylsis after precipitation with dextran
sulfate/magnesium chloride (9) and plasma triglycerides. It estimates VLDL cholesterol
as 1/5 of the triglycerides value, and LDL cholesterol as total cholesterol less HDL
cholesterol less VLDL cholesterol.

Blood lipoprotein cholesterol is far more complicated than the classification as
HDL, VLDL and LDL allows. Standard methodology does not exist for measurement of
the many subclasses which may be defined within each of the lipoprotein classes. There
exists some evidence that the protection against atherosclerosis afforded by higher HDL
cholesterol levels is actually carried in a subclass called HDL-2 while the remainder of
HDL, calied HDL-3 is less closely associated with risk. A standard methodology for the
determination of HDL-2 and HDL-3 (a second precipitation with dextran
sulfate/magnesium choloride (10)) will be used in CARDIA.

Cholesterol is carried in the blood in combination with proteins; these proteins are
called apolipoproteins. Evidence for the relationship of apoproteins to the prevalence of
atherosclerotic disease is strongest for Apo A-1 and for Apo B, among many
apoproteins. Apo A-1 is closely (see above) associated with HDL-2 and Apo B is closely
associated with LDL cholesterol. Although these associations are strong, as quoted
above, it is not known whether hypercholesterolemia is primarily a disorder of the
proteins which transport the fat, the fat itself, or both. It is possible that changes in the
lipid moiety will not be reflected in corresponding changes in the protein moiety. For
these reasons it is felt to be important to monitor these two apoproteins for which the
evidence is strongest for a relationship to the atherosclerotic process (11-13). These
apoproteins will be measured by the enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay (ELISA).

Ideally, this same battery of lipids, lipoproteins and apoproteins will be measured at
each CARDIA examination.

Rationale for Stored Blood

No study ean predict discoveries which will be made some years hence. The great
majority of blood constituents remain stable when blood is stored deep-frozen, i.e., -70
C. It may be desirable to measure blood constituents on frozen samples to investigate
discoveries yet to be made. In the second examination, CARDIA will store five vials of
frozen serum and up to two vials of frozen plasma for such future needs.

Method of Measurement
The blood drawing station is designed to obtain an adequate blood sample to test

for several important risk factors for cardiovascular disease. It is a potentially difficult
station for several reasons:

TOENAILS

The role of trace elements in human nutrition, health, and disease has been the
subject of increased research and speculation. In particular, attention has recently been
paid to the role of selenium in carcinogenesis and the pathogenesis of cardiovascular
disease. The sampling of human beings for trace element content can be a complex and
expensive task. The use of nails, however, would simplify this process. A body of
literature exists which suggests that the trace element content in nails and hair reflects
body intake.

Rationale

The role of selenium in relation to carcinogenesis and the pathogenesis of
cardiovascular disease has been of particular interest to researchers. Epidemiologic
evidence supports this association, although it is not consistent. Eeologie studies (5)
suggest a lower cardiovascular mortality in higher selenium areas compared to lower
selenium areas. In longitudinal case-control studies, a low serum concentration, i.e. less
than 45 ug/1, has been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (6-7)
and stroke (7), but in another longitudinal case-control study (8), no relationship was
observed.

Shamberger and Frost (10) were among the first to report that an inverse
relationship existed between selenium status and cancer death rates. Findings of several
selenium related case-control studies (5, 15-23) are conflicting, yet they do provide some
indication of an association between an increased risk of gastrointestinal, urinary,
mammary, and skin cancer with low selenium concentration in the body.

Accurate assessment of selenium status is crucial in studying the relationship
between selenium status and disease. Dietary selenium content has to be measured by
chemical analysis since food content varies from area to area, reflecting varying soil
levels. This poses problems for large-scale data collection needed in longitudinal cohort
studies. Biochemical assessment of tissue level of selenium should be the alternative.

Most body tissues are in a state of flux, however, nails are an exception. After the
nail is formed it is expelled from the nail bed to become isolated from the body's
continuing metabolic activities. One mm of toenail sample corresponds to more than one
month of body nutriture condition. Toenails are relatively sheltered from environmental
contaminants. They are also free from contaminants introduced through shampooing,
hair treatments, and medication.

Advances in nondestructive methods of multiple element analyses add to the
advantage of use of toenail. Other trace minerals which have been implicated as having
relevance in ischemic heart disease and cancer, include cadmium, chromium, zine,
copper, iron, ete. For example, increased cadmium levels in kidney tissue have been
associated with hypertension (38). Lower chromium levels have been observed in tissues
from patients with antherosclerosis. Chromium is also related to a glucose-tolerance
factor in insulin-stimulated oxidation of glucose (39), The availability of neutron
activation analysis provides opportunity to test these hypotheses or generate others
without additional cost.

Method of Measurement
Collection and Storage of Toenails (37,40)

Participants should be informed at the time of scheduling appointments not to trim
their toenails until they come in to the clinic. Nails are collected by clipping with a
stainless steel clipper from each of the ten toes. Instruction should be given to the
participants to obtain as much toenail as possible. The toenail elippings from the great
toes and the rest of the toes are stored separately in two 1.5" x 3" envelopes, since the
time frame represented by the great toe is different from the rest of the toenails. These
nail samples should be labelled properly and stored in the driest condition possible.

Sample Cleaning (37, 40)

Prior to the instrumental analyses, the nail samples should be cleaned with a quartz
knife by scraping off any attached gross debris on both the edge and the surface and then
rinsed with demineralized water. After air drying, the samples are placed in low trace
element plastic containers, coded and then shipped for analyses.

Sample Analyses

Our plans now are to store the toenail samples until funding for analysis is obtained
in future years. Two types of analytic methods exist: destructive and non-destructive
methods. Atomic absorption spectrometry (41) and flurometric methods (42-43) are the
most popular destructive methods. Neutron activation analysis has been used widely for
nondestructive analyses of multiple elements and selenium analysis per se. Activation
analysis has been acknowledged as a powerful method for determination of trace
elements in microgram and even nanogram concentrations (44). Typical features of
activation analysis are high sensitivity, good reproducibility, nondestructive analyses,
multi-element determination, little influence of foreign substances on analysis results,
and comparatively simple interpretation of initial data even for complex mixtures of
elements. Its nondestructive nature is desirable for a longitudinal study, so that further
measurements on other elements can be made if desired. The research reactor facility
at the University of Missouri at Columbia has been doing selenium analyses for research
purposes. The expense has ranged from 45 to 85 dollars, depending on the number of
specimens being studied,

MEDICAL HISTORY

Rationale

It is important to ascertain illnesses and medications as these may affect risk
factor levels and life style. For example, thyroid disease, oral contraceptives, and
thiazide diureties are known to affect lipid levels and should be considered when
determinants of lipid levels are assessed. Although, in the targeted age group, most
medical conditions will be infrequent, the study results will lose considerable eredibility
among the medical community if some effort to ascertain basic health status and
illnesses is not undertaken.

Consideration was given to asking for interim changes (e.g., "In the past two
years..." or "Since your last CARDIA examination, has a doctor or nurse said that you
had...?"), or asking for a lifetime history like that in Exam I (e.g., "Has a doctor or nurse
ever said that you had...?"), The main advantages of the interval history are that it
should decrease the chance of obtaining conflicting information (e.g., at Exam I subject
says he or she did have a certain condition ever, and at Exam II subject denies ever
having had that condition) and that it should lessen the chance that subjects would be
annoyed about answering some of the same questions at both exams. The advantages of
repeating the lifetime history or "ever" questions are, briefly, that (a) the redundancy
will help verify that a condition had truly been present, (b) the opportunity will be
available to study exam-to-exam reliablity of responses, (ec) considerable effort and
expense will be solved saved in revising questionnaires, (d) subjects may not clearly
remember whether a condition was first diagnosed before and reported at Exam I and
therefore give incorrect interim information or because of the nuances of questioning
temporal gaps may occur causing events to be missed. The advantages of the repeat
lifetime history outweighed the advantages of the interim history.

Smoking, particularly of cigarettes, constitutes a major established coronary risk
factor. This will be a key dependent variable in CARDIA and changes in smoking habits
will be observed in many participants as the study progresses. Therefore, it is important
to measure tobacco consumption with care and in some detail.

Alcohol consumption is another important life style component that may vary
considerably among participants and from exam to exam. It is known to positively effect
blood pressure and HDL cholesterol, and has been negatively associated with the
development of coronary heart disease in some studies. Information about intake of
different beverages, since they may have different effects, is being collected. These
questions also cover "binge" drinking and past alcohol drinking which are not covered in
the nutrition interview.

Nonmedical drugs are used by many young people. Information about this
important aspect of life style of the young will be collected. Assurance of
confidentiality will be important.

The tracking of major health events in the follow-up of the CARDIA subjects will
oceur. Whether or not the subjects report any "Other Major Health Problem", the
interviewer will ask for these events in the Interim Hospitalizations, Serious Illnesses and
Injury questionnaire. This questionnaire will ask for signed permission to obtain hospital
and medical records and contains four questions of those proposed by Polen and Friedman
to obtain additional information on injuries.

Injuries are the leading cause of death in the U.S. for people between the ages of 1
and 44 and the leading cause of pre-retirement years of life lost. Thus, information
about the injury experience of the CARDIA subjects and about factors that are thought
to increase risks for the most common types of injuries in the 18 to 30 year old
population will be obtained. Both unintentional injuries, such as those resulting from
motor vehicle crashes and falls, and intentional injuries, such as those resulting from
assaults and suicide attempts will be included.

In general, the method of administration will first be self-administered
questionnaires to screen most aspects with positive answers, followed up by interviewer
administered questions to obtain some specific details.

Questionnaires

The following questionnaires are included in this portion of the study:
1. Medical Data (including hospitalizations, weight, time of last food and
cigarette, and perceived health status)
2. Medication Use
3. Tobacco Use
4. Alcohol Use
5. Hospitalization
6. Injury
7. Pulmonary disease questions (to be administered with the pulmonary function
test)
8. Nonmedical drug use (to be self-administered with some psychosocial
questionnaires)
9. Coding instructions for medicinal drugs and cigarette brands

Training/Certification

General instructions will be provided at the major training session to be held before
each exam cycle. As part of this training, each trainee will be expected to administer
the questionnaire (if interviewer-administered) to a test participant, under supervision.
Errors in technique or interpretation will be sought and corrected. For this non-technical
segment of the exam, no special certification seems needed.

Quality Control

In addition to the inspection of forms and data to be routinely carried out at each
center and at the Coordinating Center, supervisory personnel at each center should
occasionally observe each interviewer at work to maintain high-quality performance.

Flow of Participants

If interviewer-administered, the questionnaire should be completed with the
participant seated comfortably in a quiet room. The responses are confidential and
should not be heard by anyone but the interviewer and an occasional supervisory
observer.

CARDIA QUALITY CONTROL PROCEDURES

INTRODUCTION

The CARDIA Coordinating Center will carry out quality control measures during
the course of the study. There are two primary purposes for quality control. One is for
assessing errors and historically documenting the level of quality. Second, and more
importantly, is the feedback mechanism which will provide for maintaining and improving
the quality of the study data.

Quality control involves the collection of certain types of data and the subsequent
analysis of that data. It is primarily a measure of the quality of data that is 1) being
collected by the clinical center, and 2) measured by central laboratories and centers
associated with the CARDIA study.

Quality control is accomplished in many different ways depending upon the type of
data being collected, the type of procedure being analyzed, and the associated outcome
variable in question. The types of quality contro! measures that will be used in the
CARDIA study include:

1) Monitoring reports - primarily a tool used to monitor errors in forms; also used

to document recruitment procedures.

2) Calibration of instruments - used in any section which employs a measurement
instrument, e.g. calipers, scales, sphygmomanometer.

3) Log sheets - forwarded to the coordinating center noting periodic calibration
procedures and monitoring activities such as room, refrigerator, and freezer
temperatures.

4) External surveillance ~ used when data is reported from outside the CARDIA
community, i.e. central laboratories.

A manual has been developed which outlines the particular steps that will be taken

for each of the sections of the CARDIA visit in order to assure that quality data is being

eollected and reported.

The RESPONSIBILITIES of the Coordinating Center in developing and carrying out
quality control measures are listed below:
1) Identifying and notifying clinical centers of the quality of performance of
interviewers, technicians, and other responsible personnel in upholding proper
certification standards.
2) As a back-up in identifying calibration problems and/or performing the
corrective action by notifying the clinical center and/or correcting or flagging
the data.
3) Identifying problems as they occur within the external reporting centers and
communicating this information to them for corrective action.
4) Obtaining historical data on all accounts which describes the quality and
performance of the entire CARDIA study.
5) Reporting selected information to the appropriate groups and the CARDIA
Steering Committee.
6) Design protocol and procedures for periodic site visits which check for quality
of performance and adherence to CARDIA standardized procedures within the
clinical center.
7) Develop logistics within the Coordinating Center for handling, filing, and
promptly analyzing incoming data and forms which have been created for use
in quality control.
8) Develop protocol for alerting clinical centers when periodic quality and
performance reports are past due.
9) Keep an up-to-date file of all completed personnel certification and
recertification forms.

BLOOD PRESSURE REACTIVITY

Rationale

This section reviews the relationship between blood pressure reactivity and the
incidence of CHD as well as other psychosocial risk factors including hypertension,
hostility, and Type A behavior. The general hypothesis is that blood pressure reactivity
in conjunetion with Type A behavior and hostility will predict rises in resting blood
pressure at the subsequent exams, and if the followup continues for a sufficient period
will predict the incidence of CHD.

CHD Incidence

Unfortunately only one prospective study of CHD has been conducted with blood
pressure reactivity. In this study, blood pressure reactivity predicted CHD incidence
more strongly than any other risk factors among 247 Minnesota businessmen who were
followed for 20 years (1). Individuals who had a rise of 20 mmHg or more in diastolic
blood pressure to the cold pressor test were 2.4 (RR) times more likely to have an MI
than individuals who had a reactivity of less than 20 mmHg. Resting diastolic blood
pressure was not predictive of MI's.

Hypertension

Psychophysiological theories of hypertensive etiology are founded on the
assumption that, compared to normotensives, hypertensives manifest heightened
cardiovascular reactions to psychological stressors (2-4). Research in this area by and
large supports this assumption, but there are inconsistencies. The classic studies by Brod
(5) showed no significant differences between hypertensives and normotensive controls in
mean arterial pressure to mental arithmetic and cold pressor. More recently, no marked
differences between hypertensives and normotensives have been observed in other
challenging tasks (6-9). There are several methodological explanations for these
inconsistencies including sampling problems and confounding drug therapy; however,
more important is the possibility that renal and vascular processes are more important in
established hypertension than autonomic activity.

The empirical evidence suggests that autonomic reactivity is more important as a
predictor of subsequent hypertension in individuals in the borderline or transient phase of
developing hypertension. Nestel (10) showed greater systolic and diastolic BP reactions
to a visual puzzle test from mild ("labile") hypertensives than controls, and Jern (11)
recorded greater diastolic BP reactions to mental arithmetic from young men identified
as borderline hypertensives during screening for military service.

Previous research also indicates that the nature of the task is also important for
eliciting predictive BP reactivity. It has been argued that BP responses to tasks
involving active, effortful coping are the most valid predictors of subsequent
hypertension (12-13). One of the best controlled studies of the hypothesis that
individuals with transient high blood pressure are autonomically more responsive than
individuals with stable, normal BP levels is provided in a recent study by Steptoe et al.
(14) who carefully chose three age-matched samples: mild and transient hypertensives
and normotensives. These three groups were exposed to both passive and active coping

BPR- i

7/37

tasks while autonomic measures were recorded. The results indicated that mild
hypertensives showed significantly greater pressor reactions than normotensives to tasks
requiring active behavioral coping, but not to the passive condition. The transient
hypertension group produced heightened reactions in diastolic but not systolic pressure.
Greater heart rate and pulse transit time reactions were also observed in the transient
group, suggesting that exaggerated cardiac responsiveness to active challenges may be
characteristic of the pre-hypertensive profile. Interestingly, exaggerated pressor
responses were also associated with high scores on the Hostility and Direction of
Hostility questionnaire.

Type A Behavior

The relationship between Type A behavior and blood pressure reactivity has been
researched intensively in the last ten years. Of 25 studies (not listed in references)
assessing whether Type A behavior is linked to blood pressure reactivity, 13 have found
Type A's to have a higher blood pressure reactivity than Type B's. The reasons for the
inconsistency have been attributed to differences in Type A measures and differences in
task demands.

Hostility

Clinicians have long made a connection between hypertension and suppressed
anger. The link with suppressed anger has been supported in experimental studies by
Hokanson (15) where subjects were angered by insult and allowed to retaliate or not
retaliate against the instigator. Individuals who were not given a chance to retaliate
maintained a higher blood pressure than individuals allowed to retaliate. More recently,
researchers have studied hostility in the context of the structured interview to assess
Type A behavior. Dembroski et al. (16) assessed the potential for hostility from the
Structured Interview. When confronted with three cognitive-perceptual tasks, male
college students with greater potential for hostility also had greater blood pressure and
heart rate reactivity than for any other component of Type A behavior. In a second
study, also with male students, Dembroski et al. (17) found that hostility correlated with
large blood pressure rises to both a high and low degree of challenge, whereas the Type
A's who were less hostile responded with large elevations only in the high challenge
condition. In support of these findings a subsequent study (18) linked hostility and blood
pressure reactivity in female students.

Research Questions Addressed by BP Reactivity Assessment

1. Does blood pressure reactivity predict the rise in chronic blood pressure level?
Specifically, will the young individuals in the CARDIA project who have higher blood
pressure reactivity also have a higher increase in resting blood pressure than individuals
who have lower blood pressure reactivity?

2. Does blood pressure reactivity provide a key indicator of the degree that other
psychosocial risk factors are risk inducing? This is based on the concern that no one risk
factor provides the total picture of CHD risk, and that a combination provides a more
complete and subtle picture of developing risk factors.

Methods of Measurement
Physiological Recording Apparatus
Subjects will have a total of four different physiological measures monitored during
the entire course of the reactivity protocol, including: heart rate, systolic and diastolic
blood pressure and mean arterial pressure. These measures will be monitored with the
use of a Vita-Stat automated blood pressure monitor. The Vita-Stat will be set to manual
mode so that it will inflate the cuff and determine mean heart rate, systolic and diastolic
blood pressure, and mean arterial pressure when activated by the research assistant.
During the cold pressor task, a standard mercury sphygmomanameter and stethescope
will be used to record systolic and diastolic pressure.
Tasks
A total of three tasks will be presented to subjects, including: the video-game
breakout, star-tracing, and cold pressor. The first two tasks will be presented in a
randomized order, with the cold pressor task always being the last task given. All of the
tasks will be accompanied by standardized taped instructions.
Breakout
The Atari Breakout video-game will be presented to subjects over a color monitor
which is situated directly in front of them. The paddler controller will be affixed to a
wood board.
Star-tracing
The star-tracing task involves subjects tracing the outline of a star from an image
displayed in a mirror while staying within narrow limits. If subjects move out of the
limits of the star, an error is scored.
Cold pressor
The cold pressor task is one in which subjects are asked to immerse their dominant
hand in a circulating ice-bath. A submersible pump will be used to circulate the water in
an ice-chest from one side of a mesh partition filled with ice to the other side of the
partition which is filled only with water. A submersible thermometer will be used to
ensure that the water is maintained at less than 1.5 degrees Centigrade.
Training/Certification
The training for blood pressure reactivity will take place in a one day session
following training in blood pressure measurement. Use and calibration of the Vita-Stat
will be covered as well as an explanation of the tasks to be completed by the participant
in this component of the exam. Opportunity to practice the tasks will be provided.
The certification procedures for the reactivity testing involve several stages.
These procedures are to be met by one reactivity trainee per center; once certified, this

NUTRITION

A role for diet in the development of cornary heart disease (CHD) is supported by
findings that dietary factors may influence risk factors for this disease. The CHD risk
faetors shown to be most affected by patterns of nutrient intake are serum cholestero}
and blood pressure.

Serum Cholesterol

Hypercholesterolemia is one of the three major established risk factors for CHD.
Many studies have indicated a strong relationship between dietary factors, especially
dietary lipid intake, and serum cholesterol and heart disease. These studies can be
classified in to four different categories: inter-population comparison studies, metabolic
ward studies, studies on free-living individuals, and dietary trials.

Inter-population Comparisons

Many investigators have examined the relationships among dietary factors and CHD
mortality utilizing data published by the United Nations Food and Agriculture
Organization (FAO), and the World Health Organization (WHO) (1-8). All of the studies
have consistently shown statistically significant univariate associations between dietary
constituents and mortality from CHD. These encompassed significant positive
associations between dietary saturated fat, cholesterol, animal fat, total fat, total
protein, animal protein, animal foodstuffs, refined and processed sugars, total calories
and CHD mortality rates in middle age. Significant negative correlations were observed
for vegetable protein, vegetable foodstuffs, vegetable fat and CHD mortality rates.
Intakes of these dietary factors are also related to one another, i.e., high intake of
animal fat is correlated with low intake of vegetable fat, as a reflection of the
economics of these countries. Therefore some of the relationships may be spurious. A
recent study analyzed these data using bivariate techniques (9). The results indicated
that the significant relationship between dietary lipid and CHD persisted with control for
vegetable products or refined sugars. The latter two, on the other hand, did not relate
significantly to CHD mortality when dietary lipid was controlled.

Similar comparison among living population cohorts demonstrated similar positive
associations among dietary lipid, serum cholesterol and CHD rates (10-15). For example,
the Seven Countries Study examined the 5- and 10-year incidence rates of CHD for 16
population in seven countries -- Finland, Greece, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, the
United States, and Yugoslavia (10-12). Baseline saturated fat intakes and CHD rates for
these populations samples were highly and significantiy correlated, as were saturated fat
intake and serum cholesterol, and serum cholesterol and CHD rates. The Ni-Hon San
Study compared men in Japan, Japanese-American men in Hawaii, and Japenese men in
San Francisco (13-15). Nutrient analyses indicated that the group mean intakes of total
fat, saturated fat, and animal protein were much lower in the Japanese than in the
Japanese-American men. The mean serum cholesterol level of Japanese men was 37
mg/dl lower than that of the Hawaiian men and 47 mg/dl lower than that of the
California men.

2/87

The data from the international autopsy studies, epitomized by the International
Atherosclerosis Project, also showed a relationship across populations between dietary
fat and sevee coronary atherosclerosis, and, in addition, between dietary fat and serum
cholesterol and between serum cholesterol and severe coronary atherosclerosis (16).

Within the U.S. population, comparisons of various ethnic or religious groups
yielded similar findings. For example, the comparison of vegetarians and non-
vegetarians in a Seventh-Day Adventist group, and the comparison of Boston vegetarian
commune residents with Framingham men showed that dietary fat composition and serum
cholesterol were strongly associated (17-18).

in summary, analyses of FAO-WHO data and comparisons of international living
populations, in in international autopsy studies, migrants, ethnic and religious groups
within-countries have all yielded similar findings, i.e., dietary lipid composition and
cholesterol intakes are strongly associated with serum cholesterol and CHD incidence
and mortality rates.

Metabolic Ward Studies

In a series of metabolie studies, Keys et al. showed that the mean change in serum
cholesterol in men can be expressed as a linear function of mean changes in saturated
fat, polyunsaturated fat and dietary cholesterol intakes (19). Similar findings were also
obtained by Hegsted et al. (20). Connor et al. studied the effects of dietary cholesterol
on serum lipids and showed that mean serum cholesterol levels of a group of men changed
as dietary cholesterol intake changed (21-23). Their findings were confirmed by Mattson
et al. (24). Moreover, Erickson and Mattson showed that serum cholesterol level changed
as the ratio of polyunsaturated to saturated fatty acids changed (25). In summary,
results from metabolic ward studies have indicated that dietary cholesterol, saturated
fat and polyunsaturated fat intakes have a strong impact upon serum cholesterol level.

Cross-Sectional Studies

Results of the cross-sectional studies on the relationship between dietary lipid
intake of individuals within a population and serum cholesterol are inconsistent (26-31).
Several studies, e.g., the Framingham and Tecumseh Community Studies, and the Israeli
Civil Servant Study reported no association, or a low-order non-significant association,
between the dietary lipid intake in individuals and their serum cholesterol level (26-28).
On the other hand, the Tarahumara Indian Study found a highly significant relationship,
with a very high correlation coefficient (r=.9), between dietary cholesterol and the
plasma cholesterol (29). The Western Electric Study reported a highly significant
association between dietary lipid intake and serum cholesterol at baseline (30). In the
Western Electric Study, dietary lipid intake was measured by the lipid scores derived by
Keys and Hegsted in their metabolic ward studies (19-20). These scores measure the
combined impact of the saturated fat, polyunsaturated fat and dietary cholesterol intake
on serum cholesterol. For both univariate and multivariate analyses, the lipid scores
were highly correlated with serum cholesterol level. In addition, the changes in these
lipid scores between baseline and the first year were highly significantly related to the
corresponding changes in serum cholesterol level. Similar findings were also obtained
between saturated fat, dietary cholesterol and serum cholesterol.

7/87

Several reasons may explain the inconsistent results of these studies. First, within
a homogeneous population, the intra-individual variation of dietary factor is as large as
or larger than, the inter-individual variation (32). Therefore, a single measurement—
e.g., the 24 hour recall used in the Tecumseh Study—is inadequate for validly
characterizing individuals within a population. On the other hand, the Tarahumara
Indians eat almost identically data after data. There is little intra-individual variation in
dietary cholesterol intake and thus a strong association between dietary and serum
cholesterol can be observed. Second, a large proportion of people with high serum
cholesterol levels will change their diet after being informed of their cholesterol level.
Consequently, if the dietary data are collected after the serum cholesterol data, the
relationship could be attenuated (31). Third, the intrinsic factors (under gentic influence)
of serum cholesterol may dilute a true relationship between a dietary factor and serum
cholesterol in a cross-sectional study (33). The analysis of change over time eliminates,
or at least markedly reduces, the interfering effect of genetically controlled inter-
individual differences in endogenous biochemical regulation.

The Western Electric Study did not limit itself to either a short dietary history of
what the men usually ate or to a 24-hour recall. Rather, for both the baseline and the
first year, the recent habitual diet of the participants was characterized in depth by the
modified Burke method, requiring about an hour per person. The positive findings
between dietary lipid intake and serum cholesterol and between the changes in both
variables merit emphasis.

With respect to the relationship between dietary lipid and the CHD mortality or
incidence, the results are fairly consistent. The Western Electric Study found that the
baseline lipid scores (both Keys and Hegsted) and dietary cholesterol intake (analyzed
separately) were significantly associated with the 20 year mortality from CHD (30).
These associations were independent of the three major risk factors, i.e., high blood
pressure, high serum cholesterol and cigarette smoking at baseline. Gordon et al.
analyzed the 6 year follow-up data from the Framingham Study, the Honolulu Heart
Study and Puerto Rico Heart Health Program (34). Men who developed MI or died of
CHD, consumed a significantly higher percentage of calories from total fat (in some
cases, saturated fat) and less starch than the men without CHD. In this study, the CHD
group also consumed less calories and alcohol than average. More recently, McGee et al.
found that the baseline percentage of calories from protein, fat, saturated fat and
dietary cholesterol (per 100 calories) were significantly related to the 10 year incidence
of MI or CHD death in the multivariate analysis of the Honolulu Heart Study (35).
Several other variables—calories, carbohydrates and aleohol—were inversely related to
MI or the CHD death. Similar findings were also reported by Kromhout and Coulander on
the 10 year mortality follow-up the of the Zutphen Study (36). Moreover, Cahn et al.
reported in the 21 year follow-up of adult Seventh-Day Adventists that intake of eggs
and meat were significantly positively related to, and intake of green salad was
negatively related to, the subsequent mortality from all causes (37).

In summary, the findings on the relationship between dietary lipid intake and serum
cholesterol for free-living individuals within a population are inconsistent. However, the
inconsistency ean be explained at least in part by the methodological problems in dietary
assessment and the genetic factors related to serum cholesterol. The experiences of the
Western Electric Study deserve some attention, and the positive findings need to be
confirmed.

7/B?

The results on the relationship between the baseline dietary intake of fat, saturated
fat and cholesterol, and the subsequent incidence or mortality from CHD obtained in
these prosepective studies, further support the importance of diet in relation to CHD.

Dietary Trials

Most of the dietary trials were not designed to test only the effect of dietary
change on serum cholesterol level. Usually dietary modification is a part of a
multifactor intervention program to reduce CHD. However, the National Diet Heart
Study, the Oslo Diet Heart Study, the Coronary Prevention Evaluation Program, the New
York Anti-Coronary Club Study, the Los Angels Veterans Administration Domeiliary
Facility Study, and the Lipid Research Clinic Coronary Primary Prevention Trial have all
shown that group mean serum cholesterol of free living people can be reduced
significantly by changing from a diet high in saturated fat and cholesterol to a diet low in
saturated fat and cholesterol, with or without high polyunsaturates (38-43). Results from
these studies suggest that it is feasible to change diet for a large group of people and
that the average serum cholesterol can be lowered by reducing the total fat intake and
by changing the fat composition in the diet.

Summary

The studies reviewed in this section are a few representative examples of a large
amount of literature on the relationship between diet and serum cholesterol level] and/or
CHD. It does not include studies on the relationship between dietary intake and
lipoproteins, e.g., aleohol intake increases high density lipoprotein (44). However, based
on these study results, it can logically be concluded that diet plays a very important role
in the determination of serum cholesterol and in the development of atherosclerosis and
CHD. The CARDIA study intends to identify the lifestyle or the change in lifestyle that
causes the change in the major risk factors, in young adults e.g., serum cholesterol and
blood pressure. It is therefore imperative to measure the dietary intake of these young
adults over time. In order to characterize accurately the dietary intake for individuals,
it is necessary to select an appropriate dietary assessment method.

Diet and Blood Pressure

The influence of diet on blood pressure is a complex one involving both adverse and
favorable responses to intakes of individual nutrients as well as to the interactions of one
or more of these nutrients. Nutrients shown to adversely affect blood pressure are
sodium, total calories, sucrose, alcohol and type and amount of protein: Those favorably
influencing blood pressure are potassium, calcium, magnesium, polyunsaturated fat and
fiber.

Sodium

A substantial amount of data supports an effect of dietary sodium on blood
pressure. Epidemiologic studies have shown that among populations consuming habitual
diets high in sodium, the prevalence of hypertension is high, in contrast to populations
consuming habitual diets low in sodium, where hypertension is rare and the tendency of
blood pressure to increase with age is not observed (1-6). Clinical investigations have
also shown that blood pressure may be successfully reduced in hypertensive individuals by
lowering dietary sodium intake (7-11). Studies in animals have revealed that the age at
which exposure to high sodium intake begins and the duration of this exposure may be
important factors in determining the level of blood pressure and the severity of
hypertension which develops (12-13). Intrapopulation studies of the relationship of
dietary sodium to blood pressure have yielded conflicting results (14-15). Methodological
problems with assessment of sodium intake as well as individual differences in sensitivity
to sodium and other environmental influences may have contributed to the inconsistency
in the findings from these studies (16-17).

Calories

Total ealorie intake may influence blood pressure through weight (18-22), the
amount of sodium consumed (23) and effects on sympathetic nervous system activity
(24). These factors may be interrelated in their effects on blod pressure as weight and
sodium also influence sympathetic activity (25-27). However, findings in animals suggest
a direct effect of caloric intake on sympathetic activity independent of weight or sodium
intake (28).

Sucrose

The relationship between sucrose intake and blood pressure is not well defined.
Acute pressor effects of high sucrose intakes have been demonstrated in normotensive
humans without any changes in body weight (29-30). There are no data examining long-
term effects of sucrose on blood pressure in humans, but studies in normotensive animal
models have shown increased blood pressures with sucrose supplementation over a period
of 2-3 months at constant carbohydrate intake (31-32) independent of weight (32). High
sucrose intakes also augmented the hypertensinogenie effect of high sodium intake in
monkeys (33).

Protein

Although the total amount of protein in the diet may influence blood pressure
through effects on renal funetion (34), the type of protein may be a more important
determinant of blood pressure response. Much of the evidence for this has been derived
from studies showing lower blood pressures among vegetarians compared with
omnivores. A significant decrease in diastolic pressure was noted when ominivores
consumed a vegetarian diet for six weeks, with blood pressures returning to baseline
levels when normal dietary intake was resumed (37). Although blood pressure has been
significantly associated with reported consumption of foods of animal origin (35), lacto-
ovo vegetarians who consume dairy protein also have lower pressures than omnivores
(38). In addition, fish protein fed at high levels resulted in decreased blood pressures and
complete inhibition of the development of stroke in stroke-prone spontaneously
hypertensive rats (39). However, vegetarian diets also differ from omnivorous diets in
many other factors such as P/S ratio and intakes of potassium and fiber, which have also
been shown to influence blood pressure (36, 40).

Aleohol

An association between prevalence of hypertension and regular consumption of
large amounts of aleohol has been demonstrated in several cross-sectional population
studies, independent of body weight (41-45), age (41-43), serum cholesterol, pulse (42),
sex, race, coffee use, former heavy drinking, and educational attainment (43). The
available data suggest that the relationship between alcohol and blood pressure is not a
continuous one, but that a threshold level may exist with elevated pressures at and above
these levels, and with similar pressures below these levels for drinkers compared to those
who abstain (43).

Potassium

Dietary potassium has been associated with lower blood pressure in both
normotensives (46-47) and hypertensives (48-49). Acute experiments in humans indicate
that this potassium effect on blood pressure may be related to the enhanced urinary
excretion of sodium with potassium supplementation (49-51). These findings support
early work by Dahl et al (52) showing that less hypertension developed in animals fed high
sodium diets when the Na/K molar ratio was low, than in animals fed the same level of
sodium with a high Na/K ratio.

Calcium

High intakes of calcium have also been shown to have a favorable effect on blood
pressure. Data from 24-hour recalls revealed that a group of hypertensives consumed
less calcium than a group of normotensives matched for age, sex and race (53). Caleium
intake was also significantly and inversely associated with blood pressure among a group
of normotensive men age 30-79 (54). Furthermore, calcium supplementation of young
normotensive adults resulted in a decline in mean diastolic pressure of 6% in women and
9% in men (55). This protective effect of calcium on blood pressure is also supported by
studies with animals (56-60).

Magnesium

Limited data suggest that magnesium intake may also favorably influence blood
pressure. An analysis of the epidemiologic data showing an inverse association between
lood pressure and hardness of the water supply suggested that the magnesium
concentration in the water was the important factor related to blood pressure (61), A
significant decrease in blood pressure was noted with magnesium supplementation in a
group of hypertensive patients in the absence of changes in urinary sodium and potassium
concentrations or body weight (62).

Polyunsaturated Fat

A significant negative association has been demonstrated between adipose tissue
linoleate and blood pressure in both men and women controlling for age and relative
weight (63-64). Blood pressure has also been significantly reduced in healthy adults by an
increase in the P/S ratio while decreasing intake of total fat (65-66). Similar findings
have also been reported for hypertensives with either a decrease in total fat, and
increase in P/S ratio or both (66-67). Although the amount of fat intake may also be
important, data from a study with animals indicate that the blood pressure effect is due
to the increase in polyunsaturated fat rather than to the decrease or absence of
saturated fat (68).

Fiber

Studies examining the effect of dietary fiber on blood pressure have also involved
ehanges in other dietary factors as well. However, it appears that dietary fiber may
influence blood pressure through its effect on dietary fat absorption as has been
suggested by studies with animals (69-70). Increased P/S ratio was associated with a
significant reduction in blood pressure among individuals consuming low fiber diets, but
was without a further effect on blood pressure in fiber-supplemented individuals who had
previously shown a significant decrease in blood pressure when fiber intake was increased
(71). Usual intakes of fiber were found to be signifeantly lower among a group of
hypertensives compared with normotensives (71). However, fiber supplementation of
hypertensives resulted in a significant decrease in blood pressure with a reduction in
total fat intake only if the P/S ratio was low (71). If the P/S ratio remained high, no
change in blood pressure was observed when fiber intake was increased (71), unless levels
of fiber were very high, e.g., 30-35¢ (72).

Summary

The evidence reported here supporting an association of dietary factors with blood
pressure represents only a sample of the most representative epidemiologic,
interventional and clinical research with humans. A significant amount of corroborating
findings in animals has been omitted except where these finding were provocative in
their extrapolation to humans or where research with humans was limited. With the
exception of sodium, the relationships between dietary factors and the interactions of
these factors with blood pressure have not been studied extensively and is a rapidly
growing field of investigation. CARDIA presents a unique opportunity to examine these
relationships in a young population where data concerning dietary behavior, exercise and
psychosocial factors will also be available to contribute to the interpretation of the
findings.

Method of Measurement

To assess patterns of nutrient intake of importance to the development of CHD, a
28-day dietary history based on the Western Electric dietary history format was used in
the first exam. This method was selected because it can characterize individual intakes
without the bias created by methods which increase awareness of diet or require a
minimal level of education to complete. However, due to both a reduced budget and a
reduction in the overall length of time alotted for the second exam, a shorter, self-
administered dietary method was deemed necessary. In addition, since the long term
validity of the CARDIA nutrition history is unknown, it was decided that a second
baseline of nutrient data on the CARDIA population should be obtained.

The Gladys Block questionnaire, which has typically been interviewer administered,
was modified slightly with regard to format to facilitate self-administration. The use of
such a form has a major advantage in that personnel requirements are reduced.
However, it will be necessary for clinic personnel to read the questionnaire to those
participants unable to read it for themselves.

The time frame for the dietary questionnaire in Exam Il differs from the diet
history used in the first exam. The CARDIA nutrition history focused on usual intake
using the previous 28-day period, while the Gladys Block questionnaire focuses on usual
intake over the previous year. Thus, the CARDIA history did not reflect seasonal intakes
of foods; the Gladys Block questionnaire obtains information regarding seasonal variation
in the intake of specific foods.

The CARDIA Exam II diet questionnaire consists of two parts: 1) questions
regarding usual dietary practices, including an assessment of sodium intake, and 2) a
semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire.

1) Dietary practices will be evaluated by questions pertaining to the

- use of fat in the preparation of various foods;

- addition of salt in the preparation of foods and at the table;

- use of artificial sweeteners, salt substitutes and low-sodium products; and
- frequency of eating meals in commercial establishments.

2) The semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire will obtain

- the frequency of intake over the past year of various foods to provide
qualitative and quantitative data regarding key nutrients of interest

- rough estimates of usual serving size.
Training and Certification

Interviewers will be trained at a central training session prior to the start of the
second exam. Since the form is essentially self-administered, the training will focus on
the instructions to the participants and handling those participants who cannot read.
Certification will consist of a review of a completed questionnaire with audiotaped
account of the interviewer checking the questionnaire for consistency, logic and
completeness of responses on at least one male and one female participant. The
Nutrition Coordinator will review the tapes with completed forms and provide feedback
to the interviewers.

Quality Control
The quality control procedures will consist primarily of procedures regarding

PULMONARY FUNCTION TESTING AND HISTORY

Rationale

There is little, if any, short-term information available on pulmonary function
indices in 18-30 year olds. Studies suggest that the growth and development of the
pulmonary system is still occurring among some individuals in this age range, but no data
exists to document when pulmonary function reaches its maximum, plateaus or begins to
decline within an individual. Measures of pulmonary function and history are included in
the CARDIA protocol primarily to gain a better understanding of the factors that
contribute to pulmonary growth and decay prior to middle age and only secondarily to
investigate the possible interplay between pulmonary factors and the development of
coronary heart disease and other cardiovascular outcomes. Re-examination of pulmonary
function in Exam II may serve to provide a more precise and accurate baseline for a long-
term sutdy. This added precision will enable us to relate lung function to other
parameters of cardiovascular risk such as nutrition, physical fitness and respiratory
symptoms and illness.

Numerous studies have identified cigarette smoking as an important contributor to
the decline in pulmonary function over time and to the development of chronic
obstructive airway disease (1-7). However, there is little concensus regarding other
environmental or social influences on pulmonary function or disease that might account
for differences observed between and within populations. Since the lungs continue to
develop through childhood and into young adulthood, it has been suggested that certain
factors during the formative years such as recurrent respiratory illness may predispose
individuals to later pulmonary symptomatology or disease (8,9). Existing data also
indicate that there may be racial differences in pulmonary function which are
unexplained by differences in smoking habits or simple measures of body size such as
height and weight (10-15). In addition, more research is needed on asthmatic conditions
which are poorly understood but not uncommon in younger populations, The CARDIA
pulmonary protocol has been designed to add to the existing knowledge in these areas.
Specifically, CARDIA will attempt to:

a) deseribe the evolution of pulmonary function and symptomatology
through young adulthood in relationship to influences such as early
cigarette exposure and childhood respiratory history.

b) provide data on black-white differences in pulmonary function and
change which may be related, at least in part, to differences in body
build (measured by height, frame size, girths), childhood disease
experience, and cigarette exposure.

c) gain further insight into those factors (e.g., allergies, sensitivity to
exposures) that predispose to the development of asthmatic
symptomatolgy and concomitant pulmonary function changes.

A secondary objective of characterizing the pulmonary profile of this young adult
population at baseline is to investigate the relationship between pulmonary function and
coronary risk. Some studies suggest that pulmonary function is predictive of subsequent
cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, irrespective of smoking habits (16-18). However,
it has been hypothesized that decreased pulmonary capacity is more likely an early
marker of ill-health and probably does not contribute to disease outcome either directly
or indirectly through the cardiovascular risk factors. In any event, it cannot be
anticipated that CARDIA participants will be followed for disease end points at the
present time.

Data Collection

The following pulmonary measures are part of the CARDIA examination protocol:
lung volumes and flow rates obtained from several forced expiratory maneuvers on
the Collins Survey Spirometer (forced vital capacity, forced expiratory volume in 1
and 3 seconds, peak expiratory flow rate, mid-maximal expiratory flow rate, flow
tates at 25, 50 and 75 percent of total expired volume). These measures will be
taken at the first, but not second, CARDIA examination.

respiratory sympotomatology including cough, phlegm and wheeze for

asthma.

Methods of Measurement

Accurate spirometric pulmonary function testing has three essential components:
a) a frequently calibrated spirometer that accurately records exhaled volume in relation
to time during the forced expiration; b) a subject who inspires maximally and exhales as
forefuly, smoothly, and completely as he ean; and c) a technician who can calibrate the
spirometer, coach the subject to perform maximal efforts, and detect poor subject effort
and/or expirations that are not continuous, maximal, and completely recorded. CARDIA
has as its goal to produce accurate spirometric pulmonary funetion measurements using
the Survey Spirometer and the Eagle II microprocessor (Warren E. Collins, Inc.,
Braintree, MA).

The equipment to be used in CARDIA and the supplies necessary for pulmonary
function testing will be standardized, with routine cleaning of the spirometer and
breathing tubes, plus frequent calibration of the spirometer, including cheeks of the
chart speed and volume deflection and tests for leakage. General principles of
spirometric testing, are: a) how to perform forced expiratory maneuvers; b) problems
that are often encountered in condueting the forced expiratory maneuvers; c) the number
of trials to be performed and reproducibility criteria; d) measurements of the Forced
Expiratory Volume in One Second (FEV1), the Foreed Vital Capacity (FVC), the
FEV1/FVC ratio, the Forced Expiratory Flow Rates (FEF) at 25%, 50%, and 75% of the
FVC exhaled, and the Maximal Mid-Expiratory Flow Rate (MMEF); e) correction of these
measurements to Body Temperature and Pressure, Saturated (BTPS); and f) calculation of
the predicted lung volumes and flow rates, the racial correction factor, and comparison
of the observed with these predicted values will also be detailed along with procedures to
be followed in testing study subjects using the Eagle II microprocessor and the Survey
Spirometer.

It will be seen that use of the Eagle II, in conjunction with the Survey Spirometer,
relieves the technician of hand measurement of the spirograms, BTPS correction, and
ealculation of and comparison with predicted pulmonary function values. However, it is
still essential that the technician calibrate the spirometer and that he insure, by active
eoaching and by vigilant attention to the spirograms, that maximum and good quality
forced expirations are performed and recorded.

Equipment

All pulmonary function tests will be conducted using the Collins survey 8-liter
water sealed spirometer. The expired volume is measured as it displaces a lightweight
Plastic bell riding in a narrow water well. A pen moves directly with the bell, recording
a tracing of volume versus time on a kymograph drum, rotating at a speed of 32
mm/sec. In addition to the information presented in this manual, further details of the
operation and maintenance of the spirometer are given in the Instruction Manual for the
Collins Survey Spirometer.

The Eagle Il microprocessor will be used in conjunction with the Survey spirometer
during spirometer volume calibration and patient testing. The Eagle II attaches to the
Survey spirometer via a Computer Input/Output Connector Cable. The Eagle II primarily
assists the technician in two otherwise time-consuming tasks: calculation of expired
volumes and flow rates and calculation of predicted pulmonary function values.

A linear motion potentiometer attached to the spirometer bell converts spirometer
bell volume changes into electrical signals. As the spirometer bell is displaced during a
forced expiration, signals are sent to the Eagle II through the computer connector
eable. In this way, the Eagle Il measures how fast the expiration is proceeding, and
ealeulates instantaneous flow rates at several points during the forced expiration.

In addition, using the subject's age, height and sex, which are entered into the Eagle
II prior to subject testing, the Eagle II computes the predicted pulmonary function values
using Knudson's prediction equations (16).After each expiration is recorded, the Eagle II
will print the test results and compare the subject's observed measurements with those
predicted for his age, height, race, and sex. Further details on the Eagle II are available

in the Instruction Manual for the Collins Eagle II Pulmonary Function Testing System.

Details of the approach to pulmonary function testing are outlined in the
"CARDIA" Standardized Pulmonary Function Testing Manual" which is part of the
CARDIA Manual of Operations. Pulmonary history and symptomatology questions are
part of the medica! history and medical data collection for the study.

PSYCHOSOCIAL COMPONENT

The CARDIA study presents an excellent opportunity to study the effects of life
ehange on a cohort of young aduslts prior to the exitence of major disease and in
eonjunction with an extensve set of biomedical data. The basic goas of the psychosocial
portion of the exam will be:

1. To develop basic demographic information suitable in deseribing the study
population adequately in this age group.

2. To deseribe the development of psychosocial risk factors over a minimum of
two years.

3. To identify psychosocial factors predictive of CHD risl factor development.

The basie strategy that was followed int eh selection of variables were their
demonstrated association with CHD, hypertension or other CHD risk factors in at least
two epidemiological studies. Additionally, variables were chosen that were useful or
necessary for the description of the study porpulation (socioeconomic status, race, etc).
Questionnaire selection was based on the criteria of being appropriate for the study
population in terms of age, race, gender, socioeconime status and literacy demands,
Attention to the lenght of the forms were considered as well as having documented
reliability and/or validity in prior research. While the list of variables was quite long,
the basic classes include sociodemographic indicators, life changes, and ways of coping
with life situations and life changes. Rationales and descriptions of the individual
components follow.

SOCIODEMOGRAPHIC QUESTIONNAIRE

Description
The basic sociodemographic descriptors included in this questionnaire are: age,
sex, race, marital status, socioeconomic status, parental socioeconomic status, spouse's
socioeconomic status, living situation, and residential mobility. Socioeconomic status is
measured by education, occupation and income, the traditional indicators of social
class. These measures may be analyzed separately or combined into an index of
socioeconomic status (SES). Questions on occupation have been formulated to correspond
to those used by the Bureau of the Census.
Evidence
The evidence presented here is limited to risk for CHD, in accordance with the
criteria for selection of variables set by the Psychosocial Committee. Evidence of the
association of sociodemographic characteristics with specific risk factors will be
considered by others.
Social Class
A change in the social class distribution of risk for CHD, at mid-century was noted
(Antonovsky, 1968; Jenkins, 1971; Marmot et al., 1978). Prior to the 1950's, coronary
heart disease was widely held to be a disease of affluence with upper socioeconomic
classes at elevated risk (Osler, 1910; Price, 1941; Spain, 1966). Antonovsky reported that
this perception was clearly not supported by the data. In an extensive literature review,
he found some studies reported inverse class gradients, others reported direct gradients
and still others reported no gradient at all in the association between social class and risk
for CHD. Although there was no consistency, he noted that a majority of the studies did
show class differences which were substantial. He observed that several studies done in
1930-50 reported a direct gradient for the older age group and an inverse gradient in the
younger age group. Since the 1950's there has been a marked change in the view that
CHD is a disease of the rich. CHD has been reported as progressively more common
among lower socioeconomic classes (Marmot et al., 1978; Cooper et al., 1978).
Consequently lower classes are now generally at greater risk for CHD than middle
classes. An inverse relationship between social class and CHD risk has been reported in a
number of studies (see Education and Occupation for details). Kraus and his colleagues
noted that the inverse relationship between SES and risk for CHD held for whites, Asians,
and Spanish Americans, but not for blacks (Kraus et al., 1950).
Education
An inverse relationship between education and CHD risk has been reported with
reasonable consistency in several prospective epidemiological studies since the 1950's
(Liu et al., 1981; Hinkle et al., 1968, Rosenman et al. 1975; Dawber et al., 1959). Liu and
his colleagues found an inverse association between education and risk factors at entry in
the Chicago Heart Association cohort. They also found that the inverse relationship
between education and CHD risk was independent of risk factors at entry. The
Framingham study found an inverse relationship in its six year follow-up but it was not
significant (Dawber et al., 1959).

Occupation

Differences in CHD risk have been identified both within a particular occupation,
as well as across occupations. In the Whitehall study, men in lower employment grades in
the London civil service were at higher CHD risk than men in higher employment grades
(Rose and Marmot, 1981). In comparisons across occupations, people in those which
require a higher standard of education are at lower CHD risk compared to those with
lower educational requirements (Holme et al., 1976; Sauli, 1979: Marmot et al., 1978;
Logan, 1954). On the other hand, the National Health Survey found no strong evidence of
any class gradient measured by either occupation or income with prevalence of CHD
(NCHS, Series 11, No.10, 1965).

Age-sex-race

Older people are at higher risk for CHD than younger ones, men are at higher risk
than women, black women are at higher risk than white women, and black men are
similar in risk to white men (Cooper et al., 1978; Moriyama et al., 1971; Kitagawa and
Hauser, 1973; Gillum, 1982; Gillum and Grant, 1982). Death rates for black women have
been consistently higher than for white women since the late 1940's. The picture is
different for black men. Death rates were lower than for white men in the 1940's, then
rose rapidly and exceeded the rates for white men in 1968 and 1969, and in the years
following remained lower or close to the rates for white men (Cooper et al., 1978).
Contrary to a belief held by some that blacks are immune to CHD, CHD is the leading
eause of death in blacks, as it is in whites (Gillum, 1982).

Marital Status

Death rates from CHD of the single, widowed and divorced are substantially higher
than rates for married persons (Moriyama et al., 1971). Men and women in marriages in
which the wife works out of economic necessity report more tension and negative affect
than people in marriages in which the wife works by choice (Orden and Bradburn, 1968,
1969).

Status Incongruities

Several studies indicate that men whose wives have a higher level of education than
they themselves have attained are at higher risk of CHD than men whose wives have less
education (Suarez, 1984; Haynes et al., 1983; Jenkins, 1976; Shekelle, 1969).

Occupational and Residential Mobility

Many studies have shown increased rates of disease among occupationally and
residentially mobile people (Syme et al., 1969); Syme et al., 1966; Cassel and Tyroler
1961; Kaplan 1971; Shekelle, 1979; Jahne, 1980). However several studies failed to find
increased rates of disease among mobile persons (Hinkle et al., 1968; Rosen and Rosen,
1978).

Living Situation
An association between social isolation and mortality has been shown. People
living alone are greater risk than those living with others (Gove et al., 1980; Carnahan et
al., 1974).

Hypotheses

Social class and other sociodemographic variables will be used to describe sub-
groups of the sample population and explain variations in levels of risk factors for
coronary heart disease, as well as changes in the development of risk factors over time.
The risk factors include biological and behavioral risk factors such as high blood pressure,
cigarette smoking, diet, alcohol consumption, etc.; psychological variables such as
hostility, anger, ways of coping and bringing a sense of coherence to life events; access
to and utilization of health care services; exposure to social factors such as social
supports and social disruption; and other factors yet to be identified. The pattern and
direction of the associations between sociodemographic characteristics and risk factors
for coronary heart disease will be as follow:
1. Risk factor levels in young adults will be higher in the following
sociodemographic groups:
A. black and white men (compared to black and white women)
B. black women (compared to white women)
C. black men (compared to white men)
D. single, divorced or widowed (compared to married) controlling for age
E.
men whose wives have attained more education that they (compared
to men whose wives have less education)
F. husbands and wives in marriages in which the wife works out of economic
necessity (compared to ones in which the wife works by choice)
G. people who live alone (compared to those who live with others).
2. Risk factor levels in young adults will be inversely associated with the
following sociodemographic characteristics within each age, sex, race group:
A. education
B. occupational level
3. Risk factor levels in young adults will be positively associated with the
following sociodemographic characteristics within each age, sex, race group:
A. occupational mobility
B. residential mobility
C. upward mobility
4. Risk factors in young adults will be inversely associated with education,
independent of occupation, and independent of residential occupational and/or
upward mobility.
5. Over time, changes in risk factors will follow the pattern and direction of the
associations with sociodemographic characteristics described for levels of
risk factor in the preceding hypotheses.

PSY-8

LIFE EVENTS

Description

Many studies on human behavior and social change have viewed change, especially
rapid social change as a time of stress for the individual. The most compelling evidence
for the negative impact of change on the individual comes from the literature in
psychosomatic medicine. From this developed the concept of stressful life events,
events in a person's life that, for better or worse, interrupted or changed the pattern of
usual activities. The incidence of change/interruption in usual activities leads to the
development of stress and the consequent onset of illness in the affected individual.
Recently a number of psychometric scales have been developed to measure the
magnitude of stress from a list of typical life events.

Rationale and Hypotheses

There exists a vast literature citing a positive relationship between the incidence
of stressful life events and the onset of illness - both organic and psychiatric. Several
studies (Theorell and Rahe, 1970; Rahe and Paasikivi, 1971; Theorell and Rahe 1971;
Rahe, et al., 1974; and Theorell, 1974) have found a positive relationship between
stressful life events and myocardial infaretion. The major hypothesis examined in these
studies (and many other similar investigations) is that significant stressful life events will
increase the probability of the onset of illness, including CHD. In addition, the incidence
of illness onset is a consequence of the rapid accumulation of stressful life events over
time. Finally, those stressful life events most closely related to lifestyle and lifestyle
changes will be most closely associated with illness onset, including CHD. In addition,
the incidence of illness onset is a consequence of the rapid accumulation of stressful life
events over time. The measurement of stressful life events is most important for
CARDIA as 18-30 years olds do experience rapid social change in lifestyle. Thus, for this
group the stressful effects of this change may be a definite risk factor for CHD. The
literature on stressful life events is not without its crities (Rabkin and Struening, 1974;
Wershow and Reinhart, 1974). Most of these criticisms, however, deal more with
methodological than substantive issues. Recently questions have been raised as to the
linearity of the relationship between stressful life events and illness (Wildman and
Johnson, 1977) and the additivity of the relationship (Lin, et al., 1979). These lead to
additional hypotheses concerning the meditating effects of social support mechanisms as
a buffer between stressful life events and illness onset and to the relationship between
the absence of life events and illness onset in a sub-population for which rapid social
change may be the norm.

Methods of Measuring and Scoring Stressful Life Events

Following the work by Holmes and Rahe (1967), a number of modifications of and
variations on their Social Readjustments Rating Seale have been developed in order to
measure stressful life events. To date, the revision by Dohrenwend et al. (1978) appears
to be the most successful from two perspectives: applicability to the target population
of CARDIA and methodological rigor. Each of the 102 events on the Psychiatrie
Epidemiology Rating Interview (PERI) Life Events Seale was assigned a weight,
indicating its stress magnitude. These weights were empirically derived from a sample
of persons similar in their characteristics to the proposed CARDIA population. From the
PERI scale, a sub-seale of 64 items was selected by the Psychosocial Working Group.

These events, linked to edueational attainment, family formation, and career
development, ete. may be scored by one or all of three methods. First, the number of
events experienced during a fixed time period (usually one year) may be utilized; second,
the sum of weighted life events may be used as a ratio measure; and third, the sum of the

ranks of the weighted life events may be used as an interval measure of the level of
stressful life events.

A change was made in the format for the life events questionnaire so that the
definitive time period in which the even occurred could be ascertained.

Framingham - Type A/B Assessment

CARDIA presents a unique opportunity to study the development of the behavior
pattern over time and the influence of changing life circumstances on its development.
The Framingham A/B assessment questionnaire will be re~administered in the second
CARDIA exam. This questionnaire approach to measurement will permit inexpensive
follow-up and should permit the exploration of how some components of the behavior
pattern change over time or with changes in life circumstance.
