PART

SOCIAL SUPPORT AND JOB DEMAND/LATITUDE

Rationale

The 18-30 age period is a time when young adults first assume the responsibilities
of adult life. It is a time of substantial life changes and challenge. Several sections of
the psychosocial battery identify and assess these environmental demands. The 18-30
age period also is a time when young people first need to develop adult ways of coping
with challenges and demands. We hypothesize that (a) those who cope ineffectively and
inappropriately with environmental demands will exhibit greater increases in CHD risk
and (b) those young adults who cope well, even in the face of massive demands and
burdens, will experience lower CHD risk. Several questionnaires dealing with coping
have been described elsewhere (e.g., type A behavior, hostility and anger). Here we
discuss social support and sense of coherence.

Social Support

A substantial literature exists showing that strong social support networks can act
as a mediator between environmental demands and disease (Nuckolls, Cassel, Kaplan,
1972; Boyce, Jensen, Cassel et al, 1977; Lin, Ensel, Simeone et al, 1979). Data are now
available from large prospective studies that inadequate social support networks predict
the subsequent occurrence of CHD, angina, and mortality from all with relative risks
ranging from 2 to 3 after account has been taken of other major CHD risk factors
(Berkman and Syme, 1979; House, Robbins and Metzner, 1982; Blazer, 1982). On the
other hand, research on Japanese-American men living in Honolulu found no relationship
between social support and CHD incidence (Reed, 1983). However, a 10-year follow-up
study of social support and CHD among 10,000 men and women in Finland is now nearing
completion and data from this study (after adjusting for major CHD risk factors) shows a
two-fold relative risk in disease among those with poor social support networks (Kaplan
and Syme, 1984, unpublished). Sinee young adults 18-30 tend more often than others to
leave home, leave school, get married, find jobs and move geographically, the issue of
social support is of special importance in this group.

Job Demand

In the last several years, data has been published from large prospective studies in
Sweden and the U.S. showing an increased rate of CHD among people who have
demanding and stressful jobs and who also have little latitude, flexibility or options for
coping with these demands (Karasek, 1979; Karasek, Baker, Marxer et al, 1981a; Karasek,
Theorell, Tores et al, 1981b; Alfredsson, Karasek, Theorell, in press). The issue of
options, latitude and flexibility is of particular importance in the 18-30 year age group
beeause it is at this time that demands and life changes increase and when flexibility and
options often decrease.

Method of Measurement
Social Support
A wide variety of approaches exist to assess social support, including psychosocial

assets, social network affiliation and perceived support. In a study of coronary artery
disease among people undergoing coronary angiography, all of these measures and

approaches to see which predicts disease most strongly have been used. Of all the
measures included, the importance of instrumental help and advice emerged along with
several additional questions regarding perceived support. Only these questions are
included in the CARDIA battery.

Job Demand/Latitude

The questions used to assess job demand and latitude/flexibility are those that have
been used extensively and reliably by Karasek and associates in their studies of this
concept in Sweden and the United States.

LIFE SATISFACTION

Rationale

Life satisfaction questions have been used widely in studies of quality oflife and
health. Data exists on age, sex, and race specific responses (1) .

Life satisfaction has been shown to be intermediate between the apparent
expectations and objective circumstances (achievements). The smaller the gap between
expectations and achievements, the greater the level of subjectively reported quality of
life (2).

Studies which have addressed the subjective quality of life experience hve produced
more consistent findings than those using objective social indicators (3),

A number of studies have demonstrated that the objective conditions of life (e.g.

income, education, and many other sociodemographic characteristics) are only marginally
related to the subjective experinec of a better quality of life (4-7)

A focus of the incidence study must be on patterns of elvolution of the
major risk factors and the influences that relate to these trends. In
particular, the focus must be first and foremost on patterns of evolution
of plasma cholesterol -- lipoproteins and blood pressure. Changes in
smoking habit will also be of concern although it is likely that for most
people 18-30, status in this regard was already established earlier, and
the years immediately beyond 18-30 may well witness only modest
changes. Aspects of life style related to foregoing key risk factors
(plasma cholesterol-lipoproteins and blood pressure) —e.g., eating and
dietary habits, physical activity, caloric balance, psychosocial factors
and their trends — are obviously of major concern.

Physical Activity - " We would like to examine the blood pressure
response with exercise as it relates to change in blood pressure between
the two examinations and to the inicidence of hypertension (which will of
course be low). There is evidence that individuals who have an
accelerated systolic blood pressure response to low-level exercise are at

The interaction between physical activity and lipoproteins profiles also
deserve investigation. Some studies have demonstrated an increase in
HDL cholesterol with exercise (Wood et al., 1983). It would be
interesting to examine this issue in young adults, since differences at
relatively young age might have a cumulative effect over the years and
be related to the development of CHD. It would also be of general
interest to determine the interactions with other lipoproteins and
apoproteins as little work in this area has been done with this age group,
especially with women in general, and particularly with blacks. We
hypothesize that changes in lipids and lipoproteins in the direction of
lower CHD risk will be observed in association with increased physical
activity.

It should be clear that the Physical Activity Recall (PAR) provides a
vehicle for performing the types of analyses noted above not only by
total energy expenditure and by fitness level, but also by the energy
expenditure at various levels of exercise intensity. For example, it has
been suggested that a certain weekly threshold of very hard activity (i.e.,
jogging) is associated with significant increases in HDL cholesterol (Wood
et al, 1983). The PAR ean be used to validate this and to determine
whether a high level of moderate activity might have the same effect.

A careful assessment is needed of the correlation between fitness level
as measured by the low level fitness test... and the total energy
expenditure as estimated by the PAR. If the correlation is sufficiently
high, it may be possible to use either of these methods interchangeably
as a valid measure of physical activity and fitness in future
epidemiological studies. If they do not correlate well, then it would be
necessary to use both types of methods as measurement tools in future
studies.

We would like to study the relation of job activity to fitness level as
measured by the exercise test and to CHD risk factors. Job activity will
be measured by the PAR, by a self-administered question about work
connected physical activity ... and by published information about the
energy expenditure involved in a wide variety of jobs (Durin, 1967).

Prior history of physical activity needs to be assessed in relation to the
present level of physical activity and fitness and to risk factor levels.
Prior level of physical activity will be assessed by the self-administered
questionnaire ... We would also examine whether a family history of
physical activity influences and habitual physical activity and fitness
levels of our population ... A recent survey of fitness in the USA
indicated that individuals who grew up with family members who were
interested in participating in sports and athletes were much more likely
to be physically active themselves (Perrier Study, 1978).

The relationship between physical activity and fasting blood glucose
needs to be explored. Physical conditioning may increase the insulin
sensitivity of tissues (Vranik and Berger, 1979). This could be reflected
by lower fasting blood glucose levels.

Computed Variable

algorithm:

C10SMOKE = .;
IF C10TOBAC=1 THEN C10SMOKE=0;
IF C10TOBAC=2 AND C10CIGS=1 THEN C10SMOKE=0;
IF C10TOBAC=2 AND C10CIGS=2 AND C09SMKNW=1 THEN C10SMOKE=1;
IF C10TOBAC=2 AND C10CIGS=2 AND C09SMKNW=2 THEN C10SMOKE=2;

0 = NON-SMOKERS
1 = EX-SMOKERS

C1F11 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Family History Questionnaire)

The data related to mother and father on Form 11 must be
analyzed by the status variables C11MOMLV (Is your natural mother
living?) and C11DADLV (Is your natural father living?). For
example, only one variable exists for mother's age (C11MAGE) and
one variable for father's age (C11FAGE). It means 'age at death'
when the status variable is 'no'; it means ‘age now' when the
status variable is 'yes', and it means ‘assumed age' when the
status variable is 'don't know'.

Likewise, "What was the cause of your mother's (father's)
death?" is only answered when the status variable is 'no'. Zeros
and missings will be found for this question when the status
variable is either 'yes' or 'don't know’.

C1F12PF - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Pulmonary Function Testing Data)

The following variables are the maximum values of the FVC,
FEV, and FEV, for the pulmonary function test. Reproducibility of
the maximum, time of the trial, and trial number from which the
maximum was extracted is also included. Please refer to the SAS
labels and algorithms for more detail.

Maximum: C12Fvc C12FE1 C12FE3

Reproducibility: C12RPFVC C12RPFE1 C12RPFE3
Time: C12FVCTM C12FE1TM C12FE3TM
Trial Number: C12FVCTR C12FE1TR C12FE3TR

The following variables are the flow rates extracted from the
maximum curve. Again, see SAS labels for definitions.

C12PEFR C12FF25 C12FF75 C12FRTR
C12MMEF C12FF50 C12FRTM

The header information from the Eagle II microprocessor strip
is also included in this file. This includes information such as
the technician, posture, room temperature, etc. See SAS labels for
definitions of these variables.

C12TECH C12SEX C12BPRES
C12POSTR C12RACE C12HGT
C12SPDT C12AGE C12TEMP

When performing longitudinal analysis of pulmonary function
data, note that for Exams 1 and 2, a maximum of five trials were
performed. In Exam 3, up to eight trials were performed, but only
data from the first five trials were used to maintain comparability
with past exams. Please contact the Coordinating Center if you

would like access to the complete data set for Exam 3.

MEDICAL HISTORY FOLLOW-UP FILES - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

The Medical History Follow-Up data can be found in four files.
Those files and the data contained therein include:
C1F09PER - Menstrual Period
C1F9PRG1
C1F9PRG2 Pregnancy (see following notes)
C1F9PRG3
Interviewer ID is not included in these files. This variable
was inadvertently excluded from the data entry system.

C1F09PER Computed Variables:
C09LMPDT (derived from C09LMPMO, C09LMPDY, and C09LMPYR)
- Date last menstrual period began
- Formatted as DATE7.
- Components with values of 0 (zero) are set to missing
by SAS.
- A date with any component having the special missing value
.M had the SAS date value set to .M also.

Special Notes Regarding Pregnancy File

In order to ease handling and interpretation, the pregnancy
follow-up variables have been split into three files. These files
are named: C1F9PRG1.SSD, C1F9PRG2.SSD, and C1F9PRG3.SSD. See the
PROC CONTENTS output for detailed lists of variables contained in
these files.

C1F9PRG1.SSD contains one observation for each participant who
completed a Pregnancy Follow-up form, and the variables from page
1 of the form; an observation in this file is uniquely identified
by the 5-digit CARDIA ID (SAS variable SHORT_ID).

9/91

C1F9PRG2.SSD contains one observation for each pregnancy
reported as occurring between Exam 1 and Exam 2, and the variables
from pages 2 and 4 of the form; an observation from this file is
uniquely identified by the combination of SHORT_ID and the
pregnancy number (SAS variable CO9PRGNO). Note that pregnancies
contemporaneous with the interview are identified as pregnancy "0"
(zero); other pregnancies should be numbered, beginning with "1"
(one) from earliest to latest.

C1F9PRG3.SSD contains one observation for each infant

C1F18 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Physical Activity Questionnaire)

Scoring is accomplished by adding a weighted sum of the number
of months for each activity below and again above the hours per
week cutpoint. Algebraically, where m is the number of months
below the cutpoint and n is the number of months above the
cutpoint, and the coefficients b and ¢ are described below. The
coefficient c has been selected to be 3*b for each activity.

Heavy intensity score = & bi *m +c, * n,;
for activities A-H

Moderate intensity score is similar in form, but summed over
activities I through M, and the total score is the sum of the two
subscores.

The coefficient b is the intensity level assigned to each
activity which is roughly the number of kilocalories thought to be
expended in one minute of activity by a 70 kg man. Intensities
were patterned after those used by Taylor et al and Folsom et al.
Exceptions are bicycling, which was set at an intensity code of 6
to reflect the wording "faster than 10 miles per hour"' and
vigorous work activity (which was not included in Taylor's or
Folsom's work), which was set at an intensity code of 5, somewhat
less than that for weight lifting.

In addition to the physical activity score, three indices were
developed: (1) Work Index (C18WKIDX); (2) Sport Index (C18SPIDX); and
(3) Leisure-Time Index (C18LTIDX). These indices were calculated based
on questions added from the Baecke Questionnaire of Habitual Physical
Activity (Am J Clin Nutr, 1982, 36:932-942) modified for use in the
ARIC study.

The algorithm for the Work Index (C18WKIDX) incorporates the
occupational code obtained on the Sociodemographic Questionnaire

(CO3CODE). The activity level for each occupation was coded as low,

9/91
medium, or high by the ARIC study. Low activity was given a score of
1, medium activity a score of 3 and high activity a score of 5.
C18WKIDX =
[Activity level of occupation + (6 - C1801STD) +
C1802STD + C1803WLK + C1804LFT + C1805TRE + C1806SWT +
C1807WPH]/8

NOTE: The large number of missing values for C18WKIDX is due to
errors in the coding of occupation on Form 3 (Sociodemographic
Questionnaire). Approximately 250 participant records were coded with
industry codes instead of the appropriate occupation codes. Recoding
will be performed and this data set will updated with the next release
of the data tape.

The questions from the Baecke Questionnaire regarding physical
activity were not included on the CARDIA Form 18. In place of the
simple sport score from the Baecke instrument, the algorithm for the
Sport Index (C18PIDX) uses the quintiles of the physical activity score
from Exam 1 (A18TOTAL); the cutpoints for the quintiles were scored 1
through 5.

C18SPIDX =
(Physical activity quintile + C18P1WPH + C18P2SWT +
C18P3SPT)/4

The Leisure-Time Index (C18LTIDX) was calculated using the
following algorithm:
C18LTIDX =
[(6 - C18P4WTV) + C18P5WLK + C18P6BIK + C18P7MIN]/4

C1REF - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(Demographic Data)

This file contains the demographic variables (age [Exam 1 and
Exam 3], sex, race, education [Exam 1 and Exam 3]) and should be
used in any analysis of the CARDIA cohort requiring stratification
by the demographic variables. EXAMAGE is the age of the
participant at Exam 1. EX3_AGE is the age of the participant at
Exam 3. The variables EXAMAGE, SEX and RACE are based on the
original demographic variables collected in Exam 1 and verified in
Exams 2 and/or 3. Only participants who were examined at Exam 2 or
Exam 3 have their demographic data updated. The demographic
variables for those participants who did not return for the second
and third exams are as they were recorded in the first exam. AO3ED
is the number of years of education as reported at Exam 1. CO03ED
is the number of years of education as reported at Exam 3.
Fourteen Hispanic race codes have been changed to white.

This reference file is the only file in this version of the
CARDIA data that contains information on all 5115 original
participants; all other files contain only participants examined at
Exam 3 (n=4352).

In addition to the standard demographic variables, this data
set contains the date of Exam 1 (AO2DATE), the date of Exam 2
(BO2DATE), the date of Exam 3 (CO2DATE), the participant's
birthdate (BIRTHDT), which was verified at Exam 2 and/or Exam 3,
and the participant's pregnancy status at Exam 3 (CO8PREG).

This data set also contains scheduling information on each of
the original 5115 participants seen in Exam 1 (X3DATE, X3STATUS,
X3WINDOW, and X3EXPDT). X3DATE will be the same as CO2DATE for all

examined participants. If the participant was not re-examined,
X3DATE reflects scheduling dates or pending dates, not an exam

date. X3STATUS reflects whether a participant was seen in Exam 3.

An explanation of each code is provided.

CODE | EXPLANATION
E | examined
A | abbreviated exam
1 | For participants examined in a
2 | clinic other than their home clinic,
3 | this number reflects the site of the
4 | exam (1=BHAM, 2=CHIC, 3=MINN, 4=OAKL).
D | died prior to Exam 3
N | no-show
P | pending
R | refused
L | lost

Thus, examined participants are coded as E, A, 1, 2, 3 or 4 and
those not examined are coded as N, P, R, L.

X3WINDOW reflects the participant's window status as of the
end of the exam. (See the Exam 3 Manual of Operations for more
detail on window codes.) All clinics did not use this aspect of
the scheduling system for the entire exam, thus these codes are not
all accurate. If you are planning to use these, please contact
each clinic for more specific information on how this variable was
handled.

X3EXPDT is the target week for the participant's third
examination. This is a character variable and uses codes from 'A'
through 'Z' and 'a' through 'z.' The coding scheme for each week
of Exam 3 follows.

Naming Conventions
The form set data files are named C1Fnn. 'C' signifies Exam
3, '1' signifies the first version of the data file and 'Fnn'
corresponds to the form number. Variables in each of these files
all begin with the letter 'C' followed by the two digit form
number, nn, then followed by up to five characters describing the
variable, e.g. CnnXXXXX. Variables which were collected in Exams 1,
2 and 3 are named identically except for the first character.

The demographic data are found in the file C1REF. Please
refer to the CIREF section of this documentation notebook for
detailed information regarding these important variables.

The data collected on the Medical History Follow-up forms are
distributed among numerous SAS files, each corresponding to its
data collection form. The file names are listed below under the
specific heading for which documentation can be found in this
notebook.

Number of Observations

Each file except for the Form 9 follow-ups and the substudies
(C1F31ABC, C1F39, C1F41AU, C1F41RS, C1F42, C1F43 and C1CAROTD)
contain 4352 observations (the total number of participants coded
as Examined or Abbreviated for Exam 3). If all data for a
particular participant is missing in a file, that particular record
will contain SAS missing values although an ID and CENTER variable
will be present. Recall that abbreviated exams were allowed in the
third exam, with some parts of the exam being eliminated more often
than others. Thus, some files will have a greater number of
missing data than others.

The Form 9 follow-up files and the substudy files contain only
those participants who completed the form. Most of the files are
relatively small. Some files contain multiple records per person
(e.g., medication). Please refer to the specific documentation for
more information on these files.

ID Variable
Although all the files contain an ID variable, not all contain
the 12-digit CARDIA ID (ID). A 5-digit ID (SHORT_ID) is the ID
variable in all of the Form 9 follow-up files. In order to merge
one of these files with a file containing only the 12-digit ID
variable (ID), you can use the following statement to create a new
SHORT_ID in your file:
SHORT_ID=INT(ID/10**7);
Formats
The only formats used in the SAS data sets are the
conventional SAS date and time formats identified as DATE7 and
TIME5. To determine which variables have used these formats and
which format was used, please look at the PROC CONTENTS for each
data set. When using variables that were stored with DATE7 and
TIME5 formats, we recommend using these formats since without them
the variables cannot be easily interpreted.
Sorted Files
Each of the SAS data files have been sorted by the ID variable
(either ID or SHORT_ID) to facilitate the merging of files for
analysis.
Missing Values
CARDIA data entry personnel were instructed to use the letter
'M' for missing values. Occasionally, other conventions were
followed such as the use of zero's (0) and blanks (). In addition,
skip patterns built into the data entry system appropriately filled
the skipped fields with blanks ( ). SAS sets these blank values to
the SAS missing value of a period (.).
Please refer to the 'CARDIA DATA ENTRY DOCUMENTATION' on file
at each clinic and the Coordinating Center for specific form
instructions regarding missing values and skip patterns. Files for
which specific problems with missing or skipped data have been
found and are noted in the documentation that follows.

Edits

In addition to the range checks automatically applied to the
data at entry, real-time edits were generated by the Coordinating
Center during the course of the exam on the transmission files. A
detailed listing of the "real-time" edits performed on the data can
be found in the respective documentation for that file. These
edits were corrected or verified by the clinical centers on a
monthly basis. Although all these edits were completed by the
centers, occasional out-of-range results (outliers) are still
contained in the data files because some values were verified as
being correct as entered. The data was entered correctly from the
form, although the form was obviously in error. The clinics were
instructed not to create data. Thus, only data entry errors were
corrected and not interviewer or transcription errors.

A listing of additional edits applied to the files after data
collection is found following this section.

reason, when you are making a decision regarding outliers, please
refer to these edits to see what has been done by the Coordinating

Data Dictionaries

Data dictionaries are included for each file except for the
lipid data files. Data dictionaries describe the ASCII data files
and information pertinent to their collection in the data entry
program. The first 43 bytes of information collected on each form
is referred to as "header information" specifically characterizing
the data entry process for that particular form. This data is not
included in the SAS data sets. Thus, form specific variables begin
at column 44. For each variable the following information is
included:

1. variable name (same as SAS variable name) ;

2. ASCII character definition for storing data (e.g. 'c');
number of bytes allowed for the variable; and

4. comments (begin with '/*' and end with '*/'),

a) the beginning byte count of the variable;

b) question number from the form;

qa) edit checks performed by the Forms Management

allowable character checks.

categorical data) or univariate statistics (continuous data) for
all variables in the SAS data sets are included with this
documentation. For the univariate procedure, the five highest and
lowest values are printed along with the corresponding participant
ID (first 5-digits only).

data tape. It differs from the algorithm used in Version 2.2;
the Version 2.3 data tape will use the algorithm shown here.

recalculate B07MLALC using this algorithm.

G/F1

In the process of creating the data set for Form 18 (Physical
Activity History), the Coordinating Center discovered that
approximately 250 occupational codes were erroneously coded as
industry codes by clinic personnel. The clinical centers have been
sent a list of participant IDs with the erroneous codes; all of
these files will be pulled and recoded. The corrected data will be
included in the next release of the Exam 3 data tape.

There are several ages of children and/or stepchildren that do
not seem feasible given the age range of our participants. All
such ages have been verified by the clinical centers.

A number of discrepancies between reported education at Exam
2 and Exam 3 (e.g, a lower number of years of education at the
third exam than at the second exam or increases of more than three
years) have been identified indicating that one should use caution
in using this reported education variable in analyses. The lack of
a standardized probing protocol may be the explanation for these
inconsistencies. One clinic has reported examples of problems
which were observed in reviewing some of the records sent as edits.

1. Vo-tech/business education - sometimes counted and
sometimes not counted.

2. GED - sometimes checked as 12 years of education and
sometimes not.

3. College - specific degree given various years of "credit"
- e.g., AA degree marked as 13 years when finished in
less than the usual 14 years.

4. College - 2 Bachelor degrees, 20 years of education
checked. There appears to be a tendency to give people
credit for extra degrees that are at the same level.

These comments indicate that the problem is not restricted to the
interviewers, but extends to the participants as well.

C1F05 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Phlebotomy)

The phlebotomists recorded any food and/or drink that the
participants had in the previous 12 hours. The food item(s) and/or
beverage(s) were recorded on the form and then coded for data entry
(C05CODE). The codes are provided below. If the participant had
observed the 12 hour fast, the code recorded on the form was 99.

CODES FOR FOODS EATEN
Code | Food and/or Beverages
0 | Coffee or tea w/o cream or sugar
1 | Coffee or tea w/ cream or sugar
2 | Juice or fruit
3 | Milk or milk product
4 | Candy or breakfast cake (doughnut)
5 | Cereal
6 | Eggs and/or meat
7 | Pancakes or waffles
8 | Other non-breakfast food

There are nine participants with values of 0 for C05FSTMN.
These have been verified with the clinical centers; all
participants were either chewing gum or eating candy at the time of

individual last ate and time and date blood drawn

C05FAST: fasting status based on the calculated variable C05FSTMN.
C05FAST was generated using the following statements to
indicate a 12 hour fast:

IF 720<=C05FSTMN<=2940 THEN CO5FAST = 'YES';
IF 0 < C05FSTMN < 720 THEN CO5FAST = 'NO';

CiFO8 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Medical History)

Form 8 was interviewer-administered in both Exam 1 and Exam 2.
The form was revised prior to the third exam to make it self-
administered and to reduce the number of medical conditions and
medications and thus the number of follow-up forms. In addition,
all weight and weight history questions were eliminated. In the
process of revision, several questions were re-worded so that the
comparability of the Exam 3 data for Form 8 with that from previous
exams is not possible in some instances. These cases are noted
below.

The Form 8 variable regarding high blood pressure medication
(CO8BPNOW) refers to current use, not "ever use" as in previous
exams (AO8BPMED and BO8BPMED). CO8BPNOW is comparable to the Form
9 medication follow-up variable from previous exams (AO9MDNOW
[where AOSMDTYP = HBP] and BO9HBNOW).

Likewise, variables regarding birth control use (CO8BCNOW) and
other hormone use (CO8HMNOW) refer to current use, not "ever use"
as in previous exams (AO8BRTHC and AO8HORMN). CO8BCNOW is
comparable to the Form 9 medication follow-up variable from
previous exams (AO9BCNOW and BO9BCNOW). CO8HMNOW is comparable to
AO9MDNOW (where AO9MDTYP = HORM) and BOSHMNOW.

For all Form 8 variables regarding the age at diagnosis of a
specific disease, comparable data from Exams 1 and 2 can be found
in the Form 9 follow-up data files. For example, the variable
regarding the age at which diagnosis of diabetes occurred
(CO8DIBAG) would be compared with AO9DIBAG and BO9DIBAG. Any age
at diagnosis of disease recorded as 0 was verified; these values
indicate that the participant was born with the condition or was
diagnosed before the first birthday.

F/F1

Similarly, most of the site-specific disease variables now
appearing on Form 8 can be found in Form 9 medical follow-up data
files from the first two exams. However, the variables for heart
disease and kidney disease may not be comparable between exams due
to reorganization of the form. Please compare the questions for
these diseases carefully before beginning any analysis.

and missings will be found for this question when the status

C1F12PF - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Pulmonary Function Testing Data)

The following variables are the maximum values of the FVC,
FEV, and FEV, for the pulmonary function test. Reproducibility of
the maximum, time of the trial, and trial number from which the
maximum was extracted is also included. Please refer to the SAS
labels and algorithms for more detail.

Maximum: C12Fvc C12FE1 C12FE3

Reproducibility: C12RPFVC C12RPFE1 C12RPFE3
Time: C12FVCTM C12FE1TM C12FE3TM
Trial Number: C12FVCTR C12FE1TR C12FE3TR

The following variables are the flow rates extracted from the
maximum curve. Again, see SAS labels for definitions.

C12PEFR C12FF25 C12FF75 C12FRTR
C12MMEF C12FF50 C12FRTM

The header information from the Eagle II microprocessor strip
is also included in this file. This includes information such as
the technician, posture, room temperature, etc. See SAS labels for
definitions of these variables.

C12TECH C12SEX C12BPRES
C12POSTR C12RACE C12HGT
C12SPDT C12AGE C12TEMP

When performing longitudinal analysis of pulmonary function
data, note that for Exams 1 and 2, a maximum of five trials were
performed. In Exam 3, up to eight trials were performed, but only
data from the first five trials were used to maintain comparability
with past exams. Please contact the Coordinating Center if you

would like access to the complete data set for Exam 3.

C1F18 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Physical Activity Questionnaire)

Scoring is accomplished by adding a weighted sum of the number
of months for each activity below and again above the hours per
week cutpoint. Algebraically, where m is the number of months
below the cutpoint and n is the number of months above the
cutpoint, and the coefficients b and ¢ are described below. The
coefficient ¢ has been selected to be 3*b for each activity.

Heavy intensity score = = bi *m +c, * n,

for activities A-H

Moderate intensity score is similar in form, but summed over
activities I through M, and the total score is the sum of the two
subscores.

The coefficient b is the intensity level assigned to each
activity which is roughly the number of kilocalories thought to be
expended in one minute of activity by a 70 kg man. Intensities
were patterned after those used by Taylor et al and Folsom et al.
Exceptions are bicycling, which was set at an intensity code of 6
to reflect the wording "faster than 10 miles per hour"' and
vigorous work activity (which was not included in Taylor's or
Folsom's work), which was set at an intensity code of 5, somewhat
less than that for weight lifting.

C1F36 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(CES-D Scale)

The Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression (CES-D) scale
is a self-report measure designed to assess depressive symptomology
in the general population. This instrument was not established to
designate clinical endpoints; that is, it does not define clinical
depression. The items on the scale are symptoms associated with
depression and have been previously validated in longer scales.
The range of scores is 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating more
depressive symptoms.

C36HAPPY and C36LIFE were reverse scored.

C36SCORE is missing when one or more of the variables

C1F43 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Salt Taste Test substudy)

The salt taste test was administered to participants who
participated in the urine substudy. Due to a later start date for
the salt taste test, not all participants who completed in the
urine substudy have this data.

The Form 43 variables for the saltiness rating (C43SRTR1 -
C43SRTR5) and the pleasantness rating (C43PRTR1 - C43PRTR5) for
each of the five trials were dropped from the SAS data set to avoid
use of the wrong variables in analysis. These ratings have no
meaning independent of the sequence code which varied throughout
the exam cycle. The sequence code specified the order in which the
crackers (each with a different sodium level - 0.8%, 1.6%, 2.4%,
3.2% and 4.0%) were to be administered. An algorithm which takes
the sequence code into account was used to compute the saltiness
and pleasantness rating variables included in this data set. The
saltiness rating and the pleasantness rating variables for the
trial cracker (C43SRTRO and C43PRTRO) are included as recorded on
the form; the sodium level for the trial cracker was always 2.4%.

Questions 5 through 8 regarding salt use during cooking and at
the table have been asked on both Exam 1 and Exam 2 dietary
instruments. The variables from Exam 3 and the comparable

variables from previous exams are listed below.

C1CAROTD - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Vascular Distensibility substudy)

The Biosound 2000II ultrasound system was used to obtain high
resolution B-mode images of the common carotid artery. Arterial
wall echoes from the diametrically opposite media-adventitia
interfaces of the left common carotid artery were electronically
tracked for up to 10 consecutive cardiac cycles to provide mean
values of systolic and diastolic diameters at a site 1 cm proximal
to the origin of the bifurcation.

Brachial artery blood pressure was measured at four minute
intervals during the 30 minute B-mode examination using a Model
1846SX Dinamap Vital Signs Monitor.

By combining the systolic and diastolic diameters with
concurrent measurements of the blood pressures, several parameters
commonly used to describe arterial stiffness were computed. The
variables of interest are defined below.

Mean Systolic and Diastolic Blood Pressure (C1MSBP_ and C1MDBP)
C1MSBP and C1MDBP are the averages of the blood pressures

measured by the Dinamap device. Blood pressure readings were
expressed by mmHg. When calculating the arterial stiffness
parameters, they were used as SI (Systeme Internationale) Units,
that is, in kilopascals (1 kPa = 7.6 mmHg).

Arterial Distensibility (C1DISTEN)
C1DISTEN is the percent volume increase occurring within an

arterial segment during the cardiac cycle divided by the arterial
pulse pressure. It is independent of the length of the arterial
segment. The unit of measurement is %/kPa. It is calculated as:

Vascular Increase in volume
Distensibility =
Increase in pressure x Original volume

9/91

o/F1

C1DISTEN = 100 x [D(S)? - D(D)?] / [D(D)? (CIMSBP - C1MDBP) ]
where D(S) and D(D) are the mean systolic and diastolic
diameters averaged over as many as ten consecutive cardiac

cycles.

Arterial Compliance (C1COMP)

C1cOMP is the absolute volume increase occurring within an
arterial segment during the cardiac cycle divided by the arterial
pulse pressure. It is measured in units of mm?/kPa.

Increase in volume
Vascular Compliance =

Increase in pressure
C1COMP = m (D(S)* - D(D)?) / [4 (CIMSBP - C1MDBP) ]

Pressure-Strain Elastic Modulus (C1EP)

C1EP is defined as the arterial pulse pressure divided by the
circumferential arterial strain (C1STRAIN) imposed on the artery
during the cardiac cycle. C1EP is measured in kPa. It is
calculated as:

C1EP = (C1MSBP - C1MDBP) / C1STRAIN

where C1STRAIN is the fractional increase in arterial diameter
during the cardiac cycle and is calculated as:

C1STRAIN = [D(S) - D(D)] / D(D)

Stiffness Index (C1SI)
C1sI is the natural logarithm of the ratio of systolic blood

pressure to diastolic blood pressure divided by the CAS. Cl1SI is
less dependent on arterial blood pressure within individuals. SI
is a unitless quantity. It is calculated as:

C1SI = LOG (C1MSBP/C1MDBP) /C1STRAIN

NOTE: As an artery becomes stiffer, the distensibility and
compliance decrease while the pressure-strain elastic
modulus and stiffness index increase.

The B-mode data include three measurements for five artery
segments. The three measurements are: (1) mean intima-media
thickness of the far wall of the carotid; (2) maximum thickness;
and (3) far wall depth. The segments are labeled as left (L) or
right (R) and include common carotid-optimal view (CO), common
carotid-anterior (CA), common carotid-posterior (CP), bifurcation
(B) and internal (I). Variables in the data set are labeled as
Clxxxzzz, where xxx is the segment (e.g., LCO for left carotid-
optimal view) and zzz is the type of measurement (i.e., MEN for
mean, MAX for maximum and DEP for depth).

Preliminary analysis of this data set is underway at the
Minneapolis clinical center. The data documentation will be
updated as more information of interest to data users is made
available.

C1ECHO - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Echocardiography Data)

The variables in this file do not have a distinguishing first
character as do variables in other CARDIA SAS files (e.g.,
CO2AVGSY) .

In general, M-mode parameters begin with the letters MM,
Doppler with DP, color Doppler with CD, 2-D measures with A2 or A4
(indicating apical 2-chamber oor apical 4-chamber' views),
qualitative 2-D measures with Q2D, quality scores with 98, and
segmental wall motion measures with Q.

The first diagnosis code (DC1A) is the primary diagnosis code.
Additional diagnoses are found in variables DC2A, DC3A, DC4A.
Diagnosis codes are three digit codes. An explanation of each code
is included in this documentation. In addition to diagnosis codes,
there are also two digit "protocol deviation" codes found in the
variables DC2A, DC3A, DC4A (but not DC1A). We have also included
the description of each protocol deviation code.

A large number of missing values are found for the 2-D
measures (approximately 50%). This is a result of (1) difficulty
in obtaining a clear image for measurement and (2) the reduced
reading protocol taken on by the Echocardiography Reading Center
(ERC) beginning in March 1991. Note also that color Doppler is
only conducted on those for whom regurgitation is noted, thus
explaining the large number of missing values.

The most frequently used echocardiography parameters are:

LVMASS Left ventricular mass, M-mode

MMLAD Left atrial dimension, M-mode

DPMEPKV Mitral peak velocity, early diastole, Doppler

MMLVDD Left ventricular internal dimension in diastole, M-mode
MMLVDS Left ventricular internal dimension in systole, M-mode

9/91

Quality scores are as follows: 0 - view not attempted; 1 -view
attempted, poor quality; 2 - fair; 3 - good; 4 - excellent; and
5 - view attempted, but not measured.

Wall motion scores are as follows: 0 - segment not scored due
to poor visualization of that segment, or entire view not scored
(refer to protocol deviation codes for description); 1 - normal;
2 - hypokinetic; 3 - akinetic; 4 - dyskinetic; and 5 - aneurysmal.

There is one extreme value for the variable MMLVSSFS
(LVESS/LVFS ratio). Both values (LVESS and LVFS) were verified by
the ERC.

There are two studies with a technician ID of 0; both of these
should be technician ID 447.

Questions regarding the interpretation of the various echo
parameters should be directed to Dr. Jules Gardin at the
Echocardiography Reading Center (714-634-6545).

Test Codes:

The AMU contains preset criteria which define events which
might result in the AMU recording an erroneous BP. When a
detectable event occurred during a given reading, that observation
may contain up to three "Test Codes" generated by the AMU which
identify the event(s). These test codes can be used to identify BP
observations which should be excluded or individually screened for
validity. The values of these fields are contained in the
variables C42 TCl, C42_TC2, and C42_TC3.

Note that this flagging operation is not infallible; it is
possible for the AMU to pass, without complaint, an observation
which is actually incorrect. It is also possible for a Test Code
to accompany an observation which is otherwise apparently valid.

Following are descriptions of the Test Codes (TC) which may
occur in the data. These descriptions are copied, with permission,

a/Fi

from the Accutracker II (R) PC Report Generator Software user's
guide, pp. 17-19, copyright (c) Suntech Medical Instruments, Inc.

"TC=1" = STOP KEY ENDED THIS SAMPLE. This indicates that
someone pressed the stop button and ended a_ reading
prematurely. [CARDIA Note: In most cases, TC=1 readings
should be considered erroneous. ]

"TC=2" = ECG LEADS GIVING ERRATIC HEARTBEATS OR MISSING THEM
ALTOGETHER. Indicates a problem with the ECG connections and
the reading should be considered erroneous. If this code is
displayed while the patient is still in the office, consult
the list of causes below and attempt to correct the problem.

"TC=3" = K-SOUNDS TOO WEAK...REPOSITION MICROPHONE. Indicates
that the microphone is not detecting a distinct K-sound. The
most common cause of this is incorrect microphone placement.

"TC=4" = NOT ENOUGH K-SOUNDS DETECTED FOR THIS SAMPLE.
Indicates that not enough K-sounds were detected to make a
confident reading. This code occurs when a patient's K-sound
changes dramatically from one reading to another. Because the
Accutracker II has automatic gain adjustment, this code is
usually self-correcting. If a TC=4 is obtained in the office,
take a few additional readings and it will usually go away as
the gain automatically adjusts. In most cases, TC=4 readings
should be considered erroneous.

"TC=5" = MAJOR ARM MOVEMENT OCCURRED DURING THIS SAMPLE. This
codes is seen most often after the patient has left the
office. The amount of TC=5 and TC=6 readings that occur will
depend on how much the patient moves (bends) his arm as the
cuff is deflating. TC=5 readings are usually erroneous. By
informing your patients to not bend their arm during cuff
deflation, you will minimize the amount of TC=5 readings.

9/91

"TC=6" = MINOR ARM MOVEMENT OCCURRED DURING THIS SAMPLE. This
code will probably occur the most frequently due to the fact
that some arm movement during certain readings is inevitable.
Think of TC=6 as an attribute of the reading. In many cases,
a TC=6 will be a valid reading. If the reading is similar to
those prior and after, and the activity is similar, the
reading should be considered valid. If it does not correlate
well with other readings and the activity at the time,
consider it erroneous.

"TC=7" = LOOSE CUFF OR AIR LEAK. The Accutracker II has 50
seconds to inflate the cuff to the pressure programmed into
the AMU. If the cuff is very loose, if there is a hole ina
cuff, or if any of the hoses are disconnected, the desired
pressure will never be reached. If this code occurs in the
office, check to make sure that the cuff is on firmly but not
too tight. Also check to make sure that the patient cable is
connected snugly to the fitting on the cuff hose and that the
airhose portion of the patient cable is screwed firmly onto
the AMU. If after this, you still obtain a TC=7, contact
SUNTECH.

LW BT: This TC indicates that the batteries in the AMU were
too weak to take a reading. If this condition occurs, the AMU
will abort the scan, and cease all activity.

Figure 3 is a copy of one page of a completed diary edit

A. When To Complete An Edit Worksheet.

An ambulatory blood pressure activity diary edit worksheet
should be completed if a participant's diary meets one or more of
the following criteria:

1. Reading Time(s) Skipped.
Three or more of the times generated by the ABP monitor

(the pre-printed times appearing on the participant's
worksheet) are not recorded by the participant in the
diary.

See the section below, "About Time," for instructions on
how to edit one or two skipped readings.

Exception: Times generated by the monitor while the
participant was asleep should not be included in
evaluating this criterion.

2. 12-Hour Clock Used.
One or more times were recorded by the participant using
a 12-hour "AM/PM" clock, instead of a 24-hour clock.

3. Diary Times Don't Match Monitor Times.
The participant made a diary entry for each monitor
reading, but guessed at the time, or read the time from
something other than the monitor display. This would
result in the diary times disagreeing by a few minutes
with the times from the monitor.

4. "Extended" 24-Hour Clock Used.
The participant attempted to record times using a 24-hour
clock, but times greater than "23:59" were also recorded.

B. Questionable Diary Entries and Entries That Cannot Be Coded.

You may encounter one or more items ina diary that you are
unable to edit. If you do, circle and initial the space on the
edit worksheet where the item would normally be recorded. If there
is a cluster of "uneditable items", that is, an entire line or
several consecutive lines, you may enclose them as a group.
However, if you do this, be careful to enclose only items that you
cannot edit.

Also, keep track of how many uneditable items occur ina given
diary and, when finished transcribing all the editable items, write
the number of uneditable items in the space provided at the bottom
of the last page of the participant's edit worksheet.

Note that each blank that you cannot enter a response for
counts as an uneditable item. For example, a single diary line
that you cannot transcribe counts as five (5) items: the diary time
and each of the four following columns.

pattern, or if some notation ("Don't smoke.") appears in
the diary, you may complete the "Smoked" items on the
worksheet in the manner just described.

If a participant smokes, record the "1" and "2" responses
as entered in the "Smoked" column. If an entry for a
particular time is left blank, the corresponding entry on
the edit worksheet should be left blank.

G. When the Participant is Asleep.

The usual way of recording periods of sleep on the edit

worksheet would be to match an observation's diary time with its

monitor time, and transcribe whatever the participant has recorded

in his/her diary in the other columns. Some specific situations

that you may encounter are described in the following notes.

GhFi

Some participants will record an "Activity" entry of "2"
("Lying down, but awake") for a time immediately before
falling asleep. The diary's next entry will be for a
time after they wake the next day. If this is the case,
do not impute a "sleeping" entry.

Participants may skip one or more lines in the diary
between the last entry before sleeping and the first one
after waking. The diary entries on each side of this gap
should be matched to the monitor reading times printed on
the edit worksheet; that is, do not skip the same number
of lines on the edit worksheet as the participant skipped
in the diary (unless, of course, the diary and monitor
times match).

Some participants will record one or more "sleep" entries
like this:

Location Activity Stress Smoked
1 1 (or 2) 1 1

These lines are either "dummy" entries, or were recorded
at the time of monitor readings which caused them to wake
up. If this is the case, record them on the edit
worksheet on the line with the corresponding monitor
time(s).

In general, diary entries with times during "ordinary"
sleeping hours should be recorded as they appear in the
diary, but also should be flagged as questionable ("Q").

If the participant appears, from the location and
activity entries, to have awakened during the night and
remained awake and active for two or more successive
monitor readings, the diary entries should be considered
reliable and not flagged as questionable.

9/91

In the process of creating the data set for Form 18 (Physical
Activity History), the Coordinating Center discovered that
approximately 250 occupational codes were erroneously coded as
industry codes by clinic personnel. The clinical centers have been
sent a list of participant IDs with the erroneous codes; all of
these files will be pulled and recoded. The corrected data will be
included in the next release of the Exam 3 data tape.

There are several ages of children and/or stepchildren that do
not seem feasible given the age range of our participants. All
such ages have been verified by the clinical centers.

A number of discrepancies between reported education at Exam
2 and Exam 3 (e.g, a lower number of years of education at the
third exam than at the second exam or increases of more than three
years) have been identified indicating that one should use caution
in using this reported education variable in analyses. The lack of
a standardized probing protocol may be the explanation for these
inconsistencies. One clinic has reported examples of problems

which were observed in reviewing some of the records sent as edits.

ate Vo-tech/business education - sometimes counted and

2. GED - sometimes checked as 12 years of education and
sometimes not.

Jo College - specific degree given various years of "credit"
~ €.g., AA degree marked as 13 years when finished in
less than the usual 14 years.

4. College - 2 Bachelor degrees, 20 years of education
checked. There appears to be a tendency to give people

C1APOB - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Apolipoprotein B)

This file contains apolipoprotein B measurements of frozen
Year 5 plasma speciments from 597 CARDIA participants, analyzed
by the CARL Clinical Laboratory at the Duke University Medical
Center. The sample of participants was based on the following
criteria: present for both Year 5 and Year 10 exams, fasted at
least 12 hours, no recent illness, and no current
antihypercholestorolemic or anithypertensive medication usage.
After these criteria were met, approximately 150 participants

from each race-sex group were randomly selected across all sites.

For 3 of the participants, a second vial was inadvertently
pulled and analyzed. In keeping with past decisions regarding
laboratory results, the first observations were kept and the

second observations were dropped.

There are a few important considerations regarding these
data as received from the CARL Clinical Laboratory. These
considerations are discussed in the attached memo from Dr. Bruce

Lobaugh at the CARL Clinical Laboratory.

J apologize for the lengthy delay in getting these to you. As I mentioned during our last phone
conversation, we found many specimens to be of suboptimal quality (partially clotted or jelled; fibrin

C1F31AC and C1F31B - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Injury Ancillary Study)

The injury ancillary data exists in two data sets. C1F31AC,
which contains the data from parts A and C of the form, and C1F31B,
which contains data from part B of the form. Parts A and C were to
be completed regardless of whether or not a participant had an
injury since their last CARDIA exam, while part B was to be
completed only by those participants who had an injury since their
last CARDIA exam.

C1F31AC contains just one record per participant. No edits
were done on the injury event text fields; Therefore, the injuries
may be listed in more than one way (eg. back sprain or back
strain). There are some instances where a portion of the date of
injury (i.e., the day, month and/or year) is missing. If this
occurs, the date variables (C31A_DT1 through C31A_DT6) cannot be
computed. For this reason, the day, month and year variables for
the injury event are included in this file to allow maximum
flexibility with the data.

C1F31B may contain multiple records per participant. A
separate record exists for each body part affected by an injury
event (i.e., if a participant had 2 injury events and 3 body parts
affected for each injury there will be 6 records for that
participant). The variable, C31BNPTS (number of body parts per
injury event) was calculated in order to read in the data.

All data collected in conjunction with the injury ancillary
study were reviewed by an expert in injury prevention and control,
Dr. Susan G. Gerberich. Forms were recoded, if necessary, in
accordance with injury analysis criteria commonly used in the
injury prevention and control field. For Minneapolis participants,
ongoing record review and data changes were made during the
examination period as Dr. Gerberich is located in Minneapolis. The
data collected in Oakland was reviewed periodically and recommended

data changes were sent back to Oakland.

C1F18 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Physical Activity Questionnaire)

Scoring is accomplished by adding a weighted sum of the number
of months for each activity below and again above the hours per
week cutpoint. Algebraically, where m is the number of months
below the cutpoint and n is the number of months above the
cutpoint, and the coefficients b and ¢ are described below. The
coefficient c has been selected to be 3*b for each activity.

Heavy intensity score = & bi *m +c, * n,;
for activities A-H

Moderate intensity score is similar in form, but summed over
activities I through M, and the total score is the sum of the two
subscores.

The coefficient b is the intensity level assigned to each
activity which is roughly the number of kilocalories thought to be
expended in one minute of activity by a 70 kg man. Intensities
were patterned after those used by Taylor et al and Folsom et al.
Exceptions are bicycling, which was set at an intensity code of 6
to reflect the wording "faster than 10 miles per hour"' and
vigorous work activity (which was not included in Taylor's or
Folsom's work), which was set at an intensity code of 5, somewhat
less than that for weight lifting.

In addition to the physical activity score, three indices were
developed: (1) Work Index (C18WKIDX); (2) Sport Index (C18SPIDX); and
(3) Leisure-Time Index (C18LTIDX). These indices were calculated based
on questions added from the Baecke Questionnaire of Habitual Physical
Activity (Am J Clin Nutr, 1982, 36:932-942) modified for use in the
ARIC study.

The algorithm for the Work Index (C18WKIDX) incorporates the
occupational code obtained on the Sociodemographic Questionnaire

(CO3CODE). The activity level for each occupation was coded as low,

9/91
medium, or high by the ARIC study. Low activity was given a score of
1, medium activity a score of 3 and high activity a score of 5.
C18WKIDX = [Activity level of occupation + (6 - C1801STD) +
C1802STD + C1803WLK + C1804LFT + C1805TRE + C1806SWT +
C1807WPH]/8
NOTE: The large number of missing values for C18WKIDX is due to
errors in the coding of occupation on Form 3 (Sociodemographic
Questionnaire). Approximately 250 participant records were coded with
industry codes instead of the appropriate occupation codes. Recoding
will be performed and this data set will updated with the next release
of the data tape.
The questions from the Baecke Questionnaire regarding physical
activity were not included on the CARDIA Form 18. In place of the
simple sport score from the Baecke instrument, the algorithm for the
Sport Index (C18PIDX) uses the quintiles of the physical activity score
from Exam 1 (A18TOTAL); the cutpoints for the quintiles were scored 1
through 5.
C18SPIDX = (Physical activity quintile + C18P1WPH + C18P2SWT +
C18P3SPT)/4
The Leisure-Time Index (C18LTIDX) was calculated using the
following algorithm:
C18LTIDX = [(6 - C18P4WTV) + C18P5WLK + C18P6BIK + C18P7MIN]/4

C1F39 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Urine 24 Hour Substudy)

Changes to Form 39

During January, 1991, the Coordinating Center discovered that
it would be useful to add the end dates for each collection period
to the form. Because this change was made mid-way through the
exam, calculations for some participants must be done differently
from those for other participants.

Edits Suggested by Review Committee

During January, 1991, it was found that there were many errors
made in recording the dates and times of the urine collections.
These problems often resulted in an incorrect calculation of the
length of the collection; thus, none of the remaining data would be
valid for analyses. A committee was formed to review each
problematic case and make recommendations for any changes to be
made to these cases. The changes largely involved problems with
times around midnight. Both respondents and technicians were
confused by early morning times in two ways; first, whether
midnight was 12:00 AM or 12:00 PM and second, that early morning

times occur on a different date than late evening times.

The committee made two types of recommendations. The first
were changes to the times and/or dates that at least four of the
five members agreed upon. These changes are marked by a flag
variable C39EDIT (0=No changes; 1=Changes). The second type of
recommendation involved cases for which the problems in collection
dates and times could not be resolved. These cases are marked by
a flag variable C39PROB; the committee advises deleting any
participant with C39PROB=1 from all analyses.

All committee changes were made within the SAS code that
created the data set. The original sequential file retains the
values entered on the form.

Urine samples were recorded as heights (cm). The
following algorithm transforms these heights into
volumes, based on the standardized 1 liter bottles used
throughout the study. (Heights of individual samples are
dropped from the data set.)

NOTE: After July 5, 1990, the Oakland clinical center
began using disposable bottles. These bottles are
slightly wider than the bottles the other centers used.
Thus, 0.8 centiliters is added to the volumes for all
Oakland participants who were examined after July 4,
1990.

IF HGT < 1 THEN VOL = 1.88 * HGT**3;

IF HGT >= 1 AND HGT < 2 THEN VOL = -2.52 +
(3.87 * HGT) + (0.544 * HGT**2);

IF HGT >= 2 AND HGT < 16 THEN VOL = -4.46 +
(6.06 * HGT) - (.00716 * (HGT —- 9)**2)

(.000599 * (HGT - 9)**3) +
(.000114 * (HGT - 9)**4);
IF HGT >= 16 AND HGT < 16.7 THEN VOL = 11.04 +
(5.09 * HGT);
IF HGT >= 16.7 THEN VOL = 98;
* ADD 0.8 CENTILITERS FOR OAKLAND DISPOSABLE BOTTLES;
IF CENTER=4 AND EXAMDATE > '04JUL90'D AND VOL > 0
THEN VOL = VOL + 0.8;

collection volume and collection length variables from Form 39
(Urine substudy). These were used to obtain an adjusted value for
GMP.

OVERVIEW

While increases in coronary heart disease risk factors occur
in young adulthood in conjunction with significant changes in
physiological measures and in lifestyle, the interrelationships
among these risk factors and changes have not been rigorously
investigated. Both epidemiologic and clinical research in coronary
heart disease have increased our awareness that some risk factors
for disease such as obesity, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia
many be partially determined by genetic factors or behaviors which
are formed in infancy, childhood, and adolescence. Studies to date
also suggest that some of the coronary heart disease risk factors
do not change dramatically before the late teenage years and that
differences in characteristics by sex or race emerge and are most
pronounced after this time. However, relatively little work has
been done to identify the characteristics of young adult life which
may be precursors to, or coincident with, the increase in risk
factors prior to middle age.

Cross-sectional data, for example, suggest that weight gain
is pronounced during the late teens through age 30, particularly
in males, and that positive relationships exist between weight and
lipoprotein fractions during these ages. The reasons for, and
consequences of, this increase in adiposity need further
investigation. The interaction of life events, behavior, changes
in physical activity, and dietary intake that may influence weight
gain and lipoprotein levels should be assessed as well as the
relative importance of weight gain in relationship to risk factor
changes during this age span.

Investigators have examined the consistency of blood pressure
levels in children to determine whether "tracking" occurs into the
teenage years. The results of these studies have raised other
interesting and important questions. Is there evidence for
"tracking" of other coronary risk factors? Does "tracking" persist
into young adult life, a time during which dramatic changes in

oVR - 1

&/FO

lifestyle are often taking place? Are the changes a function of
these changes?

An important component of this study is the study of young
blacks. Since the Black Health Task Force on High Blood Pressure
Control pointed out the lack of knowledge about coronary heart
disease in blacks as applied to this country, a greater focus on
the nature of disease in blacks has been a topic of increasing
consideration.

"Coronary Artery Risk Factor Development in Young Adults"
(CARDIA) is the study of the evolution of coronary heart disease
risk in a cohort of black and white men and women initially 18-30
years old. Such studies will not only contribute to our
understanding of the development of atherosclerotic disease, but
more importantly, help to suggest strategies for prevention before
individual lifestyle patterns become well established.

The original specific hypotheses set forth by each clinical

site may be found in the protocol documents from the previous two
CARDIA examinations.

OBJECTIVES

The overall goals of this study are:

1.

To document at baseline and after one or more biennial
intervals, risk factors and changes for coronary heart disease
(CHD) in young (black and white) adults, 18-30 years old.

To identify lifestyles during this age span, which influence
these changes in risk factors. The interrelationships among
risk factors and lifestyles, and changes in these
characteristics will be considered.

The secondary objectives of this study are:

1.

To observe age-related trends in risk factors during young
a@gulthood and to compare cross-sectional with longitudinal
findings.

To perform sub-population analyses on, sex, race, or
sociodemographic groupings, and to compare trends and
processes involved in risk factor development between these
subgroups.

To develop and apply effective methods of follow-up during
these young adult years to achieve maximum participation of
the study populations.

The objectives of each clinical center are:

1.

To re-examine at least 80% of the 5115 participants enrolled
in the study.

To maintain, via mail and phone calls at semi-annual intervals
during the follow-up period, contact with each participant in
order to maximize the return rate for future examinations.

To assess risk factors for CHD in these participants.

I. PURPOSE

The blood drawing station is designed to obtain a blood sample
to test for important risk factors for cardiovascular disease and
for other blood parameters of interest to CARDIA. It is
potentially a difficult station because of the anxiety caused in
many people by blood drawing and the potential for injury.
However, if carefully and professionally done, it provides a
positive safe experience for the participant. The blood drawing
station will take approximately 10 minutes of the participant's

time.

This protocol was designed as a training manual for the
phlebotomist at the clinical centers.

II. DESCRIPTION
A. Tests
The following tests are planned for the Year 5 exam:
1. LIPIDS and LIPOPROTEINS: total cholesterol,
triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, and Lp(a).
2. FIBRINOGEN; and
3. DNA (to be extracted from white blood cells for storage)

The methods of measurement for each of these tests is found in the
CARDIA Laboratory Operations Manual and the rationale for
assessment is found in the CARDIA Protocol.

B. Restrictions

The Lipid Research Clinic's Manual of Operations identifies
several factors which may influence lipid and lipoprotein values.
The following procedures are designed to standardize collection of
samples which assure the appropriateness of the measure.

1. Blood should be drawn with the participant in a seated
position. The reclining position should be allowed only
in extreme circumstances (e.g. history of fainting).

2. Elevations of 2-5% in lipid measures are observed after

two minutes of continuous venous occlusion. Therefore,

3. The state of fasting clearly influences parameters such
as triglycerides. CARDIA participants should have fasted
for 12 hours prior to blood drawing. However, blood will
be drawn on all participants, regardiess of fasting
status.

4. Participants are instructed to avoid vigorous exercise
on the day of their examination.

5. No particular restriction need be made for smoking since
the blood drawing station will be approximately one half
hour after clinic arrival.

6. Blood drawing should occur early in the CARDIA visit but
following the blood pressure measurement. It must
precede the snack.

Site: The blood drawing should take place in an isolated room
or one enclosed by dividers. Temperature should be 65-75° F.
There should be no direct sunlight. The recliner should be placed
in a space sufficient to allow the chair to fully recline. The
chair may be elevated on a wooden box to facilitate comfort of the
phlebotomist when drawing the blood.

The room should be equipped with all the necessary supplies.
A table or counter should be prepared with the materials and vials
needed for blood handling and aliquoting. The centrifuge,
refrigerator and freezer should be nearby.

Staff: This station is staffed with a technician with
documented class time and experience in phlebotomy. Certification
will occur at the centralized training session. Recertification
will occur once as requested by the Coordinating Center, and will
be authorized by the clinic supervisor or medical director. The
technician should be properly attired in a white laboratory coat.
Long hair should be tied back. Gloves should be used at all times

BLOOD PRESSURE MANUAL OF PROCEDURES
HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE (HYPERTENSION)

As blood pressure rises, so does risk of ischemic heart disease
and its complications. The range of normal blood pressures is wide.
Even within the "normal" group, risk increases as the upper limits
are approached. Usually, blood pressures are expressed as systolic
pressure/diastolic pressure; values exceeding 140/90 mmHg are
considered to be hypertensive for adults. Middle-aged persons with
a diastolic blood pressure of 90-104 mmHg or greater (so-called
"mild" hypertension) have a risk of heart attack that is about 70
percent higher than that of persons with a diastolic pressure under
80 mmHg (normal value). Persons with a diastolic blood pressure
exceeding 104 mmHg (moderately severe to severe hypertension) have
a risk more than twice that of those with a normal value.
Hypertension is an especially strong risk factor for stroke and, to
a lesser extent, for peripheral vascular disease.

Blood pressure is measured in a resting state, using three
measurements with a random zero sphygmomanometer. The random zero
machine has two advantages over the fixed zero manometer. Digit
preference does not appear in the data, though it may still exist in
the reading itself, and be randomized out of the data by the use of
the randomly chosen zero point. More importantly, it deprives the
blood pressure technician of knowledge of the actual value, and
therefore of the ability to make judgements about blood pressure
levels for readings close to critical values such as 90 diastolic.
It should be noted, however, that the random zero machines tend to
yield blood pressures which are about 1.5 mmHg less than those
obtained when using a fixed zero machine. Within person variation
in blood pressure is substantial; three replicate readings tends to

reduce this variation.

OVERVIEW OF BLOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT

The purpose of blood pressure measurements in CARDIA is: (1)
to compare levels of this risk factor between blacks and whites; (2)
to observe the interaction with other CHD risk factors over time; and
(3) to observe variables that will predict changing levels of blood
pressure.

Blood pressure measurements (systolic and fifth phase diastolic)
will be recorded with a random-zero (RZ) sphygmomanometer by trained
and certified technicians at baseline and subsequent intervals. The
methods of measurement will be standardized - as set out in the
Manual of Operations. The pulse rate for 30 seconds will be recorded
with each blood pressure measurement.

The cuff is to be inflated to 30 mmHg above the highest seated
systolic reading. As many confounders of blood pressure measurement
as possible will be controlled by standard settings and technique of
blood pressure measurement or by recording uncontrollable confounding
factors. Thus, the following will be recorded:

1). Time of day (AM/PM)

2). Room temperature

3). Arm circumference at the midpoint of the upper arm
4). Technician I.D. number

The blood pressure will be measured three times on each occasion.
Caffeine (from tea, coffee, cola beverages), eating, heavy physical
activity, smoking (30 minute proscription) and alcohol intake will
be proscribed for two hours prior to recording blood pressure level.
The requirement for a fasting state in the basic exam will assure
much of the dietary compliance. Recording of current drug intake,
including medications affecting blood pressure, non-prescription
drugs and "recreational" drugs will be made on medical history forms
on the day of the examination.

because of the known, but ill-understood, relationship of alcohol

BLOOD PRESSURE TRAINING/CERTIFICATION

Standardized training sessions are required for blood pressure
measurement. Technicians will be trained centrally prior to the
Year 5 exam in two full-day sessions with subsequent training taking
place in individual clinics. Training methods consist of a pre- and
post-test, audio cassette tape instruction and Y-tube stethoscope
testing. Blood pressure observers will be trained to observe and
record the onset of first and fifth phase Korotkoff sounds. Each
clinical center will have one blood pressure trainer (designated as
the Blood Pressure Supervisor) who will have the responsibility for
training any new blood pressure observers and for conducting
recertification procedures.

At the beginning of the first session, a description and
demonstration of the correct BP procedure is given. Trainees are to
listen to the first (training) tape, taking the test sequences until
they are comfortable with what they are listening to. Then, they
take the second tape until they have passed the test. After passing
the second tape, they are given the third tape test. Alternated with
the tapes are actual live practices under the instruction and
observation of the training supervisor. Some live practices may be
done with a standard stethoscope, but most should employ the Y-tube
stethoscope. The optimum size of a group is eight. This allows four
people to do live practices while four are on the tape training
device. The group can interchange and practice on each other.

After the first day of training, each trainee should be given
a cuff and manometer (no stethoscope) to take home and practice just

the control of the valve. This can be done by wrapping the cuff on
a jar or bottle and alternately pumping up and dropping the mercury
at a steady rate of 2 mm per second. After two or three sessions,
they could also be given a stethoscope to practice on family and/or
friends. This out-of-class practice is very important to build
confidence. The time allowed for class is not enough with outside
practice time.

Once each trainee has passed the third tape, he or she should
do at least two live readings with the training supervisor on the
Y-tube stethoscope. The readings should agree within 4 mm and the
average should agree within 3 mm. If they do not, the trainee needs
additional practice with tapes and live subjects. The training
supervisor should also assure that the trainee understands and
follows proper procedures. If the trainees are also to use the
Random Zero device, additional time should be allowed for instruction

and mastering that procedure.

Prior to certification, each technician will be tested for

Observers are certified after passing the second and third tape tests

The Coordinating Center will notify each clinical center when

STANDARDIZED CLINIC PROCEDURES

It will take approximately 10-15 minutes to make three blood
pressure measurements including the initial five minute rest and
recording of pulse rate. The blood pressure measurements will be
made very early in the clinic visit sequence immediately following
the greeting and informed consent. Measurements will be made before
the physical exam, blood drawing, or any potentially stressful
interview. The blood pressure measurements on each participant will
be made in a separate room or, at minimum, in an area properly
screened from all other activity and other participants.

Correct measurement of indirect blood pressure is of the utmost
importance and concern to the success of this study. It is essential
that the standardized format described below for measuring blood
pressure on the Random Zero be followed exactly.

Major differences in blood pressure measurement methodology among
health professionals from several countries have been observed
despite the fact that written international recommendations of blood
pressure measurement were established in 1939 by a joint committee
of the American Heart Association and the Cardiac Society of Great
Britain and Ireland. It is also well known that precision is
essential for valid comparisons of blood pressure between groups of
people and in individuals on different occasions. A number of
elements can be identified in measuring blood pressure and each is
explained briefly in subsequent subsections of this chapter ending
with a subsection on technique that is presented in detail. Study
organizers consider all of these elements equally important and ask
that the strictest attention be paid to each in order to insure that
the blood pressure measurments have a standard and high level of

accuracy and precision.

A. SOUND
For purposes of this study, SBP level is recorded at the level
when phase 1 Korotkoff sounds are first heard and DBP is recorded
at the beginning of phase 5 with disappearance of sounds. The
onset of phase 1 and 5 sounds are the points of clinical
importance.

B. EQUIPMENT
The following blood pressure measurement equipment will be used
and standardized for the study: stethoscope, random-zero and
standard sphygmomanometers, cuffs and bulb.

1. STETHOSCOPE
A standard Littman stethoscope having a bell will be used.
Korotkoff sounds are best heard with the bell because of
their low pitch. Stethoscope tubing should be about 10-12
inches from the bell piece to "Y" branching. This length

BP - ?

4/90

provides optimal acoustical properties and allows the

observer to read the sphygmomanometer at eye level and in

a comfortable position. Earpieces should fit comfortably

and snugly in the ears. Four points should be observed in

using the stethoscope.

a. The ear pieces should be directed downwards and
forwards into the external ear canal.

b. The ear pieces should be tight enough to exclude
outside sound but not so tight that they cause
discomfort.

c. The bell of the stethoscope should be placed lightly

on the skin overlying the brachial artery -
immediately below the cuff and medial to the cubital
fossa above the medial epicondyle of the radius
posterior to the biceps muscle. Light pressure
accentuates low-pitched sound and avoids compression
murmurs. Pressing too heavily with the stethoscope
over the brachial artery can also produce sounds that
can be heard by the observer by reducing the internal
diameter of the brachial artery in the same manner as
the cuff. This causes turbulent flow in the artery
and a murmur can be heard and may prolong the apparent
duration of phase 4.

d. The valve between the bell and diaphragm should be
turned in the correct direction.

SPHYGMOMANOMETERS

Standardized Hawksley random-zero instruments will be used

for all clinic visits. Standard Baum manometers will be

used for determining peak inflation level.

CUFFS AND BULBS

Clinics will have four standardized cuffs available - adult,
pediatric, large adult, and thigh cuff (by the Baum
Company). Proper size of the cuff is essential for accurate

blood pressure measurement. To select proper cuff size,

STAFF PREPARATION FOR PARTICIPANT'S VISIT

A minimum of three clinic staff persons will be responsible for
measuring blood pressure. They need not be health professionals, but
they must be trained and certified in blood pressure measurement and
technique. Observers should have some experience in relating to and
dealing with people. While it is difficult to standardize demeanor,
the observer should strive to present a non-discriminatory,
reassuring and professional approach. The observers will be required
to have a simple vision test in addition to the training process.

It should be remembered that participation in the study is a
voluntary procedure. Participants will be given full explanation and
instructions about the preparation for the blood pressure examination
as well as an opportunity for discussion. The setting for making
repeated blood pressure measurements must be standardized for clinic
visits. The examination should take place in a quiet room where no
other activity is taking place and where temperature fluctuations are
minimal. Clinic scheduling procedures will establish consistent
appointment times to minimize problems that stem from systematic
variation of blood pressure during the day.

Once the participant has been given instructions and

explanations, the equipment has been checked, and he has been sitting

in a quiet and relaxing room with no change of position or posture,
