Measurements 2 and 3: Have the participant raise
measurement arm for five seconds. Wait at least 30
seconds between readings. Repeat measurement as in 1
and disconnect cuff.

PROCEDURE FOR RECORDING

If for any reason the observer is unable to determine (or

forgets) any phase, write a dash in the space on the form. This is

the correct way to indicate missed information. If an entire reading

is missed,

completely deflate the cuff and start over with a

replacement reading. However, under no other circumstances may a

replacement reading be obtained. Always wait at least 30 seconds

between readings. After averaging the second and third corrected

R-Z readings, record the average on the forn.

Since a participant's blood pressure may be influenced by reading

the artificially uncorrected blood pressures as recorded by the

technician, the technician should tell the participant that the blood

pressure will be corrected and reported to him/her immediately
following the completion of all three measurements. When the blood
pressure is reported to the participant, the technician shoulda
indicate that the measure is normal or high. The blood pressure and
the indication of "normal" or “high" should be done prior to the
administration of Form 35, Knowledge, Attitudes and Behavior
Questions, in all clinics.

Look at the mercury columns to be certain that there is not a
lot of oxidation accumulated, and check the cap on column.
Check the standard manometer to be sure the mercury stands at

Visually check for beads of mercury on both devices.

Visually check the hoses on both devices and cuffs for cracked

The following description of RZ checks should be done only when there

seems to be a problem with a device, and then only in a proper

cleaning and repair setting, such as a chem lab where people know how

to handle mercury and have the proper equipment.

Check cap of manometer column to be sure it fits properly and is
tight. The 0 ring or seal must be seated correctly. Clean cap
of any mercury beads or dust. The cap should be firmly finger
tight. Any time the mercury seems to 'bounce' in the column of
either a standard manometer or random zero (RZ) manometer, it may
be due to a loose cap. Check the opening. If it becomes
blocked, the mercury column falls too slowly due to a vacuum
effect. This may result in false high readings and an
erratically oscillating column. This procedure should be carried
out for both standard manometers and RZ's.

Remove back of case (two screws at top of face and two at bottom
rear of case). Swing back from the left around the thumb screw
on the right side. Check for spring placement -- it should be
in line. Tighten all screws except the one holding the bellows
plate in place.

Wrap an arm cuff around a bottle or can.

With reservoir valve (newer models do not have a reservoir valve)
open and bellows valve closed, pump mercury to top of column
(270-290 mmHg). If the mercury will hold at a steady level for
10-15 seconds or drops 2-4 mm, that system is airtight.

With the high pressure still in the system, close the reservoir
valve and disconnect cuff to see if that valve will hold steady
pressure. If a leak is discovered in the reservoir valve, remove
hose and valve (with Allen wrench). Valve handle unscrews or
lifts off. There are two 0 rings on the valve stem. Clean stem
and replace 0 rings. Use stopcock grease on 0 rings and valve.
If the closed reservoir valve is tight, but there was a leak with
it open, check the inflation assembly. There may be a leak in
the bulb, valve, or cuff. To test the inflation assembly,
immerse each section, especially valves and tubing connections
in water while the pressure is high and watch for air bubbles.
To test the tubing of the mercury reservoir, put soapy water on
it. Most leaks occur at or near tubing connections or from
valves. If a valve leaks, sometimes a shot of silicone lubricant
on the thumb screw and worked in will solve the problem.
Otherwise it may need to be replaced. Tubing leaks near a
connector can be repaired by removing the connector, cutting 1/2
to 3/4 inches and replacing the connector. Lubricate a sharp
knife with soapy water to make the cut, and similarly lubricate
the cut tube to make it easier to re-attach.

Turn RZ with back toward you. With bellows valve open, retract
mercury to just below the plexiglass valve chamber. Close the
bellows valve, pump mercury to top and visually check that
leakage does not occur at that valve point. If mercury does rise
into the chamber, the valve needs repair. Replacing 0 rings on
that valve can be done locally if someone is qualified to do it.
It is a more difficult job than on the reservoir valve.
Otherwise it should be sent to Baum. A serious leak in this
valve can affect BP readings.

Whenever the manometer tube seems dirty in the area of your

‘zeroes' or if the mercury seems to hang up there, the tube

should be cleaned. A dirty tube can affect 'zero' readings. To

clean tube, set cam at lowest zero. Pump up, close bellows
valve, release pressure. This leaves little mercury in the
column. Tilt manometer, getting rest of mercury out of glass

and into reservoir. Close reservoir valve. Lean manometer at
angle so that no mercury is in glass. Remove tube and clean tube
and seats. Check to be sure the rubber gaskets are seated
properly. Replace tube.

This procedure should only be done by a qualified person in a
controlled setting. The manometer should be set in a catch basin
so that no mercury can escape and there should be a trap-type

vacuum pump available to pick up any small spills.
Check "maximum" and "minimum" zeroes and of bellows and cam

function. (This needs to be done only if there are doubts about
the values of those zeroes or functions; or if mercury has been
added or lost).

a. Release all pressure and open the bellows valve. The
large thumb wheel with the black rubber "tire" and the
cam against which it is pressed should turn freely
without binding. If they do bind, bring in the RZ.

b. Inflate the system while watching the large (about 2 -
1/4" diameter) disc above and to the left of the
bellows valve chamber. (Bellows valve is still open.)
As pressure rises you will see the disc, a piston,
pushed toward the back plate until a ring around the
center of the disc touches the forward rim of the cam.
That rim is tapered, and thus determines how far the
piston can move, depending on the position of the
taper in relation to the ring at the center of the
piston ~ a matter of chance in normal operation of the
RZ. The distance that the piston can move before
being stopped by the cam determines the volume of
mercury in the bellows chamber, hence the volume of
Hg left in the rest of the manometer.

c. To read "maximum" zero, release pressure with bellows
valve still open. Turn the cam so that the point of

4/90

its taper nearest the piston will be hit by the ring
of the piston. (It may take an inflation and
deflation or two before you find the correct cam
position, which allows the minimum volume of mercury
in the bellows chamber, hence maximum mercury in the
rest of the system.) Inflate to about 200 mmHg, close
the bellows valve, release pressure and read the zero
as usual; this is the "maximum". Repeat the procedure
once or twice, checking the cam position to make sure
you get the same reading. Note that this is not a
fixed value for if you were to inflate to 300 before
closing the bellows valve, the reading would be lower;
and inflation to 120-130 would give a higher value.
For this reason, always record what you read when
taking blood pressures.

"Minimum" zero is measured as in c above, except that
the cam is turned so that the piston can travel its
maximum. It is usually close to 20 mm lower than the
"maximum" and should not be closer than about 4 mm to
the 0 on the manometer tube scale.

Replace the rear case, putting it over the thumb wheel
first. Start all four screws before tightening any.
Take care not to cross thread.

After a series of BP readings or before transport open
the bellows valve to drain Hg from that chamber, then
close it and the reservoir valve. Between readings,
the bellows valve should be left on "open" so that
pressure on the bellows is not left in the device.

RETENTION OF PARTICIPANTS FOR THE YEAR 5 EXAM

OVERVIEW OF SCHEDULING PROCEDURES

The following retention plan is designed to maximize the

number of Year 0 exam participants re-examined five years later at

the Year 5 exam. The plan also includes steps for monitoring this

process.

1.

Each center generates a PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST by running
the program provided by the Coordinating Center. This list
orders participants by their expected Year 5 exam date which
is in the order of their participation during the first exam.
The Coordinating Center provides each center with a > 50 MILE
LIST which includes participants who have moved 2 50 miles
from their "home" center (the site of the Year 0 exam).
Participants on this list will henceforth be referred to as
2 50 mile participants.

INITIAL CONTACT LETTERS are mailed to participants selected
from the PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST and 2 50 MILE LIST at
least one week before scheduling attempts begin. (Centers
may also choose to send additional materials such as RETURN
POSTCARDS indicating ideal times to reach participants, etc.).
Recruiters make Initial Telephone Contacts with participants
selected from the participant lists and invite them to take
the Year 5 exam. The Initial Telephone Contact includes:
Introduction

Description of the Year 5 exam

Pregnancy questions

Invitation/Scheduling

Arrangements for expense reimbursement

Arrangements for reminder phone call

Review of pre-exam instructions

DETAILED INSTRUCTIONS TO RECRUITERS

PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST

The PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST can be generated using
the "expected participant" program in the CARDIA Year 5 exam
scheduling utilities directory on the CARDIA recruitment
computer. This list can be generated for any week of the exam
cycle and includes all participants whose target date is
included in the week(s) requested excluding any participant
whose status is classified as an S (scheduled), D (died), or
E (examined). This list includes the following information:
CARDIA ID, target week, birthdate, sex, race and level of
education for the participant. Space is provided on the form
for recruiters to record the participant's name, scheduled

exam date, phone number and any comments.

Once the data from the PARTICIPANT SCHEDULING LIST is
entered (i.e., status code changes and scheduled examination
dates), a list of "Participants to be Examined" for a given
week or number of weeks can be generated locally by each
center. Recruiters can generate an OVERDUE PARTICIPANT LIST
using the Coordinating Center program which includes those
participants not examined and who are four weeks past their
expected exam date. (Recruitment information will be
transmitted by phone or floppy disk to the data entry PC from
the scheduling system PC; thus, the "Participants to be
Examined" and other retention reports can be run on either

computer.)

2 50 MILE LIST

Most of the CARDIA participants will still live near
their home center during the third exam cycle and will not
need to travel extensively to participate. Others,
particularly those who have moved 2 50 miles away, are
pregnant, or are students away at school may require special
recruitment procedures and separate tracking. The primary

acceptable interval between the first and third exams. As
soon as it is feasible, starting with the participants who
were on the > 50 MILE LIST at their 54 month (or most recent)
follow-up contact, recruiters should initiate contact with
these participants by sending out initial contact letters and
making initial telephone calls to invite them to the third
exam. By using the participants contacted at 54 months first,
the best chance of examining the > 50 mile participants within
the one month target window for the Year 5 exam will be
afforded since these participants will be due for their exams
first.

The = 50 MILE LIST includes the following information:
CARDIA ID, target week, race, birthdate, sex, level of
education and space for comments. The Coordinating Center
will provide each center with a list which will be updated

had moved = 50 miles from their home center as of their last

The purpose of the Initial Telephone Contact is to

SPECIAL ARRANGEMENTS FOR PARTICIPANTS = 50 MILES AWAY

A great majority of the participants will be brought to
their home centers for the third exam within their window and
without a reimbursement of exam related expenses more than $20
or the center specific amount. The others may require special
procedures and tracking as they may require a broad window,
be examined at an alternate center and/or need to be
reimbursed more than $20 for actual travel expenses incurred.
It is expected that the majority of difficult to schedule
participants will be so because they have moved far from their

home center.

Data from the Follow-up Contacts indicate that at least
15% of the sample will live at least 50 miles from their home
center by the time they are due for the third exam. The 2 50
MILE LIST includes these participants. The following are
general guidelines for making special arrangements that
maximize the number of 2 50 mile participants that will be
brought back for Year 5 exam while minimizing the costs.
PLEASE NOTE THAT IT IS PREFERABLE TO EXAMINE PARTICIPANTS
OUTSIDE THEIR WINDOWS THAN TO PAY THEIR TRAVEL EXPENSES.

Recruiters should schedule each 2 50 mile participant
according to the following priorities:

actual travel expenses above $20.

FOLLOW-UP CONTACT PROCEDURES

Retention of the cohort is a continual focus within the CARDIA
Study. Maintaining contact with the participants is critical so
that they are available for re-examination as the study progresses.
Contact efforts are made through the mail and/or by telephone.
Each center is permitted to decide which methods achieve the best
results in their cohort. Additionally, incentive gifts (sent on
a scheduled study-wide basis), holiday cards and birthday cards
are utilized to entice the participants to remain involved with the
CARDIA study.

Contacts are attempted at scheduled six month intervals, with
the contact effort being based on the Year 0 exam date. At 66 and
78 months (following the Year 5 exam), address verifications may
be obtained from someone other than the participant (e.g., parent,
spouse, roommate, friend) although direct contact is preferable.
At the 72 month contact, direct contact with the participant is
required and a Follow-Up Questionnaire must be completed.

A participant is eligible for a period of six months at each
follow-up time frame, two months preceding the anniversary month
(which is based on the Year 0 exam date) and three months following
the anniversary month. For example, if a participant's expected
exam date is in June, he/she would be due for a follow-up contact
in December; therefore the eligible contact period would begin in
October (two months prior to December) and the deadline to complete
the contact would be March 31 (three months following December).
Thus, an un-contacted participant is always eligible for one, but
only one, follow-up at a time.

Using this method, when the deadline for an un-contacted
participant is reached, his/her Address Status will be coded as "U"
(Unable to contact) on the computer generated Follow-up Logs (see
sample), Date of Response and Mode of Response will be blank or
"missing", the Distance Moved will be coded according to the last

USING THE FOLLOW-UP LOG

In the top right corner of the log is the date and time the
log was generated. If you have more than one copy of a log you
can check the date and time to see which is the latest version.

The second line of the title gives the month (mm) and year
(yy) the participants listed are eligible for follow-up in mm/yy
format. For example, "FOLLOWUPS FOR 03/90", tells you that the
participants listed were eligible for follow-up beginning in March
1990.

The next four lines list the allowable codes and their
meanings for some parts of the log concerning the follow-up
information collected.

The "CARDIA ID" column lists the participants eligible for
follow-up for the month stated in order by their CARDIA ID.

"DATE OF FOLLOWUP" is the date follow-up is initiated for a
participant such as the date the first phone call is made or the
first letter is mailed.

"DATE OF RESPONSE" is the date the participant responds to the
follow-up and the follow-up is completed.

"MODE OF RESPONSE"' is the method that is used to obtain
completion of the participant's follow-up information. This may
be a letter received from the participant, a telephone call to or
from the participant or a visit to the participant. Some
participants may have an exam during or about the same time as they
are eligible for follow-up. Information from their exit interview
can be used to complete their follow-up. In this case the mode
should be coded as "O" for other.

GUIDELINES FOR YEAR 5 EXAMINATION

PURPOSE

The CARDIA Year 5 examinations are scheduled over a twelve-month
period (June 1990 - May 1991). This will be either the second or
third visit to the clinical center by the participant. It is
important that this experience be viewed favorably by the
participant.

The total time for the core examination should not exceed three
hours. Additional time will be required for substudies and ancillary
studies. The results of the examination will be sent to the

participant's family physician if he/she so indicates.

PREPARATION OF PARTICIPANT FOR THE SECOND VISIT

Each participant is required to fast from all food and beverage
(except water) 12 hours prior to the exam. The participant should
not have engaged in any vigorous exercise on the day of the
appointment and should not have used tobacco 30 minutes prior to the
exam. The participant should bring to the appointment a list of any
prescription medications they are currently using. Additional pre-
exam instructions will be related by phone to the participant prior
to the day of the appointment.

STAFF PREPARATION FOR THE PARTICIPANT'S VISIT

In preparation for the participant's arrival to the clinic, a
designated staff member will construct the expected participant's
file. The CARDIA forms will be arranged according to the center's
anticipated clinic flow for ease of administration. (The forms for
the core examination are collated and packaged into form sets.
Medical history follow-up forms and substudy forms are packaged
separately.) Once the form set is organized, the entire package
should be placed into a three-ring notebook provided for each

participant. Each participant's form set will accompany and be
administered to the participant throughout the course of the
examination. The form set should remain assembled in the notebook
until the Data Editor has entered all of that participant's data.
Following data entry, the form set should be filed and stored.

The identification labels to be placed on each CARDIA form will
be designed, prepared, and distributed by the Coordinating Center to
each clinical center. The identification number will consist of a
one-digit center code, a four-digit participant number, a digit check
number, a quality control number, and a five-digit cross reference.
In addition, "X3" will appear on each label to designate that forms
were completed at the third exam.

GUIDELINES FOR GREETING AND INFORMED CONSENT

GENERAL INFORMATION

The greeting is very important because it sets the tone for the
entire exam. Each participant was told during the past exams that:

* they are participating in an important national study;

* they will receive valuable information about their own
health;

* they will receive a specially designed CARDIA examination
available at only four centers in the United States; and

* if they wish, their physicians can be sent their test
results.

In the greeting for the Year 5 exam these general points should
be stressed again, but each center should do this in ways that are
most suitable for their own populations.

GUIDELINES FOR GREETING

Verify that the participant has arrived on the right day at the
right time. If the participant has not arrived on the correct day
or at the correct time, say something like, "Your appointment is not
recorded on today's exam schedule. There's a chance we may be able

to fit you in today, " or " Our records show that you are scheduled
for an exam at o'clock. There's a chance we may be able
to see you sooner." Then, consult with your Clinic Coordinator for

further instructions.

If the participant appears to be ill, verify that he/she feels
well enough to complete the examination. One way to do this is to
ask, "Do you have a fever?" If the participant answers "yes,"
reschedule the appointment according to local center appointment
procedures. If the participant fails to complete the entire exam,
reschedule the unfinished components as soon as possible according

to local center appointment procedures, and record the participant's

GUI - 2

ID, unfinished component, and reason for the incomplete exam on the

clinical center log.

A brief description of CARDIA should be given to the participant
prior to the Year 5 exam. The following is an example: "As you
know, CARDIA is a major study of the lifestyles and health of young
adults. It is sponsored by the National Institutes of Health. Here
in Chicago, the study is being conducted by the Department of
Community Health and Preventive Medicine of Northwestern University
Medical School."

"First, let me tell you again a little about what will be

included in your exam today. As you know, we will explore many
aspects of your health and your lifestyle. You will be asked
questions about:

* your current health, in general;

* any past illnesses or injuries;

* any medications you take;

*

the amount of exercise you get;

*

the way you deal with every day problems; and
* your background - your education, whether you are
married, what you do, and things like that.
We will take your blood pressure several times.
There will be a blood test to determine the amount of cholesterol in
your blood.
We will measure your height and weight.
We will test the capacity of your lungs.
We will conduct an echocardiogram which will provide an image of your
heart in motion."

GUIDELINES FOR OBTAINING INFORMED CONSENT

At this time the participant should be asked to read and sign
the consent form. Each center has a different form. It is not
enough to have the participant read and sign the form; the
participant must understand what is going to happen to him/her during
the exam and the risks involved. The greeter should make certain
that the participant is actually reading the form and then
specifically ask if he/she has any questions about it. The greeter
should be prepared to answer those questions himself/herself or have
someone else on site answer them. If it seems appropriate (i.e., the
participant is struggling to read the form), ask if the participant
would prefer that the form be read aloud. If so, the greeter should
read it aloud.

After the consent form has been read and signed, the greeter
should ask the participant if he/she would like the test results
mailed to him/her and/or to his/her physician. The responses to
these questions should be marked in the appropriate spaces on the
medical release form. If the participant would like the results
mailed to a physician, the name and address of the physician, as well
as the participants's signature on the medical release form should
be obtained at this time. Results may not be released to a physician
without the participant's siqnature on the medical release form.

VERIFICATION OF DEMOGRAPHIC DATA

After the participant has signed the informed consent, the
greeter will refer to the "Verification of Demographic Information"
form, as prepared for each individual participant by the Coordinating
Center. The participant will be asked their birthdate, sex, and race
to be compared for verification with the demographic data from their
most current exam (either Year 0 or Year 2). This form will not
require an ID label, as the ID is already on the form. The
participant is now ready to continue with the Year 5 exam.

602 Echo Diagnostic Code

The ERC has added a new code, 602, to the valid diagnostic
codes for Echo results. A diagnostic code of 602 indicates that
the M-mode readings could not be made or diagnosed because of poor
images on the tape. The "official" description of the code from
the ERC is "Sub-optimal study; any comments are only tentatively
observed".

This code is now included as a possible code for the Results
Summary program. When a diagnostic code of 602 occurs, it will
usually be the only diagnostic code given for the participant.
When it is the only code then "NO DIAGNOSIS MADE" will be inserted
into the participant's Results Summary where the evaluation would
normally occur (i.e. where the words "NORMAL" or "POTENTIALLY
ABNORMAL" are usually written). Note, there is no echo information
to send to the participant when this occurs and the echo portion
of the Results Summary should not be sent to the participant.
However, Doppler readings may be present on the physician's part
of the Summary and should be sent to the participant's physician
if they occur.

If a diagnostic code of 602 occurs and other valid diagnostic
codes also are present, the other codes are used to evaluate and
describe the participant's echo results. In this case, the 602
code will be included as a comment code on the physician's summary
and the echo portion of the results summary will be generated as

usual. Regardless of the participant's evaluation (i.e., "NORMAL",
"POTENTIALLY ABNORMAL", or "ABNORMAL"), the Results Summary should
be referred to your echo supervisor for review. The echo

supervisor should decide whether or not the letter should be sent
to the participant.

For participants with a diagnostic code of 602 only (and thus
no echo information) or participants whom the echo supervisor
advises that the echo letter not be sent, we recommend the
following actions be taken. The participant should be notified
that their echo was of poor quality and that no results can be
given to them about this component of the exam. We leave it up to
the clinic as an option to invite the participant back for a second
echo exam.

REFERRAL PROCEDURE FOR ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC
DIAGNOSIS OF MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE

The purpose of the mitral valve prolapse substudy is two-fold:
1) to assure appropriate and economical medical follow-up of CARDIA
participants who have incidental mitral valve prolapse discovered
by echocardiography and 2) to collect auscultatory and chest pain
data on these participants.

The criteria selected for the echocardiographic diagnosis of
mitral valve prolapse in the CARDIA study is as follows: 3 mm or
more of arching of the mitral leaflet behind the mitral annulus in
the two-dimensional echocardiographic parasternal long axis view.

If a participant is diagnosed with mitral valse prolapse by
the Echocardiography Reading Center, the participant will receive
a letter (see sample) from the Principal Investigator of the
appropriate CARDIA clinical center offering a free consultation
with the Echocardiography Supervisor at the clinic. The
participant may schedule an appointment on his/her own volition in
response to the letter, or the clinic personnel will call the
participant if no appointment has been scheduled within three weeks
of the mailing of the letter. If the participant does not wish to
come in to the clinic or skips his/her appointment, then only one
reschedule should be attempted.

The primary role of the Echocardiography Supervisor will be
to perform cardiac auscultation on the participants with the
echocardiographic diagnosis of mitral valve prolapse. An
auscultation form (Form 41-AUSC) will be used as a basis for this
examination. The Rose Questionnaire (Form 41-ROSE) on chest pain
and palpitations will also be administered. In addition, the
Echocardiography Supervisor will be free to provide advice
regarding future clinical management (e.g., prophylaxis against
subacute bacterial endocarditis). The cardiologist will be
instructed not to alarm the participants about this condition.

I. INTRODUCTION

Accurate spirometric pulmonary function testing has three
essential components: a) a frequently calibrated spirometer that
accurately records exhaled volume in relation to time during the
forced expiration; b) a participant who inspires maximally and
exhales as forcefully, smoothly, and completely as he can; and_ oc)
a technician who can calibrate the spirometer, coach the participant
to perform maximal efforts, and detect poor participant effort and/or
expirations that are not continuous, maximal, and completely recorded
(1,2). The goal of the present manual is to assist the technician
in producing accurate spirometric pulmonary function measurements
using the Survey Spirometer and the Eagle II Microprocessor (Warren
E. Collins, Inc., Braintree, MA).

Section II of this manual describes the equipment to be used
in the Year 5 exam, and discusses a list of supplies necessary for
pulmonary function testing. Section III presents cleaning of the
spirometer and breathing tubes. Section IV presents calibration
checks of the spirometer, including checks of the chart speed and
volume deflection and tests for leakage. Section V presents general
principles of spirometric testing, such as: a) how to perform forced
expiratory maneuvers; hb) problems that are often encountered in
conducting the forced expiratory maneuver; c) using flow-volume
curves to diagnose problems in testing; 4d) the number of trials to
be performed and reproducibility criteria; e) measurements of the
Forced Expiratory Volume in One Second (FEV1), the Forced Vital
Capacity (FVC), and the FEV1/FVC ratio; f) correction of these
measurements to Body Temperature and Pressure, Saturated (BTPS); and
g) the racial correction factor. Section VI presents the procedure
to be followed in testing study participants using the Eagle II
Microprocessor and the Survey Spirometer.

12

It will be seen that use of the Eagle II in conjunction with
the Survey spirometer relieves the technician of hand measurement of
the spirograms, BTPS correction, and calculation of and comparison
with predicted pulmonary function values. However, it is still
essential that the technician calibrate the spirometer and that he
insure, by active coaching and vigilant attention to the spirograms,
that maximum and good quality forced expirations are performed and
recorded.

II. EQUIPMENT

All pulmonary function tests will be conducted using the
Collins Survey 8-liter water sealed spirometer, shown in Figure 1.
As shown in Figure 2, the expired volume is measured as it displaces
a lightweight plastic bell riding in a narrow water well. A pen
moves directly with the bell, recording a tracing of volume versus
time on a kymograph drum, rotating at a speed of 32 mm/sec. In
addition to the information presented in this manual, further details
of the operation and maintenance of the spirometer are given in the

Instruction Manual for the Collins Survey Spirometer.

The Eagle II Microprocessor will be used in conjunction with
the Survey spirometer during spirometer volume calibration and
participant testing. The Eagle II attaches to the Survey spirometer
via a Computer Input/Output Connector Cable, as shown in Figure 3.
The Eagle II primarily assists the technician in two otherwise time-
consuming tasks: calculation of expired volumes and flow rates and
calculation of predicted pulmonary function values.

A linear motion potentiometer attached to the spirometer bell
converts spirometer bell volume changes into electrical signals. As
the spirometer bell is displaced during a forced expiration, signals
are sent to the Eagle II through the computer connector cable. In
this way, the Eagle II measures how fast the expiration is
proceeding, and calculates instantaneous flow rates at several points
during the forced expiration.

4/90 13

4/90

In addition, using the participant's age, height, and sex,
which are entered into the Eagle II prior to participant testing, the
Eagle II computes the predicted pulmonary function values using
Knudson's prediction equations (3). After each expiration is
recorded, the Eagle II will print the test results and compare the
participant's observed measurements with those predicted for his age,
height, race, and sex. Further details on the Eagle II are available
in the Instruction Manual for the Collins Eagle II Pulmonary Function
Testing System.

It is recommended that the Survey spirometer be placed on a
high surface, at least as high as a laboratory table (37" off the
floor), and preferably a surface that is 46-48" high. However, the
Eagle II microprocessor can be positioned at any level, and the
length of the computer connector cord will permit a considerable
discrepancy in height between the two units. There are two
advantages in placing the spirometer at a level well above a normal
desk level: (1) the spirometric testing can be performed in the
standing position even for tall participants without constricting the
patient breathing tube or forcing tall participants to bend over; and
(2) it is easier for the technician to watch the chart paper when it
is closer to his eye level than when he must bend over to see it.

Figure 4 presents the arrangement of patient, technician,
spirometer, and microprocessor that is recommended for testing. Such
an arrangement permits the technician simultaneously to: 1) depress
the "Fvc" button throughout the participant's expiration, 2) watch
the spirogram for the FVC plateau, and 3) watch the participant for
signs of lightheadedness. This arrangement also prevents the
participant from viewing his tracings as they are recorded on the
kymograph drum; it might interfere with his performance of the tests
if he is able to watch the tracings.

Equipment and supplies may be obtained from the companies
listed below. Extra paper, mouthpieces, and pens should be kept on
hand. One or two extra spirometer hoses also should be available

since they are inexpensive and easier to replace than to repair.
This also permits one hose to be cleaned while another hose is in
use.

To insure that the forced expirations are accurately recorded
by the Survey spirometer, daily checks of volume recording and chart
speed (time recording) should be made, as well as tests for leaks in
the spirometer. The water level, position of the pen holder,
thickness of the pen line, position of the baseline, and the
thermometer should also be checked daily. A technician self-test
should be performed once per week. The calibration log shown in
Figure 6 should be kept, recording the calibration dates, the
procedures performed, and any problems found and corrective actions
taken. A xeroxed copy of the log should be forwarded to the
Coordinating Center on a monthly basis. Adequate documentation of
the calibration procedure is essential. The paper tracings generated
during calibration should be also be saved. The following checks
should be performed on a daily basis and recorded in the calibration
log.

A. Water Level Check

The water jacket should be kept filled to about one inch
from the top of the tank. The water level should be visible
through the water level gauge on the side of the tank. Low

water jacket, "B" was recorded by the same participant on

was recorded by the same participant on a spirometer with
three-fourths of the water jacket removed.

If the spirometer water level is low, more water should be

should be recorded on the calibration log sheet. If no
water is added, the fact that the level was adequate should
be noted.

Developing a leak in the spirometer is one of the most
common technical problems that occurs, as the plastic hoses
and bells deteriorate. As shown in Figure 8, the effects
of spirometric leaks on forced expiratory tracings are
pronounced. Tracing A was recorded on an airtight
spirometer, and tracings B-F were recorded in the presence
of leaks of increasing size. The Fvc is particularly
affected by the presence of a spirometer leak. To avoid
recording tracings on leaking spirometers, the spirometers
must be checked daily for leakage and the checks must be

1) Attach a clean sheet of graph paper to the kymograph

V. THE FORCED EXPIRATORY MANEUVER
Measurements of pulmonary function made during a forced
expiratory maneuver are among the simplest and most repeatable tests
of the pulmonary mechanics of breathing. However, the accuracy of
these measurements depends, in large part,on the technician
conducting the testing. The technician must guide the participant
through the procedure, and he must be able to judge the adequacy of

the participant's effort. To make the spirometric testing results

4/90

as accurate and consistent as possible, the testing should be done

in a standardized fashion by all technicians, for all participants.

A.

Preparing for the Maneuver

The pulmonary function test should definitely be postponed
if the participant has had (1) chest or abdominal surgery
within the past six weeks, (2) is acutely ill, or (3) had
a severe respiratory infection within the past 3 weeks. If
feasible the test should be postponed if the participant has
had a heavy meal within the past two hours, smoked within
the last hour, or used a bronchodilator within the past
hour.

Whenever possible, testing should be conducted in standing
position, particularly for obese participants, since
slightly larger volumes are observed in the standing than
in the sitting posture (4). A sturdy chair, without wheels,
should be positioned behind the participant to be used in
the rare event of fainting or dizziness. Smelling salts
should always be kept on hand for this possibility.

The participant's neck should be slightly extended, the
spirometer hose should be adjustable to the participant's
height, so that he stands erect, and is not hunched over,
and his chin should be slightly elevated. The position in
which the testing is done, whether it be standing or
sitting, should be noted on the graph paper and the computer
printout.

Tight clothing, such as a tie or belt, which might restrict
the participant's maximal breathing and efforts, should be

loosened.

Dentures, if they are loose, should be removed, since they
will prevent a tight seal from being formed around the

mouthpiece. If they are not loose, they should be left in
place.

A noseclip will be used during the maneuver to prevent nasal
leakage during expiration. The best time for the
participant to put on the noseclip is just before he takes
in his maximal inspiration. This way he will avoid
swallowing while wearing the noseclip, which blocks the ears
and is uncomfortable. Though the noseclips are
"disposable", they should be cleaned and re-used for as long
as possible.

Explaining and Demonstrating the Maneuver

First, explain to the participant that he is about to doa
test to determine how much air he can exhale, and how hard
and fast he can exhale it. Then, explain to the participant
that he will (1) attach the noseclip, (2) take in as deep
a breath as possible, and when full, will (3) place the
mouthpiece in his mouth, (4) close his lips tightly around
the mouthpiece, and (5) exhale through the mouthpiece into
the spirometer, pushing his air out as hard, fast and
completely as possible. He is not to take in any additional
breaths until he has finished the forced expiration, and he
should continue to actively push out his air until the
technician instructs him to stop exhaling. He should be
able to exhale until the tracing flattens out and draws an
FVC plateau of at least two seconds in length. The
technician should continually urge the participant to "PUSH"
his air out, until the Fvc plateau is recorded. In middle-
aged participants, six seconds of expiration is usually
possible, and should be aimed for in a group of young
adults. However, some young adults with very high flow
rates reach the FVC plateau within four seconds, and this
should be accepted if it occurs. After a participant's
testing session is completed, the Exhalation Time of each
of his tracings will be measured and recorded, as described
below in Section V.F.

Quality of the Forced Expiratory Tracings

A "good quality" spirometric test requires a maximal
inspiration, to completely fill the lungs, and a subsequent
forceful, complete, and continuous expiration. The accuracy
of the measurements made from the spirograms, the Forced
Expiratory Volume in One Second (FEV1), the Forced Vital
Capacity (FVC), and the Forced Expiratory Flow Rates (FEF)
depends on the quality of the spirograms.

ae

4/90

The FEV1 is the maximum volume of air that a participant can
exhale within the first second of expiration following a maximal
inspiration. The accuracy of the FEV1 depends on whether the
participant inhales maximally and whether he expels his air as
fast and hard as he can, and not with a sub-maximal effort.

The FvC is the maximum amount of air that can be expelled in one
forced expiration after a maximal inspiration. The accuracy of
the FvcC depends on how maximal the participant's inspiration is
and how complete his expiration is.

Both of these measurements, and the flow rates, will be
discussed in more detail below. Measurement of the FEV1 and FVC

are shown in Figure 12.

There are several different types of errors that can occur
during the forced expiratory maneuver: (1) mechanical problems
with the spirometer; (2) submaximal inspirations; (3) submaximal
effort on expiration (4) hesitations, glottis closure, cough,
or tongue blocking mouthpiece during expiration; (5) incomplete
expirations; (6) taking in another breath during expiration; and
(7) procedural errors such as turning the chart drive on after
expiration has begun, or leakage through the participants nose
or around the mouthpiece. These errors, described in detail
below and pictured in Figures 13-16, may invalidate the FEV1,
Fvc, and the flow rates.

1) Mechanical Problems with the Spirometer
If the pen does not make contact with the chart paper
during the entire forced expiration, the trial should be
repeated. If the water level is low (Figure 7) or if any
other mechanical problems occur, especially if a leak
develops (Figure 13), the test should be repeated.
However, daily water level checks and leak tests should
prevent these problems from occurring during a testing

session.

Submaximal Inspirations
If this problem consistently occurs, it may not be visible

on the tracings, since tracings recorded after a submaximal
inspiration look small, but normal. Comparison of the
spirogram in Figure 14 with the normal tracing in Figure
12 reveals the effect of a submaximal inspiration on both
the FEV1 and the Fvc. The FEV1 recorded after a maximal
inspiration (2850 ml) is reduced to 2160 ml after a

Submaximal Efforts on Expiration

If the participant pushes his air out slowly during the
entire expiration (Figure 15) or gradually increases his
push (Figure 16) or purses his lips behind the mouthpiece
and blows into it like a trumpet (Figure 17), the FEV1 from
that tracing will be invalid, though the FvcC may be valid
if the expiration is complete (See (5) below). The flow
rates will be invalid. The participant must be encouraged
to blast his air out as he begins his exhalation.

Flow-volume curves are particularly helpful in diagnosing
submaximal expiratory efforts. Compare the flow-volume
inserts in Figures 15, 16A, and 16B with the insert in
Figure 12. The highest point on the flow-volume curve, the
peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR), is much greater on the
good quality expiration in Figure 12 than on Figures 15 and
16. The flow-volume curves in Figures 15 and 16 tend to
be flattened in comparison with Figure 12. And finally,
though Figure 16A has a more pronounced peak than Figures
15 and 16B, the peak is displaced to the right in
comparison with Figure 12. In Figure 12, the peak flow
rate is achieved much earlier in the expiration, i.e., the
person exhales hard and fast immediately, rather than

34

starting to exhale gradually and then exhaling more
forcefully.

4) Hesitations, Glottis Closure, Cough, or Tongue Blocking the
Mouthpiece
If the participant hesitates in his push during the first
second of expiration (Figure 18), the FEV1, the FVC, and
the flow rates generally will be invalid. A cough anywhere
during the expiration prior to the FVC plateau will usually
invalidate the FVC (Figure 19), but if the cough occurs
after the first second, the FEV1 may still be valid. A
drink of water may relieve a problem with coughing on
subsequent trials. However, if the participant stops
pushing but keeps his mouth on the mouthpiece, or has
glottis closure or his tongue blocks the airflow near the
end of the expiration (Figure 20), the FVC will be invalid,
though the FEV1 would still be acceptable. Figure 20 shows
that these problems appear in the tracing as an abrupt
flattening of the expiratory tracing, forming a "knee",
which does not occur during the usual gradual lessening of
flow rates as the FVC plateau is reached.

5) Incomplete Expirations
The expirations must be recorded to the FVC plateau, which
usually occurs after six seconds of expiration in adult
males, but may occur after a shorter exhalation time in
young adults, due to their very high flow rates during
expiration. Obstructed participants may well need 10 or
more seconds of exhalation to reach their FVC plateaus, and
they should be encouraged to exhale for this long. The FVC
plateau has been reached when a horizontal line is
inscribed on the chart paper. Incomplete expirations can
have a profound impact on the measurement of the FVC, the
FEV1/FVC, and the Forced Expiratory Flow Rates. The FVC
plateau should be maintained for at least one second before
terminating the forced expiratory maneuver. Figure 21

Taking in a Second Breath During the Expiration
As with the other hesitations in expiratory flow discussed

in (4) above, if a second breath is taken in during the
first second of expiration (Figure 22), the complete test
is invalid. However, if the second breath is taken in
after the first second of expiration, the FEV1 may be
valid, but the Fvc and the flow rates will not be valid,
unless the breath is taken in after the FVC plateau has

been drawn for at least one second. Taking a second breath
will either cause a vertical excursion of the pen (Figure
22) if the mouthpiece is not blocked by the tongue, or it
may result in a second small plateau after the FVC plateau
has already been reached (Figure 23). This will only
happen if the tongue blocks the mouthpiece and no noseclip
is used, thus permitting extra air to be taken through the
nose without being recorded as a vertical deflection. This
problem will not occur when a noseclip is used.

Procedural Errors: Turning the Chart Drive on After the
Expiration Has Begun, and Leakage Through the Nose or
Around the Mouthpiece

If the chart drive is turned on after the start of the

exhalation, the timing of the expiration is not recorded
accurately, since the onset of expiration cannot be
determined. The vertical motion of the pen resulting from
this problem is shown in Figure 24. The FEV1 is
invalidated by this problem, unless the vertical excursion
is less than 200 ml or 20% of the FVC, whichever is
smaller. However, if the expiration is complete, the FVC
may be valid. The flow rates will not be valid unless the
FEV1 is valid.

Leakage of air can occur during the forced expiration
through the hose, around the mouthpiece, or from the
spirometer. Use of a noseclip will prevent nasal leakage
from occurring; sealing the lips tightly around the
mouthpiece will prevent air from leaking around the
mouthpiece; and daily leak testing should prevent

spirometer leaks from going undetected. However, if
leakage from one of these three sources does occur, it will
appear as in Figure 13, and should be recognized.

Number, Reproducibility, and Quality of Tracings Required
Every participant should perform a minimum of five trials.

At the end of five trials, if three tracings are free of
the above mentioned procedural errors, and the maximum FVC
and FEV1 are reproduced within 5%, or 100 ml, whichever is
greater, no more trials are needed. As mentioned earlier,
the primary goal of each trial is to obtain maximal
efforts, and a series of such efforts will usually be

reproducible at this desired level.

If the first five attempts do not yield three good
tracings, up to three more attempts should be made to get
three such tracings. After eight attempts, regardless of
their quality, testing should be stopped. If the
participant refuses to continue with the required number
of trials, it should be noted on the kymograph chart paper.

Measuring the Tracings: FEV1, FVC, and Exhalation

Time

The FEV1 and FVC should be measured in all tracings that
are free of the procedural errors discussed above. Even

if the tracings are smaller or don't "look good" in
comparison with the other tracings, they should be read if
they are not technically inaccurate. Therefore, the first
step should be to look through the tracings and decide
which ones will yield invalid measurements of the FEV1 and
the FVC, based on the above mentioned categories of errors
in Section V.D.

If the spirometer is empty, the felt pen should rest at and
draw a baseline along the "0" line of the chart paper. The
measurements are easiest to read if the baseline is set at
"0" before the testing. The daily baseline check should
insure that the baseline remains on "0" line. However, if

37

4/90

the baseline was not exactly on the "oO" line during
testing, draw in the correct baseline and make all the
measurements from the corrected baseline.

The FEV1 is greatly affected by the point selected for the
start of the expiration. Therefore, a uniform method has
been established to correct for the varying degrees of
curvature that appear at the beginning of the expiration,
due to submaximal efforts in the split-second when
exhalation is starting (Figure 25). The method, called
"back-extrapolation", requires a tangent to be drawn from
the steepest portion of the curve back to the baseline.
The starting point of the expiration, the origin, is then
taken from the point where the back-extrapolation line
intersects the baseline. The curved tail to the right of
the back-extrapolation line is ignored. If the
"extrapolated volume", measured as the height of the
tracings vertically above the new origin, exceeds 5% of the
total FVC, the tracing is too curved to be back-
extrapolated, and should not be used for measurement of the
FEV1.

Having determined the onset of the expiration for
measurement purposes, the FEV1 is found by placing a "one-
second wide" (32 mm) ruler at the new origin, and reading
the FEV1 where the tracing emerges on the left side of the
ruler. Position the ruler with the right edge touching the
back-extrapolated origin for accurate FEV1 measurement.
Also, be sure that the ruler is vertical. The FEV1 shoulda
be read to the nearest 10 ml.

Measurement of the FVC is less difficult, being simply the
volume between the baseline and the tracing at the Fvc
plateau. If a plateau is not drawn the "Fvc" will be
submaximal. As with the FEV1, measure the FVC to the
nearest 10 ml.

38

Agreement between the tracings may now be checked. The
maximum FVC and FEV1 should be reproduced to within 5% or
100 ml, whichever is greater. A table showing the limits
of reproducibility is given in Appendix B. Only the best
FEV1 and the best FVC will be used to characterize the
participant's pulmonary function.

Both of these measurements - the FEV1 and the FVC - must
be corrected from room temperature to body temperature and
pressure, saturated (BTPS). Each measurement is multiplied
by the BIPS correction factor appropriate for the
spirometer temperature, inflating the measurements by 8-
10%. The BTPS-corrected measurements can then be compared
with predicted values to evaluate the state of this
participant's pulmonary function. Though the use of the
Eagle II removes the burden of regularly performing these
calculations, the technician should still know how to
measure the spirograms in case of Eagle II failure.

The Exhalation Time is the final measurement to be made on
each tracing. It is the number of seconds that elapsed
between the back-extrapolated origin of the tracing and the
Fvc. For each trial, the number of one-second intervals
crossed by the tracing are counted, to the nearest 0.25
seconds, and recorded on the computer printout, as
described in Section VI.C below. Exhalation Times are
recorded in Figures 12, 25A, and 26. Since the Eagle II
does not compute the Exhalation Time, this measurement must
always be performed by the technician.

PART I: STUDY INITIATION

SELECTION OF PARTICIPANTS

Participation in the urine substudy is completely voluntary.
Participants will be asked to participate in the substudy
consecutively as long as urine collection kits are available.
(The Clinic Coordinators may exclude from recruitment those
participants who are very hostile or those who have difficulty with
reading/following instructions. In addition, pregnant women should
be excluded from recruitment.) However, current utilization of the
collection kits will not be known until the day of the
participant's exam. In the event that all collection kits are
currently being utilized at the time of the exam, an interested
participant could return at a later date to participate in the
urine substudy. (It is not necessary to return in exactly seven
days to preserve the weekday of the initial exam.)

The timing of recruitment (e.g., prior to the clinic visit or
following the exit interview) is left to the discretion of each
clinic. The methods used to recruit and the phrasing of the
invitation to participate will thereby differ somewhat by clinic.
Whatever method is used, the content of the invitation should
include the following points:

1. This is a one-time opportunity and their participation or non-
participation will not affect their standing in CARDIA.

2. Participation requires three consecutive, complete 24-hour
urine collections. "Complete" means that every time the

participant voids during the collection period, it is into a
collection jar.

3. While this may be inconvenient, urine collection is not
difficult and the clinic will supply all the needed materials.

4. Only urinary sodium, potassium, creatinine and magnesium will
be measured (if needed, to assure the participant that we have
no intention of testing for drugs). Remind the participant
that all results are confidential and will be shared only with
him/her or authorized medical personnel.

5. Inform the participant that he/she will receive complete
results and $25.00 for participation.

URINE COLLECTION INSTRUCTIONS

Proper instructions to the participant in urine collection
procedures is of critical importance. The chief obstacles to
successful collection, in addition to incompleteness, are failure
to remember to start the first night's collection by voiding into
the toilet and failure to correctly record the times of each
collection period on the jar label. In instructing the
participant, the staff needs to make certain that the participant
clearly understands the procedures for the start of the first 24-
hour collection and the importance of accurate timing of
collections. Urine collection instructions should be reviewed with
the participant until it is clear that the participant understands
them. The instructions are as follows:

1. Inform the participant that boric acid has been added to each
jar for two reasons: (1) to control odor; and (2) to limit
the breakdown of creatinine. As you point out the warning
label on the side of a collection jar, make the participant
aware that boric acid, if ingested, will cause nausea and
vomiting, making these collection jars potentially dangerous,
especially to small children. Remind the participant of their
responsibility in keeping these collection jars out of the
reach of children.

2. Before you go to bed on (insert date), urinate into the
toilet, emptying the bladder completely. DO NOT USE A URINE
COLLECTION JAR FOR THIS VOIDING.

3. Take a jar with a green bordered label marked "FIRST 24-HOUR
COLLECTION". Record the date of the evening that you start

SPECIAL INSTRUCTIONS FOR WOMEN

There are two concerns regarding female participation in the
urine collection study: (1) menstruation and (2) use of the Speci-
Pan during urination.

MENSTRUATION

Menstruation has no effect on the measurements of sodiun,
potassium, creatinine and magnesium. However, some female
participants may feel uncomfortable participating at this time.
If this is a concern of the participant then the urine collection
may be delayed until the end of her menstrual cycle. The urine
collection should be rescheduled to start on the same weekday after

her menstrual cycle has ended. Materials and instructions should
not be given to the participant until she is ready to start
collecting urine. The decision on deferring the start of urine
collection because of menstruation is the responsibility of the
female participant and should not be interfered with or judged by
the technician.

SPECI-PAN

A Speci-Pan, a bowl shaped container into which the
participant can urinate, will be provided to each female
participant to assist in urine collection if needed. The Speci-Pan
fits between the toilet seat and the porcelain rim of the toilet.
After urinating into the Speci-Pan, the urine is transferred into
a collection jar, carefully avoiding spills. The Speci-Pan can
then be rinsed out with water and either air-dried or hand dried
with a clean cloth or paper towel. The Speci-Pan can be disposed
of at the end of the urine collection by the clinic or the
participant.

SCHEDULING THE START OF THE URINE STUDY

The start of the urine study is on the second day after the
regular clinic visit. This is to ensure that the participant has
returned to a normal steady-state after fasting for the CARDIA
examination.

Exceptions to this are menstruation and circumstances that
would otherwise prohibit participation in the urine study. These
special circumstances are abnormal variations in a participant's
schedule that affect a person's willingness to collect accurate 24-
hour urines (e.g., extended travel, field work, weddings) and will
be resolved by the passing of time.

In these cases, the participant's expected "start of
collection" date may be delayed by rescheduling the urine
collection for the most convenient time for the participant. (The
Coordinating Center will monitor the balance among the days of the
week and will inform the Clinic Coordinators if more stringent

The following procedure will be CARDIA's policy on urine

date for delivery and inquire as to the "best time" for the

3. If the participant is hostile towards self-delivery of the
urine collection or refuses to participate because of the
self-delivery, then the technician should make arrangements
for CARDIA to pick up or messenger the specimens to the
clinic. The participant will be paid $25.00 upon the
completion of the urine study.

After the participant has received a collection kit and

URINE COLLECTION COMPLETENESS

The success of the urine study depends on the completeness of
the urine collections. Participants should also be reminded that
they will be paid for incomplete collections to help ensure
truthful answers.

Since any 24-hour collection with a missing void is unusable,

PART III: STUDY PROCESSING

PROCESSING THE URINE COLLECTIONS

All technicians are required to wear gloves when handling the
urine jars and during all processing. Each 24-hour urine
collection should be processed separately. Only 24-hour urine
collections that have all urine-containing jars returned to the
clinic should be processed. If a 24-hour period has a urine-
containing jar missing, the returned jars for that 24-hour period
should be refrigerated and processed when the participant returns
the missing jar. Always process the jars in chronological order
(i.e., Day 1 first, Day 2 second, Day 3 last), only skipping those
24-hour periods with missing urine-containing jars. 24-HOUR URINE
COLLECTIONS KNOWN TO BE INCOMPLETE SHOULD NOT BE PROCESSED. AN
INCOMPLETE 24-HOUR URINE COLLECTION IS A COLLECTION WITH ONE OR
MORE MISSING VOIDS! These 24-hour collections should be disposed
of properly and the jars cleaned according to standard procedures.

There are three values which are needed to assess electrolyte
output for each collection period:
TIME (HOURS AND MINUTES)
VOLUME (MILLILITERS)
CONCENTRATION (DETERMINED BY THE LABORATORY)

MEASURING TIME

To determine the length of a collection period, enter the
"START OF COLLECTION" time and the "END OF COLLECTION" time from
any jar used in a specific 24-hour collection period in the
appropriate space in Part III, Form 39, Q#14.

MEASURING VOLUME

The next critical step is the correct measurement of volume.
Because the collection jar has been standardized, it is possible
to measure the height of the urine in the jar (in centimeters) and
convert this value to volume (in milliliters) by computer. This
eliminates the need for pouring to measure volume.

MEASURING HEIGHT

The height of the urine jar is to be determined using a
special platform with a vertical scale attached, following these
procedures:

1. Place the special platform on a level surface so that the jar
is at eye level. This means either that the observer should
be seated at a table sufficiently high to permit this, or that
there should be an eye-level shelf on which the measuring
platform could be placed.

2. Jars should be perfectly upright when read.

3. If the top of the urine falls between two 0.1 cm lines, record
the higher value. The height of the jar cannot exceed 19.5
cm. If you obtain a height of greater than 19.5 cm, re-
measure the height. Enter the height of each collection jar
in the appropriate space on the form in centimeters.

PREPARING ALIQUOTS FOR LABORATORY ANALYSIS

Aliquots for each urine collection period should be made
immediately after measuring the height of the urine in the
collection jars for that period, to avoid confusing urine specimens
from different collection periods.

Labels have been prepared in advance with the ID number and
collection period number. Three aliquot tubes (one 25-ml flat-
bottomed tube and two 4-ml cryovials) for each collection period
should be prepared with the labels secured with transparent freezer
tape. An additional aliquot will be prepared from a randomly
selected 24-hour collection period for quality control. Quality
control ID labels will be provided.

To take aliquots, pour the urine from all jars used in a
single collection period into a large plastic bucket. Since
electrolyte output may differ at different times of the day,
thoroughly mix the urine in the bucket by gently stirring with a

URN - if

plastic utensil or a glass stirring rod. To avoid frothing, the
mixing should not be done too rapidly or too vigorously. After the
urine is thoroughly mixed (generally between 10 to 15 seconds), use
a pipette to transfer urine from the bucket to the aliquot tubes.

Fill the flat-bottomed tubes to the 20 ml mark. (It is
recommended that each clinic mark a tube to be used as an example.)
Do not fill the aliquot tubes to the top, since they will break
upon freezing. Make sure the tops are pushed firmly down into the
tubes (i.e., until you hear a click) and the top is flush to the
tube.

If the participant has been selected as a quality control
participant, remove one additional aliquot (25-ml flat-bottomed
tube) and transfer it into the quality control aliquot tube.

Each clinic should have three buckets and three mixing
utensils so that all three collection days for each participant can
be processed without cleaning the equipment between collection
days. Before making aliquots for the next participant, thoroughly
wash the large buckets used to hold the urines and the utensils
used to mix the urines in warm water and the recommended cleaning
solution. Rinse well and dry with a clean cloth, paper towel or
allow to air dry. This equipment should be completely dried before
mixing the next urine collection.

Prior to washing the used bottles, the entire label should be
removed (this includes the boric acid warning label). Jars and
lids should be machine washed at temperatures exceeding 140°C using
the recommended detergent (or hand washed in hot water) and be
allowed to air dry. To remove any remaining residue, the bottles
should be rinsed in distilled water and dried before use. If jars
or lids begin to look worn, or discolored or to retain urine odor
they should be replaced and discarded.

BODY SIZE MEASUREMENTS

All measurements are to be made with the participants wearing
a short sleeve shirt or blouse (or surgical gown) , shorts and
socks and without shoes. A supply of shirts and shorts should be
maintained at the survey center for participants who forget to wear
or bring the appropriate clothes for exercise testing and body size
measurements. Men should be sure pockets are empty.

All measurements should be taken by a team of two persons, if

possible - one acting as observer and the other as recorder. The
observer takes the measurements, calling out the results to the

recorder, who repeats them and then calls out the name of the next
measurement. The observer keeps the measuring instrument in place
until the recorder repeats the number. The recorder generally
checks the examinee's position during the procedure. Any values
should be rounded to the nearest unit indicated for each measure.
If the value is exactly between two units, round up if the lower
unit is even and round down if the lower unit is odd (e.g, if value
is 10.5 round up to 11.0; if value is 11.5 round down to 11.0).

Any modification in measurement techniques~-such as left-side
rather than right-side measurements required because of amputations
or casts, abnormal conditions such as height decreased from a
hunched position, or girth increased from pregnancy--should be
noted on the recording form, where they could be taken into
consideration in data analysis.

BODY WEIGHT Be sure the scale is balanced so that the
indicator is at zero when no weight is on the scale. The scale
should be level and on a firm surface (not a carpet). The

participant should be instructed to stand in the middle of the
platform of the balance scale (Detecto, model #439) with head erect
and eyes looking straight ahead. Adjust the weight on the
indicator until it is balanced. Record the results to the nearest

0.2 pounds or 0.5 pounds according to the scale you have in your

ANT - 1

clinic. (This should follow the same procedure for your clinic as
was used the Year 0 exam.) (Rounding rules: If measuring to the
nearest half pound, half inch or half centimeter round down (to
the nearest half) if the measurement is to a quarter pound, quarter
inch or quarter centimeter. For example, 110.25 lbs should be
rounded to 110.0 and 110.75 should be rounded to 110.5. Measures
of 110.0 and 110.5 should be recorded as such. Follow a similar
rule when measuring to the nearest 0.2 lbs, that is, when a measure
falls between a graduation, round down to the nearest 0.2 lbs.)
If the participant weighs more than 350 pounds, record 350.

BODY HEIGHT The participant stands erect on the floor or the
horizontal platform with his/her back against the vertical mounted
metal centimeter ruler, looking straight ahead with his/her head
in the Frankfort horizontal plane (the horizontal plane which
includes the lower margin of the bony orbit - the bony socket
containing the eye-and the most forward point in the supratragal
notch - the notch just above the anterior cartilaginous projections
of the external ear) (Figure 1). This can also be referred to as
the upper margin of external auditory meatus (hole in ear). The
plastic triangle is brought down snugly but not tightly on the top
of the head. The participant's height is recorded to the nearest
0.50 centimeters. The participant should be instructed to stand
as straight as possible but with feet flat on the floor. A check
should be made to be sure the floor is level, the wall is at a 90
degree angle to the floor, the wall is straight and the metal ruler
is mounted perpendicular to the floor. A chart converting
centimeters to inches should be on the wall or available for use
in informing the person of his/her height in inches (Table 1).

GENERAL SKINFOLDS There are no special directions for the
participant to follow prior to this test since these are relatively
stable measurements. Skinfolds should be taken prior to active
tests since sweating and increased blood flow to the skin makes
measurement more difficult. Men can wear gym shorts for the test;

women should wear shorts and a loose fitting, sleeveless blouse or

skinfold caliper will be used for taking all skinfold measurements.
Because the calipers are delicate, they should be placed in the

Taking skinfolds requires practice to assure reliability and
validity as previously stated. The following suggestions for
taking skinfold measurements should be observed.

Make sure that the needle of the Harpenden skinfold calipers
is set at "0" before each measurement. All measurements are taken
on the right side of the person being measured. The fold of skin
should be firmly grasped between the left thumb and forefinger (for
right handed persons) and then lifted up. (Technician's elbow
should point toward the ceiling.) Firmly grasp and lift, sweeping
up the fold several times to make certain that no musculature is
grasped. When ready to take the measurement, grasp the skinfold
firmly with the thumb and finger. Do no let go of the fold and
apply the caliper. Release the grip on the caliper completely,
allowing the spring to compress the fold. Take the reading to the
nearest millimeter. Open and remove the caliper, then release the
fold. (NOTE: the Harpenden caliper needle makes more than one
revolution; the small pointer on the number of revolutions.) Each
revolution of the large needle is 20 mn. The maximum skinfold
thickness that the caliper should be opened is 50 mm. If this will
not accommodate the skinfold, mark a modification on the form. The
code '88' should be used to indicate a skinfold too large to
measure. In addition, the protocol modification question should
be checked '2' for too obese. Keeping the left hand above the
skinfold (Figure 2) allows the dial to be read easily.

The "skin" should be lifted by grasping firmly the fold
between the thumb and forefinger one centimeter above the marked
measurement site (+). A firm grip, not exceeding the pain
threshold, eliminates or at least substantially reduces the

from wide differences in the pulling force of the fingers.

The width of the skin that is enclosed between the fingers is
an important factor. It cannot be standardized, in its absolute
size, for all the sites of the body. With a thick subcutaneous
layer a wider segment of the skin must be "pinched" in order to
form a fold than when the adipose tissue is poorly developed, as
it is on the dorsum of the hand. For a given site the width of the
skinfold should be maximal, without including underlying
musculature.

The depth of the skinfold at which the calipers are placed on
the fold also requires comment. Grasping the skinfold one
centimeter above the marked measurement site (+), the calipers
should be placed at the mark, midpoint between the outer edge of
the skinfold and the body surface.

It is extremely important to measure skinfolds accurately.
Even after extensive practice it is possible to make errors due to
slight misplacement of the caliper or misreading the dial. To

avoid such errors the following procedure is recommended.

a. If possible, the person measuring the skinfolds should
not be the one to record them. An assistant should
record the values as the measurer reads them from the
caliper. It is helpful if the assistant repeats the
values aloud as they are recorded.

b. Skinfolds should be lifted two or three times to
determine the fold to be measured before placing the
calipers. Too many individuals are overly anxious to
put the calipers in place before determining what is
really to be measured. Do not lift the skinfold away

TRICEPS SKINFOLD The participant stands with his/her arms
flexed at 90°. Using the tape measure, the observer measures from
the tip of the acromion process on the shoulder to the tip of the
olecranon process on the back of the right elbow. Make this
measurement as far toward the midline of the back of the arm as
possible while still remaining anchored on the bony landmarks. If
the mark is not in the midline of the back of the arm, you may wish
to use a straight edge to make a second mark at the midline. Be
sure that the straight edge is perpendicular to the long axis of
the arm. The participant should then stand with his/her arm
hanging loosely at the side while the measurement is being made.
Using his thumb and forefinger, the observer grasps a skinfold
parallel to the long axis of the right arm over the triceps area
(back of arm, not side) and one centimeter above the mark made at
the midpoint of the upper arm. The caliper is applied at the mark
(+). The observer counts silently, 1000, 2000, 3000 (one thousand,
two thousand, three thousand) and calls out the reading (to the
nearest millimeter) to the recorder who repeats it and then records
it. The measurement is repeated a second time, releasing the
skinfold between measurements. Both measurements are recorded to
the nearest millimeter.

SUBSCAPULAR SKINFOLD This measurement is made one centimeter
below the tip of the right scapula. Palpate the bottom of the
right scapula and mark a point (+) that is one centimeter below the
tip. To aid in locating the tip of the scapula, have the
participant reach his right hand to the rear and place the back of
his hand on the middle of his back. This move will cause the tip
of the scapula to point rearward and make it easier to locate. The
observer than grasps a skinfold below the lower border of the
scapula with his fingers on top, thumb below, and forefinger at the
lower tip of the scapula. The skinfold should be angled about 45
degrees from the horizontal, going medially upward and laterally
downward. Grasp the skinfold one centimeter above the mark along
this 45 degree angle and place the calipers on the mark.
Measurement and recording are performed and recorded as for the
triceps skinfold.

SUPRAILIAC (HIP) SKINFOLD This measurement is made on the
diagonal fold one cm above the anterior iliac creast (highest peak
on the side of the pelvic girdle) on the mid-axillary line (be sure
not to make the measurement forward of this line). A measuring
tape or a straightedge directed parallel to the vertical axis of
the body with one end placed just under the mid-axilla should be
used to locate the intersection of the mid-axillary line with the
level of the suprailiac skinfold (one cm above the anteria iliac
crest). Identify this point and mark it (+). Measure this
skinfold twice, releasing the skinfold between measurements. Both

measurements are recorded.

UPPER _ARM_ CIRCUMFERENCE Arm circumference at the midpoint
of the right upper arm is to be measured using the anthropometric
tape. Using the mark made at the midpoint of the line from the
acromial process to the olecranon process on the posterior midline
of the upper arm (made for the measurement of the triceps
skinfold), measure the circumference of the arm. The arm should

CHEST GIRTH This measurement is taken while the participant
is standing relaxed, breathing normally, with arms slightly raised
to the side. (On women, the measurement is taken without a
brassiere.) A Gulick II anthropometric tape is applied, without
deforming the skin contour in the horizontal plane around the chest
at the fourth intercostal space on all participants (male and
female). If the participant is large, it is permissible to have
him/her hold one end of the tape while walking the tape around for
this measurement. The measurement is made at the end of a normal

expiration to the nearest 0.5 cm.

WAIST (ABDOMINAL) GIRTH A Gulick II anthropometric tape is
applied horizontally at a level laterally that is midway between
the iliac crest and the lowest lateral portion of the rib cage and
anteriorly midway between the xiphoid process of the sternum and
the umbilicus. This level usually is the natural waist and is
identified as the level of minimal abdominal width when the site
profiles are slightly concave (in some people it will not be
concave). Have the participant bend sideways, to identify the
natural indentation at the waist (have examiner place finger on
this spot before participant stands upright again). The objective
is to measure to smallest circumference around the waist. Be sure
that the tape is kept horizontal when making the measurement. If
the participant is large, it is permissible to have him/her hold
one end of the tape while walking the tape around for this
measurement. The measurement is made at end-expiration to the

nearest 0.5 cm. A second observer/recorder can help observe the

position of the tape. Make one measurement.

HIP GIRTH Hip girth is measured at the level of the
symphysis pubis anteriorly and posteriorly at the level of the
maximal protrusion of the gluteal muscles. This level usually is
the greatest circumference of the hips (but not always). Keep the
anthropometric tape horizontal at this level and record the
measurement to the nearest 0.5 cm. The greatest source of error

the participant is large, it is permissible to have him/her hold

the person being measured; be as discreet as possible
when using two tapes.
