TRAINING AND QUALITY CONTROL

The training and quality control program for taking body size

measurements consists of the following components:

Central training and certification of at least one technician
from each survey center before each of the two examination
cycles: This individual from each center should be designated as
that center's body size measurement primary technician.

If additional personnel are needed by a center to perform body
size measurements during the examination cycles, training will
be provided by the center's clinic supervisor and the certified
body size technician using the technician video tape. Training
includes the performance of the body size measurements on at
least five people by two technicians. Discrepancies in
measurements are to be discussed and any steps necessary to
improve the techniques should be taken. The new technician and
certified technician must complete body size measurements on five
new participants and submit the recording forms to the
Coordinating Center in order for the new technician to become
certified.

Direct observation by the supervisor of the examination
procedures on a monthly basis, with correction of errors when

necessary.

Midway through each examination cycle an intensive one day
evaluation of measurement is to be conducted by the supervisor
and an outside consultant. All body size measurements are to be
performed by each technician, supervisor, and consultant on at
least two moderately fat and two lean individuals. Discrepancies
in measurements will be discussed and any steps necessary to
improve the techniques will be taken.

A weekly instrument check is to be performed on the Harpenden
skinfold calipers using a standard lucite step wedge with widths
in increments of 10mm. A weekly check is to be performed of the

5/770

body weight scale using standard weights ranging from 50 to 200
pounds.

During each exam cycle, each anthropometry technician will be
required to obtain all body size measurements from five
individuals (i.e., clinic staff, etc.) twice with a one week time
interval between the two measurements. Analysis of the intra-
observer reproducibility of measurement will be performed by the
Coordinating Center using these data.

Four times a month (approximately once per week) each technician
will perform all anthropometric measurements on an individual
concurrently with a second technician performing these
measurements on the same individual. Copies of both forms will
be submitted to the Coordinating Center for analysis.

The Coordinating Center will direct a body size measurement
certification committee to review body size data. This committee

CARDIA AMBULATORY BLOOD PRESSURE MONITORING SUBSTUDY

The procedures for the ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
sub-study have been developed to assess the blood pressure of
selected participants over a 24-hour period after the Year 5 exam
of CARDIA. The study will be conducted at the Birmingham clinical
center. The procedure is designed to evaluate a total sample of
400 individuals with adequate readings, with 100 participants
selected from the four race/sex groups. Participation will be
voluntary, and all willing participants will be reimbursed $25 for
travel and other expenses.

METHOD
INSTRUMENTATION

The ambulatory blood pressure monitor to be used will be the
Suntech Accutracker II. This instrument is an auscultatory device
which uses a gating method, employing the EKG signal, for
determining Korotkoff sounds. Aside from standardized procedures
necessary for any blood pressure recording, the device must be
positioned on the arm so that the microphone is over the brachial
artery. Three EKG leads must also be attached to the chest area.
Monitors will be programmed to take blood pressure at an average
of every 20 minutes during the day (6:00 a.m. through 10:00 p.m.)
and at an average of every 30 minutes during the night (10:00 p.m.
through 6:00 a.m.).

PARTICIPANTS

Ambulatory monitoring will be conducted among participants
until a total of 400 acceptable recordings have been obtained with
100 of these participants in each of the four race/sex groups.
Birmingham participants from the four race/sex groups will be asked
to participate upon completion of their exam until the four cells
are filled with 100 participants each who have acceptable blood

pressure readings.

TRAINING PROCEDURES

Technicians will undergo training in the use of the ambulatory
monitor by representatives of the monitor manufacturer.
Technicians will be required to demonstrate competence in the hook-
up and demonstration of the protocol by someone already certified
in the ambulatory blood pressure monitoring procedure. Each
technician will also be required to complete the entire procedure
obtaining acceptable Office Run data (+10 mmHg), i.e., data
obtained at the time of hook-up, from at least 5 individuals prior
to certification.

PROCEDURE

Participants will be asked to participate in the substudy at
the conclusion of their exam appointments. The protocol will be
explained to them, and they will be informed that they will be
reimbursed $25 for participating in the ambulatory blood pressure
monitoring substudy. What is said to participants should be
similar to the following: "We want to ask some participants to
wear a device so that their blood pressure may be taken over the
course of the day and night. If you agree to do this, we will
reimburse you $25 for your expenses, and you will be givena print-
out of your blood pressure readings." All willing participants
will then be connected to an ambulatory monitor and the monitoring
period will begin. The four groups will be monitored as
participants successfully complete the ambulatory blood pressure
monitoring protocol. Once 100 participants have successfully
completed the protocol in a cell, recruitment of participants in
that cell will cease.

During hook-up, participants will be given an explanation of
the sub-study procedures and asked to sign a sub-study informed
consent form. The Accutracker will then be attached to
participants. Proper placement and accurate recording will be
determined from test readings and Y-tube simultaneous manual

recording of blood pressure levels. A standard sphygmomanometer

will be used in the Y-tube recording of Office Run readings. These
Office Run readings will be recorded on a data sheet; acceptable
placement of the monitor is indicated by both systolic and
diastolic values from the monitor and the mercury manometer within
10 mmHg of one another. Specifics details of the protocol are
contained in Appendix A. Participants will be given an explanation
of the monitor and instructed in procedures in case of difficulty
with the monitor (see Appendix B). Participants will be instructed
to refrain from elective strenuous activity (e.g., exercising)
during the period of recording and instructed to keep their arm in
a still and relaxed position when the monitor is recording.
Participants will also be given instructions for self-monitoring,
i.e., recording daily activities, on the ambulatory blood pressure
monitor log, and these instructions and completion of the log will
be reviewed with each participant (see Appendix B).

The ambulatory blood pressure monitor log will be used to
record their location, activity, stress level, and time when a
cigarette was last smoked (see Appendix B). Categories for
location will include: home, work, store, car, and other.
Categories to record activity will include: sleeping, lying/awake,
sitting, standing, walking at regular pace, walking at fast pace,
and other. Stress level will be assessed on a 7-point scale, and

time since last smoked cigarette will be recorded in minutes.

The monitor will be set to record on the average every 20
minutes during normal awake hours and every 30 minutes during
normal sleep hours (i.e., 10:00 p.m. through 6:00 a.m.). To reduce
the possibility that participants will anticipate the recording of
their blood pressure and systematically affect their readings, the
monitors will be programmed to record the actual readings on a
variable schedule, conforming to the overall interval averages.

Participants will be asked to wear the monitor until the next
morning when they will return to the clinic. Test readings and Y-
tube simultaneous manual recording of blood pressure levels will

also be taken and recorded prior to removing the recorders from

participants (see Appendix A for detailed procedures). The
Ambulatory Blood Pressure Questionnaire will also be administered
to participants by the technician to assess for sleep difficulties
and stress and activity factors (see Appendix C). The data will
be transferred from the Accutracker according to standard
procedures (see Appendix D).

DATA ANALYSIS

Measures of central tendency will be computed from
satisfactory blood pressure readings for daytime, nighttime, work
and home periods. Daytime levels will be compared to target organ
variables (such as LV mass index and creatinine), exam recorded BP
levels, race, Year 2 exam reactivity, and hostility and anger
measures, Differences between work and home levels will be
computed and compared between males and females, between blacks and
whites, and by other variables. Percent reduction in BP from
daytime to nighttime readings will be compared to target organ
variables and exam recorded blood pressures. Variance in daytime
readings will be examined for relations between Year 2 exam
reactivity data.

As the monitor is attached to participants, the following
description and instructions should be reviewed (these
instructions do not have to be read verbatim, but the
essentials of these instructions need to be provided to each
participant): "We are conducting this study so that we may
determine how much your blood pressure changes throughout the
day as you go through normal activities. First the microphone
will be positioned on your arm and kept in place by an
adhesive pad. The cuff will then be wrapped loosely around
your upper arm with the microphone underneath. [For females:
You will be asked to wear a gown while the monitor is attached
to you.] Three electrodes will then be attached to your chest
using adhesive pads. To avoid unnecessary discomfort and
ensure good skin contact, any hairs on the small areas of your
chest where the electrodes will be placed may have to be

your waist. At pre-set times, the control box will inflate
the cuff (it makes a humming noise while doing this) and will
record your blood pressure. The monitor is most accurate and
completes measurements most quickly when you relax your arm
to your side and stop arm movement when the cuff inflates.
Do not stiffen or bend your arm when the cuff is inflated.
At night, this should not disturb your sleep significantly.
You should try to avoid any strenuous exercise or work during
the period that you are wearing the monitor. If the monitor

not be able to take a shower while wearing the monitor, but
you may take a sponge bath, making sure that you do not get
the monitor or the devices attached to your chest wet. At
night when you sleep, it is best to not lie on the arm that
has the cuff around it, and you may want to place the control

box on the floor next to you. Placing a pillow over the
control box also helps to cover up the noise, if the noise

something other than the monitor display. This would
result in the diary times disagreeing by a few minutes
with the times from the monitor.

4. "Extended" 24-Hour Clock Used.

The participant attempted to record times using a 24-hour
clock, but times greater than "23:59" were also recorded.

B. Diary Entries That Cannot Be Coded.

Rarely, you may encounter one or more items in a diary that
you are unable to edit. If you do, circle and initial the
space on the edit worksheet where the item would normally be
recorded. If there is a cluster of items that you cannot
record, you may enclose them as a group. However, if you do
this, be careful that you do enclose only items that you
cannot edit.

Also, keep track of how many of these items occur in a given
diary and, when finished transcribing all the editable items,
write the number of uneditable items in the space provided at
the bottom of the last page of the participant's edit
worksheet.

Note that each blank that you cannot enter a response for
counts as an "uneditable item." For example, a single diary
line that you cannot transcribe counts as five (5) items: the
diary time and each of the four following columns.

Cc. Participant ID.

Check the participant's ID number. Digits 2 - 5 of the
participant's CARDIA ID are printed at the top of each page
of the edit worksheet.

For example, if the CARDIA ID is 1-1937-3223349, the digits
"1937" will appear on the worksheet's ID line.

D. First Entry on Worksheet.

Locate the pre~printed ambulatory blood pressure (ABP) monitor
time on the edit worksheet that corresponds most closely with
the first time recorded in the activity diary. you will begin
entering diary information on this line.

E. About Time.

All times in the activity diaries should be recorded using a
24-hour clock, that is, a clock with times running from 00:00
(12 midnight) to 23:59 (11:59 pm). This was not always done;
following are instructions for editing specific kinds of
miscoded times or skipped readings.

1. If the participant skipped one or two times, you may
write the skipped monitor times from the edit worksheet
in the diary between the times that the participant did
record. If you do this, also draw in blanks under the
four columns to the right of the inserted time; this will
make clear that an observation is missing. Take care
with this, so that data entry personnel will be able to
understand what you have done, and handle it
appropriately.

2. If the time recorded in the diary is from a 12-hour
clock, convert it to 24-hour clock notation.

3. If the time is recorded using an "extended" 24-hour
clock, that is, times greater than "23:59" were recorded,
you should attempt to convert these "extended" times to
24-hour clock times.

If the time recorded in the diary is exactly midway
between two monitor times, there is no way for you to
decide which of the monitor times on the edit worksheet
it should be associated with; therefore, that line in
the diary should be considered uneditable.

Circle and initial the line in the diary. Leave both of
the lines on the worksheet with times surrounding the
diary time blank, but circle and initial the lines,
adding the note, "Times Tied".

Since you cannot record any of the items on that line of
the diary, add five (5) to the count of uneditable items.

F. Smoking.

1.

If a participant does not smoke, you should record "9"
as the edit worksheet's first entry in the "Smoked"
column, and leave the following entries in the "Smoked"
column blank.

Some non-smoking participants will record "1" for all or
most of the "Smoked" items. If a diary follows this
pattern, or if some notation ("Don't smoke.") appears in
the diary, you may complete the "Smoked" items on the
worksheet in the manner just described.

If a participant smokes, record the "1" and "2" responses
as entered in the "Smoke@" column. If an entry for a
particular time is left blank, the corresponding entry
on the edit worksheet should be left blank.

G. When the Participant is Asleep.

The usual way of recording periods of sleep on the edit
worksheet would be to match an observation's diary time with
its monitor time, and transcribe whatever the participant has
recorded in his/her diary in the other columns.

Some specific situations that you may encounter are described
in the following notes.

1.

Some participants will record an "Activity" entry of "2"
("Lying down, but awake") for a time immediately before
falling asleep. The diary's next entry will be for a
time after they wake the next day. If this is the case,
do not impute a "sleeping" entry.

Participants may skip one or more lines in the diary
between the last entry before sleeping and the first one
after waking. The diary entries on each side of this gap
should be matched to the monitor reading times printed
on the edit worksheet; that is, do not skip the same
number of lines on the edit worksheet as the participant

skipped in the diary (unless, of course, the diary and
monitor times match).

Some participants will record one or more "sleep" entries
like this:

Location Activity Stress Smoked
1 1 1 1

These lines are either "dummy" entries, or were recorded
at the time of monitor readings which caused them to wake
up. If this is the case, record them on the edit
worksheet on the line with the corresponding monitor
time(s).

CARDIA QUALITY CONTROL PROCEDURES
Introduction

As in previous exams, the CARDIA Coordinating Center will
perform quality control studies during the Year 5 exam. The
Coordinating Center will be assisted in the performance of these
duties by the clinical centers and the Quality Control Committee.

There are two primary purposes for quality control. The most
important purpose is to provide feedback to the clinical centers
in order to maintain and improve the quality of the study data over
the course of the exam cycle. A secondary purpose is to
historically document the level of quality.

Quality control involves the collection of specific types of
data and the subsequent analysis of that data. It is primarily a
measure of the quality of data (1) either collected by the clinical
centers or (2) measured by central laboratories and centers
associated with the CARDIA study.

Quality control is accomplished in many different ways
depending upon the type of data being collected, the type of
procedure being analyzed, and the associated outcome variable in
question. The types of quality control measures that will be used
in the CARDIA study will assess the reliability and validity of the
data.

The tools which will be used include:

1. Monitoring -
a. instrument calibration
b. room, freezer temperatures
c. shipping schedules
da. retention efforts

ac - 1

4/90

Internal surveillance -

a. pulmonary function quality control

b. editing forms

c. laboratory internal quality control procedures
d. echo reader assessments

External surveillance -

a. inter-, intra-technician variability (blood
pressure, anthropometry, echocardiography)

b. inter-, intra-reader variability

c. measurement variability - laboratory instruments
using split pair samples

A manual following this section has been developed which

outlines the particular steps that will be taken for each of the

components of the CARDIA exam in order to assure that quality data

is being collected and reported.

Coordinating Center Responsibilities:

The responsibilities of the Coordinating Center in developing

and carrying out quality control measures are listed below:

1.

Develop a training session to teach/train standardization
of data collection.

Identify and notify clinical centers of the quality of
performance of interviewers, technicians, and other
responsible personnel.

Identify calibration problems and/or perform the

corrective action by notifying the clinical center and/or
correcting or flagging the data.

gc -2

4. Identify problems in the external reporting centers and
communicate this information to them for corrective
action.

5. Maintain historical data which describes the quality and
performance of the entire CARDIA study.

6. Report pertinent information to the Quality Control
Committee and the Steering Committee.

7. Design protocol and procedures for periodic site visits
which check for quality of performance and adherence to
CARDIA standardized procedures within the clinical
centers.

8. Develop a system for handling, filing, and promptly
analyzing incoming data and forms which have been created
for use in quality control.

9. Develop protocol for alerting clinical centers when
periodic quality and performance reports are past due.

10. Keep an up-to-date file of all completed personnel
certification and recertification forms.

11. Produce and maintain the important study documents
related to CARDIA quality control: (1) the Quality
Control Documentation presented to the Quality Control
Committee following an exam cycle; and (2) documents
found in the bi-annual report to the CARDIA Review Board.

Quality Control Committee
The Quality Control Committee, as an ad hoc committee of the

CARDIA Steering Committee, will meet bi-annually to review the
status of the study quality control monitoring. Decisions

4/90 ec - 3

regarding current and proposed techniques will be discussed, as
well as current topics. Conference calls will be organized as
needed. The Committee will be kept abreast of current issues
through frequent correspondence with the Deputy Director of the
Coordinating Center who serves as the chair of this committee. The
Committee includes members of the primary investigative group,
NHLBI staff and outside consultants.

Site Visits

Early in the exam cycle, site visits will be made to each of
the clinical centers. The primary goals of the site visits are:
(1) to observe the clinic under normal operating conditions for
adherence to protocol; (2) to increase/improve communication
between study administration and clinic personnel; and (3) to
demonstrate the study's concern for the quality of data collection.
Each site visit team will consist of one Clinic Coordinator, one
member of the Quality Control Committee (a clinical center
Principal Investigator involved in clinic operations) and one staff
member from the Coordinating Center.

Following the site visits, a formal report will be developed
and distributed to the Steering Committee, the Quality Control
Committee, the Institute and each of the clinical centers. The
Quality Control Committee will meet to discuss the site visit
reports and make recommendations for the follow-up and correction
of problem areas in a timely manner. Each Clinic Coordinator and
Principal Investigator will be asked to respond in writing in a
timely manner to the Quality Control Committee regarding the
resolution of any problems.

QUALITY CONTROL PROCEDURES MANUAL

The following manual lists the quality control procedures
which are to be carried out for specified components of the CARDIA
Year 5 exam. The list includes the specific measures and
procedures, who is responsible for the procedure and the frequency
with which the procedure should be performed.

The clinical centers are responsible for filing the proper
reports with the Coordinating Center at the indicated times. All
other reports and logs are to be kept up-to-date at the clinical
center for periodic review.

A log book must be kept for all specified exam components; the
data and actions taken (including calibrations, checks, cleaning,
problems, and solutions) should be recorded in the log. This
information is necessary to document these procedures.

Lecal clinic coordinators are requested to periodically
observe the technique in each of the following sections: blood
pressure, phlebotomy, pulmonary function and anthropometry. An
outline/check~list of the standardized CARDIA procedure for each
of these actions has been included in this section. These forms
should also to be completed at times of recertification.

Error Detection and Correction in Collected Data:

Each clinical center is required to submit a 10% sample of
form sets to the Coordinating Center on a monthly basis for a
Manual quality control review. A list of randomly generated ID
numbers for each clinic will be supplied by the Coordinating
Center. The manual review of forms by staff of the Coordinating
Center will entail a page-by-page review of the following items:

1. form completion;

2. affixed CARDIA ID and quality control labels;

3. interviewer ID's;

ec - 8&8

4. skip patterns observed;

5. medical history and tobacco follow-up forms when
applicable;

6. drugs and occupation coding; and

7. overall form consistency and preparedness for data
entry.

A report of errors and/or recommendations for improvement will be
sent to the Steering Committee, NHLBI and Clinic Coordinators
following each monthly review.

Data Entry Quality Control:

The 10% sample of participant form sets sent to the
Coordinating Center each month will be subsequently entered at the
Coordinating Center using the same data entry system resident in
the clinics and a data entry clerk trained in CARDIA data entry.
A field-by-field comparison will be made between the record entered
at the Coordinating Center and the record entered at the clinic.
A report which indicates which fields were discordant, the data
entry person responsible for the entry, and form and data entry
person-specific error rates will be generated. The first-pass
error rates will be adjudicated (via the hard-copy of the form) for
data entry errors made by the Coordinating Center data entry
person.

The resulting error rates will be summarized and forwarded to
each clinical center. All forms from a file which yields an error
rate greater than 0.50% will be re-entered in the clinic. The
double entry of the 10% sample will be an ongoing process so that
the Coordinating Center can alert the clinical centers of specific
problems, before a large number of forms have been entered.

In further analysis of this data, the Coordinating Center will
assess the quantitative effect of data entry errors by comparing
the mean value of variables from an unedited file to the mean

values from the edited (error-free) file. This analysis will be
performed for several of the classic risk factor variables,
representing both categorical and continuous measures (e.g., blood
pressure data, medical history, smoking and anthropometrics).
Statistical tests for differences between mean values will be
performed and evaluated.

orato

The Coordinating Center will receive laboratory results on
examined participants from Medlantic Research Foundation on a
monthly basis. To assess the quality of these measures, a
two-pronged system will be implemented. First, univariate analyses
will be conducted on these results. Based on these analyses,
summary statistics (means, variances, etc.) and out-of-range values
will be obtained and recorded and, if necessary, investigated
further to ensure correctness.

Second, duplicate measures will be made on a 5% random sample

of participants. These measures will be sent in separate shipments
(usually a month apart) to the laboratory and the laboratory will
be blinded as to which measures were paired. Reliability will be
assessed using correlation coefficients and the technical error
measurement. (The technical error is the square root of the pooled
between measures variance as a percent of the sample mean:
((Sqrt (= a’/2n) )/sample mean)* 100.) The technical error is
compared to the laboratories internal coefficient of variation.
If there is evidence of high technical error then the laboratory
will be contacted and queried for an explanation.

RECERTIFICATION PROCEDURES

Recertification of technicians who perform blood pressure
measures, pulmonary function measures, anthropometry measures and
phlebotomy will be required once during the Year 5 exam in December
1990. The recertification procedure involves in-house observation
of technique by a centrally trained technician (usually the Clinic
Coordinator) and completion of a station check sheet. Following
recertification, the Clinic Coordinator will forward a memorandum
to the Coordinating Center indicating the technicians which have
been recertified. A copy of the completed check sheets and copies
of any other forms or measurements taken will also be sent. A
list of the certified and recertified technicians will be
maintained at the Coordinating Center.

Portions of the Year 0 exam training video tapes will be
applicable to the Year 5 exam and should be used in re-training
technicians needing additional assistance.

Blood Pressure

Technicians are to be recertified by reviewing the videotape,
"Measuring Blood Pressure", and by completing the self-test at the
end of the tape. The videotape should be stopped immediately after
the twelfth exercise in the self-test (prior to the answers being
shown). The supervisor or Clinic Coordinator will check the
responses from each technician using the answer sheet provided by
the Coordinating Center. If any single answer (systolic or
diastolic) varies more than + 4 mm Hg, the technician will repeat
the self-test. Answers to the self-test should be forwarded to the
Coordinating Center along with the Blood Pressure Check Sheets.
In addition, each technician will complete two readings with the
supervisor or Clinic Coordinator on a Y-tube stethoscope. The
supervisor or Clinic Coordinator will use the Blood Pressure Check
Sheets in evaluating the technicians.

Anthropometry

Each anthropometry technician is required to obtain all body
size measurements from five individuals (e.g., clinic staff) twice,
with a one week time interval between the two measurements.
Information should be dated and recorded on separate anthropometry
forms and paired by subject. Concurrently, the Clinic Coordinator
or chief anthropometry technician will be required to observe and
complete one Anthropometry Check Sheet on each technician during

the recertification time period.

Phlebotomy

The Clinic Coordinator and/or phlebotomy supervisor will
observe the techniques of blood drawing and shipping as performed
by each phlebotomy technician. This observer will fill out the
following on each technician: (1) Blood Drawing Check Sheet and
(2) Blood Handling, Storage and Shipping Check Sheet. In addition,
each phlebotomy technician should view the Year 0 exam phlebotomy
training tape.

Pulmonary Function

The Clinic Coordinator and/or pulmonary function supervisor
will observe the technique as performed by each technician and will
complete the Pulmonary Function Check Sheet. Each pulmonary
function technician should also view the Year 0 pulmonary function
training tape.

INTERVIEWING PRINCIPLES AND PROCEDURES

Interviewing, in part, is a science: There are definite rules
that produce valid results. Interviewing is also an art:
Frequently there are only general guidelines to follow and much
depends on the sensitivity of the interviewer. The procedures and
techniques that follow will help you to conduct interviews which
will yield valid data.

I. DEVELOPING A GOOD INTERVIEWING RELATIONSHIP

Interviewing is one of the major parts of the CARDIA study and
therefore it is crucial that interviewers present questions
appropriately, record the participants' replies precisely and
accurately and probe meaningfully. In order to maintain an
objective information gathering atmosphere, the interviewer must
convey that he/she is an understanding person capable of accepting
information in a non-judgmental manner as well as convey an
interest in what the participant is saying. The participant must
find satisfaction in talking to a receptive person without the fear
of appearing inadequate.

It will be the interviewer's responsibility to obtain full and
accurate information by eliciting cooperation from participants,
establishing and maintaining rapport, encouraging active
participation of participants' answers in a strictly neutral way.
Interviewers are skilled professionals. Their skills make it
possible for participants to give frank, complete, relevant answers

to questions.

In general, you will find that the majority of participants
are willing to be interviewed. A confident, enthusiastic approach
which assumes people are willing to be interviewed is a most
effective technique.

4/90 INT - 2

A. Increasing the Participant's Cooperativeness. Previous

studies have identified several factors that will increase the

respondent's receptiveness.

1. Be prepared and know your material. Participants need
to feel that you are interested in the study and
interested in their opinions. Be an active listener and
establish comfortable eye contact with the participant.

2. Offer convincing statements about the purpose of the
study.

3. Discuss how the respondent was selected.

4. Describe the beneficial uses of the research findings to

both the respondent and to the community.

II. THE TWO MAIN KINDS OF QUESTIONS

A. Precoded Questions. With precoded questions, you circle the
appropriate code number (or check the right answer box). In
addition to checking a box or circling the right answer, it
is very important that you record the participant's verbatim
response whenever there is any question about which code is
appropriate.

B. Open-ended Questions. With open-ended questions, the question
is followed by a blank space for you to record the
participant's answer word for word. This kind of question
suggests no possible answers, so it is your job to fill in
that blank space with the participant's own words and to
encourage him/her to express ideas as fully and as clearly as

possible.

III. INTERVIEWER ADMINISTERED QUESTIONNAIRES

There are several standard procedures for reading questions:
Read in a natural conversation rhythm and in a normal tone of
voice. Read as if you are speaking. Be cautious about reading
questions too rapidly; the participant may not feel comfortable
asking you to repeat questions and consequently the answer will not
reflect his/her true thoughts on the issue. Be aware of the
participant's facial expressions, e.g., puzzled, confused. Repeat

4/90 INT

the question if it is answered inappropriately, but repeat it

exactly as written. Show no impatience when being asked to repeat

a question.

Each question must be asked of each participant in the same

way, and in the same order to insure that comparable information

is being obtained from all the respondents in the study.

Interview instructions are provided throughout the interview.
These instructions are not to be read to participants but are
intended to let you know what to do at each point. The
interviewer instructions appear in all capital letters.

Read only those code categories which appear in the question
and you are instructed to read UNLESS:

1. You have special instructions to the contrary.

2. There is an instruction to "READ CHOICES", or

3. A question ends with a dash or colon and it is obvious
that the codes must be read. Don NOT read any codes

which do not appear in the question.

Ask the questions exactly as worded and in the same order as
they appear in they questionnaires. Minor changes in wording
can completely change the meaning of a question. Unless each
interviewer asks the questions exactly as shown, the answers
are meaningless. Similarly, you must follow the sequence of
questions. Do not ask questions out of order unless you are
given special instructions to do so.

Ask every question. It is the interviewer's responsibility
to ask every question. Often a previous statement by the
participant will partially answer another question, but rarely

The two most effective neutral probes are silence and

repeating the original question.

Silence. The value of silence cannot be overestimated. Many
people, including interviewers, react to silence as a vacuum
that must be filled with constant chatter. The interviewer
who can wait quietly and patiently will soon find that 15
seconds of silence is more than most participants can take,
and the participant will often expand or clarify a previously
inadequate answer.

Repeating the Question or Answer Categories. Be sure to

repeat the question as stated in the questionnaire. This is

particularly useful when the participant answers a question
irrelevantly. In some cases it will be necessary to remind
the participant of your frame of reference, i.e., to
acknowledge what the participant has said and then bring the
participant back to the topic by repeating the question.

Do not Accept a "Don't Know" Answer Without Probing at Least
Once. If a response is a "don't know", probe by asking:
"Well, what do you think?" or "I'd like to know your opinion"
(if the question asks for an opinion rather than facts). If
the question deals with facts, we prefer an approximation to
no answer at all, and you might probe "what's your best
guess?" or "approximately?" to convey the idea that 100%
accuracy is not required.

Use Neutral Probes That Do Not Suggest Answers. Probes are
needed to obtain more complete, accurate answers. All probes
must be non-directive, i.e., the probe must not suggest any
particular answer to the participant. Probes should be used
whenever the participant is hesitant in answering questions;
when he/she seems to have trouble expressing him/herself; when
he/she seems too shy to speak at length; whenever there is any
reason for the interviewer to believe that the participant has
not given a complete report of his/her thoughts; and finally,
reassuring probes are needed when a participant seems to lack

confidence.

1. In what way?

3. How do you mean?

4. I would like your impression.

5. I would like your opinion.

8. Can you explain that in a little more detail?
9. How are you using the term...?

10. How is that? or How does that work?
11. Anything at all - even little things?

Always Cross Reference. When you probe to clarify a response,

interesting, but interviewers must bear in mind what

Watch for Vague, Incomplete Answers. A probe such as "tell
me more about..." is effective.

Avoid "Depends" or "Qualified" Answers. When the participant
gives a response of this nature, it is advisable to use probes
such as repeating the question; preface the question with a

HOW TO RECORD THE INTERVIEWS

The following suggestions are recommended:

1. Be prepared to write.

2. Periodically establish eye contact with the participant
while you are writing.

3. Use abbreviations to help you get down as much as
possible.

4. Always report a response using the participant's exact
words.

5S. Always record verbatim the response to a probe.

6. If you question whether you circled the correct code, be

sure to record the participant's verbatim response.

7. If you make a recording mistake, cross out the wrong part
instead of erasing: it is faster and easier to read.
Then circle and initial the correct answer. If an answer

is skipped, circle both spaces and write "NA".

VII. FOLLOWING THE CENTRALIZED TRAINING SESSION

Become familiar with the questionnaires. Read instructions
carefully. Administer questionnaires to yourself just as you would
a participant and probe yourself if an answer to a question is
uncodable or otherwise inadequate. We recommend completing the
interview with a friend. Re-read the instructions watching for any
errors you made so that you do not repeat them on subsequent
interviews. Study the instructions thoroughly so that you
understand the purpose of the questions.

You may wish to re-read this manual following the conduct of
interviews: it may provide a different perspective and reinforce
what you have experienced.

INSTRUCTIONS FOR CODING OCCUPATION

The occupation of the Respondent will be coded at the centers.
It is recommended that the person who is conducting the interviews
on the Sociodemographic Questionnaire be the person to assign the
occupation code. The interviewer will become aware of deficiencies
in responses to the occupation questions and will be sensitized to
the need for careful probing for full and accurate responses. Also
the interviewer may recall statements that were not recorded but
may provide clues to the appropriate code in uncertain cases.

The basic resource for coding occupation is the Alphabetical
Index of Industries and Occupations, 1980 Census of Population,

Final Edition, November, 1982. The document is available from the

Superintendent of Documents, U.S. Government Printing Office,
Washington, D.C. 20402, or from any U.S. Department of Commerce
District Office. (Prepayment is required if ordering by mail.)
Check price before ordering. For information call GPO, Washington
D.C., 202-783-3238.

A companion volume, the Classified Index of Industries and

Occupations, is available from the same source.

Both indexes list some 20,000 industry and 29,000 occupation
titles. The Alphabetical Index lists titles in alphabetical order,
the Classified Index lists them in numerical order. The
Alphabetical Index is the basic resource to use in identifying the
appropriate occupational code. The Classified Index helps the user
understand how the titles fit into the classification structure.
This volume is also useful when dividing between two or more
categories. It gives a broad picture of all the titles included
within a category.

Both indexes are divided into two sections: the "white pages"
list the industry codes; the "yellow pages" list the occupation

5790 INT - 18

categories. Each industry and occupation title has a 3-digit
number or a letter which can be translated into a 3-digit number.
Our task is to identify the 3-digit occupational code which best
fits the respondent's answers to the occupation questions.
Basically, the procedure is similar to looking words up in a
dictionary. Once you get the hang of using the index, the 3-digit
code is relatively simple to assign for most cases. Please note,
the Industry "white pages" has a section of SELF-EMPLOYED with an
extensive listing.

The Coder uses the description given by the Respondent to
identify the occupational code in the "yellow pages." In those
cases where specific industries are associated with an occupational
title, the Coder uses the industry information to select the
appropriate code. Industry information, even though we are not
coding it directly, may help to identify the appropriate occupation
code.

The use of the 3-digit Census occupational codes provides
maximum analytic flexibility. The codes can be aggregated into a
common system across centers or into a system tailored to
particular research objectives.

ALCOHOL USE QUESTIONNAIRE INSTRUCTIONS

In this questionnaire, respondents will be asked about alcohol use.
It is interviewer-administered.

General Instructions
(1) The path through this questionnaire is indicated by GO TO and SKIP
TO statements. These and other instructions to the interviewer are
capitalized and parenthesized. Do not read these instructions
aloud.
(2) Question 1 determines whether the respondent drank any alcoholic
beverages during the past year. Questions 2-7 apply to those who
did.
(3) Use 2 digit code. If a person drinks less than once a week, the
answers to questions 2, 3, and 4 should be 00.
(4) If person answers "2 drinks per day," interviewers should write
down the participant's answer verbatim and then convert to
appropriate time slot -- i.e. with 14 drinks/week, ask the subject,
"Is that 14 drinks per week?" Ask in a non-judgmental manner.
(5) If a person answers 10 drinks/month, say "How many would that
usually be per week?"
(6) If a person says "I drink about 50 drinks a weekend whenever
there's a party", repeat the question, placing emphasis on"per
week". Possible probe: "How many would that be per week?"
(7) The number given in answer to question 6 and only that number
should be used in asking question 7. No calculation should be made
regarding the "about" unless the participant asks what we mean by
"about" or asks a related question.

The participant may provide the total amount of hard liquor
consumed in a week. For example, the participant may say that he/she
drinks a fifth of whiskey per week. This must be converted to "drinks
per week" in order to record the data on the form. The following table
provides the necessary information to convert total amount of liquor to
number of drinks.

General Information

In this questionnaire, the respondent is asked about past
medical history and medication use. The questionnaire is divided
into two sections: self-administered initial questions and, where

Each respondent should receive a set of self-administered

GLOSSARY OF CARDIA MEDICAL TERMS

angina -- chest pain due to inadequate blood supply to part of
the heart.
aortic stenosis -- narrowing of the valve between the main pumping chamber

of the heart, the left ventricle, and the major blood vessel
supplying blood to most of the body, the aorta.

cardiomyopathy -- a disorder in which the heart muscle becomes weak. This
may be the result of any of a number of medical conditions.

chorea -- (please see rheumatic fever)

cirrhosis -- hardening of the liver with the loss of normal liver function,
often as the result of excessive alcohol intake over a prolonged
period of time; may be due to other causes, too, such as viral
infection.

congestive heart failure -- accumulation of fluid in the lungs and in other
parts of the body as a result of a poorly functioning heart.

coronary occlusion -- blockage of a blood vessel to the heart leading to death
of part of the heart muscle (heart attack, myocardial infarction).

coronary thrombosis -- same as coronary occlusion.

duodenum -- the first part of the small intestine. It is the part of the
intestinal system that occurs right after the stomach.

glomerulonephritis -- a kidney disorder characterized by inflammation of parts
of the kidney called the glomeruli. In its acute form, it is
characterized by the presence of large amounts of protein in
the urine, fluid retention (swelling of the ankles and other
parts of the body with fluid), and high blood pressure.

hepatitis -- inflammation of the liver, generally as a result of viral
infection or excessive alcohol intake.

hysterectomy -- surgical removal of the uterus (womb).

kidney stones -- stones formed in the kidney, resulting form abnormal concen-

tration of minerals and other substances; stones can cause severe
pain if released from the kidney into an area in which they
block urine flow.

mitral valve prolapse -- an abnormality, usually harmless, of the mitral valve,
which is in between the two chambers of the left side of the
heart. This abnormality is found relatively frequently in
young women and usually requires no treatment.

myocardial infarction -- death of part of the heart due to loss of blood supply
to that part of the heart (heart attack).

4490 INT - 41

GLOSSARY (2)

myocarditis -- a rare condition in which inflammation of the heart muscle
occurs, generally as the result of a viral infection.

nephritis -- inflammation of the kidney, occurring as the result of
infection or of a number of other medical conditions.

pyelonephritis -- bacterial infection of the kidney.

rheumatic fever or chorea -- an illness which may result from untreated
streptococcal (a bacteria) infections which is characterized
by fever, joint pain, and may affect the heart and cause damage
to the heart valves. If the brain is involved, chorea or
abnormal movements may occur.

rheumatic heart disease-~ abnormalities of the heart valves (valves which keep
blood moving in the right direction through the heart) resulting
from rheumatic fever. These abnormalities usually do not
manifest themselves until several years after the episode of
rheumatic fever.

sickle cel] trait -- a blood condition in which red blood cells have a slight
tendency to form sickle shapes. This conditions causes no
symptoms or physical damage, as opposed to sickle cell disease,
in which so many red blood cells can form sickle shapes that
anemia and a number of other medical problems can occur. The
presence of sickle cell trait can be determined by a blood test.

thyroid -- a gland located in the neck which helps to regulate the metabolic
rate, that is, the rate at which the body burns up energy.

valvular heart disease -- disease of the heart valves (valves which keep blood
moving in the right direction through the heart) which cause
the valves to malfunction. Valvular heart disease may result
from congenital disorders, infection, degenerative changes,
or rheumatic fever.

vasectomy -- a surgical procedure to make men sterile in which the vas deferens,
the sperm-carrying tubes, are cut.

INTRODUCTION
The Physical Activity History (PAH) was developed for CARDIA
to help determine a participant's usual activity patterns (1).

These questions focus on activities done during the past year.

Because recent longitudinal studies of physical activity and
coronary heart disease suggest that moderate intensity physical
activity has a protective effect, we have expanded this
questionnaire in the Year 5 exam to include more questions about
moderate activity (pages 6, 7 and 8 of the questionnaire). The
questions in Sections N, 0 and P are taken from the ARIC version
of the Baecke questionnaire (2).

The questions on pages 1 through 5 are identical to the

questions used in the Year 2 exam Physical Activity History.

It is important that the interviewer read each question
exactly as written, and that appropriate probes be used to elicit

answers that are as accurate as possible.

Refer to the Interview Administered Forms section of this
manual (pages INT-5, 6, 7 and 8) for acceptable probing techniques.
If the participant asks about the meaning of a term, turn the

question back to him/her: "Whatever it means to you."

QUESTION 2: SECTIONS A-M

Scores related to energy expenditure are computed from intensity
levels and the months of less frequent and more frequent performance of
each activity (see Table 1).

The intensity level assigned to each activity is roughly the number
of kilocalories expended in one minute of activity. Intensities were
patterned after those used by Taylor et al. (3) and Folsom et al. (4)
which in turn are based on formulation by Reiff et al. (5). Exceptions
are bicycling, which was set at an intensity code of 6 to reflect the
wording "faster than 10 miles per hour"; and vigorous job activity (not
included in Taylor's or Folsom's work), which was set at an intensity
code of 5, somewhat less than that for weight lifting.

Amount of activity performed is based on months of participation
and an assumption about relative duration of activity for frequent
versus infrequent participators. The duration of activity in more
frequent participation months (in which the activity was performed more
than the activity-specific cutpoint of 2 to 5 hours per week) is assumed
somewhat arbitrarily to be three times as great as the duration of
activity in less frequent participation months. The sum of the products
of Intensity * Amount is computed for each activity class A through M
("running/jogging" through "home maintenance/gardening"), i.e. bi*(mi
+ 3%ni), where i ranges through the activity classes, bi is the
intensity, mi is the number of months of less frequent participation and
ni is the number of months of more frequent participation. The Heavy
Intensity Score sums these computed values over the class of eight
vigorous intensity activities (A-H), the Moderate Intensity Score is
restricted to the class of the five remaining moderate intensity
activities, and the Total Score is the sum of these two subscores.
Since the number of minutes of performance in any month is unknown and
likely to vary substantially across activities, no interpretation as
caloric expenditure per week is available, and the score is left
unaltered in "Exercise Units".

QUESTION 2: SECTIONS N-P - INTRODUCTORY COMMENTS

Physical inactivity has been shown in several epidemiologic
investigations to be directly associated with coronary heart
disease incidence. The Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study
(ARIC) requirements for physical activity assessment were that the
instrument: (1) measure usual activity; (2) be relatively valid and

reliable; and (3) be as brief as possible (less than 10 minutes).
The ARIC Physical Activity Questionnaire is based on a
self-administered questionnaire developed for a Dutch population
by Baecke, et al. (2). A copy of the original questionnaire is
included as Appendix 1. This version of the original Baecke
questionnaire, for use by the Study of Activity, Fitness and
Exercise (SAFE), was adapted from changes made by ARIC as follows:

1. The original questionnaire had no time reference. ARIC
pretesting indicated confusion by respondents on how to
include activities that were seasonal, just taken up, or just
given up. To clarify this, ARIC instructions added that the
interest is in physical activity in the past year. This was
felt to be consistent with the intent of the original question
9.

QUESTIONS ON HOSPITALIZATIONS, SERIOUS ILLNESSES AND INJURIES

The CARDIA study will keep track of major health events that
occur in the follow-up of the CARDIA participants. Whether or not
the participants report any "Other Major Health Problem", the
interviewer should ask for these events. This questionnaire asks
for signed permission to obtain hospital and medical records.

INT - 71

KNOWLEDGE, ATTITUDE AND BEHAVIOR QUESTIONNAIRE

1. What do you think are the most important causes of heart
attack and stroke? PROBE FOR UP TO 5 RESPONSES BY SAYING:
"That's exactly what we are looking for. Can you think of
anything else?" CHECK EACH CATEGORY FOR AS MANY RESPONSES AS
THE PARTICIPANT INDICATES. DO NOT READ RESPONSES.

(Responses A through W)

Many respondents focus on prevention, not causes. The
interviewer may ask for clarification if the response is unclear.
For instance, if the respondent says "I try not to eat too much red
meat," clarify with "So do you mean eating too much red meat is a
cause of heart attack and stroke?"

The respondent is being asked opinions about the most
important causes of cardiovascular disease. The interviewer must
be familiar with the list of possible coding categories. If the
participant's answer is not sufficiently precise for coding, ask
the participant to be more specific. For instance, in follow-up
to a vague answer such as "Lifestyle," or "How people live today,"
probe for clarification by asking "What do you mean by rau

If the respondent says "Diet" or "Not eating a good diet"
probe for clarification with "What about diet? Can you give me an
example?" Use the general dietary response (Category A) only if
the participant cannot add detail; otherwise choose one of Codes
B-E. Use Code A if the response contradicts Codes B-E, i.e. for
"eating too little red meat". Select Code G for any response
involving too little exercise; Code H for too much exercise; Code
I for any response involving weight/overweight; Code J for
underweight; Code K for any response involving cholesterol which

The CES-D (Center for Epidemiological Studies) is a 20 item

PREFACE
This Year 5 Exam protocol is organized in a manner to
communicate the overall scientific rationale and objectives of
CARDIA, its organizational structure and examination components.
The evolution of the protocol has included discussions of the
competing scientific and logistic demands inherent in a study such
as CARDIA, which combines cross-sectional needs with those
necessary in a prospective longitudinal cohort study.

The protocol is organized around the basic exam components
prefaced by the organizational and policy issues. The details of
the exam procedures will appear in the Manual of Operations (MOO)
and are provided only when necessary for clarity.

4/90

OVERVIEW

While increases in coronary heart disease risk factors occur
in young adulthood in conjunction with significant changes in
physiological measures and in lifestyle, the interrelationships
among these risk factors and changes have not been rigorously
investigated. Both epidemiologic and clinical research in coronary
heart disease have increased our awareness that some risk factors
for disease such as obesity, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia
many be partially determined by genetic factors or behaviors which
are formed in infancy, childhood, and adolescence. Studies to date
also suggest that some of the coronary heart disease risk factors
do not change dramatically before the late teenage years and that
differences in characteristics by sex or race emerge and are most
pronounced after this time. However, relatively little work has
been done to identify the characteristics of young adult life which
may be precursors to, or coincident with, the increase in risk
factors prior to middle age.

Cross-sectional data, for example, suggest that weight gain
is pronounced during the late teens through age 30, particularly
in males, and that positive relationships exist between weight and
lipoprotein fractions during these ages. The reasons for, and
consequences of, this increase in adiposity need further
investigation. The interaction of life events, behavior, changes
in physical activity, and dietary intake that may influence weight
gain and lipoprotein levels should be assessed as well as the
relative importance of weight gain in relationship to risk factor
changes during this age span.

Investigators have examined the consistency of blood pressure
levels in children to determine whether "tracking" occurs into the
teenage years. The results of these studies have raised other
interesting and important questions. Is there evidence for
"tracking" of other coronary risk factors? Does "tracking" persist
into young adult life, a time during which dramatic changes in
lifestyle are often taking place? Are the changes a function of
these changes?

An important component of this study is the study of young
blacks. Since the Black Health Task Force on High Blood Pressure
Control pointed out the lack of knowledge about coronary heart
disease in blacks as applied to this country, a greater focus on
the nature of disease in blacks has been a topic of increasing
consideration.

"Coronary Artery Risk Factor Development in Young Adults"
(CARDIA) is the study of the evolution of coronary heart disease
risk in a cohort of black and white men and women initially 18-30
years old. Such studies will not only contribute to our
understanding of the development of atherosclerotic disease, but
more importantly, help to suggest strategies for prevention before
individual lifestyle patterns become well established.

The original specific hypotheses set forth by each clinical
site may be found in the protocol documents from the previous two
CARDIA examinations.

OBJECTIVES

overall goals of this study are:

To document at baseline and after one or more biennial
intervals, risk factors and changes for coronary heart disease
(CHD) in young (black and white) adults, 18-30 years old.

To identify lifestyles during this age span, which influence
these changes in risk factors. The interrelationships among
risk factors and lifestyles, and changes in these
characteristics will be considered.

secondary objectives of this study are:

To observe age-related trends in risk factors during young
adulthood and to compare cross-sectional with longitudinal
findings.

To perform sub-population analyses on, sex, race, or
sociodemographic groupings, and to compare trends and
processes involved in risk factor development between these
subgroups.

To develop and apply effective methods of follow-up during
these young adult years to achieve maximum participation of
the study populations.

objectives of each clinical center are:

To re-examine at least 80% of the 5115 participants enrolled
in the study.

To maintain, via mail and phone calls at semi-annual intervals
during the follow-up period, contact with each participant in
order to maximize the return rate for future examinations.

To assess risk factors for CHD in these participants.

ADMINISTRATIVE STRUCTURE

Role and Composition of Steering Committee

The Steering Committee is the representative body of the
CARDIA study. It is composed of eight voting members: a Principal
Investigator from each of the four clinical centers, the Director
of the Coordinating Center, the Director of the Echocardiography
Reading Center, the NHLBI Project Officer, and the Chairperson of
the Steering Committee (an individual who is not a representative
of any clinical center or the Coordinating Center). The Steering
Committee provides overall scientific direction for the study and
serves as the focal point of the organizational structure. During
the planning and the execution of the Year 5 exam phase, each
Principal Investigator will be directly responsible for
coordinating all aspects of one or more of the following designated
areas: Publications and Presentations, Content of Year 5 Exam,
Retaining Participants at the Year 5 Exam, Nutrition, Clinic
Coordinator's Issues, Lipids and Chemistries, Psychosocial, Medical
Issues, Pulmonary Function, Blood Pressure and Exercise.

The Steering Committee will meet regularly to review study
progress. Each center is required to be represented by an
investigator or proxy at each meeting of this committee. If a vote
is needed, it will require a two-thirds majority of all eight
voting members. Minutes will be taken by a member of the
Coordinating Center.

The Steering Committee will perform the following functions:

1. Guide and oversee the development of the study Protocol and
the Manual of Operations.

2. Review and approve major changes in the Manual of Operations.
3. Review and approve ancillary studies.
4. Provide advice and assistance to the Coordinating Center,

clinical centers or NHLBI on operational matters.

5. Resolve problems brought to the Steering Committee by
investigators, the Coordinating Center, and any other of the
Central units (Central labs, NHLBI, etc.).

6. Monitor the performance of all participating clinical centers
through site visits according to information provided by the
Coordinating Center in order to insure that an adequate number
of participants are retained; that the clinical centers adhere
to the protocol; and that quality data is collected.

STUDY COMPONENTS
NHLBI

The CARDIA study is a contract of the National Heart, Lung,
and Blood Institute (NHLBI). The NHLBI has assigned a Project
Officer to serve as the main scientific link between NHLBI and the
Program. It is the general responsibility of the NHLBI Project
Officer to:

1. Provide necessary scientific and administrative
communication, liaison and direction to the Principal
Investigators of the Clinical Centers and the
Coordinating Center to assure fulfillment of the
scientific objectives and administrative aspects of this
program for NHLBI and NIH review -- including protocol,
program progress, forms and publications.

2. Serve as a direct link from the organization of CARDIA
to the Director of the NHLBI, to channel inquiries,
recommendations, and policy directives.

Since this is a contract, NHLBI will be the final authority
for determining program policy and how problems should be handled.
A CARDIA Review Board composed of outside scientists will provide
advice to NHLBI on the conduct of the study.

Clinical Centers

The clinical centers are clinical research units supervised
by the Principal Investigators and supported by individual
cooperative agreement research contracts from the NHLBI. Each
clinical center is responsible for following the provisions of the
Protocol and Manual of Operations. The Principal Investigator of
each clinical center is a voting member of the Steering Committee.

Functions and Responsibilities

1. Recruit and train staff to perform the procedures of the study

effectively.

2. Retain participants according to the CARDIA Manual of
Operations (MOO) and examine/evaluate them.

3. Establish and maintain good relations with the participants,
their families, other attending physicians (if any), and the
public.

4, Collect and transmit all required data specimens, etc. in

accordance with established procedures and schedules.

5. Evaluate the progress of the study and alert the Coordinating
Center and Steering Committee to major problems.

6. Work with the Coordinating Center to maintain the quality of
data collected.

CARDIA Coordinating Center

The CARDIA Coordinating Center will be a facilitator of the
study's design, monitoring, and analysis. In this role as a
facilitator, the Coordinating Center will take the lead role in the
generation of the study Protocol and the corresponding Manual of
Operations. It will also take the organizing role for the major
training that will occur. It will have the responsibility for
developing and implementing systems necessary for data collection,
editing, management and analysis.

Staff Responsibilities

1. Prepare the Protocol and Manual of Operations with the
cooperation of the Steering Committee.

2. Prepare and implement a system for data collection,
transmittal, logging, editing, management, extraction and
analysis. (This is to include the concept of mutual access to
the database for all centers - the only caveat will be within
the restrictions and monitoring as decided by the Steering
Committee.)

3. Work with the investigators in the development, pretesting,
construction of forms and associated procedures.

a. Attempt to obtain inter-and intra-observer reliability
measurements.

b. Attempt to obtain reliability for all questionnaires and
procedures used in the study so that such information
might be incorporated into the analyses.

4. Issue requests for proposals for central laboratories as
requested by NHLBI.

5. Monitor quality control of external laboratories.
6. Interact with the Clinic Coordinators and Principal
Investigators to orchestrate the training sessions and

certification for the Year 5 exam and subsequent exams.

7. Produce minutes of the Steering Committee meetings and
conference calls.

8. Assist in the organization and conduct of site visits to each

center to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Manual
of Operations.

POLICIES
Informed Consent

In order to be eligible for the study, each participant must
be willing to sign a statement of informed consent prior to
examination/evaluation. This will document the agreement of the
subject to participate in the study activities. No subject will
be recruited who is less than 18 years of age; therefore, no parent
or guardian consent will be necessary. Changes will be adopted
only if they are required to insure participant safety or will
significantly enhance the study.

General Principles of the Informed Consent

1. Explanation of the purpose of the study.

2. A description of the primary outcome of interest, examination
schedule and follow-up methods.

3. Permission for, and information about withdrawal from
participation.

4. Participant confidentiality.

5. Participant safety measures.

6. An offer by clinic staff to answer any inquiries concerning

the study procedures.

The Steering Committee recognizes that individual
collaborating centers may require, or be required by their local
Institutional Review Boards (IRB), that the recommended Informed
Consent Form be amended to include additional statements or be
reworded to clarify existing statements. All such modifications
to the Informed Consent Form will be reviewed by the Steering
Committee, and those which do not detract from the content of the
suggested CARDIA form will be approved.

Informed Consent Procedure

No signed informed consent will be obtained for the telephone
contacts. This follows well-established principles of survey
research; however the participants will be informed of the intent
to keep the information confidential. The sequence of procedures
for obtaining the participant's consent is as follows: it is
desirable that the Principal Investigator and/or Clinic Coordinator
be involved in the early stages of the sequence. The consent form
obtains the participant's permission for the examination to be
performed.

Publications and Presentations

The success of the study depends on the adequacy of the
scientific information reported from CARDIA. These aims will be
met by encouraging and facilitating analyses subject to rules

needed to preserve the collaborative spirit. The Steering
Committee will monitor and participate in this process. The
Principal Investigator may elect to designate a substitute for this
function.

Authorship

Proposals for manuscripts and abstracts may come from any
investigators in CARDIA. These include principal investigators
and co-investigators at any clinical center and the Coordinating
Center, participating NHLBI staff, and CARDIA subcontractors.
Individuals at all the institutions listed above must be given the
opportunity to be co-authors. The initiating investigator should
contact other potential co-authors of whom he/she is aware. Final
authorship (or selection of presenter for oral papers if more than
one candidate) will be worked out among the collaborating
investigators with the Steering Committee serving as the final
arbitrator of any problems in this regard.

In general, names will be listed and papers initiated as
described below:

1. The Steering Committee's scientific interests will be
announced through conversation and communications.

2. Proposals (one to two pages) will be submitted for review by
the Steering Committee including:

a) background

b) clear statement of ideas and/or research hypotheses

c) brief description of data to be used

d) methods of analysis

e) proposed collaborators and expertise (if not apparent)

3. The Steering Committee will select the authors for a
particular area of study and establish a paper writing
committee. Other authors can be recommended to the Steering
Committee by the individual center's Principal Investigator
for approval.

4. First authorship will be assigned by the Steering Committee
based primarily on effort. It is the intent of CARDIA and
the Steering Committee that the selection of writing committee
members will be equitable and fair to all centers and
individuals participating in this collaborative program, with
due regard paid to exceptional efforts of groups or
individuals.

Submission of Abstracts/Manuscripts

All abstracts and manuscripts - mainstream, final, substudy,
local and ancillary study papers must be approved by the Steering
Committee before they are submitted to any national and/or
international organizations for publication or presentation. This
will be a funneling mechanism, NOT a censoring mechanism. In
addition, all abstracts, including all tables and charts, used for
presentation or publication will be reproduced in complete sets so
that one standard set with the data set description will be
available to all centers.

The Principal Investigator shall have the right to publish
data from his own study population after clearance by the Project
Office of NHLBI and the Steering Committee. Usually local data
presentations and publications will be limited to those data
already presented from pooled results.

Review Process for Abstracts

1. All proposed abstracts must be received for review at least
two weeks before the final submission date. Completed
documentation forms (for planned analysis) for using the data
set must be at the Coordinating Center prior to submitting an
abstract, before the Coordinating Center will give approval.
Verification of the analysis does not have to be run by the
Coordinating Center unless the data appear questionable.

2. A copy of a proposed abstract is to be sent by the senior
author or originating center Principal Investigator to each
member of the Steering Committee. It is the responsibility
of each member to communicate objections and problems to the
senior author. Approval/disapproval is granted on Steering
Committee conference calls. Absence of communication will be
construed as approved.

3. If a poster presentation is not approved two weeks prior to
the presentation date, the poster will be withdrawn. If an
oral presentation is not approved two weeks prior to
presentation, another author or senior investigator will
assume responsibility for the presentation.

Review Process for Manuscripts
1. The purpose of the review is to evaluate scientific merit and
consistency with other CARDIA findings and data. CARDIA wants

to produce publications of high scientific quality and
credibility. There is no intention to inhibit publication of

Ancillary Studies

The CARDIA Steering Committee has adopted the following policy
regarding ancillary studies:

1. CARDIA investigators are encouraged to consider ancillary
studies.
2. Any CARDIA center can conduct, or agree to participate in an

ancillary study, subject to the final approval by the Steering
Committee and the CARDIA Review Board.

3. The Steering Committee's major criterion for judging a
proposed ancillary study is its effect on the conduct and
goals of the CARDIA study itself. An ancillary study will
ordinarily be approved unless it is judged to interfere
significantly with the objectives of CARDIA. Interference
may take a variety of forms; for example, too much additional
blood to be drawn, premature thawing of frozen specimens,
excessive exam time required, or decrease in acceptability of
exam to participants.

4. If the ancillary study meets the test of non-interference with
CARDIA, it may still compete with other proposed ancillary
studies for limited additional time, blood, subject matter,
etc. Ordinarily such competition can be resolved according
to the preferences of each center. However, if this question
arises for studies requiring more than one center, we will
request that the competing applicants try to combine their
efforts. If this is not possible, the Steering Committee
members will individually assign priority scores to the
competing proposals. The proposal(s) with the highest average
priority score will be selected until the available resources
(time, blood, etc.) are exhausted. Acceptable proposals not
of sufficient priority to be included in one examination cycle
can be resubmitted to compete again for a subsequent cycle.

1. Data remains for use within study centers or NHLBI only and

2. Centers can explore the pooled data on an ongoing basis.

Training/Certification

Selected trainers in conjunction with Coordinating Center
staff are charged with the development of training procedures,
certification/recertification requirements, and selection and
assignment of other observer/trainers appropriate to the tasks
proposed.

The requirement of standardized training procedures implies
most initial training sessions should be conducted centrally with
subsequent training occurring in individual clinics. The following
rationales support centralized training: the overlap within study
centers of personnel performing specialized testing; the need to
gain understanding of the problems in implementation of the various
facets as they piece together logistically; and the psychological
benefit to the study allowing interaction to take place among study
personnel. The Steering Committee will request recommendations for
trainers from the members and the Coordinating Center will be
subsequently contact all trainers and set time schedules.

The CARDIA Coordinating Center will assume the organizing role
for centralized training. As a facilitator, the Coordinating
Center will work with the trainers and Principal Investigators to
orchestrate initial and subsequent training sessions and assist in
the monitoring of certification and recertification.

The Coordinating Center will make all reservations for
Steering Committee, Coordinating Center, trainers and trainees.
Equipment and space needs for centralized training will be handled
through a representative of the host city where training will
occur.

Privacy of Records

The CARDIA study will maintain confidentiality of stored
records according to the following guidelines: all records will
be kept by assigned study numbers. Conclusions and final results
will be presented for appropriate scientific review in conferences
and in journals in the form of statistical analyses, with no
disclosures of specific cases. Collected information will not be
released without the explicit consent of the participant, according
to the Privacy Act. The clinical centers will maintain locked
files and permit access only by authorized individuals. No
personal identifying information will be released from any clinical
center to any other clinical center, the Coordinating Center or
NHLBI.

Referral Policies
Blood Pressure
Blood pressure referral levels will follow the Joint National

RETENTION

Retention of CARDIA participants across the four clinical
centers is a primary focus of the Year 5 exam period. Participants
will be seen approximately five years from the date of their
original exam. Scheduling participants will be sequential from the
first person seen until the last participant over a twelve month
period.

Returning participants will be given a specially designed exam
which will be somewhat shorter than the Year 0 and Year 2 exams.
All participants of the Year 0 exam are eligible for the Year 5
exam. If participants are injured or ill, but willing to come for
the Year 5 exam, they will be invited. Participants must have one
unbroken arm for blood pressure testing. Pregnancy or lactation
will not eliminate a participant, but rather extend their window
of eligibility. Similarly, participants who have moved more than
50 miles from the clinic will be permitted a larger window of
eligibility in order to maximize retention of the cohort and
minimize the costs of retention. Payments will be allowed within
limits to bring participants who have moved back for examination.

The retention plan is designed to bring at least 80% of the
CARDIA cohort examined at the Year 0 exam back to be re-examined
in this examination period. The plan also provides for extensive
monitoring of the process. Each center will be provided scheduling
lists designed to achieve the completion of the re-examination
within 12 months. Participants who have moved will be monitored
so that special recruitment and cost planning can be made in
advance. Initial contact letters will be mailed to each
participant along with a series of recruitment telephone contacts.
These telephone contacts will include an introduction, description
of the examination, questions concerning pregnancy, and an
invitation and scheduling of the exam. Arrangements for expense
reimbursement and a reminder telephone call, a review or the pre-
exam instructions (i.e. fasting, etc) and any special arrangements
for exceptional participants (i.e. those moving over 50 miles,
those incarcerated, etc.) will also be discussed. Confirmation
letters, pre-exam instructions and follow-up contact worksheets are
sent to all participants one to two weeks prior to the scheduled
Year 5 exam date.

Every effort will be made to maximize the return rate of the
CARDIA cohort. The efforts will include performing a mini~exam on
participants who refuse to participate in the clinical setting, but
are willing to provide information at home or some other convenient
location. Implementation of this latter option will not be started
until sufficient documentation of the inability to complete the
regularly scheduled examination has been documented. These
specific options may include examinations administered by mobile
teams of examiners, the use of other clinics involved in NIH funded
multicenter studies, etc.
