PHLEBOTOMY

Rationale for Measurement of Lipids and Lipoproteins

CARDIA is a study in young adults of the evolution of risk
factors for coronary heart disease. Each of the major established
risk factors, including elevated blood cholesterol, are of
paramount interest in CARDIA. Evolution of risk is studied by
following the course of blood cholesterol levels and the levels of
related lipoproteins through young adulthood, and by examining the
relationships of these blood levels to other biologic and
behavioral aspects of life. Each of the blood lipid levels and the
levels of related lipoproteins are therefore primary outcome
variables in CARDIA.

Many volumes of reports have been published dealing with blood
cholesterol and its influence in the atherosclerotic process (1-
8). An exhaustive interpretative review of this body of literature
was published in 1981 by the Working Group on Arteriosclerosis of
the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (1,2). The
importance in the atherosclerotic process of blood lipids and
lipoproteins is established in the following quotation from Volume
1, pp. 16 and 17:

"The average concentration of cholesterol in the blood plasmas
of middle-aged American men is presently on the order of 210-220
mg of cholesterol per 100 ml. The risk of premature coronary heart
disease and its consequences, especially acute heart attacks,
increases rapidly as the level of cholesterol in blood exceeds 220
mg/dl in men between 40 and 49 years of age with a cholesterol
level of 240 mg/dl or above are more than twice as likely to
develop premature coronary heart disease as are men of the same age
whose blood cholesterol levels are less than 220 mg/dl. Men in the
same age group with levels of 270 mg/dl and higher have almost
three times the risk of a premature heart attack than those with
levels less than 220. The relationship is similar for women.

Cholesterol and other fats are transported in the bloodstream
in a soluble form as components of lipoproteins.
Hypercholesterolemia may reflect a disorder in the proteins
transporting the fat (apolipoproteins) and/or in the metabolism of

fat per se. The concentration of other blood fats may also be
inordinately high from a disorder of lipoprotein metabolism. For
clinical purposes, sever hyperlipoproteinemias have been

categorized using biochemical and genetic techniques. Distinctions
have been made between the common hyperlipoproteinemias in the
population and the rare genetic types. Hyperlipoproteinemias may
also result from endocrine disturbances and most commonly from
dietary excesses. These types of hyperlipoproteinemia are all
strongly related to the risk of premature atherosclerosis.

One of the several lipoproteins that transport cholesterol -
high density lipoproteins - may confer some protection against

4/90

atherosclerosis; an inverse relationship has been identified
between the concentration of HDL cholesterol in the blood ana
coronary heart disease. Thus, individuals with high levels of HDL
tend to have a lower risk of coronary heart disease compared to
those with low HDL levels. In contrast, the higher the LDL level,
the higher the incidence of coronary heart disease. Thus,
individuals with high levels of HDL tend to have a lower risk of
coronary heart disease compared to those with low HDL levels. In
contrast, the higher the LDL level, the higher the incidence of
coronary heart disease. These observations have led to a re-
examination of the interactions of the two lipoproteins with cells
of the arterial wall. Although the reasons for the different
effects of the different cholesterol-carrying lipoproteins are not
yet clear, the information provides new ways of identifying persons
at high risk and new prospects for preventing, and even reversing,
atherosclerosis."

The recent report from the National Cholesterol education
Program has re-classified risk associated with blood cholesterol.
Levels below 200 mg/dl are classified as "desirable blood
cholesterol", those 200 to 239 mg/dl as "borderline - high blood
cholesterol", and those 240 mg/dl and above as "high blood
cholesterol". The cutpoint for high blood cholesterol, the value
at which CHD risk rises steeply is the same for men and women and
corresponds to the 75th percentile for the adult U.S. population

CARDIA will measure plasma levels of total cholesterol, HDL-
cholesterol and triglycerides. LDL will be calculated by
subtraction.

Rationale for Stored Blood

No study can predict discoveries which will be made some years
hence. The great majority of blood constituents remain stable when
blood is stored deep-frozen, i.e., -70 C. It may be desirable to
measure blood constituents on frozen samples to investigate
discoveries yet to be made. In the third examination, CARDIA will
store four vials of frozen plasma (three 1/2 ml and one 2 ml
vials).

Methods of Measurement and Quality Control

Thirty ml of blood will be drawn, using two vacutainers. This
sample will be aliquotted and shipped to the Medlantic Research
Foundation for lipid determinations. The blood drawing, handling,
aliquotting, and transporting procedures have been standardized and
can be found in the Manual of Operations. Split sample quality
control measures will be employed to assure the reliability of
measurements within assays and over time. Fifteen ml of additional
blood will be drawn on 5% of the CARDIA population for these
quality control studies.

Rationale for Measurement of Fibrinogen

Fibrinogen levels are positively correlated with plasma
cholesterol(1), and raised levels of fibrinogen are found in
patients with Type II hyperlipoproteinemia(2), a disorder
associated with premature arterial disease. An association between
smoking and fibrinogen has been observed in the Northwick Park
Heart Study. Smoking initiation or cessation was associated with
an increase or decrease, respectively, of about 0.15 G/1 in plasma
fibrinogen(3). This association was confirmed by further studies
from Northwick Park(4) as well as by Wilhelmsen et al(5). The
latter investigators observed that blood pressure, degree of
smoking, serum cholesterol, and fibrinogen level were significant
risk factors for myocardial infarction, and blood pressure and
fibrinogen were risk factors for stroke as well. A direct
relationship between fibrinogen, blood viscosity and hypertension
has also been reported(6); increasing blood pressure is associated
with elevated fibrinogen concentrations and increased blood
viscosity. Persistent hypertension may induce endothelial cell
injury(7) and permit the subendothelial deposition of fibrin.
Velican and Velican(8) noted a progressive increase in such fibrin
deposition in young adults, and in those aged 31-40 these
microthrombi were found in areas of developing atherosclerotic
plaques (9). Thus, raised levels of fibrinogen increase blood
viscosity, which in turn may increase peripheral resistance and
blood pressure, alter the integrity of the endothelial cell
monolayer, and permit the subendothelial deposition of fibrin and
cholesterol.

Significance

Increased levels of fibrinogen have been observed in men who
subsequently died of ischemic heart disease and stroke. Elevated
fibrinogen concentrations increase blood viscosity, predisposing
to hypertension and resultant endothelial cell damage. When
fibrinogen is taken together with the assessment of other risk
factors such as lipids and lipoproteins, hypertension, and
cigarette smoking, a clearer picture may emerge of the young
individual likely to experience a major ischemic. event.
Measurement of fibrinogen in participants of the CARDIA study is
especially important, since all previous studies have been
performed in older individuals. Whether the alterations in
hemostasis preceed the appearance of other risk factors, or are
reactive phenomena, needs to be determined. Some recent genetic
studies(10, 11) suggest that the former may be the case, but these
must be confirmed(12). Race and sex may also be important
variables, and should be examined.

Rationale for Measurement of Lp (a)

Lp(a) lipoprotein, although resembling LDL~cholesterol because
of the apolipoprotein B on its surface, is recovered primarily
within the HDL range. It is cholesterol-rich, comprising
approximately 15% of total cholesterol. This lipoprotein has been
observed by immunofluorescence to be localized in atherosclerotic
lesions and is considered an important quantitative genetic risk
factor for CHD. Its molecular biology indicates that it plays a
role in thrombosis.

Studies since the early 1970's in Scandinavia, which
established the Lp(a) - CHD link, have been confirmed by many
investigators. Initially, studies dichotomized Lp(a) levels above
and below an arbitrary value and showed significant associations
with coronary stenosis (1). Although independent of a number of
known risk factors, the Lp(a) association was dependent upon the
LDL level. Recent studies have shown an independent association
between Lp(a) and the presence and severity of coronary artery
disease. In univariate and multivariate analyses, Dahlen (2) has
shown a correlation of Lp(a) with the presence of CAD and with
lesion scores in 307 white patients undergoing coronary
angiography. In a recent study of early onset myocardial
infarction, Lp(a) explained a good portion of the familial
disposition which strongly correlated with disease (3). Among all
the components assessed, apolipoprotein B emerged as the strongest
determinant of risk in this study.

DNA STORAGE

Rationale

With the establishment and funding of the national GENOME
project, and the forthcoming international race in sequencing the
human genome, it becomes imperative that any longitudinal study be
poised to reap the benefits from the results of the above, that is,
the sequencing and mapping of the human genes.

The sequencing of the human genome will allow researchers to
test the effects of genetic variation on the susceptibility of
individuals to many diseases both acute and chronic. of greater
importance is the capability of finding gene-environment and gene-
gene interactions.

CARDIA is unique in that it is a longitudinal study focusing
on both black and white young adults who have not entered the risk-
age for many of the chronic diseases, e.g., heart disease and
cancer. CARDIA's collection of risk factors and examination of
risk factor change will be even more important if they could be
related to various genetic disease susceptibility genes. This will
provide a valuable resource for the study of genetic interactions
with environmental and behavioral factors.

To enhance CARDIA's value as an epidemiologic resource, during
the third examination, CARDIA will establish a DNA bank, This bank
will store the DNA samples of all its participants and make them
available to researchers for testing hypotheses which are approved
by the Steering Committee and/or Review Board. This banking of DNA
will provide researchers the opportunity to determine those at risk
of certain diseases and assess the specificity and sensitivity of
these DNA markers.

BLOOD PRESSURE
Rationale

CARDIA is a study in young adults of the evolution of risk
factors for coronary heart disease. Each of the major established
risk factors, including elevated blood pressure, are of paramount
interest in CARDIA. Evolution of risk is studied by following the
course of blood pressure and the appearance of new hypertension
through young adulthood, and by examining the relationships of
these blood pressure levels to other biologic and behavioral
aspects of life. Blood pressure and hypertension are therefore
primary outcome variables in CARDIA.

Many volumes of reports have been published dealing with blood
pressure and its influence in the atherosclerotic process. An
exhaustive interpretative review of this body of literature was
published in 1981 by the Working Group on Arteriosclerosis of the
National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute (Arteriosclerosis 1981,
Volume 1, Summary, Conclusions and Recommendations, NIH Publication
Number 81-2034, June 1981; and Volume 2, Detailed Report, NIH
Publication Number 82-2035, Sept. 1981). The importance in the
atherosclerotic process of blood pressure is established in the
following quotation from Volume 1, p17:

“As blood pressure rises, so does risk of ischemic heart
disease and its complications. The range of normal blood pressure
is wide. Even with the "normal" group, risk increases as the upper
limits are approached. Usually, blood pressures are expressed as
systolic pressure/diastolic pressure; values exceed 140/90 mmHg are
considered to be hypertensive for adults. Middle-aged person with
a diastolic blood pressure of 90-104 mmHg or greater (so-called
"mild" hypertension) have a risk of heart attack that is about 70
percent higher than that of persons with a diastolic pressure under
80 mmHg. Persons with a diastolic blood pressure exceeding 104
mmHg (moderately severe to severe hypertension) have a risk more
that twice that of those with a normal value. Hypertension is an
especially strong risk factor for stroke and, to a lesser extent,
for peripheral vascular disease."

Blood pressure is measured in a resting state, using three
measurements with a random zero sphygmomanometer. The random zero
machine has two advantages over the fixed zero manometer. Digit
preference does not appear in the data, though it may still exist
in the reading itself, and be randomized out of the data by the use
of the randomly chosen zero point. More importantly, it deprives
the blood pressure technician of knowledge of the actual value, and
therefore of the ability to make judgements about blood pressure
levels for reading close to critical values such as 90 diastolic.
It should be noted, however, that the random zero machines tend to
yield blood pressures which are about 1.5 mmHg less than those
obtained when using a fixed zero machine. Within person variation
in blood pressure is substantial; three replicate readings tend to
reduce this variation.

Methods of Measurement

The purpose of blood pressure measurements in CARDIA is: to
compare levels of this risk factor between young blacks and whites;
to observe the interaction with other CHD risk factors over time;
and to observe variables that will predict changing levels of blood
pressure.

Blood pressure measurements (systolic and fifth phase

diastolic) will be recorded with a random-zero (RZ)
sphygmomanometer, by trained and certified technicians at baseline
and subsequent intervals. The methods of measurement will be

standardized - as set out in the Manual of Operations. The pulse
rate for 30 seconds will be recorded with each blood pressure
measurement.

As many confounders of blood pressure measurement as possible
will be controlled by standard settings and technique of blood
pressure measurement or by recording uncontrollable confounding
factors. So that the following will be recorded:

1) Time of day (AM/PM)

2) Room temperature
3) Arm circumference at the midpoint of the upper arm
4) Technician I.D. number

The blood pressure will be measured three times on each
occasion. Caffeine (from tea, coffee, pop) eating, heavy physical
activity, smoking, and alcohol intake will be proscribed for 30
minutes prior to recording blood pressure level. The requirement
for a fasting state in the basic exam will assure much of the
dietary compliance. Recording of the current drug intake,
including medications affecting blood pressure, non-prescription
drugs and "recreational" drugs will be made on medical history
forms on the day of the examination.

Detailed history of alcohol intake patterns will be recorded
because of the known, but ill-understood, relationship of alcohol
intake to blood pressure level. For similar reasons physical
activity will be included in a separate history.

Order of Measurement

It will take approximately 10-15 minutes to make three resting
blood pressure measurements including the initial five minute rest
and recording of pulse rate. The blood pressure measurements will
be made very early in the clinic visit sequence immediately
following the greeting and informed consent. Measurements will be
made before the physical exam, blood drawing or any potentially

stressful interview. The blood pressure measurements on each
participant will be made in a separate room or, at minimum, in an
area properly screened from all other activity and other
participants.

Training/Certification

Technicians will be trained centrally prior to participant
intake in two full day sessions. New technicians after the start
of the study will be trained locally by a designated "BP
supervisor". Recertification will occur once (at approximately six
months) during the exam cycle (details in MOO). Prior to
certification each technician will be tested for vision (reading)
and with an auditory test (by Korotkoff sound tape).

At the beginning of the first session, a description and
demonstration of the correct BP procedure is given. Trainees are
to listen to the 1st (training) tape, taking the test sequences
until they are comfortable with what they are listening to. Then,
they take the 2nd tape until they have passed that test. After
passing the second tape, they are given the 3rd tape test.
Alternated with the tapes are actual live practices under the
instruction and observation of the training supervisor. Some live
practices may be done with a standard stethoscope, but most should

employ the Y-tube stethoscope. The optimum size of a group is
eight. This allows four people to do live practices while four are
on the tape training device. The group can interchange and

practice on each other.

After the first day of training, each trainee should be given
a cuff and manometer (not stethoscope) to take home and practice
just the control of the valve. This can be done by wrapping the
cuff on a jar or bottle and alternately pumping up and dropping the
mercury at a steady rate of 2mm per second. After two or three
sessions, they could also be given a stethoscope to practice on
family and/or friends. This out of class practice is very
important to build confidence. This time allowed for class is not
enough without outside practice time.

Once each trainee has passed tape #3, he or she should do at
least two live readings with the training supervisor on the Y-tube
stethoscope. The readings should agree within 2mm. If they do
not, the trainee needs additional practice with tapes and live
subjects. The training supervisor should also assure that the
trainee understands and follows proper procedures.

Observers are certified after passing the tape tests #2 and
#3 (tape #4 is held in reserve for recertification) and at least
two live readings. Observers are recertified at six months by
taking and passing tape #3 or #4 and one or two readings with the
training supervisor on the Y-tube stethoscope.

BODY SIZE MEASUREMENTS

There are three primary reasons for including body size
measurements in CARDIA. First, they provide a standardized basis
for examining the association between physical size, stature, or
ponderosity, and risk for developing coronary heart disease,
hypertension and other diseases of interest (e.g., chronic
obstructive lung disease, diabetes). Second, repeated measurements
of body mass over time permit investigation of whether changes in
body size directly contribute favorably or unfavorably to an
individual's risk profile. Further, because the data will be
collected using standardized methods employed in previous
investigations, the representative nature of the CARDIA data set
can be determined using existing data from similar age, sex and
ethnic groups.

All of the body size measurements to be used have been
reported, either independently or collectively, to be correlated
with a specific risk factor or clinical manifestations of disease.
These measures also represent important indicators of growth and
nutritional status. Although numerous additional anthropometric
and/or body size measurements have been identified, the intent of
this study is to focus on indices particularly relevant to the risk
of developing coronary heart disease or systemic arterial
hypertension. Measurements must be limited to those that are the
most relevant and that can be performed using standardized
methodology within and between survey centers because of time
limitations and other practical constraints of the study.

Specifically, the anthropometric and body measurements
included in studies such as the Health and Nutrition Examination
Survey (HANES), Framingham, and the Lipids Research Clinics
Prevalence Survey have served as a model for the measurements
proposed (1,2,3). In addition, the age group involved in CARDIA
suggests the need for monitoring growth and development inherent
in the aging process which may be unrelated to environmental
influences such as dietary or exercise patterns.

Rationale for Specific Measurements
Body Height and Weight

Among all the possible measurements, height and weight are
universally accepted as primary indices of body size. Weight for
height standards are available for both men and women from studies
such as the Build and Blood Pressure Study and the recently updated
Metropolitan Life Insurance tables. Based on standards such as
these, relative weight can be determined. In addition, several
ratios of weight/height have been correlated with selected risk
factors. Indices such as body mass index or Quetelet's Index or
Ponderal Index also have been associated with hypertension,
hyperlipidemia and diabetes.

Not only the existence of obesity, but the age of onset of
obesity are reportedly related to susceptibility to hypertension
(5). Weight gained early in adult life may be a sensitive
indicator of increased risk for cardiovascular disease.
Hyperplastic obesity experienced during adulthood may impose
different risks than hyperplastic obesity developed during youth,
and these risks may vary among different age, sex and ethnic groups
(7). For these reasons it is important that CARDIA include
measures of height and weight during each successive examination.

However, it is well known that there are numerous limitations
to indices of relative weight (6). Although individuals may be
classified as being overweight or underweight compared to age and
sex specific means, the terms obesity and overweight are not
necessarily synonymous. Furthermore, height and weight tables do
not reflect the variations across different ethnic, socioeconomic
and/or occupational groups. Thus, in order to determine not only
body weight but also a better index of body composition, additional
measurements are proposed to CARDIA.

Skinfold Measures

No single measure of obesity or body mass is optimal or
uniformly representative for all ages, races, and sexes, making the
use of several indices desirable, if not necessary (3,8). It is
recommended that the body size index should not be dependent on
height and should have a strong association with independent
indices of fatness, e.g., skinfold thickness, body density, etc.

Blair, et al (7) reported evidence from HANES (1971-1974) that
risk for hypertension increases with centrally located body fat as
measured by triceps and subscapular skinfolds. They reported that
subscapular skinfold was a better predictor of both systolic and

diastolic blood pressure in each race-sex group ... "sharing all
the association of triceps with blood pressure and having
significant predictive power unshared by triceps" (7). The

subscapular skinfold thickness has been shown to predict the
development of CHD independent of body mass index and other
cardiovascular risk factors (9). These data support the need to
differentiate between central versus peripheral deposition of body
fat.

Despite its reported superiority in predicting hypertension,
subscapular skinfold measures may not be as sensitive in predicting
other risk factors relative to coronary heart disease. Population
data for triceps skinfold measure are available for both sexes and
race groups 18 to 30 years, thus providing a means of comparing the
data collected in CARDIA. The third most commonly measured
skinfold site is the suprailiac crest. Given its location at the
hip, it offers a means of comparing upper versus lower body fatness
and may, either separately or in conjunction with the other two

4/90

4/90

skinfold measures, provide unique information regarding the
evolution of CHD or hypertension.

Waist and Hip Girth

Measures of girth or body thickness contribute additional
information for accurately characterizing body size and
composition. Here again, numerous sites have been used in the
past, but two circumferences, one representing waist girth and the
other hip girth, will be used in CARDIA. Centralized fat
distribution, as ascertained by waist-to-hip circumference ratio,
has been associated with the development of hypertension, diabetes,
and cardiovascular diseases (9-14). The distribution of body fat
has been shown in various studies to be associated with levels of
blood lipids or lipoproteins, glucose, uric acid, blood pressure,
and serum insulin (15). At the baseline CARDIA examination, waist-
to-hip girth ratio was an independent predictor of blood
concentrations of triglyceride, total HDL cholesterol, HDL2
cholesterol, LDL cholesterol (women only), apolipoproteins A-I and
B, uric acid, and systolic blood pressure (15).

Upper Arm Girth

Upper arm girth is related to blood pressure level independent
of body weight or BMI. The size of the upper arm may be an index
of adiposity, influence the pressure needed to occlude the artery,
or influence the amplitude of the Korotkoff sounds.

Biacromial Diameter and Chest Circumference

The chest circumference/biacromial diameter ratio has been
shown to be a predictor of coronary heart disease in a cohort of
U.S. railroad workers. Biacromial diameter was measured at the
Year 2 CARDIA exam. (16)

PHYSICAL ACTIVITY QUESTIONNAIRE
Rationale

The presumption that physical inactivity is a risk factor for
coronary heart disease is strongly based on epidemiologic evidence.
This evidence suggests that inactivity is relevant to weight
control, and in turn is therefore related to the genesis of
obesity, hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Through its relationship
to HDL cholesterol, physical activity level may be related in
general to the lipid profile.

Physical activity is a behavior, consisting of many different
components. It is important for CARDIA to measure which activities
are prevalent, and how this activity spectrum changes as the CARDIA
population ages. Further it is important to reliably rank people
for overall level of all and of intense physical activity.

The existing questionnaire which might be best suited for use
in CARDIA were the Minnesota Leisure Time Physical Activity
Questionnaire and the Seven Day Physical Activity Recall. The
former, which spans 12 months, has been valided against physiologic
endpoints, but has not been shown to be adequately reliable on
reapplication, and takes too long to administer. The latter spans
only seven days, has considerable accuracy, has passed some
validity studies and is suitably brief. However, it too suffers
from low repeatability since one week's physical activity is often
not representative of general patterns.

In devising a briefer new questionnaire, it was theorized that
people could accurately recall or summarize for themselves what and

how much activity they do within broad categories. Therefore
details were avoided as being both poorly repeatable and
irrelevant.

Using an extensive database from the Minnesota Heart Health
Program, tabulations were made of activity participation for men
and women aged 25-29. Based on these tabulations questions were
worded for sets of activities which might be logically classed
together. For each, the number of months of minimal performance,
at least one hour total in the month, was queried. Finally the
number of months in which the activity was performed frequently,
i.e. at least an activity-specific number of hours/week, was
queried.

MEDICAL HISTORY
Rationale

It is important to ascertain illnesses and medications as
these may affect risk factor levels and life style. Although, in
the targeted age group, most medical conditions will be infrequent,
the study results will lose considerable credibility among the
medical community if some effort to ascertain basic health status
and illnesses is not undertaken.

Smoking particularly of cigarettes, constitutes a major
established coronary risk factor(1,2). This will be a key
dependent variable in CARDIA, and changes in smoking habits will
be observed in many participants as the study progresses.
Therefore, it is important to measure tobacco consumption with care
and in some detail.

Alcohol consumption is another important life style component
that may vary considerably among participants and from exam to
exam. It is known to positively affect blood pressure and HDL
cholesterol, and has been negatively associated with the
development of coronary heart disease in some studies
(3,4,5,6,7,8). Information about intake of different beverages,
since they may have different effects, is being collected. These
questions also cover "binge" drinking.

Genetic factors are important determinants of coronary risk
factor levels as evidenced by familial aggregation of these factors
(9,10). Therefore, some basic information about the longevity and
premature development of cardiovascular and related illness in
close relatives is essential.

Nonmedical drugs are used by many young people. Information
about this important aspect of life style of the young will be
collected. Assurance of confidentiality will be important.

The tracking of major health events in the follow-up of the
CARDIA subjects will occur. Whether or not the subjects report
any "Other Major Health Problem", the interviewer will ask for
these events in the Interim Hospitalizations, Serious Illnesses
and Injury questionnaire. This questionnaire will ask for signed
permission to obtain hospital and medical records.

Eye color has been associated with hypertension. In a study
of multiphasic health checkup examinees in the Kaiser Permanente
Medical Care Program, persons with brown eye color were 50% more
likely to develop hypertension than persons with non-brown eyes.
Eye color will be recorded on the anthropometry form.

In general, the method of administration will first be self-
administered questionnaires to screen most aspects with positive
answers, followed up by interviewer administered questions to
obtain some specific details.

PHYCHOSOCIAL COMPONENT

The psychosocial inventory chosen for the Year 5 exam includes
tests of negative affectivity and its component dimensions. This
concept refers to subjective distress, anxiety, worry, aggression,
dissatisfaction, low self esteem, interpersonal difficulties, and
a general negative psychological condition that functions like a
trait in that it is pervasive, being present even in the absence
of stress events. It is highly related to a broad range of somatic
complaints, specific health behaviors, and risk factors for CHD.
The concept is not defined by any specific component such as
anxiety, but is the overall constellation that defines the general
negative state, i.e., a group of affective factors that load on a
single dimension. This construct is helpful in understanding the
very high correlations between negative affective components
themselves, e.g., hostility, anger, depression, anxiety, and meets
our criteria of relating to CHD or to CHD risk factors. By
gathering information on these components, CARDIA will obtain
information not only on specific variables and their relationship
to other CARDIA measures, but also have the opportunity to evaluate
their roles in various combinations. The fact that negative
affectivity, as well as most of its components such as trait
anxiety, has been shown to be stable over long periods offers the
opportunity to characterize our population at one assessment. The
Year 5 exam will include measures of Depression, Trait-Anxiety,
Anger-in and Hostility.

The following is a brief summary of the inventories and
rationale for their inclusion.

Depression and Anxiety

Depression and anxiety have been related to a large number of
disease states, both as etiological factors and as determinants of
disease course. Both variables have been related to CHD, MI, and
angina, in both cross sectional and longitudinal studies. A recent
meta analysis by Booth-Kewley and Friedman (1987) show depression
to be consistently related to CHD. CARDIA will measure depression
by the CES-D scale that has wide usage among diverse populations.
The inventory is accepted well by the participants and is
relatively brief (20 items that take five to eight minutes).
Anxiety will be measured by the Spielberger Trait Inventory (1980)
that consists of 20 items that can be completed in approximately
five to eight minutes.

Anger
CHD factors are related to anger including style of coping

with anger as to whether it is expressed (anger-out), contained
(anger-in), the dimension of anger as a personality trait (trait-

4/90

anger) and the experience of anger (state-anger). Dembrowski, et
al, (in press) have shown anger-in influenced the effect of
hostility on coronary occlusions. Harburg, et al, (1979) show that
individuals in high stress areas and classified as anger-in had a
significantly higher incidence of hypertension. Johnson (1984)
found a significant positive correlation between anger-in and blood
pressure, after controlling for age, race, weight, and sex.
Framingham data show that holding anger in was predictive of
cerebral vascular accidents in women. Anger/in has been shown to
relate to systolic blood pressure and elevated cortisol levels.
Both anger and hostility have been indicated as factors related to
hypertension. Crane (1981) showed hypertensives to score higher
or both state and trait anger dimensions. A recent meta analysis
by Sommers-Flanagan and Greenberg (1989) showed that 84% of 25
studies relating anger to blood pressure showed a significant
relationship. These results are based on a broad range of
instruments and procedures.

Hostility

Anger/Hostility/Aggression (AHA) has a long history of being
related to coronary heart disease (Alexander 1939, Miller 1965).
Barefoot et al (1982) administered full scale MMPI's to freshman
medical students and recorded CHD and all cause mortality over a
25 year follow-up period. He found that hostility was the single
best predictor in a multivariate analysis using classical risk
factors of smoking, age, family history of hypertension, and
current hypertensive status. Williams et al (1984) showed that
women who were type A and hostile have a relative risk of 3.6 for

SOCIODEMOGRAPHIC QUESTIONNAIRE

Description

The basic sociodemographic descriptors included in this
questionnaire are: marital status, socioeconomic status, living
situation, and residential mobility. Socioeconomic status is
measured by education, occupation, income and surrogate measures
of income, the traditional indicators of social class. These
measures may be analyzed separately or combined into an index of
socioeconomic status (SES). Questions on occupation have been
formulated to correspond to those used by the Bureau of the Census.

Evidence

The evidence presented here is limited to risk for CHD, in
accordance with the criteria for selection of variables set by the
Psychosocial Committee. Evidence of the association of
sociodemographic characteristics with specific risk factors will
be considered by others.

Social Class

A change in the social class distribution of risk for CHD, at
mid-century was noted (Antonovsky, 1968; Jenkins, 1971; Marmot et
al., 1978). Prior to the 1950's, coronary heart disease was widely
held to be a disease of affluence with upper socioeconomic classes
at elevated risk (Osler, 1910; Price, 1941; Spain, 1966).
Antonovsky reported that this perception was clearly not supported
by the data. In an extensive literature review, he found some
studies reported inverse class gradients, others reported direct
gradients and still others reported no gradient at all in the
association between social class and risk for CHD. Although there
was no consistency, he noted that a majority of the studies did
show class differences which were substantial. He observed that
several studies done in 1930-50 reported a direct gradient for the
older age group and an inverse gradient in the younger age group.
Since the 1950's there has been a marked change in the view that
CHD is a disease of the rich. CHD has been reported as
progressively more common among lower socioeconomic classes (Marmot
et al., 1978; Cooper et al., 1978). Consequently lower classes are
not generally at greater risk for CHD than middle classes. An
inverse relationship between social class and CHD risk has been
reported in a number of studies (see Education and Occupation for
details). Kraus and his colleagues noted that the inverse
relationship between SES and risk for CHD held for whites, Asians,
and Spanish Americans, but not for blacks (Kraus et al., 1950).

4/99 PSY - 5

Education

An inverse relationship between education and CHD risk has
been reported with reasonable consistency in several prospective
epidemiological studies since the 1950's (Liu et al., 1981: Hinkle
et al., 1968, Rosenman et al. 1975; Dawber et al., 1959). Liu and
his colleagues found an inverse association between education and
risk factors at entry in the Chicago Heart Association cohort.
They also found that the inverse relationship between education and
CHD risk was independent of risk factors at entry. The Framingham
study found an inverse relationship in its six year follow-up but
it was not significant (Dawber et al., 1959).

Occupation

Differences in CHD risk have been identified both within a
particular occupation, as well as across occupations. In the
Whitehall study, men in lower employment grades in the London civil
service were at higher CHD risk than men in higher employment
grades require a higher standard of education are at lower CHD risk
compared to those with lower educational requirements (Holme et
al., 1976; Sauli, 1979: Marmot et al., 1978; Logan, 1954). On the
other hand, the National Health Survey found no strong evidence of
any class gradient measured by either occupation or income with
prevalence of CHD (NCHS, Series 11, No.10, 1965).

Age-sex-race

Older people are at higher risk for CHD than younger ones, men
are at higher risk than women, black women are at higher risk than
white women, and black men are similar in risk to white men (Cooper
et al., 1978; Moriyama et al., 1971; Kitagawa and Hauser, 1973;
Gillum, 1982; Gillum and Grant, 1982). Death rates for black women
have been consistently higher than for white women since the late
1940's. The picture is different for black men. Death rates were
lower than for white men in the 1940's, then rose rapidly and
exceeded the rates for white men in 1968 and 1969, and in the years
following remained lower or close to the rates for white men
(Cooper et al., 1978). Contrary to a belief held by some that
blacks are immune to CHD, CHD is the leading cause of death in
blacks, as it is in whites (Gillum, 1982).

Marital Status

Death rates from CHD of the single, widowed and divorced are
substantially higher than rates for married persons (Moriyama et
al., 1971). Men and women in marriages in which the wife works out
of economic necessity report more tension and negative affect than
people in marriages in which the wife works by choice (Orden and
Bradburn, 1968, 1969).

4/90 PSY - 6

Occupational and Residential Mobility

Many studies have shown increased rates of disease among
occupationally and residentially mobile people (Syme et al., 1969);
Syme et al., 1966; Cassel and Tyroler 1961; Kaplan 1971; Shekelle,
1979 Jahne, 1980). However several studies failed to find
increased rates of disease among mobile persons (Hinkle et al.,
1968; Rosen and Rosen, 1978).

Living Situation

As association between social isolation and mortality has been
shown. People living alone are greater risk than those living with
others (Gove et al., 1980; Carnahan et al., 1974).

RATIONALE FOR KNOWLEDGE, ATTITUDE AND BEHAVIOR QUESTIONNAIRE

The Knowledge, Attitude and Behavior questions, along with
several questions in other questionnaires (see Attachment) are
designed to investigate several factors which may be involved in
a participant's rational choice to engage in healthy or in risky
behaviors. The knowledge questionnaire asks about knowledge of
heart attack risk factors, perception of the level of blood
pressure and cholesterol, and seeking out cardiovascular disease
related nutrition information.

It is hypothesized that people with more knowledge about
causes of cardiovascular disease will seek to reduce risk factors.
It is hypothesized that those who seek out nutrition information
will ultimately have lower serum cholesterol. It is hypothesized
that people who think that their blood pressure or cholesterol is
high will take action to reduce it.

These hypotheses arise from psychosocial theories concerning
determinants of behavior in adults (see, for example, the review
by J. Siegrist, Models of Health Behaviour, European Heart Journal
1988;9:709-714).

PULMONARY FUNCTION TESTING

Rationale

There is little, if any, short-term information available on
pulmonary function indices in 18-30 year olds. Studies suggest
that the growth and development of the pulmonary system is still
occurring among some individuals in this age range, but no data
exists to document when pulmonary function reaches its maximun,
plateaus or begins to decline within an individual. Measures of
pulmonary function are included in the CARDIA protocol primarily
to gain a better understanding of the factors that contribute to
pulmonary growth and decay prior to middle age and only secondarily
to investigate the possible interplay between pulmonary factors and
the development of coronary heart disease and other cardiovascular
outcomes. Re-examination of pulmonary function in the Year 5 exam
may serve to provide a more precise and accurate baseline for a
long-term study. This added precision will enable us to relate
lung function to other parameters of cardiovascular risk such as
nutrition, physical fitness and respiratory symptoms and illness.

Numerous studies have identified cigarette smoking as an
important contributor to the decline in pulmonary function over
time and to the development of chronic obstructive airway disease
(1-7). However, there is little consensus regarding other
environmental or social influences on pulmonary function or disease
that might account for differences observed between and within
populations. Since the lungs continue to develop through childhood
and into young adulthood, it has been suggested that certain
factors during the formative years such as recurrent respiratory
illness may predispose individuals to later pulmonary
symptomatology or disease (8,9). Existing data also indicate that
there may be racial differences in pulmonary function which are
unexplained by differences in smoking habits or simple measures of
body size such as height and weight (10-15). In addition, more
research is needed on asthmatic conditions which are poorly
understood but not uncommon in younger populations. The CARDIA
pulmonary protocol has been designed to add to the existing
knowledge in these areas. Specifically, CARDIA will attempt to:

a) describe the evolution of pulmonary function and
symptomatology through young adulthood in relationship
to influences such as early cigarette exposure and
childhood respiratory history.

b) provide data on black-white differences in pulmonary
function and change which may be related, at least in
part, to differences in body build (measured by height,
frame size, girths), childhood disease experience, and
cigarette exposure.

c) gain further insight into those factors (e.g., allergies,
sensitivity to exposures) that predispose to the

4/90 aq

development of asthmatic symptomatology and concomitant
pulmonary function changes.

A secondary objective of characterizing the pulmonary profile
of this young adult population at baseline is to investigate the
relationship between pulmonary function and coronary risk. Some
studies suggest that pulmonary function is predictive of subsequent
cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, irrespective of smoking
habits (16-18). However, it has been hypothesized that decreased
pulmonary capacity is more likely an early marker of ill-health and
probably does not contribute to disease outcome either directly or
indirectly through the cardiovascular risk factors. In any event,
it cannot be anticipated that CARDIA participants will be followed
for disease end points at the present time.

Data Collection

The following pulmonary measures are part of the CARDIA
examination protocol:

lung volumes and flow rates obtained from several forced
expiratory maneuvers on the Collins Survey Spirometer (forced
vital capacity, forced expiratory volume in one and three
seconds, peak expiratory flow rate, mid-maximal expiratory
flow rate, flow rates at 25, 50 and 75 percent of total
expired volume).

Methods of Measurement

Accurate spirometric pulmonary function testing has three
essential components: a) a frequently calibrated spirometer that
accurately records exhaled volume in relation to time during the
forced expiration; b) a subject who inspires maximally and exhales
as forcefully, smoothly, and completely as he can; and c) a
technician who can calibrate the spirometer, coach the subject to
perform maximal efforts, and detect poor subject effort and/or
expirations that are not continuous, maximal, and completely
recorded. CARDIA has as its goal to produce accurate spirometric
pulmonary function measurements using the Survey Spirometer and the
Eagle II microprocessor (Warren E. Collins, Inc., Braintree, MA).

The equipment to be used in CARDIA and the supplies necessary
for pulmonary function testing will be standardized, with routine
Cleaning of the spirometer and breathing tubes, plus frequent
calibration of the spirometer, including checks of the chart speed
and volume deflection and tests for leakage. General principles
of spirometric testing, are: a) how to perform forced expiratory
maneuvers; b) problems that are often encountered in conducting the
forced expiratory maneuvers; c) the number of trials to be
performed and reproducibility criteria; d) measurements of the
Forced Expiratory Volume on One Second (FEV1), the Forced Vital
Capacity (FVC), the FEVI/Fvc ratio, the Forced Expiratory Flow
Rates (FEF) at 25%, 50% and 75% of the Fvc exhaled, and the Maximal

4/90 ae

4/90

Mid-Expiratory Flow Rate (MMEF); e) correction of these
measurements to Body Temperature and Pressure, Saturated (BTPS);
and f) calculation of the predicted lung volumes and flow rates,
the racial correction factor, and comparison of the observed with
these predicted values will also be detailed along with procedures
to be followed in testing study subjects using the Eagle II
microprocessor and the Survey Spirometer.

It will be seen that use of the Eagle II, in conjunction with
the Survey Spirometer, relieves the technician of hand measurement
of the spirograms, BTPS corrections, and calculation of and
comparison with predicted pulmonary function values. However, it
is still essential that the technician calibrate the spirometer and
that he insure, by active coaching and by vigilant attention to the
spirograms, that maximum and good quality forced expirations are
performed and recorded.

Equipment

All pulmonary function tests will be conducted using the
Collins survey 8-liter water sealed spirometer. The expired volume
is measured as it displaces a lightweight plastic bell riding in
a narrow water well. A pen moves directly with the bell, recording
a tracing of volume versus time on a kymograph drum, rotating at
a speed of 32 mm/sec. In addition to the information presented in
this manual, further details of the operation and maintenance of
the spirometer are given in the Instruction Manual for the Collins
Survey Spirometer.

The Eagle II microprocessor will be used in conjunction with
the Survey spirometer during spirometer volume calibration and
patient testing. The Eagle II attaches to the Survey spirometer

via a Computer Input/Output Connector Cable. The Eagle II
primarily assists the technician in two otherwise, time-consuming
tasks: calculation fo expired volumes and flow rates and

calculation of predicted pulmonary function values.

A linear motion potentiometer attached to the spirometer bell
converts spirometer bell volume changes into electrical
signals. As the spirometer bell is displaced during a forced
expiration, signals are sent to the Eagle II through the
computer connector cable. In this way, the Eagle II measures
how fast the expiration is proceeding, and calculates
instantaneous flow rates at several points during the forced
expiration.

In addition, using the subject's age, height and sex, which
are entered into the Eagle II will print the test results and
compare the subject's observed measurements with those predicted
for his age, height, race, and sex. Further details on the Eagle
II are available in the Instruction Manual for the Collins Fagle
II Pulmonary Function Testing System.

Once each month, the clinical centers will forward an

ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY
Rationale

Echocardiography has been shown to be a useful tool, both

clinically and epidemiologically, in detecting cardiac
abnormalities associated with a higher incidence of cardiovascular
events or mortality. For example, Henry and associates

demonstrated that patients with an echocardiographic left atrial
dimension of 55 mm or greater demonstrated a much lower success
rate of conversion from atrial fibrillation to normal sinus
rhythm(1). Similarly, data from the Framingham study have
suggested that echocardiographic left ventricular hypertrophy in
the general population is associated with an increased two-year
mortality, independent of standard coronary risk factor(2).

Furthermore, recent evidence has suggested that Doppler
measurements of left ventricular diastolic filling may precede and
serve as markers for the future development of hypertension.
Graettinger and associates in our group have reported that in 47
normotensive adolescents (mean age 13 years), diastolic blood
pressure was inversely related to a number of Doppler early
diastolic transmitral indices, including peak velocity, flow
velocity integral, and deceleration(3). The ratio of late-to-early
diastolic peak filling velocity was found to be directly related
to diastolic blood pressure. These Doppler left ventricular
filling velocity changes were independent of left ventricular mass
and were postulated to possibly represent early pre-hypertensive
alterations in left ventricular diastolic function.

Since echocardiography is more sensitive and specific than
such indirect tools as standard chest radiography or
electrocardiography in the detection of left ventricular
hypertrophy and left atrial enlargement, these echocardiographic
measurements may be useful as pre-clinical prognostic indicators
of the future development of hypertension, or coronary artery
disease, and overt cardiovascular events -~- e.g., myocardial
infarction and stroke -- in population of subjects such as enrolled
in the CARDIA study(4). Cardiac ultrasound is also an excellent
technique for detecting and following a wide variety of cardiac
abnormalities - including mitral valve prolapse, hypertrophic
cardiomyopathy, valvular regurgitation, and left ventricular
dysfunction.

The cardiac ultrasound technique (echocardiography and Doppler
flow recording) has the advantage of being non-invasive,
reproducible, and without known adverse effects as used clinically.
Furthermore, the ultrasound technique is less expensive, currently
yields more useful information, and is more applicable to
population studies than are either magnetic resonance imaging or
(cine) computer tomography. In a recent report from the Framingham
study, M-mode echocardiograms could be obtained in a high
percentage -- approximately 95% -- of young adults in the age group
similar to that recruited in the CARDIA study(5). Based on the
Framingham Study, the prevalence of left ventricular hypertrophy

Hypotheses
The following are major hypotheses:

1. Specific echocardiographic markers of pre~clinical and overt
cardiac disease are related to traditional risk factors (e.g.,

smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, family history
of cardiovascular disease) for coronary heart disease and

stroke.
2. One or more specific echocardiographic or Doppler
abnormalities of cardiac structure (e.g., left ventricular

mass or wall thickness) or function (systolic or diastolic)
are suitable markers of pre-clinical disease, or the
development of hypertension or non-fatal and fatal
cardiovascular events over a short term (e.g., three-year)
follow-up period.

3. Specific echocardiographic or Doppler measurements of left
ventricular structure or function are related to systolic
and/or diastolic blood pressure, or blood pressure reactivity.

Method of Measurement

The most important priority of the echocardiographic
examination is to obtain M-mode and two-dimensional
echocardiographic images (from the parasternal long-and short-axis,
and apical four-, two-chamber and long-axis views) of the left
ventricle for the evaluation of left ventricular mass, wall
thickness, dimensions and volumes, ejection fraction, and global
and regional wall motion and left atrium for left atrial size. The
second priority is the recording of the pulsed Doppler mitral flow
velocity (from the apical four-chamber view) for the evaluation of
left ventricular diastolic function and color Doppler for a
evaluation of aortic and mitral regurgitation. Measures will be
made using the Acuson 128 Cardiovascular System.

24-HOUR URINE COLLECTION FOR SODIUM,
POTASSIUM, CREATININE AND MAGNESIUM

Rationale

Hypertension is one of the major risk factors for coronary
heart disease. Extensive data from cross-population comparisons,
clinical investigations and animal experiments suggest a strong
positive association between sodium intake and blood pressure
(1-12). However, for individuals within a more or less homogeneous
population, an association has not been consistently demonstrated
(13-18). Methodological problems in assessment of sodium intake
may have contributed to the inconsistent findings of these studies
(19). Recently a large scale international collaborative study,
the INTERSALT study, has shown a significant positive association
between 24-hour sodium excretion and blood pressure for individuals
(20). Across the 52 centers of INTERSALT, median 24-hour sodium
excretion was significantly related to increase in mean blood
pressure with age. In addition, participants from the four centers
with median sodium excretion less than 50 mmol/24 hours had low
median blood pressure, low prevalence of hypertension, and little
or no increase in mean blood pressure with age. Since INTERSALT
encompassed a very large sample with a wide range of sodium
excretion and was based on a highly standardized protocol with
central training, a central laboratory and extensive quality
control, these results provide important evidence to further
clarify the sodium-blood pressure relationship.

Most epidemiologic studies on the relationship between sodium
intake and blood pressure have been based on cross-sectional data.
It remains unclear whether habitual high sodium intake during young
adulthood is related to the risk of hypertension later in life.
Most of CARDIA's 5100 young adults are normotensive. Hence CARDIA
offers a unique opportunity to examine the relationship between
sodium intake and changes in blood pressure over time, and the
relationship between sodium intake and incidence of hypertension.
Several epidemiologic studies have reported a positive association
between the sodium/potassium ratio and blood pressure (21-22).
Clinical investigations indicate that increasing dietary potassium
intake may reduce blood pressure in both normotensives and
hypertensives (23-26).

CARDIA will provide an opportunity to examine the relationship
between potassium intake and changes in blood pressure over time
and the interaction of sodium and potassium on blood pressure and
changes in blood pressure.

There is evidence that dietary magnesium may provide a cardio-
protective effect through one or more of the _ following
mechanisms:(1) metabolic effects at the cellular level in the
myocardium which reduce risk of sudden death; (2) effects on blood
pressure; and (3) alterations in lipid composition (e.g.,
increasing HDL-C and its subfractions and decreasing triglycerides,

URI - 1

4/90

LDL-C and total cholesterol). A significant consistent association
between HDL-C, HDL2-C and HDL3-C and dietary magnesium was found
in the CARDIA cohort in the Year 0 database. This intracellular
cation has received increased attention from cardiologists in the
past several years (see Am J Cardiol 63:1-45G, 1989). Asa result,
research in this area has also increased.

The kidney is the major excretory pathway for the 35-40% of
magnesium absorbed from the diet. The mean excretion ranges from
2 to 5 mmol/day, with relatively small intra-individual variation.
The kidneys are quite efficient at saving magnesium in the face of
low dietary intake, with the majority of reabsorption occurring in
the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Factors which
decrease magnesium reabsorption (thereby increasing excretion)
include sucrose intake, alcohol intake, extra supply of sodiun,
calcium or magnesium, extracellular volume expansion, osmotic
agents, loop and thiazide diuretics and digitalis. Magnesium
reabsorption is enhanced by magnesium deficiency, low magnesium
intake and parathyroid hormone in high doses.

There is relatively little data on urinary magnesium levels
in young adults nor is there data on the relationship between
urinary magnesium and risk factors for coronary heart disease.
The CARDIA study could make a significant contribution to this area
of research.

Method for Assessing Sodium Intake

The most commonly used methods for assessing sodium intake in
epidemiologic studies are timed overnight urine collections and

timed 24-hour urine collections. Overnight urine specimens are
easier to collect than 24-hour specimens, but 24-hour specimens
are considered more accurate. Several studies report that

overnight urine specimens can be used to detect large differences
in sodium intakes between groups, but do not accurately assess
sodium intakes for individuals (27-30). Moreover, two recent
studies indicate that hypertensives may excrete more sodium at
night than normotensives (31- 32). Based on these findings,
collection of 24-hour urine specimens is preferable in CARDIA.

It has been suggested that seven timed 24-hour urine specimens
are needed to accurately characterize an individual's sodium intake
(19). However, the collection of seven specimens is likely to be
very difficult in young adults. In order to avoid any adverse
effect of urine collection on cohort retention, we suggest
collecting three timed 24-hour specimens from 30% of the
participants randomly recruited from each sex-race group (n = 350).
Each participant will be paid $25 (in addition to the $20 for
reimbursement of exam related expenses) for urine collection. The
number (350) will provide 80% power to detect a correlation
coefficient of 0.15 at 0.05 level of significance between changes
in blood pressure (e.g., differences or slopes) and average sodium
excretions.

There are several reasons for choosing three 24-hour specimens
rather than some other numbers. First, under the assumption that
the ratio of intra- to inter-individual variance for 24-hour urine
sodium excretion is 3.2, the percentage attenuation of the
correlation between sodium and some variable of interest based on
1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 24-hour specimens are 51, 38, 30, 25, 22,
19 and 17, respectively (19). Three measurements are optimal since
the percentage attenuation is reduced minimally by increasing the
number of collections beyond three. Second, for those in the third
tertile of sodium intake based on three 24-hour specimens, 67% and
84%, respectively, are in the third tertile and the upper half of
the true mean sodium intake. In other words, misclassification is
minimized. Third, formulae are currently available for computing
confidence intervals for corrected simple correlation coefficients
and for computing lower bounds for corrected partial correlation
er regression coefficients (33-34). These correction procedures
require at least two measurements. Three measurements provide a
more reliable estimate of the ratio of intra- to inter-individual
variance.

Urine Collection

Urine specimens would be collected during the third
examination. For each center, a subsample of 30% of the
participants would be randomly selected from each sex-race group.
These participants would be asked to collect three timed 24-hour
urine specimens. If a participant refuses to collect specimens,
another person from the same sex-race group would be recruited.
For each selected participant, a 15 to 20 minute instruction will
be needed following the Year 5 exam. The participant would receive
instructions on how to collect urine specimens and would receive
the urine collection kit. After the participant reads the
instructions, he/she would be verbally instructed by CARDIA staff
until it is evident that collection procedures are clearly
understood. The importance of providing complete collections is
also to be strongly emphasized.

The collection kit contains instruction materials, one large
carrying case containing 12 one liter collection jars, a small
empty carrying case which can hold three collection jars and, for
women only, a plastic pan or funnel to assist in urine collection.
Additionally, each collection jar will be placed in a plastic bag
to guard against leaks and spills. Within each jar there is a
preservative to help deter odor and avoid creatinine loss. The 12
jars will be divided into three groups by color coding the labels.
Each color corresponds to one 24-hour collection. The label
contains the participant's ID, the date, and the beginning and
ending time of the collection, and the question "During this
collection period, did you always void into this jar?".

Each selected participant will start the collection on the
evening of the second day after the regular clinic visit and end

6/90

the collection on the evening of the fifth day after the visit.
In this way, urine sodium values will not be influenced greatly by
the 12-hour fast required by the CARDIA examination. The
participant begins the collection by voiding into the toilet before
he/she goes to bed. The participant then records the date and time
on the label. The participant is to void all urine into the
same-color coded jars until he/she is ready to go to bed the next
evening. At that time, he/she should void for the last time into
the jar and end the collection for the 24-hour urine specimen.
Then, he/she will write the date and ending time on the label and
the date and beginning time on the label for the second 24-hour
collection. He/she will repeat the same procedures for the second
and third 24-hour collections.

The participants will return the jars or, if necessary, the
clinic will pick-up the jars. The participant is to be carefully
questioned about the completeness of the collections and whether
or not he/she always answered yes to the question on completeness
on the jar label. The participant is also to be asked if there is
any urine missing from the collections for any reason, e.g., from
spilling. If the answer is yes, he/she is to be asked if the
amount is only a few drops or more than that. If the participant
indicates that the amount missing is only a few drops, the
collection will be considered complete. Otherwise it will be
considered incomplete and will not be processed. Clinic staff must
insure that each participant returns all urine jars.

When the urine specimens are returned, the staff will
carefully measure the volume of each specimen and prepare two
aliquots for each 24-hour collection. One aliquot from each
participant from each 24-hour collection is to be frozen and
shipped once a month to the central laboratory for the measurement
of sodium, potassium and creatinine (three total per person). The
remaining aliquots are to be frozen and stored for future use. For
every sixth participant, one extra aliquot will be prepared from
a randomly selected 24-hour collection. The one additional aliquot
will be used for external quality control of the laboratory.

At the American Health Foundation, sodium and potassium will
be analyzed by potentiometric methods. Creatinine and magnesium
will be analyzed by colorimetric methods. All analyses will be
performed on a Kodak Ektachem 400.

ASSESSMENT OF VASCULAR DISTENSIBILITY
Rationale

The CARDIA study is assessing the natural history of
cardiovascular (CVD) disease during young adulthood. Since
symptomatic cardiovascular disease is relatively rare prior to at
least ages 40-50, the assessment of preclinical measures of adult
cardiovascular disease are of interest. These more sensitive
measures of CVD disease are especially important to evaluate since
the CARDIA study was designed to assess the progression of CVD from
an asymptomatic stage in young adults through a preclinical stage
and ultimately to clinical manifestations in an adult population.

Previous investigations have detected atherosclerotic lesions
in the aortas and coronary arteries of individuals with no evidence
of cardiovascular disease. Autopsy studies of soldiers in both the
Korean and Vietnam wars have noted a substantial amount of fatty
streak development and even some significant raised lesions in the
coronary arteries of these previously healthy young adults (1,2).
Autopsy studies of children and adolescents suggest that fatty
streaks and raised lesions were present in aortas and were
associated with elevated lipids and blood pressure levels (3).
Studies of young adults have documented the prevalence of both
raised lesions and fatty streaks in young adults which increase
with age (4). However, these autopsy data were available on a
relatively small number of individuals who may not be
representative of the general population. Therefore, non-invasive
assessment of atherosclerotic lesions in the general population are
needed to provide not only a better understanding of the natural
history but also the determinants of cardiovascular disease in
early adulthood.

Animal studies have shown that carotid elasticity changes were
associated with early atherosclerotic lesions (5). Ultrasonic
assessment of the anatomy and vascular distensibility of the
carotid arterial system has been shown to be feasible for
epidemiologic studies of the general population (6,7). Previous
surveys of school-aged children have shown an association between
vascular distensibility of the carotid artery and both parental
history of myocardial infarction and elevated risk factor levels
(serum cholesterol and systolic blood pressure) (7). Several other
studies have detected age-related changes, using non-invasive
ultrasonic techniques (8-10). The CARDIA study has excellent
information on cardiovascular disease risk factors and parental
history of myocardial infarction (MI) in 5,115 young adults ranging
in age from 18 to 30 years at the initial examination (11). At the
baseline examination 15% of these participants reported a history
of MI in at least one of their parents. Of particular interest is
the assessment of whether anatomic changes related to early
cardiovascular disease can be detected in this young adult cohort.
Ultrasonic assessment of carotid artery anatomy and vascular
distensibility are potential methods for ascertaining a pre-
clinical stage of cardiovascular disease. We anticipate that there

will be virtually no detectable carotid atherosclerotic plaques in
this age group and the confirmation of this fact could act as a
baseline for later assessment by carotid ultrasound. However,
previous work has shown that children with elevated blood pressure
and cholesterol had lower levels of vascular distensibility (7).
In addition, family history of myocardial infarction was related
to distensibility even in these younger age groups (7). The
vascular distensibility substudy proposes to study carotid artery
anatomy to provide normative data on black and white young adults
and to determine if association exist between distensibility with
CVD risk factors and family history of MI in these healthy young
adults.

Research Methods

In a subset of approximately 210 volunteers from the
Minneapolis CARDIA clinic, measurements are to be made of the wall
thickness and distensibility of the carotid arteries. The protocol
is the one employed by the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities
Study (ARIC).

A B-mode ultrasound examination is performed by a trained
technician on the right and left distal common carotid,
bifurcation, and proximal external and internal carotid arteries.
The examination is recorded on videotape and measurements of wall
thickness are made by the ARIC Ultrasound Reading Center in
Winston-Salem, NC. It is not anticipated that atherosclerotic
plaques will be detectable in this age group, but some early wall
thickening may be detected.

In addition to the B-mode examination, carotid artery
distensibility will be measured using the ARIC protocol. The
ultrasound machine has a radio frequency signal produced by the
carotid artery wall excursions that can be tracked by a special
"wall tracker" developed for the ARIC Study. In each subject the
distensibility of the right and left carotid artery will be
measured as a possible early indicator of artery sclerosis. Data
are recorded electronically and transmitted to the ARIC Ultrasound
Reading Center. Measurements are made of changes in wall thickness
and are adjusted for blood pressure. The primary index of
distensibility is the "elastic strain modulus."

Hypotheses

1. Those with a positive family history of MI will have less
distensible carotid arteries than those with a negative family
history.

2. Based on data collected in adults it is anticipated that

virtually no CARDIA aged participants will have any detectable
carotid plaques.

AMBULATORY BLOOD PRESSURE MONITORING SUBSTUDY

The procedures for the ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
substudy have been developed to assess the blood pressure of
selected participants over a 24-hour period, including the period
in which they are evaluated during the Year 5 exam, i.e., both out-
of-clinic and in-clinic ambulatory measures will be taken. The
study will be conducted at the Birmingham clinical center. The
procedure is designed to evaluate a total sample of 400 individuals
with adequate readings, with 100 participants randomly selected
from the four race/sex groups. Participation will be voluntary,
and all willing participants will be reimbursed $25 for travel and
other expenses.

Rationale

While current risk factor examination of blood pressure is
almost exclusively based on casual clinic readings, there are
numerous reasons to hypothesize that ambulatory blood pressure
recordings will facilitate the characterization of blood pressure
levels in ways different from casual readings. It is well
established that for some patients casual clinic reading may be
unrepresentative of their overall level of blood pressure (1,2).
Further, these ambulatory blood pressure readings may provide other
valuable risk factor data. For example, White and colleagues (3)
have demonstrated that only those patients who remain persistently
hypertensive during ambulatory monitoring have greater left
ventricular (LV) mass indexes. Verdecchia and colleagues (4) have
recently reported among hypertensive patients an inverse
correlation between LV mass index and percentage of nocturnal BP

reduction from daytime ambulatory recordings. Blood pressure
variability during the day has been found to relate to end-organ
damage (5). As Pickering has noted (6), it may also be possible

that different aspects of blood pressure, which may be recorded
with ambulatory devices, are involved in different pathogenic
processes. Average levels may result in LVH (7), while peaks in
blood pressure may rupture atheromatous plaques (8). Ambulatory
blood pressure data may also be of value in determining relative
risk for target organ damage between blacks and whites. Murphy et
al. (9) have reported that a smaller decline in nocturnal blood
pressure occurs in normotensive and hypertensive blacks. Thus,
ambulatory blood pressure monitoring data may be of value in
determining relations between blood pressure characteristics and
echocardiography findings, other risk factors, end-organ damage,
and differences between racial groups.

ABP - 1

4/90

Hypotheses

The following hypotheses will be investigated with the
ambulatory blood pressure monitoring data:

1) LV mass index measured by echocardiography and other
target organ variables (such as creatinine) will be
related to mean blood pressure elevation recorded from
the ambulatory blood pressure monitoring;

2) participants with established hypertension will show
higher mean night blood pressure levels than

normotensives;
3) there will be a sex difference between home and work mean
blood pressure levels, with males showing less

discrepancy between home and work recorded blood pressure
than females;

4) there will be a race difference in mean ambulatory blood
pressure levels, with blacks showing a higher median
level than whites, and in decline in blood pressure at
night, with blacks showing less of a decline than whites;

5) participants who showed greater Year 2 exam laboratory
blood pressure reactivity will show more ambulatory blood
pressure variance; and

6) hostility and anger measures will be positively related
to ambulatory bliood pressure variability.

Method of Measurement
Instrumentation

The ambulatory blood pressure monitor to be used will be the
Suntech Accutracker II. This instrument is an auscultatory device
which uses a gating method, employing the EKG signal, for
determining Korotkoff sounds. Aside from standardized procedures
necessary for any blood pressure recording, the device must thus
be positioned on the arm so that the microphone is over the
brachial artery. Three EKG leads must also be attached to the
chest area. Although these leads must be attached for recording,
their placement should not interfere with echocardiography or any
other exam procedures. Monitors will be programmed to take blood
pressure at an average of every 20 minutes during the day (6:00
a.m. through 10:00 p.m.) and at an average of every 30 minutes
during the night (10:00 p.m. through 6:00 a.m.).

ABP - 2

4/90

Participants

Ambulatory monitoring will be conducted with participants
until a total of 400 good recordings have been obtained. An effort
will be made to select these 400 acceptable participants with 100
from each of the four sex/race groups. The Coordinating Center
will be asked to order randomly the Birmingham participants who
fall within these four groups, and participants will be solicited
to participate in a sequential manner until cells are filled with
100 acceptable readings.

Training Procedures

Technicians will undergo training in the use of the ambulatory
monitor by representatives of the monitor manufacturer.
Technicians will be required to demonstrate competence in the
procedure, and a procedural checklist will be developed to evaluate
their performance. Each technician will also be required to
complete the entire procedure obtaining acceptable Office Run data
(+ 10 mmHg) from at least five individuals prior to certification.

Data Analysis

Measures of central tendency will be computed = from
satisfactory blood pressure readings for daytime, nighttime, work
and home periods. Daytime levels will be compared to target organ
variables (such as LV mass index and creatinine), exam recorded BP
levels, race, exam II reactivity, and hostility and anger
measures. Differences between work and home levels will be
computed and compared between males and females, between blacks
and whites, and by other variables. Percent reduction in BP from
daytime to nighttime readings will be compared to target organ
variables and exam recorded blood pressures. Variance in daytime
readings will be examined for relations between the Year 2 exam
reactivity data.
