CARDIA SALT TASTE SUBSTUDY

Rationale and Hypotheses

Evaluation of factors affecting the development of
hypertension is a major objective of CARDIA. Salt and sodium
intake may be a determinant of hypertension and the preference for
salt may determine dietary sodium intake.

Questions and hypotheses to evaluate

1. Higher salt taste preference is related to development of
hypertension.

Early studies suggested that parameters of salt taste are
related to hypertension status (1). Sensory evaluation studies
tend to have very small samples, selected on a clinical basis,
however, and have often used weak statistical analytic/design
methods (2). Salt taste preference has been reported to be related
to dietary and urinary sodium (3,4). There are no larger
population-based cross-sectional or longitudinal studies of salt
taste parameters and hypertension. Because of the likelihood that
salt intake relates to hypertension (5), it is reasonable to
hypothesize that higher salt taste preference will lead to
increased salt intake, and thus over the long run to increased
development of hypertension.

2. Do blacks have a higher salt taste preference than whites?

At least one study suggests that 9-15 year old blacks, but not
adults, have a higher salt taste preference than equal aged whites
(6).

3. Does salt taste preference change with age?

There is considerable evidence that older children and early
adolescents have higher salt consumption than adults. Since there
are no longitudinal studies, it is not clear what happens with salt
taste preference as children move to young adulthood and to older
ages.

Method of Measurement
The proposed test will be technician administered, and will
take about 5 minutes, with an additional 5 minutes of technician

preparation and editing time.

Three standard measures will be used to evaluate salt taste.
They include: intensity judgement (saltiness), hedonic

aces

(pleasantness) rating and the sodium chloride concentration most
preferred in the taste medium. Crackers containing six different
concentrations of sodium chloride (ranging from very low
concentrations to concentrations above the mean levels found in
commercial products) will be used as the salt taste delivery
vehicle.

In the taste test, each participant will rinse twice with
distilled water, before the test, and between each tasting.
Crackers will be expectorated after tasting. Each participant will
be given one cracker to taste and rate for intensity and
pleasantness, in order to familiarize him/her with the procedure.
Then the participant will be presented with each of the five
different crackers (one at a time) and asked 1) to rate the
cracker's intensity using a 9 point Likkert type scale and 2) to
rate the cracker's pleasantness also using a 9 point rating scale.
The crackers will be presented in random order. The order will be
predetermined and participants will be blind to the ordering and
to the actual number and nature of the levels of sodium chloride
being presented. This procedure will be repeated for each cracker.
After these ratings are completed, the participant will be
presented with all five of the crackers, in a second random order,
and asked to taste each one and choose the cracker with the sodium
level he/she most prefers.

Notes on salt taste delivery vehicles

In salt taste research the most common methods for evaluating
suprathreshhold intensity and hedonic characteristics utilize taste
vehicles other than salt water solutions. Since salt water is not
a usually ingested food-beverage, preference ratings are not very
salient, and may not adequately reflect salt preference in food
systems. The most desired approach to evaluate salt taste is to
use a variety of taste vehicles such as soup, crackers, juice, etc.
However, logistics, time and cost all are important considerations
in determining the procedures. Due to the time limitations of this
trial, we think it is feasible to employ only one taste vehicle.
Crackers were chosen because they logistically will be easier to
handle and will provide a taste delivery system that will be better
standardized. Soups used as the taste medium require heating to
a standard temperature and maintenance of this temperature. Delays
in the test or overheating the soup could alter the sodium
concentration or other flavor constituents. Soups would require
additional handling and storage procedures. Tomato juice has also
been used by salt taste investigators, but is not well liked by
many individuals. Ratings of a food that is not commonly eaten or
is disliked may not represent the more general salt taste
preference. Crackers provide a taste delivery simple that does not
have specific temperature requirements. They generally store well,
ana do not have competing flavor or texture constituents that may
interfere with the salt preference ratings.

Sample size

For alpha=.05, two-sided, power=.85, in the comparison of two
equal size groups (i.e. black versus white), specific to another
grouping (i.e. gender), he difference will be declared
statistically significant if one group has 10% prevalence or
incidence (i.e. of hypertension prevalence or incidence), and the
other differs by 5% for total n=5184; if the other group differs
by 6%, n=3600 is required. Therefore it is desirable to carry out
this test in all CARDIA participants.

DATA MANAGEMENT

The data management processes of the CARDIA Year 5 exam
include the flow and management of participants' data forms and the
electronic storage and management of participants’ data. While the
first process is purely manual and occurs primarily within the
clinics and the latter process is mainly automated and includes
activities in the clinics and the Coordinating Center, the two
processes are closely associated and somewhat dependent on one
another.

Flow and Management of Data Forms

Any and all paper forms that pertain to a participant's CARDIA
examination should eventually be filed in the participant's Year
5 exam notebook. In general, when a form is completed it should
be edited, then forwarded to Data Entry.

Forms that include data to be stored in the automated data
management system should be entered within one clinic working day
of their receipt by Data Entry, then filed in their participant's
notebook. Forms that do not require entry should be filed
immediately to avoid loss or damage.

All forms should be filed in a logical and consistent manner
so as to provide accessibility for future reference. Notebooks
should be stored in a secure and accessible place and manner.
Notebooks should be filed in numerical order by participant ID
number. Data forms are to be stored in the clinics for the
duration of the Year 5 exam and thereafter until storage of the
forms is deemed unnecessary by the study.

Electronic Storage and Management of Data

The electronic storage and management of the Year 5 exam data
includes entry and temporary storage of the examination and related
data in the clinics, the transmission of this data to the
Coordinating Center, and the permanent storage and management of
the data at the CARDIA Coordinating Center.

Data Entry

The entry of participant's data is done on IBM PC/XT's located
in the clinics. There are two main parts of the CARDIA Data Entry
System, a scheduling and retention section and the entry of
examined participants' data. There are also utilities included for
the daily backup of all data entered and the transmission of data
to the Coordinating Center.

The system is menu driven consisting of customized programs
written in the C programming language. The system uses a screen
forms manager and an ISAM (Indexed Sequential Access Method) file
manager integrated within the C programs to edit and manage the
data entered.

DAT - i

4/90

The scheduling system provides the expected date of
examination for participants based on their baseline examination
date. The expected date is for a given week of the Year 5 exam.
The scheduling system also allows for the entry and retrieval of
the status of a participant contacted for an examination. This
helps to provide tracking and retention information for individual
participants and cohorts of participants throughout the study.

When a participant is examined, verification of the
demographic data and the Year 5 examination date is entered. Until
this information is entered in the data entry system, none of the
examination data may be entered.

All participant examination forms are entered on a form by
form basis within a single program. At the operator's discretion,
forms for a given participant may be displayed for entry one by one
as selected or automatically in numerical order for entry of the
entire form set. Front end edits are performed at the entry of
each piece of data to prevent the entry of invalid responses and
to verify the entry of outliers.

Data entry operators are required to backup all data entered
at the end of every clinic work day. A set of backup diskettes is
kept for each day of the week so that several backups are provided.

At the end of each week, each clinic transmits the data it has
entered to the Coordinating Center. Backups of each transmission
are made and are kept by the Data Entry Supervisor.

Data Entry of Laboratory Data

Entry of data from phlebotomy and the urine substudy is the
responsibility of the lipid laboratory and urine laboratory,
respectively. Each lab will be provided with a file of valid
CARDIA IDs to help eliminate data entry errors. Decisions
regarding software selection are at the discretion of the
laboratory. Each laboratory is required to transmit an ASCII data
file to the CARDIA Coordinating Center by modem or by mailing
diskettes. Edit and range checks are performed on this data at the
Coordinating Center after its receipt.

Data Entry of Echocardiography Data

Entry of data from echocardiography is the responsibility of
the Echocardiography Reading Center (ERC). The ERC will be
provided with a file of valid CARDIA IDs to help eliminate data
entry errors. Decisions regarding software selection are at the
discretion of the ERC. The ERC is required to transmit an ASCII
data file to the Coordinating Center by modem. Edit and range
checks are performed on this data at the Coordinating Center after
its receipt.

DAT - 2

4/90

Data Storage and Management

All clinic data is transmitted to and stored on a
microcomputer at the Coordinating Center. The data for each form
is stored in an ISAM master file associated with the clinic and the
form from which the data came. Participants' records are keyed on
the participants' twelve digit ID number.

Each week, after the clinics' data transmissions are
completed, the ISAM master files are updated from the transmission
files received from the clinics. The transmission files are then
stored in a separate directory from other data and are periodically
"backed off" the microcomputer.

The master files are monitored for completeness of forms for
examined participants and any discrepancies are made known to the
clinics concerned. Up to date sequential files are easily built
from the master files to be used with SAS or other statistical
packages and programs for data analysis.

Distributed Data Analysis

A distributed data analysis system will be utilized allowing
each individual clinic access to the CARDIA Year 5 exam data set.
Such a system will be implemented in the Year 5 exam as in the Year
O exam and Year 2 exams since the investigators have experience
with such a system, each center has adequate mainframe and
microcomputer computing resources to support such a system, and the
desire to quicken the publication process via direct access to the
data is present. In the design of such a system, the investigators
have identified three important policies to which the study must
adhere:

1. The system must give the clinical centers and the
investigators enough freedom to pursue scientific
questions in the data while at the same time exert enough
control to stave off serendipitous findings and "fishing"
expeditions.

2. Throughout the process, the Coordinating Center must
remain the clearinghouse for information regarding the
CARDIA data set which includes maintaining the updated
CARDIA database.

3. The system must minimize the duplication of efforts and
expenses.

The implementation of such a system will involve the
distribution of CARDIA data tapes or Bernoulli cartridges
containing SAS data sets to each of the clinical centers, NHLBI
and the Chairman of the Steering Committee. This method allows
flexibility to each of the clinical centers, since the data can
then be downloaded to microcomputers for analysis or analyzed at
their mainframe computing center. Existing software is available

at each of the clinical centers and the Coordinating Center and is
currently being used for analysis of the distributed Year 0 and
Year 2 exam data sets.

Monitoring use of all CARDIA exam data tapes is a studywide
concern. The Coordinating Center will be responsible for
establishing and maintaining such a system which will allow the
reporting of technical problems, initiating edits and subsequent
changes to the database, reporting areas of analyses to be
performed, and reporting the close-out of analyses irrespective of
the final outcome.

NOTE: The 14 Hispanic participants examined at the first exam
are coded as white in D1REFA.

Number of Observations

Most files contain 4086 observations (the total number of
participants coded as Examined or Abbreviated for Exam 4). If all
data for a particular participant is missing in a file, that
particular record will contain SAS missing values although an ID
and CENTER variable will be present. Recall that abbreviated exams
were allowed in the fourth exam, with some parts of the exam being
eliminated more often than others. Thus, some files will have more
missing data than others.

The Form 9 follow-up files and the substudy files contain only
those participants who completed the form. Most of the files are
relatively small. Some files contain multiple records per person
(e.g., medication). In addition, data collected at the Minneapolis
clinical center are not included in the graded exercise test data
sets. Please refer to the specific documentation for more
information on these files.

ID Variable
Although all the files contain an ID variable, not all contain
the 12-digit CARDIA ID (ID). A 5-digit ID (SHORT_ID) is the ID
variable in all of the Form 9 follow-up files. In order to merge
one of these files with a file containing only the 12-digit ID
variable (ID), you can use the following statement to create a new
SHORT_ID in your file:
SHORT_ID=INT(ID/10**7).

Formats
The only formats used in the SAS data sets are the
conventional SAS date and time formats identified as DATE7 and
TIME5. To determine which variables have used these formats and
which format was used, please look at the PROC CONTENTS for each
data set. When using variables that were stored with DATE7 and
TIME5 formats, we recommend using these formats since without them
the variables cannot be easily interpreted.

Sorted Files
Each of the SAS data files have been sorted by the ID variable
(either ID or SHORT_ID) to facilitate the merging of files for
analysis.

Missing Values
CARDIA data entry personnel were instructed to use the letter
'M' for missing values. Occasionally, other conventions were
followed such as the use of zero's (0) and blanks ( ). In
addition, skip patterns built into the data entry system
appropriately filled the skipped fields with blanks ( ). SAS sets
these blank values to the SAS missing value of a period (.).

Please refer to the 'CARDIA DATA ENTRY DOCUMENTATION' on file
at each clinic and the Coordinating Center for specific form
instructions regarding missing values and skip patterns. Files for
which specific problems with missing or skipped data have been
found and are noted in the documentation that follows.

Edits

data at entry, real-time edits were generated by the Coordinating
Center during the course of the exam on the transmission files. A
detailed listing of the "real-time" edits performed on the data can
be found in the respective documentation for that file. These
edits were corrected or verified by the clinical centers on a
monthly basis. Although all these edits were completed by the
centers, occasional out-of-range results (outliers) are still

instructed not to create data. Thus, only data entry errors were
corrected and not interviewer or transcription errors.

collection is found following this section.

D1REFA - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Demographic Data)

This file contains the demographic variables (age [Exam 1 and
Exam 4], sex, race, education [Exam 1 and Exam 4]) and should be
used in any analysis of the CARDIA cohort requiring stratification
by the demographic variables. EXAMAGE is the age of the
participant at Exam 1. EX4_AGE is the age of the participant at
Exam 4. The variables EXAMAGE, SEX and RACE are based on the
original demographic variables collected in Exam 1 and verified in
Exams 2, 3 and/or 4. Only participants who were examined at Exam
2, Exam 3 or Exam 4 have their demographic data updated. The
demographic variables for those participants who did not return for
the second, third and fourth exams are as they were recorded in the
first exam. AO3ED is the number of years of education as reported
at Exam 1. DO3ED is the number of years of education as reported
at Exam 4. Fourteen Hispanic race codes have been changed to
white.

This reference file is the only file in this version of the
CARDIA data that contains information on all 5115 original
participants; all other files contain only participants examined at
Exam 4 (n=4086).

In addition to the standard demographic variables, this data
set contains the date of Exam 1 (AO2DATE), the date of Exam 2
(BO2DATE), the date of Exam 3 (CO2DATE), the date of Exam 4
(DO2DATE), the participant's birthdate (BIRTHDT), which was
verified at Exam 2, Exam 3 and/or Exam 4, and the participant's
pregnancy status at Exam 4 (DO8PREG) .

This data set also contains scheduling information on each of
the original 5115 participants seen in Exam 1 (X4DATE, X4STATUS,
X4WINDOW, and X4EXPDT). X4DATE will be the same as DO2DATE for all
examined participants. If the participant was not re-examined,

X4DATE reflects scheduling dates or pending dates, not an exam

date. X4STATUS reflects whether a participant was seen in Exam 4.
An explanation of each code is provided.

9/93

There are several ages of children and/or stepchildren that do
not seem feasible given the age range of our participants. All
such ages have been verified by the clinical centers.

A number of discrepancies between reported education at Exam
3 and Exam 4 (e.g, a lower number of years of education at the
fourth exam than at the third exam or increases of more than two
years) have been identified indicating that one should use caution
in using this reported education variable in analyses. The lack of
a standardized probing protocol may be the explanation for these
inconsistencies. One clinic has reported examples of problems
which were observed in reviewing some of the records sent as edits.

1. Vo-tech/business education - sometimes counted and
sometimes not counted.

2. GED - sometimes checked as 12 years of education and
sometimes not.

3. College - specific degree given various years of "credit"
- e.g., AA degree marked as 13 years when finished in
less than the usual 14 years.

4. College - 2 Bachelor degrees, 20 years of education
checked. “There appears to be a tendency to give people
credit for extra degrees that are at the same level.

These comments indicate that the problem is not restricted to the
interviewers, but extends to the participants as well.

Questions 13 - 17 deal with matters of medical care and
insurance coverage. These questions are new to this form and thus

there are no comparable variables from previous exams.

D1FO6AC - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Dietary Practices, Behaviors, and Attitudes - Dietary History)

Extreme Values for Number of Meals Variables

While every attempt was made to have the values for variables
that represent the number of meals eaten (Questions 1, 2, 5, and 6)
correspond to each other (i.e., the number of meals eaten at home
plus the number of meals eaten out equals the total number of meals
reported), the complex nature of the questions made it difficult in
some cases. Values have been verified for all these variables.

Food Choice Factor Rankings

Question 102 asks participants to rank a set of factors for
how much each influences food choice. In the data set, these
variables (DO6COST, DO6TASTE, DO6NUTQ, DO6RELIG, DO6CONV, and
DO6OTHF) can have a value of 1-6 or 9. Values of 1-6 indicate the
ranking of that factor by the participant (i.e., a value of 1 means
that factor is the most important). Because participants were not
required to rank all six factors if all six did not influence food
choice, values of 9 indicate that the participant does not consider
that factor when choosing food.

Computed Variable
DO6TIME: length of the diet history interview in minutes
DO6DATE: date the diet history was administered

Note: The date the diet history was administered may be
different from the exam date for some participants.

In the years since the Year 5 exam, the profession of cardiac
ultrasound (echocardiography) has undergone changes and increased
professional recognition. In particular, the field has become a
recognized profession by the American Society of Echocardiography.
Echocardiography sonographers are now called cardiac sonographers.
In keeping with these current professional standards, the word

‘technican" has been replaced by “sonographer" throughout this text.

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

CORONARY ARTERY RISK DEVELOPMENT IN YOUNG ADULTS

1. Objectives

The Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) Study is a study of the
distribution and change in risk factors during young adulthood in black and white men and women.
The baseline CARDIA examination began in June, 1985, with participants selected to obtain a cohort
with approximate equal representation for blacks and whites, men and women, participants aged 18-24
and 25-30 years, and those with and without more than a high schoo! education. During Year 5, an
echocardiographic (echo) examination--including M-mode, two-dimensional, spectral and color Doppler
components--was performed on approximately 4,200 CARDIA participants from four Field Centers
(Appendix A).

The specific objectives for the second CARDIA echo examination, scheduled to be performed
during Year 10, might be stated as follows:

a. To develop a method, based on previous experience in performing and interpreting
echocardiograms in large-scale multicenter studies, which will result in:

1) Recording and transmitting the best echo images possible, taking into account the
importance of comparability to the CARDIA Year 5 echo protocol.

2) Measuring and coding studies with the highest possible yield, lowest error rate, and
least measurement variability, with an emphasis on measurement of left ventricular mass.

b. To identify the race-gender distribution and determinants of change in M-mode echo left
ventricular (LV) mass over a five-year period.

1) To elucidate reasons for the higher prevalence of LV hypertrophy (and increase LV
mass) in blacks and in men.

2) To determine the relationship of factors such as systolic and diastolic blood
pressure, pulse pressure, family history of hypertension, body weight and measures of obesity,

physical activity and physical fitness, alcohol intake, and change in these factors over time to change
in LV mass.

c. To determine whether there are detectible changes in LV diastolic function (mitral flow
velocity parameters) over a five-year period, any race and gender differences in these changes, and
possible determinants of these changes, e.g., systolic and diastolic blood pressure and changes in
blood pressure, physical activity and fitness, etc.

d. If the study continues beyond the current examination, to determine whether changes
(increases) in M-mode echo LV mass (or its components), and LV diastolic function (measured by
pulsed Doppler), between Years 5 and 10 can predict those who will develop subsequent changes
(increases) in systolic and diastolic blood pressure during CARDIA Years 11-13 and beyond.

e. To identify changes in common echo findings, e.g., definite and possible mitral valve
prolapse and the determinants of these changes.

1) To identify possible changes in patterns suggestive of mitral valve prolapse and
their relationship to race, gender, and changes in body weight, physical activity, and fitness, etc.

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

2) To identity possible changes (natural history) in aortic valve or LV outflow tract
gradients in participants with ultrasound evidence of aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
and the correlates of these changes if there is sufficient power.

2. Rationale

The rationale for this protocol is based on lessons learned by the Echocardiography Reading
Center (ERC) in its similar previous role for both the CARDIA and CHS (Cardiovascular Health Study)
NHLBI-sponsored multicenter studies.

a. Importance of obtaining the best possible recordings for performance of core echo
measurements: In the first CARDIA echo examination, the yield of M-mode measurements for LV mass
was approximately 95%, with even higher yields for other M-mode measurements (e.g., aortic and left
atrial dimensions), pulsed Doppler measurements of transmitral flow velocities (LV diastolic function),
and qualitative two-dimensional (2-D) assessments of left atrial and LV chamber sizes and LV systolic
function. The yield of measurements of LV mass during the first CARDIA examination was significantly
higher than that obtained in the elderly participants of the CHS (approximately 66%), or a comparably
aged Framingham cohort (1). It is clear from the previous CARDIA, CHS, and Framingham experience
that age relates directly to the inability to obtain important core echo LV measurements, e.g., LV mass
(1-4). Although in CARDIA, the younger age of the participants should foster the recording of better
images, especially of the LV, it remains important to pursue the best images possible because the goal
of the second CARDIA echo examination is to detect change in measurements such as LV mass.

Undoubtedly, the training and skill of the Field Center echo sonographers will be of great
importance in optimizing image quality. In this regard, the protocol for the Year 10 CARDIA echo
examination will maintain the initia! Orientation and Training Visit for training Field Center sonographers
at the ERC, followed by additional sonographer training at the Field Centers by the Echocardiography
Reading Center sonographers-readers. in addition, it is anticipated that, as in Year 5, local echo
Physician-Supervisors will be involved in helping to train and supervise the performance of the Field
Center sonographers. Finally, a series of quality checks on sonographer performance will be
performed at the ERC, including calculation of the components of measurement variability attributable
to Field Center intra- and inter-sonographer variability, review of echo studies by the sonographer-
readers and ERC investigators with a standardized protocol for feedback to Field Center sonographers
and their supervisors. {t should be noted that in using all of these approaches, particular attention will
be paid to training Field Center sonographers to record optimal M-mode and 2-D images of the left
ventricle (for measurements of LV wall thickness, mass, and systolic function).

b. Necessity for minimizing components of measurement variability and insuring comparability
of Year 10 to Year 5 echo measurements: Because any echo-detected changes in cardiac structure
and function occurred over this five-year period in CARDIA may, in the majority of participants, be
subtle, it is extremely important to minimize the sources of measurement variability and maximize the
comparability of Year 10 to Year 5 echo measurements. tn this regard we will maintain the same basic
reading approach as was used in CARDIA Year 5 (with a notable exception of replacing the Dextra
Offline image analysis software), including the same echo readers and investigators who have had
previous experience in the CARDIA and/or CHS ERC’s.

The comparability study planned for Phase | of the second CARDIA echo examination is
designed to measure temporal drift in measurements made by the same reader, and by different
readers, on Year 5 studies using the new Freeland workstations. In addition, anatyses of inter-reader
and intra-reader measurement variability will be buitt into the comparability study to ensure that reader
measurement variability falls within acceptable limits. Generally, our criterion for acceptable agreement

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

between readings for continuous variables will be a Standardized measurement difference (‘technical
error’) < 15%. Our approach outlines measures to assess measurement variability and comparability,
as well as allowing for retraining of Field Center sonographers or ERC readers should there be

unacceptable temporal drift in measurements, or unacceptable inter- or intra-sonographer performance
or reader measurement variability.

c. Left Ventricular Mass: The CARDIA cohort is Poised in age between adolescence, when
linear growth is the major determinant of left ventricular mass, and middle age when biood pressure,
Obesity, and other lifestyle factors are associated with progression of left ventricular mass and cardiac
morbidity. Major determinants of left ventricular mass in CARDIA at the Year 5 examination included
body size (body mass index, height, subscapular skinfold thickness) blood pressure, age, and lung
function. Additional determinants include certain lifestyle factors such as smoking, alcohol use, and
physical activity. These factors and their correlation coefficients are similar to those obtained in
Pediatric and adolescent studies of left ventricular mass (5-7). As the CARDIA cohort ages, linear
growth will have ceased. Thus, determinants of change in left ventricular mass over the 5-year interval
between Year 5 and Year 10 echocardiographic examinations are expected to be increases in body
weight and blood pressure, lifestyle factors--e.g., cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption, and
decrease in physical activity (4). The relative contribution of each of these factors to increase in left
ventricular mass, as well as the rate of change of left ventricular mass, are unknown. The CARDIA
cohort will be the largest cohort of young adults in which high quality iongitudinal data can be
collected.

Associated with the major determinants of left ventricular mass are other physiologic
measures which may explain change in mass. Left ventricular wall stress, a measure of left ventricular
afterload, could predict increase in mass as could peak exercise blood pressure (8,9). Because these
variables were measured in the CARDIA cohort at the Year 5 examination, their contribution to increase
in mass can be assessed.

In addition, the question has been raised as to whether lean body mass or total body
weight is a more important determinant of left ventricular mass (10). An attempt will be made to
assess this issue by considering the following relationship: Total body weight = lean body mass +
adiposity where height is a surrogate for lean body mass and subscapular skinfold thickness is a
measure of adiposity or fatness.

In the CARDIA cohort during year 5, significant race and gender differences are present
with regard to left ventricular mass (4). Blacks had greater left ventricular mass than whites, and males
had greater left ventricular mass than females as determined by echocardiography. In the CARDIA
cohort during Year 5, Black males had the largest left ventricular mass. The CARDIA cohort should be
of sufficient size to determine if specific determinants of left ventricular mass produce different rates of
change in left ventricular mass in different tace/gender groups.

d, Left Ventricular Function: Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction may be an end-organ
manifestation of chronic hypertension and also may be a predictor of diastolic heart failure in the
elderly. It is known that left ventricular filling changes with aging in a pattern similar to that seen with
individuals with increased Jeft ventricular mass and chronic hypertension (11). This presumed age-
related decrease in parameters reflecting left ventricular early diastolic relaxation has been well
documented. However, the factors which contribute to this impaired relaxation are unknown because
no longitudinal analyses of change in teft ventricular filling velocities--as well as the potential!
contribution of factors such as blood pressure and their interaction with aging--have been performed in
large populations.

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

The CARDIA cohort provides the unique opportunity to evaluate the strength and independence of
some of these relationships.

Because of the large statistical power in the CARDIA cohort, six variables were identified in
cross-sectional analysis as contributing to Doppler teft ventricular filling velocities measured for the first
echocardiographic examinations: age, gender, heart rate, systolic blood pressure, body mass index,
and lung function (12). The magnitude of the contribution of each of these variables independent of,
and interacting with, the aging effect can be assessed. Additional factors to consider are change in
physical conditioning, which may lead to change in resting heart rate, and changes in lifestyle, which
may have independent effects on left ventricular filling, perhaps through effects on the six variables
listed above.

e. Cardiac Disease Prevalence: In the Year 5 CARDIA examination, 1.9% of participants were
identified as having mild and otherwise asymptomatic cardiac disease, with 0.3% of the cohort having
disease identified as significant (0.1% having hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) (13-15). The latter group
included several individuals with cardiomyopathy and significant cardiac vatvular disease. The CARDIA
cohort is unique in that the cross-sectional prevalence of cardiac disease was identified Primarily by
echocardiography, rather than by other clinical criteria. The importance of these findings is unknown.
CARDIA provides the opportunity to assess prospectively the morbidity of cardiac valvular disease,
Particularly mitral valve prolapse, and also to understand changes in cardiac function in individuals with
mild aortic and mitral valve disease. Follow-up echocardiograms and questionnaire assessment can
be used to identify morbidity related to these conditions. No such data set exists in the literature and
may be important for understanding the risk for bacterial endocarditis, progression of mitral valve
prolapse, and progression and development of symptoms in individuals with mild manifestations of
cardiomyopathy--e.g.. hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

ft. New Cross Sectional Hypotheses: There is a paucity of information about the relationship
of resting insulin levels and insulin resistance to left ventricular mass. Insulin may be an important
independent determinant of increased left ventricular mass; the relationships of both fasting and
postprandial insulin to left ventricular mass can be assessed at this examination.

3. Hypotheses

The following are specific hypotheses proposed for evaluation in relation to the Year 10 (and
Year 5) echocardiography data:

a. Left Ventricular Mass

1. Change in left ventricular mass over 5 years is related to change in blood pressure
and body mass index.

2. Specific stresses on the cardiovascular system may influence change in left
ventricular mass. These include peak exercise blood Pressure (from exam Year 7), and left ventricular
wall stress (echo examination, Year 5 and Year 10).

3. Lifestyle factors shown to influence left ventricular mass in cross sectional analyses
may influence change in left ventricular mass: these include physical activity, alcohol use, and
smoking.

4. Rates of change in left ventricular mass may differ by race and gender.

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

b. Left Ventricular Function
5. Age-related changes in left ventricular diastolic function (which reflect abnormalities
of LV filling) as assessed by left ventricular inflow Doppler velocities will be greater in individuals with
increases in blood pressure and increases in weight, as opposed to individuals with unchanged or
lower blood pressure and less weight gain (between Years 5 and 10).
Cc. Disease Prevalence

6. Individuals with identified possible or definite mitral valve prolapse will have
progressive changes in mitral valve prolapse grade.

d. New Cross Sectional Hypotheses

7. Elevated insulin levels will be associated with increased increments in left ventricular
mass.

4, Background
The recording of echocardiograms with acceptable measurement accuracy and reproducibility
will be accomplished using a protocol! based on studies previously published by the principal

investigator and other workers (2,3,16-19).

4.1 Standardization of Quality Contro!

Definition of Acceptable Quality: The quality control of M-mode echocardiograms will be
assisted by using a uniform definition of a technically satisfactory echocardiogram. This definition will
be based on our own experience as well as that of Schieken and associates who have defined a
technically satisfactory M-mode echocardiogram to include the following:

Generation of a single dominant line representing each interface being imaged,

Demonstration of continuous interface lines at least 5 mm in length at the point of
measurement, and

Demonstration of interfaces with the motion pattern characteristic of a specific cardiac
structure being imaged.

In addition, these workers required a simultaneous recording of electrocardiographic QRS
complexes with readily identifiable onset and peak deflections for use in timing echocardiographic
measurements (20). These criteria were said by Schieken, et al to result in high reproducibility in
measurements of the left ventricle, left atrium, aortic root and left ventricular ejection indices. Our
experience is similar. Aso Devereux and Reichek have Proposed analogous criteria for making
measurements of left ventricular mass fram M-mode echocardiography (21). These workers required
that left ventricular echocardiograms demonstrate continuous motion of tight and left septal surfaces
and endocardial and epicardial interfaces of the posterior left ventricle wail throughout the cardiac
cycle. In 24 echocardiograms deemed technically adequate by these criteria, measurements of left
ventricular mass exhibited good reproducibility (r= 0.94, P < 0.001) between two experienced
observers (22). We propose to use the criteria of Schieken, et al in CARDIA Year 10 as was done in
Year 5 to guide the recording and interpretation of echocardiograms.

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

It would be projected on the basis of data reported from the Framingham study in
subjects aged 17 to 29 years that, although during the initial learning curve (pilot study) should be in
the range of 85%, the percentage of acceptable echocardiograms recorded during the examination
period should be in the range of 96% (23). During CARDIA Year 5, the retrieval rate for

echocardiographic tracings of acceptable quality for making left ventricular measurements exceeded
95%.

4.2 Equipment Factors

Periodic instrument calibration is another extremely important factor in assuring accurate
and reproducible echocardiographic measurements. We will Periodically calibrate the ultrasound
equipment with an acoustic phantom. Such a phantom will be used initially to calibrate new
echocardiographic equipment and at six month intervals to check horizontal and vertical distance
calibrations, as well as resolution in the different axes (24).

In addition, it is well known that changes in dynamic range and gain settings on a given
instrument will result in differences in the appearance of echocardiographic interfaces and, hence, in
the measurements derived from these recordings. The use of different echocardiographic instruments
with different transducers and recording and display characteristics may result in variability in
echocardiographic measurements for the same heart. It is therefore apparent that standardization of
equipment among centers in a multicenter, multi-year trial is important and should reduce this potential
source of echocardiographic measurement variability. The same ACUSON machines used in Year 5
will be used again in Year 10.

4.3. Technical Factors

In addition to the equipment factors noted, various technical factors involved in the
performance of the echocardiographic study impact significantly on measurement accuracy and
reproducibility. The position of the patient and the location and angulation of the transducer on the
patient's thorax or subcostal area can greatly influence the echocardiographic image obtained and the
measurements that are made. A number of studies have documented the need to record accurately
both the patient and bed position resulting in the most optimal echocardiographic tracing (25,26).
Although various patient and bed positions, as well as transducer locations and angulations, may
produce adequate echocardiographic images of the same structure, these images may resutt in
somewhat different echocardiographic measurements (27,28). Consequently, we plan to have the
sonographers record information for each study about the patient’s position and inclination of the head
of the bed, as well as about transducer position and angulation (See Appendix B: Echocardiographic
Sonographer’s Worksheet).

Various workers have recommended either a partial left lateral decubitus (30 to 45
degrees) (19) or extreme left lateral decubitus position for recording the M-mode echocardiogram and
the majority of two-dimensional echocardiographic views (24,25). The degree of body rotation in the
left lateral recumbent position can be standardized by using one or more wedges placed under the
patient's back. With the patient in the extreme left lateral decubitus position, the apex impulse comes
close to the surface of the mattress. The construction of many transducers makes it impossible to
obtain images in this position with the standard mattress. Consequently, Schiller has recommended the
use of a 12-inch thick mattress that has a removable "scoop", i.e., a segment that can be removed after
the patient is in position--located in the area where the apex impulse approximates the mattress with
the patient in the left recumbent position (24,25). This type of mattress will be used at both Field
Centers for the subjects to lie on during performance of their echocardiograms.

Probably even more important than the position of the patient is the position and
angulation of the transducer during echocardiographic imaging. Popp and Feigenbaum initially
recommended that for optimal M-mode echocardiographic recording of the left and right ventricle, the
transducer be placed in the third or fourth interspace at the left sternal border to allow simultaneous
recording of continuous endocardial echoes from both the left ventricular posterior wall and the
interventricular septum (29,30). It was later noted, however, that left ventricular echocardiograms
satisfying these criteria could be obtained from various interspaces with corresponding differences in
left ventricular dimensions. Popp and co-workers showed that the measurement obtained for left
ventricular dimension depends on whether the echocardiographic beam is parallel to the left ventricular
minor axis or is angled obliquely to it, resulting in an overestimation of left ventricular internal
dimensions and wall thickness (28). These workers demonstrated excellent reproducibility of left
ventricular end-diastolic dimensions and fractional! shortening on different strips recorded from the
same chest wall location, while considerable scatter in the measurements was noted when dimensions
were obtained from other transducer locations. Hoenecke and co-workers demonstrated that once the
echo beam diverges by more than 25% of the distance between the true ventricular meridian and
either papillary muscle at the side of the ventricle, there is a progressive artifactual increase in percent
fractional shortening (31). The approach in CARDIA Year 10, as in Year 5 is to have the sonographers
use two-dimensional echocardiography to locate the M-mode beam along the true meridian of the left
ventricle as well as other structures being imaged.

Variations in body habitus, or in disease states such as emphysema or ascites, are known
to shift the heart inside the thorax. These alterations in cardiac position may require recording
echocardiographic structures from other than the standard interspace, using different
transducer angulation. Consequently, it is important, as noted by Clark, et al, that patient position,
head angulation, and transducer location and angulation be recorded as part of the echocardiographic
record. These workers showed that when these variables were properly accounted for, measurement
reproducibility was such that serial measurements of left ventricular end-diastolic dimension producing
differences greater than 3 mm could be labelled a true change in dimension, since they fell outside the
95% confidence limits (defined as + 2 standard deviations) for normal measurement variability. These
workers also concluded that differences in left ventricular fractional shortening greater than 5.5%
reflected a real physiologic change (26). As noted in CARDIA Year 10, the sonographer performing the
echocardiogram will record the position of the patient, the elevation of the head of the bed, and the
transducer locations (Appendix B-1: Echocardiographic Sonographer'’s Worksheet).

With regard to Doppler measurements of early or late diastolic transmitral flow velocity,
Gardin and co-workers have shown that recording from either the apical four-chamber, two chamber or
long-axis views yield similar values. On the other hand, the location of the sample volume--e.g. on the
teft atrial side of the mitral leaflets versus at - the mitral leaflet tips--makes a significant difference in
values for mitral early and late diastolic mitral flow velocity (p < 0.005). Specifically, increases in the
range of 22-25% in both early and late diastolic peak flow velocity were noted when moving the
sample volume from the left atrial side of the mitral valve to the mitral orifice near the leaflet tips (32).
Presumably, the early and late diastolic flow velocity measurements were higher in the mitral orifice
than in the left atrium because of the smaller flow area in the orifice: The continuity equation dictates
that in a closed system, (mitral) flow remains a constant product of the mean (mitral) flow velocity and
(mitral) flow area. The recording of Doppler mitral flow velocity measurements will be standardized by
having the sonographers place the sample volume in the mitral orifice near the leaflet tips.

44 Physiologic Variables

Physiologic variables, such as heart rate and respiration, have been previously shown to
affect echocardiographic measurements of left ventricular internal dimension and Doppler
measurements of transmitral flow velocity. DeMaria and co-workers performed right atrial pacing in
normal! subjects at increments of ten beats per minute to a maximum of 150 beats per minute. They
demonstrated a 2.7% decrease in left ventricular internal dimension, occurring virtually linearly, for each
10 beats-per-minute increase in heart rate (33).

Other workers have not detected significant changes in left ventricular diastolic dimension
in patients in whom the heart rate varied in the normal range of 110 beats per minute between serial
echocardiograms (34). Based on a reported mean intra-subject difference in heart rate of less than ten
beats per minute between annual examinations, it has been suggested that no greater than a 2-3%
variation in left ventricular diastolic dimension should be expected based on fluctuations in heart rate
(36). More recently, heart rates in the range of 70 to 110 beats per minute in norma! subjects were
shown to have no significant effect on Doppler early and late diastolic transmitral fiow filling velocities
and velocity integrals (37).

Respiratory variation has also been reported in echocardiographic measurements of left
ventricular internal dimension and in Doppler mitral flow velocity measurements. Brenner and Waugh
have demonstrated a 6% decrease in the left ventricular end-diastolic dimension at peak inspiration
compared to end expiration (38). This finding is similar to the 5% decrease in mitral early and late
diastolic peak flow velocities at end-inspiration, compared to end- expiration, noted in our laboratory
(39). The general approaches that have been recommended to standardize echocardiographic
measurements for the effects of respiratory variation include: 1) recording the ultrasound data at a
fixed time in the respiratory cycle e.g., at end-expiration; and 2) attempting to record measurements on
3-6 consecutive beats, in order to obtain representative measurements during all phases of the
respiratory cycle.

In order to standardize the procedure for making echocardiographic measurements, as
well as diminishing the time necessary to make these measurements, in CARDIA Year 10 (as in Year 5)
echocardiographic recordings will be performed during held-expiration (i.e., the end of the expiratory
phase during quiet respiration). This will obviate the need for standardizing the recording of multiple
beats during phases of the respiratory cycle.

In addition to heart rate and respiratory variation, variables such as preload, afterload, and
blood volume status are known to influence measurements of left ventricular anatomy and function.
Although pre-load and volume status are not generally measured by echocardiography as used
Clinically, various workers have demonstrated the utility of measurements of left ventricular end-systolic
(meridional) wall stress as an index of left ventricular afterload. This wall stress parameter is best
determined by combining M-mode or two-dimensionai echocardiographic measurements of left
ventricular wall thickness and cavity dimension with simuttaneously-determined cuff blood pressure.
Measurement of left ventricular end-systolic wall stress will be an integral part of this study (40,41).

45 Echocardiographic Conventions

A number of different measurement conventions have been proposed for making M-mode
echocardiographic measurements (30,31,32). Our initial studies using M-mode echocardiography to
define cardiac anatomy and function in younger and older subjects without clinically apparent heart
disease involved the convention that has become known as the National Institutes of Health (NIH)
Convention (21,42,43). In this initial measurement, convention, left ventricular internal dimensions in

-12-

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

diastole and systole were measured immediately below the mitral leaflet tips as the maximum and
minimum internal dimensions between the ventricular septum and endocardium of the left ventricular
free wall. The thicknesses of the ventricular septum and left ventricular free wall, however, were ”
measured at an earlier time in diastole, just prior to the thinning of the wall related to atrial systole. A
switched-gain circuit developed by Griffith and Henry was used to simplify identification of the
epicardium of the posterobasal left ventricular free wall (44). This switched-gain technique was very
helpful in defining the thickness of the left ventricular free wall. Although the NIH Convention proved to
be extremely useful in population studies of normal subjects (16,17), patients with systemic
hypertension (45) and patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (46), this convention has, by and
large, been replaced. A major weakness of the initial NIH measurement convention was the fact that
the left ventricular interna! dimensions and wall thicknesses were measured at slightly different times in
the cardiac cycle, which presented a theoretical problem in using these measurements to calculate left
ventricular mass. In addition, the NIH measurement convention for left ventricular mass has never
been directly validated against necropsy data.

Another measurement technique for estimating left ventricular muscle mass by
echocardiography, known as the Penn convention, was proposed after a comparison, in 34 patients, of
eight alternative echocardiographic mass measurement methods to actual necropsy measurements
(21) The Penn convention takes left ventricular diastolic measurements at the peak of the R-wave, and
arbitrarily excludes the thickness of the endocardial interfaces from wall thickness measurements. More
recently, the American Society of Echocardiography (ASE) has formulated a set of recommendations
based on the measurement reproducibility of 76 readers for a set of sample echocardiograms (43).
The ASE measurement convention takes M-mode echocardiographic measurements from the leading
edge of the more anterior echo interface to the leading edge of the posterior interface. The onset of the
QRS complex was used to define end diastolic measurements. Finally, the time of most posterior
displacement of the ventricular septum was used to determine end-systole for the measurement of left
ventricular systolic dimension.

Various studies have compared the accuracy and reproducibility of measurements made by the
ASE convention to angiographic and necropsy reference standard (21 47,48). Although left ventricular
volume estimates derived by cubing left ventricular internal dimension measurements made by the ASE
convention have been shown to overestimate ventricular volume determined by angiography, these
overestimations are highly reproducible (47). Furthermore, although echocardiographic measurements
of left ventricular mass using the ASE convention also overestimate left ventricular mass measured at
necropsy. the correlations using the two methods are excellent (21,48,49). The over-estimation of left
ventricular mass by echocardiography can be corrected using a simple regression equation described
by Devereux, et al (22). Because the ASE convention is widely accepted in laboratories throughout the
country and because measurements made using this method are highly reproducible, we used this
convention during Year 5, and will do so again in Year 10 as the standard for making measurements in
this protocol.

4.6  Intra-observer, Inter-observer and Temporal Variability

An important factor in the quality of interpretation of echocardiographic and Doppler
measurements involves the degree of intra-observer, inter-observer, and inter-test (temporal)
measurement variability. The same observer making measurements on the same echocardiogram or
Doppler study on multiple occasions will undoubtedly produce some degree of variability in these
measurements. We have previously evaluated the variability in making Doppler aortic flow velocity
measurements. Measurement variability was defined as the difference between measurements on
different studies (or on different reading of the same study) divided by the mean measurement for all

-13-

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

studies expressed as a percentage. The intra-observer variability was in the range of 5% (50). The
degree of inter-observer variability for M-mode echocardiographic measurements has also been well
described in the literature. For example, Vignola, et al (51) described inter-observer variability in
measurements of left ventricular end-diastolic dimension, ventricular septal thickness, and left
ventricular wall thickness of 5.2, 10.0 and 16.4%, respectively. The American Society of
Echocardiography measurement convention was determined to be the measurement convention that
produced the smallest percentage uncertainty between different observers (43). In the studies of Sahn
et al and Vignola et al, the measurement of left ventricular end-diastolic dimension exhibited the least
inter-observer variability, while measurements of teft ventricular posterior wail thickness and excursion,
and mitral E-F slope produced the greatest inter-observer variability.

Various workers have documented that reader experience tends to diminish the degree of
inter-observer measurement and variability (19,51). Vignola, et al have demonstrated that
echocardiographic readers with at least two years reading experience in a laboratory which performed
greater than 800 echocardiograms per year demonstrated less inter-observer variability than another
group of readers with less experience. Clark, et al, reported that two readers, each reading a given
echocardiogram twice on different occasions, or three readers, each reading a given echocardiogram
once, resulted in the best measurement reproducibility (26). Lapido, et al and Pietro, (52,53) evaluated
the inter- and intra-observer variability of M-mode echocardiographic measurements utilizing the quality
contro] measures recommended by Schieken (20) using the American Society of Echocardiography
measurement convention. In these studies, measurements on multiple beats were averaged to obtain a
data point. These workers obtained excellent intra-observer and inter-observer measurement
reproducibility.

Fortunately, intra- and inter-reader measurement variabilities for important echo
components were with acceptable limits during the first CARDIA echo examination. Of note, overall
CARDIA inter-reader variability for LV mass was 13%; for LV posterior wall thickness in diastole, 10%;
for variability for LV mass was 13%; for LV posterior wall thickness in diastole, 10%; for ventricular
Septal thickness in diastole, 11%; for LV internal dimension in diastole, 4%; and for 2-chamber Simpson
LV ejection fraction, 9%;. These variabilities compare very favorably to inter-reader measurement
variabilities previously reported in small, young adutt, non-population based studies - including 16%
reported for M-mode posterior LV wall thickness (51), and 27% for 2-D LV mass (52). Overall CARDIA
intra-reader variability for LV mass was 7%; for LV posterior wall thickness in diastole, 8%; for
ventricular septal thickness in diastole, 8%; for LV internal dimension in diastole, 2%; and for 2-
chamber Simpson LV ejection fraction, 6%. Overall CARDIA inter-reader measurement variabilities for
mitral early and late peak flow velocities were 6-9%, and intra-reader variabilities tanged from 3-6%,
considered to be in the acceptable range.

Various workers have attempted to study the inter-test or temporal variability of
echocardiographic measurements made on serial echocardiographic studies. Clark and associates (26)
expressed their results in terms of a coefficient of variation defined as "The standard deviation of all the
Presented data in a given case divided by the mean of those measurements". These workers
determined that a change in left ventricular end-diastolic dimension of 3 mm or greater represented a
biologically significant difference. Similarly, a change equal to or greater than 5.5% in left ventricular
percent fractional shortening was also considered to be biologically significant. One approach that has
been suggested to decrease temporal variability on serial echocardiograms is to have the entire series
of tracings on the same subject read at the same time (54,55). Although this approach has been
suggested as possibly reducing temporal variability by 50% (18), care must be taken not to inform the
reader of the sequence in which the echocardiograms were recorded to avoid any possibility of
observer bias. While this precaution is not possible in such circumstances where the subject has had

valve--it should be possible to follow this convention in studies in which the changes are more subtle.

4.7 Role of Two-Dimensional Echocardiography

Two-dimensional echocardiography has the advantage over M-mode echocardiography of
allowing better spatial orientation of structures, since it affords a second dimension in which to view
these structures. For example, the use of orthogonal views of the left ventricle might eliminate some of
the errors of improper angulation of the transducer beam relative to the left ventricle which may result
in erroneous M-mode measurements of left ventricular dimension and wall thickness in-some patients.
In this regard, Hoenecke and associates have shown that when measuring left ventricular percent
fractional shortening, there is a progressive artifactual increase in this measurement once the echo
beam diverges in the parasternal short axis from the true ventricular meridian by more than 25° of the
distance between the meridian and either papillary muscle (31). Angulation of the ultrasound beam
obliquely to the true ventricular meridian will result in decreases of both left ventricular diastolic and
systolic dimension, but in a greater decrease in systolic dimension--and hence, an artifactual increase
in left ventricular percentage fractional shortening. The parasternal long axis view will be used in Year
10 (as in Year 5) to orient the ultrasound beam initially for M-mode recording perpendicular to the
ventricular septum and left ventricular wall just below the mitral leaflet tips. The transducer will then be
turned 90 degrees to confirm in the parasternal short axis view that the echo beam, in fact, passes
through, or near, the largest diameter (meridian) of the ventricle. Clearly, a comparability study
comparing readings of Year 10 readers on Year 5 echocardiograms with those of Year 5 readers on
Year 5 echocardiograms is necessary, and will be performed, to study the effects of temporal and
reading systems (Freeland versus Dextra) on measurement variability.

Although it appears logical that the use of two-dimensional echocardiography should
result in greater accuracy and reproducibility of left ventricular size and function compared to M-mode
measurements, this is not entirely the case since two-dimensional echocardiography has its own
limitations. Although reasonable correlations have been reported between cineangiographic and two-
dimensional echocardiographic estimates of left ventricular volume--two dimensional echocardiography
tends to underestimate true left ventricular volume--even as documented by myocardial markers
(56,57) For example, as noted by Schnittger, et al, echocardiographic transducers with large beam
width characteristics may result in underestimation of true ventricular cavity size due to the lateral
target spread of the endocardial image which appears to encroach on the ventricular cavity.
Furthermore, improper apical transducer placement proximal to the true anatomic apex may produce a
foreshortened view and a reduced left ventricular image area.

Erbel and associates have shown that echocardiographic imaging from the so called
“apical window’ may miss the true left ventricular apex (as defined by angiography) in many patients
(58). Another problem encountered with two-dimensional echocardiography is that the third dimension
is not displayed in the planar images that are recorded. Although the transducer may be properly
Placed at the apex, the orientation of the scan plane may be oblique to the maximal cross-section of
the left ventricle and result in a reduced image of the ventricular cavity. Finally, the fact that the
interstices between the trabeculae carnae are included in volume estimates by angiography, but
excluded during volume determination by echocardiography, might be expected to result ina
comparatively smaller echocardiographic volume measurement when compared to angiography.
Furthermore, it should be noted that many of the difficutties inherent in M-mode echocardiography are
also present with two-dimensional echocardiography--e.g., the necessity for image quality control and
standardization of measurement technique, presence of intra-observer, inter-observer, and temporal
measurement variability, etc.

4.8 Influence of Age, Body Surface Area, Race, and Gender on Echocardiographic
Measurements

Various studies have evaluated the effects of such variables as age, body surface area,
race, and gender on both M-mode and Doppler echocardiographic measurements in subject
populations without clinically apparent heart disease (16-18,59,60).

In our own experience, comparing an older adult age group (over 70 years) with a
younger age group (21-30 years), significant (P< 0.01) increases in aortic root (22%) and left atrial
(16%) dimensions, in ventricular septal (20%) and left ventricular free-wall (18%) thicknesses, and in
estimated left ventricular mass (15%) were noted. In addition, significant (P< 0.01) decreases in mean
mitral EF slope (43%) and in mean left ventricular systolic and diastolic internal dimensions (5% and
6% respectively, P< 0.05) were noted. Left ventricular ejection fraction and percentage fractional
shortening were found to be independent of age.

In our studies of 136 normal adults, we noted approximately a 15% increase in mean left
ventricular mass in going from the 21-30 age year to the over 70 year age group after normalizing for
body surface area. In our studies, we normalized our echocardiographic data base using regression
equations on body surface area or body weight derived specifically for each measurement. This
increase in left ventricular mass was related to an increase in wall thickness (mean 19%) that was
relatively greater than the decrease in {eft ventricular diastolic dimension (mean decrease 6%) noted
between the two age groups (16,61). Subsequent echocardiographic studies in normal individuals also
have concluded that both posterior left ventricular wall thickness (59) and left ventricular mass (62)
increase significantly with advancing age. These findings are compatible with autopsy experience.
However, it should be noted that there is one conflicting study of 225 normal subjects, age range 18-
72 years, by Devereux and associates who suggested that age had no significant effect on
measurements of left ventricular mass (63).

There are various reports that have documented a relationship between body surface area
and both cardiac chamber dimensions and left ventricular wall thickness. We have previously
published equations with 95% prediction intervals for normal echocardiographic values derived from 92
younger normal subjects (ages 1 month to 23 years) (17,18) and 136 older norma! subjects (ages 20-
97 years) (16,18). These equations use a bi-variate regression model in which echocardiographic
measurements are expressed as a function of the subject's age and either body weight or body
surface area, The echocardiographic measurements include left ventricular end-diastolic and end-
systolic dimension, ventricular septal and left ventricular free wall thickness at end-diastole, aortic root
and left atrial dimensions, mitral E-F slope and left ventricular mass (17,18). These M-mode
echocardiographic measurements were obtained using the American Society of Echocardiography
convention (43). We found that estimated left ventricular mass varied linearly with body surface area,
but was 7.2% less in adult normal females than in males of the same age and body surface area (P <
0.05). This finding suggests a small but significant relationship between sex and echocardiographic
measurements of left ventricular mass that cannot be eliminated by correction for body surface area.

Devereux and associates also found that left ventricular dimensions and mass were
closely related to body surface area (63). Although, indexing by the body surface area eliminated sex
differences in LV wall thickness and internat dimension, a significant sex difference remained in left
ventricular mass index (89 + 21 g/m? in men versus 69 + 19 g/m2 in women, p< 0.0001). However,
when left ventricular mass was indexed by lean body mass in this study, no sex difference persisted.
On the other hand, Valdez and co-workers, in their study of a normal population, found differences
between men and women in left ventricular echocardiographic measurements such as wall thickness

-16-

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

and internal dimension, but noted that these differences were eliminated by merely indexing for body
surface area (60). In this study, we propose to compare three alternative anthropometric
measurements for "indexing" echocardiographic measurements for body size: 1) body surface area
estimated from the Boothby and Standiford modification (64) of the Dubois formula; 2) weight; and 3)
height which proved to be the strongest correlate of the three anthropometric measurements to left
ventricular mass in the first CARDIA and CHS echocardiography examinations. Levy and associates
have demonstrated in the Framingham original cohort and offspring a higher prevalence of left

ventricular hypertrophy when using the LV mass height ratio, rather than LV mass/body surface area
to correct for body size (65).

A number of studies have noted that age influences Doppler transmitral and aortic flow
velocity measurements (66-69). In our laboratory, Doppler measurements of transmitral flow velocity
were made at the level of the mitral leaflet tips in 66 adult men and women, ages 21-78 years. Mitral
peak flow velocity in early diastole was significantly lower (P< 0.01) in the 61-70 year age decade (45
+ 10cm/sec) than in the 21-30 year age decade (66 + 11¢m/sec). Mitral peak flow velocity in late
diastole (atrial systole) was significantly higher (P< 0.05) in the 61-70 year age decade (55 +
14cm/sec) than in the 21-30 year age group (41 + 7cm/sec). Consequently, the ratio of late-to-early
diastolic peak flow velocity (A/E ratio) was significantly higher (P< 0.01) in the oldest (1.2 + 0.3)
compared to the youngest (0.6 + 0.1) age group. In these subjects without clinical evidence of
cardiovascular disease, we could detect no significant relationship between body surface area and
gender and the Doppler mitral flow velocity parameters. There was, however, a significant relationship
between systolic (but not diastolic) blood pressure and the mitral A/E ratio (r=0.67, P< 0.001).
Miyatake et al, who reported similar findings, have postulated that the increase in the late diastolic
peak transmitral flow velocity with aging reflects an augmentation of ventricular filling by atrial
contraction which compensates for the decreased early diastolic ventricular filling. In our study of mitral
measurements, we demonstrated not only age-related increases in late diastolic peak flow velocity, but
also in late diastolic flow time and flow velocity integral. In a similar study of Doppler measurements
performed in the ascending aorta in 97 adults aged 21 to 78 years, age demonstrated a significant
inverse relationship with various aortic Doppler measurements. Peak flow velocity, flow velocity
integral, and average acceleration (all P <0.001). The CARDIA study will allow us to extend our
previous Doppler findings to a large, free-living young adult population.

4.9.2 Qualitative Two-Dimensional Echocardiographic Scoring

Severe LV function will be assessed from two-dimensional echocardiographic images in al!
available reading views. As in Year 5, readers will subjectively score (without quantitative
measurement) left ventricular ejection fraction as normal, abnormal or borderline (Appendix C).
“Normal” will generally correspond to the readers quantitative assessment that ejection fraction is
>55%. "Borderline" will correspond to a quantitative assessment of an ejection fraction of 40 to 50%,
and "abnormal" will correspond to an ejection fraction < 40%. In addition, readers will score left
ventricular segmental wall motion quantitatively as normal, borderline, or abnormal, based on a 2-D
segment reader proposal by the American Society of Echocardiography (72) (Appendix D-1). Each
segment will be visually scored as follows: normal, hypokinetic (decreased wall motion), akinetic
(absence of wall motion), and dyskinetic (paradoxical wall motion). Normal wall motion in all segments
or hypokinesis in at most one segment, will correspond to a score of "normal". A "borderline" score will
correspond to hypokinesis in two segments. Akinesis or dyskinesis in any segment, or hypokinesis in
more than two segments will resutt in a score of “abnormal’.

4.10 Doppler Evaluation of Left Ventricular Diastolic Function

With regard to left ventricular diastolic function, Snider et al have demonstrated ina
Pediatric population with hypertension that transmitral late diastolic flow velocity and velocity integral
are more sensitive indicators of filling abnormality than early diastolic flow velocity and velocity integral
(73) In a series of adult patients with mild hypertension, we have reported that late diastolic transmitral
flow velocity integral but not velocity, was significantly correlated with left ventricular mass. More
recently, Graettinger and associates in our group have reported that in 47 normotensive adolescents
(mean age 13 years), diastolic blood pressure was inversely related to a number of Doppler early
diastolic transmitral indices, including peak velocity (r=- 0.44, p<0.005), flow velocity integral (r=0.40,
p<0.01), and deceleration (r=- 0.32, p<0.05) (74). The ratio of late-to-early diastolic peak filling
velocity (A/E) was found to be directly related to diastolic blood pressure (r=0.48, p<0.001). In 22 of
these 47 subjects who had bimodal P-waves in Lead V1 on their electrocardiogram, there was even a
stronger correlation between AVE ratio and diastolic blood pressure {r = 0.63). These Doppter left
ventricular filling velocity changes were independent of left ventricular mass and were felt to possible
represent early pre-hypertensive alterations in left ventricular diastolic function. Because of the large
Statistical power in the CARDIA cohort, six variables were identified in cross-sectional analysis as
contributing to Doppler left ventricular filling velocities measured in the first echocardiographic
examination: age, gender, heart rate, systolic blood pressure, body mass index, and tung function (12),
In CARDIA Year 10, we will study whether Doppler transmitral early or late diastolic flow velocities, flow
velocity integrals, or their ratios have changed since Year 5, and whether any significant Doppler
changes are associated with changes in risk factors such as hypertension, obesity, etc.

It has been reported that aortic flow velocity integral alone, even without muttiptying by the
flow area, is useful in predicting changes in stroke volume and systemic vascular resistance in patients
with heart failure who have received vasodilators (75). In addition, an index percent total systemic
resistance can be estimated by dividing the mean arterial pressure (estimated using an arm
sphygmomanometer) by the aortic flow velocity integral. Aortic flow velocity integral and total systemic
resistance index are expected to prove useful in evaluating such issues as the hemodynamic correlates
(‘volume-dependent" versus "vasoconstrictor" forms) of hypertensive and "pre-hypertensive" states.

5.1. Background

The two basic approaches considered in terms of echo data acquisition at the Field Center
and transmission to the Echocardiography Reading Center were: (1) digitization of (analog) images
directly from the ultrasound scanner by the Field Center sonographers onto optical disks in addition to
sending the backup videotape to the Echocardiography Reading Center; and (2) sending the video
cassette tape recorded on a super VHS video tape recorder to the Echocardiography Reading Center
where selection of images to be digitized for data analysis would be made by the Echocardiography
Reading Center readers.

After extensive consideration of the two options, it was decided that it would be preferable
for the data to be recorded on super VHS video tape at the Field Center and sent to the
Echocardiography Reading Center (as was done during Year 5). The videotapes will then be analyzed
by readers at the Echocardiography Reading Center on a Tomtec/Freeland off-line image analysis
system (See Section 5.1.2). Both the images selected in each view and measurements made will be
stored at the Echocardiography Reading Center on an optical disk.

5.2 Offline Image Analysis System

The basic "work-horse” of our off-line image analysis system is the Horizon offline analysis
system manufactured by Tomtec/Freeland Imaging. This system has a frame grabber which can digitize
30 frames per second in real time with 640 x 480 x 8 bit resolution. The system is equipped with a
mouse, high resolution monitor, printer/plotter and, importantly, a super VHS video tape recorder. The
Horizon system has an IBM compatible computer with an Intel 80486 50 MHz processor. The system
comes configured with 4 mbyte system memory and 360/1.2/1.44 mbyte disk drives. The system also
is configured for our purposes with a 650 mbyte optical disk. Two major advantages of this system are:
(1) Measurement data obtained from image analysis can go directly into an ASCII database for storage
and additional statistical analysis: There is a no need for a person in addition to the echo reader to enter
data into the computer. (2) With its “open architecture”, the computer is fully programmable so that
programs can be written to merge files, do additional measurement calculations based on desired
formulae for LV mass, wall stress, do statistical calculations, etc.

The commercially available software on the system allows performance of all the direct M-
mode measurements proposed as part of this study. In addition, the following derived M-mode
measurements will be correlated after transmission of the primary measurement data to the UCI
Epidemiology Program or the CARDIA Coordinating Center: 1) M-mode LV end-systolic meridional wall
stress calculation; and 2) an equation to index the left ventricular percent fractional shortening for LV
end-systolic stress, as described by Borow et al (see Section 4.10).

The Doppler measurements recommended in our proposal will all be made on the
Tomtec/Freeland offline analysis system.

Parcel Service, or an overnight mail delivery service. These videotapes should be accompanied by a
packing slip listing the videotapes by number. Upon arrival at the Echocardiography Reading Center,
