5.4 Sequence of Recording Echocardiographic Examination (Appendix D)

As part of each participant's echocardiographic record, the following information will be
recorded: Participant’s initials, identification number, date of study, patient position, number of wedges,
inclination of head of bed, chest deformities,lung disease, arm cuff blood pressure, frequency of
transducers used, and technica! rating (quality of the study). In addition, for each M-mode, two-
dimensiona! or Doppler recording sequence, the transducer location--in terms of interspace and
approximate distance from various landmarks such as the sternal border, mid-clavicular line, anterior
axillary lines, etc.--will be recorded on the Echocardiographic Sonographer Worksheet (See Appendix B).

Each M-mode, two-dimensional and Doppler study will be recorded in its entirety on a
videotape as outlined in Appendix D. The following M-mode and pulsed Doppler tracings that are felt to
be of optimal quality will be recorded (Appendix D): (1) M-mode echocardiogram at the level of the left
atrium and aortic root; (2) M-mode echocardiogram of the mitral valve showing the anterior and the
posterior mitral valve leaflets; (3) M-mode echocardiogram of the left ventricle at the level of the papillary
muscle with visualization of the ventricular septum and posterior wall in both systole and diastole; (4)
pulsed Doppler transmitral flow velocity in the apical four-chamber view; and (5) pulsed Doppler
recording at a sweep speed of 100 mm per second in the left ventricular outflow tract proximal to the
aortic leaflets.

The videotaped data will allow the echocardiographic readers to determine that the M-
mode, two-dimensional and Doppler studies have been recorded using the two-dimensional
echocardiogram to optimize the echo beam angulation and Doppler sample volume positioning.
Specifically, the left atrial and aortic root M-mode dimensions will be derived by two-dimensional
scanning, first in the parasternal long axis to localize the M-mode beam at the level of the aortic leaflets.
The transducer will then be turned 90-degrees to the parasternal short axis view to determine that the M-
mode beam passes through the meridian (center) of the aortic root and left atrium. M-mode
measurements will generally be made from images derived from the parasternal short axis view.

Similarly, the two-dimensional echocardiogram will be used to image the left ventricle in the
parasternal long axis view and to locate the M-mode cursor just below the mitral leaflet tips. This long
axis view will be used to assure that the echo beam is not passing through the left ventricle at an
oblique angle. If an oblique angle is noted, the transducer will be moved to position the echo beam
perpendicular to the left ventricle. The transducer will then be turned 90-degrees to the parasternal short
axis view to confirm that the M-mode beam is passing through the meridian (center) of the left ventricle
just below the mitral leaflet tips.

5.5 Protocol! For Making Echocardiographic and Doppler Measurements

5.5.1 General Approach

From our previous work and from the recommendations developed by other laboratories as
discussed in detail above under Section 4 Background, we propose a general approach to the recording
and scoring of the M-mode, two-dimensional and Doppler echocardiographic data.

All recordings will be performed at end-expiration, obviating the need for using a
resplrometer and making measurements at defined points in the respiratory cycle.

For M-mode echocardiographic and pulsed measurements will be made, when possible,

from 3 consecutive beats as noted below. The American Society of Echocardiography Standards will be
used for making all M-mode echocardiographic measurements.

For M-mode measurements of the !eft ventricle, left atrium and aorta, all of which will be
derived from a cursor positioned on the two-dimensional image, measurements will not be made from
beats recorded with the cursor at a greater than 20° angle to the meridian. In addition, in the two-
dimensional parasternal short-axis view, M-mode left ventricular measurements will not be made when, in
the absence of wall motion abnormalities, there is an eccentricity index of 1.3 - i.e., when the radius of
the left ventricular cavity in one axis is_> 1.3 times the radius of the cavity in another axis.

The criteria for quality control suggested by Schieken and associates will be used as a gold
standard to determine acceptable quality of M-mode echocardiograms of the left ventricle. These criteria
are: (1) generation of a single dominant line representing each interface being imaged; (2) demonstration
of continuous interface lines at least 5 mm in length at the point of measurement; and (3) demonstration
of interfaces with the motion pattern characteristic of the specific cardiac structure being imaged. (See
also Section 7, Quality of Data Score)

For pulsed Doppler measurements of aortic and mitral peak velocities and flow velocity
integrals, spectral curves will be traced using peak velocity conventions. Measurements will not be
performed from pulsed Doppler beats demonstrating maximum spectral dispersion greater than 30% of
peak velocity.

After each super VHS tape is logged in, it will be given to the echocardiography readers.
The entire Tomtec/Freeland offline analysis system is turned ON via a single power switch on the plug
strip supplying power to all the system components. This causes components to power up
simultaneously avoiding any possible initialization problems. Before powering the Tomtec/Freeland, all
system components are confirmed to be ON: computer, monitor, and VCR. Normally there should be no
diskette inserted in the floppy drive of the computer at power up. All the operating programs are loaded
automatically from the hard disk. The opening menu is displayed a short time after the power is turned
ON.

The echocardiographic measurements to be made are described below:

The American Society of Echocardiography (ASE) measurement conventions will be used-~
including leading-edge to leading-edge methodology, and measuring the aortic root dimension at the
onset of the QRS complex and the left atrial dimension at its maximum during systole (43).

The left ventricular internal dimension at end-diastole will be measured at the onset of the
QRS complex. Similarly, the thickness of ventricular septum and left ventricular posterior wall at end-
diastole will be measured at the onset of the QRS using the leading-edge to leading-edge convention.
The left ventricular internal dimension at end-systole will be measured as a perpendicular line drawn
between the septum and left ventricular posterior wall at the time of the most posterior motion of the
ventricular septum. The ventricular septal and posterior left ventricular wall thicknesses at end-systole
also will be measured from leading edge to leading-edge. A simultaneous electrocardiogram, recorded
on the videotape, will be used to measure the preceding R-R interval and to derive the approximate
heart rate. An attempt will be made by the readers to average three beats at end-expiration which meet
the definition for acceptable quality of interface definition outlined previously.

Flow velocity integrals (j.e., the areas in cm, under the flow velocity curves) for LV outflow
tract flow in systole and transmitral flow in early and late diastole will be planimetered using the off-line
analysis system. The R-R interval will be measured from the Doppler tracing and the heart rate will be
calculated.

6. Quality Control Procedures

Detailed documentation of quality control is particularly important. Relatively little experience
exists with the use of echocardiography in multicenter studies and it is essential to determine the
comparability of measurements made in different locations and by different sonographers. In addition,
it is important to document comparability of measurements made during Year 10 (or Year 9) using the
Tomtec-Freeland offline analysis system with measurements made on the same studies during Year 5
using the Dextra offline analysis system. Despite increased experience and improvements in
equipment and technique, questions remain about the utility of the technique in multicenter studies
including CARDIA. Strict quality control procedures for echocardiography performed in CARDIA should
Provide quantitative documentation of the reproducibility of procedures and will be of great importance
in interpreting data from the study.

6.1 Comparability Study

July through August 1994, a comparability study will be performed involving
remeasurement of CARDIA Year 5 studies, plus a blind duplicate sample to be selected by the
Coordinating Center. The comparability study will also include assessment of intra- and inter-individual
variability of echo measurements. Two readers will each read 100 studies initially. The 100 studies
would include 25 studies read by the second reader, yielding a total of 50 studies read in common that
could be used for assessment of Year 9 inter-reader variability. Furthermore, each of the readers
would re-read the same 25 of the initial 125 studies to provide data for Year 9 intra-reader
measurement variability.

In addition, a comparison would be made in 100 studies for each reader of measurements
made using the Tomtec-Freeland software during Year 9 with readings previously made on these same
Year 5 CARDIA studies using the Dextra software during Year 5. Furthermore, because
Echocardiography Reading Center reader Paynter read nearly 300 Year 5 CARDIA studies during Year
5, we would select a subsample (e.g., 50) of these studies to be included among the 125 studies that
he would read as part of the comparability study. This would provide a comparison of the differences
between a single reader, versus a second reader, re-reading a Year 5 study approximately four years
later using a different offline analysis system. This proposal would result in a comparability study
involving a total of 250 studies read.

Analysis and Recommendations from Comparability Study. The data from the
comparability study will be analyzed and results and recommendations presented to the Steering
Committee. This analyses will be performed at the UC! Epidemiology Program by Dr. Hoda Anton-
Culver and Dr. Tom Kurosaki, with input solicited from the Coordinating Center. The comparability of
measurements made by readers during Year 5 will be assessed by calculating "technical error" (the
standardized measurement difference) for continuous variables, such as LV mass. For qualitative
measurements (normal, borderline, abnormal) of left ventricular ejection fraction, and segmental wall
motion, a composite Kappa statistic and 95% confidence limits will be calculated.

“Agreement” between readings can be defined as differences in continuous variable
measurements of less than or equal to 10%, "borderline" agreement as differences of 11-15%, and
“disagreement' as differences greater than 15%. For qualitative variables, “agreement” can be defined
as occurring when the 95% confidence limits for the Kappa statistic overlap 1.0 (i.e., perfect
agreement). Using this approach, "disagreement" would be defined as occurring when the 95%
confidence limits for the Kappa overlap 0. Finally, "borderline" agreement would be defined as
occurring when the 95% confidence limits overlap neither 1 nor 0 (76). Another approach might be to

6.2 Training of Echocardiography Reading Center Readers

Our objective is to certify at least three trained sonographer-readers at the
Echocardiography Supervisor Center in addition to the Center Principal and Associate Principal
Investigator. The advantage of having multiple certified echocardiography readers available at any
given time is that one of the echocardiography sonographer-readers may be travelling to a Field Center
to either certify or recertity sonographers or to monitor protocol adherence and perform general quality
control. In addition, having more than one certified reader will minimize any potential disruption to the
study related to iliness or departure of echocardiography readers.

Training of the Echocardiography Reading Center readers will be supervised by Drs.
Gardin and Reid. This will be accomplished through an intensive two month training period. Training
sessions, held twice each week, will be supervised by Drs. Gardin and Reid. These training sessions
will include review of teaching tapes and echo studies of varying image quality. One important goal of
the one-month training period is to have readers develop efficiency in making measurements on the
Tomtec-Freeland analysis work stations. A second goal of this training is to allow the readers to
perform a final check on the performance of the Tomtec-Freeland software. A third important goal is to
have each of the ERC readers receive intensive training related to the appropriate performance of M-
mode and 2-D echo measurements and scoring of the left ventricle (mass, wall motion, etc.) specified
in the CARDIA protocol.

63 Assessment of Inter- and Intra-Field Center Sonographer Variability During the Pilot Period

Measurement variability between studies on the same patient performed by different Field
Center sonographers (inter-sonographer) and within the same sonographer (intra-sonographer) will be
assessed during the pilot study. After completion of the training program at the Echocardiography
Reading Center, sonographers will return to the Field Centers where each will perform
echocardiograms on 20 volunteer participants who are not enrolled in CARDIA (see Appendix M).
Each sonographer will also perform repeat studies, during a different clinic visit within one week if
possible, on these 20 participants. Assuming there are two sonographers at a Field Center, there will
be 60 studies from each Center or a total of 120 studies to be read at the Echocardiography Reading
Center. Videotapes will be sent to the Echocardiography Reading Center, coded with arbitrary ID
numbers, and measurements will be performed. Estimates will be made of inter- and intra-
sonographer measurement variability among key echocardiographic variables. Each reader will read
initial and repeat studies performed by Field Center sonographers on selected volunteers, with the
combined data from all readers used to assess inter- and intra-sonographer variability. An outline of
this scheme appears in Appendix M. Additional repeat echocardiogram will be scheduled during the

Reader variability will also be assessed during the pilot study. Each Echocardiography
Reading Center reader will read the same sample of 40 echocardiograms performed by the first Field
Center sonographer, and 20 echocardiograms performed by the second sonographer at each Field
Center. Each reader will than re-read 20 echocardiograms for determination of intra-reader variability.

6.5 Pilot Study Analysis and Follow-Up

A similar strategy will be used as during the previous CARDIA echo examination to partition
the various components of variability into inter-sonographer, intra-sonographer, inter-reader, and intra-
reader variability (see Appendix N). It is anticipated that these analyses will be performed by Dr. Anton-
Culver and associates at the UCI Epidemiology Center with appropriate input from the Coordinating
Center. If inter- or intra-sonographer, or inter- or intra-reader measurement variability, calculated as the
technical error for continuous measurements, is found to be greater than 15% (or if the Kappa statistic
falls into the “disagreement” range for qualitative measurements), this will trigger additional re-training of
the appropriate personnel with regard to making or reading the specified measurement(s). It is
anticipated that for many continuous echo variables, the individual technical errors will be in the range of
10%, or less.

Echocardiography Reading Center principal investigators and readers will review the pilot
studies very closely to determine whether there are any protocol deviations (Appendix J) committed by
Field Center sonographers. In the event of a protocol deviation, Field Center sonographers will be
phoned directly to advise them of the problem. A log will be kept of these phone calls and of the
problem(s). If the problem cannot be corrected within one week, a written notice describing the
problem will be sent to the Field Center sonographer, clinic supervisor, and local echo Physician
Supervisor. If the echo reader feels that the problem is unsolved over a two-week period, it will be
reviewed with the Echocardiography Reading Center Principal Investigator, and additional measures
taken. These measures might include additional work locally by the Field Center sonographer with the
local echo physician-echocardiographer or a trained local sonographer, or as a worst case, an
emergency visit of the Echocardiography Reading Center sonographer-trainer to the Field Center for re-
training.

6.6 Echocardiography Reading Center Staff Visits to Field Centers

Echocardiography Reading Center supervisor will visit Field Centers at least twice during
the examination year to insure that Field Center sonographers are performing examinations in
compliance with the protocol and to attempt to correct any problems that may be associated with
performance of poor quality studies. The sonographer-trainer will supervise the performance of
echocardiograms by each Field Center sonographer and make any necessary instructional comments,
using a supervisory protocol similar to that used during the initial training period in Phase |. Finally, on
the last day of the visit, a formal test will be performed in which the sonographer-trainer supervises the
performance of at least four echocardiograms by the Field Center sonographer and scores them
according to the Phase ! protocol. These reports will be sent to the Field Center Clinic Supervisor,
Principal Investigator, local Physician-Echocardiographer, and to the Project Office or the Quality Control
Committee as directed. If problems with supervisor variability are identified during the pilot study, the
Echocardiography Reading Center sonographer will visit the Field Center in an attempt to upgrade skills
of the Center’s sonographer. The echocardiography equipment will be calibrated at the time of these
visits using an RMI model 400F tissue-mimicking or equivalent, phantom (Appendix N).

6.12 Analysis of Data Quality

Three major steps be undertaken to evaluate the quality of data from readings of
echocardiograms in this study. The first step is to evaluate distributional characteristics of the various
measures. The second step is to determine the relative consistency of reliability of data across
sonographers and readers between reading years (using different offline analysis brochures), and
within the same set of echocardiograms. The third step is to assess validity, or the degree to which
readings by the other readers agree (or depart) from those of the Director of the Echocardiography
Reading Center. (Intra- and Inter-reader variability will also be assessed for the Director and Associate
Director during the pilot study).

The Echocardiography Reading Center personnel will note the general form of the
distributions of the various echocardiographic measures. The presence of data points that, in the
opinion of the Echocardiography Reading Center Director, are felt to be clinically implausible, and any
reader-specific pattern apparent among such outliers, will be noted and feedback will be directed to
the reader or sonographer.

Important sources of reliability to be assessed during the pilot study and the Year 10
echocardiography examination include:

. Agreement in interpretation of an echocardiogram by different readers at the same
time (inter-reader variability)

. Agreement in interpretation of an echocardiogram by the same reader at different
times during the second echocardiography examination (intra-reader variability)

- Agreement between studies performed by two sonographers at the same time
{inter-sonographer performance variability)

- Agreement between studies performed by the same sonographer at different times
(intra-sonographer performance variability)

An assessment of sonographer- and reader-specific differences in echocardiographic
parameter distribution will be included in quarterly Quality Control Reports.

Because a different set of echocardiograms is performed at each center, inter-center
reliability is best assessed by comparing the distributions of echocardiographic parameter across Field
Centers in large samples. Nevertheless, because of different study population characteristics that
maybe inherent in each Field Center, analysis of covariance design adjusting for these characteristics
(age and sex} may need to be employed.

Validity for echocardiography readers is defined as agreement by other readers with
measurements made by the Director of the Echocardiography Reading Center (inter-reader variability
with the Director as one reader). The Director's interpretations will serve as a standard against which
to evaluate other interpretations of echocardiograms. Overall, validity cannot be high without high

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

reliability. However, some readers may exhibit more agreement with the Director than others, and so
validity scores will be determined for each reader separately.

6.14 Data Quality Score

A scoring system will be used by the Echocardiography Reading Center to describe the
quality of the echocardiographic data received (Appendix H). Specifically, each echocardiogram
projection or view read in M-mode, Doppler, or 2D will be coded with respect to the clarity of the
various interfaces (e.g., the endocardial LV cavity interface, and. the LV epicardial-pericardial interface)
integral to making M-mode, Doppler, and two-dimensional echocardiographic measurements related to
the left ventricle. The system will consist of codes ranging from 1 to 4, based on whether a view was
poor to excellent and not measured and the quality of image definition of the various structures in each
study. This coding system will allow us to monitor on-line the quality of studies obtained from each
Field Center. Specific views currently stored based on the current release (7 views) of Tomtec-Freeland
software include,..M-mode LA, M-mode LV, 2D parasternal, 2D apical, and Doppler apical. Specifically
the following scoring system will be used for M-mode, 2-Dimensional and Doppler, and color Doppler.

Grade 0 = View not attempted

Grade | = Unsatisfactory/Uninterpretable: either because a) interfaces are not recorded
sufficiently weil to make LV measurements, or b) the M-mode cursor was positioned at greater than a
20° angle to the meridian through the left ventricle in either the parasternal long axis or short axis
views. The latter situation would result in M-mode dimensions and wall thickness measurements which
are unreliable due to the oblique angle of the ultrasound beam to the left ventricular structures.

Grade 2 = Fair/Satisfactory: measurements can be made with reasonable certainty;
demonstration of interfaces of at least 5 mm in length representing endocardium and epicardium.
These criteria may be fulfilled if interfaces of 5 mm in length for endocardium of the right and left side
of the septum and left ventricular posterior wall, and for epicardium of the LV posterior wall, are
present during any portion of three contiguous beats.

Grade 3 = Good: measurements are relatively easy to perform; fulfillment of the Schieken
criteria (20) on at least one beat -including imaging 5 mm of continuous interface for all of the above
left ventricular structures on the same beat.

Grade 4 = Excellent: publishable quality images; fulfillment of the Schieken criteria (10) on

7. Quality Control Procedures

Detailed documentation of quality control is particularly important. Relatively little experience exists
with the use of echocardiography in multicenter studies and it is essential to determine the comparability
of measurements made in different locations and by different sonographers. in addition, it is important
to document comparability of measurements made during Year 10 (or Year 9) using the Tomtec-
Freeland offline analysis system with measurements made on the same studies during Year 5 using the
Dextra offline analysis system. Despite increased experience and improvements in equipment and
technique, questions remain about the utility of the technique in multicenter studies including CARDIA.
Strict quality control procedures for echocardiography performed in CARDIA should provide quantitative
documentation of the reproducibility of procedures and will be of great importance in interpreting data
from the study.

7.1. Comparability Study

July through August 1994, a comparability study was performed involving remeasurement of
CARDIA Year 5 studies. !n Phase | of the comparability study, reader Jim Paynter re-read 50 randomly
selected studies which he had previously read in Year 5 to assess the difference between the Dextra and
Tomtec-Freeland difference analysis systems. The first 25 readings were measured, first using the
Dextra software, and then repeated on the Tomtec-Freeland software to be used in Year 10; the second
25 echoes were read first on the Tomtec-Freeland and then the Dextra system. In Phase ll, readers
Peggy Knoll and Beverly Jamison read 50 studies from Year 5 on the Tomtec-Freeland system only.
Twenty-five of these studies had previously been read in Year 5 and Phase | by Jim Paynter; the
remainder were selected from the range of readers in Year 5 with a large proportion of measurements
from the upper end of the distribution for LV mass. In addition, Dr. Julius Gardin read the same 25
studies common to all three readers.

This design allowed comparisons in Phase | to be made on 50 studies from the same
reader for measurements made in Year 5 CARDIA studies using Dextra software versus Year 9 Dextra
software and the new Tomtec-Freeland software systems. In Phase Il, comparisons were made between
inter-reader variabllity from Year 5 Dextra software and Year 9 Tomtec-Freeland software readings.

Finally, each of the three readers were compared to readings performed by Dr. Gardin as the "gold
standard."

Analysis and Recommendations from Comparability Study. The data from the comparability
study was analyzed at the Echocardiography Reading Center by Dr. Hoda Anton-Culver and Dr, Tom
Kurosaki, with input solicited from the Coordinating Center. Phase | results summarized in Table 1
were evaluated by the mean per cent differences by the same reader on the Dextra and Tomtec-
Freeland systems. The comparability of measurements made by readers during Year 5 was assessed by
calculating “technical error” (the standardized measurement difference) for continuous variables, such as
LV mass.

Based on the results of the comparability study, it was decided by the Steering Committee
to retrieve Year 5 echocardiogram videotapes for each participant on whom a study is performed during
Year 10 examination. The same reader will perform the measurements on both Year 5 and Year 10

7.2 Assessment of Inter- and Intra- Field Center Sonographer Variability During the Pilot
Period

Measurement variability between studies on the same patient performed by different Field
Center sonographers (inter-sonographer) and within the same sonographer (intra-sonographer) will be
assessed during the pilot study. After completion of the training program at the Echocardiography
Reading Center, sonographers will return to the Field Centers where each will perform echocardiograms
on 20 volunteer participants who are not enrolled in CARDIA (see Appendix M).
Each sonographer will also perform repeat studies, during a different clinic visit within one week if
possible, on these 20 participants. Assuming there are two sonographers at a Field Center, there will be
60 studies from each Center or a total of 120 studies to be read at the Echocardiography Reading
Center. Videotapes will be sent to the Echocardiography Reading Center, coded with arbitrary ID
numbers, and measurements will be performed. Estimates will be made of inter- and intra- sonographer
measurement variability among key echocardiographic variables. Each reader will read initial and repeat
studies performed by Field Center sonographers on selected volunteers, with the combined data from all
readers used to assess inter- and intra-sonographer variability. An outline of this scheme appears in
Appendix M. Additional repeat echocardiogram will be scheduled during the examination period to
further monitor inter- and intra-sonographer performance variability.

7.3 Assessment of Inter- and Intra-Reader Variability During the Pilot Study

Reader variability will also be assessed during the pilot study. Each Echocardiography
Reading Center reader will read the same sample of 40 echocardiograms performed by the first Field
Center sonographer, and 20 echocardiograms performed by the second sonographer at each Field
Center. Each reader will then re-read 20 echocardiograms for determination of intra-reader variability.
The Echocardiography Reading Center Director will also read 40 echocardiograms and re-read a sample
of 20. These readings will become the "gold standard" for interpretation. An outline of this scheme
appears in Appendix M.

7.4 Pilot Study Analysis and Follow-Up

A similar strategy will be used as during the previous CARDIA echo examination to partition
the various components of variability into inter-sonographer, intra-sonographer, inter-reader, and intra-
reader variability (see Appendix M). It is anticipated that these analyses will be performed by Dr. Anton-
Culver and associates at the Echocardiography Reading Center with appropriate input from the
Coordinating Center. If inter- or intra-sonographer, or inter- or intra-reader measurement variability,
calculated as the technical error for continuous measurements, is found to be greater than 15% (or if the
Kappa statistic falls into the "disagreement" range for qualitative measurements), this will trigger
additional re-training of the appropriate personnel with regard to making or reading the specified
measurement(s). It is anticipated that for many continuous echo variables, the individual technical errors
will be in the range of 10%, or less.

Echocardiography Reading Center principal investigators and readers will review the pilot
studies very closely to determine whether there are any protocol deviations committed by Field Center
sonographers. In the event of a protocol! deviation, Field Center sonographers will be phoned directly to
advise them of the problem. A log will be kept of these phone calls and of the problem(s). If the
problem cannot be corrected within one week, a written notice describing the problem will be sent to the
Field Center sonographer, clinic supervisor, and Jocal echo Physician Supervisor. If the echo reader
feels that the problem is unsolved over a two-week period, it will be reviewed with the Echocardiography
Reading Center Principal Investigator, and additional measures taken. These measures might include
additional work locally by the Field Center sonographer with the local echo

7.5 Echocardiography Reading Center Staff Visits to Field Centers

Echocardiography Reading Center sonographers will visit Field Centers at least twice during
the examination year to insure that Field Center sonographers are performing examinations in
compliance with the protocol and to attempt to correct any problems that may be associated with
performance of poor quality studies. The sonographer-trainer will supervise the performance of
echocardiograms by each Field Center sonographer and make any necessary instructional comments,
using a supervisory protocol similar to that used during the initial training period in Phase |. Finally, on
the last day of the visit, a formal test will be performed in which the sonographer-trainer supervises the
performance of at least four echocardiograms by the Field Center sonographer and scores them
according to the Phase | protocol. These reports will be sent to the Field Center Clinic Supervisor,
Principal Investigator, local Physician-Echocardiographer, and to the Project Office or the Quality Control
Committee as directed. If problems with sonographer variability are identified during the pilot study, an
Echocardiography Reading Center sonographer will visit the Field Center in an attempt to upgrade skills
of the Center's sonographer. The echocardiography equipment will be calibrated at the time of these
visits using the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine 100 mm test object, or an equivalent
phantom.

7.6 Overview of Clinical Year Tasks

The Echocardiography Reading Center will process approximately 42 studies per week, with
two readers making measurements on one Freeland offline analysis system. The total number of studies
to be read is comprised of approximately: 1) 2,000 initial studies; 2) 200 blind duplicate readings; and 3)
120 sonographer performance quality control studies. The blind duplicate and quality control studies will
be selected on an ongoing temporal basis, at random, by the Coordinating Center. We propose dividing
the 10% blind duplicate sample into a 7% sample for inter-reader measurement variability and a 3%
sample for intra-reader measurement variability.

7.7. Assessment of Inter- and Intra-Field Center Sonographer Variability During the Examination
Period (Quality Control Studies}

Inter- and intra-sonographer variability will be assessed during the examination period by
performing a series of quality control echocardiograms in three volunteers per month during months 1,
2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 10. These participants can be obtained from one of three different sources: 1) CARDIA
participants; 2) pilot study participants; and 3) volunteers. CARDIA participants will use their existing
CARDIA 1D number. The pilot participants and the volunteers will use a QC number assigned to their
Field Center by the Coordinating Center. The volunteers used for these studies will be between 20 and
45 years of age. Each volunteer will undergo a total of three echocardiograms, the initial study and two
repeat studies, [It is expected that 10 of the initial 20 echocardiograms performed at each Field Center
will be done by each Field Center sonographer. In case there is only one Field Center
echocardiography sonographer, no inter-sonographer assessment studies will be performed. At the
Echocardiography Reading Center, the same reader who reads the initial echocardiogram will read each
of the repeated echocardiograms. Field Center sonographers will fil! out a Echocardiographic
Sonographer Worksheet for Quality Control studies, noting their sonographer ID #, as well as whether it
is their initial or second study (Appendix C). Of the two repeat studies, the second echocardiogram will
be performed by the same sonographer who did the initial study to assess intra-sonographer variability,
and the third echocardiogram will be done by the other sonographer to assess inter-sonographer
variability. The repeat studies will be performed within two weeks following the initial

7.9 Maintenance or Certification by Field Center Sonographers

To maintain certification, a Field Center sonographer must consistently:

- Use proper imaging view to record images

- Maintain the quality of echocardiographic recording (e.g., left ventricular endocardial
or epicardial interfaces)

- Follow imaging protocol

- Perform at least five studies every two weeks

- Maintain acceptable levels of intra- and inter-sonographer measurement variability

7.10 Supervision of Field Center Sonographers by Echo Supervisor

A physician-echocardiographer has been identified at each Field Center. This physician
will oversee the performance of the Field Center sonographers to see that they perform examinations
according to the protocol, providing assistance and additional training when necessary, and
collaborating with the Echocardiography Reading Center in correction of any problems which develop.

The physician-echocardiographer are responsible for meeting weekly for the first three
months, and biweekly thereafter with the sonographers at their Field Center. The purpose of these
meetings is to identify deficiencies--such as using improper imaging views, or poor quality recordings,
and/or failure to follow the imaging protocol (e.g., omission or improper sequence of views, etc.). In
these sessions. the physician should review a minimum of three echoes with the sonographer. At that
time, a Quality Control Supervisor Checklist (Appendix M) should be filled out and returned to the
Echocardiography Reading Center. These sessions are designed to provide the sonographer with
feedback on how they are doing and how they can improve in any deficient areas.

As each video tape is reviewed at the Echocardiography Reading Center, the reader will
fill out a tape evaluation form identifying any areas that need improvement. At the end of each month
{every two weeks in months 1 and 2), the Echocardiography Reading Center Supervisor will send out a
summary to the Field Center physician supervisor identifying a plan of action to correct the problems
noted on the tape evaluations. The Field Center physician will monitor the sonographers’ work for
progress in the areas identified. This should be recorded on the Supervisor Checklist. The following
protocol will be utilized as a guide for immediate corrective action:

Immediate Action: The Echocardiography Reading Center Supervisor will:
Phone and/or fax the Field Center sonographer, describe the problem and suggest a

course of corrective action. Documentation of this conversation will be maintained in the
Echocardiography Reading Center logbook.

7.11 Analysis of Data Quality

Three major steps be undertaken to evaluate the quality of data from readings of
echocardiograms in this study. The first step is to evaluate distributional characteristics of the various
measures. The second step is to determine the relative consistency of reliability of data across
sonographers and readers between reading years (using different offline analysis brochures), and
within the same set of echocardiograms. The third step is to assess validity, or the degree to which
readings by the other readers agree (or depart) from those of the Director of the Echocardiography
Reading Center. (Intra- and Inter-reader variability will also be assessed for the Director and Associate
Director during the pilot study).

The Echocardiography Reading Center personnel will note the general form of the
distributions of the various echocardiographic measures. The presence of data points that, in the
opinion of the Echocardiography Reading Center Director, are felt to be clinically implausible, and any
reader-specific pattern apparent among such outliers, will be noted and feedback will be directed to
the reader or sonographer.

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

important sources of reliability to be assessed during the pilot study and the Year 10
echocardiography examination include:

- Agreement in interpretation of an echocardiogram by different readers at the same
time (inter-reader variability)

- Agreement in interpretation of an echocardiogram by the same reader at different
times during the second echocardiography examination (intra-reader variability)

- Agreement in interpretation of an echocardiogram between readers and the
Echocardiography Reading Center Director

. Agreement between studies performed by two sonographers at the same time
(inter-sonographer performance variability)

- Agreement between studies performed by the same sonographer at different times
(intra-sonographer performance variability)

An assessment of sonographer- and reader-specific differences in echocardiographic
parameter distribution will be included in quarterly Quality Control Reports.

Because a different set of echocardiograms is performed at each center, inter-center
reliability is best assessed by comparing the distributions of echocardiographic parameter across Field
Centers in large samples. Nevertheless, because of different study population characteristics that may
be inherent in each Field Center, analysis of covariance design adjusting for these characteristics (age,
sex, height and/or weight) may need to be employed.

Validity tor echocardiography readers is defined as agreement by other readers with
measurements made by the Director of the Echocardiography Reading Center (inter-reader variability
with the Director as one reader). The Director's interpretations will serve as a standard against which
to evaluate other interpretations of echocardiograms. Overall, validity cannot be high without high
reliability. However, some readers may exhibit more agreement with the Director than others, and so
validity scores will be determined for each reader separately.

7.12 Routine Quality Control Reporting to the Field Centers

When transmitting echocardiographic data from studies read during the previous week to
the Coordinating Center, the Echocardiography Reading Center will also E-mail or fax a note to the
Quality Control Supervisors at the Field Centers to let them know of problems encountered during that
period. A system will be established at the Echocardiography Reading Center so that readers are
consistently reading a sample of studies received from each Field Center during the previous week. If
a problem arises, the Echocardiography Reading Center will first call the clinic to provide immediate
feedback. in their report, the Echocardiography Reading Center will then list problems encountered,
sonographers that dealt with the problems, and what was done to solve the problems. A copy of the
telephone log may be included with this report, or it may be summarized in the report. If the
Echocardiography Reading Center encountered no problems, they will still send a note to the Field
Centers to inform them. Detailed Quality Control Reports will also communicate this information,
including suggestions for sonographer improvement in performing specific echocardiographic views
which were identified to be a problem.

APPENDIX D

CARDIA YEAR 10 ECHO/DOPPLER
SCANNING AND RECORDING SEQUENCE

Parasternal Long-Axis View

a.

b.

Two-dimensional echocardiography during quiet respiration: Record 10 beats on tape.

M-Mode cursor perpendicular through aorta and left atrium: Record 10 beats of 2-D
update image side-by-side with M-mode recording during quiet respiration, then record 10
beats of full-screen M-mode during held-expiration; finally, record a full-screen freeze-
frame M-mode image for 5 seconds at held-expiration.

M-mode cursor perpendicular through the mitral valve at the level of the leaflet tips:
Record two-dimensional update image on the screen next to the M-mode images of the
mitral valve (five beats recorded at a sweep speed of 50 mm per second during quiet
respiration). Subsequently, record a full-screen, freeze-frame M-mode image of the mitral
valve for 5 seconds at held-expiration.

M-mode cursor perpendicular through left ventricle just below the level of the mitral leaflet
tips. Record: 10 beats of 2-D update image side-by-side with M-mode recording during
respiration, and another 10 beats at held-expiration; finally record a full-screen, freeze-
frame (3 beats) M-mode image for 5 seconds at held-expiration onto tape.

Turn 90° into parasternal short-axis view.

Parasternal Short-Axis View

a.

Two-dimensional echocardiography during quiet respiration at level of aorta and left
atrium: 10 beats.

M-mode cursor perpendicular through aorta and left atrium: Record 10 beats of 2-D
update image side-by-side with M-mode recording during quiet respiration, then record 10
beats of full-screen M-mode during held-expiration; finally, record a full-screen freeze-
frame (3 beats) M-mode image for 5 seconds at held-expiration on tape.

Two-dimensional echocardiography at level of papillary muscles at quiet respiration:
Record 10 beats on tape.

M-mode cursor through the meridian of the left ventricle at level of papillary muscles:
Record 10 beats of 2-D update image side-by-side with M-mode recording of left ventricle
during quiet respiration; then record 10 beats of full-screen M-mode during held-
expiration; finally, record a full-screen freeze-frame (3 beats) M-mode image for 5 seconds
at held expiration on tape.

- §8 -

CARDIA ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY READING CENTER MANUAL - FEBRUARY 27, 1995

I. Apical Four-Chamber View

a.

Two-dimensional echocardiography at quiet respiration: Record 10 beats with maximum
chamber dimensions and good LV endocardial definition on tape.

Pulsed Doppler transmitral flow recording with sample volume at leaflet tips during
diastole: Using a 2.5 MHz transducer, record 10 beats of 2-D update image side-by-side
with Doppler recording during quiet respiration and another 10 beats full-screen Doppler
at held-expiration; finally, record a full-screen freeze-frame Doppler image for 5 seconds
at held-expiration on tape. If the heartrate is less than 60 beats per minute, change the

sweep speed from 100 mm/sec to 50 mm/sec in order to obtain two full beats on the
freeze frame.

Color flow Doppler recording for absence or presence and severity of mitral regurgitation
in the apical four chamber view.

Turn approximately 90° into apical two-chamber view.

IV. Apical Two-Chamber and Apical Long-Axis Views

a.

Two-dimensional echocardiography in the true apical two-chamber view during quiet
respiration: Record 10 beats with maximum LV chamber dimensions and good LV
endocardial definition on tape.

Two-dimensional echocardiography in the apical long-axis view during quiet respiration:
Record 10 beats taking care to include the left ventricle, left atrium, aorta and right
ventricle in the image.

Pulsed Doppler recording in the apical long-axis view: Record 10 beats of 2-D update
image side-by-side with pulsed Doppler recording in the left ventricular outflow tract 0.5-
1.0 cm below aortic valve annulus at quiet respiration, then record 10 beats of full-screen
Doppler during held-expiration on tape; finally, record a full-screen, freeze-frame Doppler
image for 5 seconds at held-expiration on tape.

Color flow Doppler recording for absence or presence and severity of aortic regurgitation
in the apical long axis view.

V. Subcostal Four-Chamber View

Two-dimensional echocardiography during quiet respiration: Record 10 beats with maximum
chamber dimensions and good LV endocardial definition. This view will only be obtained in cases
in which other 2-D imaging views are suboptimal. (For use only in participants in whom
unmeasurable images of the left ventricle are obtained from the parasternal views).

CODE DESCRIPTION

Aortic Dissection - is characterized by dilatation of the aortic root; and by a separation of the normal

single dominant echo from the aortic wall into two discrete echos that move in unison with one
another.

Flail leaflet - is characterized by a whipping motion of the tip of the affected leaflet through a 180-
degree or greater arc about its point of attachment. This pattern is in contrast to the prolapsing leaflet
in which the leaflet body always remains concave toward the left ventricle.

Significant Arrhvthmia - Ventricular ectopic beats that occur in groups of 3 or more, and/or ventricular
ectopic beats that occur at a rate of 6 beats per minute, and/or episodes of complete heart block.

Vegetation - an irregular mass of echos that is usually attached to the valve leaflet and moves with the
valve. The vegetation will vary in size and shape and may have a "shaggy" appearance. Regurgitation
is often associated with this lesion.

Thrombus - appears as a echo-producing mass superimposed on and interrupting the
normal endocardial contour of the ventricle in regions of akinesis or dyskinesis. When thrombus is
suspected, confirmation usually requires its visualization in at least one other projection.

Tumor (intracardiac mass) - Usually a myxoma may be intracavitary, intramural, or extramural. Most
tumors that involve the left ventricle are extramural, arising within the posterior mediastinum and
deforming the left ventricular chamber by external compression.

Pericardial Tamponade - a large pericardial effusion that restricts proper filling of the heart. Suspected
pericardial tamponade will be defined echocardiographically as the presence of a pericardial effusion
with right atrial and right ventricular chamber collapse and respiratory variations exceeding 40% in
Doppler peak velocities recorded at any cardiac valve site.

Other - findings that do not fit into a specific category.

APPENDIX N
QUALITY ASSURANCE IMAGING PHANTOM PROCEDURE
ACUSON 128
Introduction
Acuson will provide complete system operational verification and preventive maintenance as outlined in
Sections 6 and 7 of the ACUSON 128 Service Manual. These procedures, listed below, will be
performed two times per year.
Transducers
Each transducer will be verified using the procedure outlined in Section 7 of the Acuson 128 Service
Manual using an RMI Model 400F tissue mimicking phantom, supplied by ACUSON. Photographs will
be taken at each preventive maintenance call and sent to the Echocardiography Reading Center to
demonstrate consistent image quality. It is important that the photos be taken of the same phantom
views with the same setup each time to properly determine total system performance.
Diagnostics and Performance Checks
These steps are performed to verify the integrity of the actual electronics involved in forming the
ultrasound image and displaying it on a monitor. Proprietary diagnostic test equipment known as the
Flow Test Board and PROM Board are used interactively with onboard diagnostics to determine
operational status. The tests are extensive and allow each subassembly to be individually tested and
interrogated for outright failures as well as subtly degraded performance which may or may not be
visible in an ultrasound image. All modes of operation are tested (two-dimensional, Doppler, color).
The Doppler verification tests consist of individual linear and sector test suites using the Flow Test
Board, as this provides more accurate operational verification than a Doppler flow phantom.
Mechanical/Visual Inspection
These steps assure that system controls and mechanical hardware are operating correctly in good
repair. Operational tests will be performed as outlined in Section 7 of the ACUSON 128 Service
Manual. Filters are inspected and cleaned to ensure cooling air circulates unimpeded. This is
necessary for stable operation and long component life.
Electrical
These steps verify that any peripherals connected to the ACUSON 128 are operating correctly, that the
environment in which the unit is operating meets minimum specifications, that the power supplies are
operating within specifications and that any mandatory field upgrades or enhancements have been
installed.
Peripheral Equipment Service
These steps involve testing and performing preventive maintenance on all peripherals attached to the
ACUSON 128. As delivered, these peripherals are: Panasonic S-VHS VCR and Honeywell strip chart
recorder.

D1F07 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Alcohol Use Questionnaire)

Extreme Values

For all the alcohol consumption variables (Questions 2-6), the
data entry system will only accept values less than 100. Thus,
there may be some underreporting of alcohol consumption.

Computed Variables

D07MLALC: total amount of absolute alcohol consumed in milliliters
per day; calculated using the following algorithm:
(D07BEER/7*16.7) + (D07WINE/7*17.02) + (D07LIQR/7*19.09)

IF D07DRINK = 1 THEN D07MLALC = 0;

NOTE: This algorithm is the same that was used in the Version 1.4
and Version 3.1 data tapes. It differs from the algorithm
used in Version 2.2; the Version 2.3 data tape will use the
algorithm shown here. Anyone analyzing alcohol consumption
with Exam 2 data should recalculate B07MLALC using this
algorithm.

D1F06/D1F06V_ - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Nutrient Data - Dietary History)

There are two nutrient datasets: (1) nutrients with the
vitamin supplement data excluded (D1F06, variable prefix: D06);
and (2) nutrients with the vitamin supplement data included
(DIFO6V, variable prefix: DV6). The SAS code and PROC CONTENTS
for these files are located in this section.

General Considerations and Comments

Dietary data were collected using a dietary history method.
Nutrients were calculated with Version 20 of the Food Table from
the Nutrition Coordinating Center at the University of Minnesota.
Appropriate use of these data should consider the following
factors.

1. Absolute mean intakes may be overestimates of actual
intakes obtained as other dietary methods, e.g., 24-hour
recall or food records. This should not interfere with
analyses comparing means for various subgroups within the
CARDIA population. However, mean nutrient intakes of the
CARDIA population may be higher than that of other
populations if methodology other than the history was
used.

2. Nutrient densities (intakes expressed relative to caloric
intake) may be used to adjust for the tendency towards
overestimation of actual intakes in the dietary history
methodology.

3. Although group mean intakes may be overestimated, ranking
of individual intakes should be preserved. This permits
analyses of relationships between nutrient intakes and
other variables for the individuals.

3/94

The dietary history referenced intake for the previous month.
When average daily intake was calculated, it was assumed that one
month had 30.42 days and 4.35 weeks.

General information about the dietary interview, such as
length of interview and nutritionist's rating of the participant's
ability to recall information, as well as data concerning dietary
practices and attitudes, can be found in D1FO6AC.

Comparison with Exam 1 Data

Every effort was made to make the Exam 1 dietary history
comparable with the Exam 4 dietary history. Minor changes were
made to the foods listed on the form for Exam 4 due to changes in
the food supply, but the overall organization of the form was

maintained. The database used to calculate the nutrients is by
necessity different from Exam 1 to reflect changes in the food
supply.

Between Exam 1 and Exam 4, the Nutrition Coordinating Center
modified the formulae for calculating fat added during the
preparation of food. The new formulae are based on laboratory
analyses and, thus, are more accurate. The Coordinating Center has
recalculated the added fat for the Exam 1 data and redistributed
the nutrient data. Please only do longitudinal analyses with the
version of the Exam 1 data created in 1994 (A4FO6A, A4FO6VA).

Qutliers and Missing Values

In accordance with the decisions made by the Nutrition Working
Group during Exam 1, we have made the following decisions regarding
outliers and missing values.

1. Include all out-of-range amounts in the participant

records. These values have been checked for data entry

errors and have been verified.

3/94

Do not exclude any participant from the data set.
Outliers will be handled in the analysis of the data.

Do not impute values for missing serving amount or
frequency data.

Edits of Participant Food Records

Prior to nutrient processing, the participants' food records
were extensively edited. The following describes the edits done

for each of the data fields from the Quantitated Food Frequency
portion of Form 6.

B/94

1.

NCC Code: Check that the code is in the NCC Version 20
database.

Serving Size Amount: Check that the amount is non-
missing and greater than 0.

Serving Size Unit: Check that the unit is valid for the
specific food in the NCC Version 20 database.

Frequency Unit: Check that the unit is D, W, or M.

Prep Code: Check that the code is a valid code (APF,
BDF, BVF, NAP, PAN, SES) and that it is allowable for
that food in the NCC Version 20 database.

Fat Code: Check that the code is a valid code in the Ncc
Version 20 database.

Average Daily Intake (calculated from serving amount and
frequency amount): Check that the average daily intake
is less than or equal to the maximum intake amount
specified in the NCC Version 20 database.

Processing of Food Items with Errors

Included in the data set is information regarding the total
number of food items reported, the number processed with errors,
and the number of food items processed for each specific error
(Dx6ERR1 Dx6ERR16). The following are the error codes used:
1 = Missing/Invalid Food Code
2 = Serving Size missing
3 = Frequency Size missing
4 = Frequency Unit missing
5 = Serving Unit missing; Multiple Serving Units available in
database
6 = Serving Unit missing; only one Serving Unit available in
database
7
=
Amount eaten > maximum allowed in database
8 = Prep Code of BDF for a vegetable
9
= Prep Code reported for food that does not allow added fat
10 = Prep Code missing or invalid
11 = Prep Code present, Fat Code missing
12 = Fat Code invalid
13 = Prep Code is SES or BVF but CP not valid Serving Unit
14 = Prep Code is PAN but OZ not valid Serving Unit
15 = Fat Food Code not found
16 = Fat Food Code does not have needed Serving Unit
Foods with Errors 1-5 are not processed when calculating
nutrients. Foods with Error 6 are processed with the default
Serving Unit. Foods with Error 7 are processed with no changes.
Foods with Errors 9-16 are processed without the added fat.

Computed Variable

D06PRCOR: percent of the total number of food items reported by the
participant that were processed without error(s)

MEDICAL HISTORY FOLLOW-UP FILES - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

The Medical History Follow-Up data can be found in four files.
Only women who completed these forms are included in the files.
Those files and the data contained therein include:
D1F09PER - Menstrual Period
D1F9PRG1
D1F9PRG2 | Pregnancy (see following notes)
D1F9PRG3

Special Notes Regarding Pregnancy Files

In order to ease handling and interpretation, the pregnancy
follow-up variables have been split into three files. These files
are named: D1F9PRG1.SSD, D1F9PRG2.SSD, and D1F9PRG3.SSD. See the
PROC CONTENTS output for detailed lists of variables contained in
these files.

D1F9PRG1.SSD contains one observation for each participant who
completed a Pregnancy Follow-up form (whether or not they answered
'Yes' to Question 38 on Form 8) and the variables from page 1 of
the form; an observation in this file is uniquely identified by the
5-digit CARDIA ID (SAS variable SHORT_ID).

D1F9PRG2.SSD contains one observation for each pregnancy
reported as occurring between Exam 3 and Exam 4, and the variables
from pages 2 and 4 of the form; an observation from this file is
uniquely identified by the combination of SHORT_ID and the
pregnancy number (SAS variable D09PRGNO). Note that pregnancies
contemporaneous with the interview are identified as pregnancy "0"
(zero); other pregnancies should be numbered, beginning with "1"
(one) from earliest to latest.

D1F9PRG3.SSD contains one observation for each infant
resulting from each pregnancy, and the variables from page 3 of the

3/94

form; observations are uniquely identified by the combination of
SHORT_ID, D09PRGNO, and the infant number (SAS variable D09WHICH).

D1FO8A - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Medical History)

New Release of Version 4.1

After D1F08 was distributed in September 1993, it was
discovered that the breastfeeding variables had not been included
in the data set.

Comparability of Variables with Previous Exams

Form 8 was interviewer-administered in both Exam 1 and Exam 2.
The form was revised prior to the third exam to make it self-
administered and it remained so for the fourth exam. Also,
additional medical conditions and some questions regarding weight
and weight history questions were added to the form since Exam 3.
All of the questions that appear both in the Exam 3 and the Exam 4
questionnaires are directly comparable. There are several
questions for which the comparability of the Exam 4 data for Form
8 with that from Exams 1 and 2 is not possible. These cases are
noted below.

The Form 8 variable regarding high blood pressure medication
(DO8BPNOW) refers to current use, not "ever use" as in Exams 1 and
2 (AO8BPMED and BO8BPMED). DO8BPNOW is comparable to the Form 9
medication follow-up variable from Exam 1 (AO9MDNOW) [where
AOOMDTYP = HBP] and Exam 2 (BO9HBNOW).

Likewise, variables regarding birth control use (DO8BCNOW) and
other hormone use (DO8HMNOW) refer to current use, not "ever use"
as in Exam 1 (AO8BRTHC and AO8HORMN). DO8BCNOW is comparable to
the Form 9 medication follow-up variable from Exams 1 and 2
(AO9BCNOW and BO9BCNOW) . DOSHMNOW is comparable to AO9MDNOW
(where AO9MDTYP = HORM) and BO9HMNOW.

For all Form 8 variables regarding the age at diagnosis of a

3/94

specific disease, comparable data (if collected) from Exams 1 and
2 can be found in the Form 9 follow-up data files. For example,
the variable regarding the age at which diagnosis of diabetes
occurred (DO8DIBAG) would be compared with AO9DIBAG and BO9DIBAG.
Any age at diagnosis of disease recorded as 0 was verified; these
values indicate that the participant was born with the condition or
was diagnosed before the first birthday.

Similarly, most of the site-specific disease variables now
appearing on Form 8 can be found in Form 9 medical follow-up data
files from the first two exams. However, the variables for heart
disease and kidney disease may not be comparable between exams due
to reorganization of the form. Please compare the questions for

these diseases carefully before beginning any analysis.

NOTE: One participant (410801625346) recorded her maximum body
weight (DO8MAXWT) as 30 pounds. Since we know this value
is incorrect, we have set the value to missing in the
data set.

D1F10 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Tobacco Questionnaire)

Any value greater than 10 for the variable D10LVHME (the
number of persons that the participant lives with that smoke
cigarettes) was verified by the clinical centers. These three
participants were either in the service or in prison.

For the variable D10EXHME (number of hours of exposure to
smoke at home), the data entry system will only accept values less
than 100. Thus, there may be some underreporting of smoke
exposure.

Computed Variable

D10SMOKE: reported smoking status; calculated using the following
algorithm:

D10SMOKE = .;
IF D10TOBAC=1 THEN D10SMOKE=0;
IF D10TOBAC=2 AND D10CIGS=1 THEN D10SMOKE=0;
IF D10TOBAC=2 AND D10CIGS=2 AND D09SMKNW=1 THEN D10SMOKE=1;
IF D10TOBAC=2 AND D10CIGS=2 AND D09SMKNW=2 THEN D10SMOKE=2;

0 = NON-SMOKERS
1 = EX-SMOKERS
2 = SMOKERS
. = UNABLE TO CODE

MEDICATION FOLLOW-UP - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

The Medication Follow-Up data can be found in six files.
Those files and the data contained therein include:

D1F9MHBA - Antihypertensive medications

D1F9MCHA - Cholesterol lowering medications

D1IF9MASA - Medications for asthma or other breathing
problems

D1F9MOTA - Other prescription medications

D1F9MBCA - Birth control pills

D1F9MHMA - Hormones other than birth control pills

NOTE: Multiple records per participant are allowable for all
medications except birth control pills.

The variable DO9MDQNO indicates which question on Form 8 led
to the completion of that Medication Follow-up form.

Medication codes are derived from the chapter titles of Drug
Evaluations, Annual 1992 prepared by the American Medical

Association. (A copy of the table of contents from this book is

included.) The medication codes for Exam 3 are taken from the 6th
edition Drug Evaluations (1986); the codes used in Exams 1 and 2
are from the 5th edition (1983) of this book. Thus, Exam 4

medication codes are not directly comparable with any of the
previous exams.

New Release of Version 4.1

After data was distributed in September 1993, it was
discovered that medication name was truncated and Interviewer ID
was inadvertently dropped from the data sets. Also, the variable
DO9RESO (reason for taking medication) was not included on
D1FO9MOT. Please note the new names of the data sets.

D1F18 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Physical Activity Questionnaire)

Scoring is accomplished by adding a weighted sum of the number
of months for each activity below and again above the hours per
week cutpoint. Algebraically, m is the number of months below the
cutpoint and n is the number of months above the cutpoint. The
coefficient b is described below. The coefficient ¢ has been
selected to be 3*b for each activity.

Heavy intensity score = 2b, * m, +c, * n,

for activities A-H

Moderate intensity score is similar in form, but summed over
activities I through M, and the total score is the sum of the two

subscores.

The coefficient b is the intensity level assigned to each
activity which is roughly the number of kilocalories thought to be
expended in one minute of activity by a 70 kg man. Intensities
were patterned after those used by Taylor et al and Folsom et al.
Exceptions are bicycling, which was set at an intensity code of 6
to reflect the wording "faster than 10 miles per hour"' and
vigorous work activity (which was not included in Taylor's or
Folsom's work), which was set at an intensity code of 5, somewhat
less than that for weight lifting.

D1F20A - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Anthropometry)

New Release of Version 4.1

The variable D20HTMOD was not included in the original release
of this data set.

Comparability of Variables Across Exams

In Exam 4, two measures were taken for each of the girth
variables (chest girth was not done at Exam 4). The average of the
two measures at each site was used to compute variables for use in
analysis. This was the protocol used in both Exam 1 and Exam 2.
In Exam 3, only one measure of hips (C20HIPS1) and waist (C20WST1)
was made. Thus, the Exam 4 waist and hip computed variables
(D20WST and D20HIP) can be compared directly with those from Exams
1 and 2, but these Exam 4 variables should not be compared with the
Exam 3 girth measurements.

Protocol Modifications

When revising Form 20 for Exam 4, it was decided to indicate
whether the value recorded for a measurement was an estimate due to
inability to measure the participant (i.e., participant was too
heavy for the scale). In order to not offend participants, we
tried to make this indication vague on the form. Thus, Questions
1.b., 2.b., 3.d., 4.c., and 6 were added. The following are the
specific interpretations.

D20HTMOD: Participant is taller than the centimeter ruler;
D20HGT should have a value of 200

D20WTMOD: Participant weighs more than 350 pounds; D20WGT
should have a value of 350

D20SKMOD: Calipers could fit around participant's skinfold;
both trifold (D20TRI1, D20TRI2), subscapular

3/94

(D20SUB1, D20SUB2), and/or suprailiac (D20SUP1,
D20SUP2) measurements should be missing
D20GRMOD: Participant's waist or hip girth was too large to
be measured with one measuring tape; both waist
(D20WST1, D20WST2) and/or hip (D20HIPS1, D20HIPS2)
measurments should be greater than 150
D200TMOD: Some problem other than the above occurred when
taking the participant's measurments

Computed Variables
D20TRICP: mean of two triceps measures
D20SUBSC: mean of two subscapular measures
D20SUPRL: mean of two suprailiac measures
D20WST: mean of two waist measures
D20HIP: mean of two hip measures
D20BMI: body mass index computed as:
[(weight(kg)/2.2)/ (height(cm)/100)²]

******************************************
Questions regarding skin color (reflectance) were added at
Exam 4. Because data collection and analyses regarding skin color
are relatively sparse, we have not attempted to transform the data
in any way. Therefore, no computed variables have been created
with these data.

D1F22 - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(Treadmill Exercise Test)

Excluded Data

During preliminary analyses of the treadmill performance data,
it was discovered that the data from participants examined in
Minneapolis were quite different from those examined at the other
centers. Neither cohort effects nor technician/mechanical effects
could adequately explain the differences. Thus, the Steering
Committee decided to closely monitor analyses of this data. Asa
result, the data from participants examined in Minneapolis are not
included in this data set but are stored at the Coordinating Center
(D1F22M). Use of the Minneapolis data requires prior approval of
the Steering Committee. Similar restrictions apply to D1F21
(Treadmill Exercise Test).

Missing Values

Values of 0O for heart rate (pre-exercise, exercise, or
recovery), SBP, or rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were set to
missing. DBP was set to missing if the DBP was recorded as 0 and
SBP was also recorded as 0 (or missing).

Because BP measures were taken at 1:30 minutes into each
stage, SBP and DBP will be missing for a participant’s last stage
if the participant stopped before 1:30 minutes.

Variable Names

For each stage (#), the variables collected are recorded as
D22_S#. For example, for stage 2, the variables collected are
D22HRS2, D22SBPS2, D22DBPS2, and D22RPES2. These correspond to
heart rate, SBP, DBP, and RPE (a scale from 6-20) for stage 2,
respectively.

Change in ECG Criteria for Stopping Treadmill Test

During Exam 4, it was observed that many more participants
were being stopped during the treadmill test due to ECG criteria
than had been stopped during Exam 1. A panel of physicians
determined that the ECG criteria could be relaxed with no increased
risk to participants.

In order to make the data comparable, the Minnesota ECG Coding
Center reviewed the ECG strips of all participants who had been
stopped due to ECG criteria before the criteria changed (N=40) to
determine which participants would have been allowed to continue
the test with the relaxed criteria. The variable D22CRIT reflects
this review with the following coding.

1 = Would have been stopped with relaxed criteria

2 = Would have been allowed to continue with relaxed criteria
= Was not stopped due to ECG criteria

Computed Variables

D22HRMAX: Maximum heart rate recorded for stage 1 through stage 9
D22HRMAX = MAX (D22HRS1, D22HRS2, ..., D22HRS9)

D22STGFN: Number of stages (2 minute periods) completed
D22STGFN = FLOOR (D22DURTN/60/2)
where D22DURTN = exercise test duration in seconds

D22DATE: Date the treadmill test was administered

Note: The date the treadmill test was administered may be
different from the exam date for some participants.

**In Memorcito: A Journey of Love, Remembrance, and Gratitude**

---

**Overview**: This poignant tale follows the journey of two children as they tenderly recall their departed grandmother (Abuelita), who passed away on May 21, 2018. Through vivid storytelling and heartfelt reflections, the reader is invited to witness how they navigate the grieving process, celebrate their beloved Abuelita's life, and find comfort in the enduring bonds of family and love.

**The Tale:**

*"Abuelita", she said on the 21st of May, 2018, "I love you!"*
*But my mom was very sad and so was I...*

**(Scene: The day Abuelita left)**
*The date of May 21st, 2018 was when Abuelita left.*
*My mom said: "Oh, mom" and so did I.*
*I was so sad because she was gone.*
*My brother was sad and so was my dad.*

**(Scene: A precious memory)**
*I remember when she brought me a little truck.*
*I still play with the truck, it has no wheels now...*
*I had it since I was 3, but it broke when I was 5.*
*But I still remember Abuelita!*

**(Scene: Memories in the garden)**
*I remember when she made the garden with the flowers.*
*I watered them and she sat down with me.*
*We had lots of fun with the flowers.*
*The flowers are still growing, but she is gone.*

**(Scene: The beautiful dress)**
*I remember when she made me the dress that was so pretty.*
*I wore it to school, but it doesn't fit me now.*
*I think it was when I was 4.*
*But I still remember her.*

**(Scene: A place in our hearts)**
*She is still in my heart.*
*She is still in my soul.*
*She is still in my dreams.*
*She is still in my every thought.*

**(Scene: A message of love)**
*I love you, Abuelita!*
*I miss you, Abuelita!*
*Thank you, Abuelita!*
*We will never forget you!*

**(The End)**

For Exam 4, a coding system (included with this documentation)
was developed to identify reason(s) for hospitalization(s). This
system allows for coding of specific problems, medical procedures,
and body parts. There is no comparability with previous exams
other than to determine whether a hospitalization was the result of
a pregnancy, an illness or an injury.

For each hospitalization (#), the date of event (D31EVDT#) and
the date of care (D31CADT#) are SAS date variables, which require
a month, day, and year. However, because participants often cannot
remember exact dates, variables have been included on the data set
for month, day, and year that correspond to each of the date

variables (D31EVMO#, D31EVDY#, D31EVYR#, D31CAMO#, D31CADY#,
D31CAYR#) .

D1F46_- NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(Weight Change Questionnaire)

Only participants who attended both Exams 3 and 4 completed this

questionnaire. D46X3WGT and D46X4WGT are the respective weights the

participant; all other participants have missing values. D46WDIFF, the

difference in the exam weights, is calculated by the data entry system.

The three levels of D46WCODE indicate whether the participant’s weight

increased, decreased, or remained stable between exams:

A: > 3 or more pound increase
B: > 3 or more pound decrease

C: change of < 3 pounds, increase or decrease.

D46WINT indicates if this change was intentional or not.

is possible that the weights recorded on Form 46 are a result
of self-report. Until they can be verified, all of the
variables for these participants have been set to missing in

Longitudinal Analyses

LINCO Research was the sub-contractor for insulin analyses
during Exam 4. This is not the same laboratory that performed the
analyses during Exam 1. To avoid problems of laboratory
comparability, stored samples from Exam 1 for which there were also
Exam 4 samples were analyzed at LINCO Research in the same assay as
the Exam 4 samples. Thus, when performing longitudinal analyses,
use the variable D1L7INSO for baseline values, not the values in
the A4INS data set.

Missing Values

For some people, the insulin values were too low to measure.
These people have a value of 'L' in the data set. All other
missing values denote people who did not have a sample available
for analysis.

D1HCY - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(Homocysteine)

This file contains the homocysteine measurement made from
frozen Year 7 samples of 805 CARDIA participants. To be included
in the sample, an individual must have been examined and had
dietary history data at both the baseline examination (Year 0)
and the third exam (Year 7). Participants with self-reported
renal disease were excluded prior to the sample selection. From
the eligible participants, approximately 200 individuals were

randomly selected from each race-gender group.

Samples were analyzed by the Nutrition Research Support
Laboratory. The assay used was a high performance liquid
chromatograpic method as published by Cornwell et al. This isa
nonstandard assay for homocysteine. If two readings were done of
the same sample, the value included in this file is the average
of those readings. For further details on the assay, please

contact the CARDIA Coordinating Center.

DILEPTIN - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES

(Leptin)

This file contains leptin measurements from a pilot study of
400 CARDIA participants. The residual frozen serum samples from
a previous pilot study of proinsulin (performed in 1995 on these
same participants) were analyzed for leptin as a courtesy by Dr.
Ron Gingerich at Linco Research, Inc. in 1997. These
measurements were obtained to determine whether leptin could
effectively replace BMI as a covariate in multiple regression
models of the relationship between proinsulin and CVD risk
factors. Missing values were included in this data set to

indicate that a measurement was attempted.

There are a few important notes regarding these data as
received from Linco Research. The data contained the value
“<1.0" for seven participants (10836, 20327, 20782, 30001, 30151,
30583, 30985). Each value was changed to 1.0 in this data set
per discussion with Dr. Gingerich. Similarly, there were values
of “<2.5" for two participants (10312, 30564). Each value was
changed to 2.5 in this data set. Also, Dr. Gingerich has
indicated that analyses of leptin should be stratified by gender,
because values in women are higher than values in men by a factor

of 2 to 3.

DIDEXA - NOTES AND COMPUTED VARIABLES
(DEXA/Bone Mass)

Ancillary Study Design and Exclusion Criteria

During Exam 4, participants from the Oakland clinic were
recruited to participate in the DEXA study, provided that they
met specific study criteria. Data collected for the ancillary
bone mass study were (1) DEXA bone and body composition data, (2)
laboratory blood and urine chemistry data, (3) muscle strength
data, and (4) data from data collection forms specific to the
bone mass study. Because of financial constraints, blood and
urine chemistry studies were planned for a core group of
approximately 100 in each sex-race subject group who satisfied
stringent criteria established for the study. Muscle strength
testing and limited DEXA testing were also offered to
participants who did not satisfy the stringent criteria, as
clinic scheduling and staff availability permitted.

While bone mass data were collected for 799 participants,
only the data for the core group with blood and urine chemistry
data are included in this dataset. All participants had to be
less than 37 years old at the time of the exam. Additional
critera for female participants were (1) not currently pregnant,
(2) no birth delivery within 335 days prior to the exam, (3) > 10
menstrual periods in the year prior to the exam, (4) blood
specimen obtained between day 3 and day 11 of menstrual cycle,
and (5) not currently breast-feeding. For the core group whose
data are included here, female participants also had to be not
currently using birth control pills. The core group had at least
one non-missing value of total BMD for the whole body, spine, or
hip; blood and urine chemistry data; and muscle strength data.
Subjects in the full cohort also had at least one non-missing
value of total BMD for the whole body, spine, or hip and some,
but not all, had muscle strength data.
