Data Processing and Compilation

Bone densitometry data were collected on a dedicated PC with
software provided by HOLOGIC. An extract ASCII file was created
and used as input to a SAS program, also provided by HOLOGIC, to
create HOLOGIC source SAS data sets of the data collected (6 data
sets). Processing of the source data sets identified CARDIA
participants and identified data by exam. Subsequent processing
merged variables from the different source data sets to create a
merged data set with 1 rec/ID.

The variable BENTKNEE, which is =1 for ID with knees bent,
was added to the data set BMWB created for the cc. The mass
values in the data set remain unchanged from those in the
extract. A calibration phantom, a spine shaped material embedded
in a plexiglass cube, was used as a standard for quality control
to detect change in the sensitivity of the instrument. During the
period 02/25/93 -03/06/93, PA spine phantoms decreased and
lateral spine phantoms increased. Scans done at that time were
corrected by the following factors(per Dr. Ettinger):

-For hip, total body, and PA spine:

(BMD) density value x 1.0475/1.0368
-For lateral spine:
(BMD) density value x 1.0657/1.0710
The product of the two correction factors were used for the whole
vertebrae and sub region volume variables. “FIX” variables

indicate if the correction was applied (see below).

CONSENT FORM

You are invited to participate in the fourth examination of a research study of the
health status of young adults, for which you were selected randomly. The purpose
of the study is to learn how the beginning stages of heart disease develop in healthy
young adults. The clinic examination will last about three hours.

Blood Drawing. This examination will include having a 4 tablespoon sample of
blood drawn to measure blood cholesterol and other blood substances. Slight
bruising or fainting may occur in some people when blood is drawn. These are
usually minor and have no lasting effects. We will make every effort to prevent
these from happening.

Exercise Treadmill. In addition, an exercise test will be done to evaluate your heart's
response to a standardized amount of stress. This test is performed by having you
walk or jog on a treadmill and is designed to gradually increase the heart’s
workload. Before the test, you will be interviewed to determine if you should not
take the test. Should symptoms such as chest discomfort, unusual shortness of
breath or fatigue develop during the test, the staff will stop the test. Also, if at any
time during the test you feel you would like to stop, you can stop.

Certain changes in body function normally take place when any person exercises.
Occasionally, abnormal changes may occur in blood pressure or heart rate. Very rare
instances of heart attack have occurred, as in any other moderately strenuous
exercise activity. Every effort will be made to minimize possible problems by the ,
preliminary examination and constant supervision during testing.

Seismocardiogram. A seismocardiogram will be performed to measure the
mechanical function of your heart. This test records heart vibrations, uses no x-rays,
and is entirely safe.

Other Procedures. There will also be a measurement of your blood pressure, skin
folds, and some questions concerning your health, diet, and the stresses of everyday
life. You will also be asked about medical care and accidents or injuries you may
have had since your last CARDIA examination. There are no known significant
complications from these procedures.

In the event that this research activity results in physical injury, medical treatment
will be available, including first aid, emergency treatment, and follow-up care as
needed. Payment for follow-up care must be provided by you or your third party
payor (such as health insurance, Medicare).

OVERVIEW

While increases in coronary heart disease risk factors occur
in young adulthood in conjunction with significant changes in
physiological measures and in lifestyle, the interrelationships
among these risk factors and changes have not been rigorously
investigated. Both epidemiologic and clinical research in coronary
heart disease have increased our awareness that some risk factors
for disease such as obesity, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia
may be partially determined by genetic factors or behaviors which
are formed in infancy, childhood, and adolescence. Studies to date
also suggest that some of the coronary heart disease risk factors
do not change dramatically before the late teenage years and that
differences in characteristics by sex or race emerge and are most
pronounced after this time. However, relatively little work has
been done to identify the characteristics of young adult life which
may be precursors to, or coincident with, the increase in risk
factors prior to middle age.

Cross-sectional data, for example, suggest that weight gain is
pronounced during the late teens through age 30, particularly in
males, and that positive relationships exist between weight and
lipoprotein fractions during these ages. The reasons for, and
consequences of, this increase in adiposity need further
investigation. The interaction of life events, behavior, changes
in physical activity, and dietary intake that may influence weight
gain and lipoprotein levels should be assessed as well as the
relative importance of weight gain in relationship to risk factor
changes during this age span.

Investigators have examined the consistency of blood pressure
levels in children to determine whether "tracking" occurs into the
teenage years. The results of these studies have raised other
interesting and important questions. Is there evidence for
"tracking" of other coronary risk factors? Does "tracking" persist

lifestyle are often taking place? Are the changes a function of

An important component of this study is the study of young
blacks. Since the Black Health Task Force on High Blood Pressure
Control pointed out the lack of knowledge about coronary heart
disease in blacks as applied to this country, a greater focus on
the nature of disease in blacks has been a topic of increasing
consideration.

"Coronary Artery Risk Factor Development in Young Adults"
(CARDIA) is the study of the evolution of coronary heart disease
risk in a cohort of black and white men and women initially 18-30
years old. Such studies will not only contribute to our
understanding of the development of atherosclerotic disease, but
more importantly, help to suggest strategies for prevention before
individual lifestyle patterns become well established.

The original specific hypotheses set forth by each clinical

site may be found in the protocol documents from the first and
second CARDIA examinations.

OBJECTIVES

The overall goals of this study are:

1.

To document at baseline and after one or more biennial
intervals, risk factors and changes for coronary heart disease
(CHD) in young (black and white) adults, 18-30 years old.

To identify lifestyles during this age span, which influence
these changes in risk factors. The interrelationships among
risk factors and lifestyles, and changes in these
characteristics will be considered.

The secondary objectives of this study are:

1.

To observe age-related trends in risk factors during young
adulthood and to compare cross-sectional with longitudinal
findings.

To perform sub-population analyses on, sex, race, or
sociodemographic groupings, and to compare trends and
processes involved in risk factor development between these
subgroups.

To develop and apply effective methods of follow-up during
these young adult years to achieve maximum participation of
the study populations.

The objectives of each clinical center are:

1.

in the study.

To maintain, via mail and phone calls at semi-annual intervals
during the follow-up period, contact with each participant in
order to maximize the return rate for future examinations.

To assess risk factors for CHD in these participants.

the function of your heart. Some of you will be asked to volunteer for an optional study
which will require collection of all your urine over a 24 hour time period plus the

FOLLOW-UP CONTACT PROCEDURES

Retention of the cohort is a continual focus within the CARDIA
Study. Maintaining contact with the participants is critical so
that they are available for re-examination as the study progresses.
Contact efforts are made through the mail and/or by telephone.
Each center is permitted to decide which methods achieve the best
results in their cohort. Additionally, incentive gifts (sent ona
scheduled study-wide basis), holiday cards and birthday cards are
utilized to entice the participants to remain involved with the
CARDIA study.

Contacts are attempted at scheduled six month intervals, with
the contact effort being based on the Year 0 exam date. At the 90
month contact (following the Year 7 exam), address verifications
may be obtained from someone other than the participant (e.g.,
parent, spouse, roommate, friend) although direct contact is
preferable. At the 96 month contact, direct contact with the
participant is required and a Follow-Up Questionnaire must be
completed. (See Sample 72 and 90 Month Follow-Up Questionnaires.)

A participant is eligible for a period of six months at each
follow-up time frame, two months preceding the anniversary month
(which is based on the Year 0 exam date) and three months following
the anniversary month. For example, if a participant's expected
exam date is in June, he/she would be due for a follow-up contact
in December; therefore the eligible contact period would begin in
October (two months prior to December) and the deadline to complete
the contact would be March 31 (three months following December).
Thus, an uncontacted participant is always eligible for one, but
only one, follow-up at a time.

Using this method, when the deadline for an uncontacted
participant is reached, his/her Address Status will be coded as "U"
(Unable to contact) on the computer generated Follow-up Logs (see
sample), Date of Response and Mode of Response will be blank or

"DATE OF RESPONSE" is the date the participant responds to the
follow-up and the follow-up is completed.

"MODE OF RESPONSE" is the method that is used to obtain
completion of the participant's follow-up information. This may be
a letter received from the participant, a telephone call to or from

GUIDELINES FOR YEAR 7 EXAMINATION

PURPOSE

The CARDIA Year 7 examinations are scheduled over a twelve-month
period (June 1992 ~ May 1993). This will be the second, third or
fourth visit to the clinical center by the participant. It is
important that this experience be viewed favorably by the
participant.

The total time for the core examination should take
approximately three to three and one-half hours. Additional time
will be required for ancillary studies. The results of the
examination will be sent to the participant's family physician if
he/she so indicates.

PREPARATION OF PARTICIPANT FOR THE VISIT

Each participant is required to fast from all food and beverage
(except water) for 12 hours prior to the exam. The participant
should not have engaged in any vigorous exercise on the day of the
appointment and should not have used tobacco 30 minutes prior to the
exam. The participant should bring to the appointment a list of any
prescription medications and the medication bottles that they are
currently using. Additional pre-exam instructions will be related by
phone to the participant prior to the day of the appointment.

STAFF PREPARATION FOR THE PARTICIPANT'S VISIT

In preparation for the participant's arrival to the clinic, a
designated staff member will construct the expected participant's
file. The CARDIA forms will be arranged according to the center's
anticipated clinic flow for ease of administration. (The forms for
the core examination are collated and packaged into form sets.
Medical history follow-up forms are packaged separately.) Once the
form set is organized, the entire package should be placed into a

4/92 GUI - 4

three-ring notebook provided for each participant. Each
participant's form set will accompany and be administered to the
participant throughout the course of the examination. The form set
should remain assembled in the notebook until all of the
participant's data has been entered on the computer. Following data
entry, the form set should be filed and stored.

The identification labels to be placed on each CARDIA form will
be designed, prepared, and distributed by the Coordinating Center to
each clinical center. (Label sets for participants who are examined
at sites other than their "home" clinic will be sent by the "home"
clinic to the center who is to perform the Year 7 exam. ) The
identification label will consist of a 12 digit number (ID number)
which identifies the participant. The first digit of the ID
represents the center where the participant was initially recruited
and examined (1 = Birmingham; 2 = Chicago; 3 = Minneapolis; 4 =
Oakland). In addition, “CARDIA IV" will appear on each label to
designate that forms were completed at the fourth exam.

The following guidelines should be remembered when monitoring

the exam flow for each participant:

1. Blood pressure measurements should be made very early in
the clinic visit sequence immediately following the
greeting and informed consent. Measurements will be made
before blood drawing and any potentially stressful
interview.

2. Phlebotomy should occur early in the exam flow, prior to
the snack, as the participants have been instructed to come
to the clinic in a fasting state.

3. A snack should be provided very soon after blood draw.

4. It is preferable to measure skinfolds and girths prior to
the treadmill test, since sweating and increased blood flow
to the skin makes measurement more difficult.

5. The treadmill test should not be performed in a fasting
state, and at least 30 to 40 minutes should elapse between
the snack and testing where at all possible.

GUIDELINES FOR GREETING AND INFORMED CONSENT

GENERAL INFORMATION

The greeting is very important because it sets the tone for the
entire exam. Each participant was told during the past exams that:

they are participating in an important national study;
they will receive valuable information about their own

health;
* they will receive a specially designed CARDIA examination
available at only four centers in the United States; and
* if they wish, their physicians can be sent their test
results.

In the greeting for the Year 7 exam these general points should
be stressed again, but each center should do this in ways that are
most suitable for their own populations.

GUIDELINES FOR GREETING

Verify that the participant has arrived on the right day at the
right time. If the participant has not arrived on the correct day or
at the correct time, say something like, "Your appointment is not
recorded on today's exam schedule. There's a chance we may be able
to fit you in today, " or " our records show that you are scheduled
for an exam at o'clock. There's a chance we may be able
to see you sooner." Then, consult with your Clinic Coordinator for
further instructions.

If the participant appears to be ill, verify that he/she feels
well enough to complete the examination. One way to do this is to
ask, "Do you have a fever?" If the participant answers "yes,"
reschedule the appointment according to local center appointment
procedures. If the participant fails to complete the entire exam,
reschedule the unfinished components as soon as possible according to

local center appointment procedures, and record the participant's ID,

4/92 SUI - 3

unfinished components, and reason for the incomplete exam on the
clinical center log.

NOTE: Pregnancy, regardless of gestational stage, excludes
a participant from all anthropometric measurements and
the treadmill. It would be wise to ascertain
pregnancy status during the greeting in order to plan
the exam flow appropriately.

A brief description of CARDIA should be given to the participant
prior to the Year 7 exam. The following is an example: "As you
know, CARDIA is a major study of the lifestyles and health of young
adults. It is sponsored by the National Institutes of Health. Here
in Chicago, the study is being conducted by the Department of
Community Health and Preventive Medicine of Northwestern University
Medical School."

"First, let me tell you again a little about what will be
included in your exam today. As you know, we will explore many
aspects of your health and your lifestyle. You will be asked
questions about:

* your current health, in general;

* any past illnesses or injuries;

* any medications you take;

* the amount of exercise you get;

* the way you deal with every day problems; and
*

your background - your education, whether you are
married, what you do, and things like that.

We will take your blood pressure several times.

There will be a blood test to determine the amount of cholesterol in
your blood.

We will measure your height and weight.

We will interview you regarding the usual foods that you eat.

A treadmill test will be conducted to measure your physical fitness.

GUIDELINES FOR OBTAINING INFORMED CONSENT

At this time the participant should be asked to read and sign
the consent forn. Each center has a different form. It is not
enough to have the participant read and sign the form: the
participant must understand what is going to happen to him/her during
the exam and the risks involved. The greeter should make certain
that the participant is actually reading the form and then
specifically ask if he/she has any questions about it. The greeter
should be prepared to answer those questions himself/herself or have
Someone else on site answer them. If it seems appropriate (i.e., the
participant is struggling to read the form), ask if the participant
would prefer that the form be read aloud. If so, the greeter should
read it aloud.

After the consent form has been read and signed, the greeter
should ask the participant if he/she would like the test results
mailed to him/her and/or to his/her physician. The responses to
these questions should be marked in the appropriate spaces on the
medical release form. If the participant would like the results
mailed to a physician, the name and address of the physician, as well
as the participants's signature on the medical release form should be
obtained at this time. Results may not be released to a physician

without the participant's signature on the medical release forn.

VERIFICATION OF DEMOGRAPHIC DATA

After the participant has signed the informed consent, the
greeter will refer to the "Verification of Demographic Information"
form, as prepared for each individual participant by the Coordinating
Center. The participant will be asked his/her birth date, to be
compared for verification with the demographic data from his/her most
current exam (Year 0, Year 2 or Year 5). Changes for sex and race
should only be questioned if an obvious error has been made. This
form will not require an ID label, as the ID is already on the form.

The participant is now ready to continue with the Year 7 exam.

CONSENT FORM

You are invited to participate in the fourth examination of a research study of the
health status of young adults, for which you were selected randomly. The purpose
of the study is to learn how the beginning stages of heart disease develop in healthy
young adults. The clinic examination will last about three hours.

Blood Drawing. This examination will include having a 4 tablespoon sample of
blood drawn to measure blood cholesterol and other blood substances. Slight
bruising or fainting may occur in some people when blood is drawn. These are
usually minor and have no lasting effects. We will make every effort to prevent
these from happening.

Exercise Treadmill. In addition, an exercise test will be done to evaluate your heart’s
response to a standardized amount of stress. This test is performed by having you
walk or jog on a treadmill and is designed to gradually increase the heart’s
workload. Before the test, you will be interviewed to determine if you should not
take the test. Should symptoms such as chest discomfort, unusual shortness of
breath or fatigue develop during the test, the staff will stop the test. Also, if at any
time during the test you feel you would like to stop, you can stop.

Certain changes in body function normally take place when any person exercises.
Occasionally, abnormal changes may occur in blood pressure or heart rate. Very rare
instances of heart attack have occurred, as in any other moderately strenuous
exercise activity. Every effort will be made to minimize possible problems by the .
preliminary examination and constant supervision during testing.

Seismocardiogram. A seismocardiogram will be performed to measure the
mechanical function of your heart. This test records heart vibrations, uses no x-rays,
and is entirely safe.

Other Procedures. There will also be a measurement of your blood pressure, skin
folds, and some questions concerning your health, diet, and the stresses of everyday
life. You will also be asked about medical care and accidents or injuries you may
have had since your last CARDIA examination. There are no known significant
complications from these procedures.

In the event that this research activity results in physical injury, medical treatment
will be available, including first aid, emergency treatment, and follow-up care as
needed. Payment for follow-up care must be provided by you or your third party
payor (such as health insurance, Medicare).

BLOOD PRESSURE MANUAL OF PROCEDURES
HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE (HYPERTENSION)

As blood pressure rises, so does risk of ischemic heart disease
and its complications. The range of normal blood pressures is wide.
Even within the "normal" group, risk increases as the upper limits
are approached. Usually, blood pressures are expressed as systolic
pressure/diastolic pressure; values exceeding 140/90 mmHg are
considered to be hypertensive for adults. Middle-aged persons with
a diastolic blood pressure of 90-104 mmHg or greater (so-called
"mild" hypertension) have a risk of heart attack that is about 70
percent higher than that of persons with a diastolic pressure under
80 mmHg (normal value). Persons with a diastolic blood pressure
exceeding 104 mmHg (moderately severe to severe hypertension) have a
risk more than twice that of those with a normal value. Hypertension
is an especially strong risk factor for stroke and, to a lesser
extent, for peripheral vascular disease.

Blood pressure is measured in a resting state, using three
measurements with a random zero sphygmomanometer. The random zero
machine has two advantages over the fixed zero manometer. Digit
preference does not appear in the data, though it may still exist in
the reading itself, and be randomized out of the data by the use of
the randomly chosen zero point. More importantly, it deprives the
blood pressure technician of knowledge of the actual value, and
therefore of the ability to make judgements about blood pressure
levels for readings close to critical values such as 90 diastolic.
It should be noted, however, that the random zero machines tend to
yield blood pressures which are about 1.5 mmHg less than those
obtained when using a fixed zero machine. Within person variation in
blood pressure is substantial; three replicate readings tends to
reduce this variation.

4/98

OVERVIEW OF BLOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT

The purpose of blood pressure measurements in CARDIA is: (1) to
compare levels of this risk factor between blacks and whites; (2) to
observe the interaction with other CHD risk factors over time; and

(3) to observe variables that will predict changing levels of blood
pressure.

Blood pressure measurements (systolic and fifth phase diastolic)
will be recorded with a random-zero (RZ) sphygmomanometer by trained
and certified technicians at baseline and subsequent intervals. The
methods of measurement will be standardized - as set out in the
Manual of Operations. The pulse rate for 30 seconds will be recorded
with each blood pressure measurement.

The cuff is to be inflated to 30 mmHg above the highest seated
systolic reading. As many confounders of blood pressure measurement
as possible will be controlled by standard settings and technique of
blood pressure measurement or by recording uncontrollable confounding
factors. Thus, the following will be recorded:

1). Time of day (AM/PM)

2). Room temperature
3). Arm circumference at the midpoint of the upper arm
4). Technician I.D. number

The blood pressure will be measured three times on each occasion.
Caffeine (from tea, coffee, cola beverages), eating, heavy physical
activity, smoking (30 minute proscription) and alcohol intake will be
proscribed for two hours prior to recording blood pressure level.
The requirement for a fasting state in the basic exam will assure
much of the dietary compliance. Recording of current drug intake,
including medications affecting blood pressure, non-prescription
drugs and "recreational" drugs will be made on medical history forms
on the day of the examination.

BLOOD PRESSURE TRAINING/CERTIFICATION

Standardized training sessions are required for blood pressure
measurement. Technicians will be trained centrally prior to the
Year 5 exam in two full-day sessions with subsequent training taking
place in individual clinics. Training methods consist of a pre- and
post-test, audio cassette tape instruction and Y-tube stethoscope
testing. Blood pressure observers will be trained to observe and
record the onset of first and fifth phase Korotkoff sounds. Each
clinical center will have one blood pressure trainer (designated as
the Blood Pressure Supervisor) who will have the responsibility for
training any new blood pressure observers and for conducting
recertification procedures.

At the beginning of the first session, a description and
demonstration of the correct BP procedure is given. Trainees are to
listen to the first (training) tape, taking the test sequences until
they are comfortable with what they are listening to. Then, they
take the second tape until they have passed the test. After passing
the second tape, they are given the third tape test. Alternated with
the tapes are actual live practices under the instruction and
observation of the training supervisor. Some live practices may be
done with a standard stethoscope, but most should employ the Y-tube
stethoscope. The optimum size of a group is eight. This allows four
people to do live practices while four are on the tape training
device. The group can interchange and practice on each other.

After the first day of training, each trainee should be given a

cuff and manometer (no stethoscope) to take home and practice just

4/92 BP - 4

4/92

the control of the valve. This can be done by wrapping the cuff on
a jar or bottle and alternately pumping up and dropping the mercury
at a steady rate of 2 mm per second. After two or three sessions,
they could also be given a stethoscope to practice on family and/or
friends. This out-of-class practice is very important to build
confidence. The time allowed for class is not enough with outside
practice time.

Once each trainee has passed the third tape, he or she should do
at least two live readings with the training supervisor on the Y-tube
stethoscope. The readings should agree within 4 mm and the average
should agree within 3 mm. If they do not, the trainee needs
additional practice with tapes and live subjects. The training
supervisor should also assure that the trainee understands and
follows proper procedures. If the trainees are also to use the
Random Zero device, additional time should be allowed for instruction

and mastering that procedure.

Prior to certification, each technician will be tested for
vision (reading) and with an auditory test (by Korotkoff sound tape).
Observers are certified after passing the second and third tape tests
(tape 4 is held in reserve for recertification) and at least two live
readings. Observers are recertified once during the exam cycle by
taking and passing tape 3 or 4 and one or two readings with the
training supervisor on a Y-tube stethoscope.

The Coordinating Center will notify each clinical center when
recertification is required. It will be the responsibility of each
clinical center to conduct these procedures at the specified times
and to notify the Coordinating Center when the procedures are
complete.

The Coordinating Center will review blood pressure data,

monitoring digit preference, inter- and intra-technician variability

and distributional characteristics on a monthly basis.

USING THE CRONUS STOP WATCH WITH THE PRINEAS BLOOD PRESSURE TAPES

Turn on the stop watch and press reset button.

Start the tape, wearing headphones. At the beginning of each
tape is a timing sequence, with no Korotkoff sounds. When you
hear the beep, start the watch by pressing the button at the top.
Stop the watch with the button at the top when you hear the
second beep. Record the time elapsed to the nearest tenth of a
second on the top of the student form.

Press reset button. When the tape announces sequence 1, start
the watch at the beep.

When you hear the first Korotkoff sounds, stop the watch with the
button at the top. Record the time elapsed to the nearest tenth
of a second. The watch continues to run internally.

When you hear the Phase 4 (muffling), stop the watch. There will
not be enough time between Phases 4 and 5 to record - so just
remember that number until Phase 5 (disappearance). Then stop
the watch again and record the remembered number for Phase 4 and
the final one for Phase 5 on the stop watch. Press reset.
Repeat steps 3 through 5 for each sequence. Remember that the
tapes were designed for a special timing device. The answers
given will be double the stop watch values. At the end be sure

to turn off the stop watch in order to save batteries.

There are a series of four tapes of Korotkoff sounds. Tape 1 is

six month recertification. Tapes 3 and 4 are to be alternated

EQUIPMENT MAINTENANCE

Each clinical center is responsible for the proper operation and
maintenance of its equipment. Maintenance responsibility should be
assumed by the quality control officer and all staff should be
instructed to report any real or suspected equipment problems to
that person promptly.

All checks, inspections, cleanings and problems indicated will be
documented and recorded by date in a permanent log. Problems and
solutions should also be recorded. The local quality control officer
will send copy of this log monthly to the Coordinating Center.

An inspection and maintenance schedule is summarized below.
Specific instructions for the cleaning and maintenance of R-Z and
standard sphygmomanometers is found in Appendix 1.

A. Random Zero and Standard Sphygmomanometers

These devices will be checked thoroughly and cleaned if necessary
every three months. The R-Z manometer should be inspected once
a week and the Standard device once a month. In general, these
inspections should include a check of zero levels of standard
manometers, mercury leakage, operation of valves, manometer
columns for dirt or mercury oxide deposit, and condition of all
tubing and fittings. More specific instructions are included
later in this chapter.

BLOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT PROCEDURES
STANDARDIZED CLINIC PROCEDURES

It will take approximately 10-15 minutes to make three blood
pressure measurements including the initial five minute rest and
recording of pulse rate. The blood pressure measurements will be
made very early in the clinic visit sequence immediately following
the greeting and informed consent. Measurements will be made before
the physical exam, blood drawing, or any potentially stressful
interview. The blood pressure measurements on each participant will
be made in a separate room or, at minimum, in an area properly
screened from all other activity and other participants.

BP 8

4/92

Correct measurement of indirect blood pressure is of the utmost
importance and concern to the success of this study. It is essential
that the standardized format described below for measuring blood
pressure on the Random Zero be followed exactly.

Major differences in blood pressure measurement methodology among
health professionals from several countries have been observed
despite the fact that written international recommendations of blood
pressure measurement were established in 1939 by a joint committee of
the American Heart Association and the Cardiac Society of Great
Britain and Ireland. It is also well known that precision is
essential for valid comparisons of blood pressure between groups of
people and in individuals on different occasions. A number of
elements can be identified in measuring blood pressure and each is
explained briefly in subsequent subsections of this chapter ending
with a subsection on technique that is presented in detail. Study
organizers consider all of these elements equally important and ask
that the strictest attention be paid to each in order to insure that
the blood pressure measurements have a standard and high level of
accuracy and precision.

A. SOUND
For purposes of this study, SBP level is recorded at the level
when phase 1 Korotkoff sounds are first heard and DBP is recorded
at the beginning of phase 5 with disappearance of sounds. The
onset of phase 1 and 5 sounds are the points of clinical
importance.

B. EQUIPMENT
The following blood pressure measurement equipment will be used
and standardized for the study: stethoscope, random-zero and
standard sphygmomanometers, cuffs and bulb.

1. STETHOSCOPE
A standard Littman stethoscope having a bell will be used.
Korotkoff sounds are best heard with the bell because of
their low pitch. Stethoscope tubing should be about 10-12
inches from the bell piece to "Y" branching. This length

BP - 9

4/92

provides optimal acoustical properties and allows the

observer to read the sphygmomanometer at eye level and in a

comfortable position. Earpieces should fit comfortably and

snugly in the ears. Four points should be observed in using

the stethoscope.

a. The ear pieces should be directed downwards and
forwards into the external ear canal.

b. The ear pieces should be tight enough to exclude
outside sound but not so tight that they cause
discomfort.

c. The bell of the stethoscope should be placed lightly

on the skin overlying the brachial artery -
immediately below the cuff and medial to the cubital
fossa above the medial epicondyle of the radius
posterior to the biceps muscle. Light pressure
accentuates low-pitched sound and avoids compression
murmurs. Pressing too heavily with the stethoscope
over the brachial artery can also produce sounds that
can be heard by the observer by reducing the internal
diameter of the brachial artery in the same manner as
the cuff. This causes turbulent flow in the artery
and a murmur can be heard and may prolong the apparent
duration of phase 4.

d. The valve between the bell and diaphragm should be
turned in the correct direction.

SPHYGMOMANOMETERS

Standardized Hawksley random-zero instruments will be used

for all clinic visits. Standard Baum manometers will be

used for determining peak inflation level.

CUFFS AND BULBS

Clinics will have four standardized cuffs available - adult,
pediatric, large adult, and thigh cuff (by the Baum
Company). Proper size of the cuff is essential for accurate
blood pressure measurement. To select proper cuff size,

BP - 10

4/92

hold the end of the cuff containing the rubber bladder over
the upper arm and pull the other end toward the subject
under the arm. The top edge should lie within the range
markings for cuff size. If it does not, select the next
smaller or larger cuff. The range markings which are on the
commercial cuffs actually overlap from size to size and are
not considered to be optimum correct measurements. The
pediatric cuff should be used for an arm circumference (AC)
of <24.5 cm. The standard adult cuff should be used for AC
of 24.5 - 32.5 om, large adult cuff for Ac of >32.5 - 41.0
em, and thigh cuff for AC of >41 cm.

STAFF PREPARATION FOR PARTICIPANT'S VISIT

A minimum of three clinic staff persons will be responsible for
measuring blood pressure. They need not be health professionals, but
they must be trained and certified in blood pressure measurement and
technique. Observers should have some experience in relating to and
dealing with people. While it is difficult to standardize demeanor,
the observer should strive to present a non-discriminatory,
reassuring and professional approach. The observers will be required

to have a simple vision test in addition to the training process.

It should be remembered that participation in the study is a
voluntary procedure. Participants will be given full explanation and
instructions about the preparation for the blood pressure examination
as well as an opportunity for discussion. The setting for making
repeated blood pressure measurements must be standardized for clinic
visits. The examination should take place in a quiet room where no
other activity is taking place and where temperature fluctuations are
minimal. Clinic scheduling procedures will establish consistent
appointment times to minimize problems that stem from systematic
variation of blood pressure during the day.

Prior to seating the participant and giving explanations about
blood pressure measurement, the arm circumference measurement should
be made so that the appropriate arm cuff can be selected. Following
describes the measurement technique:

UPPER ARM CIRCUMFERENCE Arm circumference at the midpoint of
the right upper arm is to be measured using the anthropometric tape.
The participant stands with his/her arms flexed at 90°. Using the
tape measure, the observer measures from the tip of the acromion
process on the shoulder to the tip of the olecranon process on the
back of the right elbow. Make this measurement as far toward the
midline of the back of the arm as possible while still remaining
anchored on the bony landmarks. If the mark is not in the midline of
the back of the arm, you may wish to use a straight edge to make a
second mark at the midline. Be sure that the straight edge is
perpendicular to the long axis of the arm. Using this mark, measure
the circumference of the arm. The arm should be hanging loosely at
the person's side. Make the measurement and record it to the nearest
0.5 centimeter on the blood pressure recording form.

Once the participant has been given instructions and
explanations, the equipment has been checked, and he has been sitting
in a quiet and relaxing room with no change of position or posture,
blood pressure measurement can begin. The following steps should be
followed as precisely as possible.

1. Seat the participant with right arm on table. The
inner aspect of the bend at the elbow (cubital fossa)
should be at heart level. (If the right arm is
missing or injured, reverse chairs and use left arm -
noting this change on the form.) Legs should remain
uncrossed, feet on floor.

2. Palpate for the brachial artery (just medial to and
above the cubital fossa). Choose the correct cuff
size and wrap the cuff on the arm with the center of
the bladder over the brachial artery. If the
participant seems particularly apprehensive or
nervous, wait until after the five minute wait to wrap
cuff.

3. Record the time. There must be a five minute wait
before taking the pulse and blood pressure.
Conversation should be limited. However, a brief
explanation of the procedure can be repeated at this
time if necessary.

PROCEDURE FOR RECORDING

If for any reason the observer is unable to determine (or
forgets) any phase, write a dash in the space on the form. This is
the correct way to indicate missed information. If an entire reading
is missed, completely deflate the cuff and start over with a
replacement reading. However, under no other circumstances may a
replacement reading be obtained. Always wait at least 30 seconds
between readings. After averaging the second and third corrected
R-Z readings, record the average on the forn.

pressure is reported to the participant, the technician should
indicate that the measure is normal or high.

With reservoir valve (newer models do not have a reservoir valve)

With the high pressure still in the system, close the reservoir

Most leaks occur at or near tubing connections or from valves.
If a valve leaks, sometimes a shot of silicone lubricant on the

b. Inflate the system while watching the large (about 2 -

As pressure rises you will see the disc, a piston,
pushed toward the back plate until a ring around the
center of the disc touches the forward rim of the cam.
That rim is tapered, and thus determines how far the
piston can move, depending on the position of the
taper in relation to the ring at the center of the
piston - a matter of chance in normal operation of the
RZ. The distance that the piston can move before
being stopped by the cam determines the volume of
mercury in the bellows chamber, hence the volume of Hg
left in the rest of the manometer.

c. To read "maximum" zero, release pressure with bellows
valve still open. Turn the cam so that the point of
its taper nearest the piston will be hit by the ring
of the piston. (It may take an inflation and
deflation or two before you find the correct cam

position, which allows the minimum volume of mercury

the bellows valve, release pressure and read the zero
as usual; this is the "maximum". Repeat the procedure
once or twice, checking the cam position to make sure
you get the same reading. Note that this is not a
fixed value for if you were to inflate to 300 before
closing the bellows valve, the reading would be lower;
and inflation to 120-130 would give a higher value.
For this reason, always record what you read when
taking blood pressures.

"Minimum" zero is measured as inc above, except that
the cam is turned so that the piston can travel its
maximum. It is usually close to 20 mm lower than the

I. PURPOSE

The blood drawing station is designed to obtain a blood sample
to test for important risk factors for cardiovascular disease and
for other blood parameters of interest to CARDIA. It is
potentially a difficult station because of the anxiety caused in
many people by blood drawing and the potential for injury.
However, if carefully and professionally done, it provides a
positive, safe experience for the participant. The blood drawing
station will take approximately 10 minutes of the participant's
time.

This protocol was designed as a training manual for the

phlebotomist at the clinical centers.

II. DESCRIPTION
A. Tests

The following tests are planned for the Year 7 exam:

1. LIPIDS and LIPOPROTEINS: total cholesterol,
triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, Lp(a) isomers and
apolipoprotein E phenotype;

2. INSULIN; and

3. GLUCOSE.

The methods of measurement for each of these tests is found in the
CARDIA Laboratory Operations Manual and the rationale for

assessment is found in the CARDIA Protocol.

B. Restrictions
The Lipid Research Clinic's Manual of Operations identifies
several factors which may influence lipid and lipoprotein values.
The following procedures are designed to standardize sample
collection.
1. Blood should be drawn with the participant in a seated
position. The reclining position should be allowed only
in extreme circumstances (e.g., history of fainting).

4/92 PHL ~ 1

2. Elevations of 2-5% in lipid measures are observed after
two minutes of continuous venous occlusion. Therefore,
a total tourniquet time of less than two minutes is
required.

3. The state of fasting clearly influences parameters such
as triglycerides. CARDIA participants should have fasted
for 12 hours prior to blood drawing. However, blood will
be drawn on all participants, regardless of fasting
status.

4. Participants are instructed to avoid vigorous exercise on
the day of their examination.

5. No particular restriction need be made for smoking since
the blood drawing station will be approximately one half
hour after clinic arrival.

6. Blood drawing should occur early in the CARDIA visit but
following the blood pressure measurement. It must
precede the snack.

c. General Preparation

Site: The blood drawing should take place in an isolated room
or one enclosed by dividers. Temperature should be 65-75° F.
There should be no direct sunlight. The recliner should be placed
in a space sufficient to allow the chair to fully recline. The
chair may be elevated on a wooden box to facilitate comfort of the

phlebotomist when drawing the blood.

The room should be equipped with all the necessary supplies.
A table or counter should be prepared with the materials and vials
needed for blood handling and aliquoting. The centrifuge,
refrigerator and freezer should be nearby.

4/92 PHL ~- 2

Staff: This station is staffed with a technician with
documented class time and experience in phlebotomy. Certification
will occur at the centralized training session. Recertification
will occur once as requested by the Coordinating Center, and will
be authorized by the clinic supervisor or medical director. The
technician should be properly attired in a white laboratory coat.
Long hair should be tied back. Gloves should be used at all times
while handling blood specimens.

The Daily Temperature Record must be completed each day the
Clinic is in operation. Freezer, refrigerator and room
temperatures should be recorded. The expected temperatures are:
freezer: ~75° to -65°C; refrigerator: 35° to 40°F; room: 65° to 75°F.

D. Blood Volume To Be Obtained
All participants will have 38 ml of blood drawn, using:
one 15-ml lavender top (EDTA) vacutainer tube;
one 13-ml red top (SST) vacutainer tube;
one 10-ml lavender top (EDTA) vacutainer tube (filled in
this order).
Participants selected for quality control will have an additional
16 ml of blood drawn, using:
one 10-ml lavender top (EDTA) vacutainer tube; and
one 6-ml red top (SST) vacutainer tube.

III. Procedure For Blood Drawing

The following steps outline the procedures for blood drawing:

1. Wash hands at the beginning of the work day and as needed
after processing specimens. Smoking is not allowed in this
area.

2. Greet the participant. Confirm that you have the correct

envelope of ID labels. Locate the phlebotomy form (Form 5) in
the participant's form set and check that it has been properly
labeled. Fill in the phlebotomist ID. Ask the participant
question 1 (whether he/she has been ill in the past 24 hours),

5/92

question 2 (the time and date he/she last ate) and question 3
(whether he/she has any bleeding disorders). If the
participant reports a history of bleeding disorders, the
participant should be sampled under the supervision of a

physician.

Explain the procedure. An example might be: "I am going to
be drawing some blood from the vein in your arm. The purpose
of this is to check levels of blood fats such as cholesterol.
I will be taking three tubes -- about 3 and 1/2 tablespoons of
blood. Are there any questions?" (NOTE: The number of tubes
and the total amount of blood drawn will vary depending on
whether the participant is tagged for QC. Also, three of the
clinics will draw additional blood for ancillary studies.)

If the participant asks when he/she will receive the results
of this test, direct the participant to ask the Clinic
Coordinator at the exit interview.

With jackets removed, have the participant sit upright in the
recliner with the sleeves rolled up to expose the antecubital
fossa (elbow). The recliner should be in a complete upright
position.

Only when the participant has indicated that he/she has a
history of fainting, should the technician recline the
participant for the whole procedure. The technician may
recline the participant by: (1) pulling the lever forward;
(2) pulling up and forward on the arm rest; or (3) pushing
back smoothly on the chair back. This reclining position is
an exception to the protocol and should only be allowed in
extreme circumstances. Its use is left to the discretion of
the technician. It may be helpful to reassure an apprehensive

participant that he may recline following the blood drawing.
The chair position should not be changed from sitting to
reclining during the blood drawing. Try to draw as much blood

as possible when the participant is in the upright position.

PRECAUTIONS IF A PARTICIPANT FEELS FAINT OR LOOKS FAINT

FOLLOWING THE BLOOD DRAWING:

a. Have the person remain in the recliner, recline the chair
if necessary or have him/her sit with their head between
their knees.

b. Take an ampule of smelling salts and crush it and wave it

under the person's nose for a few seconds.

c. Provide the person with a basin if he/she feels nauseous.

d. Have the person stay reclined until the color returns and
he/she feels better.

e. Place a cold wet rag on the back of the person's neck.

f. If the person continues to feel sick, take a blood
pressure and pulse reading. Contact a medical staff

member, who will advise you on further action.

HANDLING PARTICIPANTS WHO ARE EXTREMELY APPREHENSIVE ABOUT
HAVING BLOOD DRAWN: Do not, under any circumstances, force
the participant to have blood drawn. It is sometimes best to
let the participant go on with another part of the visit, and
have them return when the phlebotomist has more time to talk
with the person. (However, the participant should not be
given a snack until a final decision regarding the blood draw
has been reached.) It also helps to have the participant
recline in the blood drawing chair just so the phlebotomist
can check the veins in the participant's arms, without

19. CAUTION IN HANDLING BLOOD SAMPLES: Improper handling of blood
collection tubes and needles is extremely dangerous. All
blood samples should be handled as though the participant has
a blood-borne transmissible disease. Therefore, the following
procedures should be observed.

a. Needles must be disposed of in proper disposal
containers.

b. Avoid contact with plasma. Gloves should always be worn
when handling samples.

c. If the phlebotomist accidentally sustains a contaminated
needle stick, the wound should be thoroughly cleansed
with soap and water. The medical director should be
notified immediately.

d. All used vacutainer tubes and blood products are to be
placed in biohazard bags for disposal.

Iv. BLOOD HANDLING
A. Description

The proper handling of the collected samples is critical
because deviation from the protocol can significantly affect the
parameter being measured in the blood. It is particularly
important that time deadlines in handling be observed and that
samples not be left open to the atmosphere longer than necessary.
A total of ninety (90) minutes is permitted between blood drawing
and final placement of samples in the freezer, so schedule your

PHL 10

5/92

time accordingly.

B. Procedure

1.

Immediately after drawing the sample, affix one of the
large plain white labels with the participant's ID to
each of the three blood tubes. This is necessary to

identify which tubes belong to which participant.

Immediately place the two lavender top tubes into a
container of water and ice. Cool the sample on water and
ice for 30 minutes but not more than 60 minutes.

Place the red top tube in the test tube rack. Allow the
sample to clot by standing for at least 30 minutes but
not more than 60 minutes at room temperature (65-75°F).

Do not let the samples stand in direct sunlight or at
extreme temperatures.

Cc. Operating The Centrifuge

1.

To pre-cool the centrifuge, close and lock the cover, set
the TEMPERATURE control at 4°C, set the SPEED control to
1000 RPM, set the TIMER control to 20 minutes, and push
the RUN button. If the chamber is already cool, begin
operation at #2. (NOTE: The shields should be
refrigerated if they are removed from the centrifuge, so
that they will be chilled prior to spinning blood.)

Set the POWER switch to ON.

Balance the load.

a. Place opposite shields containing filled
vacutainers on the balance.

b. To the lighter centrifuge shield, add water (or
50/50 water/alcohol) around the vacutainers, but no
closer to the top of the container than 1/4 inch.
Add same solution to the other centrifuge shield
until the two are balanced.

4. Load the rotor, being careful to place balanced shields

directly opposite each other.

5. Set the TEMPERATURE control at 4°C. Set the SPEED
control at 3,000 RPM (1,500 g, 5.0" rotating radius).
Set the TIMER to 20 minutes. Set the BRAKE control to
the MAX position.

6. Close cover and lock.

7. Push the RUN button to begin the run cycle. Record the
time the samples were placed in the centrifuge in the
TIME SPUN section on the Phlebotomy Form.

8. The centrifuge will stop automatically at the preselected
time and the stop indicator will light. Remove samples
one at a time.

9. Consult the Centrifuge Service Manual for other
guidelines and for troubleshooting.

VIII. LABORATORY QUALITY CONTROL

In order to assess the reproducibility of the measurements
made at the centralized laboratories, a split sample external
surveillance program has been developed. The purpose of the
program is to produce data which may be used: (1) to identify
problems as they occur and to communicate this information to the
clinic and laboratory for corrective action; and (2) to document
the performance of the entire process, i.e. sample collection,
preparation, handling, shipping an@ analytical performance.

The quality control procedures will consist of providing the
laboratories with duplicate specimens, one sample labeled with the
participant ID and the other with a fictitious ID. Duplicate
samples will also aid in measuring “across assay" reproducibility.
In order to accomplish this, the duplicate blood specimens must be
split across shipments to the laboratories. Otherwise, the sample
is analyzed in the same manner as all other specimens in that
particular month.

A. Duplicate Specimens

The volume of additional blood that will be drawn for quality
control is: one 15-ml lavender top (EDTA) vacutainer tube for
duplicate lipid, apolipoprotein E phenotype and Lp(a) isomer
measures and one 6-ml red top (SST) vacutainer for duplicate
insulin and glucose measures. The plasma is aliquoted into a red-
labeled 8-ml screw-top tube, a red-labeled 2-ml cryovial and a
lavender-labeled 2-ml cryovial. The appropriate color stripe
quality control labels are affixed to these vials.

Each of the clinical centers will draw the quality control
tube on an approximate fourteen percent sample of the participants
for the first three months (generally one out of every seven
participants per week) and an approximate nine percent sample of
the participants for the remainder of the exam cycle (generally one
out of every 11 participants per week). The quality control
participant will be identified at the time of the clinical center's

PHL - 24
4/92

weekly phone call to the Coordinating Center. In the event that
the additional sample could not be drawn on the identified
participant, the phlebotomist should draw the quality control
sample on the NEXT PARTICIPANT.

The participant need not be told that he/she is having extra
blood drawn for quality control. The consent form covers the
maximum amount of blood that could be drawn on any participant.

B. Shipping Duplicate Specimens

When an additional amount of blood is drawn for a quality
control duplicate specimen, it is to be submitted with the
following month's shipment. That is, duplicate specimens should
not be shipped together, but separated by one month. Review the
quality control shipping schedule in the preceding Transporting
Samples section (VII).

c. Internal Quality Control

The laboratory will supply the Coordinating Center with
periodic reports of their internal quality control. These reports
will be reviewed by the Quality Control Committee to insure that
contract requirements are met and that action is taken when
problems arise.

IX. RESULTS REPORTING
A. Laboratory Results Submitted To The Clinical Centers

Each clinical center should receive from the Coordinating
Center via Northwest Lipid Laboratory individual results reports of
the lipid and lipoprotein measurements within 4 weeks following
shipment of the specimens for analysis. Serum glucose results will
be sent to the Coordinating Center via “hard copy" by Linco
Research, Inc.; thus, Coordinating Center staff will need to data
enter the results for transmission to the centers. Results will be
transmitted to the clinics within 6 weeks following shipment of the
specimens for analysis.

5/93 PH - 25

B. Reviewing Laboratory Results
When the participant results arrive at the clinical center,
several items should be checked:
1. Indicate on your inventory forms that the results have
been received to confirm that all specimens which were

shipped were also analyzed.

2. Scan all reports for obvious laboratory errors.

3. Report any missing results or errors to the contact
person at the laboratory and to the quality control
person at the Coordinating Center.

4. File the report in the participant's form set.

A sample of the results will be reviewed on a monthly basis at
the Coordinating Center and periodically by the Quality Control

Committee.

C. Reporting Results To Participants And Referrals

The clinical center is responsible for reporting specific
laboratory test results to their participants. Participants with
an LDL level of 160 mg/dl or greater will be referred to an
appropriate medical care provider. Participants with a
triglyceride level greater than 500 will be referred. In addition,
participants with a glucose level of 140 or greater will be
referred to an appropriate medical care provider. The clinical
center may offer to re-evaluate the participant's lipid and/or
glucose levels for public relations purposes, as deemed necessary.
Please contact the Coordinating Center for an ID to be used for the
re-analysis sample. DO NOT USE THE PARTICIPANT'S CARDIA ID FOR THE
RE-ANALYSIS SAMPLE. If repeat results are above these thresholds,
participants will be referred to an appropriate medical provider.
